en: The Newly Compiled Catalogue of Śākyamuni’s Teachings, Volume One, compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xīmíng Monastery in the Western Capital.
I respectfully consult the old catalogues, which state: "The emergence of catalogues was primarily intended to distinguish between the authentic and the spurious."
Clarifying right and wrong,
recording the antiquity and modernity of persons and eras,
and marking the extent of the volumes and sections.
I have gathered what was omitted and supplemented what was missing, while excising redundancies and superfluities.
My aim is to ensure that the orthodox teaching accords with principle and that the golden words follow a coherent sequence,
so that the essential framework and core points may be clearly perceived.
However, because the Dharma gates are profound and subtle and the net of transformation is vast and expansive,
as the translations were carried out over successive generations across the passage of time,
they have frequently suffered dispersal and destruction, resulting in a disordered arrangement of the scrolls.
Furthermore, there are other individuals who, from time to time, increase their fabrications and falsehoods,
causing such confusion that it becomes difficult to investigate their origins.
For this reason, the virtuous scholars of former generations compiled these records.
Currently, those that remain are perhaps six or seven families;
yet even these do not exhaust the fundamental sources and still contain many omissions and deficiencies.
I, Sheng, being of mediocre and shallow capacity, have long devoted myself to their study and investigation.
I have examined the similarities and differences in practice and pointed out their strengths and weaknesses,
compiling this collection of volumes so that one may avoid errors and contradictions.
I hope that all you wise scholars will deign to examine this together in detail.
Now, observing that the works composed by the former sages stand preeminent among all the eminent,
I have humbly followed the passage of time since the year Gengwu, adding seventy years to their count.
The Tripitaka masters have succeeded one another down to the present four reigns.
Our sagacious Sovereign, reverent and enlightened, has overseen successive translations,
through which more than one hundred sections of Sūtras and Vinaya have been particularly clarified.
By imperial decree, we have been granted the profound favor of being permitted to compile and compose this work.
However, the talents and wisdom of Yuanzhao and his colleagues are shallow and limited; our thoughts do not extend far enough to produce elegant prose.
I reverently receive the Imperial Grace and humbly comply with Your Majesty’s command.
As for the present translation, I have categorized the texts according to their types.
I have appended these according to the textual sequence of the Tripiṭaka.
I reflect upon this as using a rope to continue a silken cord,
or placing pebbles alongside gold.
Where there is doubt, let it remain unrecorded,
awaiting future sages.
I prostrate to the Sugata, the Muni, the Unsurpassed Hero, the Tamer of Men.
I also pay homage to the pure and wondrous Dharma of the Three Vehicles, The secret gateways of the five families and the dhāraṇīs,
And the Saṅgha of the eight classes of noble Arhats; To Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and all the Bodhisattvas,
Whose five eyes and three bodies illuminate the world— With utmost sincerity I take refuge, praying that you will bestow your majestic power.
I have compiled this catalogue of scriptures to protect the city of the Dharma; may the Triple Gem bestow compassion and grant me secret protection.
May the lamp of the Dharma shine long through the dark night, so that deluded followers may thereby attain the clarity of wisdom.
May the True Dharma abide for a vast duration within the world, and by relying upon its study, may all swiftly ascend to the Unsurpassed Ground.
From the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Xiaoming of the Later Han, the year being Dingmao,
until the sixteenth year of the Zhenyuan era of the Sage, Divine, Martial, and Civil Emperor of the Great Tang, the year being Gengchen.

In total, there have been seven hundred and thirty-four years; from the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, the Gengwu year, until the present Gengchen year, seventy-one years have been added. During this interval, a total of one hundred and eighty-seven individuals, both monastics and laypeople, engaged in the transmission and translation [of Buddhist texts].
The holy teachings of the Tripitaka of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles that have been produced,
including the collected biographies of worthy sages as well as those of unknown translators,
total two thousand four hundred and forty-seven works; with one hundred and thirty-nine new additions, they comprise seven thousand three hundred and ninety-nine fascicles.
Regarding the deficiencies in the *Jianhang* (Catalogue of Inspection), all are included within the aforementioned figures, with three hundred and forty-two new volumes added.
The newly established catalogue consists of thirty volumes,
which are divided into general and specific categories.
The General Record is divided into two parts.
First, the reception of imperial decrees;
second, the compilation of various scriptures.
The Supplementary Records also consist of two parts:
the first distinguishes the various divisions of the Piṭaka;
the second elucidates the collected biographies of the worthy and holy ones.
The general division consists of nineteen fascicles,
while the specific division is divided into eleven fascicles.
Within the specific division of the Vehicle-piṭaka (Yānapiṭaka), there are further seven sections.
Now, first I shall set forth the remaining categories and articles,
which will subsequently be compiled and recorded in the two upper volumes of the General Record.
First, those specifically received by imperial decree, totaling three items:
first, the newly translated *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*;
second, the translations of sūtras, vinaya, and śāstras from the Three Dynasties; and third, [the remaining works].
The *Mahābuddhanāmasūtra* in one fascicle, etc.— three works in total—
all of these were specially granted imperial edicts permitting their inclusion in the catalogues.
The details are listed as follows.
Second, the General Catalogue of the Collected Scriptures (*Zongji qijing lu*):
the above comprises all translations and expositions from the Han through the Tang dynasties.
Complete.
[This includes] the eras of emperors, the original accounts of the translators, the teachings produced, and so forth,
arranged in chronological order according to the sequence of the dynasties.
Without following the sequence of the Tripiṭaka,
I have also recorded the catalogues, noting the similarities and differences between the old and new versions,
following the two texts of the Separate Record.
The first section: A Record of the Differences in the Piṭaka of Vehicles.
Within this separate record, the Inner Scriptures (Nèidiǎn) are divided into seven categories.
First: those that have been translated and possess extant texts.
Second, there are translations for which no original manuscripts exist;
third, the texts circulate according to their respective sectarian lineages;
fourth, they have been abridged to eliminate redundancy and prolixity.
5. Supplementary Omissions;
6. Re-examination of Doubts;
7. Perversion and Heresy Distorting the Correct.
Within these seven gates,
there are distinctions between the two vehicles and different classifications among the three piṭakas.
All details are fully provided,
including a clear explanation of the various sections.
Second, the Record of the Collections and Transmissions of Worthies and Sages.
Within this compiled commentary, there are two points of difference.
First, regarding the translation from the Sanskrit original:
this refers to the collection having been transmitted from the Western Regions to the Eastern Land (China).
The Tripitaka master of profound virtue translated and promulgated it.
Second, compositions of this land,
meaning the biographies compiled by eminent monks of this territory.
The Three Jewels and the Three Baskets were all clearly discerned;
his spiritual wonders, responsive communications, and practices of precept, concentration,
and wisdom were fully set forth as listed in the text, providing a detailed mirror for all to observe.

This morning, the Tripitaka Master Prajñā and others of the Kapiśa kingdom translated seventy fascicles of Mahāyāna scriptures, including the *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the *Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Sovereign Protecting the Realm* in ten fascicles, the *Sūtra on the Original Ground of the Mind* in eight fascicles, the *Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Six Pāramitās of the Principle of Interest* in one volume of ten fascicles, the *Sūtra of the Great Avataṃsaka on the Nārāyaṇa Power Asked by the Elder* in one fascicle, and the *Heart Sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā* in one fascicle. Furthermore, there is a newly translated version of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in one volume of forty fascicles. These six works, totaling seventy fascicles, were all translated by the Tripitaka Master Prajñā under imperial decree.

The *Daśabala-sūtra*, one fascicle. The above sutra was translated at Anxi by the Tripiṭaka Master Muditaśrī from the country of Kucha—whose name means "Lotus-Vīrya" in the language of Tang. The *Pariṇāmacakra-sūtra*, one fascicle; the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, nine fascicles. These two sutras together comprise ten fascicles.
Translated together with the Tripiṭaka Master Śīladharma of Khotan at Beiting.

"Brahmā" means "pure.
In the past, at the beginning of the kalpa, when the Ābhāsvara gods from the Brahma-world descended to that land, there were those who consumed the "earth-fat.
Their bodies became heavy and they could no longer return; consequently, they became human beings.
He is the progenitor of the Five Indias;
his title was established in accordance with their celestial designation.
If it were otherwise, from what source would the title "Hu" (Hū) have emerged?
However, when they employ Sanskrit terms, it is like what is called "Han" (Chinese) in this land;
there is indeed a basis for this and it is not erroneous.
For instance, in former times, monks all referred to their secular surnames.
During the Fu Qin period, there was the śramaṇa Dao’an,
who stood out as preeminent among his contemporaries and possessed a transcendent realization.
Having shaved his head and entered the monastic life, he succeeded to the lineage of the sons of Śākyamuni, yet remained distinct from their fathers.
How could it be said that this is merely a matter of inherited tradition?
Now, those who have left the household life should all be called "Śākya" (Shi).
Furthermore, when translating the *Caturāgama*, the text indeed states: [the passage follows].
Those who have left the household life from the four castes are all of one Śākya lineage.
The multitude all sighed in admiration and submission; the four castes are: first, the Kṣatriya; second, the Brāhmaṇa; third, the Vaiśya; and fourth, the Śūdra.
During the era of the Jin and Qin dynasties, Dao’an established a definitive catalog and edited the sūtras and śāstras;
he styled himself "The One Under Heaven" (Mitiān),
serving as a model for later generations.
It is as if one were saying that translating from the Hu (foreign) language into Qin (Chinese) involves "five losses and three difficulties.
Is this perhaps a universal shortcoming of translators, such that they have not yet reached perfection?
Since ancient times, wherever there has been the Hu language, [this issue has persisted].
Now, all have been revised into Sanskrit script,
so that there may be no further errors and those who discuss them may attain the correct version.
Furthermore, there are the records of Sengchang and others.
Among the translations by Zhi Chen, there is also one fascicle of the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*.
Since this is the same text as the *Buddhavaṃśa-maṇiratna-sūtra*, it is not appropriate to publish it again.
Furthermore, upon examining the text and its phrasing, it was not translated by Dharmarakṣa;
within the *Bielu* (Separate Catalog), it is classified as a work of lost translation.
Since we now rely on the *Bielu* as authoritative, the *Chenlu* (Dharmarakṣa’s Catalog) has excluded it.
*Mahāyāna Vaipulya-uttama-prajñā Sūtra*, one fascicle; first translated, identical in text to the "Assembly on the Eight Dharmas" in the *Ratnakūṭa*, as recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*.
*Prince Mupò Sūtra*, one fascicle; first translated, included among the alternative translations in the *Liùdù jí*, as recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*.
*The Scripture of the Elder’s Son Zhì*, one fascicle; also known simply as *Zhì jīng*; first translated, identical in text to the *Shì* [Sūtra].
The *Kumāra-sūtra* and others share the same original text; see the *Chángfáng-lù*.

The *Ratnakūṭa-samādhi-mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-dharmakāya-sūtra*, one fascicle—also titled *Yìrì-bǎo-samādhi-mañjuśrī-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-dharmakāya-sūtra*—is seen in the *Chángfáng-lù* as having originally shared the same text as the *Dharmadhātu-svabhāva-sūtra*. The *Svayaṃpratijñā-samādhi-sūtra*, one fascicle.

The note beneath the title states: "The fourth chapter, 'The Chapter on Sole Testimony,' appears within the 'Pure Conduct of Bhikṣus. Its initial appearance is largely the same as that of the version translated by Dharmarakṣa, with minor differences;
see the *Chángfáng Lù*. There is also one fascicle of the *Wēnshì Xǐyù Zhòngsēng Jīng* (Sūtra on the Bathing of the Monastic Community in the Warm Chamber), which is simply called the *Wēnshì Jīng*;
its initial appearance is recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. There are also two fascicles of the *Míngdù Wǔshí Jiàojì Jīng* (Sūtra of the Fifty Calculations of the Perfection of Wisdom)."

Some simply call it the *Mingdu jiaoji* (Examination of the Perfection of Wisdom), while others simply call it the *Wushi jiaoji* (Fifty Examinations). It was translated in the first year of the Yuanjia era.
It appears in Zhu Shixing’s *Han lu* and Sengyou’s *Lu*. There is one fascicle of the *Foyin sanmei jing* (Buddha-Seal Samādhi Sūtra) seen in Changfang’s *Lu*;
one fascicle of the *Badarenjue jing* (Sūtra on the Eight Great Persons’ Awakening) seen in Baochang’s *Lu*; and also one fascicle of the *Shelifu huiguo jing* (Sūtra on Śāriputra’s Repentance).

The *Zhíyún huìguò jīng* (Sutra on Directly Confessing Transgressions), one fascicle; first appeared in the *Chángfáng lù* (Record of Sengchangfang); originally intended as a *shēngjīng* (sutra for recitation). Translated in the second year of the Yǒngshòu era.
The tenth fascicle of the *Cháng āhán jīng* (Dīrgha Āgama), a different translation, contains the commentary by Dào'ān and his preface;
this is recorded in Zhū Shìxíng’s *Hàn lù* (Han Record) and Sēngyòu’s *Lù*. The *Shījīáluè yuè liù xiàngbài jīng* (Sutra on Śikhālāvaṣṭaka’s Sixfold Prostrations), one fascicle; also known as...
The *Śukarātya-ṣaḍdigvidhi-sūtra* (尸迦羅越六方禮經), translated from the eleventh fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*; a variant translation found in the *Chángfáng Lù*.
The *Daśottara-dharma-sūtra* (十報法經), two fascicles—also titled *Bahudhātuka-mārgavibhaṅga-sūtra* (多增道章經) or simply *Daśottara-sūtra* (十報經)—translated from the ninth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*;
an earlier catalog also states it was translated from the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

The *Yīqièliúshè shǒuyīn jīng* (Sūtra on the Guarding of Causes Collected from All Outflows), one fascicle, is included in Sengyou’s Catalogue (*Chūsānzàngjìlù*) and appears as the second fascicle of the *Zhōngāhán jīng* (Madhyama Āgama) with a different translation.
Old records state it is the *Yīqièliúshè jīng*; the Wu Record calls it the *Liúshè shǒuyīn jīng*, also known as the *Shòugù*.
There are also those who call it *Liúshè* or *Yīqièliúshè shǒugù*. This is seen in Zhu Shixing’s record.
Additionally, there is the *Catuḥsatya-sūtra* in one fascicle by Saṃghavarman; it appears as a variant translation in the seventh fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.

According to the record of Saṃghavarman, Master Dao’an stated that it was translated from the *Dīrgha Āgama*, though this may be an error. There is also the *Mūlapratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* in one fascicle;
it appears as a variant translation in the tenth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*. The *Wu lu* (Record of Wu) states that the *Mahāpratītyasamutpāda* is the same as the *Mūlapratītyasamutpāda* sūtra.
The original manuscript sometimes uses the character "yi" (倚); this is seen in Zhu Shixing’s *Han-lu* and Sengyou’s *Lu*. *The Scripture on Dharma and Non-Dharma*, one fascicle:
translated from the twenty-first fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*; a variant translation seen in the records of both Zhu Shixing and Sengyou.
*The Scripture on the Distribution of Leaks*, one fascicle: translated from the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*; a variant translation seen in Zhu [Shixing’s] record.
In the *Xing Han Lu* and the *Sengyou Lu*, it is recorded that An Shigao stated this was translated from the *Dīrgha Āgama*; however, this may be an error.
The *Bāramoṇ Zizi Mingzhong Ainian Buli Jing* (One Scroll), translated from the sixteenth scroll of the *Madhyama Āgama*, appears as a variant translation in the *Changfang Lu*.
The *Shizhi Jushi Bacheng Ren Jing* (One Scroll) is found in the sixth scroll of the *Madhyama Āgama*.

A ten-fascicle variant translation is recorded in the *Chángfáng lù* (Catalogue of Dharma-pāla). There is also a one-fascicle *Pǔfǎyì jīng* (Sūtra on the Meaning of Universal Dharma), also called the *Pǔyì jīng* (Sūtra on Universal Meaning), with the alternative title *Jùfǎxíng jīng* (Sūtra on the Practice of Endowed Dharma).
In this version, "Pǔfǎyì" is rendered as Śāriputra, while "Jùfǎxíng" is rendered as Śāriputra; all other details are the same.
It is said to have been translated during the second year of the Yuánjiā era and is identical to the *Guǎngyì fǎmén jīng* (Sūtra on the Gate of the Vast Meaning of Dharma) from the Táng dynasty.

The *Bāramon Bishisō-kyō* (Sūtra on the Brāhmaṇa Avoiding Death), one fascicle; listed in the two catalogs of Zhu Shixing and Sengyou, it is an alternate translation appearing in the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
It is recorded in the Changfang Catalogue. The *Anabhintu-kwa-shichi-shi-kyō* (Sūtra on Anāthapiṇḍada Transforming His Seven Sons), one fascicle;
listed in the fourth and ninth fascicles of the *Ekottarika Āgama*, it is an alternate translation appearing in the Changfang Catalogue. The *A...* [text ends].
*The Sūtra on Difficult-to-Practice Learning*, one fascicle; its title states it is extracted from the *Ekottarika Āgama*, though it is not found [in the extant version].
It is recorded in Changfang’s catalogue. *The Sūtra on the Seven Places and Three Contemplations*, one fascicle; it is extracted from within the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

In total, there are thirty sūtras from beginning to end, as they are titled at the outset. Alternatively, it consists of two fascicles. It was translated in the first year of the Yuanjia era, as seen in Zhu Shixing’s *Han Record* and the *Monk* [catalogue].

*Sūtra on the Parables of the Five Aggregates* (Wǔyīn pìyù jīng), one fascicle; alternatively, it lacks the character "pì" (parable). Also known as the *Sūtra on Being Drifted by Water Foam* (Shuǐmò suǒpiāo jīng).
Translated from the seventh fascicle of the *Āgama*; a variant translation found in Zhu Shixing’s *Han-lù* and Sengyou’s *Lù*.

*Sūtra on Turning the Dharma Wheel* (Zhuǎnfǎlún jīng), one fascicle; alternatively, it is called the *Sūtra on the Revolving of the Dharma Wheel* (Fǎlún lúnzhuǎn jīng). Translated from the fifteenth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*; a variant translation.
The translation is identical to its corresponding text in the original sūtra, though it differs from the previous version.
It is recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue as the *Aṣṭāṅgamārga-sūtra* (One Scroll), appearing as a variant translation in the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Saṃyuktāgama*.

It is also listed in the catalogues of Shi Xian and Sengyou as the *Mātṛceṭī-sūtra* (One Scroll), alternatively titled *Māyā-dārikā-sūtra* or *Ānanda-vaśīkaraṇa-strī-mohanaka-sūtra*; it is found in the *Chang [zhuan]*.
The *Ghosts Ask Maudgalyāyana Sūtra* (一卷), one fascicle; its initial appearance was recorded as being the same text as the *Maudgalyāyana Sūtra*.
It is noted in the *Chángfáng Lù* [Catalogue of Dharma Hui-chang]. The *Ānanda Asks about the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha Sūtra* (一卷);
some call it the *Ānanda Asks about the Sūtra*, while others call it the *Sūtra on the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha*. It is also noted in the *Chángfáng Lù*.

The *Nai-nü-zhi-yu-yin-yuan-jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Maiden Nai and Jiyu), one fascicle, which was among the first translations and is identical to the *A-na-fen-bie-jing* (Sūtra on the Separation from Ānanda);

alternatively, it may lack the characters "causes and conditions" (*yin-yuan*). Also, the *Nai-nü-jian-fang-lu-zui-ye-ying-bao-jiao-hua-di-yu-jing* (Sūtra on the Teaching and Transformation of Hell through the Maiden Nai Seeing Her Own Room and Recording Her Karmic Offenses and Retributions), one fascicle, which was among the first translations and is also called the *Di-yu-bao-ying-jing* (Sūtra on the Retribution of Hell); this is recorded in the *Chang-fang-lu*. Firmly [established].
*Yijing* (Scripture on the Mind), one fascicle; first appearance, also titled *Jianxin zhengyi* (Firm Mind and Right Intention) or *Jianxin jing* (Scripture on Firm Mind); seen in the Changfang lu.
*Dà ān bān shǒuyì jīng* (Great Ānāpāna Scripture on Guarding the Mind), two fascicles—sometimes one fascicle, or lacking the characters "shǒuyì" (guarding the mind);

sometimes called the *Ānbān jīng* (Ānāpāna Scripture). Master Dao’an stated it was the "Small Ānāpāna" along with commentary and a preface. The Yù lu (Yaoxian’s Catalogue) records the *Dà ān* separately.
The *Fanglu* (Record of the Library) contains one fascicle; it is recorded again as a duplicate in another fascicle. It is seen in the three catalogs of Shi Xing, Sengyou, and Li Kuō.
The *Yin-chi-ru-jing* (Sūtra on the Bases of Mindfulness and Elements) is in two fascicles, or sometimes one; Sengyou states that "Ji-chi-ru" is an error for "Yin-chi-ru.

He also mentions an annotated version of the *Yin-chi-ru-jing* with a preface composed by Master Dao’an. In the *Fanglu*, apart from the *Yin-chi-ru-jing*, there exists separately the *Ji-chi-ru-jing*.

*Wu ye jian shi xing* (Erroneous Views of Śrāvakas), one fascicle; seen in the *Sengyou lu*. *Sichuchu jing* (Scripture on Various Places), one fascicle; seen in the *Changfang lu*. *Mayi jing* (Scripture on the Meaning of Abuse), one fascicle;
seen in the *Changfang lu*. *Fenbie shane suoqi jing* (Scripture on the Arising of Good and Evil), one fascicle; seen in the *Changfang lu*.
*Chujia yuan jing* (Scripture on the Causes and Conditions for Leaving Home), one fascicle—also titled *Chujia yinyuan jing*; seen in the *Changfang lu*. *Axiang zheng...* [text fragment]
*Xiáng jīng* (Sutra on Practice), one fascicle; also titled *Zhèngyì jīng* (Sutra on Rectifying the Intention); listed in the Chángfáng Lù. *Nǐlí jīng* (Sutra on the Eighteen Nirayas), one fascicle;

alternatively titled *Shíbā dìyù jīng* (Sutra on the Eighteen Hells); listed in the Chángfáng Lù. *Fǎshòuchén jīng* (Sutra on the Dust of Receiving the Dharma), one fascicle; listed in the Sēngyòu Lù.
*Cánxíngfǎxiǎng jīng* (Sutra on the Dhyāna Practice of Mental Conception), one fascicle; listed in both the Sēngyòu and Bǎochàng Lùs. *Chángzhězǐàonǎo* (The Elder’s Son’s Distress).
*The Sūtra on the Three Places* (one fascicle), also titled *The Sūtra on the Elder’s Distress in Three Places*, or simply *The Sūtra on Distress in Three Places*;
seen in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *The Sūtra of King Kānta* (one fascicle); sometimes the character for "king" (*guó*) is omitted; seen in the *Chángfáng Lù*.
*The Sūtra on the Difficulty of Repaying Parental Kindness* (one fascicle); also called *Qín bào* (Diligently Repaying); seen in the *Chángfáng Lù*. Translated from the *Madhyama Āgama*.

*Jianwu jiuheng jing* (Sūtra on Examining the Nine Untimely Deaths), one fascicle; Fang states it was extracted from the *Madhyama Āgama*, but it is not found [in the current canon]. See Changfang’s record. *Chanxing san shiqi jing* (Sūtra on the Thirty-seven Practices of Dhyāna), one fascicle;
sometimes the character "pin" (chapter) is added. See Baochang’s record. *Fanjie baoying qingzhong jing* (Sūtra on the Lightness and Heaviness of Retribution for Violating Precepts), one fascicle;
extracted from the *Maudgalyāyana-paripṛcchā-vinaya-sūtra*. It is also called *Fanjie zui bao qingzhong* (Lightness and Heaviness of the Sinful Retribution for Violating Precepts). Or...

*Yunmuliwen jing* (The Scripture on Maudgalyāyana’s Questions), recorded in Changfang’s catalogue; *Dabiqiusanqianwei yi jing* (The Scripture on the Three Thousand Dignified Deportments of Great Bhikṣus) in one or four fascicles, also called *Sengwei yi jing* (The Scripture on the Dignified Deportment of the Saṃgha);
*Daodi jing* (The Scripture on the Stages of the Path) in one fascicle, initially issued with the character "Da" (Great) prefixed, recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue;
*Jiaye jie jing* (The Scripture on Kāśyapa’s Council) in one fascicle, initially issued, recorded in Changfang’s catalogue; *Abhidharma Wufa xing* (The Fivefold Practice of Abhidharma).
One fascicle; alternatively, it lacks the character "wu" (without). Seen in Sengyou’s Catalogue. The above exists; the following are missing texts.

*The Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, two fascicles. Its initial translation was identical to the *Immeasurable Life* [chapter] of the *Ratnakūṭa*. Fang says it is seen in a separate catalogue. *The Sūtra on the Illusory Samādhi*, two fascicles, or one fascicle.
Its initial translation was identical to the "Assembly of the Well-Abiding Mind" (*Susthitamati-parivarta*) of the *Ratnakūṭa*.

Identical to the original; recorded in the *Chángfáng lù* as the two-fascicle *Yuedēng sānmèi jīng* (Moon-Lamp Samādhi Sūtra), a variant translation of the seventh fascicle of the *Dàrìdēng jīng* (Great Sun-Lamp Sūtra).

Recorded in the *Chángfáng lù* as the one-fascicle *Shí èryīnyuán jīng* (Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination); its initial appearance was also titled the *Wénchéng shí yīnyuán jīng* (Sūtra on the Ten Links of Dependent Origination from the City of Hearing).
Recorded in the *Sēngyòu lù* as the one-fascicle *Nèizàng jīng* (Inner Treasury Sūtra); its second appearance is also known by the name *Nèizàng*.

The *Bai-pin* (One Hundred Items), also known as the *Bai-bao* (One Hundred Treasures). In the tenth month of the second year of the Yuanjia era, it appeared; this is recorded in Zhu Shixing’s catalogue.

The *Si-buke-de-jing* (Sūtra on the Four Unobtainables), one fascicle. Its initial appearance may have lacked the character "ke" (obtainable); this is seen in Fang’s catalogue. From the first fascicle of the *Zhenyuan-xin-ding-shi-jiao-mu-lu* (Newly Compiled Catalogue of the Buddhist Teachings of the Zhenyuan Era).
The Newly Compiled Catalogue of Śākyamuni’s Teachings from the Zhenyuan Era, Scroll Two.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xīmíng Monastery in the Western Capital.
General Collection of Records of the Various Scriptures, Part Two of the First Section.
*Guān yàowáng yàoshàng púsà jīng* (Sūtra on the Visualization of the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata), one fascicle; first appeared in the *Chángfáng lù*.

*Kōngjìng tiān gǎnyìng sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Response of the Emptiness-Purity Heaven), one fascicle; the old catalogs call it the *Kōngjìng sānmèi jīng*; first appeared in the *Chángfáng lù*.

*Zúféng zéi jiéyīdài zhòujīng* (Sūtra on the Incantation for Binding Robes with Belts When Suddenly Encountering Bandits), one fascicle; appears in the *Chángfáng lù*. *Zhòuzéi jīng* (Sūtra on Incantations Against Bandits), one fascicle; [first appeared in the *Chángfáng lù*]. One.

The *Zhuzui jing* (Sutra on Exorcising Demons), titled *Bichuzaihaimian*, is recorded in Sengyou’s *Chusanzangji ji*; it appears twice in Sengyou’s lost-translation catalog under the same title, *Zhuzui*.

Here, only one version is retained. The *Shisiyi jing* (Sutra of the Fourteen Intentions) in one fascicle; the old catalogs state it is the *Pusa shisiyi jing* (Bodhisattva Sutra of the Fourteen Intentions), as seen in Sengyou’s catalog.
The *Falü sanmei jing* (Sutra of the Samādhi of Dharma-Rules) in one fascicle; its initial appearance is noted in Fa Shang’s catalog as the *Daoyi*.
The *Dvādaśamukha-sūtra* (Twelve Gates Sutra) in two fascicles, or one fascicle, is seen in the catalogs of Dao’an and Sengyou; Faxiang states it was translated from the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
The *Mahā-dvādaśamukha-sūtra* in two fascicles, or one fascicle, was translated from the *Dīrgha Āgama*;
Dao’an provided a commentary and also composed a preface, as seen in the catalogs of Sengyou and Baochang. The *Laghu-dvādaśamukha-sūtra* in two fascicles was also translated from the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
Master Dao’an’s commentary on this work lacks a preface; it is recorded in the catalogs of Sengyou and Baochang. There is one fascicle of the *Saptadharma-sūtra*;

old catalogs refer to it as the *Abhidharma-saptadharmaprakaraṇa-sūtra* or simply the *Saptadharmaprakaraṇa-sūtra*, as seen in Sengyou’s catalog. According to Fang, it was extracted from the *Dīrghāgama*.
There is one fascicle of the *Bahu-dharmacakra-sūtra*; old catalogs lack the character "dao" (path), referring to it instead as the *Yijing* (Different).

The *Chushi fajianfang lu* (Record of the Ten Dharmas and the Vision of the Abode) states: "The *Yijue lü jing* (Sūtra on the Decisions of Meaning in the Vinaya), one fascicle—sometimes without the character 'sūtra' (*jing*)—also called the *Yijue lü faxing jing* (Sūtra on the Practice of Dharma in the Decisions of Meaning in the Vinaya).
Master Dao'an stated it was excerpted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

The *Sengyou lu* (Sengyou’s Catalogue) lists it as "the *Jiaosi shisi pian jing* (Sūtra in Forty-four Miscellaneous Sections), one fascicle," or alternatively, "the *Zajing sishisi pian* (Forty-four Miscellaneous Sections of the Sūtra). Since its specific title is not clearly manifest, [it remains unidentified].
It is unknown which sūtra this refers to; Master Dao’an stated it was translated from the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
One fascicle of the *Sūtra of One Hundred and Sixty Chapters* appears in Sengyou’s catalogue; the old catalogues state it was translated from the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
One fascicle of the *Śatruñjaya-sūtra* (She-tou-jian jing) appears in the old catalogues; its second entry states: "The Śatruñjaya Prince [sūtra] explains two [matters]."
The *Eighteen Lunar Mansions Sūtra* (*Shibabaxiu jing*) also mentions it; the *Prince Venus and Sixteen Lunar Mansions Sūtra* (*Taizi mingxing shiliu xiu jing*) also mentions it;

the *Tiger-Ear Sūtra* (*Huer jing*) and the *Lapis Lazuli King Sūtra* (*Liulijwang jing*), one fascicle—sometimes titled *Lapis Lazuli Chamber* (*Liulifang*)—are said to have been extracted from the *Ekottarika Āgama*, but they are not found upon examination.
The *Prince’s Dream Sūtra* (*Taizimeng jing*), one fascicle, first appeared in the *Changfang lu*. The *Dhyāna Sūtra* (*Chan jing*), two fascicles, is the second [entry].
The *Chūbō-ungen-betsuroku* (Record of Separate Translations from the Chūbō-ken) lists one fascicle of the *Gangajikyō* (Sutra of the Ganges). Its initial appearance also mentions the *Gangajikyō*.

The *Kensōroku* (Record of Fa Shang) and the *Hōshōroku* (Record of Baochang) state that there is a one-fascicle *Gangajikai-kyō* (Sutra of Precepts for the Ganges), which is the *Kaigahō-kyō* (Sutra on the Method of Repentance);

this is found in the *Chōbōroku* (Record of Daochang). There is also a one-fascicle *Gohō-kyō* (Sutra of the Five Dharmas) found in the *Sōyūroku* (Record of Sengyou), and a one-fascicle *Gyōgyō-kyō* (Sutra of the Five Practices) found in the *Chōbōroku*.
*Record of the Short Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, one fascicle. Fang states that it is seen in the *Bie lu*.

You’s record states that it is also called the *Sūtra on the Various Bhikṣus after the Nirvāṇa*, or the *Sūtra on Transformations after the Nirvāṇa*, or the *Sūtra on the Worldly Changes of the Bhikṣus after the Nirvāṇa*, or the *Sūtra on the Worldly Changes of the Bhikṣus after the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa*. *Zhengzhai jing*, one fascicle.

One fascicle of the *Jianzhai fuzhi jing* (Sūtra on the Distinction of Sin and Merit), recorded in the *Changfang lu*. One fascicle of the *Nantijia zuiqi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of Sin for Nandika), recorded in the *Changfang lu*.
One fascicle of the *Chanding fangbian cidi jing* (Sūtra on the Sequential Stages of the Expedient Means of Dhyāna), recorded in the *Sengyou lu*.

He was the crown prince of the principal consort of the King of Anxi.
From childhood, he harbored pure filial piety and served his parents with utmost sincerity;

In his speech and conduct, he moved as if following a compass and a square;
moreover, endowed with a brilliant intellect and industrious diligence,
he applied himself to study with such devotion that there were no foreign scriptures he did not master.
He thoroughly mastered the symbolism of the seven luminaries and the five elements,
as well as the divinations of wind-angles and atmospheric phenomena,

Furthermore, he was thoroughly versed in medical arts and exceptionally skilled in acupuncture and pulse diagnosis;
by observing a person's complexion, he could discern their ailment, and his administration of medicine invariably brought salvation.
He even understood the inner thoughts of birds and beasts upon hearing their cries.
Once, while traveling, he saw a flock of swallows and suddenly said to his companions,

Shortly thereafter, he indeed received such [offerings],

Possessing high talent and quick discernment, he was able to grasp the meaning upon hearing it once.
Not long after his arrival, he became thoroughly proficient in the Chinese language.
Reflecting upon how the True Dharma is profound and subtle, he extensively undertook its translation and propagation.
His lofty realization reached the ultimate depths of principle and the full extent of human nature;

At first, he claimed that in a previous life he had already been the prince of Parthia,

Although Hui-gao repeatedly admonished and exhorted him, he never reformed.

He then took leave of his fellow students, saying:

"Furthermore, his nature was prone to anger, and upon passing away, he was destined to receive an evil form.

This divine consciousness returned to become the crown prince of King Anxi;

Once, there was someone who begged for the divine bamboo.

because of his past practice of giving, precious objects and luxuries abound.

The Upāsaka An Xuan was a native of Parthia (Anxi).

He constantly made Buddhist affairs his primary concern.
Gradually mastering the Han language, he resolved to propagate the scriptures.
He frequently engaged in discussions on the principles of the Way with śramaṇas.
He was what the world calls a Commandant (duwei).

The *Sūtra on the Horse Having Eight Bear-like Traits in Man*, one fascicle—also simply titled the *Sūtra on the Horse Having Eight Vicious Habits*—is a variant translation of the thirty-third fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. It is recorded in the *Wu lu* (Records of Wu) as having been seen by Fang.

The *Sūtra on the Horse Having Eight Bear-like Traits in Man*, one fascicle—also simply titled the *Sūtra on the Horse Having Eight Vicious Habits*—is a variant translation of the thirty-third fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
It is recorded in the *Wu lu* (Records of Wu) as having been seen by Fang.
*Xiǎodàodì jīng* (Sūtra on the Stages of the Lesser Path), one fascicle; Fang states it was seen in the *Wùlù* (Record of Wu); prior to this it existed, but thereafter its loss was heard of.
*Dì'èr chū shìgāo yì shí'èr yīnyuán jīng* (The Second Translation of the Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination by Lokakṣema), one fascicle;

identical in text to the *Shí'èr yīnyuán jīng* translated by An Shigao; Fang states it was seen in the *Wùlù*. *Dàmóyé jīng* (Mahāmāyā Sūtra), one fascicle—sometimes the character "Dà" (Great) is omitted—or in two fascicles.

The first [text], the *Mahāmāyā-sūtra*, shares the same original source; Fang says he saw it in the *Wu lu* (Records of Wu), and it is the one-fascicle *Ratthapāla-sūtra* appearing in the thirty-first fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
Regarding the variant translations, Fang says he saw them in the *Wu lu*, while An says they appear in the Vaipulya section—this may perhaps be an error.
There is also the one-fascicle *Kṣudraka-vastu-utpatti-sūtra*, which some call the *Pratipad-bhūmi-sūtra*.

*Qishi* (The Arising), also known as *Xingxiu benqi* (The Original Arising of Practice); it is merely a minor supplement to the original text. Its initial publication was identical to the *Ruixing benqi jing* (Sūtra on the Auspicious Response of the Original Arising).
This is seen in the old catalogs and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. *Duoluo youposai jing* (Sūtra of the Fallen Upāsaka), one fascicle;
also known as the *Upāsaka jing*. Sengfang states that he saw it in the *Wulu* (Records of Wu). The above comprises ten works in ten fascicles, belonging to the stage of the Lesser Path (*xiao dao*).
Five sections in five fascicles currently exist; the five sections in five fascicles following those from the city of Wencheng are missing.
The śramaṇa Zhiyao was a man from the Western Regions.
He was profoundly learned in the various classics and possessed a subtle understanding of their profound mysteries.
In the second year of Zhongping of Emperor Ling’s reign,
the year of Yichou (189 CE), he translated ten scriptures, including the *Juguangming jing* (Sūtra of Complete Radiance),

at Luoyang. In the catalogues of Sengchang and others, there is also the *Shouzhiwenfo shisi shi jing* (Scripture on the Fourteen Matters Heard from the Buddha), which sometimes lacks the character "Buddha" (*Fo*).
I have personally seen that its original was actually a compilation of excerpts from a sutra;
it has already been included within the *Biesheng lu* (Record of Additional Works),
so I have omitted it here without recording it.
*Wen dizhu shi jing* (Sutra on Questions Concerning the Matters of Hell), one fascicle; seen in Zhu Shixing’s *Han lu* and the *Gaoseng zhuan*. This one work in one fascicle was originally missing.
The śramaṇa Kangchen (alternatively written as Ju) was a man from the Western Regions; it is not yet clear which version is correct.
With his heart set on wandering to convert others and his resolve fixed on propagating the Dharma,
in the fourth year of the Zhongping era of Emperor Ling (the Dingmao year),
he translated the *Yiqiendiyu jing* (Sūtra on the Inquiry into the Hells) in Luoyang; its words were direct and its principles profound, without any further embellishment.
*The Sutra of the Supreme Pure Alms-round of the Bodhisattva Niu-shou*, two fascicles; also titled *The Sutra on Resolving that All Dharmas are Like Illusions and Transformations through Samādhi*.
Its initial translation was identical to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Nāgaśrī-bhāgavata-parivarta*, etc., or it appears as one fascicle in the *Chángfáng-lù*.
*The Sutra of the Bodhisattva Hui-shang’s Inquiry into Great Skillful Means*, two fascicles; its initial translation was identical to... [text fragment ends].
The *Ratnakūṭa Mahāyāna Upāya-parivarta* (寶積大乘方便會) is identical in substance to the aforementioned [text], though it may lack the word "bodhisattva" or consist of one fascicle;

this is recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. The ancient *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* in two fascicles was the first translation produced and is identical in substance to the Tang dynasty translation, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*;
this is seen in ancient catalogs and Zhusi Xing’s *Hàn lù*. The *Siyì jīng* (思意經) in one fascicle is also called the *Yìyì jīng* (益意經).
The first work to appear is the *Pusa nei xi liu boluomi jing* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Internal Practice of the Six Pāramitās), one fascicle, recorded in the *Changfang lu*.
Of the five works totaling eight fascicles mentioned above, the first four comprise seven fascicles whose originals were missing; the last one is one fascicle and is currently extant.
The śramaṇa Yan Fotiao also states that according to Sengyou’s catalog and the *Gaoseng zhuan*, these were combined by the śramaṇas Changfang and others.
The record states that "the lay devotee" is incorrect;
he was a native of Linhuai Commandery.
From his youth, he was exceptionally intelligent and quick-witted, possessing a fondness for learning.
His faith was such that his wisdom arose spontaneously;
he subsequently left the household life to practice the Way, became proficient in translating the scriptures, and was held in high esteem by his contemporaries.
He was ordained in the fifth year of Zhongping of Emperor Ling’s reign, the Wuchen year (188 CE).
In Luoyang, he translated five scriptures, including the *Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Śrīmati*.
The world has praised the three—An Houshu, Duwei, and Fotiao—for their translations, declaring them difficult to emulate.
Master Dao’an praised the sūtras translated by Zhu Fashu,
noting that they were concise rather than prolix and were complete with elegant phrasing.
Furthermore, the catalogs of Sengchang and others list an additional *Kāśyapa Questions Ānanda Sūtra*.
It is also said to have been translated by Buddhabhadra.
I personally examined its original manuscript, which was a compilation of various sutras containing several items of fact.
The *Sui zhong lu* states:
This is excerpted from the *Saṃyuktāvadāna*.
Both An Shigao’s and Nie Chengyuan’s catalogs contain this scripture;
it is an error on the part of those catalogers.
Since this is a separately produced apocryphal scripture,
it should not be counted among the authentic translations.
Furthermore, there is the *Śrāmaṇera-daśajñāna-sūtra*.
It is said that this was composed and annotated by the monk Foutiao himself;
since it is not the word of the Buddha and its original manuscript is missing,
I have now deleted it entirely.
*Śāriputra-mahāmaudgalyāyana-catuṣpatha-saṃcāra-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated from the forty-first fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*;
see separate record for alternative translations. *Xingqi xing jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of Deeds), two fascicles, also titled *Yanjie suyuan jing* (Sūtra on the Solemn Admonition of Past Causes);
the title states it was translated from the *Kṣudraka Piṭaka*; see the Wu Record. *Fanwang jing* (Brahmajāla Sūtra), two fascicles; initially appeared as three fascicles.
The *Wulu* (Records of Wu) lists one fascicle of the *Catuḥsatya-sūtra*, translated in the first year of the Xingping era;
this third translation is slightly different from the seventh fascicle of the *Āgama* translated by Shigao.

It is also seen in Zhu Daozu’s *Hanlu* (Records of Han), where there are two fascicles of the *Rāstrapālaparipṛcchā-sūtra* (also called the *Ruiying benqi*), a second translation that corresponds to the *Guoxian yinguo* (Causes and Effects of Past and Present).

The *Jing* (Sūtra) and others state that this is identical to what is recorded in the *Sanzang ji* (Record of the Tripitaka). However, according to Sengyou’s *Sanzang ji*, Meng Xiang produced the *Zhong benqi* (Middle Account of Past Deeds), which is not the *Shuiying benqi* (Miraculous Response Account of Past Deeds).
The *Baofu jing* (Sūtra on the Requital of Blessings), one fascicle; some say it is the *Fubao*. This is seen in the *Wulu* (Records of Wu). The above six works comprise nine fascicles.
The first two works, comprising three fascicles, are extant as the *Xingqixing jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of Practice). The latter four are the *Fanwang jing* (Brahmajāla Sūtra).
The sixth fascicle of this section is missing.
The śramaṇa Kang Mengxiang was originally from the kingdom of Kangju and enjoyed a reputation for his wisdom and learning.
From the first year of Xingping of Emperor Xian (Jiaxu) to the fourth year of Jian’an (Jimao),
he translated six scriptures, including the *You sifu* (Wandering through the Four Quarters), at Luoyang.
Master Dao’an remarked: “The translations produced by Meng Xiang are fluent and sufficient to convey the profound mysteries.

The *Xiuxing benqi jing* (Sūtra on the Original Acts of Practice) in two fascicles—also known as the *Suxing benqi*—is the third version to emerge; it shares the same source as the *Ruixing benqi jing*. This one work in two fascicles is listed in the *Shi xing lu* (Record of Shixing), and its manuscript currently exists.
The śramaṇa Zhū Dàlì was a man from the Western Regions.
By nature he loved to travel afar and felt no dread of hardships or perils.
In the third month of the second year of the Jiàn'ān era of Emperor Xiàn (the Dingchou year), he departed.
In Luoyang, he translated the *Sūtra on the Original Acts of Practice* (*Xiuxing benqi jing*).
The Sanskrit manuscript of this sūtra was likewise brought from the kingdom of Kapilavastu by Dharmaphala and Kang Mengxiang.

Kang Mengxiang translated the *Zhongbenqi jing* (Sutra of the Middle Origination) in two fascicles, also known as the *Taizi zhongbenqi jing* (Sutra of the Middle Origination of the Prince); it is listed in the *Shixing lu*. The title at the beginning of the sutra states that it was extracted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*. This one work in two fascicles is extant.
The śramaṇa Dharmaphala was a man from the Western Regions.
His learning encompassed both the inner and outer teachings, and his understanding penetrated both the ultimate and conventional truths.

Carrying a Sanskrit manuscript of the sūtra from the kingdom of Kapilavastu, he arrived in Luoyang and, in the twelfth year of Emperor Xian’s Jian’an era (the Dinghai year), translated the *Madhyamāgama-sūtra* (Zhongbenqijing).
Kang Mengxiang translated the *Duyu*.
In the *Neidian lu*, Tan’guo is recorded as having produced this work together with Mengxiang;
however, it is incorrect to merge this with the *Taizi benqi ruishying jing* (The Auspicious Response of the Prince’s Original Arising) into a single volume.
The two sūtras differ entirely and cannot be conflated.
Dao You’s statement that the *Madhyamāgama* was translated by Kang Mengxiang is based merely on the fact that they were co-translated.
*The Sūtra on the Great Expedient Means for Repaying the Buddha’s Kindness*, seven fascicles;

*The Mahāyāna Sūtra of Jewel Adornment*, one fascicle—also known as the "Chapter of Mahākāśyapa," the second part of which was produced from the same source as the *Sūtra of the Universal Gate Bodhisattva Assembly* within the *Ratnakūṭa*.

It is stated that these were compiled together during the Jin dynasty according to the Jin records. For now, I follow the old records. Xu You states that the *Mahāyāna Sūtra of Jewel Adornment* appeared later than the [other] *A* [sūtras].
*The Sūtra of Verses on Amitābha Buddha*, one fascicle (sometimes without the word "sūtra"), excerpted from the second *Sūtra of the Unprecedented*;
one fascicle, first translated and identical to the *Sūtra of the Extremely Rare* in the Tang translation.

*The Sūtra of the Image of the Buddha*, one fascicle—also known as the *Sūtra of King Udayana Making an Image of the Buddha*, or the *Sūtra of the Causes and Conditions for Making an Image*—concerning the construction of images.

*The Scripture on the Requital of Merit* (1 fascicle); *The Scripture on the Dhāraṇī for Securing One’s Dwelling*, same text as above (1 fascicle), also called *The Method for Securing One’s Dwelling with Dhāraṇīs*;

*The Scripture on Receiving the Ten Good Precepts through the Dhāraṇī for Securing One’s Dwelling* (1 fascicle); *The Scripture on the Darkness of Suffering* (1 fascicle), translated from the twenty-fifth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*;
*The Scripture on the Disturbance by Māra* (1 fascicle), an alternative translation of the same text, also known as *The Trial by the Wicked Māra*.
*Maudgalyāyana Sūtra* (also titled *The Sūtra on the Demon King Entering Maudgalyāyana’s Abdomen*), translated from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume 30;
*Śrāmaṇerī-śīla Sūtra* (one volume, sometimes without the word "Sūtra"); *Upāli Asks the Buddha Sūtra* (one volume, sometimes without the name Upāli);
*Vinaya-vibhaṅga-guṇa-vibhāga Śāstra* (four volumes, also called *Vibhaṅga*).

*Gongde jing* (Sutra on Merit), either in three fascicles or five fascicles; *Chan yao he yu jing* (Sutra on the Essentials of Dhyāna and the Reproach of Desire), one fascicle, titled *Chan yao jing*, "Chapter on the Reproach of Desire";

*Neishen guan zhangju jing* (Sutra on the Contemplation of the Internal Body in Verse), one fascicle, or [variant] "without verses"; *Za poyu jing* (Miscellaneous Sutra of Parables), two fascicles, also known as *Pusa du ren jing* (Sutra of the Bodhisattva Saving Humans);
*Liupusa ming* (Names of the Six Bodhisattvas), one fascicle. The catalogue records it as entering the canon under the heading "Bodhisattva."
The *Banzhou sanmei nianfo zhangju jing* (Sutra on the Recitation of the Phrases of the Pratyutpanna Samādhi on Mindfulness of the Buddha) in one scroll;

the *Xingpin biefan di si chu Amituofo jie jing* (Sutra on the Verses of Amitābha Buddha from the Fourth Separate Translation of the Chapter on Practice) in one scroll; and the *Chu xianjie qianfo ming jing* (Sutra on the Names of the Thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa) in one scroll.

Daoyou states that these contain only the names of the Buddhas, which correspond to the *Sishidi jing* (Sutra of the Four Noble Truths) and the *Qianfo ming jing* (Sutra of the Names of the Thousand Buddhas) produced by Dharmarakṣa.

A different translation from the *Bhadra-kalpika-sūtra* (Xianjie jing), a variant Sanskrit manuscript in four fascicles; formerly called the "Hu-ben" (Hu-language manuscript), newly revised as "Fan" (Sanskrit).
Also, the *Nirvāṇa-sahasravarṣa-vikāra-sūtra* (Chang'an zhong chu niepan hou qiansui bianjing) in four fascicles, also known as the *Qiansui bianjing*.
Sengyou states: the *Zhongbian ji* (Record of Transformations During the Thousand Years After Nirvāṇa) in one fascicle, and the *Foming* (Names of Buddhas) in two fascicles, which are now [included].

It is suspected that there is one fascicle of the *Acintyaguṇa-sūtra* (The Sūtra of Inconceivable Merit) titled *The Names of Three Thousand Buddhas*, and one fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Praise of the Names of One Hundred and Seventy Buddhas*, which is also simply titled *The Names of One Hundred and Seventy Buddhas*. It is now suspected that this [latter] was extracted from the *Sūtra of the Praise of Merit*.
There is also one fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Names of Southern Buddhas*, formerly called the *Treatise on Cheng City Temple Sūtra*; however, this is incorrect.
Then he inscribed the temple with a record; these were not alternative names for sutras: *The Sutra of the Buddha’s Name for Extinguishing Sin and Attaining Blessings*, one fascicle;
*The Sutra on the Methods of Practice Spoken by Avalokiteśvara*, one fascicle; this was a dharani sutra; *The Sutra of the Image of the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita Seeking Deep Prajñā*, one fascicle;
and *The Sutra on Not Falling into Evil Realms by Upholding the Names of Buddhas*, one fascicle. Five.

*Longzhou dujing* (Dragon Spell for Subduing Poison), one fascicle; *Qu xueqi shenzhoujing* (Spell for Taking Vitality and Qi), one fascicle—the old catalog states it is the *Xuezhou zhuzei zhufa jing* (Blood Spell and Thieving Spell Ritual Scripture);
Fang says it is a different edition; Yu Zhi says it is the *Zhuzei qifo anzhai shenzhoujing* (Thieving Spell of the Seven Buddhas for Pacifying the Dwelling), one fascicle;
*Pusa shoujie jing* (Bodhisattva Precept Receiving Scripture), one fascicle—Yu’s catalog omits the character “scripture” (*jing*); Fang says it is a different [edition].
*The Ten Methods for the Successive Stages of Receiving the Bodhisattva Precepts*, one fascicle; *The Method for the Bodhisattva’s Repentance*, one fascicle;
*The Bodhisattva Who First Resolves His Mind Constantly Practices Five Matters During the Six Periods of Day and Night*, one fascicle;

*The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of King Mūrdhaja*, one fascicle (the old catalog refers to it as the *Sūtra of King Mūrdhaja*); *The Sūtra of the Elder Bhadramukha*, one fascicle; and *The Brahmin Who Lost His Daughter*.
*Sūtra in One Scroll*: *The Sūtra of the King Bitten by a Hyena and a Dog*, one scroll; *The Sūtra of the Diligent Suffering of Niraya*, one scroll; *The Sūtra of Hell*, one scroll;

*The Sūtra of the Eleven Causes and Conditions*, one scroll—the old catalog states it is the *Sūtra of the Eleven Causes and Conditions*, or alternatively the *Sūtra of the Twelve Ascetics as the Twelve Dhūtas*, one scroll;
*The Enumeration of Monastic Names and Matters of Conduct*, one scroll. [End of] Comparison.

*Qiu zhujinlü* (The Various Prohibitions and Precepts of the Buddha), one fascicle; *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-bhikṣu-yaoji* (Essential Collection from the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya for Bhikṣus), one fascicle—also titled *Mahāsāṃghika-bhikṣu-suiyong-yaojifǎ* (The Essential Collection of Methods for the Daily Use of Bhikṣus in the Mahāsāṃghika School);

*Śrāmaṇera-daśa-śīla-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Ten Precepts for Śrāmaṇeras), one fascicle—the old catalog states it is the *Śrāmaṇera-jie-xianzhe-wujie-jing* (Sūtra on the Five Precepts of the Worthy Śrāmaṇera);
*Upāsaka-vaipulya-vidhi-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Dignified Conduct of Upāsakas), one fascicle; [Compiled by] Yu.
*Ghasamasūtra*, one fascicle; translated as *Brief Exposition on Practice*, also known as *The Dhyāna Method of Dharmatrāta*, or alternatively said to be compiled by Bodhisattva Dharmatrāta;
*Essential Collection of Dhyāna Sūtras* (in Sanskrit verse), one fascicle;
formerly called *Hymns in Hu-Speech Praising the Seven Buddhas*, one fascicle; *One Hundred Phrases of the Tathāgatī*, one fascicle; *Five-Character Odes and Hymns*.

*Benqi jing* (Sutra on the Original Arising), one fascicle; one hundred forty-two chapters. *Duxing pin* (Chapter on the Course of Practice) and *Zhujing fanyin jie* (Explanation of the Sanskrit Sounds of Various Sutras), one fascicle;
formerly called *Huyin*. *Faju piyu jing* (Sutra of Dharma Verses with Parables), one fascicle; the Sengyou Catalogue states it contains seventeen parables.

The fifty-nine works above, including those with the character "喻" (*yu*) as the first character, are all found in Sengyou’s *Shiyi lu* (Record of Lost Translations). The above fifty-nine works comprise seventy-six [fascicles].

According to the *Fǎlù* (Record of the Dharma), the total number of fascicles should be seventy-seven. However, the *Fēnbié Gōngdé Lùn Lù* (Record of the Treatise on the Distinction of Merit) states there were five fascicles;
since only four fascicles currently exist, the total is seventy-six. Regarding the titles of the Bodhisattvas: the first sixteen divisions comprise twenty-six fascicles and are extant;
the forty-three divisions below the *Bānzhòu* (Pratyutpanna) comprise fifty fascicles, but these are missing from the original.
Sengchang and others recorded that these were translations lost after the Han dynasty,
totaling one hundred twenty-five works in one hundred forty-eight fascicles;
of these, sixty-six works in seventy-one fascicles remain today.
A detailed collation that does not lose the source, recording the full particulars as listed below:

*The Sūtra of the Sun-like Maṇi Jewel Bequeathed by the Buddha*, translated by Zhi Chen of the Han; *The Sūtra on the Birthplace of the Bodhisattva*; and *The Miscellaneous Difficulties Regarding the Sun*.
Regarding the two aforementioned sutras translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty: the *Vajrasamādhi-svabhāva-viśuddhy-avināśy-aniruddha-sūtra* (also known as the *Vajra-viśuddhi-sūtra*).
The catalogs of Changfang and others state it was translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu period;
however, it is also recorded in the list of lost translations from the Later Han. Upon careful examination, this sutra is neither a lost source from the Han dynasty nor a work by Zhi Qian.
That which was produced by Qian consists of translations by Master Kumārajīva and others since the Yao Qin dynasty; these are currently classified as "lost sources" and included in the Qin Records.
The two volumes of the *Old Miscellaneous Parables Sūtra* were translated by Kang Senghui during the Wu dynasty.

The *Sūtra of the Names of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions* and the *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Thirty-two Marks*—these two sūtras above were translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. The *Bodhisattva-xiu*... [text fragment].
The *Caryā-sūtra*, also known as the *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Practice Asked by the Elder Vaisya*, or the *Sūtra on the Practice of the Elder*, has already been translated three times;
one version survives while two are missing, as recorded in full in the *K'ai-yüan shih-chiao lu*.

The *Sūtra on Kāśyapa’s Journey to the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa*, also known as the *Sūtra on Kāśyapa’s Journey to the Buddha at the Time of His Parinirvāṇa*. The *Sūtra on the Iron City Hell*, also known as...
The *Āgama-niraya-sūtra*, the *Śramaṇaphala-sūtra*, the *Saptatriṃśat-pakṣa-sūtra*, and excerpts from various sūtras compiled in the *Bie sheng lu* (Record of Separate Translations),
including the *Seven Buddhas’ Oil-Mantra*.
The Illusionist’s Bhadra Dhāraṇī;
the Tooth-Decay Dhāraṇī—also known as the Tooth-Worm Dhāraṇī or the Direct Tooth-Dhāraṇī; the Toothache Dhāraṇī; the Eyeache Dhāraṇī;
the Ten Sūtras on Kāśyapa’s Descent; translated by Zhu Tanwulan of the Eastern Jin Dynasty; The Causes of the Thousand Buddhas.
The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* and the *Aṣṭaguṇa-sūtra*; the above two sūtras were translated by Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin, according to the record of Fashang.
The *Bodhisattvotpatti-sthāna-sūtra* and the *Mahākṣudraka-sūtra*; the above two sūtras were translated by Śramaṇa Jian of the Qifu Qin.
[Regarding the name] "Jitiào-yì," it should be pronounced as "Héyīn"; "Shǒuyì" is an error. The *Paripṛcchā-sūtra*, also known as the *Tathāgatopadeśa*.
*The Sutra on Purifying and Subduing*, also known as *The Sutra on the Bodhisattva Turning the Female Body*;
also known as *The Sutra on the Expedient Means of Adorned Joyful Necklaces*, or *The Sutra on Women Adorned with Joyful Necklaces*. The above two sutras were translated by Fǎhǎi of the Song dynasty.

*The Sutra on the Demeanor of Śrāmaṇeras* (sometimes omitting the word "sutra"); translated by Guṇavarman of the Song dynasty. *The Sutra of the Four Heavenly Kings*; translated by Zhī... of the Song dynasty.
The *Sūtra on the Five Messengers of King Yama* translated by Yan [Fayou], also known as the *Parable of the Five Celestial Messengers Sūtra*;
the above three sūtras were translated by Hui Lan of the Song dynasty. The *Sūtra of the Names of Eight Buddhas* was translated by Gautama Dharmarakṣa of the Northern Wei.

The *Sūtra on the Visualization of Amitāyus Buddha*: this sūtra had previously been translated twice; one version survives while the other is missing, and it is recorded in the *Beiqie Jing Luchu*. The *Prajñāpāramitā*... [text truncated].

The *Prajñāpāramitā-mantra-sūtra* is excerpted from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. The *Sūtra on the King of Merit-Adornment Inviting the Buddha for Eighty-four Thousand Years* is excerpted from the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*.

The *Tathāgatagarbha-prabhava-guhyakośa-sūtra* in two fascicles—also simply called the *Tathāgatagarbha-prabhava-sūtra*—is the "Tathāgatagarbha-prabhava" chapter of the old version of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, combined with the "Dao-shen" [chapter].
The *Catur-pāda-sūtra* in four fascicles—also known by the alternative title *Sudarśana-ṛddhi-vikurvāṇa-ananta-sūtra*, which is another name for the *Sudarśana-ṛddhi-sūtra*;

these two versions are not distinct; the *Upoṣadha-sūtra*, which is an alternate name for the *Upoṣadha-sūtra*; the *Past-Gandha-padma-buddha-loka-sūtra*, which appears in the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
the *Sadguṇa-brāhmaṇa-śarīra-prārthana-sūtra*; and the *Puruṣa-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*. These have already been [translated].
The first two sutras are from the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*. The [sutras] on the names of the fifty-three Buddhas are from the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-bhaiṣajyasamudgata-sūtra*.

In total, over a period of forty-six years during the reigns of the Five Emperors,

The śramaṇa Dharmakāla (translated into Wei as Fashí),
a native of Central India.
His family had been immensely wealthy for generations and constantly cultivated the merit of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Since his youth, Kāla was exceptionally gifted and discerning;
his physical bearing surpassed that of ordinary men, and upon reading a book only once, he mastered both its literary style and its meaning.
He was well-versed in the four Vedas and mastered all aspects of wind,
clouds, constellations, diagrams, prophecies, and the movements of fortune and change.
He claimed that the principles and patterns of the entire world were already contained within his belly.
When he reached the age of twenty-five,
he entered a monastic quarters and happened to see the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā* by Dharmatrāta;
he took it up for a brief look, but was utterly bewildered and could not understand it.
As he reflected with earnest and repeated care, his state of mental confusion increased even further.
He then sighed and said,
"I have accumulated learning for many years."
I have long directed my aspirations toward the ancient classics and wielded my skills with ease through the scriptures;
yet, meaning did not require further reflection and no passage was read twice.
Now, beholding these Buddhist texts, they suddenly transcend the reach of my understanding.
When he applied his reasoning to probe the profound and discern the essential points of sentient beings' conditions,
he took up the documents and entered the quarters to request a bhikṣu to provide a brief explanation. Thereupon,
he deeply awakened to the law of cause and effect and attained a subtle mastery of the three periods of time.
Only then did he realize that the Buddhist teachings are vast and expansive, beyond the reach of secular texts;
he consequently renounced worldly glory, left the household life to practice asceticism,
and recited the sūtras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as the various sections of the Vinaya.
He was always fond of traveling to convert others and did not delight in remaining in one place.
In the third year of the Huangchu era of Emperor Wen (the Renyin year), he arrived in Luoyang;
at that time, although the Buddha-dharma existed within the Wei realm, it was still in its early stages.

Yet the influence of the Way has declined and been corrupted; there are also many monks who have not received the precepts of taking refuge, regarding the mere shaving of their heads as a distinction from the common people.
Even when they perform rites of fasting and repentance, these are identical to the sacrificial offerings of the secular world.
Once Kāla had arrived and was extensively propagating the Buddha-dharma,
the monks requested him to bring forth the Vinaya.
Kāla [responded that] the Vinaya-piṭaka was bound by its intricate regulations and its extensive phrasing and wording.
If Buddhism had not yet flourished, this would certainly not have been accepted and employed.
Consequently, in the second year of the Jiaping era of Emperor Fang of the Qi dynasty, the Gengwu year,
he produced the *Sengqi jiejing xin* (The Heart of the Mahāsāṃghika Precepts) at the Baima Monastery in Luoyang.
He provided for their morning and evening needs.
Thereupon, he further assembled Indian monks to perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and confer the precepts;
thus did the Vinaya tradition first begin in the Eastern Land (China).
It is unknown where this Kāla ended his life. *The Sūtra on the Questions of the Householder Ugga*, one or two fascicles;

third translation, also titled *The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Practice as Asked by Uggarava*; appeared in the fourth year of the Jiaping era. It is found in Zhu Daozu’s *Wei Lu* and is now included in the nineteenth assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa*. *The Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, two fascicles; fourth translation; seen in Zhu Daozu’s *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty* and Baochang’s *Record*. It differs slightly from the version by Shi Huchao. *The Miscellaneous Karma of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, one fascicle; the title reads *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya School Miscellaneous Karma*; it begins with the "Binding of the Precept Field" (*sīmābandha*). Newly appended. These three sections comprise four fascicles, and their texts are all extant.
The śramaṇa Kang Seng-kai was a native of India.
He studied the various sūtras extensively and thoroughly elucidated their profound meanings.
In the fourth year of the Jiaping era, the Ren-shen year, he...
At Baima Monastery in Luoyang, he translated three works, including the *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra*.

This is corroborated by the *Weijin lu* (Record of the Wei and Jin) by Zhu Daozu and the *Liangdai lu* (Records of the Liang Dynasty) by Sengyou and Baochang.

and Jingmai all state that there were two divisions;

I have not yet seen it verified.

The *Dharmaguptaka-karman* in one fascicle, titled simply *Karman*, is extracted from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*; it begins with the "Binding of the Great Boundary" (*mahā-sīmā-bandha*). It is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Wei lu*. This single work in one fascicle currently exists.
The śramaṇa Dharmatāta—
also called Tandi;
in the Wei language, "Dharma-Truth" (Fashi).
An inhabitant of the country of Anxi,
he was well-versed in the Vinaya Piṭaka and had profoundly mastered its subtle and profound mysteries.
In the first year of the Gao-gui-xiang-gong era (the Jia-xu year), he arrived in Luoyang.
At the Baima Temple, he translated one fascicle of the *Dharmaguptaka Karmavācanā*.
He also produced two fascicles of the *Amitābha-samyaksambuddha-sūtra*, the fifth version to appear;

its similarities and differences with the versions produced during the Han dynasty by Zhi Chen and others, as well as with the *Ratnakūṭa* and *Amitāyus-parivarta*, are recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty*.
Furthermore, according to Sengyou’s *Chu sanzang jiji*, there is one fascicle of the *Sūrala-sūtra* (also titled *Wuyou*;
Sengyou’s record reads *Chaya*), first appearing in the records of Zhu Daozu and Sengyou;
and one fascicle of the *Bodhisattvacaryā-sūtra* (also titled *The Questions of the Elder Veda on the Bodhisattva Practice* or *The Elder’s Practice Sūtra*), the second appearance.
