*Shoulengyan jing* (Śūraṅgama Sūtra), two fascicles. Fifth appearance; same text as the version produced during the Han dynasty by Zhi Chen and others, though the wording differs.
See Zhu Daozu’s *Jinshi zalu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) and Sengyou’s Record. The above comprises five works.
The seven fascicles of this section are all missing from the original manuscripts.
The śramaṇa Baiyan was a man from the Western Regions;
his talent and fame surpassed those of his contemporaries, and his profound understanding exceeded that of his peers.
In the third year of the Ganlu era of Emperor Gaogui Xianggong, the year Wuyin,
he traveled to Luoyang for the purpose of proselytization and stayed at Baima Temple,
where he translated five scriptures, including the *Wuliangqingjing jing* (Sutra of Immeasurable Purity).
The records of Sengchang and others also include one fascicle of the *Pingdengjue jing* (Sūtra of Equal Enlightenment),
which is likewise said to have been translated by Bo Yan;
it is now identified as being the same as the *Qingjing pingdengjue jing* (Sūtra of Pure Equal Enlightenment).
However, because the titles vary between extensive and abbreviated versions, they are no longer preserved.

The *Luo-mo-jia jing* (Rāma-ga Sūtra) in three fascicles appears in the four catalogs of Zhu Daozu, Baochang, Fashang, and Lingyou; it was first excerpted from the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter (*Praveśa-dharmadhātu-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and the second version is an abridgment of the earlier chapters of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. These three fascicles appear in Zhu Daozu’s *Wei-lu* (Wei Dynasty Catalog). Thus, these two works comprise five fascicles in total, and their original texts are all missing.
The śramaṇa An Faxian was a man from the Western Regions.
His mastery of the arts and learning was profound, and his wisdom and understanding were exceptionally lofty.
Carrying his mendicant’s staff, he traveled through various lands, arriving here from afar.
He translated two sections of scriptures, including the *Rāmāyaṇa*.
Various catalogs all state that these were produced during the Wei dynasty,
though they do not specify the reign of which emperor.
Now, following the compilation at the end,
the records of the various feudal lords' translations are also separately recorded and listed collectively after the *Wu lu* (Records of Wu).
*The Newly Compiled Catalogue of Śākyamuni’s Teachings from the Zhenyuan Era*, Volume Two.
The Newly Compiled Catalogue of Śākyamuni’s Teachings from the Zhenyuan Era, Volume Three.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xīmíng Monastery in the Western Capital.
General Collection of Records of the Various Scriptures, Part Three of the Upper Section.
The Wu state, the Sun clan: formerly the capital was Wuchang; later the capital was Jianye.
Following Sun Quan, posthumously titled Emperor Taizu Wen (太祖文), from the first year of Huangwu (Renyin) until Sun Hao, there were no posthumous titles.
In the fourth year of the Tianji era, the gengzi year,
a total of four rulers had presided over fifty-nine years;
there were five individuals, both monastics and laypeople.

Including the sūtras translated by others as well as those of unknown translators, there are a total of one hundred and eighty-nine works comprising four hundred and seventeen fascicles; among these, sixty-one works totaling ninety-two fascicles are currently extant, while one hundred and twenty-eight works totaling three hundred and twenty-five fascicles are missing.

The Śramaṇa Weizhinan of Wu compiled two collections of six fascicles each; the Śramaṇa Zhulüyan compiled four collections of six fascicles each; the Upāsaka Zhi Qian compiled eighty-eight collections totaling one hundred and eighteen fascicles of sūtras and vinaya;
the Śramaṇa Kang Senghui compiled seven collections totaling twenty fascicles of sūtras; and the Śramaṇa Zhi Jiangliangjie compiled one collection.

Six fascicles of scriptures translated by various anonymous translators during the Wei and Wu dynasties: eighty-seven works totaling two hundred and sixty-one fascicles. The *Akṣayamati-bodhisattva-sūtra* in four fascicles was first produced;

it is the same text as the *Akṣayamati-sūtra* and the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin, as seen in the two separate records of the Wu dynasty. The *Dharmapada-sūtra* in two fascicles was also first produced; it is also called the *Dharmapada-saṃgraha*.

It was compiled by the Venerable Dharmarakṣa and produced jointly with Kālayaśas and Zhi Qian; Qian composed the preface, as recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue. The Wu record states it is in five fascicles, though this remains uncertain.
The above constitutes two sections comprising six fascicles.
The *Dharmapada-sūtra* in two fascicles is extant;
the *Aksayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra* in four fascicles is missing its original text.
The śramaṇa Vighna— translated in the Wu dialect as "Obstruction"—
was originally from India. His family had followed heterodox paths for generations, regarding fire worship as supreme.

At that time, there was a Śramaṇa from India who had studied the Hīnayāna and practiced many magical arts. As his long journey drew to a close and evening approached, he wished to seek lodging at the house of Nanda.
However, having followed a heterodox path, he harbored suspicion and prejudice toward the followers of the Śākya.
He then stayed outside the gate on the bare ground for the night.
During the night, the śramaṇa secretly employed incantations and spells,
causing the fire worshipped by the Nanda family to suddenly vanish and be extinguished.
Thereupon the entire family went out together and requested the śramaṇa to enter their home to receive offerings. The śramaṇa,
in turn, used his incantations to transform the fire so that it would arise.
Having witnessed the superior supernatural powers of the śramaṇa,
Nandika conceived great faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma;
he then abandoned his former pursuits and left the household life to practice the Way.
Taking this śramaṇa as his preceptor,
he studied the Tripiṭaka and became profoundly skilled in the four Āgamas;
wherever he traveled to convert and teach in various kingdoms, there was no one who did not revere him.
Together with his companion Zhu Lüyan, he set out from the Western Regions and arrived in Jiangyou.
In the third year of Sun Quan’s Huangwu era, the Jiachen year,
at Wuchang Commandery, he and Lüyan jointly translated two sections of the *Acāra-mātṛkā* and other sutras.
However, since Zhi Nan and Yan had not yet mastered the local dialects,
there were some omissions during the translation from Sanskrit;
their intent lay in the fundamental meaning, and their phrasing was relatively plain and simple.

The *Madengjia jing* (Mātṛkā-sūtra) in three fascicles is listed in the *Fashang lu*; it was translated jointly by [Dharmakṣema] and Zhi Qian. It shares the same original text as the *Shetoujian jing* and others, or consists of two fascicles; this is the fourth translation. The *Samajie jing* (Sāmāji-sūtra) in one fascicle first appeared in the *Shixing lu*. It shares the same original text as the *Fennu dantanwang jing* but is a different translation. It is also known as the *Sumati nǚ jing*, the *Nanguo wang jing*, or the *Nuhedantanwang jing*. It was translated jointly with Zhi Yue; it is not a complete canon but was extracted from a larger scripture. The *Foyi jing* (Buddha-vaidya-sūtra) in one fascicle, also known as the *Foyiwang jing*, is listed in the *Baoshang lu*. The *Fanzhi jing* (Brāhmaṇa-sūtra) in one fascicle is listed in the *Shixing lu*. Of these four works totaling six fascicles, the first three consist of five fascicles and are extant; the last one consists of one fascicle and is missing.
The śramaṇa Dharmaratna was a native of Central India.
His understanding and practice were pure and vigorous,
and he was extensively learned in both internal and external teachings.
He traveled together with Vighna throughout the territory of Wu.
After Vighna passed away,
in the second year of Sun Quan’s Huanglong era, the gengxu year, he...
In the capital city of Yangdu, he translated four scriptures, including the *Mātanga-sūtra*;
their titles differ across various catalogs,
with some referring to him as Jiangyan.
Some say it is *Chiyen* (持炎),
while others say it is *Lüyian* (律炎);
it is not yet clear which is correct.
Therefore, these are listed in full.
The *Damingdu wuji jing* (Sutra of the Great Perfection of Wisdom) in four fascicles is the second translation; it is also found in six fascicles and is simply called the *Damingdu jing*.
It is the same text as the *Daofxing* and *Xiaopin* [versions of the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*], as seen in the *Wei-Wu lu* by Zhu Daozu and the records of Sengyou and others.
The *Record of the Amitābha Sūtra* in two fascicles; its internal title reads:

*The Buddha-Spoken Sūtra on the Path for the Transcendence of Humans by the Buddhas, the Amitābha Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas*, Part Three. It is also titled *The Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*.
It appears in the records of Zhu Daozu and Sengyou, and differs slightly from the version translated by Shi Heng. The *Sūtra on the Original Vocation of Bodhisattvas*, Fascicle One.
This scroll is also directly titled the *Benye jing* (Sutra on Original Vows) and is also called the *Jingxing pin jing* (Sutra on the Chapter of Pure Conduct).

It is a separate translation of the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, as recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue. It is an error for Changfang to list the *Jingxing pin* separately outside of the *Benye*.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* in two scrolls is titled the "Inconceivable Dharma-gate Spoken by Vimalakīrti"; it is also known simply as the *Foshuo wuming jing* (Sutra on the Five Wisdoms Spoken by the Buddha).
*Fǎpǔrùdàomén sānmèijīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Universal Entry into the Gate of the Path), fascicle 2, also appearing in three fascicles;

seen in the catalogs of Zhūdào zǔ and Sēngyòu, it differs slightly from the version by Fótíáo of the Wèi and Hàn dynasties. *Huìyìn sānmèijīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom), one fascicle;
also simply called *Huìyìn jīng*, alternatively titled *Bǎoyīn huìyìn sānmèijīng*. Its initial appearance was as the *Rúláizhìyìn jīng* (Sūtra of the Tathāgata’s Seal of Wisdom).

The *Jiǔsèlùjīng* (Sūtra of the Nine-Colored Deer), one fascicle, is found in both the *Dàozǔ lù* and the *Sēnyòu lù*; it is an alternate translation of the *Liùdù jí* and appears in the *Fǎshàng lù*.
The *Lǎonǚrén jīng* (Sūtra of the Old Woman), one fascicle, was said by Master Ān [Shìgāo] to have been translated from the *Āpítán*;

the *Wú lù* simply calls it the *Lǎonǚ jīng*, though it is also called the *Lǎomǔ jīng*. Its initial appearance is recorded in the *Sēnyòu lù*. The *Dúzǐ jīng* (Sūtra of the Vatsiputriya), one fascicle.

*Jianfashang lu*: "The first appearance of the *Sūtra on Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination under the Peepal Tree*, which is identical in its original text to the *Sūtra of the Buddha of Radiant Milk-Light*.
One fascicle. *Changfang lu*: "The third appearance of the *Sūtra on the Noble Path of Dependent Origination*, which is identical in its original text to the Chinese translation [of the same title].
One fascicle. *Sūtra on the Completion of Birth and Death*: "Master An said it was the *Shengsheng jing* (Sūtra on the Production of Beings). Master You examined it..."

The *Wǔjuǎnshēng jīng* (Sūtra of Five Volumes on Birth) does not have this title; it is seen in Sengyou’s catalogue as a different translation of the same original text as the *Dàmiǎn jīng* (Sūtra of the Rice Seedling).

Zhiqian himself annotated it and composed a preface, stating: "It was translated at the end of the Han dynasty; Zhiqian annotated the *Lóngshī nǚ jīng* (Sūtra of the Daughter Lóngshī) in one volume. When it first appeared, it shared the same original text as the *Lóngshī púsà běnqǐ jīng* (Sūtra on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Lóngshī).

Sengyou says that while it is recorded in the *Bié lù* (Separate Catalogue), it is not found in Daoan’s catalogue. [Note: The character "八" (eight) appears to be an error for "吉" (auspicious) in the context of the "Eight Auspiciousnesses" (*bājì*).]

*Śāṅg-shén-zhòu-jīng* (Sūtra of the Auspicious Divine Spell), one fascicle; first appearance. Sometimes the character "shén" (divine) is omitted, or it is called the *Jíxiáng-jīng* (Auspiciousness Sūtra).

It is the same text as the *Bāyáng-shénzhòu-jīng* (Eight-Sun Divine Spell Sūtra), etc. Fáng says he saw it in an ancient catalog. *Wúliàngmén-wēīmìchí-jīng* (Sūtra of the Subtle and Secret Retention of the Gate of Immeasurability), one fascicle;
also simply called *Wēīmìchí-jīng*. Also named *Chéngdào-jìngmó-dé-yīqièzhì-jīng* (Sūtra of Attaining Enlightenment, Subduing Māra, and Obtaining All-Knowledge). First appearance.
*Yūshōshutsu-muryōmon-dōhon* (The Same Original as the Gate of Producing Immeasurable [Buddhas]), one fascicle; seen in the *Sōei-roku* (Monk Rui’s Record) and the *Sōyū-roku* (Monk Sōyū’s Record).
*Kegashaku-daarani-jinjū-kyō* (The Flower Accumulation Dhāraṇī Divine Spell Sūtra), one fascicle; seen in the *Hōshō-roku* (Monk Hōshō’s Record); sometimes the character "jin" (divine) is omitted.

It is the same original as the *Kegeshū-daarani* (Flower Cluster Dhāraṇī). *Jiku-gu-jinjū-kyō* (The Divine Spell Sūtra of Holding Phrases), one fascicle; first appeared in the *Chōbō-roku* (Monk Chōbō’s Record). It is the same as the *Da...* (Dhāraṇī...).
The *Linibao jing* (Āṭānāṭīya-sūtra) and other texts of the same lineage also state: *Dhāraṇī-śīkha-samādhi-sūtra*, one fascicle, the second edition;
alternatively, it is called *Śīkha*, also known as *Bodhisattva-mārga-vṛkṣa*, or *Mārga-vṛkṣa-samādhi*.
This is recorded in the three catalogs by Dao’an, Zhi Min-du, and Sengyou. Sengyou states: "This sūtra is precisely the *Bodhisattva-mārga-vṛkṣa*."

*The Sūtra on the Birthplace of the Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; also known as the *Cāmara-sūtra*. Its initial appearance is recorded in the *Wu lu* (Record of Wu) by Zhu Daozu and the *Sengyou lu* (Catalogue of Sengyou).
*The Pāyāsi-sūtra*, one fascicle; also called the *Pāyāsi-compiled Sūtra*. Sengyou states: "The current single-fascicle *Pāyāsi-sūtra* is precisely this [text].
Its second appearance is recorded in the *Sengyou lu* and the *Bie lu* (Separate Catalogue). *The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Candraprabha*, one fascicle.
The scroll may also include the word "samādhi"; it is also titled *Candraprabha-kumāra-sūtra* or *Candraprabha-kumāra-bhikṣu-sūtra*.
It is recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue as the one-fascicle *Śrāvaka-trividha-śikṣā-sūtra*, also known as the *Śrāvaka-trividha-śikṣā-sūtra*.
It is recorded in Changfang’s catalogue as the one-fascicle *Vinaya-dharma-samādhi-sūtra*, also simply called the *Vinaya-dharma-sūtra*; this is the third edition.
The *Fanzhi Abo jing* (Sūtra of the Brahmin Aśvaka) in one fascicle, also titled the *Abo Mana jing*;
An’s catalogue simply calls it the *Ababa jing*, and it is also known as the *Fowen Fanzhi Abo jing*. It appears in the thirteenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama* as a variant translation;
see Sengyou’s *Chu sanzang jiji* (Catalogue of Tripitaka Translations). The *Fanwang liushi'er jian jing* (Sūtra of the Sixty-two Views of the Brahmajāla) in one fascicle, also titled the *Fanwang*.

The *Jingfang* (Scripture Chamber) records that it appears in the *Bielu* (Separate Record); it is a different translation of the fourteenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, titled the one-fascicle *Qizhi jing* (Sūtra on the Seven Knowledges), though some versions call it the *Qizhijian jing*.
It also appears in the *Changfang lu* (Changfang Record) as a different translation of the first fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, titled the *Shi Monan benjing* (Original Sūtra of Śreṇika’s Son).

According to Sengyou’s record, this title does not exist; it is also known as the *Wuyin yinshi jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Five Aggregates). An’s record states it appears in the *Zhong* (Middle) [Āgama].
The *Zhufa ben jing* (Sūtra on the Origin of All Dharmas), one fascicle; translated by Zhu Daozu during the Wu dynasty, recorded in the *Wu lu*.
This is a variant translation of the twenty-fifth sūtra of the *Āgama*. The *Bimoshishi mulian jing* (Sūtra on the Evil Māra Tempting Maudgalyāyana), one fascicle;
also known as the *Mochao luan jing*. Recorded in the *Changfang lu*. Faxian states it was seen in the old catalog. This is a variant translation of the thirtieth sūtra of the *Madhyamāgama*.
*The Sūtra of Rāṣṭrapāla*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Sūtra of the Arhat Rāṣṭrapāla*.
It differs slightly from the version translated by Zhi Yao of the Later Han dynasty. It appears in the third volume of the *Madhyama Āgama* (No. 31).
Sengyou states that it is recorded in the *Bie lu* (Separate Catalog) but is not found in Dao’an’s catalog. *The Sūtra of Brahmāyu*, one fascicle; alternatively written as "Yu" (渝). Seen.
The *Zhāijīng* (Upoṣadha-sūtra), one fascicle, also known as the *Chízāijīng*, translated by Dao’an and Sengyou from the thirty-first [section] of the *Madhyamāgama*;
see the *Bielù* and the *Sengyùlù*. The *Xumotínnǚjīng* (Sūmāgadhāvadāna-sūtra), one fascicle, translated by [others] from the fifty-fifth [section] of the *Madhyamāgama*;
also found as a variant translation in the twenty-second [section] of the *Ekottarikāgama*.

The *Jian Changfang Lu* (Catalogue of Jian Changfang) records the *Buzi shouyi jing* (Sūtra on Not Guarding One’s Intentions) in one fascicle; some versions omit the character "yi" (intention), while others read "zishou" (self-guarding) instead, thus titled *Buzi shou jing*.

It appears as a variant translation in the eleventh fascicle of the *Za ahan jing* (Saṃyukta Āgama). The *Wumuzi jing* (Sūtra of the Five Mothers and Sons) in one fascicle is recorded in the *Jian Changfang Lu*;
its initial translation was the same text as the *Shami luo jing* (Śāmilaka Sūtra). The *Taizi ruixiang* (Auspicious Signs of the Crown Prince) [is also recorded therein].
The *Yingbenqi jing* (Sūtra on the Original Arising) in two fascicles, translated during the Huangwu era;

this fourth edition is also titled *Taizi benqi ruisheng* (Auspicious Responses to the Prince’s Original Arising), or simply *Ruisheng benqi* (Auspicious Responses to the Original Arising). It differs slightly from the version produced by Meng Xiang.
Recorded as having been transcribed by Xie Qiang of Chenjun and Zhang Xi of Wujun, and collated by Cao Zhi of Dong’e of Wei. It is found in the two catalogs compiled by Sengyou of Shixing. Dragon.

*The Sūtra of the King’s Brothers* (one fascicle), also known as *The Sūtra of the Dragon King Nāga*, or alternatively without the character "king" (*rājan*), also known as *The Sūtra of the Subduing Dragon King*;
first appeared in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *The Sūtra of the Householder Ghosila* (one fascicle), also known as *The Sūtra of the Householder Ghosila and Uruvilvākāśyapa*, or simply *The Ghosila Sūtra*;
first appeared in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *The Seven Daughters...* [text fragment].
One fascicle; also called the *Saptakanyā-sūtra*. Master Dao’an says it was translated from the *Abhidharma*.
Its initial appearance is recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue. One fascicle of the *Aṣṭācārya-sūtra*; recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Wu-lu* and Sengyou’s catalogue. Its initial appearance.
One fascicle of the *Piṅśarāja-pañcapraṇidhāna-sūtra*, or written with the character "píng"; also known as the *Puṣya-rāja-sūtra*. Recorded in the [Cháng] catalogue.

When the *Fanglü* (Record of the Canon) first appeared, Seng'an's record stated that it was derived from the *Zhong ahan* (Madhyama Āgama). Upon examination, the two-fascicle *Yizu jing* (Sūtra on the Meaningful Footsteps) was not found there;
however, it is seen in Zhu Daozu’s *Wulu* (Record of Wu) as well as in the two records of Sengyou and Baochang.

When it first appeared, there were sixteen sūtras, including the two-fascicle *Sumati gāzhăng jing* (Sūtra of the Elder Sumati), which is also titled *Huizhu fujian* (Assembly Before All Buddhas) and is further named *Rulai suoshuo shi* (The Teaching Spoken by the Tathāgata).
*The Scripture on the Four Matters of Ānanda* (一卷), seen in the *Chángfáng Lù*; also seen in the *Sēngyòu Lù* and the *Bièlù*.
*The Scripture on Ajātaśatru* (一卷), seen in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *The Scripture on the Four Vows* (一卷), seen in the *Zhūdào Zǔ Wú Lù* and the *Sēngyòu Lù*.
*The Scripture of the Kṛṣṇa Brahmin* (一卷); the *Fáng Lù* states it is seen in the *Bièlù*. *The Scripture of the Mad Dog* (一卷).
*Āṭānāṭīya Sūtra*, one fascicle; listed in the *Chángfáng lù*. *Sūtra on Sundarika-putra*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *Sūtra on the Brahmin Sundarika-putra*; listed in the *Chángfáng lù*.
Master Ān said it was extracted from the *Madhyama Āgama*, but it cannot be found there.

*Sūtra on the Precepts for Eliminating Calamities*, one fascicle; also titled *Sūtra on the Precepts for Subduing and Eliminating Calamities*; listed in the old catalogs. *Saṃyuktaśataka-vyākaraṇa Sūtra*, ten fascicles.
The *Bodhisattvapūrvapraṇidhānasūtra* (or *Bodhisattvapūrvapraṇidhānasaṃgrahasūtra*) in three fascicles—also said to be in two or four fascicles—compiled by the Indian śramaṇa Saṃghasena;
recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. The *Vairōcanavyākaraṇasūtra* (or *Vairōcanavyākaraṇanānāvidhaduṣkarasūtra*) in one fascicle;
recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitāmantrasūtra* in one fascicle.
Alternatively, there is no entry for the *Mahā* (摩訶) character; the *Baochang lu* lists the *Fajing jing* (法鏡經) in two fascicles—or one fascicle—stating it is the second edition.

Sengyou says he saw it in the *Bielu* (別錄), but it is not found in the *Anlu* (安錄). Furthermore, the *Changfang lu* (長房錄) additionally lists the *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra* (郁伽長者經) in two fascicles, also attributed to Zhi Qian;
this is precisely this same scripture and should not be recorded twice. [The entry for] the Daughter of King Ajātaśatru...

*Āśudá púsà jīng* (The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Āśudá), one fascicle; first appearance in the *Chángfáng lù*. *Āchāmò púsà jīng* (The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati), four fascicles; appears in the *Wú lù*.
This second appearance is identical in text to the version translated by Vighna, differing only slightly. *Xiǎo āchāmò jīng* (The Minor Sūtra of Akṣayamati), two fascicles;
appears in the *Bié lù* and the *Sēngyòu lù*. It includes the "Small" (Xiǎo) characters and should correspond to the aforementioned sūtra.

This is not the same as the original two-fascicle *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*; the third edition produced here consists of this abbreviated version, with its introductory section and the "Chapter on Lamentation" (*Śoka-parivarta*) forming two fascicles.
The final three sheets differ from the [standard] view. According to Zhu Daozu’s *Wu lu*, An says it was translated from the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
Sengyou says that the *Dīrgha Āgama* differs from this [text]. The *Sūtra of the Three Chariots Summoned by the Buddha* in one fascicle is found in the *Changfang lu*.
*Yun chū fǎhuá yīng chū dì èr juàn pìyù pǐn* (The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Two: Parables), one fascicle; first appearance in the *Bǎochàng lù*.
*Sūlàijīng* (Sūrya-sūtra), one fascicle; alternatively called *Xūlàipúsà jīng* (Sūrya-bodhisattva-sūtra);
third appearance, same text as those translated by Bái Yán and others; recorded in Zhú Dàozǔ’s *Wǔlù* and Sēngyòu’s catalog under the Bodhisattvas.
*Xiuxing jing* (Sutra on Cultivating Practice), one fascicle; first appearance in the *Baochang lu*. *Yan daosu ye jing* (Sutra on Expounding the Practices of Monastics and Laity), one fascicle;

first appearance in the old catalogs, though some versions omit the character "ye" (practice). *Fangdeng shoulengyan jing* (Prajñāpāramitā Śūraṅgama Sūtra), two fascicles; translated during the Huangwu era.
This second edition is the same text as that produced by Zhi Chen and others of the Later Han, as recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Wu lu* and the *An lu*.
Sengyou’s catalogue states there is no title "Wufang" (No Direction); see the *Bielu* (Separate Record). *Weiming ershi ji jing* (The Sutra of the Twenty Verses on Only Clarity), one fascicle;
first appeared, though some omit the word "jing" (sutra); see Sengyou’s catalogue. *Famiejin jing* (The Sutra on the Extinction of the Dharma), one fascicle;

first appeared, though some call it *Famojin* (The Dharma is Exhausted) or *Kongji pusa suowen jing* (The Sutra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Śūnyatā-viśrānta); see Changfang’s catalogue. *Qifo shenzhou* (The Divine Incantations of the Seven Buddhas).
One fascicle; one manuscript lacks the character "sūtra" (jing). Recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. *Mahā-vīrya-sūtra* (Móhē jīngjìn jīng), one fascicle;

The Upāsaka Zhi Qian, courtesy name Gongming,
also known as Yue,
was a native of the Great Yuezhi.
His grandfather, Fadu, led several hundred people from his state to submit to Han rule during the reign of Emperor Ling.
He was appointed General of the Household for Leading the Well-Governed (Shu-shan Zhong-lang Jiang).
At the age of seven, Yue played at a neighbor’s house on a bamboo horse.
He was bitten by a dog, which shattered the bone of his shin.
A neighbor wished to kill the dog to take its liver and apply it to the wound.
Yue said:
Heaven created this creature to guard and bark for man.
Had you not gone to your master’s house, the dog would never have bitten you.
Thus, the fault lies with me; it does not concern the dog.
If even killing it would not lead to recovery, one should not do so;
how much less should one act when it benefits neither oneself nor others, while only inviting great sin?
Furthermore, since animals lack awareness, how can they be held accountable through reason?
Because of this, his neighbor was moved by the sincerity of his words and consequently ceased killing [animals] altogether.
At ten years of age, he studied the Chinese classics;
at thirteen, he studied the Brahmanical scriptures.
He attained a refined and exquisite mastery,
and was furthermore proficient in the spoken languages of six kingdoms.
During the reigns of Emperors Huan and Ling, Zhi Chen translated the scriptural canons.
There was Shi Liang, whose courtesy name was Jiming;
he was endowed with the learning of [Dao]can and [Zhi]qian,
and furthermore received his instruction from Liang.
He had extensively read and thoroughly mastered all the classical scriptures,
and he was well-versed in many worldly arts and crafts. As for his physical appearance,
he was slender, tall, dark-complexioned, and thin.
His eyes had much white sclera and were yellow;
at that time, people spoke of him, saying:
"Zhi Lang, Zhi Lang, the yellow in his eyes!"
Although his physical frame was small, he was a treasury of wisdom.
By nature, he revered the Great Dharma and refined his mastery of the essential meanings of the sutras.
Toward the end of Emperor Xian’s reign, the House of Han fell into great chaos.
He fled to Wu together with several dozen fellow villagers.
On the day he first set out, he had only a single blanket,
and a traveling companion followed him.
During a great cold snap, Yue called out to him to sleep together as they had no blankets.
When the night was half over, the guest snatched the blanket and departed.
The next morning, his companions asked where the blanket was.
Yue said,
"Last night it was taken by a guest.
My companions all asked, 'Why did you not inform us?'"
He replied,
"If I were to expose you all, you would surely be punished with the crime of *kalpa*-sins.
How could it be appropriate to kill one person for the sake of a single garment?"
Those who heard of him, whether from afar or nearby,
were all moved to admiration and submission. Later, when Sun Quan, the ruler of Wu, heard of his extensive learning and talent,
he summoned him for an audience and questioned him on the profound and obscure meanings within the scriptures.
Huiyue responded to the occasion by resolving the difficulties without hesitation or analysis;
the Prince was greatly pleased and appointed him as a *boshi* (Confucian scholar),
charging him with the task of instructing the Crown Prince.
He was bestowed with exceptional honor and rank,
yet he surpassed others in the Great Teaching;
for although the scriptures were being practiced, most were in Sanskrit and none could interpret them.
Being proficient in both Chinese and non-Chinese languages,
he collected various versions and translated them into the Wu dialect.
This work spanned more than thirty years, from the second year of the Huangwu era (Gui-mao) under Sun Quan to the second year of the Jianxing era (Gui-you) under Sun Liang.
He translated eighty-eight works, including the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others,
skillfully capturing the sacred meaning while rendering the phrasing and style elegant and refined.
Furthermore, he relied upon the *Amitāyus-sūtra* and the *Madhyama-āgama* (Middle-length Discourses).
He composed the "Verses in Praise of the Bodhisattva" (Zhì zàn púsà lián jù) and the "Three Rituals for Chanting Sanskrit Hymns" (Fàn bèi sān qiè),
as well as a commentary on the *Sūtra on the Fundamental Nature of Birth and Death* (Zhù liǎo běn shēng sǐ jīng);
all of these were practiced throughout the world.
Later, when the Crown Prince ascended the throne,
he retired to Mount Qiong’ai and no longer involved himself in worldly affairs. There,
he followed the Daoist monk Zhu Falan to further refine his practice of the five precepts.
All those he traveled with were exclusively śramaṇas.
Later, he passed away in the mountains at the age of sixty.
Sun Liang, the ruler of Wu, wrote to the assembly of monks, saying:
"Zhi Gongming did not survive his illness;
yet his practice was pure and simple from beginning to end, and may well be held in high esteem."
I am moved by such deep compassion that I cannot restrain myself;
such was the esteem in which he was held by his contemporaries.

Furthermore, the *Vajraviśuddhi-sūtra*—also titled the *Vajrasamādhi-prakṛtiviśuddhy-aniruddhāvināśa-sūtra*—is recorded in the Later Han lost translations catalog.

They are now reclassified under the Qin Records. The three sūtras added above—namely, the *Mahāśakuntaka-śyena-mṛga-sūtra*, the *Ulūka-pakṣi-vastu-sūtra*, and the *Śuṣka-vṛkṣa-sūtra*—are all found in the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
The *Rūpam-anitya-sūtra* and the *Sarvāsrava-kṣaya-sūtra* (or the *Anāsrava-sūtra*).
The *Himavat-na-markaṭa-sūtra* (sometimes titled *Na-markaṭa* or *Na-markaṭa-sūtra*). The *Na-mātṛputra-sūtra*. And the *Aśubha-bhāvanā-sūtra*—these are the three types.

These are the *Sūtra on What Belongs to Me* and the *Sūtra on the Brahmin*; these two sūtras are both... [text ends]... included therein.

The *Mukha-manas-sūtra*, the *Brahmacāri-paripṛcchā-buddhaguru-dharma-sūtra*, the *Dāna-viśeṣa-sūtra*, the *Udaka-phena-sūtra*, the *Andha-kūrma-sūtra*, and ten other sūtras such as these, all appear in the *Abhidharmadīpa* (or *Udānavarga*).

The aforementioned *Mahāmaitry-aparihāṇa-sūtra* and others [are likewise found there].

The *Bodhisattva-viśuddhacaryā-sūtra* in two fascicles is an alternative translation of the "Ratna-keśa-parivarta" chapter of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, or is simply titled the *Viśuddha-vinaya-sūtra*;

his father moved to Jiaozhi for commercial purposes.
When he was about ten years old, both of his parents passed away.

he dispatched a messenger to the monastery to inquire after the various monks and to invite them for a gathering to hear the Dharma.
Senghui followed him into the palace, where Sun Hao questioned him in detail regarding the causes of his offenses and merits.
Senghui provided a detailed exposition, the words of which were exceedingly refined and essential.
Hao, who already possessed a talent for understanding, was filled with joy and great delight.
Because he sought to examine the precepts of the śramaṇas,
and as the text of the precepts was strictly guarded and could not be lightly proclaimed,
he instead took up the one hundred and twenty-five vows of the *Karma-śataka*.
These were divided into two hundred and fifty matters.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, he constantly made vows for all sentient beings.
When Hao saw these compassionate vows so vast and universal, his own wholesome intentions increased even further.
He immediately attended the assembly and received the five precepts; within ten days, his illness was cured.
He then further renovated the site where the assembly had been held and named it Tianzi Temple (Heavenly Son Temple).
He proclaimed that all members of the imperial clan must respectfully uphold [the teachings].
Later, during the Wu dynasty, he frequently preached the True Dharma;
however, because Emperor Huo’s nature was fierce and coarse, he could not grasp the subtle meanings.
He recounted only matters of immediate retribution to open his mind.
In the third month of the fourth year of the Tianji era of the Wu dynasty, Sun Hao surrendered to the Jin.
In the ninth month, Hui fell ill and passed away.
This was the first year of the Taikang era of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty.
Later, during the Xianhe era of Emperor Cheng,
Su Jun incited a rebellion and burned down the stupa built at the assembly hall.
He Chong, the Minister of Works, reconstructed it once again.
Zhao You, General Who Pacifies the West, was a man of his generation who did not honor the Dharma and utterly despised the Three Jewels;
upon entering this temple, he said to the various monks:
"I have long heard that this stupa frequently emits radiance;
however, as such accounts are hyperbolic and lack scriptural basis, I have been unable to believe them.
If I were to witness it for myself, there would be no need for further discussion."
As soon as he finished speaking, the stupa emitted light of five colors that illuminated the hall and the spire.
Dao You was so moved by solemn awe that his hair stood on end.
Consequently, out of faith and reverence, he erected another great stupa to the east of the temple.
In the distant past, this was due to the spiritual resonance of the Great Sage;
in the recent past, it was likewise through the power of Kanghui.
Therefore, his image was depicted and transmitted to the present day.
Sun Chuo composed a eulogy for him, saying:
"Master Hui’s air was serene and refined; he was truly possessed of noble substance.
His mind was free from immediate burdens, and his spirit possessed abundant leisure."
He illuminated this dark night and shook off those who were most depraved;
he transcended to reach afar and rose loftily above all.
This occurred in the first year of the Dàyuán era of Emperor Huìwǔ, the year of Xīnwèi.
In the first temple he established, he translated seven scriptures, including the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*,
attaining an exquisite mastery of their essential character such that both the phrasing and the meaning were perfectly accurate.
Furthermore, he transmitted the melodic chanting style of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Its purity, elegance, pathos, and resonance served as a model for an entire generation.
Furthermore, according to the records of Changfang and others,
there were additionally the *Ānanda-nianmi jing*, the *Jingmianwang jing*, the *Chaweiwang jing*, and the *Fanhuanwang jing*.
Although the four aforementioned scriptures are said to have been translated together,
they all originate from the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya*; therefore,
they should not be counted among the number of authentic translations.
These are now included in the Separate Record (*bie lu*).

Furthermore, there are two fascicles of commentary on the *Fajing jing* (Sūtra of the Dharma Mirror), one fascicle of commentary on the *Daoshu jing* (Sūtra of the Tree of the Path), and one fascicle of commentary on the *Anban jing* (Sūtra of Ānāpāna).
The above three sutras were compiled together and provided with prefaces.
Although the commentaries for these three compiled sutras were not originally translated by the Sangha,
they are nonetheless not counted among the works of collective translation.
Including the previous seven sections, all are now deleted.

The *Fahua sanmei jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi-sūtra), six fascicles; one copy contains the character "zheng" (correct). translated into Wu as Zheng Wuwe (Righteous Fearlessness),
was a man from the Western Regions.
In the second year of the Wufeng era of Sun Liang, the year of Yihai,
the *Fahua sanmei jing* was translated at Jiaozhou;
the śramaṇa Zhu Daoxin acted as the scribe.

Thus, the above eighty-seven works totaling two hundred and sixty-one fascicles are recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue (*Chu sanzang jiji*).

Of these, eight works totaling six fascicles—the *Bukongyi* (Inconceivable) and others—are extant; eighty-three works totaling three hundred and fifty-five fascicles, including the *Puyao* (Universal Radiance) and others, are missing.
The catalogs compiled by Sengchang and others record that these were lost translations from the Wei and Wu periods,
totaling one hundred and ten works in one hundred and ninety-one fascicles;
it is said that they are all ancient translations of various sūtras.
I have now appended these here to demonstrate that for many years there has been no basis for them;
meanwhile, as for the remaining twenty-three sections in thirty fascicles,
their translations possess a verifiable source.
Some have alternative names or different titles;
some are extracts from larger works;
others are suspected of being apocryphal rather than authentic.
These are now all deleted to avoid redundancy and complexity.
A brief summary follows below.
The *Avaivartika-sūtra* in four fascicles, translated during the Northern Liang dynasty (translator lost), contains this same material; thus, it is recorded here again as a duplicate.

Sengyou’s *Lu* (Catalogue) states: "Master Dao’an’s *Liangshi yijing* [Scripture on the Extraordinary Matters of the People of Liangzhou] currently exists; it has been excluded from this [present] *Liang lu* [Catalogue of Liangzhou].

The *Xiaobenyiqing jing* (Smaller Sūtra on the Origin of the World), two fascicles, translated by Zhi Yao of the Later Han. The *Sibei jing* (Sūtra of the Four Classes), also called the *Sibei dishi jing* (Sūtra of the Disciples of the Four Classes) or the *Sibei xue jing* (Sūtra of the Learning of the Four Classes).
According to the upper catalogue, it was translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. It is also known as the *Jianhui sanmei jing* (Sūtra of the Samādhi of Building Wisdom). One name... [text ends].
The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-bodhisattva-daśakriyā-sūtra* (one fascicle), also known by the alternative titles *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*,
*Dhyānakrama-cittasaṃgraha-sūtra*, or *Dhyānakrama-cittaparīkṣā-sūtra*; the *Ānanda-vinaya-aṣṭasmṛti-sūtra*,
also known by the alternative title *Ruciraketu-bodhisattva-sūtra* (two fascicles)— this is simply an abbreviated name for the *Ruciraketu-bodhisattva-pariśuddha-piṇḍapāta-sūtra*.

*The Sutra on the Simile of the Infinite Deliverance*, three fascicles (or four fascicles), translated from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. *The Sutra of King Śikhāvin*, also written with the character "Ni" (尼).
*The Sutra of Prince Dharmamati*, also written with the character "Hui" (惠). The two sutras concerning Śikhā and others are found in the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-saṃcaya-sūtra*.
*The Sutra of the Lustful Man Walking with His Heels Dragging*, found in the *Arthavargīya-sūtra*. *The Sutra of the Man Falsely Claiming the Name of the Way*. *The Poor Woman*.
*The Sutra on Listening to the Dharma*;
*The Sutra on a Poor Woman Who Died from a Snakebite and Was Reborn in Heaven after Listening to the Dharma*; *The Sutra on the Foolish Consort of the King*;
*The Sutra on Selling Wisdom*; *The Sutra on First Receiving the Way*; *The Sutra on Learning the Dharma*; and *The Sutra on the Merit of Learning*. These are all included together.
The eight sūtras consisting of the *Saṃgharakṣitāvadāna*, the *Upamānasaṃcodana* (also called the *Upamānopadeśa*),
the *Puruṣavyañjanādi*— these eight sūtras are all from the *Kṣudrakavyākaraṇa*; the *Pañcaśatabrāhmaṇapraśnavidyāvidyāstīti-nāsti-sūtra*,
the *Pañcaśatabrāhmaṇasūtra*, the *Sahampati-bodhisattva-sūtra* (also called the *Rājā-sahampati-bodhisattva-prajñāsamādhi-viśvabhū-sūtra*).
The *Ṣaḍabhijña-bodhisattva-sūtra* is also called the *Huiding pǔbiàn guótǔ shéntōng púsà jīng*;
the *Daridra-strī-sūtra* is also called the *Nanda-daridra-strī-sūtra*; and the *Ajuna-sūtra* is also called the *Ajuna-samādhi-sūtra*.

These five sūtras, including the *Pañca-brāhmaṇa-sūtra*, are all listed in the *Yìwěi lù* (Record of Doubtful and Spurious Works). [Compiled during] the Western Jin dynasty. [Compiled by] Sīxíng of the Western Jin.

The Ma clan’s capital was Luoyang; it is also said that Northern Jin began in the first year of the Taishi era of Emperor Wu, the year of Yiyou (345 CE), and lasted until the fourth year of the Jianxing era of Emperor Min, the year of Jingzi (396 CE).
In total, four emperors reigned for fifty-two years.
Twelve individuals, both monastics and laypeople,
compiled the sūtras, precepts, anthologies, and various newly and formerly translated scriptures of unknown translators,
totaling three hundred and thirty-three works comprising five hundred and ninety fascicles.
Among these, one hundred and fifty-six works totaling three hundred and twenty-one fascicles are extant;
one hundred and seventy works totaling two hundred and sixty-nine fascicles are missing.
The Śramaṇa Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin translated one hundred seventy-five works totaling three hundred fifty-four fascicles of sūtras and precepts;
the Śramaṇa Qiang Lianglouzhi compiled one work in one fascicle; the Śramaṇa An Faqin compiled five works totaling sixteen fascicles of sūtras;
and the Śramaṇa Wuluocha compiled one work of thirty fascicles of sūtras for lay practitioners (upāsakas).
Two sections and five fascicles of sutras by Zhu Shulan; sixteen sections and eighteen fascicles of sutras by the śramaṇa Bai Fazang;
four sections and twelve fascicles of sutras compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Fali;
forty sections and fifty fascicles of sutras and vinaya by the śramaṇa Shi Faju; and two sections and three fascicles of sutras by the lay devotee Nie Chengyuan.
The lay practitioner (upāsaka) Nie Daozhen [translated] twenty-four works totaling thirty-six fascicles of sūtras and vinaya;
the śramaṇa Zhi Fadu [translated] four works totaling five fascicles of sūtras; the śramaṇa Jueluoyan [translated] one work totaling one fascicle of sūtra;

and various previously and newly translated works of unknown translators totaling fifty-eight works in fifty-nine fascicles—specifically, three works in three fascicles and fifty-three works in fifty-six fascicles.

The *New Translation of the Sūtra of the Radiant Praise of the Prajñāpāramitā*, in fifteen fascicles (originally issued in ten fascicles), is identical in its original text to the second assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the "Chapter on the Emission of Light" (*Prabhāsa-parivarta*).

It is also titled the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and consists of twenty-seven chapters. It was issued on the twenty-fifth day of the eleventh month in the seventh year of the Taikang era.

According to the An lu (An’s Catalogue), the Sengyou lu (Sengyou’s Catalogue), and the Miji jinganglishi jing (Sūtra of the Secret-Trace Vajra-Powerful One)—which exists in versions of seven, five, four, or eight fascicles—it was translated on the eighth day of the tenth month of the first year of the Taikang era.
Some catalogs simply refer to it as the *Miji jing* (Secret-Trace Sūtra). It is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa* collection as the third [sūtra].

The *Pusa shu meng jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Explaining Dreams) in two fascicles, recorded by Fashang; now included in the *Ratnakūṭa*, it is renamed the "Assembly of the Śuddhāvāsakāyika Devaputra.
Fashang’s record states it was produced by Master Hu; however, a detailed examination of the text reveals this is not the case.
For now, I follow Fashang’s record as definitive. The *Baoji pusa suo wen jing* (Sūtra Asked by the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin) in two fascicles, also known as the *Pusa jing*.

The *Xingjing jiulü* (Record of the Former Catalogues of Translated Scriptures) simply states that the *Baoji jing* (Ratnaśikhara Sūtra) is a separate translation of the "Ratnaśikhara Chapter" from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*.

It was brought out on the fourteenth day of the seventh month of the first year of the Dayi era. According to the records of Daozhen and Sengyou, it is now included as the forty-seventh assembly in the *Ratnakūṭa*.

The *Puming pin jing* (Sūtra of the Chapter on Universal Radiance), one fascicle, was also initially called the *Pumen jing* (Sūtra of the Universal Gate), and its text is identical to that of the *Ratnakūṭa*.
The *Potaṃśi jing* (Sutra on the Womb) in one fascicle, translated by Shu and others, was revealed on the eleventh day of the first month of the eighth year of Taikang;

this is recorded in the catalogues of Nie Daozhen and Sengyou. An older record states that the *Potaṃshou shen jing* (Sutra on Receiving a Body in the Womb) was revealed on the first day of the eighth month of the second year of Taikang;
it was initially revealed as being the same text as the *Baoci chutai hui* (Assembly on the Womb of the Ratnakūṭa). This is recorded in the catalogues of Nie Dao[zheng].
The *Zhēnlù* (True Record) and the *Sēngyòulù* (Sēngyòu’s Record) list the *Wénshūshīlì Fótǔ Yánjìng Jīng* (Mañjuśrī Buddha-land Adornment and Purity Sūtra) in two fascicles—
also simply titled *Yánjìng Fótǔ Jīng* or *Fótǔ Yánjìng Jīng*— translated in the first year of the Tàixī era.

Its initial appearance was identical to the *Wénshū Shòujì Huì* (Mañjuśrī Prophecy Assembly) within the *Bǎojí* (Ratnakūṭa), as seen in Zhūdǎozǔ’s *Jìnshì Zá Lù* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) and the *Sēng*.
Sengyou’s Catalogue records the *Yugavarya-putra-paripṛcchā-bodhisattvacaryā-sūtra* in two fascicles, also known as the *Yugavarya-gṛhapati-sūtra*, which is the same as the *Mahāyugavarya-sūtra*.
Fascicle four is an excerpt that appears identical in its original text to the *Fajing* (Dharmakṣema) and *Ratnakūṭa-yugavarya-gṛhapati-parivarta*.
This is seen in the three catalogues of Daoan, Mindu, and Sengyou. It also includes the *Māyāvi-jīvaka-sūtra*.

One fascicle; alternatively called the *Renxian Huanshi Jing* (Sūtra of the Illusionist Renxian). Its initial translation was the same text as the "Chapter on the Prophecy Bestowed upon the Illusionist" (*Shou Huanshi Ji Hui*) from the *Ratnakūṭa*.
This is seen in the records of Nie Daozhen and Sengyou. The *Sumati Jing* (Sūtra of Sumati), one fascicle;

its initial translation simply called it the *Sumo Jing*, and it is also called the *Sumati Pusa Jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Sumati). It is the same text as the "Chapter on Wondrous Wisdom" (*Miaohui Hui*) from the *Ratnakūṭa*.
The *A-jü-dá púsà jīng* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Aśokadatta), one fascicle, daughter of King Aśoka; second edition.
Also called the *A-jü-shè nǚ jīng* (Sūtra on the Daughter of Aśoka) and the *Ā-shù-dá nǚ jīng* (Sūtra on the Daughter Aśokadatta).
Translated in the first year of the Jianwu era. Recorded in the three catalogs by Nie Daozhen, Zhu Daizu, and Sengyou. Included in Sengyou’s preface and the separate records of the three catalogs.
The *Cun wuyou shijing* (Sūtra on the Gift of Fearlessness) was recorded by Sengyou, yet it further contains the *Ajase king*; both are erroneous.
The *Li gou shi nü jing* (Sūtra of the Woman Vimaladattā), one fascicle, first appeared on the second day of the twelfth month of the tenth year of Taikang.

It is identical in substance to the *Pao chi wugou shi hui* (Assembly of Vimaladattā in the Ratnakūṭa). This is seen in Daoxuan’s *Zhenseng lu* and within Sengyou’s two records (*Neidian lu*), where it is further recorded as being without [the title] "Wu" (Fearless).
The *Gouchi yingbian jing* (Sūtra on the Discernment of Defiled Offerings) is an error; it was translated by Daozhen, as seen in the subsequent translations.

The *Ruhuan sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Illusion-like Samādhi) exists in two fascicles, or alternatively in three or four fascicles, and is the same text as the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra: The Assembly of the Well-Abiding Mind*; this is recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue.
The *Taizi shuhujing* (Sūtra of the Crown Prince Brushing the Teeth) exists in one fascicle; its initial appearance is recorded in Fashang’s catalogue.

The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, the Assembly of Prince Ajātaśatru, etc., identical to the original; the *Sūtra on the Great Skillful Means* (Mahopāyakauśalya-sūtra) asked by Bodhisattva Hui-shang, in two fascicles, the second edition;
or in one fascicle, translated on the seventeenth day of the sixth month in the sixth year of the Taikang era.
It is also called the *Sūtra on the Great Skillful Means*, the *Sūtra of Bodhisattva Hui-shang*, the *Sūtra on Skillful Expedients*, or the... [etc.]
*Upāyakauśalya-aparimita-darśana-tattva-āyuṣya-sūtra*, two fascicles; *Maitreya-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-pūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra*, one fascicle.
First brought out on the eleventh day of the fifth month in the second year of the Taian era. Translated [by Dharmarakṣa]. Some editions omit the characters "paripṛcchā" (所問).
It is also called the *Maitreya-pūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra*, or alternatively the *Maitreya-vinaya-sūtra*. It corresponds to the *Ratnakūṭa-maitreya* [section].

The *Sūtra of the Questions* (So-wen-hui) is identical to the original *Sūtra of the Path of Seeing* (*Jian-dao zhen-dao jing*). According to the three catalogs of Sengyou, the *Aca-mo jing* consists of seven fascicles;
its title is rendered as "Wujin-yi" (Inexhaustible Intention) in the Jin translation, though it is also recorded as being in four or five fascicles.

It is the third translation from the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, produced on the first day of the twelfth month of the first year of Yuanshou, or alternatively with the word "Bodhisattva" added [to the title], as seen in the two records of Zhenyong.
It is an error for the two records of Sengyou and Dao’an to list the *Wujinyijing* (Sutra of Akṣayamati) in four fascicles twice.

Regarding the *Dayijing* (Sutra of Great Compassion) in eight fascicles, the old catalog states that the *Rulai Dayaijing* (Tathāgata-sūtra on Great Compassion) was translated from July 7th to August 2nd of the first year of Yuankang;
it consists of twenty-eight chapters. It was also separately translated in either six or seven fascicles, as seen in the records of Zhu Daozu of the Jin dynasty.

In the *Zalu* and the *Sengyou Lu*, it is recorded that the *Baoṇu Suowen Jing* (Sūtra of the Questions of the Precious Woman) in three fascicles was translated on the twentieth day of the fourth month in the eighth year of the Taikang era.

It is an alternative translation of the "Precious Woman Chapter" from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, though it is sometimes listed as four fascicles, or simply titled the *Baoṇu Jing* (Sūtra of the Precious Woman), or the *Baoṇu Wenhui Jing* (Sūtra of the Questions of the Precious Woman on Wisdom), or the *Baoṇu Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra of the Samādhi of the Precious Woman). See Daozhen and Sengyou, fascicle two.

*Lu wuyan tongzi jing* (Record of the Scripture of the Silent Boy), two fascicles; also known as *Wuyan pusa jing* (Scripture of the Silent Bodhisattva). This is an alternative translation of the "Chapter on the Silent One" from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*.
It may also consist of one fascicle, according to the *Nie Daozhen lu* and the *Sengyou lu*. *Bodhisattva shizhu xingdao pin* (Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Practice of the Ten Stages), one fascicle.
This is an alternative translation of the "Ten Stages Chapter" from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. It is recorded in the *Sui Shaomen Fajing lu* and the [Seng]you [lu].

The *Fangji* (Record of the Storehouse), fascicle 2, states directly that the "Ten Abodes of the Bodhisattva" (*daśabhūmi*) is precisely this *Dàopǐn* (Chapter on the Path). The *Jiàn bèi yīqiè zhìdé jīng* (Sutra on the Gradual Preparation of All Wisdom Virtues) is in five fascicles;
it is also titled *Shízhu* (Ten Abodes) or *Dàhuìguāng sānmèi* (Samādhi of Great Wisdom Light), and is sometimes in ten fascicles.

It was translated on the eleventh day of the eleventh month of the seventh year of Yuankang. This is a different translation of the "Ten Grounds Chapter" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, as noted by Niè Dàozhēn.

Furthermore, according to the catalogs of Sengyou and others, there is the *Boshu suowen sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi Asked by Samantabhadra) in two fascicles—also titled *Puxian pusa dingyi* (The Concentrated Intent of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra), or simply *Dingmu pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra)—or in three fascicles. This is a different translation of the "Ten Samādhis" chapter from the new *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*;
this chapter did not exist in the old translation. See Sengyou’s catalog for the *Rulai xingxian jing* (Sūtra of the Manifestation of the Tathāgata) in four fascicles.

One title is *The Sūtra on the Manifestation of Arising Like an Illusion*. On the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month of the first year of the Yuankang era, this *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, specifically the "Chapter on the Arising of the Tathāgata-nature" and the "Ten Endurances," was translated as a separate version; these are seen in the records of Nie Daozhen and Sengyou.

The *Dushi pin jing* (Sūtra on the Chapter of Transcending the World) consists of six fascicles—also called the *Dushi jing* (Sūtra on Transcending the World)—or alternatively five fascicles, [translated] in the first year of the Yuankang era.

On the thirteenth day of the fourth month, this *Lokottara-parivarta* (Chapter on Leaving the World) from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* was translated; it is seen in the two catalogs of Nie Daozhen and Sengyou.

The *Vaipulya-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* in two fascicles first appeared with the same original text as the *Four Boys* (*Caturdāraka*) translated during the Sui dynasty—sometimes without the character "Parinirvāṇa" (*ban*), making it three fascicles—or it is called the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, [translated] in the seventh month of the fifth year of the Taishi era.
On the twenty-third day, the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* (Pu-yao jing) in eight fascicles was brought forth; it is also known as the *Vaipulya-pūrvaprabhava*.
Master Dao’an categorized it as belonging to the *Vaipulya* section. It was translated on the fifth day of the fifth month in the second year of the Yongjia era at Tianshui Temple.
This second translation is identical in content to the Tang dynasty translation of the *Vaipulya-prabhāsa-alaṃkāra-sūtra*. Translated by the śramaṇas Kangzhu Bai and Faba.

According to the records of Sengzhu and others, as well as the *Zhēnyòu* catalogues, there was a *Zhèngfǎhuá jīng* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) in ten fascicles—also called the *Fāngděng Zhèngfǎhuá*—or in seven fascicles consisting of twenty-seven chapters.
It was translated on the tenth day of the eighth month in the seventh year of the Tàikāng era.
The third translation was received by the lay believer Zhāng Zhōngzhèng, Niè Chéngyuǎn, and others, as recorded in the two *Tán* catalogues.
Sui recited it until he had mastered it entirely, whereupon he was moved by a divine response.

When the ninety days were completed, he was granted one white horse, five sheep, and ninety-six bolts of silk, as well as a single scroll of the *Mahāvaipulya-uṣṇīṣarāja-sūtra*. When first brought out, Master Dao’an categorized it as belonging to the *Vaipulya* section;
it is also simply called the *Uṣṇīṣarāja-sūtra*, alternatively titled the *Vimalakīrti-putra-prcchā-sūtra*, and is also said to be excellent.

The *Sìtóngzǐ jīng* (Sūtra on the Youth Si) has four titles in total. According to the catalogs of Zhi Min-du and Sengyou, it is the *Fóshēng Dàolìtiān wèimǔ shuōfǎ jīng* (Sūtra of the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother), in two fascicles;
when first translated, it was sometimes in three fascicles. It is also said that the "Chapter on the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven" is the same text as the *Dàoshénqiě jīng*.
It appeared in the first year of the Taishi era, as recorded by Nie Daozhen and Seng [you].
The *A-vyavartana-śāstra-sūtra* (阿惟越致遮經), three fascicles (initially four fascicles), translated by Zhi Yao;
also known as the *A-vyavartana-sūtra* (阿惟致經). It was produced at Dunhuang on the fourteenth day of the tenth month in the fifth year of Taikang.

It is a different translation of the same text as the *Avivartana-sūtra* (不退轉經) and the *Vipula-vyūha-pariśuddha-sūtra* (廣博嚴淨經), as seen in the catalogs of Sengzhao and others. [It is also included in] the *Ji-zhongde-sanmei-jing* (集眾德三昧經).

The first fascicle of the *Samantabhadrapuṇyasaṃbhāra-sūtra* (or simply the *Samantabhadra-sūtra*) is stated in the older catalogs to be identical in text to the *Sarvapuṇyasamuccaya-sūtra* and others;
it appears in two fascicles in the *Nie Zhen lu* and the *Sengyou lu*.
The *Brahmadeva-cittadhara-sūtra* is in four fascicles; it is also titled *Zhuangyan Fofa* or *Dengyu Zhufa*, totaling ten [titles].

The *Saptavarga* (Seven Chapters) consists of either six fascicles; its initial translation may include the two characters "Suowen" (Questions) or simply be titled the *Chixin jing* (Sūtra on Holding the Mind).
It was issued on the tenth day of the third month in the seventh year of the Taikang era, with Nie Chengyuan serving as the scribe. This is recorded in the older *Zhenyou Sanlu*.

The *Chiren pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīdhara) consists of four fascicles; its initial translation includes the passage: "Dhāraṇīdhara Bodhisattva questioned [the Buddha] regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*) in order to bring them to full understanding."
The *Dàohuì jīng* (Sūtra on the Wisdom of the Path) was first translated in three fascicles; it is a different recension of the same text as the *Chíshì jīng* (Sūtra on Upholding the World).

Sengyou’s catalogue records the *Jì zhū fāngděng xué jīng* (Sūtra for Assisting All Mahāyāna Students) in one fascicle, which was orally transmitted by the Indian Śānavīrmika Saṃghaka (also known as Wúxué) and transcribed by Zhu Fashou.
Its initial translation is the same text as the *Fāngguǎng zǒngchí jīng* (Sūtra of the Universal Dhāraṇī of the Vaipulya), as seen in the catalogue of Zhu Daozu.

Sengyou’s Catalog records the *Mañjuśrī-prabhāsa-ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* in three fascicles; its initial translation may have lacked the character "prabhāsa" (manifestation), as it shares the same text as the *Vaipulya-ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra*.
It was translated in the tenth month of the sixth year of the Taishi era, though some versions consist of two fascicles and simply call it the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra*.
This is seen in Sengyou’s *Changfang lu*, where a separate entry for a two-fascicle *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* appears—an error that is quite egregious.
*Wújí bǎo sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Ultimate Treasure), one fascicle; first appearance. Some say it is the same text as the *Bǎo rúlái sānmèi jīng*.
It appeared on the third day of the third month of the first year of the Yongjia era; see the *Bié lù* (Separate Record) by Niè Dàozhēn and Sēngyòu’s two catalogs.
*Pǔyuè sānmèi jīng* (Samādhi of Universal Joy), three fascicles; second appearance. Alternatively, four fascicles; also known by another name.
The *Aśokarāja-parivarta* (Chapter on King Aśoka). Translated on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month in the seventh year of Taikang.
Some editions omit the characters for "samādhi," while others prefix the title with "Mañjuśrī. The catalog records state that this is a re-translation of the *Aśokarāja-sūtra*.

It is found in the two catalogs of Zu and You. The *Wusuoxiwang jing* (Sūtra on Having No Hopes), one fascicle; the second translation, where "hope" is sometimes written as "desire" (*xī*), also known by another name.
The *Hastipadopama-sūtra* and the *Hastikakṣya-sūtra* are identical texts, as recorded in the catalogues of Nie Daozhen and Sengyou.

The *Mahāviśuddhi-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*, one fascicle, titled "The Chapter on the Great Gate of Purity" (*Mahāviśuddhi-dharmaparyāya-parivarta*), Part One, is the Questions of the Girl Suvarṇottamaprabhā and the Conversion by the Youth Śiṣyaka;
its initial translation is identical to the *Mahāvyūha-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*.
On the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month of the first year of the Jianxing era, it was brought out and seen by Nie Daozhen and Sengyou.

It consists of two fascicles of the *Shunquan fangbian jing* (Sūtra on Following Expedient Means), also titled the *Zhuan nüshen pusa jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Transforming Female Gender), or sometimes written as the *Weiquan*.
The old catalogues state it is the *Shunquan nü jing*, also called the *Suiquan nü jing*. This is the second appearance; it is also seen as one fascicle.
The *Sengyou Er-lu* (Two Records of Sengyou) and the *Yufang Er-lu* (Two Records of Yufang) separately preserve the *Suiquan Nü-jing* (Scripture on the Woman Suiquan), which is an error.

The *Taizi Mupò-jing* (Prince Mupò Scripture), the third [entry], appears as a variant translation in the fourth fascicle of the *Liudu ji* (Collection of the Six Pāramitās). Some editions read "Mupò" as "Mùpò.

It is recorded in Sengyou’s catalog that the *Yuanguang Tongzi-jing* (Moonlight Youth Scripture), one fascicle, was first produced; it is also titled *Yueming Tongzi-jing* (Moon-Bright Youth Scripture) or *Shen*.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (Rìjīng) is seen in Sēngyòu’s Catalog as being the same text as the *Sūtra of the Elder Dharmapāla*; it is the second translation.

Also, the *Kṣīraprabhāsa-buddha-sūtra* (Yùguāng fó jīng), one fascicle, is the second translation; it is also called the *Kṣīraprabhāsa-sūtra* and is seen in Sēngyòu’s Catalog as being the same text as the *Vatsa-sūtra*, though a different translation.
The *Vimaladatta-bhikṣuṇī-sūtra* (Wúgòu xián nǚ jīng), one fascicle, is the second translation; it is also called the *Garbha-sūtra* (Tāizàng jīng) and is the same text as the *Strīvivarta-sūtra*.

The *Shen jing* (Scripture on the Body) is the same text as the *Ben jian nie dao zhen lu* (Record of Nie Daozhen’s Original Vision) and the two records by Sengyou; it is the *Tai zang jing* (Womb Treasury Scripture), which is this very *Wugou xian nü jing* (Sūtra of the Stainless Noble Woman).

It is a single fascicle of a definitive compendium (*jueding zong jing*). Its initial appearance was such that some called it the *Jue zongchi jing* (Sūtra of the Decisive Dhāraṇī), while others called it the *Jueding zongchi jing* (Sūtra of the Definitive Dhāraṇī);
it is the same text as the *Bangfo jing* (Sūtra on Slandering the Buddha), as seen in the *Sengyou lu* (Sengyou’s Catalogue). [It concerns] the Tathāgata alone...

*Zheng zishì sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Self-Aspiration Realization), one fascicle; also called *Dú zhèng zishì sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Solitary Self-Aspiration Realization) or *Rúlái zishì sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Tathāgata’s Self-Aspiration Samādhi).
The second edition is the same text as the *Zishì sānmèi jīng* translated by An Shigao of the Han dynasty, as recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue.
*Lóngshī púsà běnqǐ jīng* (Sūtra on the Previous Life of the Bodhisattva Nāgadatta), one fascicle; old catalogues refer to it as the *Lóngshī běn*.

The scripture is sometimes called the *Longshi jing* (Sutra of Nāgadatta); its second translation is identical to the *Longshi nü jing* (Sutra of the Daughter Nāgadattā), as recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue.
The *Bāyáng shénzhòu jīng* (Sutra of the Eightfold Auspicious Divine Incantation) in one fascicle is also simply titled the *Bāyáng jīng*;

its second translation is identical to the *Bājiǎxiáng zhòu jīng* (Auspicious Incantation of the Eight Buddhas), as recorded in Changfang’s catalogue. The *Yúlánbō jīng* (Ullambana Sutra) in one fascicle is also simply titled *Yúlán*.
The *Jing* (Sūtra) is the same text as the *Bao'en fengpen jing* (Sūtra on Repaying Kindness by Offering the Bowl), according to the *Fang lu* (Record of Fang);

it is the second appearance [of this text], translated by Nie Daozhen. The *Buke de jing* (Sūtra on the Four Unobtainables), one fascicle, is the first appearance; it is recorded in the three catalogs of Sengyou and others. The *Fannü shouyi jing* (Sūtra of the Brahman Woman Shouyi), one fascicle, is the first appearance;
it is also known as the *Shouyi nü jing* (Sūtra of the Woman Shouyi) and is recorded in Sengyou’s catalog. The *Baowang jing* (Jewel Net Sūtra), one fascicle, is also the first appearance.

*Yun bao wang yi zi jing* (Cloud Jewel Net Son of the Mind Sūtra), seen in the two catalogs of Nie Dao-seng; *Pusa xing wu shi yuan shen jing* (Sūtra on the Fifty Bodhisattva Practices of the Body), one fascicle.

Its initial appearance in the old catalogs states it is also called *Pusa xiang shen wu shi shi jing* (Sūtra on the Fifty Matters of the Bodhisattva’s Image-Body) or *Wu shi yuan shen xing jing* (Sūtra on the Practice of the Fifty Conditions of the Body);
seen in the catalogs of Zhu Daozu and Sengyou. *Xu zhen tian zi jing* (Sūtra of the Heavenly Son Susīma), three fascicles. Initial [appearance].
It was translated in two fascicles, or with the addition of the two characters "Suowen" (Questions), also known as the *Sūtra on the Four Questions*.
On the eighth day of the eleventh month of the second year of the Taishi era, it was translated at the Baima Monastery outside the Qing Gate in Chang’an;

the monk An Wenhui and others acted as the oral reciters, while Nie Chengyuan and others served as the scribes. It was completed on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month. This is recorded in the works of Daozu and Sengyou.
*Lu hai long wang jing* (Record of the Sutra of the Sea Dragon King), four fascicles; originally three fascicles, translated on the tenth day of the seventh month in the sixth year of Taikang.
Recorded by Nie Daozhen and in the *Sengyou lu*. *Zhu fo yao ji jing* (The Essential Collection of All Buddhas), two fascicles.
In Indic: *Buddha-saṃgīti*; also simply called *Yaoji jing*. Originally recorded in the *Sengyou lu*. *Xian jie jing* (Sutra of the Worthy Kalpa), ten [fascicles].
The title of the three-fascicle work reads *Bhadra-kalpa-samādhi-sūtra*; in the Jin [translation], it is called *Xianjie dingyi jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Worthy Kalpa).
It was brought forth on the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the first year of the Yongkang era, with Zhao Wenlong serving as the scribe.

When first published, it appeared in either seventeen fascicles or ten fascicles, as seen in the records of Daozhen and Sengyou; the *Fang lu* preserves it separately under the title *Bhadra-kalpa-samādhi-sūtra*, which is an error.

*Yehongdao Guangxian Sanmei Jing* (The Sutra on the Samādhi of Widely Propagating the Way and Manifesting It), four fascicles; also known as *Anouda Longwang Suowen Juezhu Huxi Qingjing Pin* (The Questions of the Dragon King Anavatapta Resolving All Doubts:
Chapter on Purity) or *Rujingang Wen Dingyi Jing* (The Sutra on Entering the Diamond-like Questioning of the Concentrated Mind).

It consists of twelve chapters or two fascicles. It was translated in the twelfth month of the second year of the Yongjia era. It appears in the *Zhenyou Lu* and the *Neidian Lu*, with a separate entry recorded therein.

The *Anoutada Jing* (Aṇavatapta Sūtra) is an error. The *Xinming Jing* (Heart-Illumination Sūtra), one fascicle—also known as the *Xinming Nü Fanzhi Fu Fanzhi Shi Jing* (Sūtra on the Brahmin Woman Heart-Illumination Offering Rice-Water)—is found in Sengyou’s Catalogue.
The *Mie Shifang Ming Jing* (Sūtra on Extinguishing the Darkness of the Ten Directions), one fascicle, was produced on the fourteenth day of the eighth month of the first year of Guangxi;

some call it the *Shifang Mie Ming Jing* (Sūtra on the Extinction of Darkness in the Ten Directions) and it is found in Nie Daozhen’s Catalogue as well as Sengyou’s Catalogue. The *Lu*... [text fragment].
*The Sūtra of the Mother*, one fascicle; furthermore, there is separately *The Sūtra of the Deer Son*, one fascicle, which is identical to this [text], as seen in Sengyou’s Record.

*The Sūtra of Māra’s Rebellion*, one fascicle; on the second day of the twelfth month of the tenth year of Taikang, it was translated at the White Horse Monastery west of the city of Luoyang, with Nie Daozhen serving as scribe, as seen in Sengyou’s Record and the colophon of the scripture. Prince De Guang.
One fascicle; alternatively titled *The Sūtra on the Questions of Rāṣṭrapāla* or *The Sūtra of Prince Prabhāśrī*.
It appeared on the third day of the ninth month of the sixth year of the Taishi era. Recorded in the catalogs of Zhu Daozu and Sengyou.

*The Sūtra on the Offering of Wax after the Parinirvāṇa*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Sūtra on the Offering of Wax by the Four Classes after the Parinirvāṇa*, or simply *The Sūtra on the Offering of Wax*.

*Jianfang lu*: *Sijie jing* (Scripture on the Four Classes), one fascicle; also called *Sijie dishi jing* (Scripture on the Disciples of the Four Classes) or *Sijie xue jing* (Scripture on the Learning of the Four Classes).
*Danglai bian jing* (Scripture on Future Transformations), one fascicle; also called *Danglai bian shi jing* (Scripture on the Consciousness of Future Transformations).
Recorded in the *Dazhuan lu* and *Shengji lu*. *Guoqu fo fenwei jing* (Scripture on the Past Buddha’s Almsround), one fascicle; old records call it *Guoshiji fo* (Buddha of the Past World).
*Piṇḍapāta-sūtra* (contained in Sengyou’s *Chu sanzang jiji*). *Mañjuśrī-viśuddha-śīla-sūtra*, one fascicle; first translated. Also simply titled *Viśuddha-śīla-sūtra*.

On the eighth day of the fourth month in the tenth year of Taikang, it was produced at Baima Temple. The elder Lu encountered the Western Region śramaṇa Jizhi, who recited the original text of the sūtra.
There were still several chapters remaining, but the person forgot them; he only proclaimed what he could recall. The Way [thus remained incomplete].
One fascicle of the *Mañjuśrī-pratideśanā-sūtra* (The Scripture on Mañjuśrī’s Confession of Transgressions), transcribed by hand;
it first appeared with the character "Śrī" added [to the name], and is also called the *Mañjuśrī-pañcāṅga-pratideśanā-sūtra*. It is recorded in the *Sengyou lu* (Catalogue of Sengyou).

One fascicle of the *Vibhinna-sūtra*, appearing as the twentieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*; it is a variant translation recorded in the *Fang lu* (Catalogue of Fang). One fascicle of the *Poṣadha-sūtra*, appearing in the *Madhyama Āgama*.
Included in the twenty-third fascicle; a different translation seen in Fang’s Catalogue. *Sukhasaññā-sūtra*, one fascicle; found in the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*;
a different translation seen in Fang’s Catalogue. *Abhyudgata-sūtra*, one fascicle; found in the forty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*;
a different translation seen in Fang’s Catalogue. *Anudharma-sūtra*, one fascicle; also found in the [forty-third] fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.

Forty-five alternative translations are recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue: *Aṅgulimāla-sūtra*, one fascicle—sometimes written with the character "mā" (魔) instead of "ma" (摩), also called *Aṅguli-keśa-sūtra* or *Aṅgulimāla-sūtra*;
it appears as an alternative translation in the thirty-first section of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
Also, *Balavardhana-parvata-saṃkramaṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle—also simply titled *Parvata-saṃkramaṇa-sūtra*; it is recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue.

Extracted from the *Ekottarika Āgama*, Chapter 36, as a variant translation of the *Sūtra on the Four Unprecedented Dharmas* (1 fascicle), sometimes titled *Sūtra on the Four Non-existent Dharmas* or *Sūtra on the Four Unprecedented [Dharmas]*; also recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*.
Also extracted from the *Ekottarika Āgama*, Chapter 36, as a variant translation of the *Sūtra on the Holy Seal of Dharma* (1 fascicle); the Indic title is *Acchadharma*.
The illustration is from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, fascicle 3; alternatively, it is titled the *Huiyin jing* (Sūtra on the Seal of Wisdom).

On the twentieth day of the twelfth month of the fourth year of Yuankang, at Liquan Commandery, it was transcribed by Zhu Fashou based on the oral recitation of Jian Zhenyou. It appears in the *Sanlu*.
One fascicle of the *Shetoujian jing* (Sūtra of Śatruñjaya), titled *Shetoujian*; in Jin, it is called *Taizi ershiba xiu* (The Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions of the Prince).
A sūtra titled *The Tiger-Ear Sūtra* (*Hujing*), which is the same text as the *Mātanga Sūtra* (*Modengjia jing*) and others, is the fifth [text] produced;

it differs slightly from that of An Shigao of the Han dynasty. Dao’an’s catalogue records it. Sengyou states: *The Tiger-Ear Intention Sūtra* (*Huer yijing*) and *The Sūtra on What One Desires to Cause Suffering* (*Suyuzhihuan jing*), one fascicle.
It was first produced and translated in the first month of the third year of the Taian era. It appears in the three catalogues of Daozhen, Wangzong, and Sengyou. [Recorded by] Liu.

*Li wang jing* (The Sūtra of King Li), one fascicle; second edition, also known as *Liu li* [or *Ryūri*], listed in Sengyou’s Catalogue. *Seng jing* (Sūtra on Birth), five fascicles; first edition, also in four fascicles.
Translated on the nineteenth day of the first month in the sixth year of the Taikang era. It is said that there were fifty-five sūtras [in this collection];
listed in the Zhen Catalogue and Sengyou’s Catalogue. *Fen bie jing* (Sūtra on the Separation), one fascicle; formerly titled *Fen bie yu Anan* (Separation with Ānanda).

The claim that this scripture is identical to the original is incorrect. According to the *Fánglù* (Record of Fáng), there is the *Wǔbǎi Dìzǐ Zìshuō Běnpǐ Jīng* (Scripture of the Five Hundred Disciples’ Own Account of Their Past Lives) in one fascicle, translated in the fifth month of the second year of the Dà'ān era.

It is also called the *Fó Wǔbǎi Dìzǐ Zìshuō Běnpǐ Jīng* (Old Scripture of the Buddha’s Five Hundred Disciples’ Own Account of Their Past Lives), or the *Wǔbǎi Dìzǐ Běnpǐ Jīng* (Scripture of the Five Hundred Disciples’ Past Lives). This is recorded in the *Zhēnlù*.
*Yaoxing jing* (Sūtra on the Practice of Yoga), one fascicle; also called *Jiaye ben jing* (Sūtra of Kāśyapa’s Origin) or simply *Kāśyapa ben jing*, recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue (see entry no.

4). *Sizhen jing* (Sūtra on Self-Inflicted Harm), one fascicle; Master Dao’an states it is from the *Abhidharma*; recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue. *Shenguang jing* (Sūtra on Contemplating the Body), one fascicle;

said to be extracted from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*; not found when checked against Fang’s catalogue. *Xingxiu daodi jing* (Sūtra on the Stages of the Path of Practice), six fascicles; the title of the first fascicle is as follows: [text continues].

*Yunyouzhengjiamijing* (The Sūtra of the Cloud-Brandished Encouragement and Subsequent Attainment); translated in the Jin dynasty as *Xiuxingdaodi* (The Stages of Cultivating the Path) on the twenty-third day of the second month in the fifth year of Taikang;
alternatively in seven fascicles and twenty-seven chapters. This is the third edition, also simply titled *Xiuxingjing* (Sūtra of Cultivation).

It is recorded in the catalogs of Sengyou and Huichang. *Faguanjing* (Sūtra of Dharma Contemplation), one fascicle; recorded in the catalog of Daofang. The above are extant; the following are missing.
The *New Version of the Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Xīndàoxíng jīng), one fascicle—also called the *Xiǎopǐn* (Small Version)—or seven fascicles.
Sengyou states that this is a further edition of the *Xiǎopǐn*, translated in the eighth year of the Tàishǐ era; it is the fourth appearance and is identical in text to the old *Dàoxíng*.

Fǎfáng says that the inclusion of a seven-fascicle *Xiǎopǐn* is an error. Those found in the catalogs of Fǎfáng and Sengyou are not this version, as they previously lacked the *Renwáng* and *Bānruò* [sections].
This scripture consists of one or two fascicles and thirty-one sheets. Dao’an initially noted it in his *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty* (*Jin shi zalu*).

It is the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* in two fascicles, also titled the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment*. It was produced on the twenty-first day of the first month of the second year of Yongjia.
This is the sixth translation, corresponding to the versions produced during the Han dynasty by An Shigao, Zhi Qian, and others.
The same text with different titles: the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* in three fascicles, first appearing in the *Fáng Lù* (Fáng Shí’s Catalog) and subsequently in the *Yù Lù* (Dào Yù’s Catalog);
the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra* in two fascicles, which Ān said was a later edition; the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra* (fifth appearance) listed in the *Yù Lù*;
the *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmi-sūtra* in one fascicle, also called the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra*, or simply the *Daśabhūmi*.
The *Dìjīng* (Earth Sūtra) first appeared in Sengyou’s catalogue; the *Sāyuṇfēnduólì jīng* (Saṃpuṇḍarīka Sūtra) in six fascicles was translated in the first year of the Tàishǐ era.

It is recorded in the second section of the *Jìnshì zá lù* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) by Dào zǔ, which states that the title *Sātán yún* is likely an error, as it does not appear in Sengyou’s catalogue.
The *Wéimójié suǒshuō fǎmén jīng* (Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra) in one fascicle was translated on the first day of the fourth month in the second year of the Tài'ān era.
Translation: The fourth appearance [of this text] is recorded in the *Nie Daozhen lu*, which simply calls it the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra*. The *Sengyou lu* also records the *Na-vimalakīrti-sūtra*;
Sengyou states that he believes the previously translated *Vimalakīrti* was redundant, and thus Na translated the omitted verses.

The ten-fascicle *Xianju jing* (Sūtra on Dwelling in Solitude) is a different translation of the same original text as the *Beihua jing* (Sūtra of the Compassionate Flower); its initial appearance is recorded in the *Sengyou lu*, and it appeared again later.
*Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra*, two fascicles; fourth entry in the *Xiàn-yòu-lù*.
According to the *Ān-lù*, there is only the *Ajātaśatru-jǔ-wáng-jīng* (Ajātaśatru Sovereign King Sūtra), while the *Pǔchāo-sānmèi-jīng* (Samādhi of Universal Transcendence) is not listed.

Since both sūtras are recorded together in the *Yòu-fáng-lù*, and as their Sanskrit originals are identical, it is inappropriate to record both as separate translations. (*Zhēnyuán-xīndìng-shìjiào-mùlù*, Fascicle 3).
The Newly Compiled Catalogue of Śākyamuni’s Teachings from the Zhenyuan Era, Volume Four,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xīmíng Monastery in the Western Capital.
Section on the Comprehensive Collection of Records of the Various Scriptures, Part Four of the First.
