*Maitreya-buddhatva-sūtra*, one fascicle; first translation, also titled *Maitreya-āgami-janma-sūtra*; translated in the second year of the Tà'ān era (303 CE); appears in the records of Niè Dàozhēn and Sēngyòu; seventeen sheets.
*Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna* (or *Dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*), one fascicle; fourth translation; also called *Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination under the Peiḍuō Tree*;

appears in the record of Sēngyòu. *Jentāka-snāna-bhikṣu-saṃgha-sūtra*, one fascicle; second translation; also simply titled *Jentāka*; appears in the records of Niè Dàozhēn and Sēngyòu. *Buddha-nāma-śata-sūtra*, one fascicle; first translation; [appears in the] record of Sēngyòu.

*The Scripture on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta* (Guānshìyīn dàshèzhì shòujué jīng), one fascicle. It first appeared during the Yuánkāng era; some versions simply call it *The Scripture on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara*.

It is recorded in the catalogs of Zhēnyòu and others. *The Scripture on the Subduing of the Brave and Resolute* (Yǒngfú dìng jīng), two fascicles. Master Ān stated that this was a further translation of the *Śūraṅgama*. It appeared on the ninth day of the fourth month of the first year of Yuánkāng, with Niè Chéngyuǎn serving as the scribe.

This is the sixth translation. It is recorded in the catalogs of Zhēnyòu and others. The inclusion of a separate entry for the two-fascicle *Śūraṅgama* in the catalogs of Zhòu and Fáng is an error. *The Inconceivable* (Wúsīyì).

*Guang haotong pusa jing* (Sutra of the Radiant Child Bodhisattva), one fascicle; also called *Wusi yi haotong jing* (Inconceivable Child Sutra) or *Wusi yi guang jing* (Inconceivable Light Sutra). The old catalogs simply call it the *Haotong jing*. Its initial appearance is recorded in the *Yao lu* (Catalogue of Yao).

*Chao riming sanmei jing* (Sutra of the Samādhi of Transcending the Sun’s Brilliance), two fascicles; translated in the first month of the seventh year of the Taishi era. Its initial appearance is in some records as three fascicles, or simply as the *Chao riming jing*. It is found in the *Zhen* and *Yao* catalogs.

*Zhao ming sanmei jing* (Sutra of the Samādhi of Illuminating Wisdom), one fascicle; its initial appearance is in the *Yao lu*. *Weiming shier jie jing* (Sutra of the Twelve Verses on Solemn Clarity), one fascicle; or sometimes without the word "sutra."

The third translation by Zhi [Yao] is largely identical to that produced during the Wu dynasty by Zhi Qian; it is recorded in the Fang Lu as the *Famojin jing* (Sūtra on the Extinction of the Dharma) in one fascicle, though some call it the *Kongji pusa suowen jing* (Sūtra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Emptiness-and-Quietude).

The second translation is the same text as that produced by Zhi Qian, though some call it the *Famiejìn jing*. It is recorded in the Sengyou Lu. The *Zhu shenzhou jing* (Sūtra of Various Divine Spells) in three fascicles is recorded in the Sengyou Lu.

The *Wenshushili pusa jing* (Mañjuśrī-bodhisattva-sūtra) in one fascicle is recorded in the Fang Lu. The *Xiaoyuqia jing* (Shorter Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra) in one fascicle differs from the *Dayuqia jing* (Longer Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra); it is recorded in the Sengyou Lu, where it is sometimes titled differently.

*The Scripture on the Names and Merits of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions Beginning with the Syllable Ka*, one fascicle; the character "merit" (gōngdé) is absent in the records of Sengyou and Huìfáng. *The Scripture on the Names of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions*, one fascicle;

the character "scripture" (jīng) is absent in the records of Sengyou and Huìfáng. *The Scripture on the Eighty Minor Marks as Questioned by Maitreya*, one fascicle; alternatively titled simply *The Scripture on the Eighty Minor Marks*; found in the records of Dào'ān and Huìfáng.

*The Scripture on the Causes and Conditions of the Thirty-two Major Marks*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Scripture on the Bodhisattva’s Thirty-two Major Marks*; found in the records of Dào'ān and Huìfáng. *The Scripture on the Samādhi of Pure Adornment*.

One fascicle; also titled *Xushi jing* (Sūtra on the Introduction to the World); listed in Sengyou’s catalogue. *Baoshi nü jing* (Sūtra of the Daughter Baoshi); one fascicle; also titled *Sumati fǎlǜ sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra of the Samādhi of the Dharma-Rule of Sumati); listed in the catalogues of Sengyou and Zhizhen. *Jinyi zhǎngzhězǐ jīng* (Sūtra of the Elder’s Son Jinyi);

one fascicle; listed in Sengyou’s catalogue. *Líjiù gài jīng* (Sūtra of the Immaculate Canopy); one fascicle; listed in Sengyou’s catalogue. *Huìmíng jīng* (Sūtra of Wisdom-Brightness); one fascicle; listed in Sengyou’s catalogue. *Zhòngyòu jīng* (Sūtra of the Multitude of Protectors);

one fascicle; listed in Sengyou’s catalogue. *Sānzuǎnrì míng jīng* (Sūtra of the Three Turnings of the Sun-Brightness); one fascicle; Sengyou’s catalogue states it is the *Yuèmíng* (Moon-Brightness). *Shídēngzàng jīng* (Sūtra of the Tenfold Treasury); one fascicle; listed in [Sengyou’s catalogue].

*Yùlù jué dàosú jīng* (Scripture Resolving Matters for Monastics and Laity), one fascicle; seen in the *Yùlù*. *Zhí zhòngdéběn jīng* (Scripture on Planting the Roots of All Merits), one fascicle; seen in the *Yùlù*. *Xiǎofǎ mièjìn jīng* (Scripture on the Extinction of the Lesser Dharma), one fascicle;

seen in the *Yùlù*. *Měngshī jīng* (Scripture on Fierce Giving); the old catalogs state it is the *Měngshī dàozhì jīng*; seen in the *Yùlù*. *Mùlián shàng jìngjūtian jīng* (Scripture on Maudgalyāyana Ascending to the Pure Abodes), one fascicle;

one version lacks the character "heaven" (*tiān*). Fáng says it appears in the *Fó běnxíng jí jīng*; seen in the *Yùlù*. *Bōsà zhāifǎ jīng* (Scripture on the Bodhisattva’s Method of Fasting), one fascicle; sometimes the character "scripture" (*jīng*) is omitted, or sometimes the character "dharma" (*fǎ*) is omitted. Also known as the *Bōsà* [scripture].

The *Sawangzhai jing* (also known as the *Chizhai jing* or the *Xianshou pusa zhai fa jing*). Its initial appearance is recorded in the two catalogs [of Fajing and Yancong], though it is erroneously listed separately as the *Pusa zhai jing*.

The *Shelifu huiguo jing*, one fascicle; its second appearance is simply titled the *Huiguo jing*, as seen in the catalog of Sengyou. The *Fohuiguo jing*, one fascicle; seen in the catalog of Sengyou.

The *Daliu xiangbai jing*, one fascicle; not found in the old catalogs. Translated in the first year of the Taitai era. Some say it is the *Shijialuoyue liu xiangbai jing*, which appears in the *Chang [a-han]*.

The *Āgama*, Volume 11: A different translation of the *Sixty-two Views Sūtra* (in one fascicle) is found in the three catalogs of Zhi Min-du, Seng You, and Bao Chang; it is also called the *Brahmajāla Sixty-two Views Sūtra*.

It is recorded in the catalogs of Daozu, [Dao]you, and [Hui]yu as being from the fourteenth part of the *Dīrgha Āgama*. A different translation of the *Loutan Sūtra* (in six fascicles, or five, or eight) was originally the fourth section of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, titled the *Jishi Sūtra*.
It is recorded in the catalog of Zhen and You as a different translation. Master An stated that its claim to be from the Vaipulya division is incorrect. This is the *Fapufa* (Universal Dharma).

*Yijing* (Sūtra on Meaning), one fascicle; also called *Puyijing* (Sūtra of Universal Meaning). The second edition, which largely agrees with minor differences from that produced by Dharmakṣema during the Han period, appears in the *Zhen* and *Yu* catalogs.

*Śāriputramaudgalyāyanayouzhuguo jing* (Sūtra of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana Traveling Through Various Countries), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Śāriputramaudgalyāyanayousizhu jing* (Sūtra of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana Traveling Through the Four Crossroads). This variant translation of the forty-first chapter of the *Ekottarika Āgama* appears in the *Yu* catalog.

*Nainüqiyu jing* (Sūtra of the Maiden Nāi and Jīvaka), one fascicle; also called *Nainü jing* (Sūtra of the Maiden Nāi). Translated during the Taian era; this is the second edition, appearing in the *Zhen* and *Yu* catalogs. *Qinnü jing* (Sūtra of the Seven Daughters).

*Ben jing* (Original Scripture), one fascicle; the second translation, which largely agrees with that translated by Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty, appears in the Fang lu. *Wu gai yi jie shi xing jing* (Scripture on the Five Coverings, Doubtful Ties, and Lost Practice), one fascicle;

translated on the twelfth day of the fourth month in the second year of Yongning. The first translation; Master Dao’an remarked that it does not resemble those produced by Master Dharmarakṣa; appears in the Zhenyou lu.

*Fo wei pusa wu meng jing* (The Buddha’s Five Dreams for the Bodhisattva), one fascicle; translated in the fifth month of the second year of Tai’an. The second translation; also known as *Fo wu meng jing*, *Taizi wu meng jing*, or *Xianren wu [meng jing]*.
The *Dream Sūtra* (one fascicle), seen in the *Jiùlù* and the *Zhēnyòulù*; the *Mó Mùqiéluán Běnjīng* (one fascicle), also titled *Yǒuhēzì Wújiànzì*, seen in the *Yòulù*;

the *Wǔfúshījīng* (one fascicle), seen in the *Yòulù*; the *Guānxíngbùyísìshìjīng* (one fascicle), seen in the *Yòulù*; the *Sìfùyùjīng* (one fascicle), seen in the *Yòulù*; the *Lúyīzhèngjīng* (one fascicle), seen in the *Yòulù*;
the *Héluówángjīng* (one fascicle), seen in the *Yòulù*; the *Tányuèjīng* (one fascicle), seen in the *Yòulù*; and the *Lóngshījīng* (one fascicle), [seen] today in the *Yòulù*.

*Yi shi long shi pusa benqi jing* (The Sūtra on the Original Arising of the Bodhisattva Nāga-dāna), one fascicle; seen in the Yù-lù (Record of Yù). *Ji gudu mingde jing* (The Sūtra on the Virtuous Deeds of Anāthapiṇḍada), one fascicle; the old records say it is the *Ji gudu shi jing*. Seen in the Yù-lù.

*Longwang xiongdi tuoda jie wang jing* (The Sūtra on the Elder Brother Dragon King Tuḍa Admonishing the King), one fascicle; seen in the Yù-lù. *Quan hua wang jing* (The Sūtra on Exhorting and Transforming the King), one fascicle; seen in the Yù-lù. *Yan wang jing* (The Sūtra of the Goose King), one fascicle; seen in the Yù-lù.

*Yan wang wubai yan ju jing* (The Sūtra of the Goose King and Five Hundred Geese Together), one fascicle; seen in the Yù-lù. *Jie wuchang jing* (The Sūtra on Explaining Impermanence), one fascicle; seen in the Yù-lù. *Cheng yu jing* (The Sūtra of the City Parable), one fascicle; seen in the Yù-lù.

*Lu Jianglong jing* (Record of the Scripture on Subduing Dragons), one fascicle; listed in the You-lu. *Xiefajing* (Scripture on Evil Dharmas), one fascicle; listed in the You-lu. *Zuifajing* (Scripture on Committing Offenses), one fascicle; listed in the You-lu. *Kuyingjing* (Scripture on the Response to Suffering), one fascicle;

listed in the You-lu. *Sanpinxiuxingjing* (Scripture on the Threefold Practice of Cultivation), one fascicle; also called *Sanpinhuiguo jing* (Scripture on the Threefold Repentance). Master Dao’an stated that this was a recent compilation from the *Daxiuxingjing*.

It is an error to maintain separate entries for the *Sanpinhuiguo jing* in the two catalogs of the Fang-lu. *Nalujing* (Nāla Scripture), one fascicle; listed in the You-lu. *Jiakijing* (Scripture on the Merchant), one fascicle; listed in the Fang-lu. *Sha...* [text fragment]

*Men-guo-zheng-jing* (Sūtra on the Realization of the Fruits of the Gate), one fascicle; listed in the *Yù-lù*, now suspected to be the same text as the *Jì-zhì-guǒ-jīng*. *Bìn-nǚ-wèi-guó-wáng-fū-rén-jīng* (Sūtra of the Poor Woman Who Became the King’s Consort), one fascicle; listed in the *Fáng-lù*. *Jiè-wáng-jīng* (Sūtra of Admonishing the King), one fascicle; listed in the *Yù-lù*.

*Jiè-jù-jīng* (Sūtra of Admonishing the Fully Equipped), one fascicle; listed in the *Yù-lù*. *Jiè-luó-yún-jīng* (Sūtra of Admonishing Rāhula), one fascicle; listed in the *Yù-lù*. *Bhikṣuṇī-jie* (Bhikṣuṇī Precepts), one fascicle;

the *Yù-lù* states that this *Bhikṣuṇī-jie-jīng* was extracted from the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-vinaya* (or *Daśādhyāya-vinaya*) and differs slightly from that produced by Dharmagupta. Its initial appearance is recorded in the *Yù-lù*. *Kāśyapa-jie* (Kāśyapa’s Compilation), [one fascicle]. Listed in the *Yù-lù*.

*Jichuan jing* (Sūtra of the Collection of Transmissions), one fascicle; alternatively, it lacks the character "chuan" (transmission). The old catalog states it is the *Kāśyapa-jie-jing* (Kāśyapa’s Vinaya Compilation Sūtra); others say it is the *Jiejiji-jing* (Compilation of the Precepts Sūtra). Sengyou says it is the *Kāśyapa-jijie-jing* (Kāśyapa’s Compiled Vinaya Sūtra). This second appearance is found in the *Zhenyou lu*.

*Qisheshuwoshan jie* (Explanation of Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain), one fascicle; found in the *Sengyou lu*. *Zapiyuyou sanbaiwushou jing* (Sūtra of Three Hundred and Fifty Miscellaneous Parables), twenty-five fascicles.

Sengyou says it is the *Piyu sanbai shou jing* (Sūtra of Three Hundred Parables). Found in the *Sengyou lu*. Fang says it is found in the *Bielu* (Separate Catalog). The above totals one hundred and seventy-five works in three hundred and fifty-four fascicles, according to Faquan.
Of the scriptures, ninety collections comprising two hundred and eight fascicles are currently extant; eighty-four collections comprising one hundred and forty-six fascicles are missing.
[Compiled by] the śramaṇa Zhu Tanmoluocha.
His name in the Jin language was Dharmarakṣa.
His ancestors were people of the Yuezhi state;
his original surname was Zhi.
His family had lived in Dunhuang Commandery for generations.
At the age of eight,
he left the household life and took the foreign śramaṇa Zhu Gaosuo as his teacher.

He subsequently adopted the surname Zhu; prior to the Qin and Jin dynasties, śramaṇas mostly followed their teachers' surnames, but later, due to Mīlān and Dao’an, they all collectively came to be called Śākya.
He could recite ten thousand words of scripture daily, mastering them upon a single reading.
By nature he was pure and noble, and his conduct was refined and austere.
With resolute dedication to learning, he sought out teachers even ten thousand *li* away;
thus, he read extensively the Six Classics and allowed his mind to roam through the Seven Documents.
Although worldly affairs such as praise and blame never entered his heart,
it was during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty that temples and sacred images were highly revered in the capital.
However, the profound Vaipulya sutras were still hidden beyond the Onion Kingdom (Kashmir).
Consequently, Senghu was filled with lamentation and indignation, resolving to propagate the Great Way;
he thus followed his master to the Western Regions.
Having traveled extensively through various foreign lands, he encountered thirty-six different types of foreign languages, and their written scripts were likewise diverse.
Dharmarakṣa studied them all thoroughly and mastered them;
there was no glossary, phonetic meaning, or character form that he did not fully understand.
He then brought a great number of Sanskrit scriptures back to the eastern lands;
traveling from Dunhuang to Chang’an,
he subsequently arrived in Luoyang and proceeded to the region south of the Yangtze River.
Along the route, it was translated and transcribed into the language of Jin,
beginning in the Jingshu year (366 CE) of the second year of Emperor Wu’s Taishi era,
and ending in the Guiyou year (313 CE) of the first year of Emperor Min’s Jianxing era.
Chū-kō translated one hundred and seventy-five scriptures, including the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others.
The lay devotee Nie Chengyuan and his son Daozhen [assisted him].
Zhu Fashou,
Chen Shilun,
and Sun Bohu.
Yu Shuya and others collectively received the Master’s instructions and took up their pens to carefully collate the texts;
yet the Master, with diligent devotion, made the propagation of the teachings his sole vocation,
writing and translating until the end of his life without ever complaining of fatigue.
That the sutras and dharmas have spread widely throughout the Eastern lands is due to the power of [his] protection.
In his later years, he lived in seclusion deep in the mountains;
there was a clear mountain stream where he constantly took water for washing and rinsing.
Later, a woodcutter defiled the side of the water,
and in an instant it dried up.
Guhā then paced back and forth, sighing and saying:
That people lack virtue has caused the clear spring to cease its flow.
If the water were to dry up forever, it would truly have no means of sustaining itself;
it is only right that it should move elsewhere.
Having finished speaking, a spring gushed forth and filled the ravine.
Such were the manifestations of his profound sincerity.
Thus, Zhi Dun composed a eulogy for his portrait, saying:
Master Hu was serene and tranquil, his virtue profound and beautiful.
He chanted softly in secluded valleys, as withered springs murmured their waters—how remote he was!
Master Hu was naturally endowed with vast nobility.
He washed his feet in the shifting sands and extracted the profound essence from its depths.
Later, he established a monastery outside the Qing Gate in Chang’an and applied himself with diligent devotion to the Way.
Thereupon, his virtuous influence spread far and wide, and his reputation covered the four quarters.
The several thousand monks all followed him with devotion.
When Emperor Huai of the Jin dynasty traveled west to Chang’an,
the region of Guanzhong fell into desolation and the common people were displaced.
Dharmarakṣa and his disciples fled eastward to seek refuge.
Upon reaching Mienchi, he fell ill and passed away at the age of seventy-eight.
It is said that during the reigns of Emperors Huai and Min, Dharmarakṣa once again produced translations of sutras and treatises when Emperor Hui traveled west to Chang’an.
As for the claim that Master Hu fled the chaos eastward and died upon reaching Mianchi,
this may not be the case.
Hu was originally from Dunhuang.
His transformative teachings were pervasive and thorough;
people of the time all called him the "Dunhuang Bodhisattva," while some records refer to him as the "Yuezhi Bodhisattva."
They are also called "Bodhisattvas of India";
these are all instances of honoring their virtues and praising their titles.
Now, as for Dharmarakṣa:
In this land, he is translated as *Dharmarākṣasa*.
This is his name in the Western Brahma-language.
However, in the Liang dynasty’s *Sengyou lu* and the Sui dynasty’s *Fajing lu*, he is established as two separate individuals.
To claim that these were translated as separate sutras is not a detailed or careful assessment.
Now, having carefully examined various catalogs:
The number of sutras translated by Dharmarakṣa is indefinite, being sometimes many and sometimes few;
in Sengyou’s *Chū sānzàng jìjí*, their count is even more numerous.
Now, upon careful examination, there are among those titled as "separately produced" (biéshēng) and other such categories that were not actually translated by Dharmarakṣa.
These cannot be counted as part of the standard canon;
however, for the sake of an authentic record,
they have all been omitted here as described below.

The *Sūtra on the Previous Life of the Buddha Siṃhacandra*—some catalogs omit the character "original" (ben) [in its title]—is recorded in the catalogues of Fang and others as translated by Master Hu. However, a detailed examination of the text reveals it is not [a genuine translation]; it has therefore been classified as a work of lost translation within the Qin records. The *Commentary on the World* (*Shijie*) regarding the *Dharmasamaya-sūtra* identifies it as doubtful; having personally seen its manuscript, I find it was composed by a human author. It is now included in the "Records of Doubtful Works. The same applies to the *Sūtra of the Questions of Ratnāvalī on Wisdom*.

The *Brahmā-rāja-vikurvita-sūtra* (upper volume); these two sūtras are from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*. The *Catur-vaśitā-abhijñā-sūtra* is from the *Īśvararāja-sūtra*. The *Vajragarbha-bodhisattva-caryā-sūtra* is from the *Anupūrva-saṃpada-sūtra*. The *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* is from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The *Ratnādityaprabhāsa-bodhisattva-sūtra* is also called the *Ratnādityaprabhāsa-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-padma-loka-vyūha-sūtra*; it is from the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The *Samantamukha-kumāra-sūtra*—sometimes written with the character "薄" (*bo*)—is from the *Samantābhibhū-sūtra*. The *Sulambha-mūla-sūtra*.
The *Aśvavarga-sūtra*;
the *Maitreya-bodhisattva-nārī-bhāva-sūtra*;

the *Mahākṣatrapa-rāja-sūtra*; and the four sūtras beginning with *Suyāma*—all these were translated together as the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-saṃgraha-bodhisattva-pāpadeśanā-dharma-sūtra*, though some versions omit the word "sūtra. Also included are the *Nāgārjuna-daśabhūmi-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Puruṣa-āgata-sūtra* (also titled *Puruṣa-āgamana-sūtra*), the *Puruṣa-mūla-kāma-utpatti-sūtra*, and the *Daridra-sūtra*.

The *Kehuking* (Sūtra on the Suffering of Poverty), the *Pingqiong deng er jing* (Two Sūtras on Poverty, etc.), both appear in the *Madhyamāgama*; the *Qibao jing* (Sūtra of the Seven Jewels) appears in the *Ekottarikāgama*; the *Yiwang jing* (Sūtra of the King of Physicians);
and the *Xibili tianzi yi fo shuo jie jing* (Sūtra of the Devaputra Śibiṛi Visiting the Buddha to Recite Verses).
The *Sūtra on the Four Types of People*, the *Sūtra on the King of Physicians and Others*, and three other sūtras all appear in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
The *Dhāraṇī Sūtra*—also known as the *Buddha-mind Dhāraṇī Sūtra* or the *Abushishi Jing*—is also included therein.
The *Madhuvāsiṣṭha-sūtra*,
the five sūtras including the *Miśrakastotra* and the *Viveka*, the *Utpatti-sūtra*, the *Strīkāma-tīvra-moha-sūtra*,
and the *Bahuśruta-sūtra*.

The *Wuyijing* (Sūtra on Awakening the Mind) has already been listed above; the three preceding sūtras are from the *Chuyao jing* (Sūtra of Luminous Verse), while the twenty-seven sūtras following "Bao nü" (Jewel Woman) are all separately extracted excerpts taken from larger collections, which are now being deleted.

*Zhong jing mulu* (Catalogue of All Scriptures), one fascicle; compiled by Master Hu himself, not a translation from an Indic original. It was listed among the introductory catalogues but no longer exists.
*Shi er you jing* (Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings), one fascicle; first brought out. This one work in one fascicle is originally missing.
The śramaṇa Jiangliánglóuzhì (疆梁婁至),
whose name means "True Joy" (Zhēnxǐ) in the Jin language,
was a man from the Western Regions.
With a mind free from worldly attachments and a profound commitment to spreading the Dharma,
in the second year of the Taikang era of Emperor Wu (the *xinchou* year),
he translated the *Dvādaśavyākaraṇa-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Twelve Wanderings) in one fascicle at Guangzhou.
According to the *Shixing lu* and the *Baocang lu*,
the *Daoshenzu wuji bianhua jing* (Sūtra on the Infinite Transformations of the Divine Footsteps of the Way) in four fascicles, the second [translation], is also known as the *He daoshenzu jing*.
It consists of either two or three fascicles and is identical to the *Fosheng daoli tian wei mu shuo jing* translated by Zhu Fahu.
The *Dharmaparyāya-sūtra* (Fǎjīng) is a different translation of the same text as seen in Zhūdào zǔ’s catalogue;

the *Aśokarāja-avadāna* (Āyùwáng zhuàn) in seven fascicles—sometimes titled with the character "Great" (*Dà*) as the *Mahā-aśokarāja-sūtra*—or in five fascicles, was first produced and is of the same text as the *Aśokarāja-sūtra* translated during the Liáng dynasty;
it was translated in the Guāngxī era, as recorded in Zhūdào zǔ’s catalogue. The *Mañjuśrī-prabhāsa-ratnagarbha-sūtra* (Wénshūshìli xiàn bǎozàng jīng) in two fascicles [is also recorded therein].
The first edition was also called the *Xian baozang jing* (Sutra on Manifesting the Treasure Treasury), in three fascicles;

it is the same text as the *Baobie jing* (Sutra of the Jewel Casket) and others, translated during the Dà'ān era, as recorded in Zhūdǎozǔ’s catalogue. The *Āshèshì wáng jīng* (Sutra of King Ajātaśatru), in two fascicles, was translated during the Dàkāng era, as recorded in Zhūdǎozǔ’s catalogue.
The third edition is the same text as the *Puchao jing* (Sutra of Universal Transcendence) and others. The *Ānán mùqiéluó jīng* (Sutra of Ānanda Mukhara), in one fascicle... [text ends].
Volume Three: This is a different translation corresponding to the *Weimi shi jing* (Sūtra on the Subtle and Secret Time). It is recorded in the *Zhu Daozu lu*.
Of the five works totaling sixteen fascicles mentioned above, the first two works comprising eleven fascicles are extant; the latter three works comprising five fascicles are missing.
The śramaṇa An Faqin was a native of the country of Parthia (Anxi).
Having studied various scriptures, his profound insight was unimpeded.
From the second year of Taikang of Emperor Wu (the *xinchou* year) until the first year of Guangxi of Emperor Hui (the *jǐngyin* year),
he translated five scriptures, including the *Daoshenzu jing*, at Luoyang.

The *Fangguang Banruo Boluomi Jing* (Luminous Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) in thirty fascicles; the second translation, which is identical in substance to the *Guangzan* and the *Dapin* [versions], or in twenty fascicles, also called the *Fangguang Mahāprajñā Sūtra*, or the *Mahāprajñā Fangguang Sūtra*. Translated in the first year of the Yuan [era]; see the postscript to the sūtra. This one work in thirty fascicles is extant. Regarding the śramaṇa Mokṣala, the postscript to the sūtra states: "Mokṣala."
A man from the kingdom of Khotan,
on the fifteenth day of the fifth month of the first year of the Yuankang era (the *xinhai* year) of Emperor Hui’s reign,
translated the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* at the South Temple of the Yuan River, based on the records of the Cangheng Monastery in Chenliu.
It was completed on the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month.
Transmitted orally by the lay devotee Zhu Shulan of Henan,
and recorded in writing by Zhù Taixuan and Zhōu Xuánmíng.
The Sanskrit manuscript of this sūtra was originally [brought by] the śramaṇa Zhushixing of Yingchuan.
He once lectured on the *Daoxing jing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra) in Luoyang;
however, he frequently encountered difficulties in understanding its profound meanings.
Every time he sighed over how this sūtra was the essential core of the Mahāyāna yet its principles had not been fully translated,
he vowed to sacrifice his life and set his mind upon seeking it out. Thus,
in the fifth year of the Ganlu era of the Cao Wei dynasty, the Gengchen year, he departed.
Setting out from Yongzhou and crossing the shifting sands to the west,
he reached Khotan, where he transcribed the authentic Sanskrit text consisting of ninety chapters and over six hundred thousand words.
This was done in the third year of the Taikang era of the Jin dynasty, the Renyin year.
He dispatched ten disciples, including Pútúndán (whose name means "Dharmādarśa" in the Jin language), to escort him back.
Before they had even departed from Luoyang,
the community of Hinayana scholars in Khotan reported the matter.
The King said, "The śramaṇas of the land of Han wish to delude and confuse the orthodox scriptures with the books of the Brahmins.
As the King is the lord of the earth,
if you do not restrain them, the Great Dharma will be severed."
"The deafness and blindness of the land of Han are the fault of the King.
If the King will not permit the scriptures to be taken, I shall seek to prove my point by burning them. Filled with indignation, Sengxing then requested to burn the scriptures as a testament.
The king, wishing to test him,
piled firewood in the palace courtyard and set it ablaze.
Sengxing approached the steps and made this vow:
If the Great Dharma was destined to flow into the land of Han,
the sutras would not have been burned;
if it were not destined by fate, what could be done?
Having spoken these words, he threw the scripture down without damaging a single character;
the leather binding remained as it was, yet appeared even more radiant and fresh.
The great assembly was struck with awe and submitted, praising this as a divine response.
He was subsequently escorted to Luoyang, where he resided for three years.
He then traveled to Xuchang for two years, after which he arrived at Shuinan Temple in Chenliu.
There, the assembly requested that Dharmarakṣa and others translate [the scriptures].
The various catalogs by Zhu Daozu, Sengyou, Wang Zong, Baochang, Li Kuò, Fashang, Lingyu,
and others all state that [the *Dīrghāgama*] was translated by Zhu Shixing;
this is likely because they attributed the merit to him based on the fact that he was the original seeker after the text.
According to the postscript to the sutra and the *Zhimiandu lu* (Record of Zhi Min-du), as well as various other catalogues,
this was translated by An Wuluo (An Shigao) and Zhu Shulan together.
As for Zhu Shixing, he remained in Khotan for eighty years before passing away.
According to the Western method of cremation, when the firewood was exhausted and the flames extinguished, the remains of the corpse were still intact.
The assembly was all struck with wonder and astonishment, and they uttered this incantation:
"If you have truly attained the Dharma, you should be destroyed."
At his command, [the remains] were shattered and scattered;
he then collected the bones and erected a stupa over them.
Having thus passed away in Khotan, [he was buried there].
That sūtra is certainly not a translation by him. It differs from the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* in three fascicles;

Sengyou states it differs from the *Weiqie jing* (or sometimes written with the character "si"), or it consists of two fascicles and was translated in the sixth year of the Yuankang era. This third edition differs from the original texts produced by Zhu Fashu and others; this is seen in the records of Daozu and Sengyou. The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* in two fascicles appeared in the first year of the Yuankang era; this seventh translation differs in wording from the versions produced by Zhi Chen, Bo Yan, Dharmarakṣa, and others; this is seen in the *Zhen* and *Sengyou* records. These two works, totaling five fascicles, are both currently missing.

Regarding the Upāsaka Zhu Shulan: according to Sengyou’s *Lù* (Catalogue), the biography of Zhu Shixing, the biography of Zhu Shulan, the postscript to the *Fàngguāng jīng* (Prabhūtaratna-sūtra), and Zhi Mindu’s record on the compilation of the *Shòulènyán jīng*, all state that Shulan was a lay devotee (*báiyī jūshì*). The records of Changfang and other Buddhist bibliographies claiming he was a śramaṇa are erroneous.
He was originally a native of India.
His grandfather, Lou-tuo, was earnest in his aspirations and fond of learning; he was pure, simple, and possessed of high integrity.
At that time, the king was unrighteous and the common people longed for chaos.
There was a rebel minister who had led troops and committed an offense;
fearing execution, he summoned the country's powerful leaders to join him in rebellion.
Louta said in anger,
"You rose from humble origins to hold a position of high office;
instead of repaying this kindness with virtue, do you instead plot treason?"
"I would rather die maintaining my loyalty than live by betraying it.
A traitor fears that his plot might be leaked, so he kills [his master] and then incites a rebellion.
Louduozi Damashiluo (婁陀子達摩尸羅)—which in the Jin language means Fashou—was previously in another country.
Her two brothers-in-law were both śramaṇas.
Upon hearing that her father had been killed and the country was in revolt,
they immediately fled with the two śramaṇas to the Jin territory, settling in Henan, where they gave birth to Shu Lan.
Shulan was intelligent and eloquent from childhood;
she studied the sutras and the Dharma under her two maternal uncles,
attaining realization upon hearing them but once.
He was proficient in the Sanskrit language and its script,
as well as various secular histories and literature;
however, by nature he was somewhat flighty and impulsive, and his hunting excursions were unrestrained.
Once, while pursuing a deer on horseback alone, he encountered a tiger and fell from his mount;
his right arm was broken, but after a long time it healed.
Subsequently, he continued to gallop and race without ceasing.
His mother repeatedly scolded and admonished him, but he would not change;
she only stopped when she took up a vegetarian diet for his sake.
By nature he was fond of wine, drinking five or six *dou* before he felt satisfied.
Once, while heavily intoxicated, he lay by the side of the road;
he then entered the gate of Henan Commandery and began shouting.
The officials arrested him and sent him to the Henan prison.
At that time, Yue Guang, the Governor of Henan,
was drinking with his guests until they were all intoxicated;
he then said to Lan:
"You, a guest from afar, why do you learn to drink wine?
Shulan replied, "Du Kang brewed this wine for all under heaven to drink; what does it have to do with you, an old man from Qi?"
Guang said again,
"Drinking wine may be permissible, but why does it cause such madness and confusion?
He replied:
"Though the people are wild, they are not disordered;
it is like the Magistrate, who though drunk, is not mad.
He called out loudly.
At that time, a guest at the gathering asked,
"How can a foreigner have such white skin?
Shulan replied:
"A person from Henan has a dark face, yet you do not doubt him;
I have a white face—what is there to find strange about that?
Thereupon, the host and guests marveled at his quick wit and eloquence, and finally released him.
Shortly thereafter, he died suddenly without illness.
After three days, he revived and recounted his experience:
he had entered a vermilion gate where a hall made of gold and silver stood.
He saw a man who said of himself,
"This is my grandfather," and addressed Shulan, saying,
"I practiced good for many years, yet now I receive this retribution."
"You, you sinner, how have you come here?
At that time, the gatekeeper drove him with a staff into the bamboo grove.
There he saw his hunting companions being pecked and bitten by hawks and dogs; bleeding profusely, they cried out for help to Shulan.
He fled for several dozen paces, where he encountered a man with an ox head who intended to pin him down.
Xulan said,
"I have been a disciple of the Buddha for successive generations and have always made offerings to two śramaṇas."
"What offense has been punished?
The ox replied,
"Although this brings me merit, it is not related to the crime of hunting."
Shortly thereafter, his two maternal uncles appeared and said to Niutou,
"The two of us have constantly received offerings from him."
"Since his evil deeds were few and his good deeds many, he may be spared.
He then followed the practitioner back home,
and upon returning, he revived.
Thereupon, he changed his ways, cultivated compassion, and devoted himself exclusively to the sutras and the Dharma.
In the first year of the Yuankang era of Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty,
he collaborated with Mokṣala to produce the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (the *Fàngguāng jīng*).
Later, in Luoyang, he personally produced two distinct versions of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and other scriptures.
Since his learning encompassed both Sanskrit and Chinese, his translations were precise and authoritative in meaning.
Later, encountering a period of great hardship, he intended to move for burial within three months.
A neighbor said to him, "The current month and year are unfavorable; you should wait until next year.
Shulan replied:
Now, those who are born must inevitably die;
once dead, they do not return to life again.
That the realms of humans and spirits follow different paths is the natural order of things.
If my deceased mother could find a place for her spirit to rest, my filial heart as a child would be fully satisfied.
If we wait until next year, I fear there will be no place left for us to flee;
how then would I have the leisure to attend to her grave?
The burial was thus completed.
The following year, Shi Le indeed incited a rebellion;
as bandits and marauders roamed unchecked, [he] fled to Jingzhou to seek refuge.
Later, without any illness or suffering, he suddenly informed his acquaintances,
saying, "I am about to die.
A few days later, he passed away.
Those who understand consider this to be the knowledge of destiny (*jñāna-mṛtyu*).

*The Sūtra on the Departure of the Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; the third translation, also called *The Sūtra of the Vow of the Youth* or simply *The Sūtra on Departure*, is the same text as *The Sūtra on the Restriction for the Son of the Elder*, as seen in the Fang Catalogue. *The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Practice*, one fascicle; the third.

The *Sūtra on the Elder Vaiśya’s Questioning of the Contemplation of the Body* (also known as the *Sūtra on the Elder’s Cultivation of Practice*), recorded in the Fang-lu, is also said to be among the three extant translations.

The two-fascicle *Buddha-parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, recorded in the Fang-lu, is an alternate translation of the first part of the *Caturvargika-vinaya* (the *Parivarta-sūtra*) and is also simply titled the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The one-fascicle *Mahāprajāpatī-parinirvāṇa Sūtra* is also extant.
The *Ekottarika Āgama*, fascicle 50, has alternative translations also titled *Nirvāṇa* and *Seeing the Five Blessings of the Worthy One*;
these are recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. The above are extant; the following are missing:

the *Sūtra on Purifying the Buddha-field*, two fascicles, the second translation of which is also called the *Pure Land Sūtra*, identical to the *Mañjuśrī’s Sūtra on the Adornment and Purity of the Buddha-field*, etc.
The *Yugalarāja-paripṛcchā-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle, first seen in the Fáng-lù;
the fifth edition, identical in substance to the *Fǎjìng-jīng* translated by Ān Xuán of the Hàn dynasty. The *Dùjí-sāmādhi-jīng*, one fascicle, second edition, seen in the Fáng-lù.
The *Wúliàng-pòmó-duōluóní-jīng*, one fascicle, fourth edition, identical in substance to the *Weí...* [text fragment].

The *Mimi-chi jing* (Secret Holding Sūtra) is a variant translation of the same text as seen in the Fang-lu; one fascicle of the *Dafangdeng rulai zang jing* (Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra), its second appearance, is seen in the Fang-lu;
one fascicle of the *Weijian pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Weijian) is seen in the Biographies of Eminent Monks (*Gaoseng zhuan*) and the Sengyou-lu;

one fascicle of the *Tanchi tuoluoni jing* (Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of Tanchi) is seen in the Fang-lu; and one fascicle of the *Rulai xingxian jing* (Sūtra of the Manifestation of the Tathāgata) is seen [in the Fang-lu].
*Fánglù shànquán jīng* (The Scripture on the Good Power), one fascicle; recorded in the *Fánglù*. *Hǎilóngwáng jīng* (The Scripture of the Sea Dragon King), one fascicle; recorded in the *Fánglù*.
*Chíxīn fànlì zhī jīng* (The Scripture of the Brahmāṇa Holding the Mind), one fascicle; recorded in the *Fánglù*. The above consists of sixteen works in eighteen fascicles.
Regarding the "Five Blessings of the Worthy," the first five works comprise six fascicles currently extant in the Pure Buddha-land; the remaining eleven works comprise twelve fascicles.
The original manuscript is missing.
The śramaṇa Baiyuan, whose courtesy name was Fazǔ,
was originally surnamed Wàn.
He was a native of Henei.
His father, Wei Da, was renowned for his refined scholarship and elegant character;
he declined all appointments offered by the provincial and regional governments.
From his youth, Daozu conceived the aspiration for the Way and petitioned his father to leave the household life;
his arguments were so earnest and profound that his father could not resist him, and he consequently changed his robes to follow the Way.
Daozu’s literary talent and insight were brilliant and penetrating, surpassing all others in their keenness and clarity.
He recited eight or nine thousand words daily from the sutras.
He studied and savoring the Vaipulya scriptures, he attained profound mastery of their subtle mysteries.
He was extensively versed in and thoroughly conversant with the secular classics and treatises.
He then constructed a vihāra in Chang’an, making the study and exposition of the teachings his primary occupation.
Monks and laypeople who took him as their spiritual guide numbered nearly a thousand.
Toward the end of the reign of Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty, the Grand Chancellor, Prince of Hejian, Yao Yong, was stationed in Guanzhong.
With an open mind and deep reverence, he treated him with the respect due to a teacher or a friend.
Whenever there was leisure time or a quiet night, they would invariably discuss the Way and its Virtue.
At that time, the Western Capital had recently been established, and the assembly of eminent talents was exceedingly flourishing.
All eloquent scholars were humbled by his profound ancestry; he was widely learned, versatile, and proficient in both Sanskrit and Chinese.
During the reign of Emperor Hui, he translated sixteen works, including the *Bodhisattvagaty-uttara-sūtra*.
Later, he suddenly said to his disciples and fellow practitioners,
"In a few days, my karmic retribution from past lives will arrive.
He then took his leave, requested writing materials, and completed the distribution of the scriptures, images, and his personal assets.
At that time, Zhang Fu was the Regional Inspector of Qinzhou.
Zu went there with him;
at dawn the next morning, he visited Fu and conversed with him.
Suddenly, having offended the will of his patron, he was consequently harmed by him.
People of the time considered this to be knowledge of past lives.
A short while later, there was a person...
His surname was Li and his name was Tong.
After dying, he revived and said that he had seen Dharma Master Zu at the abode of King Yama, where the Master was preaching the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* for the king.
It is said that after the lecture concluded, he should have ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Furthermore, he saw the ritual master Wang Fu and the Daoist priest Ji Gong,
who were subsequently bound in shackles and manacles, seeking the patriarch’s repentance.
In the past, during his ordinary days, Sengzu and Daofu frequently debated matters of heterodoxy and orthodoxy.
Having been repeatedly defeated by Sengzu, Daofu could not restrain his anger;
he consequently composed the *Laozi huahu jing* (The Scripture of Laozi Converting the Barbarians) to slander the Buddha-dharma.
Since retribution has its destination, it is only at the point of death that one thinks of repentance.
Furthermore, the records of Zhang Fang and others include seven additional scriptures that also claim to originate from Zu;
however, as these are all separate apocryphal productions, they have been deleted.
These refer to the *Buddha-questions-the-Four-Boys Sūtra* and the *Sūtra on Subduing the Prince’s Resolve for the Path*; both of these sūtras appear in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*.

The *Sūtra on the Five Hundred Princes Making Vows for a Pure Land* appears in the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka*. The *Sūtra of the Three Young Boys*—sometimes titled *The Young Boys*—appears in the *Samantabhadra-abhyudgata*.
The *Sūtra of the Two Boys Seeing the Buddha, Speaking Verses, and Making Offerings* appears in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
The *Śatapañcāśatka-bāladāraka-sūtra* (also known as the *Kumāra-śuddha-sūtra* or *Vaiśravaṇa-mārga-sūtra*) and the aforementioned two sūtras were all translated from the original Indic texts.
The *Sarvaguṇa-puṇyakṣetra-sūtra* in one fascicle was first translated; it is sometimes titled the *Sarvapuṇyakṣetra-sūtra* or simply the *Puṇyakṣetra-sūtra*.
It was produced by Dharmayaśas and Dharmaprabha, as recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue. [The *Loutan jing* (Lokadhātu-vibhāga-sūtra) is also mentioned.]
The *Loutan jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra) in six fascicles, the second edition, is also called the *Daluotan jing*.

It is said to be a different translation from the fourth division of the *Dīrghāgama*, sharing the same original text as the *Jishi jing* (Saṃjñeya-sūtra). It differs slightly from the five-fascicle version translated by Dharmarakṣa;

it appears in Sengyou’s catalog as being either in five or eight fascicles. The *Dafangdeng rulaizang jing* (Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra) in one fascicle; old catalogs state it was translated by the Buddha.
Regarding the first appearance of the Mahāvaipulya sūtras from the Tibetan [tradition], as recorded in the *Jiyou lu*: the four sections above comprise twelve fascicles;
of these, the first three sections totaling eleven fascicles are extant, while the final section, one fascicle, is missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Falì was a man of unknown origins.
His wisdom and path were profound and eminent, and he prioritized awakening sentient beings.
During the reign of Emperor Hui, together with Faju and others, he translated four scriptures, including the *Sarvapuṇyakṣetradharmaparyāya*, at Luoyang.
*The Sūtra of King Udayana*, one fascicle; first translated, identical in substance to the *Assembly of King Udayana* in the *Ratnakūṭa*, as seen in the Fang Record.

*The Sūtra of the Three Turnings of the Wheel of Dharma in Previous Lives*, one fascicle; first translated, identical in substance to the *Sūtra of the Silver-Colored Woman*, as seen in the Fang Record.

*The Sūtra of King Ajātaśatru Receiving the Prediction*, one fascicle; first translated, identical in substance to the *Sūtra of King Vaiśravaṇa Gathering Lotus Flowers*, as seen in the [Fang] Record.

*Fánglù Guànxǐ Fóxíngxiàng Jīng* (The Scripture on the Ritual Bathing of the Buddha’s Image), one fascicle; its initial appearance also refers to it as the *Sìyuèbārì Guàn Jīng* (Scripture on the Bathing of the Eighth Day of the Fourth Month) or simply the *Guàn Jīng*.

It is of the same text as the *Mahāsthāman Sūtra*, according to the *Fánglù*. *Héngshuǐ Jīng* (Scripture on the Ganges Water), one fascicle; also called the *Héng héyù Jīng* (Scripture on the Parable of the Ganges).
It appears in the ninth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama* as a variant translation, according to the *Fánglù*. *Jǐng* (Crown), one fascicle.

*The Sūtra on the Story of King Jāta* (one fascicle), also simply titled *The Sūtra of King Mūrdhaja*; translated from the eleventh fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, a variant translation seen in the Fang record.
*The Sūtra on Seeking Desire* (one fascicle); translated from the twenty-second fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, a variant translation seen in the Fang record.
*The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Aggregate of Suffering* (one fascicle); translated from the twenty-fifth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
The *Jianpō Bǐqiū Jīng* (Sāṃkāśyaka-bhikṣu-sūtra), one fascicle, translated by [anonymous], also known as the *Jianpō Chūzhōng Āhán* (Sāṃkāśyaka from the Madhyamāgama), fascicle 29;
a variant translation seen in Fánglù. The *Fúyín Jīng* (Subduing Lust Sūtra), one fascicle, from the *Zhōng Āhán*, fascicle 30; a variant translation seen in Fánglù.
The *Shù Jīng* (Enumeration Sūtra), one fascicle, from the *Zhōng Āhán*, fascicle 35; a variant translation seen in Fánglù.
The *Dust-Bedewed Body Sūtra* (Chen-tun-shen jing), one fascicle, concerning the death of Queen Mother of King Prasenajit, is found in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, Volume 18;
it is recorded as an alternative translation in the Fáng Catalogue (*Fáng lù*).

Furthermore, the *Sūtra on King Prasenajit’s Mourning for His Mother* is identical to this *Dust-Bedewed Body Sūtra* and is not a redundant or repeated entry. [There is also] the *Sūtra on King Bimbisāra Visiting the Buddha to Make Offerings*.
*Yǎng jīng* (Sūtra on Nurturing), one fascicle; also called *Pínpó chū* (The Emergence of Bimbisāra). A variant translation of the twenty-sixth chapter of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
Recorded in Fáng’s catalogue. *Āngqǐjì jīng* (Sūtra of Aṅgulimāla), one fascicle. Largely identical with minor differences to Dharmarakṣa’s *Zhǐjì jīng* (Sūtra of the Finger-Ring).
A variant translation of the thirty-first chapter of the *Ekottarika Āgama*. Recorded in Fáng’s catalogue. *Nántíshì jīng* (Sūtra of Nandika), one fascicle. Extracted [from the Āgamas].
*Saṃyukta Āgama*, Volume 30, translated differently; listed in the Fang-lu (Catalogue of Fang); *Xiāngyìngxiāngkě jīng* (Sūtra on Corresponding Characteristics), one fascicle;
included in the single-fascicle *Saṃyukta Āgama* with different translations; listed in the Fang-lu; *Màn fǎ jīng* (Sūtra on Arrogance toward the Dharma), one fascicle;

third translation, same text as the *Ānànfēnbié jīng* (Sūtra on the Separation from Ānanda) and others; listed in the Fang-lu; *Fǎhǎi jīng* (Sūtra of the Dharma Ocean), one fascicle; second translation, same text as [the above].

The *Sūtra on the Eight Virtues of the Ocean* (same text as seen in the Fang-lu); the *Sūtra on King Ajātaśatru Asking about the Five Heinous Crimes*, one fascicle, second edition (seen in the Fang-lu);
the *Sūtra on Rāhula’s Patience*, one fascicle, also simply titled the *Sūtra on Patience* (seen in the Fang-lu);
the *Sūtra on the Buddha Explaining Righteous Matters to Young Bhikṣus*, one fascicle (seen in the Fang-lu); [and] the Bhikṣu Śaha.
*Gongde jing* (Sūtra on Merit), one fascicle; Fang states it was seen in the old catalog. *Qunniu pi jing* (Sūtra of the Parable of the Herd of Cows), one fascicle; seen in Fang’s catalog.
*Biqiu bi nü eming yu zisha jing* (Sūtra of the Bhikṣu Who Attempted Suicide to Avoid a Woman’s Ill Repute), one fascicle; seen in Fang’s catalog. The above are extant; the following are missing.
*Futian jing* (Sūtra on Fields of Merit), one fascicle; also titled *Zhude futian jing*. Second edition, translated by Fali.
These differ slightly from the *Zhudaozu Jinlu*. The *Bujing Pusa ming jing* (Sutra on the Names of Bodhisattvas in Various Sutras), one fascicle, is found in the Fanglu;
the *Zhengyi jing* (Sutra of Correct Meaning), one fascicle, is also found in the Fanglu, with a note stating it is the second translation, though it is unclear which was the original version.
The *Mingdishi shi jing* (Sutra on the Offering of Indra to the Buddha), one fascicle, is found in the Fanglu; the *Loutan jing* (Loutan Sutra), eight fascicles, is the third translation.
This is a different translation of the *Ji-shi jing* (Sūtra on the Record of the World), the fourth division of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, which largely agrees with that produced by Fa-li.
Previously, [this text] was translated together with Fa-li; however, because his understanding was not yet complete, I have consulted the two catalogs of Min-du and Bao-chang extensively.
The *Śuddhodana-rāja-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle, first appeared in the Fang-lu (Fang-gu’s Catalog). The *Daridra-vṛddha-puruṣa-sūtra*, one fascicle, first appeared [there].

*Chūjiensōroku* (Record of the Appearance of Dharmottara): *Weichui jing* (Sutra on Fragility), one fascicle; seen in the Fang record. *Dashé pìyù jīng* (Sutra of the Parable of the Great Snake), one fascicle;
also simply called *Dashé jīng*. The Fang record notes it was seen in the old records. *Luóhàn Jiāliútáiyī jīng* (Sutra of the Arhat Kālodāyin), one fascicle;
sometimes the word "Arhat" is omitted; seen in the Fang record. *Zhuǎjiǎ qíngtǔ pìjīng* (Sutra of the Parable of the Nail-Parable of Lifting Soil), one fascicle; also called *Zhǎojiǎ*.

The *Qutu jing* (Scripture on Taking Earth) states that it was seen in the *Jiulu* (Record of Old Catalogs): one fascicle of the *Shaili jing* (Scripture on Decline and Benefit), seen in the *Fanglu* (Record of the Fang Family);

one fascicle of the *Zhongsheng muyan sanman jing* (Scripture of the Three Men of Sentient Beings Yet to Be Enlightened), seen in the *Fanglu*; one fascicle of the *Yuqiu shuofa jing* (Scripture on Seeking to Preach the Dharma), seen in the *Fanglu*;

and one fascicle of the *Luoxunyu jing* (Scripture of the Parable of Rāhu). I now suspect this last is an alternative title for the *Lomi shou jing* (Scripture of Rāmaśūra) found within the *Biesheng jing* (Scripture of Separate Births), as seen in the *Fanglu*.

*Yijiao falü jing* (Sūtra on the Law and Discipline of the Bequeathed Teaching), three fascicles—also called *Yijiao falü sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Law and Discipline of the Bequeathed Teaching) or *Yijiao sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Bequeathed Teaching)—in two fascicles;
recorded in the *Shixing lu*. [Total: forty works, fifty fascicles.
[The following] twenty-four works, twenty-four fascicles, by the bhikṣu Bi-nü, are extant. [From the *Futian jing* onwards: sixteen works.
The twenty-sixth fascicle is missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Faju’s clan and lineage are also not clearly known.
Possessing a lofty capacity and harboring a deep resolve for the propagation of the Dharma,
he initially translated scriptures together with Fali during the early years of Emperor Hui’s reign.
After Fali passed away, Daohui himself subsequently translated forty scriptures, including the *Udrāyaṇa-rāja-sūtra*.
Furthermore, the records of Sengchang, Fang, and others state that various other sūtras were all translated by Zhu Faju;
however, since these are all apocryphal texts produced separately,
the cataloguers have erroneously attributed them to him.
Now, all of these have been deleted,
as described below.

The *Sūtra on Time and Non-Time* is also simply called the *Sūtra on Time*; according to the postscript of that sūtra, it was not translated by Faqu. A detailed account is provided below. The *Sūtra on the Demoness Hearing the Buddha’s Dharma and Attaining a Male Body* is from the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*. The *Sūtra on the Original Vows of the Compassionate Bhikṣu* is from the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. The *Sūtra on Past Deeds* and the *Sūtra on Holding the Alms Bowl*—these two sūtras are both from the *Samantaprabhā-samādhi Sūtra*. The *Sūtra on Using Gold to Redeem Sins at Mount Tai* and the *Sūtra on Devadatta Teaching Others to Commit Evil*—these two sūtras are both from the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-saṃgraha*. The *Sūtra on the Buddha Subduing Aṅgulimāla* and the *Sūtra on the People’s Joy* (also known as the *Sūtra on Aṅgulimāla’s Conversion*)—these two sūtras are both from the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra*. The *Sūtra on Vaidehī’s Son Asking about the Lady Under the Moonlight* (alternatively titled the *Sūtra on Heaven and Humans*) is from the *Dīrgha Āgama*. The *Sūtra on Meritorious Conduct* is from the same source.

The *Āpadā-sūtra* (Sutra on Evil Paths), also known as the *Duṣṭa-citta-sūtra* (Sutra on Evil Intentions); the alternative title *Duṣṭa-citta* is likely an error. It is incorrect for both titles, "Evil Paths" and "Evil Intentions," to be recorded together in the catalog. [Also] the *Krodhopaśama-sūtra* (Sutra on the Cessation of Anger).
The *Mṛdusūtra*,
the *Dhāraṇīsūtra*,
and the *Yaśasūtra*.
The *Pūmī-sūtra*, the *Sūtra on Meritorious Conduct* (the latter seven sūtras all appearing in the *Madhyama Āgama*),

the *Sūtra of the Simile of the Flying Bird*, the *Sūtra of the Burning Pile of Wood*— also known as the *Sūtra of the Great Withered Tree*— and the *Sūtra on King Prasenajit Approaching the Buddha with Five Modes of Deportment*.
The four sūtras beginning with the *Flying Bird Simile* from the *Ekottarika Āgama* are all found in the *Pushi jing* (Universal Bestowal Sūtra) of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
Also included is the *Sūtra on the Monk Kṣema Recovering from a Serious Illness*.
The Buddha spoke the *Śīrṣa-dāha-upama-sūtra* for the bhikṣus.
He spoke the *Udāyin-vṛkṣamūla-pratisaṃlayana-damana-sūtra*.
The Buddha spoke the *Mahābala-sūtra* for the bhikṣus.
The Sūtra on Developing Disenchantment toward the Material Body of the Four Great Elements;
the Sūtra on Different Faiths and Different Desires;
and the Sūtra on Three Dharmas Spoken by the Buddha for the Bhikṣus.
There are several sutras using the analogy of leaves:
the *Sūtra on the Extremely Deep, Precipitous, and Difficult Places* spoken by the Buddha for the bhikṣus;

the *Sūtra on Not Contemplating the World* (alternatively titled *The Sūtra on Not Contemplating the World or Contemplating [It]*), spoken by the Buddha for the bhikṣus; and the *Sūtra on the Impurity of the Sentient Being’s Body*.
The Discourse on the Eye and Visible Forms;
the Discourse on the Bhikṣu’s Disenchantment with Visible Forms;
and the Discourse on Abandoning All Worldly Affairs.
The Sūtra of the Simile of the Infant;
the Sūtra on the Appearance of the Seven Jewels of a Wheel-Turning Sage King in the World;
and the Sūtra on Turning Toward the Erroneous and Contravening the Dharma.
The Sūtra of the Simile of the Farmer;
the Sūtra on the Faults Arising from the Five Faculties in Those Who Have Faith;
and the Sūtra on the Few and Many Precepts.
The Sūtra on the Beginningless Fundamental Limit;
the Sūtra on the Arhat Meeting King Bimbisāra;
and the Sūtra on the Venerable Gautika’s Solitary Contemplation.
The Sutra on the People’s Plague Receiving the Three Refuges;

the Sutra on the Flowing Stream (alternatively titled the Sutra on the River of Ashes from Flowing Trees, which is erroneously listed as a separate title in the *Pi-yu-jing-lu*); and the Sutra on the Death of King Prasenajit’s Grandmother.
The Sūtra of the Simile of Casting Gold;
the Sūtra of the Simile of the Wooden Pestle;
and the Sūtra of the Venerable Elder’s Illness at the Goldsmith’s Monastery.
The Sūtra of the Simile of the Flock of Sheep;
the Sūtra on Practicing the Middle Way;
and the Sūtra on King Prasenajit’s Daughter Who Passed Away and Went to the Buddha.
The *Bhikṣu pṛcchati bahūpāsaka-prayāṇa-sūtra*, the *Sarvadāna-sūtra* (the twenty-fifth sūtra in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Bhikṣu-varga), the *Bhikṣu-piṇḍapāta-sūtra*,
and the *Upananda-sūtra*.
The Scripture on Sustaining Oneself through Improper Livelihood;
the Scripture on the Vows of the Bhikṣus;
and the Scripture of Upāli, the Śākya.
The Bhikṣu-ābādha-sūtra (The Discourse on the Illness of a Bhikṣu),
the Abhaya-sūtra (The Discourse on Fearlessness), and the Viṣa-vyañjana-upama-sūtra (The Discourse on the Simile of the Poisonous Herb).
The *Poison Simile Sūtra*, the *Horse Simile Sūtra*,

ten sūtras including the *Bhikṣu Begging for Alms*, the *Birth of the Sūtra of Parables*, the *Sūtra of the Six Men*, the *Sūtra on Selling Intentions*, and the *Sūtra on King Ajātaśatru Asking from What Anger Arises*.
The Mahābhikṣu-sūtra; the Upāli-sūtra (or Tiao-da-yu-jing);

the three sūtras beginning with Ajātaśatru; the Minor Vehicle excerpted sūtras including the Candanānulipta-caitya-sūtra, the Śata-varāha-sūtra, the Anityatā-sūtra, and the Bhikṣu-pramāṇārthika-sūtra.
The Discourse on the Bhikṣu Abhaya’s Impermanence;
the Discourse on the Bhikṣu Asking the Buddha Why He Abandoned the World to Study the Path;
the Discourse on the Buddha Visiting a Sick Bhikṣu Who Refused an Invitation from an Elder.
The Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Practicing Meditation Passing Away to Be Reborn in Heaven;
the Sūtra on Heedlessness;
the Sūtra on the Bhikṣus of Shallow and Deep Learning; and the Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Kūṭi.
The *Pālibhikṣu-brahmacaryā-dūṣaṇa-sūtra*,
the *Uttarapatha-seṭṭhi-sūtra*,
and the *Devadatta-rāja-śākyaputrīya-abhighāta-sūtra*.
The Sūtra on Faith Being Able to Cross the River;
The Sūtra on Sentient Beings Committing Evil in the Three Times;
The Sūtra on the Wise Bhikṣu.

The *Sūtra on the Difficulty of Encountering the Dharma* (Fǎshuō nánzhì jīng); the *Sūtra on Tíduó Questioning the Buddha’s Complexion* (Tiáodúo wèn fó yánse jīng) and seventeen subsequent sūtras on impermanence (*wúcháng*) all appear in the *Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Chūyào jīng); the *Sūtra on the Morning Meal* (Xiǎoshí jīng) appears in the *Śrāvakabhūmi* (Xiūxíng dàozhì jīng); the *Sūtra of the Simile of the River* (Xūhé yù jīng) appears in the *Saṃyukta-avadāna* (Zá pìyù jīng); the eighty-nine sūtras following the "Māra-daughter" section are all excerpted from the *Mahāsūtra* and recorded in the *Biesheng lu*, which are excluded here; the *Sūtra of the Surpassing Sun Radiance Samādhi* (Chāorìmíng sānmèi jīng), two fascicles—the second edition sometimes simply called the *Chāorìmíng jīng*, or in three fascicles—this sūtra was previously translated by Master Hù, but as its language and meaning were cumbersome and redundant, it was later revised and refined by Master Chéngyuǎn, resulting in a text superior to the former; this is recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gāosēng zhuàn) and Sēngyòu’s catalog; the *Sūtra of Overcoming Difficulties* (Yuè nán jīng), one fascicle—also known as the *Sūtra of the Elder Nán* or simply the *Nán jīng*—appears in Fáng’s catalog; these two works, totaling three fascicles, both have their original texts extant.
The lay devotee Nie Chengyuan was intelligent and talented,
and he was devoted to the study of the Dharma.
When Master Hu translated the scriptures, Chengyuan frequently participated in correcting the wording and phrasing.
He concurrently served as Penchi Chengzhi (Director of the Imperial Secretariat).
Later, during the reign of Emperor Hui,
he personally translated two scriptures, including the *Chāorìmíng jīng* (Sūtra of Transcending the Sun’s Radiance).
Furthermore, the records of Sengchang and others state that Chengyuan further translated the *Kāśyapa-anuyoga-ānanda-sūtra*. This, however,
is an excerpt from the *Saṃyukta-avadāna* and is not a separate translation.
Furthermore, it is a great error that the three catalogs from the Han period— those of Fotiao, An Shigao, and this Chengyuan— all record [this work].

The *Wugoushi pusa fenyingshenbian jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Vimaladatta’s Discernment of Responsive Eloquence), one fascicle, was the second production, translated by Dharmarakṣa as the *Ligou*.
The *Śīla-sūtra* (or *Dāna-sūtra*) and its counterparts also state that [the Buddha] distinguished the retributions; it is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa* as the thirty-third assembly.
There are records stating it was translated by Zhu Fahu, but this is an error, as seen in the catalog of Fang [Yong].

The *Sūtra on the Fundamental Activities of All Bodhisattvas Seeking Buddhahood*, one fascicle—some versions omit the word "all" (*zhū*)—is an alternative translation of the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" from the *Avataṃsaka*, attributed to Mañjuśrī.
*The Sūtra on Beneficial Parinirvāṇa*, one fascicle; listed in the Fang Catalogue. *The Sūtra on the Original Arising of Bodhisattvas*, one fascicle;
alternatively titled without the character "arising" (*qi*); listed in the Fang Catalogue. *The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra*, one fascicle;
listed in the Fang Catalogue. *The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Receiving the Fast*, one fascicle; the second edition; listed in the Fang Catalogue. *The Vaipulya Bodhisattva Ten Stages*.
One fascicle; the second translation, which is largely identical with slight variations to that by Dharmarakṣa, is recorded in the Fang-lu.

*The Sūtra on the Ten Dharma Abodes of Bodhisattvas*, one fascicle: a variant translation of the "Ten Abodes Chapter" of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*; the third translation, recorded in the Fang-lu. *The Sūtra on the Ten Abodes*, twelve fascicles:
a variant translation of the "Ten Grounds Chapter" of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*; the second translation, recorded in the Fang-lu.

*The Scripture on the Fifty Matters Concerning the Body of a Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; second translation, largely identical with slight differences to the *Scripture on the Fifty Conditions of the Body*, as noted in the Fang Catalogue.
*The Scripture on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara*, one fascicle; second translation, as noted in the Fang Catalogue.

*The Scripture on the Essential Collection of All Buddhas*, two fascicles; second translation, as noted in the Fang Catalogue. *The Scripture on the Vows of the Bodhisattva Śāntasvara*, one [fascicle].

*Pusa qiuyan fa jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Method for Seeking the Five Eyes), one fascicle; the character “jing” (sūtra) is absent in the [Dao]you catalogue, though some call it the *Wuyan wen* (Text on the Five Eyes).

Seen in the Fang catalogue. *Pusa daoxing liufajing* (Sūtra on the Six Dharmas of the Bodhisattva’s Practice of the Path), one fascicle. Seen in the Fang catalogue. *Pusa chudi jing* (Sūtra on the First Stage of the Bodhisattva), one fascicle.
Seen in the Fang catalogue. *Pusa shidao di jing* (Sūtra on the Ten Stages of the Bodhisattva’s Path), one fascicle. Some say this was a previous translation.
The *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmi-vimalakīrti-nārī-saṃvāda* (Discourse on Mañjuśrī and the Woman Vimalā), one fascicle, recorded in the Fang-lu;

examining the current canon now, the discourse concerning the woman Vimalā appears in the lower fascicle of the *Sarvabuddha-sāra-saṃgraha-sūtra*, and it is suspected that this text was excerpted from that sūtra.
The *Bodhisattva-vividhacaryā-dharma* (Dharma of the Various Practices of Bodhisattvas), one fascicle, recorded in the Fang-lu.
*Record of the Four Dharmas Practiced by Bodhisattvas*, one fascicle; listed in the Fang Catalogue. *Bodhisattva’s Sutra of Past Lives*, one fascicle;
listed in the Fang Catalogue. *Mañjuśrī’s Sutra on the Pure Vinaya*, one fascicle; the second edition differs slightly from that of Dharmarakṣa; listed in the Fang Catalogue.
*Text for the Sole Reception Platform of the Bodhisattva Precepts*, one fascicle; listed in the Fang Catalogue. *Bodhisattva’s Method of Repentance*, one fascicle.
The scroll states that these were transcribed from different original versions as seen in the Fang-lu (Fangguang Record).
Of the twenty-four works in thirty-six fascicles listed above, the first six works totaling six fascicles are extant; the remaining eighteen works totaling thirty fascicles are missing.
The lay devotee Nie Daozhen was the son of Chengyuan.
Father and son were both pure and enlightened, and both took the transmission of the Dharma as their vocation.
This spanned from the beginning of the Dakang era of Emperor Wu to the end of the Yongjia era of Emperor Huai.
During that interval, in addition to the texts he consulted, received, and had Dharmarakṣa transcribe,
after Dharmarakṣa’s death, Zhu Fonian himself translated twenty-four scriptures, including the *Vimaladattāparipṛcchā* and the *Pratibhānamati*.
Master Hugu truly lived up to his title;
he was quite skilled in literary composition, and his phrasing and meanings were clearly distinguished.
Furthermore, the catalogs of Sengzhang and others list twenty-nine additional scriptures.
It is also said that these were produced by Daozhen.
Since they are all separately compiled excerpts from scriptures,
I have deleted them and do not retain them.
The *Bodhisattva-pūjā-pratimā-stūpa-praṇidhāna-sūtra*,
the *Siṃhakrama-garjitasvara-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-cittotpāda-sūtra*, and the *Bodhisattva-tridharma-sūtra*—
these three sūtras, including the *Bodhisattva-pūjā-sūtra*, are all extracted from the *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-vyūha-pariśuddhi-sūtra*.
The *Bodhisattva-dāna-pratideśanā-dharma* from the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā-sūtra*;
the *Vaiśravaṇarāja-bodhisattva-tathāgata-avavāda-sūtra*, also known as the *Bodhisattva-kāya-avavāda-vaiśravaṇa-sūtra*.
The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Guidance and Instruction in Practice;
the Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Initial Resolve;
and the Sūtra on the Bodhisattva of Silence Disseminating the Dharma.
The *Avyākṛta-bodhisattva-sūtra*,
the *Bodhisattva-niryāṇa-asaṅga-dharmamukha-sūtra*, the *Prabhārasmi-bodhisattva-saptaratna-sopāna-sūtra*,
and seven other sūtras including the *Vajrarāja-bodhisattva-sūtra* were all extracted from the *Mahāsannipāta*.
The *Bodhisattva-ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa-sūtra* and the *Bodhisattva-śīla-vaśitā-sūtra*;
these two sūtras are extracted from the *Vaśavarti-rāja-sūtra*.
The *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Śāntisvara’s Inquiry into the Five Corruptions*, also known as the *Śāntimati-sūtra*.
The *Sūtra on the Wheel-Turning Sage King’s Resolve to Seek the Pure Land* (upper volume) and the second sūtra are both from the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka*.
The *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Mahāmegha-Guhyagarbha Asking about the Samādhi of the Great Ocean* is from the *Mahāmegha Sūtra*.
The *Puśu tóngzhēn jīng* (Sūtra on the Youthful Puśu) is extracted from the *Pǔchāo jīng* (Sūtra on Universal Transcendence).
The *Rútóng púsà jīng* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva儒童) sometimes omits the word "Bodhisattva" and is extracted from the *Liùdù jí jīng* (Compendium of the Six Pāramitās).
The *Bōsìní wáng yù fá yāngjué móluó jīng* (Sūtra on King Prasenajit’s Intention to Attack Aṅgulimāla) is extracted from the *Yāngjué móluó jīng* (Sūtra on Aṅgulimāla).
The Sūtra of the One Hundred Forty-Eight Vows of the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha;
the Sūtra on the Six Dharmas of Bodhisattva Practice;
the Sūtra on the Chapter of the Original Vow Practice of Bodhisattvas.
The *Bodhisattva-duṣkaracaryā-sūtra*, the *Bodhisattva-nindāsvapna-sūtra*, the *Bodhisattva-nindāgṛhadoṣa-sūtra*,
and the *Mahāprabhāsa-sūtra*— these six sūtras, according to the *Yùlù* (Catalogue of Translations), are designated as "extracts" (*chāo*). They are now all classified as Mahāyāna excerpted sūtras.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-saṃgraha-sūtra* is extracted from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*;
the *Bodhisattva-pañcadharma-caryā-sūtra* and the *Prathamacittotpādika-bodhisattva-carita-sukhacaryā-dharma-sūtra*— these two latter sūtras are both extracted from the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
The *Cakravartin-rāja-saptaratna-paripūrṇa-sūtra* appears in the *Saṃyukta-āgama*.

The *Zhongjing mulu* (Catalogue of Various Scriptures) in one fascicle was compiled by Daozhen himself; it is not a translation from an Indic original. In Daozhen’s preface and catalogue, this title is listed, yet it no longer exists. The *Changfang deng lu* (Catalogues of Changfang and Others) states: [as cited above].
The Upāsaka Weishi translated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-mārgacaryā-sūtra* in two fascicles during the reign of Emperor Hui.

It is said that this was an abridged extraction from the original *Mārgacaryā-sūtra*. Sengyou’s Catalogue states: "Various scriptures all refer to the *Mārgacaryā-sūtra* in two fascicles as having been abridged by Weishi."
Since this was an abridgment of an existing scripture and not a separate translation from a Sanskrit original,
it is now included in the *Biesheng lu* (Record of Additional Translations).
This no longer exists.

The *Śrī-śreṣṭhi-dāraka-sūtra* (The Scripture of the Deceased Youth), one fascicle, is the fourth [translation] to appear; it is also titled *The Scripture of the Elder’s Regulation*, or simply *The Scripture of Regulation*;
it is also titled *The Bodhisattva Śrī-sūtra*, or simply *The Śrī-sūtra*. These five versions are largely identical, differing only in their alternative titles and translations.
The *Śūreṇa-jātaka-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Birth Story of Śūra), one fascicle. Its initial translation was the same text as those produced by Jītamitra and Zhú Nántí;
it appears in the thirty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama* as a different translation.
It is recorded in the three catalogs of Zhī Mǐndù, Zhú Dàozǔ, and Bǎochàng. The *Mañjuśrī-prabhāsa-ratnagarbha-sūtra* (The Sutra of Mañjuśrī Revealing the Treasure Treasury), two fascicles. Third.
Translated by Zhu Fahu; identical to the *Ratnakara-sutra* (Baozang jing). Translated by Zu Chang; listed in the two catalogs, the *Jin lu* and the *Baocang lu*.
One fascicle: *Sutra on the Ten Good and Ten Evil Deeds*. The above four works comprise five fascicles.
Two works comprising two fascicles, including the *Sutra of the Youth Śrī*, are extant. Two works, including the *Mañjuśrī-parivarta-ratnakara-sutra*, are extant.
The third fascicle of this section is missing.
The śramaṇa Zhī Fǎdù is of unknown provenance.
In the first year of the Yongning era (the *xin-you* year) during the reign of Emperor Hui,
he translated four works, including the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra*.
Furthermore, according to the catalogs of Sengyou, Fazang, and others, at that time during the reign of Emperor Hui, there was the śramaṇa Zhimin-du.

Regarding the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, there were four versions—those of Zhi Liang, Zhi Qian, Zhu Fahu, and Zhu Shulan—which the Fang Catalogue further adds the "White" version to make five. Now, according to the You Catalogue and the *Hejing ji* (Record of Combined Scriptures), there are only four versions combined, as the "White" and "Yan" versions are absent. Regarding the *Śūraṅgama*, it consists of eight fascicles; You’s commentary states that it may also consist of five fascicles. There were three versions of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*: those of Zhi Qian, Zhu Fahu, and Zhu Shulan, which together comprise five fascicles.
Since these were neither separate translations from Sanskrit originals nor do their original texts exist,
they have been omitted and not included in this catalog.
The *Śīla-akāla-sūtra* (or simply the *Kāla-sūtra*), one fascicle; see the postscript to the scripture. This one work, consisting of one fascicle, its manuscript is currently extant.
The śramaṇa Yeluo Yan was a man from a foreign land.
One fascicle of the *Yishi feishi jing* (Sūtra on the Timely and Untimely).
The postscript to the sūtra states:
"The foreign Dharma Master Yeluo Yan held the Hu manuscript in his hand and orally translated it himself."
The Daoist monk Lüzhèn (also written as Lüzhen) of Liangzhou recorded this in the city;
Fang and others all state that it is an error to claim this was translated by Faju.
Since their imperial origins are unknown, they are appended here within the records of the Western Jin dynasty.

One fascicle of the *Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one fascicle of the *Ratnavyūha Sūtra*, and one fascicle of the *Sūtra on the Five Meritorious Virtues*—these three works in three fascicles are all missing from their original texts. According to the catalogs of Senglang and others, they were lost translations of the Western Jin period.
It is stated that [this work] consists of eight sections in fifteen fascicles.
Both the *Wu lu* and the *Bie lu* record it as having been produced during the Yuankang era, though they do not specify the translator.
A detailed examination of the records reveals no definitive attribution.
Therefore, the individual items remain distinct and their translators lost.
Now, having examined various catalogs and consulted the scriptural texts, [I have identified] the remaining five sections comprising twelve fascicles.
Since all [of these works] have a basis for their attribution, they are not translations of unknown origin.
A detailed account of their origins is set forth as follows:
*The Scripture on the Chapter of Transcending the World*, six fascicles.

The *Anavatapta-nāgarāja-sūtra* in two fascicles is another name for the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-samādhi-sūtra*. The above two sūtras were translated by Dharmarakṣa. The *Tathāgata-rahasya-garbha-sūtra* in two fascicles—also titled the *Mahāvaipulya-tathāgata-gotra-utpatti-sūkṣma-rahasya-garbha-sūtra*, or simply the *Tathāgata-gotra-utpatti-sūtra*—is the "Tathāgata-gotra-utpatti" chapter of the old version of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. It was already lost during the Later Han dynasty; its reappearance here is a grave error. It is now appended to the section on separately produced texts. The *Prabhāsa-saṃtati-vimukti-bhūmi-pāramitā-sūtra* in one fascicle was translated by Guṇabhadra of the Song dynasty. The *Sūtra on the Three Grades of Disciples* in one fascicle is another name for the *Sūtra on the Three Grades of Disciples*; it was translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. The following entries are newly appended to this catalogue.
*The Sutra of Prince Hehu*, one fascicle; second edition, identical in text to the *Sutra of Prince Shuhu* and others.
*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one fascicle; old catalogs refer to it as the *Sayun Pun-ta-li Sutra*, or simply the *Puṇḍarīka Sutra*.

It corresponds to the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Dharma" and the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa" of the *Lotus Sutra*, being minor partial translations of the *Devadatta* chapter. *The Sutra of the Alms Bowl*, one fascicle.

One fascicle of this scripture is an alternative translation of the "Chapter on Holding the Alms Bowl" from the *Puchao jing* (Sūtra of Universal Transcendence). The first fascicle was annotated by Master Dao’an as belonging to the Vaipulya section.
The *Śānta Sūtra* (or *Xiàozǐ Shàn jīng*, also simply called *Shàn jīng*) in one fascicle is the second [entry];

it is an alternative translation of the second fascicle of the *Liùdù jí* (Compendium of the Six Pāramitās). The *Chángshòu wáng jīng* (Sūtra of King Long-Life) in one fascicle is the third; it concerns the permanence of the Dharma.
*Sūtra on the Simile of Salt Water*, one fascicle; *Sūtra of Dautiya*, one fascicle; translated separately from the fourteenth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*:
*Sūtra on the Ten Dreams Seen by the King of Śrāvastī*, one fascicle (also simply called the *Sūtra of the Ten Dreams*;
the old catalogues call it the *Sūtra of the Ten Dreams of the King of Śrāvastī* or the *Sūtra of the Ten Dreams of King Prasenajit*).
Extracted from the *Ekottarika Āgama*, fascicle 51; translated by An Gong.

It is said to be the *Apidan Yujie Nü Jing* (Sūtra of the Girl Yujie) in one fascicle, or alternatively the *Yuyejing*. Its initial translation was the same text as the *Aduda Jing* (Āṭānāṭīka Sūtra).

Also, the *Xiaozijing* (Sūtra of the Filial Son) in one fascicle, also known as the *Xiaozibaoen Jing* (Sūtra on the Filial Son’s Requital of Kindness); and the *Atuoduheji Jing* (Āṭānāṭīka Sūtra) in one fascicle.

*The Scripture of King Puda*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on the Enshrinement and Funeral Rites after the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa*, one fascicle—also titled *The Scripture of the Bhikṣu Teacher* or *The Scripture of the Teacher Bhikṣu*;
*The Scripture of Kūṣmāṇḍī*, one fascicle; *The Scripture of King Brahmānanda*, one fascicle;
*The Scripture of Kātyāyana’s Verses on the Extinction of Phenomena through the Teaching of the Dharma*, one fascicle—the title states: "Sent by the Buddha, [spoken by] a bhikṣu."
The *Kātyāyanīputra-dharmaparyāya-śatakṣaya-gāthā* in one hundred and twenty chapters;

also simply titled the *Kātyāyana-buddha-deha-cikitsā-sūtra* in one fascicle, or sometimes without the word "Buddha. The old catalog records it as the *Buddha-deha-cikitsā-sūtra*, while other catalogs agree with this.
There is also the *Citta-cikitsā-sūtra* in one fascicle; the old catalog records it as the *Buddha-citta-cikitsā-sūtra*, while other catalogs agree with this. Both of these currently exist.
The end is missing.
*Mile dang lai xia sheng jing* (Sūtra on Maitreya’s Future Descent), one fascicle; the first edition, identical in text to the *Mile lai shi jing*.
*Shiliyue jing* (Śrīlaṅkā Sūtra), one fascicle; the second edition, identical in text to the *Yueguang tongzi jing*, though differing slightly.

*Ben sheng si jing* (Sūtra on the Fundamental Cycle of Birth and Death), one fascicle; same text as the *Śālistamba-sūtra*. *Nai zang da fang deng jing* (Mahāvaipulya Sūtra from the Inner Treasury), one fascicle;
now suspected to be the *Buddhapiṭaka-mahāvaipulya-sūtra*. *Xiao a she shi jing* (Sūtra of the Young Ajātaśatru), one fascicle.
