*Xiao xu lai jing* (Sūtra of the Young Sudāna), one fascicle. *Yin qie jing* (Sūtra of Ingada), one fascicle. Master Dao’an stated that these were produced from the Mahāvaipulya section; they are now suspected to be the works of Ānanda.
*Mukha-sūtra* (目佉經), one fascicle; Maitreya-sūtra (彌勒經), one fascicle—Master An says these are from the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
*Pātala-sūtra* (墮藍經), one fascicle—Master An says it is from the *Madhyama Āgama*. *Saptavastu-sūtra* (七事經), one fascicle—Master An says it is from the *Madhyama Āgama*.
*Rāṣṭrapāla-sūtra* (賴吒謣羅經), one fascicle—Master An says it is from the *Madhyama Āgama*. *Ānanda-sūtra* (歡豫經), one fascicle—Master An says it is from the *Madhyama Āgama*. *Fajing* (法經).
The Catalogue states: *Huanyu* says there is one fascicle of the *Dwenty-second Sūtra on Death from the Āgama*. I now suspect this is the *Sūtra on the Twelve Stages of Birth and Death*.
There is also one fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Seven Wives*, and one fascicle of the *Sūtra of Ānanda-Bhāradvāja’s Fourfold Almsgiving*.
The old catalogues state: the *Sūtra of Ānanda-Bhāradvāja’s Fourfold Almsgiving* and the *Sūtra of the Seven Chariots*. I now suspect [these are the same].
Among these are: the *Saptasāra-sūtra* (The Simile of the Seven Chariots) from the *Madhyamāgama*; the *Samudra-aṣṭa-vastu-sūtra* (The Sūtra on Eight Matters Concerning the Ocean), one fascicle;

the *Durgati-ādi-sūtra* (The Sūtra on Difficulties, etc.), one fascicle; the *Ānanda-kāśyapa-prathama-bhāṣita-sūtra* (The Sūtra Spoken by Ānanda and Kāśyapa as the First), one fascicle—formerly recorded as the *Vilīya-rāja-sūtra*;
the *Gṛhapati-durga-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Householder’s Difficulties), one fascicle—formerly recorded as the *Vilīya-rāja-sūtra*; and the *Kālodayin-rāja-sūtra*, one fascicle.
*The Sūtra of the Brahmin Ācārya’s Grandson*, one fascicle; the ancient catalog records it as *The Sūtra of the Brahmin Ja-sun*.

*The Sūtra of King Pāṭha*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of the Melancholy Compassionate Heart*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra on the Path to Transcendence*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of the Householder’s Power*, one fascicle.
*The Sūtra of the Dullness-Infusion*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of Devadatta*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of Udraka*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of Patu*, one fascicle.
*Sāstra-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Śarīra-vibhāga-sūtra*, one fascicle (alternatively titled *Vibhakta-śarīra-pratipatti-vinaya*, one fascicle);
*Siddham-mukha*, two fascicles; *Kalyāṇa-dharma-pratyaya*, one fascicle; *Mouth-Transmission on the Arising and Exhaustion of Kalpas*, one fascicle;
*Method for Striking the Ghaṇṭā*, one fascicle. The above fifty-five works comprise fifty-six fascicles. From the *Citta-pariśodhana-sūtra* onwards, there are nineteen works.
Nineteen fascicles are currently extant; thirty-six works in thirty-seven fascicles are said to be among those that Maitreya will bring in the future, while thirty-seven fascicles are missing.
This is according to the *Liang Sengyou Lu*.
Among the scriptures whose translators were lost in Seng’an’s catalog,
only those recorded in Huiguo’s catalog are preserved;
the catalogs of Baochang and others are all deficient in this regard.
In the *Yòuzǎi Ān gōng shīyì zǒng* (The Total of One Hundred Forty-Two Scriptures with Lost Translators by Master Ān),
there are now eighty-seven remaining sections;
upon examining various catalogs, it is found that most have their translators identified.
Alternatively, there may have been separately produced transcribed scriptures or biographies compiled by others;
since these provided a basis for verification, they were deleted and not included.
Since Dao’an did not specify the historical period [of the original sources], [I have omitted them].
For now, these are appended to the end of the Jin period.
Together with the three previously lost translations of old, totaling three works in three fascicles,
there are fifty-eight works in fifty-nine fascicles in all.
And it is said that the Western Jin lost its source.
*The Newly Compiled Catalogue of Śākyamuni’s Teachings from the Zhenyuan Era*, Fascicle Four;
*The Newly Compiled Catalogue of Śākyamuni’s Teachings from the Zhenyuan Era*, Fascicle Five.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xīmíng Monastery in the Western Capital.
Volume One, Part Five of the *Zǒngjíqīnjīnglù*.
Eastern Jin (Eastern Jin: the Sīmǎ clan; capital at Jiānkāng, also known as Southern Jin). From the first year of Yuándì’s Jiānwǔ era, the *Dīngchū* year.
Up until the second year of the Yuexi era of Emperor Gongdi, the year Gengshen,
there had been eleven emperors for a total of one hundred and four years,
and sixteen individuals, both monastics and laypeople.

The sutras, vinayas, and śāstras translated herein—including those from both the new and old collections as well as various scriptures of unknown translators—total one hundred and sixty-eight works comprising four hundred and sixty-eight fascicles; of these, eighty-five works comprising three hundred and thirty-six fascicles are extant, while eighty-three works comprising one hundred and thirty-two fascicles are missing.
The *Three Collections of Fourteen Volumes of Sūtras* by the Eastern Jin śramaṇa Śrīmitra;
the *Two Collections of Seven Volumes of Sūtras* by the śramaṇa Zhidao Gen; the *Sixty-one Collections of Sixty-three Volumes of Sūtras* by the śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan;
and the *Five Collections of One Hundred and Eighteen Volumes of the Vinaya-piṭaka* by the śramaṇa Gautama Saṃghadeva.
*Jinglun jiaofa* (Scriptural and Treatise Teachings), translated by the śramaṇa Kālodaka: one fascicle; *Xian sheng ji* (Collection of Worthies and Sages), translated by the śramaṇa Kang Daohuo:
three fascicles; various scriptures, translated by the śramaṇa Buddhayaśas: thirteen works totaling one hundred twenty-five fascicles;
*Jinglü lunji* (Collection of Scriptures, Vinaya, and Treatises), translated by the śramaṇa Dharma: two fascicles; *Lüyao* (Essentials of the Vinaya).
The *Vinaya-mātṛkā* in two sections and five fascicles by Upagupta; the *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* in seven sections and twenty-six fascicles by the śramaṇa Shi Faxian;
the *Sūtra-śīla-śāstra-saṃgraha* in twenty-three sections and forty-five fascicles by the śramaṇa Zhi Damo;
the *Sūtra* in three sections and five fascicles by the layman Zhu Nanti; and the *Sūtra* in one section and one fascicle by the śramaṇa Zhu Fali.
The *Sāṃghika-śramaṇa Śākya Sōng* compiled three works in three fascicles; the *Sāṃghika-śramaṇa Śākya Tù* compiled one work in one fascicle;
the *Sāṃghika-śramaṇa Śākya Fǎyǒng* compiled one work in one fascicle;

and forty works in forty-eight fascicles by various anonymous translators of both new and old editions, consisting of two works in three fascicles from the old collection and twenty-eight works in forty-five fascicles from the new collection.
Attached is the *Mahā-abhiṣeka-sūtra* in twelve fascicles; alternatively, the catalog [without the character "da" (great)] states it is in nine fascicles, the details of which are unknown.

This *Abhiṣeka* comprises twelve sections of sūtras in total, which were later divided by others into separate fascicles, each kept in a different repository. It is said that this is seen in the *Zalu*.
The *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra* in one fascicle is found in the catalogs of Zhu Daozu and Sengyou; it was first brought out by Kong [Leizi].
*The Sūtra of the Miscellaneous Divine Incantations of the King of Sparrows*, one fascicle; recorded in the catalogues of Zhu Daozu and Sengyou as the third appearance.
Of the three sections totaling fourteen fascicles mentioned above, the first section of twelve fascicles currently exists, while the latter two sections comprising two fascicles are missing.
The śramaṇa Bośiliduo, whose name means Jizhi in the Jin language,
was a native of the Western Regions.
The prince, having inherited the succession,
yielded the kingdom to his younger brother,
the elder brother An-quǐ.
Soon thereafter, he realized that his mind had been divinely enlightened and thus became a śramaṇa.
Hui-mi was naturally brilliant and lofty, with a spirit that transcended the ordinary;
even upon first meeting him, one could see how he stood out preeminently from all others.
How much more so for those who were awakened by his eloquence and wisdom?
During the Yongjia era of the Western Jin dynasty, he first arrived in this land;
subsequently, he crossed the Yangtze River and settled at Jianchu Monastery.
When Prime Minister Wang Dao saw him once, he marveled at him,
thinking, "He is one of my own kind.
From this, his fame became manifest.
Taiwei Yu Yuan gui,
Guanglu Zhou Bo ren,
and Dacang Xie You yu.
Huan Moulun, the Minister of Justice, was both a renowned scholar of his generation;
upon meeting him, he sighed repeatedly throughout the entire day and opened his heart to form a deep bond with him.
Sengdao once visited Zhu Fami.
Huiyi untied his sash, lay down prostrate, and engaged in a conversation of divine understanding.
At that time, Bian Wangzhi, the Imperial Secretary for the Promotion of Literature, was also on friendly terms with Huiyi.
Shortly thereafter, Wangzhi arrived.
Buddhamitra then composed his demeanor, adjusted his appearance, and sat upright facing him.
When someone asked him the reason for this,
Buddhamitra said:
The Prince and Duke [Wang] aspired to the Way and its influence;
Magistrate Bian regulated things according to the standard.
It was for this reason that it was so.
Thereupon, the gentlemen marveled that his spirit was so free and unrestrained that he had attained his true place.
Once, the Magistrate of the Court of Justice, Huan, wished to compose a descriptive epitaph for Mi,
but after a long time he could not find the right words.
Some said that Śrīmitra could be described as "exceedingly brilliant.
Thereupon, Huan sighed with deep admiration,
considering him the pinnacle of those who set forth titles.
The Grand General Wang Chuchong was in the Southern Xia;
hearing that the various lords, including Wang Zhou, all held Sengmi in high esteem,
he suspected they had failed to exercise proper discernment.
When he personally saw Huimi, he was filled with joy and rushed to one side,
paying him the utmost reverence. The King once said to Huimi,
"In foreign lands, you alone are such a person."
Mili smiled and replied,
"If I were like you gentlemen,
how could I be here today?"
At that time, this was considered an excellent response.
Mi Xing was lofty and simple by nature;
he did not learn the language of Jin.
Whenever I engaged in discourse with these gentlemen,
although it was conducted through interpreters, my spirit grasped the essence and my mind understood the meaning so thoroughly that the transmission seemed entirely natural.
His physical appearance was extraordinary, beyond the comprehension of ordinary people.
He was skilled at maintaining incantations and mantras, which were invariably effective in every instance.
His contemporaries called him the Dharma Master of the High Seat (Gaozuo Fashi).
During the reign of Emperor Yuan, he translated three sections of scriptures, including the *Abhiṣeka-sūtra*.
Furthermore, he taught his disciple Mili the art of chanting the Sanskrit liturgy (*brahmaghoṣa*) in a resonant voice,
a tradition that has continued to resound to this day.
At over eighty years of age, he passed away during the Xiankang era.
When the various officials heard of this, they mourned him with deep sorrow and shed tears.
Huiyi had frequently practiced *dhūta* austerities on the eastern side of Shizigang Hill.
After his death, he was buried here.
Emperor Cheng, admiring his character, erected a stupa at the site of his tomb.
Later, there was a śramaṇa from Guanyou.
Upon arriving to travel to Jiankang, he established Chaoshi at the site of the tomb;
Xie Hun of Chenjun assisted in completing his work and posthumously honored these past events by renaming it Gaozuo Temple.

*The Sūtra on the Bodhisattvas’ Attainment of Fruition in the Buddha-field of Akṣobhya*, two fascicles; translated during the Taikang era, the second translation, which is largely identical with minor differences to that produced by Zhi Chen of Han; recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty*. *The Vaipulya Lotus Sūtra*, five fascicles. These two works, totaling seven fascicles, are both missing their original texts.
The śramaṇa Zhidao’gen traveled to various regions to cultivate the Way and benefit sentient beings.

In the first year of Emperor Cheng’s Xiankang era (the year of Yiwu), he translated two sections of the *Akṣobhya-buddhakṣetra-sūtra* and other scriptures. Both the catalogues of Changfang and others state that the *Akṣobhya-buddha-sūtra* was translated during the Taikang era under Emperor Wu of the Western Jin, which would place it approximately sixty years prior to the Xiankang era. To suggest that these were both produced by the same person during two different reigns seems highly improbable; this is likely due to errors in transcription, and the dates should mostly be attributed to the Xiankang era.
*The Scripture on the Prediction Bestowed upon King Utpalavaktra for Plucking Lotus Flowers*, one fascicle; also simply titled *The Scripture on King Utpalavaktra*. Second translation;
same text as the *Scripture on the Prediction Bestowed upon King Ajātaśatru*. *The Scripture on the Dhāraṇī-bhājana*, one fascicle;
also called *The Scripture on the Dhāraṇī-mantra of the Bhājana*. Second translation; same text as the *Scripture on the Divine Mantra of Holding the Phrases*, etc.

Regarding the fact that the *Dharani-pata Sutra* recorded in the *Benfang lu* (Record of the Original Office) further preserves what is called the *Chiju Shenzhou Jing* (Sutra of the Mantra of Holding Phrases), this is incorrect.
There is also one fascicle of the *Maniluo-dan Jing* (also called the *Maniluo-tan Shenzhou Jing*), and one fascicle of the *Shenzhou Jing Spoken by the Master Bhadra*.
The record states that it contains the words "Spoken by the Illusionist," though some versions have the character "Ba" (拔) instead; it is also called "Bo" (波).

The *Tuogulü* states: the *Huàn wáng fántuó jīng* (Sūtra of King Bhadra) and the *Jìzhì guǒ jīng* (Sūtra on the Fruits of the Śramaṇa), one fascicle each, are from the seventeenth fascicle of the *Dīrghāgama*;

the *Tiěchéng nílí jīng* (Sūtra of the Iron City Hell), one fascicle, is from the twelfth fascicle of the *Dīrghāgama* and is a different translation of the same text as the *Wǔtiānshǐ jīng* (Sūtra of the Five Messengers);
the *Ānòufēng jīng* (Sūtra of the Anupama Wind), one fascicle—“Anupama” being the Jin translation for “successive”—is from the *Madhyamāgama*.
Included herein is the *Ekottara-varga* (Volume 27), an alternative translation of the *Brāhmaṇa Ārāḍa-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, also known as the *Ārāḍa-sūtra*; one fascicle.
Also included is the *Niraya-sūtra*, an alternative translation of the thirty-seventh fascicle of the *Madhyama-āgama*, also known as the *Madhyama-āgama Niraya-sūtra*; one fascicle.
Alternatively, it is an alternative translation of the fifty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama-āgama*, titled the *Śīla-sūtra*.
*Śīlagandha-sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *Śīlaguṇa-sūtra*. Translated from the thirteenth fascicle of the *Ekottarika-āgama*;
a variant translation of fascicle fifty-one. *Phenapiṇḍa-parivarta-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Mahāphenapiṇḍa-sūtra* or the *Phenapiṇḍopama-sūtra*.
This shares the same original text as the *Pañcaskandhopamā-sūtra* and was translated from the *Saṃyukta-āgama*.

The tenth fascicle of the *Sūtra* (alternate translation): *The Sūtra of Yuyé* (one fascicle), also titled *The Sūtra on the Elder Visiting the Buddha to Speak of His Son’s Wife’s Lack of Reverence*, or alternatively called *The Sūtra of the Woman Yuyé*; second edition, same text as the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra*.
*The Sūtra of the Five Kinds of Suffering* (one fascicle); first edition, also titled *The Sūtra of the Five Sufferings of the Heavens*, or alternatively titled *The Five Realms*.
*Zhangju jing* (also titled *Jingchu zuigai yule fofa jing*, *Ziai jing*), one fascicle; alternatively called *Ziai buziai jing*.
Sengfang states that it was seen in the old catalogs. *Zhongxin jing*, one fascicle; alternatively called *Zhongxin zhengxing jing*.
The old catalogs state it is also called *Dazhong jing* or *Xiaozhongxin jing*. Sengfang’s catalog states it was translated by [An] Faxian.
In the *Six Perfections Compendium* (*Liùdù jí*), I have now examined and found the following works that were not previously seen as authentic scriptures:
one fascicle of the *Samsāra-pariṇāma-vijñāna-sūtra* (also known as the *Mahāmatsya-vastu-sūtra*); one fascicle of the *Ānanda-sapta-svapna-sūtra* (sometimes simply called the *Sapta-svapna-sūtra*);

one fascicle of the *Krauñca-anāgāmin-sūtra* (also known as the *Hédiāo*, though sometimes the character is written as *Kē*); and one fascicle of the *Navavarṣa-sūtra*. [Also listed: the *Bhikṣu-...*.
*Śrāvaka-dāna-sūtra*, one fascicle; also titled *Śrāvaka-bhikṣu-dāna-sūtra*. *Buddha-parinirvāṇa-mahākāśyapa-gamana-sūtra*, one fascicle;
also titled *Kāśyapa-gamana-buddha-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*. *Vatsa-sūtra*, one fascicle;
also known as the *Vatsaputra-sūtra*. Second edition; same text as the *Kṣīraprabhāsa-sūtra*. *Rājñī-mayūra-indra-mantra-sūtra*.
One fascicle; the third [fascicle] is the same text as that translated by Ji-zhi. *The Sūtra on the Seven Buddhas’ Binding of the Sesame Oil* (one fascicle);
the translator is lost, though it is recorded twice in the catalogs, one being called a different version. *The Sūtra of the Great Goddess Mother’s Vow-Mantra* (one fascicle).
*The Sūtra of the Divine Mantra of the Dharma-Vow of Uruvilvā*. *The Divine Mantra for Resolving the Calamity of the Sun*. One [fascicle].
*The Scripture on the Names of Deities and Divine Mantras*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on the Mantra for the Art of Tāṇḍila’s Sesame Oil*, one fascicle;
*The Scripture on the Mantra for the Description of Sesame Oil*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on the Case of the Maṇidhāna Deity and Divine Mantras*, one fascicle;
*The Scripture on the Divine Mantras of the Physician King Vailokyaprabha*, one fascicle—or alternatively titled *The Divine Mantras of the Physician King Vailokyaprabha as Asked by Ānanda*.

*Jīng lóngwáng zhòushuìyù jīng* (Sutra on the Dragon King’s Incantation for Bathing with Water), one fascicle; *Shíbā lóngwáng shénzhòu jīng* (Sutra of the Divine Incantations of the Eighteen Dragon Kings), one fascicle; *Qǐyǔ zhòu jīng* (Sutra of the Incantation for Requesting Rain), one fascicle;

*Zhǐyǔ zhòu jīng* (Sutra of the Incantation for Stopping Rain), one fascicle; *Qīnshuǐ jīng* (Sutra on the Offering of Water), one fascicle; *Huànshī Āiyínà shénzhòu jīng* (Sutra of the Divine Incantation of the Illusionist Āyina), one fascicle;

*Zhòushuǐ jīng* (Sutra of the Incantation for Water), one fascicle; *Yàozhòu jīng* (Sutra of the Incantation for Medicine), one fascicle; *Zhòudú jīng* (Sutra of the Incantation against Poison), one fascicle.

*Jiù shí qì bìng jīng* (Sutra on the Incantation for Wind Illnesses), one fascicle; *Jiù xiǎo'ér jīng* (Sutra on the Incantation for Infants), one fascicle; *Jiù chǐ jīng* (Sutra on the Incantation for Teeth), one fascicle.
In Sengyou’s *Shīyì lù* (Record of Lost Translations), another version with the same title is additionally recorded, though it is noted as a different manuscript.

One source calls it *Chóngchǐ* (Worm Teeth), while another calls it *Yúzhòu yá tòng jīng* (Incantation for Toothache). One fascicle. In Sengyou’s *Shīyì lù*, another version with the same title is additionally recorded.
It is said that there are variant versions titled *The Sutra on the Incantation for Toothache* (one fascicle) and *The Sutra on the Five Eyes* (one fascicle);

these are now suspected to have been produced by Nie Daozhen. There is also *The Text on the Method for Seeking the Five Eyes*, alternatively titled *The Text on the Precepts for Laymen and Laywomen Free from Desire* (one fascicle), also known as *The Text on the Twenty-two Precepts for Complete Practice*.
Furthermore, there is *The Sutra on the Retribution of Sinful Karma* (one fascicle).
*Jǐuàn yǔ zuìyè yīngbào jiàohuà dìyù jīng* (The Sutra on the Rebirth in Hell as Retribution for Karmic Offenses Corresponding to the Scroll), same text as [the above], one fascicle;

*Bāshī jiè jīng* (The Sutra of the Eight Preceptors’ Precepts), one fascicle, second edition; *Píngshā wáng wǔyuàn jīng* (The Sutra of King Bimbisāra’s Five Vows), one fascicle, also titled *Fúshājiā wáng jīng*, second edition;

*Yìzú jīng* (The Sutra of the Meaningful Feet), two fasciles, recorded by Fáng as being seen in the *Wǔlù* (Records of the Wu Kingdom), also said to be a different edition, second edition; *Shíshàn shí* (Ten Good Deeds, Ten [Evils]), second edition.
*Ējīng* (Sūtra on Evil), one fascicle; second translation. The *Wùlù* (Record of Wu) states it is the *Yìzhì chánfǎ jīng* (Sūtra on the Method of Contemplation for Different Treatments).

*Fàntiàn cèshù jīng* (Sūtra on the Numerical Calculations of Brahmā), one fascicle. The old catalog states it is the *Zhūtiān shì jīng* (Sūtra on the Affairs of Various Heavens) or the *Zhūtiān dì jīng* (Sūtra on the Grounds of Various Heavens), one fascicle.
*Shísòng bǐqiū jièběn* (Ten Recitations Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa), one fascicle. In the sixth year of the Dàyuán era, the monks from the three houses—Cún, Tánmótuō, and Zhú Sēngshū—combined [these texts].
I originally thought that this fascicle, as recorded in Baochang’s catalogue, should be the second edition;
it consists of two fascicles titled *The Concordance of the Three Versions of the Two Hundred and Sixty Precepts*, with the preface enlarged by the title "Da" (Great) and the character "Bhikṣu.

On the twentieth day of the sixth month in the sixth year of the Dàyuán era, at Xiè Zhènxi Sī, I collated the monks and carefully re-examined it, consulting the old records and those of Baochang. [Total: sixty-one items.]
Section Sixty-three: twenty-four works totaling twenty-four fascicles, beginning with the *Buddha-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* (upper part), are extant. Section Sixty-four:
thirty-seven works totaling thirty-nine fascicles, following the *Go-vatsa-sūtra*, are missing.
The śramaṇa Dharmarāta—
translated into Chinese as Fǎzhèng—
was a man from the Western Regions.
From the *xin-si* year, the sixth year of the Dàyuán era of Emperor Xiāowǔ,
until the *yì-wèi* year, the twentieth year of the same era, sixty-one sūtras,
including the *Cāiliánwéiwáng jīng* (Sūtra of King Pāriyātra), were translated at Xiè Zhèn-xī Temple in the capital of Yáng.
I have consulted the *Chángfáng lù*.
Furthermore, the *Chángfáng* and other records list forty-eight additional scriptures,
which are likewise said to have been translated by Fǎzhèng.
Since these are all separately produced excerpts from scriptures,
or are perhaps of doubtful or spurious origin,
they have all been deleted.

As described below, the *Shenming jiuhu jing* (Sutra on Saving and Protecting Life) and the *Jiuhu shenming ji renbing ku'e jing* (Sutra on Saving and Protecting Life and Relieving Humans from the Calamities of Sickness) were likewise compiled and included in the catalog of the True Scriptures (*zhengjing*). The old catalogs classify them as spurious; here, they are retained according to the old tradition. The *Zhuitian wen rulai jingjie bukeshiyi jing* (Sutra of the Gods Questioning the Tathāgata on the Inconceivable Admonitions) and the *Jian shui shijie jing* (Sutra on Seeing the Water World)—these two sutras both originate from the *Daji longwang jieyuan wulong shenzhou jing* (Great Collection Sutra on the Dragon King’s Vow and the Five Dragon Deity Spells).
The *Mahāsenāpati-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, the aforementioned two sūtras, the *Abhiṣeka-nirātma-sūtra*, the *Samantābhibhu-sūtra*, and the *Milinda-sūtra*—also called *Miliyan* or *Miliyan*.

The *Sūtra of the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven*, the *Ānapanasmi Sūtra*, and the *Milaṇḍa Sūtra*—these three sūtras were all translated together. The *Sūtra of the Names of the Thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa* was extracted from the *Sūtra of the Collection of the Six Pāramitās*. The preface to the *Bhadrakalpa Sūtra* states: "The *Bhadrakalpa Sūtra* explains two thousand one hundred *pāramitās*, with Krakucchanda Buddha as the first. This *Sūtra of the Thousand Buddhas' Names* has a separate translation that takes Krakutsunda Buddha as the initial head. Regarding the *Sūtra on the Thirty-three Heavens and Their Gardens*, Master Dao’an stated it was extracted from the Vinaya scriptures; Sengyou’s catalogue records that it was compiled at Xie Zhenxi Temple in the sixth month of the year Jingshen (the 20th year of the Dàyuán era of the Jin dynasty).
The Sūtra on the Five Dharmas by Which a Bhikṣu Enters Hell;
the Sūtra on the Disciple with a Disturbed Mind; the aforementioned three sūtras from the Ekottarika Āgama; and the Sūtra on the Great Heating Hell Spoken by the Buddha for the Bhikṣus.
The *Sūtra on Śakra Devānām Indra Visiting Maudgalyāyana and Emitting Light*;
the *Sūtra on Maudgalyāyana Seeing a Great-bodied Being with Burning Iron Wrapped Around Its Body*;
and the *Sūtra on Seeing a Being with Its Entire Body Smeared with Excrement*.
The Sūtra on the Iron Mill with Blazing Fire atop the Heads of Sentient Beings;
the Sūtra on the Rāva Bird Being Seized by a Hawk;
and the Sūtra on Entering Hell through the Accomplishment of Ten Unwholesome Deeds.
The Scripture on the Method of Serpent-Walking;
the Scripture on a Bhikṣu Encountering a Heavenly Son Emitting Light;
the Scripture on Devas and Asuras Desiring to Engage in Battle.
The Sūtra on Śakra Devendra Receiving the Precepts;
the Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Questioning the Buddha Concerning the Causes and Conditions of Śakra Devendra;
the Sūtra on the Four Heavenly Kings Inspecting the World.
The *Buddha Sees the Crown of the Brahmā Heaven Sūtra*,
the *Sūtra on Śakra’s Compassionate Heart and Victory in Battle*,
and the *Sūtra on the Celestial Deities’ Prohibited Jewels*.
The Sūtra on King Aśoka’s Offering to the Bodhi Tree;
the Sūtra on Exhorting Practice with Realization;
and the Sūtra on Dharmas Corresponding to the Precepts.
The *Dhyānapāripūri-sūtra*, spoken by the Buddha for the bhikṣus; the following twenty sūtras are all also found in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*:
the *Tittira-sūtra*, the *Kūrma-markaṭa-sūtra*, and the *Kīṭa-śṛgāla-kāka-sūtra* (or, as some versions read, the *Vihaga-sūtra*).
The Discourse on the Death of a Disciple;
the Discourse on the Donkey and the Camel;
and the Discourse on the Crow King of Kosala (or without the character "wu").
The *Mayūra-jātaka*,
the *Dampati-jātaka*, the *Tittira-jātaka*, and the other eight sūtras are all contained within the *Jātaka-nidāna*.
The *Go-sahasra-jātaka* [is also included therein].
The *Saṃyuktacaryābhūmi-sūtra*,
the *Kapotamāṃsa-sūtra*, and the *Gośālaka-sūtra*— these three sūtras are all found in the *Avadāna-śataka*.
The *Nāraka-sattva-parasparavihiṃsana-sūtra* appears in the *Caryābhūmi-śāstra*.
The *Āṭānāṭīya Sūtra* (赤𭉨烏喻經) and the *Ānanda-uruvilvā-mātṛ-sūtra* (阿難多洹羅云母經).
These two sūtras, including the *Āṭānāṭīya*, appear within the *Za piyu jing* (雜譬喻經);
they are the second [sūtras] extracted from the sixty-fascicle *Madhyama Āgama* (or the fifty-eight fascicle version), translated in the eleventh month of the first year of the Long’an era.
Recorded on the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month in the second year [of the Yixi era] at Heng Temple in Tokyo on the tenth day of the month.
Transmitted by Dharmaratna; the śramaṇas Tóngdào and others acted as scribes. Preface composed by Dàocí. See the *Jùlù* (Record of the Patriarchs).
The *Ekottarika Āgama*, fifty-one fascicles, second edition, produced in the first month of the first year of the Lóng'ān era.
This differs slightly from the version by Nandi; it was transcribed by Zhu Daozu.
It is not fixed at either forty-two or thirty-three fascicles, though there are also versions consisting of sixty fascicles, as seen in the records of Zhu Daozu and Baochang.
The *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* in four fascicles—also called the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*—was composed by the Venerable Dharmasri during the sixteenth year of the Dàyuán era.
In his sixtieth year, at Mount Lu, he translated the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Fǎdù lùn) in two fascicles for Dharma Master Huìyuǎn;
Dào cí acted as the scribe and Master Yuǎn composed the preface, as recorded in Sēngyòu’s *Lù*.

This second translation, produced in the sixteenth year of the Dàyuán era at Mount Lu for Dharma Master Yuǎn—whose preface was also composed by Master Yuǎn—is largely identical with slight variations to that by Nántí, or perhaps it is the third [translation].
The *Bié lù* (Separate Record) states: "One fascicle," or simply "Three Dharma-Degree Treatises" (*Sān fǎ dù wú lùn*), without the character "lùn";
or it is called a "sūtra" (*jīng*) or a "sūtra-treatise" (*jīng-lùn*). See Sengyou’s record. *Jiào shòu bǐqūní fǎ* (Methods for Instructing Bhikṣuṇīs), one fascicle;

Sengfang says it is seen in the *Bié lù*, and it is also said to have been produced at Mount Lu. Thus, these five works comprise one hundred and eighteen fascicles; the first four works comprise one hundred and ten [fascicles].
The seven-fascicle version is preserved, while the latter one-fascicle version is missing.
The śramaṇa Saṃghadeva, whose name is translated into Chinese as Zhòngtiān (Assembly of Gods),...
Some call him T'i-ho;
this is due to a corruption of the pronunciation.
He was a native of Kaśmīra.
Having entered the Way to practice and study, he traveled afar to seek out an enlightened master.
His learning encompassed the Tripiṭaka, which he had extensively memorized and mastered;
he was particularly adept at the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*, penetrating its most subtle nuances.
He constantly recited the *Tridharmaka-śāstra*, sighing over and savoring its meaning day and night,
regarding it as the treasury of the Way.
He was a person of brilliant character and profound discernment.
His deportment was mild and respectful, and he was dedicated to instructing others;
he was diligent and never weary.
During the Jianyuan era of the Fu Qin dynasty, he came to Chang’an.
He propagated the Dharma and translated two treatises,
both of which are recorded in the *Qin lu*.
Later, during the sixteenth year of the Taiyuan era (the *xinmao* year) of the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty, he traveled to propagate the teachings in the Jiangzuo region.
Previously, Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu had been devotedly diligent regarding the sublime scriptures and had extensively collected the Tripitaka.
With an open mind and a seat prepared for him, he looked out expectantly for eminent guests from afar.
Upon hearing that [the Master] had arrived, he immediately invited him to enter Mount Lu.
In that same year, he requested the translation of the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*, the *Tridharmaka-śāstra*,
and other texts. Vasubandhu then, at the Prajñā Terrace,
held the Sanskrit manuscripts in his hands while orally proclaiming them in the Jin language.
He discarded the ornamental to preserve the practical and exhausted the root of the meaning;
what is transmitted today is largely his literary style.
In the first year of the Long’an era of Emperor An, the Dingyou year, he came to travel in Jiankang.
Among the princes and eminent scholars of refined elegance during the Jin dynasty, there were none who did not attend his gatherings and pay their respects.

At that time, the Minister of the Household, General of the East, and Marquis of Dongting, Wang Xun of Langya—according to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*), the *Record of Sengyou* (*Sengyou lu*), the *Record of Changfang* (*Changfang lu*), and others—all stated that Wang Xun composed the preface to the *Madhyama Āgama*. Furthermore, it says "Wang Yuanlin"; Yuanlin was indeed the courtesy name of Xun.
Ya possessed faith and wisdom;
he upheld the True Dharma, established a vihāra, and widely invited a multitude of students.
Once Deva arrived, Yao Xun immediately extended an invitation to him.
He continued to lecture on the Abhidharma in that residence,
where eminent monks gathered in great numbers.

As Vasubandhu’s doctrinal principles were refined and his arguments were clear and incisive, he illuminated the profound depths of the meaning, and the assembly was all moved to joy and enlightenment.
That winter, Yao Xun gathered more than forty śramaṇas of the Institute for the Study of Meaning, including Shi Huichi and others,
and again invited Guṇabhadra to translate the *Ekottarika-āgama* at that monastery.
The Śramaṇa Saṃgharakṣa from Kaśmīra held the Sanskrit original,
while Deva translated it into the language of Jin;
it was not completed until the following summer.
The śramaṇa Daoci of Yuzhou received [the teachings] in writing;
Li Bao and Tang Hua of the Wu region transcribed them together.
Deva produced five works totaling one hundred and eighteen fascicles at both Mount Lu and Jiankang.
Deva traveled extensively among both Chinese and foreign lands, becoming thoroughly acquainted with their customs.
He was composed, quick-witted, and skilled in conversation;
his reputation for spiritual transformation and renown was heard everywhere.
Its conclusion is unknown.

One fascicle of the *Dvādaśavyūha-sūtra* (Twelve Wanderings Sutra), the second translation produced by [An]Shigao, differs slightly from that translated by Kang Senglang; this is noted in Zhu Daozu’s *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty* and the *Record of Baochang*. This one work in one fascicle is extant.
The śramaṇa Kālodāyin— translated into Chinese as Shishui (Time-Water)—
was a man from the Western Regions.
Hongyu was a man of skillful means who traveled through various kingdoms while cherishing the Way.
In the seventeenth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu, the Renchen year,
he translated the *Dvādaśavyākaraṇa-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Twelve Wanderings), one fascicle.

*Yìyì jīng* (Sūtra on Increasing the Mind), three fascicles; second appearance in *Zhūdào zǔ Jìnshì zá lù* (Zhu Daozu’s Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty). *Zhū Shíxíng Hàn lù* (Zhu Shixing’s Han Records) states it consists of two fascicles, and the translator is not specified. This one work in three fascicles is currently missing.
The śramaṇa Kang Daohe possessed the dignity of preceptual virtue and served as a model for all beings.
In the year of Jingshen, the twenty-first year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu.
He translated one fascicle of the *Yiyi jing* (Sūtra on the Meaning of Benefit).
Regarding the *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra* in sixty fascicles: it was initially produced in fifty fascicles during the Yuan era;
later, people divided it into sixty. The śramaṇa Zhifaling obtained the Sanskrit original from Khotan in the third year of the Yixi era.

On the tenth day of the month, at Daochang Temple, the translation of the *Birth of the Immeasurable Gate Dhāraṇī Sūtra* (or, as some say, the *New Secret Dhāraṇī Sūtra*) was completed on the tenth day of the sixth month of the second year of the Yuexi era;
it was transcribed by Faye. It is recorded in the two catalogs of Zu and You.
This fifth edition is identical to Zhi Qian’s *Immeasurable Gate Secret Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, which was translated at Mount Lu.

The *Dafangdeng rulai zang jing* (Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra), one fascicle—also simply called the *Rulai zang jing*, third [in the collection]—was translated at Daochang Monastery in the second year of the Yuanxi era.

It is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Jin shi za lu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) and Sengyou’s *Lu* (Catalog). It is also found in the *Guanfo sanmei hai [jing]* (Sūtra on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha).
Note: The entry in the *Zu you fang deng lu* (Record of the Zu and You Monasteries) that lists it separately as the *Xin weimi chi* (Newly Compiled Secret Retention) is an error.

The *Sūtra* consists of ten fascicles; it is also called the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* or the *Guanfo sanmei jing*, and it appears in the *Jin shi lu* (Catalogue of the Jin Dynasty) by Zhu Daozu as well as in the *Sengyou lu*.
It is also said to have appeared during the Song dynasty.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* consists of forty fascicles—or thirty fascicles—and its Sanskrit original was brought from the kingdom of Magadha by Faxian in the tenth month of the twelfth year of the Yixi era.
In the first month, at Daochang Temple, he [Dharmarakṣa] produced [the *Mahāsāṃghika-bhikṣu-prātimokṣa*] together with Faxian; this is seen in the record of Zhu Daozu.

Sengyou’s record places it under Faxian because it was translated jointly. One scroll of the *Mahāsāṃghika-bhikṣu-prātimokṣa*, also titled the *Mahāsāṃghika-śīla-mūla*, is the second production from Daochang Temple;
this is seen in Baochang’s record. Sengyou places it under Faxian and Juexian as having been translated together.
In the [relevant] year, he obtained two fascicles of the *Dharmatrāta-dhyāna-sūtra* (also known as the *Yogācārabhūmi*, translated as "The Stages of Practice"), which was produced at Mount Lu;
it is also called the *Aśubha-bhāvanā* and the *Yoga-upāya-dhyāna-sūtra*.
Sengyou states that it has seventeen common names, including "The Stages of Practice," and that Master Huiyuan composed its preface, which is preserved among the monastic records.
*Sūtra on Mañjuśrī’s Aspiration* (一卷), or with the character "gāthā" added; translated at Douchang Temple in the second year of the Yuánxī era.

According to the *Sēngyòu Lù* and *Bǎochàng Lù*, the postscript to this scripture states that when the four assemblies of foreign lands pay homage to the Buddha, they frequently recite this sūtra to make aspirations and seek the Buddha-way. *New Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* (二卷).
In the second year of the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty (421 CE), it was brought out at Daochang Monastery by Sengyou and Baochang.
It is the eighth translation and is identical in text to the *Bodhisattva-mūla-karma-sūtra* (one fascicle) produced by Lokakṣema, Zhi Chen, Zhi Qian, Sengyi, and others;
it is also simply titled the *Benye jing*. This is seen in the *Changfang* and other records of Sengyou.
The *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra* (Great Perfection of Wisdom Entering the Canon) currently lacks [certain portions], yet they have been preserved.

The *Sūtra on the Purification of the Six Pāramitās*, one fascicle, appears in the catalogs of Sengyou and Changfang. The *Upāyahṛdaya-śāstra* (Treatise on the Mind of Skillful Means), one fascicle, was translated by Dharmaya; it appears in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
Initially, the *Past Causes and Effects Sūtra*, four fascicles, was produced; Changfang states it appears in the *Bie-lu* (Separate Catalog). The above comprises ten items.
Three sections totaling one hundred and twenty-five fascicles; the *Mañjuśrīpraṇidhāna* (upper) in eight sections totaling one hundred and sixteen fascicles currently exists;
the *Amitāyus Sūtra* (lower) in five sections totaling nine fascicles is missing.
The śramaṇa Buddhayaśas— known in the Jin language as Juexian (Awakened Virtue)—
was originally of the Śākya clan.
He was a native of Kapilavastu and a descendant of King Amṛtodana. His grandfather,
Dharmadeva— translated into Chinese as Fǎtiān (Dharma-Heaven)— once engaged in trade with Northern India and settled there.
His father, Dharmasūrya—translated here as "Dharma Sun"—died when he was young; the virtuous Tripiṭaka Master Xian lived in solitude with his mother.
After five years, his mother also passed away, and he was raised by his maternal relatives.
His great-uncle Kumāralīva, having heard of his intelligence and feeling pity for him as an orphan,
welcomed him back and ordained him as a śrāmaṇera.
When he reached the age of seventeen, he and several fellow students devoted themselves solely to the task of memorizing and reciting the scriptures.
The assembly all completed their recitation in one month, while Bhadra finished it in a single day.
His teacher sighed in admiration and said,
"Bhadra in one day is the equal of thirty men."
Upon receiving full ordination, he applied himself with diligence to his practice;
he studied the various scriptures extensively and attained profound mastery in many areas.
From his youth, he was renowned for his expertise in meditation and the Vinaya.
He once traveled together with his fellow student Saṃghadatta to Kaśmīra, where they lived together for many years.
Although Saṃghadatta admired his talent and brilliance, he did not yet fathom his true character.
Later, while sitting in meditation in a private room with the door closed, he suddenly saw Xian arrive;
startled, he asked where he had come from.
Xian replied:
He briefly went to Tuṣita Heaven to pay his respects to Maitreya;
having finished speaking, he vanished.
Upatiṣya knew him to be a holy man, yet he could not fathom the depth of his realization.
Later, having repeatedly witnessed his noble spiritual transformations, he began to revere him and inquire after his realization;
only then did he learn that [the Master] had attained the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmin).
He constantly desired to travel abroad to propagate the teachings and observe the customs of various lands.
There was a monk from the Qin dynasty named Mingyan who traveled west to Jibin.
Beholding the purity and excellence of the Dharma assembly there, he looked toward the east with a sigh of longing and said,
"Among my own peers here, there are those with such aspirations for the Way."
However, not having encountered a true master, he had no means by which to attain awakening.
He therefore inquired among the people of the kingdom as to who was capable of propagating the teachings in the eastern lands,
and they all replied:
There was one named Buddhabhadra,
born in the city of Nagarahāra in India;
his lineage had been hereditary for generations, and they followed the path of learning.
Having left home at the age of seven, he thoroughly mastered the sūtras and śāstras.
In his youth, he received instruction from the Great Dhyāna Master Buddhadasa,
who was also then residing in Kaśmīra.
He then said to Yan,
"The one who can revitalize the monastic community and proclaim the transmission of the Chan dharma is none other than Buddha-tuo.
Yan’s requests were so earnest and persistent that he could not refuse.
Xian was moved by compassion and granted his request.
Thereupon, he left the community, took leave of his master, packed his provisions, and set out toward the east.
He traveled for three years, enduring the full cycle of cold and heat.
Having crossed the Pamir Mountains, he traveled through six kingdoms;
their rulers, admiring his far-reaching mission, were all delighted to provide him with provisions and stipends.
Upon reaching Jiaozhi, he boarded a ship and proceeded by sea, arriving at an island.
The worthy one pointed with his finger toward the mountain and said,
"You may stop here.
The ship's captain replied:
Travelers on the road cherish their time, for a favorable wind is difficult to encounter and one must not stop.
After traveling more than two hundred li, the wind suddenly shifted and blew the ship back toward the island.
Only then did the people realize his divine power; they all took him as their teacher, following his every move and decision.
Later, when a favorable wind arose and his companions all set sail,
Xian said, "It must not be moved," and the ship's captain accordingly halted.
Subsequently, those who had set out first were all defeated at once.
Later, in the midst of the dark night, he suddenly ordered all the ships to depart together,
but none were willing to comply.
Xian personally took up the hawsers and set out alone on a single ship.
Before long, the pirates arrived; those who remained were all plundered and killed.
Shortly thereafter, they reached Donglai Commandery in Qingzhou.
Upon hearing that Kumārajīva was in Cháng'ān, he immediately went to join him.
Kumārajīva was greatly delighted to engage in discussions on the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Sengzhēn brought forth the profound and subtle mysteries, gaining much insight and benefit.
Tanyou said to Kumārajīva, "Your exegesis does not go beyond what others have conceived; why then have you attained such high renown?
Kumārajīva replied:
"It is simply because I am old; how could I possibly be expected to engage in elegant discourse?
Whenever Kumārajīva encountered points of doubt, he would invariably consult with him to reach a resolution.
At that time, Yao Xing, the ruler of Qin, was single-mindedly devoted to the scriptures and the Dharma, providing offerings to more than three thousand monks.
He traveled back and forth between the palace and the inner quarters, diligently attending to worldly affairs;
only Xian maintained stillness and did not join the multitude.
Later, he said to his disciples:
Yesterday, I saw five ships set sail together from my native region.
Subsequently, my disciple informed outsiders of this.
The veteran monks of Guanzhong all considered it a display of supernatural wonders intended to delude the masses.
Furthermore, while Xian resided in Chang’an, he widely propagated the practice of dhyāna.
Those from all quarters who delighted in tranquility came to him upon hearing his reputation.
However, there were differences in the depth of their engagement with the study and the intensity of their realization of the Dharma.
Deceitful and hypocritical individuals took advantage of this to act with guile and craftiness. One disciple,
having practiced contemplative conduct for a short time, claimed for himself that he had attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin.
Before Xian could investigate the matter, rumors spread abroad.
He was subjected to such widespread slander and vilification that he faced the threat of unforeseen calamity.
Consequently, some of his disciples hid their names and departed in secret.
Some even scaled walls and fled in the night;
within half a day, the crowd had almost entirely dispersed.
Yet Xian remained composed and indifferent, not taking it to heart at all.
At that time, the senior monks Sengqie and Daoheng said to Xian,
"The Buddha himself did not permit [his disciples] to preach the Dharma they had attained themselves.
Previously, you spoke of five ships that were about to arrive, but it proved to be empty and without substance."
Furthermore, as the disciples deceive one another and give rise to mutual disagreements and contradictions,
and since they thus violate the Vinaya and their views on principle are discordant,
you should depart at once and not remain for long.
Xian said, "My body is like a drifting water lily; it is very easy for me to go or stay.
I only regret that my inner aspirations have not yet been fully realized, which is why I feel such deep sorrow.
Thereupon, he set out together with over forty disciples, including Huiguan.
His countenance remained composed and showed no sign of distress;
those who recognized the truth all sighed with lamentation.
The funeral procession, consisting of both monastics and laypeople, numbered several thousand.
Upon hearing of his departure, Yao Xing was filled with regret and said to Daoheng,
"The śramaṇa Fotuoxian has come here from afar, carrying the Way, wishing to proclaim the bequeathed teachings."
That these words remained unspoken is truly a matter of deep regret.
How could the fault of a single person’s speech cause ten thousand men to be without a guide?
Consequently, an imperial edict was issued to recall him.
The worthy one said to the messenger,
"I truly understand your gracious intent and shall not presume to seek further instructions. Thereupon,
he led his companions and set out on the journey under the cover of night.
Pointing south toward Mount Lu,
the śramaṇa Huiyuan, who had long admired his reputation and virtue,
dispatched a messenger to the Guanzhong region to deliver a letter of entreaty.
Later, when he arrived at Mount Lu, Huiyuan greeted him with joy as if they were old acquaintances.
Huiyuan maintained that Huixian’s expulsion was due to the transgressions of his disciples;
furthermore, regarding the prophecy of the five ships, it refers only to those who share the same intent.
He was likewise not in violation of the Vinaya;
he then dispatched his disciple Tanyong to deliver a letter to the Yao ruler and the monastic community of Guanzhong to resolve the matter of his suspension.
Huìyuǎn subsequently requested the translation of various sutras on meditation and Abhidharma.
Xian’s intention was to travel and convert others, never seeking comfort in his dwelling.
After staying at the mountain for about a year,
he traveled west to Jiangling, where he encountered a foreign shipowner.
Shortly thereafter, upon further inquiry,
it was confirmed that these were indeed the five ships from India he had previously seen.
People throughout the entire region vied with one another to come and pay their respects.
He would not accept any offerings that were presented to him.
Carrying his alms bowl, he went on his rounds for food regardless of whether the donor was noble or humble.
At that time, Yuan Bao of Chen County served as the Chief Secretary to the Grand Marshal of Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty.
When Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty went south to campaign against Liu Dun,
Bao followed the provincial administration to Jiangling.
There, the disciple Huiguan of the eminent general went to Bao to beg for food.
Liu Bao was by nature neither reverent nor trusting and treated him with great scantiness.
Before he was satiated, [the monk] took his leave;
Liu Bao said, "It seems you have not had enough."
Furthermore, please stay a little longer.
Xian said:
"Because the donor's intention for giving is limited, what has been prepared is now exhausted."
Bao immediately called his attendants to bring more rice.
When the rice was indeed exhausted,
Bao felt great shame.
Shortly thereafter, he asked Huiguan,
"What kind of person is this śramaṇa?
Huiguan replied:
His virtuous measure was so lofty and remote that it could not be fathomed by ordinary men.
Bao deeply marveled at his extraordinary nature and informed the Grand Marshal (Taishou).
The Grand Marshal invited him for an audience and revered him with the utmost sincerity, providing him with the most excellent provisions.
Shortly thereafter, the Grand Marshal returned to the capital.
He invited [Kumārajīva] to return with him and settled him at Daochang Temple.
Kumārajīva’s ritual protocols were simple and austere, differing from Chinese customs.
His aspirations were pure and far-reaching, and he possessed a refined and profound elegance.
Fǎshī Sēngbì of Yángdū wrote in a letter to the śramaṇa Bǎolín:
"The Meditation Master of Dòuchǎng possesses a truly great resolve."
"He was indeed a man of such refined elegance, a king of India.
Such was the acclaim he received.

Previously, the śramaṇa Zhi Falin had obtained a Sanskrit manuscript of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* consisting of thirty-six thousand verses in the kingdom of Khotan, but it had not yet been translated into Chinese.
In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, Meng Yi, the Interior Prefect of Wu Commandery, and Chu Shudu, General of the Right Guard, invited him to serve as the master translator.
He then personally held the Sanskrit texts and, together with more than one hundred people including the śramaṇas Faye, Huiyan, and Tanyi, translated [the work] at Daochang Temple.
He elucidated the meaning of the texts and harmonized the traditions of China and the Western Regions, masterfully capturing the essence of the sutras;
thus, the Huayan Hall still exists at Daochang Temple today.
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Faxian requested Xuanzang to translate the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, which he had obtained in India as a Sanskrit manuscript.
From the second year of Long’an (wùxū) during the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty until the second year of Yongchū (xīn yǒu) of the Song dynasty,
Xuán translated thirteen works in total, including the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, at two locations: Yangdu and Mount Lu.

He thoroughly investigated its profound purport and exhaustively realized the meaning of the text. Buddhabhadra entered *nirvāṇa* in the sixth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty at the age of seventy-one.

Furthermore, the two catalogs by Sengyou and Changfang state that Buddhabhadra produced a "new" version of the *Mimi chi jing* (Sūtra on Holding the Subtle and Secret), which is the *Sheng wuliangmen chi jing* (Sūtra on Producing Immeasurable Doors). This is because it does not correspond to the earlier translation by Zhi Qian; thus, the word "new" was added to distinguish it from that. Moreover, there are the *Bodhisattva shizhu jing* (Sūtra on the Ten Stages of the Bodhisattva) and the *Benye jing* (Sūtra on Original Vows). These two sūtras are both separate chapters of the *Avataṃsaka*. Since Buddhabhadra had already translated the main body of the *Avataṃsaka*, it was inappropriate to produce these sūtras separately. Regarding the *Benye jing*, it is included in the catalog of the canon and remains preserved as its original text has not yet been seen. As for the *Shizhu jing*, it was deleted and not established [in the canon].
*Zawen lushi* (Miscellaneous Questions on Vinaya Matters), two fascicles; first appeared in the *Changfang lu*. This one work in two fascicles was originally missing.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Dharma (translated into Chinese as "Dharma") during the Jin dynasty.
He was well-versed in the Vinaya teachings.
On the second day of the third month of the fourth year of the Long’an era (the *gengzi* year) of Emperor An’s reign,
he [passed away] at the monastery of Wang Fadu, the Minister of the Secretariat, in Yangdu.
More than twenty virtuous monks, including the śramaṇa Shi Sengzun, requested the translation of the *Zawen lushi* (Miscellaneous Questions on Vinaya Matters).
The preface at the beginning of the volume clarifies the boundaries regarding the mutual interactions between the property of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
The distinctions [between these] are of great importance and must be carefully guarded against.

The *Vinaya-śāstra-pūrvapīṭhikā* (序) in three fascicles of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (十誦律)—also known as the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya-pūrvapīṭhikā*—is now combined with the final three fascicles of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. This is what Fǎng calls the *Vinaya-bhāṇaka*; the commentary states it is the "Excellent Bhāṇaka" (*Subha-bhāṇaka*) following the *Daśabhāṇavāra*. This *Subha-bhāṇaka* consists of four fascicles and corresponds to the tenth bhāṇaka within the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. According to the *Lidai sanbao ji* (二秦錄), there were also two fascicles titled *Vinaya-vastu-saṃyukta-praśna* (雜問律事). Of these two sections totaling five fascicles, the former—the *Vinaya-pūrvapīṭhikā* in three fascicles—is currently extant; however, the latter—the *Vinaya-vastu-saṃyukta-praśna* in two fascicles—is originally missing.
The śramaṇa Vimalākṣa—
translated into Chinese as Wugouyan (Stainless Eye)—
was a native of Jibin.
He was serene and possessed great resolve and vigor.
Having left the household life to tread the Way, he achieved his purpose through rigorous asceticism.
His eyes were blue, and thus he was also known as the Vinaya Master Blue-Eye (Qingyan Lishi).
Previously residing in Kucha, he extensively propagated the Vinaya and other teachings;
scholars from all quarters vied with one another to go and study under him,
and Kumārajīva was among those who participated at that time.
When Kucha fell, he fled to Uḍḍiyāna; shortly thereafter,
he heard that Kumārajīva was in Chang’an, extensively propagating the treasury of the sūtras.
Furthermore, wishing to cause the supreme teachings of the Vinaya to once again permeate the Eastern lands,
he took up his staff and traveled through the drifting sands, braving dangers as he entered the East.
In the eighth year of the Hongshi era of the Yao Qin dynasty, he arrived in Guanzhong.
Kumārajīva treated him with the respect due to a teacher;
moreover, he was delighted to have met him from afar.
When Kumārajīva passed away, [the Master]...
Furthermore, during the Yixi era of Emperor An’s reign, he traveled to the region west of the Passes.
He halted at Shouchun and stayed at Shijian Temple,
where his disciples gathered like clouds as he extensively propagated the Vinaya.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* in fifty-eight fascicles translated by Kumārajīva has its final section called the "Bhāṇavāra on Goodness" (*Kalyāṇa-bhāṇavāra*).
This refers to the exposition of the methods for receiving the precepts and various matters concerning the accomplishment of wholesome dharmas;
it is named "Bhāṇavāra on Goodness" according to its essential meaning.
Furthermore, because the later revision changed the "Recitation" (Sūtra-piṭaka) into the "Vinaya Recitation," both names have persisted.

There was also a three-fascicle *Vinaya Preface* which was placed at the end, making a total of sixty-one fascicles. However, the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* and the *Catalogue of Zhangfang* claim that the original fifty-eight fascicles were expanded into sixty-one; this is not entirely accurate. Regarding the three-fascicle *Vinaya Preface*, some recent editions of the scripture place it after the ninth recitation and before the tenth recitation, corresponding to fascicles 55, 56, and 57, but this is incorrect. Upon examining an ancient copy of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is found after the tenth recitation, corresponding to fascicles 59 through 61. What I have done now is to follow the ancient manuscript as the correct version. Recently, I traveled south to Jiangling.
At Xinsi Temple, he opened a summer lecture on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
Having mastered the Jin language, he was exceptionally adept at receiving and explaining it;
he extensively expounded upon the subtle essence of "unconditioned action" (*avijñapti*) at that time, and those who analyzed the text to seek its principles gathered there like a forest.
Those who clearly understood the articles and knew the prohibitions were also numerous;
this was due to the great propagation of the Vinaya-piṭaka by Saṃghavarman.
Later, he produced two fascicles titled *Zawen lushi* (Miscellaneous Questions on Vinaya Matters).
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) records that Daochang Huiquan,
having thoroughly investigated the essential tenets, compiled his writings on the gravity of internal prohibitions into two fascicles.
Upon its return to the capital, monks and nuns searched for it and vied with one another to copy it.
At that time, a popular saying among the common people went:
"Biluo’s vulgar words were recorded by Huiquan’s talent."
The people of the capital copied it so extensively that the price of paper rose as high as jade.
It is said that these miscellaneous inquiries regarding Vinaya matters were made by Daochang Huiguan, who, having doubts concerning the teachings, consulted on them according to specific issues.
Vimalākṣa provided the definitive explanations, which [Huiguo] recorded as he heard them;
he compiled them into two fascicles that circulated throughout the world.
There was no separate Sanskrit manuscript for this;
it was translated by Vimalākṣa.
As for the one attributed to Dharmaruci, that too was likely an erroneous entry by the cataloguer. Later, he moved to Shouchun, where he passed away at Shijian Temple.
He was seventy-seven years old.
Regarding the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* in six fascicles, the *Jingji* (Record of the Scripture) states that the *Vaipulya-mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* consists of ten fascicles;

this fourth translation was produced by [Dharmakṣema] together with Juexian at Daochang Temple on the first day of the tenth month in the thirteenth year of the Yixi era, under the auspices of Baoyun.
The transcription was completed on the second day of the first month of the fourteenth year.

According to the two catalogs by Daozu and Sengyou, there are three fascicles—or perhaps two fascicles—of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which is an alternative translation of the initial section of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the *Cankrama-sūtra*.
Both detailed records state that this is the *Vaipulya Nirvāṇa* revealed [by the Buddha], and it is not simply the aforementioned *Mahānirvāṇa-sūtra* with the term "vaipulya" added.
The title of this text on the *nirvāṇa* of the Hīnayāna appears to be a literal translation;
it is seen in the two catalogs of Sengyou and Baochang as the first volume of the *Zazang jing*, where its second appearance is identical to the *Guiwen Mulian Egui Baoying jing*.
It is also seen in the two catalogs of Sengyou and Baochang as the first volume of the *Shengqi biquni jieben*, which is also called the *Biquni [jieben]*.
The *Prātimokṣa-saṃghī-śīla-mūla* (Bōluómìjī sēngqījìběn), translated jointly by [Guṇabhadra] and Juéxián; recorded in the Chángfáng Catalogue.

The *Record of Travels to India* (Lìyóu Tiānzhú jìchuán), one fascicle, also known as the *Faxian Zhuan*; records Faxian’s own account of his travels to and from India, recorded in the Chángfáng Catalogue.
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* (Zá āpítán xīn), thirteen fascicles; the second edition, translated during the Fúqín period by Saṃghavarman.

The versions produced by Deva and others are identical; see Sengyou’s Catalogue. Faxian states that he co-translated the *Buddha-you-tianzhu-ji* (Record of the Buddha’s Travels in India) in one fascicle with Juexian;

see Sengyou’s Catalogue. Of the seven works totaling twenty-six fascicles mentioned above, the first five works totaling twelve fascicles are extant, while the latter two works totaling fourteen fascicles are missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Faxian’s original surname was Gong;
he was a native of Pingyang.
Faxian had three elder brothers, the second of whom passed away when he was still a young child.
His father, filled with fear, allowed him to go forth into homelessness when he was several years old.
After living as a householder for several years, he fell gravely ill and was on the verge of death.
He was sent back to the monastery, where he recovered after staying for two nights;
however, he refused to return home.
His mother longed to see him, but she was unable to do so.
He built a small hut outside the gate to accommodate those coming and going. At the age of ten, he encountered the sorrow of his father's death.
Because his mother was a widow with no other support, his uncle pressured him to return to secular life.
Huiyan said,
"It was not because I had a father that I left the household life;
it was precisely because I wished to distance myself from the dust of the world and depart from secular life that I entered the Way."
His uncle approved of his words and desisted.
Shortly thereafter, his mother passed away;
his natural filiality exceeded that of ordinary men.
Once the funeral rites were completed, he immediately returned to the monastery.
On one occasion, while he was harvesting rice in a field with several dozen fellow students,
some starving bandits appeared, intending to seize their grain.
All the śrāmaṇeras fled in every direction;
only Huixian remained alone and said to the bandits,
"If you require grain, take as much as you wish."
"It is simply because you did not practice giving in the past that you are now born into this life of hunger and poverty.
If you continue to seize from others now, it will be even more severe in future lives.
I have spoken to you out of concern for you in advance."
Having finished speaking, he immediately returned.
The bandits abandoned the grain and departed.
Among the several hundred monks, there was none who did not express deep admiration and submission.
Having received the full precepts, his aspirations and conduct were pure and his ritual observances were solemn.
He often lamented that the sūtras and vinaya were incomplete and discordant, and he vowed to seek them out.
In the third year of the Long’an era of Emperor An’s reign, he set forth.

Together with his fellow students Huijing, Daozheng, Huiying, Huiwei, and others, he set out from Chang’an and crossed westward through the River of Sand; above there were no flying birds, and below there were no running beasts.
Looking out in all four directions, the vast expanse was boundless and its destination unfathomable;
one could only rely on the sun to determine east and west,
and use human bones to mark the path.
There were frequent hot winds and malevolent spirits; anyone encountering them would surely die.
Xuǎn entrusted himself to his karmic conditions and surrendered his life, truly passing through these perils and hardships.
After a while, he reached the Pamir Mountains (Congling), where snow accumulates throughout both winter and summer.
There were malevolent dragons that spat forth poisonous winds and rains of sand and gravel.
The mountain path was perilous, with cliffs rising sheer for thousands of fathoms.
In the past, someone had carved a passage through the rock and constructed a flight of stairs alongside it, totaling more than seven hundred steps.
Furthermore, he traversed the river by treading upon a suspended rope for more than several dozen li—
places that neither Zhang Qian nor Ganfu had reached during the Han dynasty.
Next, as he crossed the Lesser Snow Mountains, a violent cold wind suddenly arose.
Huìjǐng’s teeth chattered with fear and he could not move forward.
He said to Fǎxiǎn, "I am about to die; you should leave at once so that we do not perish together."
His words ended and he passed away.
Sengxian stroked him and wept, saying, "Our original plan has not been realized; what can be done about this fate?"
Furthermore, relying on his own strength and traveling alone, he eventually crossed perilous mountain passes.
Having traversed more than thirty kingdoms in total,
he reached Northern India and subsequently proceeded to Central India.
When they were still more than thirty li away from the city of Rājagṛha,
they stayed at a monastery as evening approached.
The following morning, Xuán intended to go to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.
The temple monks remonstrated with him, saying,
"The road is extremely perilous and there are many black lions that frequently devour people;
by what means could you possibly reach it?"
Xian said:
"I have traveled tens of thousands of li from afar, vowing to reach Vulture Peak;
I do not expect to preserve my life, nor can I guarantee that my next breath shall remain."
"How can the sincerity cultivated over many years be allowed to fail now that it has reached its fulfillment?
Though there be peril and hardship, I shall not fear them.
Since no one could stop him, he sent two monks to escort him.
When Faxian arrived at the mountain, the sun was already setting;
he intended to stay the night there, but two monks, filled with fear, abandoned him and departed.
Faxian remained alone in the mountains.
He burned incense and prostrated himself, feeling a profound sense of longing for the ancient traces as if he were beholding the actual presence of the Sage.
When night fell, three black lions came and crouched before the manifest image, licking their lips and wagging their tails.
Xian continued reciting the sutras without ceasing, single-mindedly mindful of the Buddha.
Thereupon, the lion lowered its head and tail and prostrated itself before Xian’s feet.
Xian stroked it with his hand and recited a mantra, saying:
"If you wish to harm me, wait until I have finished reciting.
When the Lion saw that he was being tested, he withdrew; after a long while, he departed.
At dawn the next morning, he returned, his path leading into a remote and deep wilderness.
The land was overgrown with hazel thickets and brambles, and birds and beasts roamed across it;
there was only a single path by which one could pass.
When he was less than a *li* away from his destination, he suddenly encountered a Daoist practitioner who appeared to be about ninety years old.
His appearance and clothing were coarse and plain, yet his spirit and bearing were noble and far-reaching.
Although Xian perceived that his air was lofty, he did not realize it was this very man.
A moment later, as he moved forward, he encountered a young monk.
Xian asked,
"Who was that elder just now?
He replied:
The head-dhūta disciple was Mahākāśyapa.
Xianfang lamented for a long time; when he finally reached the foot of the mountain, there was a massive rock lying across the entrance of the cave, so that he could not enter.

Faxian then shed tears, paid his respects, and departed. It is now said that the place Faxian visited was Mount Kukkuṭapāda, where Mahākāśyapa entered parinirvāṇa, and not Gṛdhrakūṭa Parvata, the former residence of the Buddha. Furthermore, in a monastery within the kingdom of Kāśi, there was a white-eared nāga.
Every time he made an agreement with the assembly of monks to ensure the domestic harvests were bountiful, there was always faith and efficacy.
He built dragon-shelters for the śramaṇas and provided them with meritorious food.
This occurred every time the summer retreat (varṣā) had concluded.
The dragon immediately transformed into a small snake with both ears entirely white;
everyone recognized it as the dragon and placed it inside a copper bowl filled with curd.
Starting from the senior-most monk and proceeding down the line as if to pay his respects,
he would vanish once he had gone around the entire assembly;
he did this once every year.
Xian also personally saw this dragon, after which he returned to Central India.
He was at the Deva Temple south of King Aśoka’s stūpa in the city of Pāṭaliputra in Magadha.
He obtained the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya;

furthermore, he obtained the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha*, the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-sūtra*, and the *Vaipulya-mahāparinirvāṇa*. This *Vaipulya-nirvāṇa* is the Sanskrit original of the six-fascicle *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*; according to the postscript of that scripture, it is titled the *Vaipulya-mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, and does not refer to the two-fascicle *Vaipulya-nirvāṇa*. He stayed for three years to study Sanskrit script and language, personally transcribing the texts himself.
Thereupon, he entrusted the sutras and images to a merchant caravan and arrived in the Kingdom of Siṃhala.
Of the dozen or so fellow travelers, some remained behind and others perished;
looking at his own reflection as he was left all alone, he was constantly filled with sorrow and lamentation.
Suddenly, before the jade image,
he saw a merchant who offered him a white round fan from the land of Jin;
unconsciously, he was moved to tears of sorrow.
After staying for two years, he further obtained the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya and the two Āgamas—the Dīrgha-āgama and Saṃyukta-āgama—as well as the Kṣudraka-piṭaka;
all of these were previously unavailable in the land of Han.
Furthermore, in the Kingdom of Siṃhala, there was a tooth of the Buddha.
Every year in the third month, ten days prior [to the festival],
the king of that land would have a noble, eloquent, and wise minister—
adorned in royal attire and mounted upon a white elephant— strike a drum and proclaim with a loud voice:
The Tathāgata remained in the world for forty-five years,
preaching the Dharma and delivering countless billions of people.
When his karmic affinity with sentient beings was exhausted, he entered parinirvāṇa.
From that time until now, one thousand four hundred and ninety-seven years have passed;
the world remains in long-lasting darkness, and sentient beings are to be pitied.
Ten days hence, the Buddha’s tooth relic shall emerge from the Abhayagiri Vihāra.
"You may prepare incense and flowers, each coming to make offerings.
At that time, it was precisely the first year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty;

calculating from the first year of Yixi, the year of the *jiashen* cycle (*yisi*), until the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, the year of the *gengwu* cycle, [one hundred and fifty-nine years have passed].
Thus, one thousand eight hundred and twenty-two years had passed.
Subsequently, he boarded a large merchant vessel and returned eastward by sea;
there were approximately two hundred people on board the ship.
Encountering a great tempest, the ship was wrecked and water poured in;
the multitude were struck with terror and immediately began casting away miscellaneous goods.
Xian feared that the merchants would discard his scriptures and images.
With single-minded devotion,
they invoked Avalokiteśvara and took refuge in the Sangha of the land of Han; thus,
the ship was carried by the wind and reached its destination without damage or destruction.
After traveling for ninety days, he reached the kingdom of Yavadvīpa and stayed there for five months.
He then joined another merchant caravan and headed east toward Guangzhou.
After the sails had been raised for over a month, a great wind suddenly arose day and night, and the entire ship was struck with terror.
The multitude deliberated together, saying,
"This śramaṇa sits upon us and has brought us to such disorder;
we cannot allow the entire group to perish for the sake of one man."
He intended to cast him out.
Dharma-xian’s lay supporter rebuked the merchants in a stern voice, saying,
"If you would cast out this śramaṇa, you should likewise cast me out as well."
Otherwise, you shall be put to death.
The emperors of the land of Han revere the Buddha and honor the Sangha;
when I arrive there and inform the king, he will surely punish you.
The merchants looked at one another in terror and reluctantly ceased their efforts.
Once their water was exhausted and their provisions depleted, they could do nothing but let themselves drift with the wind and current.
Suddenly, they reached a shore where they saw that the wild herbs, beans, and leeks remained as they had been before.
He knew this was the land of Han,
but he did not yet know which direction it lay in.
He immediately boarded a small boat and entered a bay to search for a village, where he encountered two hunters.
Xian asked, "What place is this?
The hunter replied,
"It is on the southern shore of Laoshan in Changguang Commandery, Qingzhou."
The hunter returned and reported this to the Prefect, Li Yi.
Having always been one who revered and placed his faith [in the Dharma],
upon suddenly hearing that a śramaṇa had arrived from afar, he personally went out to welcome and greet him.
Having displayed the scriptures and images, Xian intended to return south after a short while.
At that time, the Regional Inspector requested that he remain for the winter.
Xian said:
This poor monk has cast himself into a place from which there is no turning back, his resolve being to propagate and spread [the Dharma].
Since my aspirations have not yet been fulfilled, I cannot remain for long;
I have therefore traveled south to Jiankang.
At Daochang Monastery, he worked with the foreign meditation master Buddhabhadra to translate six scriptures,
including the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra,
and compiled one fascicle of the *You Tianzhu zhuan* (Record of Travels to India).
Having produced the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra,
Xuán circulated it for the purpose of teaching and transformation so that all might see and hear it;
there was one family whose name has been lost.
Living near the Zhuque Gate in the Yangdu capital, his family had long upheld the orthodox teachings.
He personally transcribed a copy [of the scripture] for recitation and veneration;
he possessed no separate library, as it shared a room with miscellaneous books.
Later, wind and fire suddenly broke out and spread to his house.
All his possessions were consumed, yet the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* alone remained intact.
The embers did not touch it, and the color of the scroll was no different from before.
Throughout the capital at Yangdu, everyone transmitted his teachings and praised him as divine and wondrous.
Later, he went to Jingzhou and passed away at Xin Temple at the age of eighty-six.
The multitude was deeply moved and lamented his passing with grief.
*The Sutra on the Ten Abodes of the Bodhisattva*, one fascicle: a different translation of the "Ten Abodes Chapter" from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*; recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*.
*The Sutra on the Samādhi of the Treasure Tathāgata*, two fascicles (or one fascicle): also known as the *Sutra on the Samādhi of the Infinite Treasure*; second [in the sequence].
The *Chū yǔ wújí bǎo jīng* (Sutra on the Emergence of the Ultimate Treasure) shares the same original text as [the *Dà zhì dù lùn*], according to the *Fáng Lù*;

it is the fifth [translation] produced, sharing the same original text as Zhi Chen’s *Dàoxíng jīng* and the fourth assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Fáng states that he saw it in the "New Records from the South.
The *Pǔmén pǐn jīng* (Sutra of the Universal Gate Chapter), one fascicle, is the first [translation] produced, sharing the same original text as Dharmarakṣa’s *Pǔmén pǐn* and the *Bǎo...* [text].
The *Ji Wenshu Pumen Hui* (Accumulated Mañjuśrī Universal Gate Assembly) is the same text as [the *Aśokadattā Sūtra*]; see the catalogs of Sengyou and Zhu Daozu.
The *Ashudada Jing* (Aśokadattā Sūtra), one fascicle, is the third translation; it is the same text as the *Ratnakūṭa Bhayaparitrāṇa-guṇa-parivarta*; see the Changfang catalog.
The *Ruhuan Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Illusory Samādhi), two fascicles, is the third translation; it is the same text as the *Ruhuan Sanmei* translated by An Shigao and the *Ratnakūṭa*.
The *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-praṇidhāna-sūtra* (一卷), translated by Zhú Dàozǔ during the Jìn dynasty;

its original text is identical to that found in the *Fǎhù* translation of the *Maitreya-praṇidhāna* and the *Ratnakūṭa-maitreya-paripṛcchā*. This is recorded in the *Chángfáng-lù* as the second appearance [of this text].
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* (一卷), translated by Fǎhù; its original text is identical to that of the *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmi* [translated by Dharmarakṣa]. This is the third appearance [of this text].
The *Dì jīng* (Earth Sūtra) and others share the same original text as seen in Sengzhao’s *Chángfáng lù*;

the four-fascicle *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the fifth translation, shares the same original text as the ancient *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* by Yan Fotiao; Sengzhao notes that it is not found in the *Nán lái xīn lù*.

The *Wú suǒ xīwàng jīng* (Sūtra on Having No Expectations), one fascicle, the third translation, shares the same original text as the *Xiàng zhí jīng* (Elephant-Arm Sūtra); this is seen in Sengzhao’s *Chángfáng lù*. The *Fúguāng jīng* (Floating Light Sūtra).
One fascicle; alternatively titled *Rulguang* (Milk-Light). The fourth appearance is the same text as the *Duzi jing* (Sūtra of the Calf), according to the Fang lu.

*Rulai duzheng zishì samèi jing* (Sūtra of the Tathāgata’s Sole Realization of the Self-Vow Samādhi), one fascicle; the third appearance is the same text as the *Zishì samèi jing* (Sūtra of the Self-Vow Samādhi) by An Shigao, according to the Changfang lu.
*Puxian guan jing* (Sūtra of the Contemplation of Samantabhadra), one fascicle; the first appearance, also known as *Guan puxian pusa* (Contemplation of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra).

Safang states that he saw the *Jian Daohui Lu* (Record of Daohui’s Observations) regarding the twelve fascicles of the *Yingluo Jing* (Garuḍa-Necklace Sūtra), also known as the *Xianqian Bao* (Manifest Retribution);
