its first appearance was together with the *Pusa Yingluo* (Bodhisattva Necklace) translated by Zhu Fonian, though it is sometimes in fourteen fascicles. Safang states that he saw it in the new records from the South.

The *Zhaoming Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Clarifying Wisdom), one fascicle, is the second appearance, seen in the Changfang Lu (Changfang’s Record). The *Chan Jing* (Dhyāna Sūtra), four fascicles, [is recorded in] the [Chang]fang [Lu].
The *Yunjian Nainlai Xinlu* lists one fascicle of the *Famen Jing*; the *Changfang Lu* lists one fascicle of the *Pusa Zhengzhai Jing*, noted as the third appearance;
the *Changfang Lu* lists one fascicle of the *Weige Zhangzhe Liuxiangbai Jing*, also known as the *Weihua*, noted as the second appearance.
These appear in the thirty-third fascicle of the *Zhong Ahan*.
*Finger-Garland Sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *Finger-Bun [Sūtra]*, translated from the thirty-first section of the *Ekottarika Āgama*;
a variant translation recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *Suyòu Zhìhuàn Jīng* (Sūtra on the Troubles Caused by Desires), one fascicle; the second translation, recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*.

*Wǔgài Yíjié Shīxíng Jīng* (Sūtra on the Five Hindrances, Doubts, and Knots that Cause the Loss of Practice), one fascicle; the second translation, recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *Bēnwèi Jīng* (Sūtra on Almsround), one fascicle.
According to the Record of Changfang (Chángfáng lù), the above twenty-three sections comprise forty-five fascicles;
the first two sections, totaling three fascicles, are extant within the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàzhìdù lùn), while the remaining twenty-one sections, totaling forty-one fascicles, are missing.
The śramaṇa Jīvaka (or Jīvadatta);
in the Jin language, Geyi.
A man from the Western Regions,
his cognitive nature was versatile and sharp, and his understanding was profound and far-reaching.
His ambition lay in spreading the transformative teachings, and he undertook distant travels without hesitation.
During the Jin dynasty, twenty-three scriptures, including the *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmika-sūtra*, were translated;
all catalogs state they were translated by Jītamitra during the Jin period, though it is not specified under which emperor.
If it was not Xian or Luo, it must have been Jiangnan.
This account appears in Sengyou’s *Lu*.
Fang said:
All other works have been clearly identified in various miscellaneous catalogs.

Furthermore, since the *Ratnadattā-sūtra* is extracted from the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* and the *Mādhyantika-rāja-sūtra* is extracted from the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-saṃgraha*, these derivative texts have been omitted and not recorded here.

The *Mahāyānopāya-sūtra* (Dacheng fangbian jing), three fascicles, translated in the second year of the Yuandi era (420 CE); this is the third translation, though some versions consist of two fascicles. It is identical to the *Mahopāya-kauśalya-sūtra* (Dashanquan jing) translated by Dharmarakṣa; see the Shixing lu. It is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* as the thirty-eighth assembly. The *Āryāvalokiteśvarabodhisattvaviṣavināśanadharanī-mantra-sūtra* (Qing guanshiyin pusa xiaofu duchai tuoluoni zhou jing), one fascicle, also simply titled *Qing guanshiyin jing*. This is the second translation; see the Fashang lu. The *Vaiśālī-ṣaḍabhimukha-praṇāma-sūtra* (Weige changzhe lixiang bai jing), one fascicle, translated during the Jin and Song dynasties at Guangzhou. It is an alternative translation of the thirty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*; see the Shixing and Baochang lu. The above three works comprise five fascicles in total. Of these, the first two works were originally four fascicles each, while the latter work was originally one fascicle but is currently missing.
The layman Zhu Nanti—
translated into Chinese as Hǐ (Joy)— was a man from the Western Regions.
He was unwearied in his aspiration for the Way and was able to find peace while traveling great distances.
Having realized the profound essence of the teachings, his speech was fluent in the customs of the Jin dynasty.
From the year Jiwu (459 CE), the first year of the Yuanxi era of Emperor Gong,
until the Song period, he translated three works, including the *Mahāyānopāya-kauśalya-sūtra*.

*The Sūtra of the Tathāgata Amitāyus, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha*, in one fascicle; also known as *The Sūtra of the Joyful Buddha-land* or *The Sūtra of the Land of Ultimate Bliss*. This is the seventh translation, recorded in the *Zhengdù lù* (Record of Correct Translations) as being the same text as those produced by Lokakṣema, An Shigao, Zhi Qian, Saṃghavarman, Bai Yan, Dharmarakṣa, and others. This single work in one fascicle is currently missing.
The śramaṇa Zhu Fali was a man from the Western Regions whose conduct was pure and lofty, and whose wisdom and realization of the Way stood towering high.
He was proficient in various foreign languages and excelled in elucidating the subtle points of the sūtras.

In the second month of the first year of the Yuanxi era of Emperor Gong (the Jiwu year), he translated the *Wuliangshou zhizhen dengzhengjue jing* (The Sūtra of the Immeasurable Life, the Perfectly True, Equal, and Right Enlightenment) in one fascicle.

*The Sūtra on the Difficulties of the Sun*, one fascicle; the second translation, which is the same as the *Sūtra on the Difficulties of Yue*, with slightly different details following it. Found in the Zhao lu and the Shixing lu. *The Sūtra on the Five Vows of King Piṅgala*, also known as the *Sūtra of King Puṣya*, one fascicle; the third translation. Found in the Zhao lu and the Shixing lu. *The Kāśyapa’s Compilation of the Precepts*, one fascicle; the third translation. Found in the Zhao lu and the Shixing lu. These three works, totaling three fascicles, are all currently missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Sōnggōng—
also known as Gāogōng—
translated three scriptures, including the *Rì nán* (Sūtra on the Sun), during the end of the Jìn dynasty.
Various catalogs all state it was produced at the end of the Jin dynasty, though the specific reign of which emperor is unknown.

*The Scripture on Kāśyapa’s Prohibitions* (one fascicle), also titled *The Scripture on the Great Bhikṣus* and *The Scripture on Authentic and Spurious Śramaṇas*. Its initial appearance is recorded in the Shixing lu. This one work, consisting of one fascicle, is currently missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Tuigong translated one fascicle of the Kāśyapa-vinaya-sūtra during the end of the Jin dynasty.
The imperial reign during which this was translated is unknown.

*The Scripture on the Buddha’s Explanations for the Brahmin Āṣāḍha*, one fascicle; a variant translation of the thirteenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*. Recorded in the *Zhao Lu* (Catalogue of the Zhao Dynasty). This single work, consisting of one fascicle, is missing from the extant canon.
Translated by the śramaṇa Shi Fayong.
One fascicle of the *Fanzhi Ahan jing* (The Sūtra of the Brahmin Aśvaghosa).
It is said to have appeared at the end of the Jin dynasty.
It is also not detailed under which emperor’s reign it was produced. The *Nāgasena Bhikṣu Sūtra* (two fascicles), also called the *Nāgasena Sūtra*, or in three fascicles;

first appeared in Sengyou’s *Record of Lost Translations*, and is seen in the *Collection of Holy and Sage Works*. The *Dhāraṇī-pada-sūtra* (one fascicle); Sengyou’s catalog lacks the character "zhāng" (chapter/section). It is seen in Sengyou’s *Record of Lost Translations*. Third appearance: it is the same text as the *Cihou Shenzhou Jing* (Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī-mantra of Holding Phrases) and others. This Mahāyāna sūtra is missing its original manuscript. The above two works comprise three fascicles.
Sengchang and others recorded that these were translations from the Eastern Jin dynasty whose translators were lost;
in total, there are fifty-three works in fifty-seven fascicles.

some had already been recorded in the catalogues of lost translations from the Later Han dynasty.

which are listed in detail as follows.
[The *Guan wuliangshoufo jing* (Sūtra on the Contemplation of Amitāyus Buddha):]...

the Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of the Thousand Buddhas;

the Sutra on the Names of the Buddhas of the Southern Quarter;
and the Sutra on the Names of the Buddhas for Eradicating Sin and Attaining Merit.
The Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra;
the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-bhikṣu-saṃgraha; the Upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra;

The *Anzhai zhou* (House-Blessing Dhāraṇī). The above twenty dhāraṇīs comprise twenty-nine fascicles. Since these were already included in the *Lost Translations of the Later Han* catalog, we know they are duplicates. [Next is] the *Sanguo wujie daipei hushen zhoushen jing* (Sutra of the Dhāraṇīs for Wearing and Carrying for Protection of the Body through the Three Refuges and Five Precepts).
The *Dharani Sutra for Protecting Bhikṣus by Seventy-two Thousand Divine Kings*;
the *Dharani Sutra for Protecting Bhikṣuṇīs by One Hundred and Twenty Thousand Divine Kings*;
and the *Dharani Sutra for Protecting the Body by One Hundred Knot Divine Kings*.
The Scripture on the Palace and Dwelling Spirit-Kings Guarding and Pacifying the Left and Right;
the Scripture on the Causes and Conditions for Blocking Tombs and the Four-Directional Divine Mantras;
and the Great Divine Mantra Scripture on Subduing Demons and Sealing with Mudrās.
The Mahāmaṇivipula-dhāraṇī Sūtra; the Maṇidhara Great Divine Incantation Sūtra for Summoning the Dragons of the Five Directions and Subjugating Pestilence and Toxicity;
and the Brahmā Deva’s Celestial Divination Sūtra.

The eleven sections and eleven fascicles listed above, beginning with the *Puguang jing* (Universal Radiance Sutra) and ending with the *Daguanding jing* (Great Consecration Sutra), are all translations by Śrīmitra. From the first fascicle to the eleventh is the *Yijiao sanmei jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of the Bequeathed Teaching) in two fascicles; it is also known as the *Yijiao sanmei falü jing* (Sutra on the Law and Vinaya of the Samādhi of the Bequeathed Teaching), translated by Dharmakṣema of the Western Jin, and it is also included among the spurious records.
The *Anāgāmi-sūtra* in two fascicles, translated by Zhiyan of the Jin dynasty; it is also listed in the spurious records.

The *Adbhuta-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* in two fascicles, also simply titled the *Adbhuta-sūtra*, was previously translated twice—once extant and once missing. The *Dhyāna-samādhi-upāya-anupūrva-dharma-sūtra* was translated by An Shigao of the Later Han.
*The Scripture on the Divine Incantations of the Seven Buddhas*, translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty;
*The Scripture on the Five Blessings of the Venerable One*, translated by Bai Fazang of the Western Jin dynasty;
*The Scripture on the Incantation of the Divine King Maṇibhadra*, also known as *The Scripture on the Case of Maṇibhadra* (sometimes omitting the word "King"), translated by Zhu Tanwulan.
*The Sutra on the Original Practice of the Six Pāramitās*, translated by Guṇabhadra of the Song dynasty;
*The Sutra on the Five Precepts for Upāsakas*, translated by Juqu Jingsheng of the Song dynasty;
and an excerpt from the *Sutra on the Names of the Divine Kings of the Three Refuges and Five Precepts*, compiled from the *Guanding Jing*.

The *Dingyi Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Concentrated Mind) appears in the *Shizhu Duanjie Jing* (Sūtra on the Ten Stages of Severing Bonds); the following are newly appended to this catalogue.

The *Jueding Bini Jing* (Sūtra on the Decisive Vinaya), one fascicle—also known as the *Pohuai Yiqie Xinshi Chushi* (Initial Emergence of the Destruction of All Consciousness)—was originally translated concurrently with the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Chapter on Upāli;
it is a different translation. Dao You states that various catalogues all say it was produced at Dunhuang, though its provenance is not explicitly stated.
The Biography of the Translator states that during the Jin dynasty, it is not detailed under which emperor this occurred. *The Sūtra on the Arrival of Maitreya* in one fascicle;

third appearance, identical to the *Sūtra on Maitreya’s Descent to Be Born* translated by Kumārajīva. *The Sūtra on the Rice Seedling* in one fascicle, identical to the *Sūtra on the Understanding of Birth and Death*.
*The Sūtra on the Merit and Retribution of Constructing Images* in one fascicle, identical to [the corresponding text].

*The Sūtra on the Making of Buddha Images*, same text as *The Sūtra on Repaying Kindness by Offering the Bowl*; one fascicle. *The Sūtra on the Offering of the Alms Bowl*, same text as the *Ullambana Sūtra*.
*The Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāmin*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī-mantra of the Accumulation of Flowers*, one fascicle.
(The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations. *The Sūtra of the Six-Syllable King of Mantras*, one fascicle; same text as the *Six-Syllable Divine Mantra*.
*The Sūtra on the Dhāraṇī of Skillful Means for Good Dharmas*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on the Dhāraṇī of the Auspicious Gate of Vajra Secrets*, one fascicle.
The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations. *The Sūtra on the Original Deeds of the Bodhisattva*, three fascicles;
*The Sūtra on the Divine Incantations Spoken by the Seven Buddhas*, four fascicles. The former was also titled *The Sūtra Spoken by the Seven Buddhas and Eleven Bodhisattvas*.
The *Mahādhāraṇī-mantra-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Sālā-rāja-sūtra*.
The *Parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, two fascicles; also simply called the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* or the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

This is a variant translation of the first part of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the *Caryā-sūtra*. Among the various collections, the single-fascicle version contains only the upper fascicle and is incomplete.

The lower fascicle: *Yuanbenzhijing* (Scripture on the Original Causes), one fascicle; translated from the tenth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, with an ancient variant translation. *Gulaishijijing* (Scripture on the Times of the World), one fascicle;
translated from the thirteenth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, with an ancient variant translation. *Fanzhijishuijing* (Scripture on the Brahmin’s Calculation of Water Purity), one fascicle;
translated from the twenty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, with an ancient variant translation. *Sanguiwujiaicixin* (The Three Refuges, Five Precepts, and Compassionate Mind).
*The Sūtra on the Merit of Renunciation*, one fascicle; translated from the thirty-ninth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
*The Sūtra of the Arrow Simile*, one fascicle; translated from the sixtieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.

*The Sūtra on Obtaining Five Blessings by Bestowing Food*, one fascicle—also known as the *Sūtra on Bestowing Physical Strength* or the *Sūtra on Merit*; translated from the twentieth fascicle of the *Ekottara Āgama*.

*The Sūtra of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra*, one fascicle, translated differently from the four-fascicle [version]; it appears in Sengyou’s *Record of Lost Translations* as having a "Jin" (Chinese) title, hence it is moved here.
*The Sūtra on the Six Matters Concerning the Dissolution of the Body by the Woman Māndhārī*, one fascicle, translated differently from the thirteenth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*;
this is the fifth appearance, being the same text as the *Sūtra of Māndāravā and Śikhin*, etc. *The Retribution of the Hungry Ghosts*.

*Ying jing* (Sūtra on Correspondence), one fascicle; third appearance, also titled *Maudgalyāyana’s Discourse on the Causes and Conditions of Hell and Hungry Ghosts*, which is the same text as the *Ghosts Question Maudgalyāyana Sūtra*.
*Dedao ticheng xizhang jing* (Sūtra on the Ladder to the Path and the Religious Staff), one fascicle; its title reads "Chapter Twelve:
The Ladder to the Path and the Religious Staff," though it is also simply called the *Xizhang jing* (Sūtra on the Religious Staff). *Senghu jing* (Sūtra of Saṃgharakṣita), one fascicle.

Some say there are the *Senghu yinyuan jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Saṃgharakṣita), one scroll; the *Hujing jing* (Sūtra on Protecting Purity), one scroll; the *Muhuanzi jing* (Sūtra on the Wood Beads), one scroll;

the *Wushangchu jing* (Sūtra on the Supreme Abode), one scroll; the *Luzhi Zhangzhe yinyuan jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Elder Luzhi), one scroll; the *Wuwang jing* (Sūtra of the Five Kings), one scroll;

and the *Shami shijie fa bing weiyi* (The Dharma of the Ten Precepts for Śrāmaṇeras and their Deportment), one scroll—also known as the *Shami weiyi jieben* (Śrāmaṇera Deportment and Code of Precepts)—and the *Shamini li*... [text ends].
*Śīla-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Pañcaśata-praśna-vastu-sūtra*, one fascicle;

*Aśoka-rāja-avadāna-sūtra*, one fascicle—titled *Tianzun shuo Aśoka-rāja-avadāna-jing* (The Scripture on the Similes of King Aśoka Spoken by the Celestial Honored One). Since ancient scriptures referred to the Buddha as the "Celestial Honored One," this is actually spoken by the Buddha.
Also, *Zhuanjji sanzang ji zanzang zhuan* (Biographies of the Compilation of the Tripiṭaka and the Miscellaneous Piṭaka), one fascicle.

It is said that the *Zuàn sānzàng jīng* (Compendium of the Tripiṭaka Sūtras) and the *Zá zàng jīng* (Sūtra of the Miscellaneous Piṭaka) consist of one fascicle each, titled *Mílè zuò fó shì shí jīng* (Sūtra on the Events of Maitreya Becoming a Buddha).
This is not listed in Sengyou’s catalogue; it is the second appearance [of this text] and is identical to the *Mílè lái shí jīng* (Sūtra on Maitreya’s Arrival), as noted in Bǎochàng’s catalogue.

The *Dàoshù sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Bodhi Tree) consists of two fascicles; it is the second appearance [of this text] and is identical to the *Sīhāmèi jīng* (Sīhāmèi Sūtra), as noted by Zhīmǐndù.
The above records thirty-eight sections totaling forty-five fascicles;
the final two sections, comprising three fascicles, are missing, while the remaining thirty-six sections, totaling forty-two fascicles, are all extant.
This scripture, which has entered the canon, is unknown as to its translator;
it is omitted from the various catalogs of lost translations and was not recorded there.
As it appears to be a scripture from a remote era, it has been compiled here at the end of the Jin period.
May there be no omissions or errors.
Including the two sections in three fascicles previously translated by those of unknown translators,
the total comprises forty sections in forty-eight fascicles.
It is also said that the Eastern Jin lost its source [at this point].

The Qin of Fu (the Fu Qin) had its capital at Chang’an; it is also called the Former Qin, which began with Fu Jian, posthumously titled Emperor Ming. Its first year was the Gengxu year, the first year of Huangshi.
It reached the reign of Fu Deng, who was posthumously titled Taichu; it was the Jiawu year of the ninth year [of that era].
In total, five rulers presided over forty-four years.
There were six śramaṇas.
The total number of translated sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras is fifteen works comprising one hundred and ninety-seven fascicles.

Among these, seven works totaling sixty-five fascicles are extant, while eight works totaling one hundred and thirty-two fascicles are missing. The Fang catalogue states that the first year of Yuanshi was Jia-yin and the first year of Yanchu was Ding-you; these differ from the chronological records of various houses by three years. Subsequently, following the official record, one preface has been added; thus, the Jia-zih date in the Fang catalogue is erroneous.
The Śramaṇa Dharmadhara of the Fu Qin [dynasty] translated three works in three fascicles: the *Śīla-sūtra* (Precept Manual) and the *Mandala-text*.
The Śramaṇa Kumārabuddhi translated one work in three fascicles: the *Saṃyukta*. The Śramaṇa Saṃghabhūti translated three works in twenty-seven fascicles: the *Śāstra-saṃgraha*.
The Śramaṇa Dharmapriya translated one work in five fascicles: the *Sūtra*. The Śramaṇa Guṇavṛddha translated two works in forty [fascicles].
The *Ṣaṭ-varga-śāstra* by the śramaṇa Dharmanandi; the collection of one hundred and fourteen fascicles of sūtras and śāstras from the five schools;
the *Daśabhāṇavāra-bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra*, one fascicle—also called the *Daśabhāṇavāra-mahābhikṣu-prātimokṣa*, first appearing in Sengyou’s catalogue;
the *Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa*, one fascicle—also called the *Daśabhāṇavāra-bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa*, second appearance.

The *Jian sengyou lu* records one fascicle titled *Jiaochou biquni ersui tanwen* (Text on the Two-Year Ordination Platform for Teaching Bhikṣuṇīs), though some versions lack the character "ni" (bhikṣuṇī).
Sengchun obtained the Sanskrit original in the kingdom of Kucha; Buddhanandi translated the oral terminology, and Huichang acted as the scribe.
This is recorded in the *Baoshang lu*. These three sections comprising three fascicles are all currently missing.
The śramaṇa Dharmadhara,
also called Shi (Attendant);
in the Qin language, Dharmamati (Dharma-Wisdom).
Also known as Fahai (Dharmasāgara),
he was a man from the Western Regions who was skilled at upholding the Vinaya-piṭaka and transcribing it into the Sūtras.
During the third year of the Jianyuan era (dingmao) and the fourth year (wuchen) of Fu Jian’s reign, when he was posthumously titled Emperor Zhuanglie Tianwang,
he translated three works, including the *Sūtra of the Ten Recitations* (*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya-mātṛkā*), at Chang’an.
Zhú Fóniàn acted as the oral interpreter, while Huìcháng transcribed [the text] in writing. In Seng’ān’s "Preface to the Monastic Precepts," it says:
"Fóniàn copied out its Sanskrit text."
Daoxian served as the translator,
and Huichang recorded the text in writing for the Bhikṣuṇī-Prātimokṣa.
Sengyou’s Catalogue states:
During the reign of Emperor Jianwen of the Jin dynasty,
the śramaṇa Sengchun obtained a Sanskrit manuscript in the kingdom of Kuci in the Western Regions.
Upon arriving in Guanzhong, he commissioned Fonian, Dharmadhara, and Huichang to produce a Chinese translation together.
I have carefully examined the records of Sengchang and others, all of which designate Huichang as the primary translator.
However, the current text was translated by Dharmakṣema in collaboration with Dharmamitra and Zhu Fonian.
Since the Qin monk Huichang never traveled to India, he could not have been the primary translator.
Although Huichang was always present when the *Bhikṣuṇī-śīla* was translated—having personally recorded the oral dictation (bishou) as a transcription—it is identical to the *Bhikṣu-śīla*.
This is merely citing the names of Huiyao and Huichang.
By collating the beginning and end of the text, the matter became clear.
[Kumārajīva] frequently assisted with the translation,
while Dharma served as the principal authority.
Therefore, it was included in the catalog of Dharmarakṣa (Tánmó).
Huìcháng did not separately preserve it.

There is also the *Sī-āhán mù-chāojiě* (Explanatory Abstract of the Four Āgamas) in two fascicles, also called the *Sī-āhán mù-chāojīng* (Scripture of the Abstract of the Four Āgamas), for which Master Ān composed a preface; this is recorded in Sēngyòu’s catalog. This one work in two fascicles currently exists.
The śramaṇa Kumārabuddhi— translated into the language of Qin as "Child-like Enlightenment"—
was a man from the Western Regions.

In the eighth month of the eighteenth year of Fu Jian’s Jianyuan era, the year of Renwu, he translated the *Ekottarika-āgama-saṃgraha* (Ahan mu chao) at the Ye Monastery; it was completed in the eleventh month of winter.
Buddhabhadra held the Sanskrit manuscript;
Buddhasmṛti and Baohu translated it into the Qin language;
and the śramaṇas Sengdao, Sengrui, and Tanjiu received the text by brush.

The *Ācārya Vasumitra-bodhisattva-saṃgīti-śāstra* (尊婆須蜜菩薩所集論) in ten fascicles—also known as the *Vasumitra-sūtra* (婆須蜜經)—in twelve or fourteen fascicles, was translated from the original manuscript by the three masters Sanghabhadra, Saṃghadeva, and Saṃghabhūti, with Zhu Fonian acting as oral translator and Huichong as scribe.
It began on the fifth day of the third month in the twentieth year of the Jianyuan era and was completed on the thirteenth day of the seventh month. Master Dao’an composed the preface;
this is recorded in Sengyou’s *Lu*. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (鞞婆沙論) in fourteen fascicles—sometimes omitting the character "wu" (無)—is also called the *Vibhāṣā-abhidharma* (鞞婆沙阿毘曇) or the *Pṛthu* (廣).
It is said to consist of either fifteen or nineteen fascicles. It was produced beginning in the fourth month of the nineteenth year of the Jianyuan era and completed at the end of the eighth month.

Nanti recorded it from the Sanskrit text; Fotuo Locha (Buddharakṣa) acted as the oral translator, Minzhi as the scribe, and Master Dao’an composed the preface. This is found in Sengyou’s *Lu* (Catalogue). The *Sengqialuocha Suoji Jing* (Saṃgharakṣasa-saṃgīta-sūtra) consists of three fascicles, though some say it was originally five fascicles.

It was produced in the twentieth year of the Jianyuan era, beginning on the twentieth day of the eleventh month and concluding that same month. Fonian acted as the oral translator, Huichong as the scribe, and Master Dao’an [composed the preface].

The preface states that according to Sengyou’s Catalogue (*Chu sanzang jiji*), these were produced at Shiyang Monastery in Chang’an; it is also said that Buddhagupta translated them. The three sections comprising twenty-seven fascicles are all extant;
some say they were translated by Ba-teng.
His name in the language of Qin was Zhongxian.
A native of Jibin,
he possessed a resolute character and a profound, noble capacity.
He traveled extensively to seek out renowned masters, training until his practice reached the highest level of refinement.
He read widely across many scriptures and was particularly proficient in several sutras.

By heart he recited the *Vibhāṣā*, penetrating its subtle principles—this refers to the *Vibhāṣā* (not the *Mahāvibhāṣā*). Constantly setting his mind on traveling to various regions, he observed local customs to propagate the teachings.
At the end of the Jianyuan era of Fu Jian, he entered Guanzhong.
Previously, the rise of the Mahāyāna had not yet been widespread;
instead, the study of dhyāna and saṃkhyā was very prevalent.
Upon arriving in Chang’an, everyone acclaimed him as a master of the Dharma. Wenye,
a Librarian and Rectifier of Characters in the Secretariat under Yao Xing,
was a man of broad learning and talent who held the Great Dharma in high esteem.
I have heard that in foreign lands the *Vibhāṣā* is the primary object of study, and that Saṃghabhūti could recite it from memory.
Consequently, he was honored with the fourfold offerings and requested to translate the Sanskrit text.
In the seventeenth year of the Jianyuan era, the year of Xinsi (381 CE), Saṃghabhūti...
In the twenty-first year, the year of Yiyou (485 CE),
together with the eminent and virtuous Dharma Master Shi Dao’an and others,
he translated two works, including the *Vasumitra-śāstra*.
The śramaṇa Zhu Fonian from Liangzhou and the foreign śramaṇa Buddharakṣa acted as interpreters;
the śramaṇa Minzhìhuì, Sōng, and the Secretariat Clerk Zhao Wényè received the oral transmission in writing.
Master Dao’an and Master Fǎhé collated and finalized [the text] together.
Saṃghabhūti’s precepts and virtue were upright and lofty; he was serene and detached from the mundane world.
The monastic community in Guāngōng took him as their model.
His ultimate end was unknown.
Fotu Locha was a man of unknown nationality;
his virtuous deeds were pure and refined, and he had thoroughly mastered the Buddhist scriptures.
Having traveled extensively through the Central Lands (Madhyadeśa), he was well-versed in the language of Qin.

His translation of the Sanskrit texts was highly acclaimed in his time; while various catalogs such as those by Sengyou and others state that the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* was translated by Saṃghadeva, the preface to the treatise by the Duke of Huai’an states it was translated by Saṃghabhūti. Following the preface to the treatise, I consider this to be correct. Furthermore, the various catalogs of Sengyou and others state that the fourteen-fascicle *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* translated by Saṃghabhūti is precisely this *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra-śāstra* (or *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra-śāstra-saṃkṣepa*), five fascicles—sometimes without the character "śāstra" (*chao*)—or seven fascicles; also called the *Prajñā* [Sūtra], the "Subhūti Chapter," or the "Chang'an Sixth Translation"; identical in substance to the *Dōgyō*, *Shōhon*, and *Myōdo* [versions]. Seen in Sengrui’s *Record of the Two Qin Periods* and Sengyou’s *Catalogue*. This one work in five fascicles currently exists.
The śramaṇa Dharmapriya— translated into Chinese as Fashou (Dharma-Reception)—
was a native of India.
He was of brilliant and sensitive character, and his aspirations were set upon broad and profound exposition.
In the eighteenth year of Fu Jian’s Jiayuan era, the *Renwu* year, he translated one fascicle of the *Prajñā-pāramitā-saṃgraha-sūtra*.

Buddhagupta acted as the oral translator—Buddhagupta being none other than Buddharakṣa—and Huijin received the text in writing; Master Dao’an then verified and finalized the work, composing a preface for it.

It is commonly transmitted that this [text] shares the same original as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Prabhāsa*, and the *Guangzan*; however, it is feared that those who have examined it have not yet done so with full precision.

The *Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra* (Treatise on the Eight Sections of Abhidharma) consists of thirty fascicles—though some omit the word "wu" (treatise)—or twenty fascicles; it is also called the *Kātyāyanīya-abhidharma* or the *Abhidharma-sūtra*. Its first section was initially produced at the same time as the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* translated by Saṃghadeva. It began on the twentieth day of the fourth month in the nineteenth year of the Jiànyuán era and was completed on the twenty-third day of the tenth month, according to Sēngyòu’s catalog. The *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* (Heart of Abhidharma) consists of sixteen fascicles—though some say thirteen—and was initially produced in Luoyang during the final years of the Jiànyuán era, according to Sēngruì’s *Two Qín Records* and Sēngyòu’s catalog. Of these two works totaling forty-six fascicles, the former work of thirty fascicles currently exists, while the latter work of sixteen fascicles is missing.
The śramaṇa Saṃghadeva—also called Tihua or Sengyou; "Deva" is merely a difference in dialect between the Chu and Xia regions—is in the language of Qin called "Zhongtian" (Multitude of Heavens).
He was a native of Jibin.
He was of the Gautama clan.
In the nineteenth year of Fu Jian’s Jianyuan era, the year of Guiwei,
he traveled to Chang’an.
The śramaṇa Fǎhuó requested that he be commissioned to translate [the texts].

From the nineteenth year [of the Jiànyuán era] until its conclusion in the final year of Jiànyuán, he produced two treatises, including the *Aṣṭagrantha* (Eight Chapters). Regarding the fourteen fascicles of the *Vibhāṣā*, based on Master Ān’s preface, these were translated by Saṃghabhūti; they are excluded from the present collection.
Translated by the śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou;
received in writing by Hui-li and Seng-mao, and its essential meaning refined by Fa-he.
Master Dao-an composed the preface.
Later, in the sixteenth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty,
he traveled to Mount Lu and proceeded to Jiankang, where he further produced various sutras and treatises,
as evidenced by the Jin lu (Records of the Jin).
The Madhyama Āgama, fifty-nine fascicles, was produced in the twentieth year of the Jianyuan era; this is the first translation.
Zhu Fonian transcribed it while listening to the oral recitation. This is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty* and Sengyou’s *Catalogue*.

The Ekottara Āgama, fifty fascicles, was the first translation; it began production in the summer of the Jia-shen year of the twentieth year of the Jianyuan era and was completed by the following spring.
The *Fonien zhuan* (Biography of Fonian) in forty-one fascicles was translated by [Fonian] with Tanshung serving as the scribe.

It appears in the prefaces to the scriptures by Master Daoan, and is recorded in the catalogs of Sengrui, Sengyou, and Baochang. Sengyou states that the thirty-third and twenty-fourth fascicles are likely erroneous.

The two-fascicle *Sanfadu lun* (Treatise on the Three Dharma-Levels) first appeared; some omit the character "wu" (treatise), calling it simply the *Sanfadu lun*. It was translated by Saṃghadeva during the Jin dynasty.
The first appearance of this work was slightly different [from the current version] and is recorded in Senglang’s *Lu* (Catalogue);
it consists of two fascicles of the *Saṃgharakṣa-saṃgraha*, composed by Saṃgharakṣa seven hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. The second appearance was recorded in Baochang’s *Lu*;

it is the one-fascicle *Aśokarāja-suta-vimūrdha-hetu-pratyaya-sūtra*. The third appearance occurred in the sixth year of the Jianchu era of the Yao Qin dynasty, the *Xinmao* year, at the city of Anding.
For Yao Min, the Director of the Secretariat, [the work] began on the eighteenth day of the second month and was completed by the twenty-fifth.

Fo-nian acted as both the oral translator and the author of the preface. This is seen in the *Qin lu* (Record of Qin); it should properly be included among the Later Qin records, but following the majority of sources, it is appended here.
Of the five sections totaling one hundred and fourteen scrolls, the first four sections comprise one hundred and thirteen scrolls; the final section is missing.
The fascicle is extant.
Translated by the śramaṇa Dharmaratna,
whose name means "Dharma-joy" in the language of Qin.
Dharmagupta was a native of the country of Kucha.
Having left secular life in his childhood, he possessed an intelligence that was precociously developed;
he devoted himself to the study and recitation of the scriptures with single-minded dedication.
He examined the Tripiṭaka thoroughly and could recite the Aṅguttara Nikāya from memory;
he was profoundly learned and widely erudite, with no aspect of the teachings that he had not mastered.
For this reason, those within the kingdom have recently come to universally respect and admire him.
In his youth, he traveled abroad to observe the ways of others, visiting various countries.
He often maintained that the essence of propagating the Dharma should be proclaimed and made known;
therefore, he braved the shifting sands from afar, carrying his precious treasure as he journeyed eastward.
In the twentieth year of Fu Jian’s Jianyuan era, he arrived in Chang’an.
Since Nandi’s scholarly achievements were already eminent and his reputation for the Way was very great,
Fu Jian received him with profound courtesy and provided him with generous offerings and support.
Previously, among the various scriptures in the Central Land, the four Āgamas had not yet appeared.
Zhu Fajian’s attendant, Zhao Zheng, the Governor of Wuwei, possessed a profound aspiration for the treasury of the Dharma;
he therefore joined forces with An Gong to request the translation of the scriptures.
In the city of Chang’an, he assembled monks who were experts in the study of the Dharma;
they transcribed the two *Piṭakas* from their Sanskrit manuscripts and also began the work of translation.
Buddhabhadra orally transmitted the words, while Huisong recorded them in writing.
This spanned from the year Jiashen, the twentieth year of the Jianyuan era of Fu Jian,
to the year Xinmao, the sixth year of the Jianchu era of Yao Chang.
He translated five sections of the Madhyama Āgama and other sūtras.
After completing these, he returned to the Western Regions, where his final destination remains unknown.
*Zhenyuan xinding shijiao mulu*, Volume Five.
The Catalogue of the Newly Established Buddhist Teachings Compiled in the Zhenyuan Era, Volume Six.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xīmíng Monastery in the Western Capital.
Part Six of the Upper Section: General Collection of Records of the Various Scriptures.

The Yao Qin dynasty was established by the Yao clan with its capital at Chang’an; it is also referred to as the Later Qin. It began with Yao Chang, who was posthumously titled Emperor Zhaowu. Its first year was the White Sparrow (Baique) era, the Jia-shen year. It continued through Yao Hong, whose reign included the Yonghe era, ending in the Ding-si year, the third year of that era.
In total, under three successive rulers, for a period of thirty-four years,
five śramaṇas produced various sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras.
In total, there are ninety-four works comprising six hundred and twenty-four fascicles.

Among these, sixty-six works totaling five hundred and twenty-eight fascicles are extant; twenty-eight works totaling ninety-six fascicles are missing. According to the postscript to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the year was the cyclical year *Xinchou* (辛丑) in the third year of Hongshi. Wang Gui states that the years given by Fang and Zhen Luan differ from this by two years; here, I follow Dao Gui’s account as correct and have arranged them in sequence accordingly.
The Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of the Yao Qin translated twelve sections comprising seventy-four fascicles of sūtras and vinaya;
the Śramaṇa Kumārajīva compiled seventy-four sections comprising three hundred and eighty-four fascicles of sūtras, vinaya, and śāstras;
the Śramaṇa Puṇyatāra [translated] one section comprising fifty-eight fascicles of vinaya; and the Śramaṇa Buddhayaśas [translated] four sections comprising eight... [fascicles].
The *Sāmaññaphala Sūtra* and the *Vinaya* translated by the śramaṇa Dharmayaśas comprise fourteen fascicles in three sections totaling twenty-four fascicles.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-saṃyojana-prahāṇa Sūtra* consists of ten fascicles; its opening states:

*Vijayaparipṛcchā-bodhisattva-daśabhūmi-malāpahāra-saṃyojana-prahāṇa Sūtra*, also known as *Daśasahasra-sūryaprabhā-samādhi-samāpatti*, or alternatively called *Daśabhūmi-saṃyojana-prahāṇa*. It is also found in versions of eleven fascicles.
In fourteen fascicles; second appearance. Recorded in the *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Record of the Three Jewels Through the Ages) and the *Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks).
The *Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra-sūtra* in twelve fascicles—also known as the *Xianzai Bao* (Retribution in the Present)—second appearance. It appears in twelve, fourteen, or sixteen fascicles.
Translated in the seventh month of the twelfth year of the Jianyuan era of the Fu Qin dynasty. Recorded in the *Lidai Sanbao Ji* and the *Gaoseng Zhuan*.

The *Pusa chutai jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Dwelling in the Womb) in five fascicles, as recorded in the *Chusanzang jiji*, states at its beginning that the Bodhisattva descended from Tuṣita Heaven into his mother’s womb;

it is also referred to simply as the *Guangpusa jing* (Extended Sūtra of the Bodhisattva) or the *Taijing* (Womb Sūtra), appearing in four or eight fascicles according to the *Qin lu* and the *Gaoseng zhuan*.
The *Zhongyin jing* (Sūtra of the Intermediate State) in three fascicles, as recorded in the *Qin lu* and the *Gaoseng zhuan*, is also included in the *Sengyou lu*.
*The Sutra on the Original Action of the Bodhisattva’s Necklace Ornament*, two fascicles; alternatively titled simply *The Sutra on the Original Action of the Necklace Ornament*.

Its initial appearance is recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *The Vinaya of Piṇāya*, ten fascicles; also known as the *Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of Testing*, also called the *Piṇāya Sutra*, and also called the *Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of the Fruits of Precepts*.
Translated by the monk Fónién with the scribe being the śramaṇa Tánjǐng; recorded in the *Ān Lù*.

The Preface to the *Gāthāsaṃgraha-sūtra* (Chūjō-kyō) states that on the twelfth day of the first month of the fourteenth year of Jianyuan of the Fu Qin dynasty (the Renwu year), twenty fascicles were produced;
it is also called the *Gāthāsaṃgraha-śāstra*. It was produced in the tenth year of Jianyuan of the Fu Qin dynasty, as recorded in the *Erqin lu* and the *Gaoseng zhuan*.
According to the records of Sengyou, Baochang, and others, the above [entries] are extant, while those below are missing.

*The Scripture on the Bodhisattva Dharanimdhara*, three fascicles; the second translation, produced by Dharmarakṣa. It shares the same original text as *Dharanimdhara* and *Lokadhara* translated by Kumārajīva;
this is noted in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *The Mahāvaipulya Nirnimitta Sūtra*, five fascicles—also titled *Mahāmegha Sūtra*—or four fascicles;

it shares the same original text as the *Mahāvaipulya Mahāmegha Sūtra* translated by Dharmakṣema. Its initial appearance is recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *The Universal [Bodhisattva]...* [text fragment].
*Chujing* (Sūtra on Abodes), three fascicles; recorded in the *Changfang lu*. *Shisong biquni jie suochu benmo* (The Origin and End of the Ten Recitations Bhikṣuṇī Precepts), one fascicle;

the third edition produced by Sengchun, who obtained the Sanskrit manuscript in the country of Wuyi. Fonian translated the text, which was later revised and corrected by Zhu Fonian, with a preface composed by him;
recorded in the *Baoshang lu*. *Wangzi fayi huaimu yinyuan* (The Causes and Conditions of Prince Fayi’s Loss of Sight).
One fascicle; alternatively titled *The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of King Aśoka’s Son Losing His Sight*. Third appearance in Sengyou’s Catalogue.
Of the twelve works totaling seventy-four fascicles listed above, seven works totaling sixty-one fascicles from the *Chuyao* (Udānavarga) section are extant;
five works totaling thirteen fascicles from the *Chizhi* (Dharmatrāta) section are missing.
The śramaṇa Zhu Fonian was a native of Liangzhou.
He entered the monastic order at a young age, and his aspirations and practice were pure and steadfast.
Outwardly harmonious and inwardly luminous, he possessed a penetrating and discerning intelligence.
He recited and studied various sutras and had a general familiarity with non-Buddhist classics;
he was particularly well-versed and refined in the glossaries and commentaries of the *Cangjie* and *Yaya*.
From his youth, he delighted in traveling abroad to fully observe local customs.
His family lineage was from Xihe;
he thoroughly understood foreign languages, and there were no phonetic meanings of either Chinese or non-Chinese tongues that he did not explain.
Thus, although his reputation for scholastic learning was lacking, [his linguistic mastery was renowned].
The fame of his extensive learning was very prominent.
During the Jianyuan era of the Fu clan's reign, Dharmadhara, Kumārabuddhi, Saṃghabhūti, Deva, and Nandi arrived and entered Chang’an.
Dharmarakṣa (An Gong) and Zhao Zheng and others requested that he translate various sūtras;
at that time, none of the renowned and virtuous masters were able to undertake the transmission and translation.
The assembly unanimously recommended Dharmamitra (Nian) as the master craftsman for the task.
Since the time of An Shigao and Zhi Qian, none has surpassed Zhu Fonian.
During the two reigns of Fu Jian and Yao Xing, he was the preeminent master among translators;
thus, the monastic community in Guanzhong all rejoiced together in his presence.

I have reflected that among the twelve sections of sutras such as the *Ten Stages of Severing Bonds* translated during the two reigns of Fu Jian and Yao Xing, the eleven-fascicle *Sutra on the Ten Stages of Severing Bonds* preserved separately in Daolun’s catalog is incorrect; for there is no distinction between the two meanings of "stages" (*zhù*) and "grounds" (*dì*). Thus, I have retained the *Ten Stages* and deleted the *Ten Grounds*. Later, he fell ill and passed away in Chang’an.
People far and near, both white and black, all sighed with regret.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* consists of forty fascicles and is also known as the *Dapin Banruo Jing*.
Dao You states that this is the third translation of the *New Dapin Jing*, which shares the same source text as the *Fangguang Jing*; it is either in thirty fascicles or twenty.

[The translation] was completed in four [years], or twenty-seven [months], beginning on the thirteenth day of the fourth month of the first year of Hongshi (the Gui-mao year) and ending on the twenty-second day of the fourth month of the sixth year.

As seen in the preface by Sengrui and the records of Dao’an and Sengyou, the ten-fascicle *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Small Version) has the title *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*; the term "Small Version" (*xiao pin*) is absent from the record of Sengyou.
The *New Shorter Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Xīn xiǎopǐnjīng) is identical in its original text to the *Dàoxíng míngdù*; it is the seventh translation, consisting of either seven or eight fascicles.
It was translated from February 6th to April 3rd of the tenth year of the Hongshi era.
Sengrui’s preface notes that this is seen in the two Qin catalogs and in Sengyou’s *Jīngāng bōluómì jīng*, one fascicle, which is also called the *Jīngāng*.

Regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* where the Buddha was in Śrāvastī: the first translation is identical in its original text to that produced by Dharmaruci and others during the Yuan-Wei period, as seen in the *Catalogue of the Two Qin Dynasties* (*Er Qin Lu*) and the *Catalogue of Sengyou* (*Seng You Lu*).

The *Renwang Huguo Banruo Boluomi Jing* in two fascicles is also called the *Renwang Banruo Jing*, or sometimes said to consist of one fascicle; this second translation is by Dharmarakṣa from the Jin dynasty.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitāmahāvidyāmantra-sūtra* (one fascicle), also known as the *Mahāvidyāmantra-sūtra*, was translated by Paramārtha during the Liang dynasty from the same original text as [the *Heart Sūtra*];
Fang reports seeing it in the *Bielu*. Its initial translation is identical in substance to the *Prajñāhṛdaya-sūtra* translated during the Tang dynasty;
see the title of this scripture. Also, the *Bodhisattvapitaka-sūtra* in three fascicles, also named [the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*].
The *Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, also titled the *Mahākaruṇā-citta-sūtra*, is now included as the seventeenth assembly in the *Ratnakūṭa* collection, titled the "Pūrṇa Assembly.

It was translated in the seventh year of Hongshi; it consists of either two fascicles and is a second translation identical in text to that produced by Dharmarakṣa, as seen in the *Two Qin Records* and the *Fajing Record*. The *Subāhu-bodhisattva-sūtra* in two fascicles is now also included.
*The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Sumati*, one fascicle, recorded in the *Fajushu* (Catalogue of the Dharma Treasury) as the twenty-sixth assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa*;
the second translation, identical to the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra on Sublime Wisdom*. Recorded in the *Changfanglu* (Catalogue of the Library of the Longfang).

*The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Īśvararāja*, two fascicles; sometimes the word "Bodhisattva" is omitted. The first translation was identical to the *Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Vikrāntagāmin*. Translated in the ninth year of Hongshi.
In the [X]th year, under the supervision of Yao Xian, the Minister of State, Seng Rui transcribed the text and composed the preface; this is recorded in the *Erqin lu*.

Furthermore, there is one fascicle of the *Zhuangyan pútíxīn jīng* (Sūtra on Adorning the Bodhicitta) by Sengyou, which is the fourth translation and shares the same source text as the *Fahù púsà shìdì jīng* (Dharmarakṣa’s Bodhisattva Ten Stages Sūtra).
According to the *Bie lu*, there is also a *Shízhu jīng* (Ten Abodes Sūtra) in four or five fascicles, which is the Chinese version.

The *Yán shí dì pǐn* (Chapter on the Adornment of the Ten Stages) was translated by Kumārajīva together with Buddhayaśas; this is recorded in the two *Qín lù* (Records of the Qín Dynasty) and the *Sēng yòu lù* (Record of Sēngyòu).

Regarding the eight-fascicle *Mìofǎ liánhuá jīng* (Lotus Sūtra of the Wondrous Dharma), the *Sēng yòu lù* states that when the new *Fǎhuá jīng* first appeared, it consisted of seven fascicles and twenty-seven chapters.
Later, the "Tiānshòu pǐn" (Chapter on Bestowed by Heaven) was added as the twenty-eighth chapter in the eighth year of the Hóngshǐ era.

In the summer, at the Great Monastery (Dà sì), it was produced with Sengrui serving as the scribe and composing the preface; this fifth translation is recorded in the *Lù of the Two Qins* and the *Sēngyòu Lù*.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* consists of two fascicles; it is also titled *Acintyavimokṣa* or simply *Vimalakīrti-sūtra*.
The *Sēngyòu Lù* states that the new *Vimalakīrti* was translated in the eighth year of Hóngshǐ at the Great [Monastery].

The sixth translation, produced at the temple with Sengzhao transcribing and composing the preface, is recorded in the *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Records of the Three Jewels through the Ages) and the *Sengyou Lu* (Catalogue of Sengyou).
The *Mahādruma-kinnara-rāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in four fascicles— also titled *Acintya-varga-nirdeśa* or simply *Mahādruma-kinnara-sūtra*—
is the second translation, which is identical to the *Candraprabha-kumāra-bodhisattva-sūtra* translated by Zhi Chen.
The *Chángfáng lù* records that the three-fascicle *Jí yīqiè fúdé sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Collecting All Merit) was translated by Zhu Fahu and others;
it is a different version of the same text as the *Jí zhòngdé jīng*. This second translation is recorded in the *Zhēnjì sì lù*.

The four-fascicle *Sīyì fàntiān suǒwèn jīng* (Sūtra of the Questions of Brahmā Viśeṣacinti), also simply called the *Sīyì jīng*, is what Sengyou refers to as the *Sīyì yì jīng*. It was propagated widely.
On the first day of the twelfth month of the fourth year, at the Xiaoyao Garden, the second translation was produced;

it is identical in its original text to the earlier translations by Dharmarakṣa, Saṃghavarman, and Guṇabhadra. Sengrui composed the preface, as recorded in the *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Records of the Three Jewels Through the Ages) and the *Sengyou Lu* (Catalogue of Sengyou).

The *Holding the World Sūtra* (*Chishi jing*) consists of four fascicles—also known as the *Dharmamudrā Sūtra* (*Fayin jing*)—or alternatively three fascicles; this second edition was produced alongside the version by Dharmarakṣa.

The *Puruṣasūtra* (人經) and others share the same original text as the two fascicles of the *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa-sūtra* (諸法無行經)—or one fascicle—found in the records of the Two Qin dynasties and the catalogue of Sengyou;

it is identical in origin to the *Sarvadharmāmūlanirdeśa-sūtra* (諸法本無經) translated by Jñānagupta during the Sui dynasty. Its initial appearance is recorded in the catalogues of the Two Qin and Sengyou.
The *Amitābhasūtra* (阿彌陀經), also titled the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (無量壽經), consists of one fascicle and was translated in the fourth year of the Hongshi era.

The first translation was produced on the eighth day of the second month of that year; it is identical in text to the *Sūtra of Praise for the Pure Land* translated during the Tang dynasty, as seen in the *Two Qin Records* and Sengyou’s *Catalogue*.

The second translation, one fascicle of the *Sūtra of Maitreya’s Attainment of Buddhahood*, is identical in text to Dharmarakṣa’s *Sūtra of Maitreya’s Attainment of Buddhahood* and was produced in the first year of Hongshi; it is recorded in the *Qin Records* and Sengyou’s *Catalogue*. Maitreya... [text ends]

*Xiasheng jing* (Sūtra on the Descent [to Birth]), one fascicle; also known as *Mile shoujue jing* (Sūtra on Maitreya Receiving the Prediction). It begins with "The Great Wisdom Śāriputra... and is the fourth [text] translated.

It shares the same original text as the *Mile lai shi jing* (Sūtra on Maitreya’s Coming) and is also called the *Mile chengfo jing* (Sūtra on Maitreya Attaining Buddhahood), or the *Xiasheng chengfo* (Attaining Buddhahood upon Descent), or the *Dangxia chengfo* (Attaining Buddhahood upon the Current Descent).
This is recorded in the catalogs of the Two Qin dynasties and the *Sengyou lu*. Mañjuśrī...

The *Lìwèn pútí jīng* (Sūtra on Questions Regarding Bodhi), one fascicle—also simply called the *Pútí jīng* (Bodhi Sūtra), alternatively titled the *Gāyashīrṣa sūtra* (Sūtra of the Summit of Gayā) or the *Pútí wúxíng jīng* (Sūtra on the Non-practice of Bodhi)—was originally a translation identical in text to the *Gāyashīrṣa sūtra* and the *Hastikṣaya sūtra*.

This is recorded in Sengyou’s *Chū sānzàng jìjí* (Collection of Records Concerning the Translation of the Tripiṭaka) within the *Yìjīng tújù* (Illustrated Record of Translated Scriptures). Any separate listing of a one-fascicle *Pútí jīng* elsewhere is an error.

*The Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī Sūtra*, one fascicle; the fourth edition, also titled *The Great Golden Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī Sūtra*, produced at the Xiaoyao Garden, including the complete methods for establishing the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*). Fang says it is seen in the *Bielu*.
*The Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*, three fascicles (or two fascicles); also simply called *The Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Sengyou says it is a new [translation].
The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, fascicle nine; this is the same text as the *Śūraṅgama-vīravikrāmiṇa-samādhi-sūtra* and others.

According to Sengyou’s Catalogue, there is also the *Acintyaprabhāsa-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in one fascicle, also titled the *Acintyaprabhāsa-bodhisattva-bhāṣita-sūtra*, and also called the *Acintyaprabhāsa-kumāra-bodhisattva-sūtra*. This is the second appearance [of this text].
It is the same text as the *Acintya-bāla-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa; this is recorded in the *Changfang lu*.

The *Huashou jing* (Flower-Hand Sūtra) consists of thirteen fascicles, though it is sometimes titled *Huashou jing*, also known as the *Shezheshangen jing* (Sūtra on Gathering All Roots of Goodness) or the *Shefude jing* (Sūtra on Gathering Merit).
It is also found in eleven or twelve fascicles, translated in the eighth year of Hongshi, as recorded in the *Erqin lu* and the *Sengyou lu*.

*The Sutra on the Brief Exposition of the Teaching and Admonition as the Buddha Was About to Enter Parinirvāṇa*, one fascicle; also known as *The Sutra on the Buddha’s Imminent Parinirvāṇa* or *The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching*.
Recorded in the *Sengyou lu*. *The Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of the Thousand Buddhas*, one fascicle. Recorded in the *Fashang lu*. *The Brahmajāla Sūtra*, two fascicles;
also known as *The Sutra on the Selection of All Dharmas*. Sometimes in three fascicles or sometimes in two. Translated in the sixth month of the seventh year of Hongshi.
The appearance of the *Dvādaśāditya-sūtra* on the thirteenth day of the sixth month in the seventh year of Hongshi (385 CE), as recorded in the *Two Qin Records* and the *Sengyou Record*.

The ten precepts were transcribed by Sengzhao; this appears in the preface to the sutra. The *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* in four fascicles—also known as the *Sarvadharmaparīkṣā-sūtra*—or in three or two fascicles, was translated on the same date and is found in the *Two Qin Records* and the *Sengyou Record*. [The *Qingjing-jing*...]
*Vinayavaipulya-sūtra*, one fascicle; same text as the *Mañjuśrī-viśuddha-vinaya*, third edition, appearing in the *Fǎshàng-lù*.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, one hundred fascicles; also called the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra-śāstra*, or the *Mahāprajñā-vyākhyā-śāstra*;
alternatively in seventy or one hundred ten fascicles. Translated in the summer of the fourth year of Hongshi at...
The translation at Xiaoyao Garden was completed on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month of the seventh year. Sengrui composed the preface;

it is recorded in the two Qin catalogs and the Sengyou lu. Regarding the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* in four fascicles—also called the *Zhongguan lun* (Treatise on the Middle Way)—it was translated at the Dasi Monastery in the eleventh year of Hongshi.
Sengrui composed the preface; it is recorded in the two Qin catalogs and the Sengyou lu, as well as the aforementioned *Zhi*.
The *Dulun* (Treatise on the Stages of Liberation), composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;

the *Shiermen lun* (Twelve Gate Treatise), one fascicle, composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, translated at the Great Monastery in the eleventh year of Hongshi with a preface written by Sengrui—both are recorded in the *Sengyou lu* and the *Baochang lu*;

and the *Bailun* (Hundred Verse Treatise), two fascicles, composed by the Bodhisattva Āryadeva, translated in the sixth year of Hongshi with a preface written by Sengzhao—these are both recorded in the aforementioned catalogs.
The *Qin lu* and the *Sengyou lu* record the *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra* in fourteen fascicles;
it is attributed to Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, though some versions omit the word "vibhāṣā," while others list it as twelve or fifteen fascicles, as seen in the *Changfang lu*.

The *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* in fifteen fascicles—or without the word "vyūha"—is attributed to Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, though some versions list it as ten fascicles, as seen in the *Changfang lu*. [Then follows: *Fā...* [text truncated].
*The Treatise on the Bodhicitta*, two fascicles; also called *The Sūtra on Generating the Bodhicitta* or simply *The Sūtra-Treatise*;
see Li Kuò’s Record. *The Sūtra on Tending Cattle*, one fascicle; also called *The Sūtra on Herding Oxen*; translated from the forty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*;
alternative translation; see Fang’s separate record. *The Sūtra on the Eight Virtues of the Ocean*, one fascicle; third translation, same as the *Dharmasāgara*.

The *Jing deng ben jian fa shang lu chan mi yao jing* (Scripture on the Secret Essentials of Dhyāna Recorded by Fashang Based on the Original Text) in three fascicles—also referred to as the *Chan mi yao fa* (Secret Essentials of Dhyāna) without the word "jing" (scripture)—or in four fascicles, is the same text as that translated by Zhi Qian and others;
the second edition was seen by Fang in the *Bie lu* (Separate Catalog).

The *Deng zhi yin yuan jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Lamp-Pointing) in one fascicle is found in Li Kuò’s catalog. The *Shisong biqiu jieben* (Ten Recitation Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa Sūtra) in one fascicle... [text continues].
The scroll also states that the *Daśabhāṇavāra-prātimokṣa-śīla* was translated by Dharmatrāta and others from the same original text as previously mentioned;
this is recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* consists of twenty, twenty-four, twenty-seven, sixteen, or fourteen fascicles.
On the eighth day of the ninth month of the thirteenth year of Hongshi, the Minister of the Secretariat, Yao Xuan, [recorded it].

The invitation to produce [this text] was completed on the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the fourteenth year. Transcribed by Tan-gui. Composed by Harivarman nine hundred years after the Buddha’s passing;

recorded in Sengyou’s Catalogue (*Chu sanzang jiji*). The *Zuochan sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seated Meditation) in three fascicles, also titled the *Pusa chanfa jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Methods of Meditation).
When first produced, it was sometimes simply called the *Chan jing* (Meditation Sūtra), sometimes the *Chanfa yao* (Essentials of Meditation Methods), or sometimes the *A...* [text fragment].
*Āraṇyaka-caryā-dhyāna-vidhi*. Three titles for one work. Translated on the fifteenth day of the first month in the fourth year of Hongshi (402 CE).
Re-edited on the fifth day of the intercalary month in the ninth year. Preface by Sengrui. Recorded in the catalogs of Sengyou, Baochang, and the two Qi dynasties.
*Bodhisattva-kutsita-rūpa-kāma-dharma*, one fascicle; also called *Bodhisattva-kutsita-rūpa-kāma-sūtra*. Or...
The *Direct Discourse on the Bodhisattva’s Rebuke of Form and Desire* (Zhíyún púsà hē sèyù) first appeared in Sēngyòu’s Catalogue;
it is also called the *Essential Explanation of Dhyāna Methods* (*Chánfǎ yàojiě*) in two fascicles, or the *Sūtra on the Essentials of Dhyāna* (*Chányào jīng*).

The *Brief Essential Method of Contemplation* (*Sīwéi lüeyào fǎ*) in one fascicle, also called the *Sūtra on the Brief Essentials of Contemplation* (*Sīwéi yàolüè fǎjīng*), or simply the *Sūtra of Contemplation* (*Sī jīng*), was the second appearance, found in Zhǎngfáng’s Catalogue among the *Miscellaneous Parables* (*Zápìyù*).
*Sūtra* in one fascicle; translated in the tenth month of the seventh year of Hongshi. *Biography of Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa* in one fascicle, collected from the *Daolüe*;
recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *Biography of Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna* in one fascicle; recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *Biography of Bodhisattva Āryadeva* in one fascicle;
recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *Dharmadhātusvabhāvanirvikalpa-sūtra* in two fascicles; identical to the *Ratnakūṭa-dharma*.
The *Jiè tǐ xìng huì tóng běn chū xiàn* (The Essential Nature of the Realms: A Compendium of Original Appearances), recorded in the *Fǎshàng lù* (Record of Fǎshàng); the following portion is missing.
The *Dà shànquán jīng* (Sutra of Great Skillful Means) in two fascicles is the same text as the "Skillful Means Assembly" (*Fāngbiàn huì*) of the *Bǎojí jīng* (Ratnakūṭa Sūtra).

The fourth [entry], the *Dàfāngdáng dàjí jīng* (Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra) in thirty fascicles—or twenty-four fascicles with the addition of the character "New"—is the same text as that of [Zhi]... recorded in the *Lǐ kuò lù* (Record of Lǐ Kuò).

The *Cen* (Prophecy) and the *Wu cen* (No Prophecy) are of the same original text as those translated by Dharmarakṣa and others; this is seen in the *Lü of the Two Qin Dynasties* and the *Record of Li Kuò*.
The one-fascicle *Mahāvaipulya Uṣṇīṣarāja Sūtra* is of the same original text as that translated by Dharmarakṣa and others; it is the second translation, as seen in the *Record of Changfang*.
The two-fascicle *Ajātaśatru Sūtra* is of the same original text as that translated by Lokakṣema and others; it is the fifth translation, and Changfang notes that it appears in a separate record.

*Lu shan benqi jing* (Record of the Original Arising of Śyāma), one fascicle; also simply titled *Śyāma jing*, translated from a different version than that found in the *Liudu ji jing* (Collection of Six Perfections), second appearance, recorded in Li Kuò’s catalog.
*Qing guanshiyin jing* (Sutra on Entreaty to Avalokiteśvara), one fascicle; first appearance, same text as that produced by Zhu Fonian, recorded in Li Kuò’s catalog.
*Bawang jing* (Jewel Net Sutra), one fascicle; second appearance, same text as that produced by Dharmarakṣa.
The *Sūtra on Praising the Merits of All Buddhas* in three fascicles, also titled the *Sūtra of Collected Flowers*, is recorded as having been translated in the seventh year of the Hongshi era;
it appears in the *Records of the Two Qin* and the *Record of Sengyou*.

The *Sūtra on Contemplating the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra* in one fascicle is the second translation, appearing in the *Record of Li Kuò*. The *Sūtra on Unprecedented Causes and Conditions* in two fascicles was the first translation.
The *Jianfashang lu* records that the second volume of the seven-fascicle *Bhadra-kalpa-sūtra* was produced on the fifth day of the third month in the fourth year of Hongshi;
it shares the same original text as the translation by Dharmarakṣa, with Tanguo acting as the scribe. This is recorded in the *Sanqin lu* and the *Sengyou lu*.
It has three names: the *Bhadra-kalpa-samādhi-sūtra*, the *Bhadra-kalpa-samāpatti-sūtra*, and [the aforementioned title]. The *Sengyou lu* states this.
*The Sūtra of the New Bhadrakalpa* (Shin xianjie jing), *The Mahāvidyā-mantra Sūtra of Good Faith* (Shanxin mahashenzhou jing), two fascicles;

listed in Li Kuò’s record. *The Sūtra of the Earth-holding Bodhisattva* (Chidi jing), one fascicle; listed in Changfáng’s record. *The Sūtra on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha* (Gufo sanmei jing), one fascicle;

listed in Changfáng’s record. *The Bodhisattva Precept Text* (Pusa jieben), one fascicle; first appearing in Changfáng’s record. It is now suspected that this *Bodhisattva Precept Text* is identical to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
*The Sūtra of Mañjuśrī’s Repentance*, one fascicle; the second appearance, listed in the *Chángfáng lù*.
*The Sūtra of Śāriputra’s Repentance*, one fascicle; the third appearance, listed in the *Fǎshàng lù*. *Treatise on the Ten Stages* (*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*), ten fascicles;

composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, translated during the Hongshi era [of the Later Qin], though not yet completed. The end of the tenth fascicle appears similar to the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya*; listed in the two *Qin lù*.

According to Sengyou’s Catalogue, I now suspect that this *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* is the same as the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*. I have examined the ten fascicles of the *Zhuzui-fu jing* (Sūtra on Various Sins and Merits);
Sengfang says he saw it in the *Bielu* (Separate Catalogue). There is one fascicle of the *Dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, seen in Sengchang’s *Bielu*.

There is one fascicle of the *Vasu-bandhu-zhuan* (Biography of Vasubandhu), first appearing in the *Fanjing tu* (Diagram of Translated Scriptures). Altogether, these seventy-four works comprise three hundred [fascicles].
The *Biography of Bodhisattva Deva*, eight volumes and four scrolls; fifty-two works totaling three hundred and two scrolls currently extant;
and twenty-two works totaling eighty-two scrolls for which the texts are missing.

The śramaṇa Kumārajīva—“Jiushou” (Child-Life) in the language of Qin—and also known as Kumārajīva, took his name by combining elements from both his parents, as it was the custom in foreign lands to base names upon one's parents: his father was named Kumāra and his mother’s name was Jīva. Thus, he was given this combined name.
He was a man from India whose family had served as ministers of state for generations.
Kumārajīva’s grandfather was Datta.
He was unconventional and stood apart from the crowd, his reputation being esteemed throughout the realm.
His father, Kumārajīva, was intelligent and possessed noble character; he was about to succeed to the position of Prime Minister.
He then took his leave to renounce the world and travel east across the Pamir Mountains.
When the King of Kucha heard that he had abandoned his glory and forsaken secular life, he held him in profound reverence and admiration.
He went out from the capital to welcome him and invited him to serve as National Preceptor.
The King had a younger sister who was twenty years of age;
she possessed such brilliant intelligence that she could recite anything after a single glance and memorize it upon hearing it once.
Furthermore, her body bore a vermilion mole, a sign that she would give birth to a son of wisdom.
Kings from various nations sought her hand in marriage, but she refused them all.
When she saw Yanxin, however, she desired to become his wife.
Upon hearing this, the king was greatly delighted and compelled him to take her as his wife.
Subsequently, Kumārajīva was born;
while he was still in the womb, his mother’s wisdom and understanding were twice as great as usual.
He went to the Great Kaniṣka Monastery to listen to the sutras,
whereupon he suddenly attained spontaneous mastery of the Indian language;
whenever he posed difficult questions or inquiries, his interlocutors were invariably left at a loss.
The assembly all marveled at this in astonishment.
A *arhat* named Mākuṣa said,
"This woman must surely be carrying a child of wisdom."
He recounted the evidence regarding Śāriputra’s time in the womb;
yet after being born, Kumārajīva was as precocious as a deity,
and once he was born, he forgot the previous words.
Shortly thereafter, his mother left the household life to practice the Way and attained the first fruit of enlightenment.
When Kumārajīva was seven years old, he also left the household life;
under his teacher, he received the sūtras and recited a thousand verses daily.
The verses consist of thirty-two characters and total thirty-two thousand words.
Having recited this Abhidharma, one has already surpassed what was transmitted by the teacher.
The meaning of these principles was naturally and thoroughly understood by him; there was nothing obscure that he could not elucidate.
At that time, because his mother was the King’s daughter and her offerings were exceedingly abundant, the people of Kucha took Kumārajīva along with him to avoid [the king].
At the age of nine, he proceeded to Jibin,
where he met the renowned and virtuous Dharma Master Bandhudatta,
who was the younger brother of the King of Jibin.
Profound and pure, he possessed a vast capacity for understanding.
There was nothing among the Tripiṭaka or the nine divisions of the scriptures that he did not master in detail.
He could also recite a thousand verses daily, and his fame spread throughout many countries.
Once Kumārajīva arrived, he served him as his teacher.
He subsequently recited the *Madhyama Āgama* and the *Dīrgha Āgama* from within the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka*, totaling four million words.
Guṇabhadra would often engage Kumārajīva in debate and always deeply admired and respected him.
The sound reached the King.
The King immediately invited him to enter and assemble the non-Buddhist masters (*tīrthika-ācāryas*) to engage in mutual debate.
As the exchange of words began, the non-Buddhists, looking down upon his youth, spoke with considerable insolence.
Kumārajīva took advantage of this opening to defeat him.
The non-Buddhist was humbled and subdued, remaining speechless with shame and regret.
The King’s respect and admiration increased daily; he subsequently provided him with a pair of goose haunches, three *dǒu* each of non-glutinous rice and flour, and six *chǔn* of clarified butter.
Furthermore, as a supreme offering to the foreign country,
the monks of the monastery where he resided dispatched five senior monks and ten śrāmaṇeras to attend to him,
sweeping and cleaning for him as if they were his own disciples.
He was thus held in such high esteem.
When he reached the age of twelve, his mother took him back to Kucha.
Upon arriving at the Northern Mountains of the Yuezhi, an arhat saw him and marveled at his extraordinary nature.
He said to his mother,
"You must always protect him;
if this śrāmaṇera reaches the age of thirty-five without breaking the precepts,"
He shall greatly propagate the Buddha-dharma and deliver countless people,
no different from Upagupta;
yet if his precepts are not complete, he will be unable to achieve this.
It was fitting that only the brilliant and eminent Dharma Master [Moksala] should have arrived.
As Kumārajīva proceeded to the kingdom of Kāśagarhṣa, he took up the Buddha’s almsbowl upon his head and thought to himself:
"The shape of this bowl is very large; why is it so light?
He immediately felt it was too heavy to bear, let out a cry, and dropped it.
His mother asked him the reason.
He replied,
"It is only because my mind harbors discrimination that the bowl appears to have weight.
In the country of Kashgar, Kumārajīva recited the six *pāda* treatises of the Abhidharma and the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
Upon his return to Kucha, his fame eclipsed that of all other nations.
At that time, the monastic community of Kucha, numbering more than ten thousand, suspected he was no ordinary person;
they all venerated him and dared not occupy a position above him.
Consequently, he was not included among those who burned incense;

instead, he extensively read the four Vedas, the treatises on the five sciences, and the scriptures of non-Buddhist paths, mastering everything from the principles of yin and yang and stellar calculation without exception.
He was profoundly adept at discerning auspiciousness and misfortune, his words matching reality as if by a tally.
By nature, he was straightforward and forthright, not adhering strictly to minor restraints;
consequently, practitioners of the Way somewhat criticized him for this.
Kumārajīva attained realization within his own mind and never gave such matters a second thought.
He studied the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* under Vimalākṣa and further received instruction in the Mahāyāna from Śūryasoma.
He then sighed and said:
"In the past, my study of the Hīnayāna was like a person who does not recognize gold and mistakes brass for something exquisite.
Thereupon, he extensively sought out the essential meanings and recited the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Śata-śāstra*, the *Dvādaśanikāya-śāstra*, and other such works.
After a short while, Kumārajīva’s mother took her leave to travel to India.
She said to Bai Chun, the King of Kucha, "Your kingdom will soon decline; it is time for me to depart."
While traveling through India and advancing to the third fruit of the path,
Kumārajīva’s mother said to him as she was about to depart,
"The profound teachings of the Vaipulya sutras should be extensively propagated in China."
"That you have transmitted [the teachings] to the Eastern lands is solely due to your power.
However, as it brings no benefit to yourself, what can be done?
Kumārajīva replied:
The path of a Great Being benefits others even at the cost of his own life.
If it is necessary to cause the Great Transformation to spread and wash away the ignorance of the common people,
he would feel no regret even if his body were cast into the cauldrons of hell.
Thereupon, he remained in Kucha at the King’s New Monastery.
Having obtained the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, he began to study it;
however, Māra came and obscured the text so that he saw only blank pages.
Kumārajīva knew this was the work of Māra, yet his vow became even more firm.
After Māra departed, he continued to practice and recite it;
later, at the Mahāvana Monastery in Kaniṣka, he read the Mahāyāna sūtras.
Suddenly, a voice was heard from the air saying, "You are a wise man; why do you read this?
Kumārajīva replied, "You are a minor demon; you should depart at once."
"My mind is like the earth; it cannot be turned.
He remained there for three years, extensively reciting Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras until he had thoroughly penetrated their secret mysteries.
The King of Kucha constructed for him a golden lion throne.
A fine Chinese brocade mat was spread out for him, and Kumārajīva sat upon it as he preached the Dharma.
Later, he went to Kaśmīra and fully explained the wondrous meaning of the One Vehicle to his teacher, Bandhudatta.
The Master was awakened to the truth and submitted with heartfelt devotion, immediately prostrating himself before Kumārajīva as his teacher.
He said, "I am the Upādhyāya’s teacher of the Hīnayāna;
the Upādhyāya is my teacher of the Mahāyāna."
The various kingdoms of the Western Regions were all converted by Kumārajīva’s divine brilliance; they all held him in the highest esteem and veneration.
Whenever he gave a lecture, the kings would kneel on their right knees beside his seat and have Kumārajīva step upon them to ascend.
His reputation was esteemed in such a manner.
Kumārajīva’s fame shook the Western Regions and his influence spread to the Eastern Kingdoms.
In the first month of the year Dingchou, the thirteenth year of the Jianyuan era of the Fu clan, the Grand Astrologer submitted a memorial.
A star was seen in the celestial division corresponding to foreign lands,
which indicated that a man of great virtue and wisdom would enter to assist the Central Kingdom.
Yao Xian had long heard of Kumārajīva’s reputation.
He then realized and said,
"I have heard that there is Kumārajīva in the Western Regions; could this not be him?"
In the nineteenth year, Jian dispatched the General of the Light Cavalry Lü Guang and others with seventy thousand troops to campaign westward against the kingdoms of Kucha, Karashahr, and others.
As they were about to set out, he said to Guang:
I have heard that there is Kumārajīva there,
who deeply understands the characteristics of dharmas and is well-versed in the principles of yin and yang, serving as the preeminent master of learning for that land.
I am thinking of him.
If Kucha were captured, Kumārajīva would have been sent there immediately by post.
Before King Guang’s army arrived, Kumārajīva said to its king, Bai Chun:
"The destiny of your nation is declining; you shall soon face a formidable enemy."
A man from the land under the sun came from the east;
it would have been appropriate to receive him with respect rather than oppose his advance.
Because [Fu] Chun did not comply and instead fought, Guang subsequently defeated Kucha, killed Chun, and captured Kumārajīva.
Daōguāng’s nature was aloof, yet he could not fathom Kumārajīva’s measure of wisdom.
Seeing that he was still young in years, Daōguāng treated him as an ordinary man and mocked him.
When Kumārajīva was thus driven to the limit, he ultimately compromised his integrity.
Some attempted to cause him to fall by having him ride an ox or mount a vicious horse;
however, Kumārajīva always maintained patience and showed no sign of agitation.
Fǎguāng felt ashamed and desisted.
On the way back, Guang halted the army at the foot of a mountain;
once the officers and soldiers had rested,
Kumārajīva said:
"We cannot remain here; we will surely suffer a disastrous defeat.
It is best to move the army to the heights of Longshan.
Guang did not accept this advice, and when night fell, rain indeed came, and a sudden flood of torrential waters arose.
The water was several zhang deep, and thousands had perished there.
Dao-guang treated Kumārajīva with exceptional reverence and wonder.
Kumārajīva said to Dao-guang:
This is a place of misfortune and death; it is not fitting to linger here.
Calculating the numbers and discerning the destiny, you should speak of returning home at once.
Along the way, there will surely be a blessed land where you may dwell.
Kumārajīva followed this light and reached Liangzhou, where he heard that Fu Jian had already died;
he subsequently established a foothold in the land of Liang and exercised authority over that corner of the realm.
Kumārajīva remained in Liang for many years.
After he had spoken these words several times, everything occurred exactly as he had said.
Since Lü Guang and his son did not propagate the Way,
they kept the scriptures and teachings hidden, with no means to spread their transformative influence.
Fu Jian had already perished before they could ever meet.
When Yao Chang heard of his eminent reputation, he sincerely invited him with open-mindedness.
The various Lü brothers [of Fu Jian] considered that because Shi possessed many strategic insights and understandings, [they feared for their safety].
Fearing that this was a plot by Yao, he did not permit [Fu] Chang to enter the east.
When Chang died, his son Xing succeeded him, posthumously titled Emperor Wenzu;
he then sent envoys again to invite [Fu Jian].
In the third year of Hongshi, the year being Xinchou, in the third month,
a tree with interlocking branches grew in the courtyard of the temple;
furthermore, in the Xiaoyao Garden, the leeks transformed into *zhuan* (a type of aromatic plant).
Considering this a most auspicious omen, he declared that a man of wisdom should enter [the capital].
On the twentieth day of the twelfth month of that year, Kumārajīva arrived at Cháng'ān.
Fǎxìng treated him with the etiquette due to a National Teacher and showed him the highest honor and favor.
