When we converse face-to-face regarding the realization of the truth, we linger together all day long;
when we investigate the subtle and reach its ultimate limit, we exhaust the year without forgetting our diligence.
Since the Great Dharma was first transmitted to the East during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, it has been thus.
Having traveled through the Wei and Jin dynasties, he gradually acquired many sūtras and śāstras;
however, those translated by Zhi Qian and Dharmarakṣa were often hindered by archaic phrasing and interpretive schemata (gēyì).
Huixing, from his youth, revered the Triple Gem and was resolute in his commitment to lecturing and compiling commentaries.
When Kumārajīva arrived at Jiankang, he was invited to enter the Ximing Pavilion and the Xiaoyao Garden to translate various scriptures.
Kumārajīva mostly recited them from memory; there were none that he did not master thoroughly.
He became proficient in the phonology of the Qin language and fluent in translation.
Upon examining the old scriptures, he found that their meanings were frequently erroneous;
this was entirely due to the fact that previous translators had missed the essential intent, such that their versions did not correspond with the Sanskrit originals.

Emperor Xiaowen dispatched over eight hundred people, including the śramaṇas Sengzhao, Sengqie, Sengmiao, and Sengrui, to receive Kumārajīva’s instructions and have him retranslate the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Kumārajīva held the Sanskrit manuscript while Emperor Xiaowen held the previous Chinese version, and they compared them against one another.
The new texts differed from the old ones, yet their meanings were all perfectly comprehensive;
everyone was filled with admiration and did not fail to rejoice in and praise them.
Emperor Xing [recognized that] the Buddha-way is profound and subtle, and its practice consists solely of goodness.
Faith is the bridge and ferry for escaping suffering and the grand standard for looking up to the world; therefore,
he entrusted his intent to the Nine Classics and let his mind roam through the Twelve Divisions of Scripture,
subsequently composing the *Tongsanshi Lun* (Treatise on the Three Times) to exhort and demonstrate the principle of cause and effect.
From the princes and dukes downward, all admired and praised his character; among them were Xian, Duke of Changshan of the Imperial Clan,
and Song, Marquis of Ancheng,
both of whom possessed profound faith in the principle of causes and effects.
He repeatedly invited Kumārajīva to the Chang’an Great Monastery to lecture on the newly translated scriptures.
This occurred from the fourth year of Hongshi, the Renyin year,
until the fourteenth year, the Renzi year.

He translated seventy-four works totaling more than three hundred and eighty fascicles, including the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
In all of these, he thoroughly elucidated the divine source and brought forth its profound subtleties.

At that time, more than three thousand monks from all four directions—renowned for their learning and outstanding in virtue who had traveled from as far as ten thousand *li*, including the two masters Cai and Chang, as well as Daoheng, Sengbiao, Huiyi, Sengdun, Sengbi, Sengzhao, and others—gathered there.
He received instructions and conducted profound research, striving to exhaustively fathom the subtle meaning.
As the dharma career of Huiyuan of Mount Lu was pure and refined,
he dispatched an envoy to inquire after him.
The Daoist Huixie of Longguang Temple, who had profound insight into the subtle mysteries, also entered the Pass to seek instruction.
His magnificent achievements have endured for a long time and remain vast; even today, people look up to him as a model.
Initially, the śramaṇa Huìyuǎn, whose talent and insight were exceptionally brilliant, constantly accompanied Kumārajīva to transcribe his works.
Kumārajīva frequently engaged in discussions with Yuǎn regarding the literary styles of the Western regions, deliberating upon their similarities and differences.
The customs of the kingdom of India place great importance on literary elegance.
Regarding the tonal patterns and rhythmic cadences, they consider it excellent when these are set to stringed instruments.
Whenever one has an audience with the King, there must be a hymn of praise for his virtues.
The ritual for beholding the Buddha takes the chanting of praises as its preeminent form;
the verse hymns found throughout the sūtras all follow this model.
However, by transcribing the Sanskrit into the Qin language, their elegant refinement has been lost.
Although you have grasped the general meaning, it is utterly divorced from the literary style;
it is like chewing food for someone else.
Not only do you fail to convey the flavor, but you actually cause the person to vomit.
Kumārajīva composed this verse as a gift for the śramaṇa Fǎhuá:
"The mountain of mind nurtures virtue and its fragrance permeates;
Its sweet scent flows forth for ten thousand yojanas."
The grieving phoenix cries upon the solitary paulownia;
its pure resonance pierces the nine heavens.
In all, there are ten stanzas.
This applies to both his terminology and his metaphors.
Kumārajīva was deeply fond of the Mahāyāna and was committed to its propagation;
he once sighed and said:
If I were to take up my pen to compose a Mahāyāna Abhidharma, it would not be comparable to that of Kātyāyanīputra.
At present, those with deep understanding are few in this land of Qin;
with my wings broken here, what would there be to discuss?
He then desisted in sorrow and wrote only the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Realization of True Reality) in two fascicles for Yao Xing;
his words flowed into elegant composition without the need for any deletion or revision.
His diction and metaphors were elegant and refined, all of them profound and subtle.
Kumārajīva was a man whose spirit and character were transparently brilliant;
he was loftily eminent among his peers, responding to circumstances with instantaneous comprehension.
Rarely has there been his equal.
Moreover, he was sincere by nature, benevolent and kind, with universal compassion as his core motive.
He humbled himself to guide others well, never growing weary throughout the entire day.
At that time, the śramaṇas Sengrui and Xing were greatly delighted.
Sengrui participated in the verification and correction of all the sūtras translated by Kumārajīva.
Previously, in the "Chapter on Receiving the Prediction" (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa, it was said:
"The heavens see humans, and humans see the heavens.
When Kumārajīva reached this passage in his translation, he remarked:
"The meaning of these words is identical to that of the Sanskrit original."
However, when [the monk] spoke words that were overly plain, Huì responded at once, saying,
"Is it not that humans and devas have met, so that both may see one another?"
Kumārajīva was greatly delighted and said, "It is indeed so.
Such were the instances in which Huì and Kumārajīva mutually inspired and enlightened one another.
Once, he listened to the Qin monk Dàoróng lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Kumārajīva then sighed and said,
"The flourishing of the Buddha-dharma depends upon its people.
Shortly thereafter, there was a Brahmin from the Kingdom of Siṃhala.
He was intelligent and eloquent, having studied many secular texts of the Western lands, few of which he had not read and recited.
However, when the non-Buddhist masters abroad heard that Kumārajīva was widely propagating the Buddha-dharma in Guanzhong, they were deeply concerned.
He then sighed with deep emotion and said to his disciples:
"How can it be that the teachings of the Śākya alone have spread throughout China,
while our own scriptures of the True Dharma have not yet reached this eastern land?"
Consequently, he traveled far on a camel carrying his books and arrived in Chang’an.
When Yao Xing saw that his mouth and eyes were so clever and persuasive, he was somewhat deluded by him.
The Brahmin then addressed Yao Xing, saying:
"The Ultimate Way has no fixed direction, and each honors their own practice.
I have therefore come from afar to request a contest of dialectical power with the monks of Qin."
Whenever there was someone capable, they would immediately transmit the mission to them,
and Yao Xing granted his permission.
At that time, the monastic community from all four directions in Guanzhong looked at one another with a sense of deficiency, none daring to accept the task.
Kumārajīva said to Tanyu:
"This non-Buddhist is exceptionally clever; in a contest of speech, he will surely prevail.
It would be truly lamentable if we, who uphold the unsurpassed Great Way, were to yield to him."
If we were to allow the non-Buddhists to act according to their whims and achieve their ambitions,
it would mean that our Wheel of Dharma has broken its axle;
how could such a thing be permitted?
"As I have observed, you alone possess this quality.
Dao Rong considers his own talent and ability to be no inferior [to yours],
yet he has not yet fully read the scriptures of the non-Buddhist outsiders of the Western Regions."
He then secretly ordered someone to transcribe the titles of the scriptures read by the Brahmin; upon a single glance, [the monk] could recite them from memory.
Subsequently, the date for the formal debate was set, and Yao Xing came in person, with all the high officials assembled.
The monastic community of Guanzhong gathered from all directions;
at that time, Daorong engaged in debate with the Brahmin,
his soaring and profound eloquence surpassing what the other could reach.
At that time, although the Brahmin recognized for himself that his arguments were already defeated,
he still took pride in his extensive learning.
Daorong then laid out the texts he had written.
Furthermore, he generally discussed how the titles and volumes of the scriptures and histories in the land of Qin were three times greater than those [in India].
Kumārajīva, seizing the opportunity, satirized him by saying,
"Have you not heard that the Great Qin is vast in its learning?"
Having come from afar so unexpectedly and lightly,
the Brahmin felt shame and submission;
he prostrated at Huirong’s feet and departed within ten days without further ado.
The resurgence of the Dharma during the Age of Images was due to the power of Kumārajīva’s harmonizing influence.
Furthermore, when the Bhikṣu Beidu was in Pengcheng, he heard that Kumārajīva was in Chang’an and sighed, saying:
"I have been separated from this disciple for more than three hundred years in play.
We are now lost in obscurity, with no set time for reunion; we shall likely meet again in a future life.
As Kumārajīva was nearing death, he summoned his strength to bid farewell to the assembly of monks, saying:
Meeting through the Dharma, we have by no means fully exhausted our mutual intentions;
now that we shall be separated in different worlds, my grief is profound—
what more can be said?
I have, out of my own ignorance, mistakenly served as a translator.
If what I have transmitted is free from error, may my tongue not be scorched or withered after my body is cremated.
On the thirteenth day of the fourth month in the fifteenth year of Hongshi, he passed away at the Great Monastery at the age of seventy.
His body was cremated according to foreign rites within the Xiaoyao Garden.
The firewood was consumed and its form transformed, yet only the tongue remained unchanged;
this truly provides evidence for the efficacy of propagating the Dharma. When Master Kumārajīva passed away, various records were inconsistent.
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* states that he died in Chang’an on the twentieth day of the eighth month in the eleventh year of Hongshi.
Some say seventy,
others say eighty;
the tradition takes eleven as the correct number.
This is not so. According to the postscript to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*,
it was written on the eighth day of the ninth month of the year Shiwei, the thirteenth year of Hongshi during the Qin dynasty.
Yao Xian, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, requested that the treatise be published.
It was completed on the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the following year.
According to this, Kumārajīva had not yet passed away at the end of the fourteenth year.
Furthermore, according to the memorial submitted by Sengzhao to Yao Xing, the ruler of Qin,
regarding the "Treatise on the Namelessness of Nirvāṇa," it states that Sengzhao remained in the school of Master Kumārajīva for over ten years.
If Kumārajīva produced the scriptures in the fourth year [of the Jianyuan era],...
He passed away in the eleventh year.
From his beginning, eight years had elapsed,
but he had not yet completed ten years.
How can it be said that [he lived] for more than ten years?
Now, according to Kumārajīva’s eulogy, he passed away on the thirteenth day of the fourth month in the year Guichou;
this Guichou year was the fifteenth year of Hongshi.
However, regarding the various recensions of the scriptures translated by Kumārajīva, the number of fascicles differs considerably according to various accounts;
in the *Chángfáng lù*, the count is even more extensive.
Upon careful examination, it appears that most of these are merely derivative versions.
Some volumes contain multiple titles,
or there are errors in the headings;
the specific items are listed below.
I have now deleted them all.
Regarding the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* in sixty-one fascicles, Sengyou’s catalog states it was translated by Kumārajīva;

however, since there are currently only fifty-eight fascicles, these were merely transcribed by Kumārajīva and not his direct translation. The final three fascicles were subsequently produced by Vimalākṣa.

Having set this aside for later, I have recorded other works here that are no longer extant. The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Fàngguāng) in twenty fascicles was the second translation;
it appears in the *Bié lù* (Separate Record). Now, the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Fàngguāng* is identical to that of the *Dàpǐn*.

When the *Dàpǐn* was being produced, Kumārajīva translated the new version while the old version already existed. If one asks which of these was the old version translated by Kumārajīva regarding the *Fàngguāng*: [the answer follows].

Because this is so, we know that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) is the new version and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Fangguang) is the old; it is a grave error to load both versions together.
Regarding the twenty-fascicle *Collection of Prajñā Sūtras and Treatises*, Fang states that he saw it in the *Wulu*.

This current collection is actually the work of Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu, who, seeing that the textual phrases of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* were excessively voluminous and difficult for beginners to seek out, deleted the redundancies and trimmed the excesses.

Regarding the current edition, which clarifies the substance and form and consists of twenty fascicles—also known as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra-saṃgraha* or the *Vyākhyā-śāstra-saṃkṣepa*—this was a condensation of the previous treatise by Master Huiyuan and not a separate translation by Kumārajīva.
The *Chánfǎ yào* (Essentials of Dhyāna Methods) in three fascicles states that it was previously translated;
it was re-edited in the ninth year of Hongshi, and Sengrui composed its preface. Since it explicitly mentions "previously translated," [it confirms this].

In the subsequent collation, two titles were retained that do not accord with one another; according to Sengrui’s preface to the sutra, the *Zuochan sanmei jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of Seated Meditation) is the same as the *Aluonuo xichanfa jing* (Sutra on the Methods of Practice for Meditation in Āraṇya), in two fascicles.
Fang states that he saw it in the *Bielu* (Separate Catalogue), though some versions lack the character "jing" (sutra).

This [latter title] shares the same root text as the *Zuochan* [sutra] but was issued separately. I now maintain that this is not so; rather, it is simply an alternative name for the *Zuochan sanmei*. Upon investigation...
The phrasing at the beginning and end of this text is identical to that of the original edition; it was not produced by a collator.

One fascicle of the *Lèyíngluòzhuāngyán jīng* (Sūtra of the Adornment of Necklaces) is recorded in the catalog of Fang [Xuanling]. According to the postscript at the end of the sūtra, however, it was translated by Dharmayaśas and was not a translation by Kumārajīva.
It is now moved and appended to his catalog. One fascicle of the *Bǎoxiàng lùn* (Treatise on the Precious Marks) is mentioned in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
The two fascicles translated by Kumārajīva for Yao Xing were not from Indic originals; they are thus omitted [from the standard canon].

In ancient times, there were the *Fo guo yuan xing fa dian jing* (Sutra on the Dharma Canon of Vows and Practices in the Buddha-land), also known as the *Sheng he chu wen shu fo tu yan jing* (Sutra on the Adornment and Purity of Mañjuśrī’s Buddha-land Spoken by Śākyamuni), and the *Fo qing kai che shi fang jing* (Sutra on the Buddha’s Laughter Resonating Throughout the Ten Directions).
The *Buddha-zi-hua-chu-pusa-jing* (Sutra on the Buddha’s Equal Transformation and Emanation of Bodhisattvas),
the *Mo-yeh-jing* (Sutra on the Deeds of Māra),
and the *Guoqu-wubian-guangjing-fotu-jing* (Sutra on the Immeasurable Radiance Pure Buddha-land of the Past).
The *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-śravaṇadhāraṇī-sūtra*,
also known as the *Sūtra on Attaining Merit* or the *Sūtra on Attaining Blessings*,
and the *Sūtra on Transcending the Realm of Mara*.
The Sūtra on the Demon King Śukra’s Firm Faith;
the Verse Recitation Sūtra on the Buddha’s Disciple Transforming the Demon Son;
and the Sūtra on Converting Demons.
The *Māraparivarta-sūtra* emerged from the Buddha’s coughing and sneezing; ten sūtras subsequently issued forth from the *Mahāsannipāta*.
The *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* emerged from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, as did the *Ṣaḍvidha-kampana-sūtra* on the dharma-gate of dhāraṇīs.
The *Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Original Vow to Await the Time for Attaining Buddhahood Sūtra*,
the *Sūtra on the Buddha Transforming the Assembly’s Bodies*,
the *Sūtra on the Eastern World of Good Flowers and the Buddha’s Seat Trembling*, and the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra*— these four sūtras were all extracted from the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The *Sūtra of the King of Sparrows*,
the *Sūtra of the Buddha’s Former Life as the King of Deer*,
and the *Sūtra of the Bodhisattva’s Body as the King of Pigeons*— these three sūtras, including the *Sūtra of the King of Sparrows*, are all contained within the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya*.
The *Amitābha-sukhāvatī-vyūha-sūtra* also states that the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* appears in the *Madhyama-āgama*.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Buddha Asking the Asura about the Ocean Decreasing* appears in the *Madhyama-āgama*.
The *Sūtra on Seeing the Mark of the Thousand-Spoked Wheel on the Buddha’s Footprints*, from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*;
the *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Mind-Totality-Dhāraṇī*;
and the *Sūtra on the Water Buffalo King*.
The *Śaśarāja-sūtra*, the *Buddhacitta-samādhi-ādi-trisūtra*, and others are all extracted from the *Utpatti-sūtra*.
The *Markaṭa-dāsī-sahapradāna-vikāra-sūtra* and the two sūtras concerning the Queen and the Cockroach,
as well as the *Markaṭa-sūtra* and others, are all extracted from the *Saṃyukta-avadāna*.

The *Bhikṣu-ārya-dharma-caryā-sūtra* was recorded by Sengyou as a doubtful scripture and is currently included in the Catalogue of Doubtful Scriptures (*Yi lu*). Altogether, there are thirty-five works comprising one hundred and thirty-six fascicles.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), fifty-eight fascicles, was translated at Zhong Temple on the seventeenth day of the tenth month in the sixth year of Hongshi. It is recorded in the *Qin Lu*. This one work, consisting of fifty-eight fascicles, is extant.
The śramaṇa Puṇyatāra—
translated into the language of Qin as Guǒdéhuā (Flower of Merit)—
was a native of Jibin.
He left home to become a monk at a young age and was renowned for his observance of the precepts.
He was thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka and specialized in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya),
becoming a preeminent master for foreign teachers.
At that time, people all said he had already attained the fruits of sainthood. During the Hongshi era, he took up his staff and entered Guanzhong.
Emperor Xing of the Qin treated him with the etiquette due to a guest of highest honor.
Kumārajīva also held him in high esteem for his precepts and conduct, honoring him with profound reverence.
Previously, although the sūtras and dharmas had been transmitted, the Vinaya Piṭaka had not yet been expounded.
Hearing that Mātṛceṭa was well-versed in this section, everyone felt a shared longing for him.
On the seventeenth day of the tenth month in the sixth year of Hongshi (the Jiachen year),
More than six hundred śramaṇas specializing in the study of the Vinaya gathered at Chang'an Temple to invite Dharmanandin and orally recite the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
Kumārajīva translated it into the language of Qin,
achieving two-thirds of the work.
Then, Dharmatāra fell ill and suddenly passed away.
Because the great undertaking was not yet completed when the master artisan passed away,
the depth of their grief and regret surpassed that of ordinary sorrow.
Next, there was the śramaṇa Dharmaruci from the Western Regions—translated into Chinese as Fale—who had left home to enter the Way.
He was particularly renowned for his mastery of the Vinaya Piṭaka.
In the autumn of the seventh year of Hongshi, he arrived at Guanzhong.
When Shi Huiyuan of Mount Lu heard that Zhi was well-versed in the Vinaya and hoped to obtain a definitive understanding of the Vinaya-piṭaka,
he sent a letter to establish friendly relations, saying:
Since the rise of Buddhism first spread to the superior kingdoms and its subsequent division, more than four hundred years have passed.
Yet, regarding the attainment of the precepts by śramaṇas, there remain many deficiencies.
Recently, the Western Region monk Puṇyatāra, a native of Kaśmīra, arrived here.
He recited the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* from its Sanskrit original;
the Dharma Master Kumārajīva, a man of versatile talent and vast learning, served as its translator.

However, before more than half of the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra* had been completed, Mātara was prematurely lost to death, and the work was suspended mid-course, such that the great undertaking could not be brought to completion.
My regret and resentment are truly profound.
I have heard it said that you, O Benevolent One, carry this sutra with you at all times.
How could such a joyful encounter and the arrival of this hidden destiny be anything other than the work of the Unseen? It cannot be explained merely by human effort.
I consider that propagating the Way involves responding to the needs of beings by acting according to the occasion;
when one is struck by others, there must be no resentment in one's heart.
If you are a follower of the Vinaya school, you should complete this text.
He reveals the holy life to cleanse their ears and eyes,
ensuring that those who have first entered the stream do not lose the bridge to the Unsurpassed.
For those who harbor superior aspirations, the sun and moon shine ever more brightly.
This is indeed a case where grace is profound and virtue is deep, such that both humans and deities are moved in common.
I hope you will graciously extend your consideration and not depart from your previous intention.
Thus, Kumārajīva received the letter from Yuán as well as the invitation from Yáo Xīng.
He then completed the translation of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* together with Kumārajīva.
They scrutinized, examined, and cross-referenced the text, refining and finalizing its regulations;
yet Kumārajīva still regretted that the phrasing was cumbersome and not yet perfected.
Shortly thereafter, as Kumārajīva had passed away, the text could not be edited or refined.
Dharmaruci resided at the Great Monastery of Chang’an;
Huiguan wished to invite him to the capital of Yangdu.
Zhi said,
"That land possesses both people and the Dharma sufficient to benefit the world;
I shall instead travel to places where there is no teaching of the Vinaya."
Thereupon, he traveled and transformed others in other regions, with no one knowing where he had gone.
The *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle—initially appearing perhaps without the word "Bodhisattva"—is the same text as the *Ākāśa-sūtra*.
It is a separate division of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*. Later, having returned to his country, he obtained this sūtra at Kaśmīra and sent it along with a merchant caravan.

A person sent [the manuscript] to Liangzhou to see Daohui. According to the *Song Qi Lu* and Sengyou’s record, the *Dīrgha Āgama* in twenty-two fascicles was translated beginning in the fourteenth year of Hongshi and completed in the tenth year.

The Liangzhou śramaṇa Zhu Fonian acted as the oral translator, the Qin-kingdom śramaṇa Daohan served as the scribe, and Sengzhao composed the preface. This is recorded in the works of Sengrui, the two Qin records, and Seng...
The *Yùlù Gāosēngzhuàn* (Record of the Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks) and other sources state that the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* consists of sixty fascicles;
it is also said to be the *Tánwúdé lǜběn* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya Text), translated in forty-five fascicles, or forty, or forty-four. There are also versions today in seventy fascicles.
It was produced at Zhōng Temple in the tenth year of the Hóngshǐ era, translated by Huìbiàn, with a preface composed by Sēngzhào. This is seen among the miscellaneous records of the Jin dynasty.
The *Sifen sengjieben* (Four-Part Monastic Precept Manual) in one fascicle— sometimes omitting the character "seng" (monastic)—
also known as the *Wude jieben* (Precept Manual for Those Without Virtue), is found in the *Jin shi zalu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) and the *Sengyou lu* (Monk You’s Catalog).
The above four works comprise eighty-four fascicles, all of which are extant.
The śramaṇa Buddhayaśas—“Buddha” means “Awakened” (Jue) in the language of Qin, and “Yaśas” means “Renown” (Cheng).

Although some say it means “Renowned,” the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* translates it as “Awakened Brilliance” (Jue Ming), which is slightly inconsistent with the original meaning. He was a native of Kaśmīra.
He was of the Brahmin caste.
While his family followed non-Buddhist paths, a certain śramaṇa came to their house to beg for alms.
His father, filled with rage, ordered someone to strike him.
The father’s hands and feet subsequently became withered and paralyzed,
so that he could no longer walk or stand. He then consulted a diviner,
who replied, "This is caused by his offense against a worthy man and the local spirits."
He immediately invited this śramaṇa to sincerely repent his transgressions;
after several days, he was healed.
Consequently, he caused Yaśas to leave the household life and become his disciple.
At that time, he was thirteen years old.
Once, while traveling a long distance with his teacher through a vast wilderness, they encountered a tiger.
His teacher wished to run away to avoid it.
Yaśas said, "This tiger is already satiated and will certainly not harm people.
Shortly thereafter, the tiger departed; as he proceeded forward, he indeed saw the remains of meat.
The Master [Dao’an] privately marveled at this.
By the age of fifteen, he could recite fifty to sixty thousand words of scripture each day.
However, because the monastery where he resided frequently sent him out for alms, his practice of recitation was neglected.
There was an arhat who,
valuing his intelligence and quick wit, constantly begged for food to provide for him.
For nineteen years, he recited several million words from the sūtras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
However, by nature he was haughty and disdainful, regarding himself as possessing superior knowledge and insight, and claiming that few were capable of being his teachers;
consequently, he was not held in high esteem by the monks.
He was valued only for his elegant deportment and his skill in conversation and laughter.
Those who saw him forgot their deep resentment.
When he reached the age for receiving the full precepts, no one came to preside over the ordination platform;
thus, even at the age when one should stand as a teacher, he remained a śrāmaṇera.
He then studied the treatises on the five sciences under his maternal uncle.
He became extensively proficient in various worldly arts and techniques.
It was not until he was twenty-seven years old that he finally received full ordination.
He was constantly devoted to the task of reading and reciting, never letting his hands leave the scrolls.
Whenever he sat upright to contemplate the meaning of the texts, he would not notice the passage of time as the days slipped away in emptiness.
Such was his single-minded dedication.
Later, he arrived at the kingdom of Kāśmira (Shale).
At that time, the crown prince Dharmavatsa (in the language of Qin, "Dharma-son") saw that his appearance was dignified and elegant, and asked where he had come from.
Guṇabhadra (Yeshe) responded with clear eloquence, which pleased the prince; he subsequently invited him into the palace to provide him with offerings and treatment of great magnificence.
Kumārajīva arrived later and studied under him, holding him in great respect.
As Kumārajīva followed his mother back to the east, Guṇavarman remained behind.
Shortly thereafter, the king passed away and the crown prince ascended the throne.
At that time, Fu Jian dispatched Lü Guang to attack Kucha.
Kucha urgently sought military aid from the King of Śāla,
who personally led his troops to rescue them.
He sent Yaśas to remain and assist the Crown Prince, entrusting him with the subsequent administration.
Before the relief army could arrive, Kucha had already been defeated.
Upon his return, the King related in detail how Kumārajīva had been captured by Guṇabhadra.
He then sighed and said:
"Although I have known Kumārajīva for a long time, we have not yet fully expressed our innermost thoughts.
How unexpected that we meet now as a captive; when shall we see each other again?"
After staying there for more than ten years, the king passed away.
Consequently, Kumārajīva traveled to Kucha, where the propagation of the Dharma flourished greatly.
At that time, while Kumārajīva was in Guzang, he dispatched a messenger to invite him.
He packed his provisions and intended to depart.
The people of the country requested that he remain, so he stayed for another year or so.
Later, he said to his disciples:
"I wish to seek out Kumārajīva; you should pack secretly and set out at night so that no one knows.
My disciple said, 'I fear that if they pursue us tomorrow morning, we will not escape being forced to return.'"
Yaśas then took a bowl of clear water,
cast medicinal herbs into it, and recited incantations several dozen times.
He gave it to his disciple to wash his feet, and they set out that very night.
By the time dawn arrived, they had traveled several hundred li.
He asked his disciples,
"What have you perceived?"
He replied,
"I have heard nothing but the sound of a violent wind;
it is only that tears have fallen from my eyes."
Yaśas then used consecrated water to wash his feet and rested.
At dawn the next day, the people of the country pursued him,
but he had already traveled several hundred *li* and they could not catch up.
When Faxian reached Guzang,
Kumārajīva had already entered Chang’an.
Upon hearing that Faxian had arrived at Guzang, Kumārajīva urged Yao Xing to welcome him.
Xing did not accept it.
Shortly thereafter, he ordered Kumārajīva to translate the scriptural canon.
Kumārajīva said:
In propagating the teachings of the Dharma, one should ensure that both the text and its meaning are perfectly integrated.
Although I, this poor monk, recite the text, I have not yet mastered its underlying principles;
only Buddhayaśas has a profound understanding of the essential purport of the scriptures.
He is currently in Guzang.
I wish for an imperial edict to summon him;
let his words be examined three times with great detail before being committed to writing.
He thought, "I must ensure that these subtle words do not fall into oblivion, so as to inspire confidence for a thousand years.
Xing followed his advice and immediately dispatched an envoy to invite him;
the master was presented with lavish gifts, all of which he refused to accept.
Only after repeated expressions of faith and earnest exhortations did he finally reach a state of constant peace.
Emperor Xiaowen personally went out to visit and inquire after him;
although a separate administrative office was established for him in the Xiaoyao Garden and the four requisites of monastic life were provided, he accepted none of them.
When it was time for his alms-round, he would take but a single meal.
At that time, Kumārajīva was producing the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*;
for over a month, he remained hesitant and in doubt, as yet unable to set pen to paper.
Yaśas arrived first;
through their mutual inquiry and resolution, the arguments were finally settled.
More than three thousand monastics and laypeople all marveled at the excellence and precision of his discourse.
Śīha was a man with red hair who was highly proficient in the *Vibhāṣā*;
thus, the people of the time called him "Red-Bearded Vibhāṣā.
He subsequently became the teacher of Kumārajīva.
He was also called Mahāvibhāṣa.
Although the fourfold assembly provided him with offerings of robes, alms bowls,
and bedding that filled three rooms, he did not set his mind upon them.
Xing established a monastery south of the city for the purpose of producing this translation.
Yaśas had previously recited the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya;
Yao Shuang (also known as Yao Shi), the Commandant of the Imperial Secretariat, requested that he bring it out.
Xing suspected that there might be errors or omissions, so he had Guṇabhadra recite from the Tibetan medical texts,
each of which was over forty pages long.
After three days, Xing compared the recitation with the written text and found not a single character was mistaken.
The assembly marveled at his prodigious memory.
Consequently, in the tenth year of the Hongshi era, the Wushen year,
he translated the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* along with the *Dīrgha-āgama* and other texts.
It was finally completed fifteen years later, in the year Gui-chou (493).
The śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou translated it into the Qin language,
while Daohan received the oral dictation by pen.
When the translation was completed, they broke the session.
Daoxing offered Yashas ten thousand bolts of raw silk as a religious gift (dakṣiṇā),
but he would not accept any of it at all.
The Buddha thought of the sentient beings and bestowed one thousand rolls of fine silk upon each;
he also gave generous offerings to five hundred śramaṇas of renowned virtue.
Later, Yaśas returned to Kaśmīra.
His ultimate end is unknown. The Preface to the *Four-Part Vinaya* states:

"In the year of Renchen, there was the Śramaṇa Zhīfǎlǐng of the Jin state, who traveled west across the shifting sands to seek the distant land of India. On his journey, he passed through Khotan and encountered the Śramaṇa Buddhayaśas, a Tripitaka master of the Mahāsāṃghika school and a proponent of the Mahāyāna, whose talent and character were renowned, and who was thoroughly versed in the Sūtras and Vinaya."
He had thoroughly mastered the recitation of the Tripiṭaka and the Vaipulya sūtras.
He then extensively collected various scriptures in that country at a monastery, and in the year Wushen, he finally arrived in the kingdom of Qin.

The Qin ruler Yao Xian immediately requested that the Vinaya Piṭaka be translated in that same year. He assembled more than three hundred śramaṇas who were experts in the Vinaya at Zhong Temple in Chang’an;
he then appointed his own disciple, Huibian, as the translator.
The year Renchen corresponds to the seventh year of the Jianchu era of the Qin dynasty.
The year Wushen corresponds to the tenth year of the Hongshi era.
Furthermore, there is another account stating that Guṇavarman, together with Fonian and others, collated the Sanskrit manuscripts brought by Faxian before finally translating them.
Various accounts differ slightly;
it is not yet clear which is correct.
Furthermore, according to both Sengzhao’s preface to the *Dīrgha Āgama* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, it is stated:
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* in four fascicles, translated during the twelfth year of Hongshi, likely refers to the time when that specific section was finalized.
The *Kṣema-sūtra*, one fascicle, reached Guangzhou during the Long’an era of the Eastern Jin; it was translated at Baisa Temple for the laywoman Zhang Puming.
This should have been included in the Jin catalog, but it was subsequently appended to the Qin records, as seen in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* and the *Chang [Ahan]*.
*Fánglù yuèyíngluò zhuāngyán fāngbiàn pǐn jīng* (Sūtra on the Chapter of the Skillful Means of Adornments of Necklaces of Music Recorded in the Chamber), one fascicle;

also titled *Zhuǎnnǚshēn púsà wèndá jīng* (Sūtra of the Questions and Answers of the Bodhisattva Who Transforms the Female Body). Third, it was produced as a counterpart to the *Shùnquán fāngbiàn jīng* (Sūtra on Accordant Expedient Means) translated by Dharmarakṣa.

Li Kuò’s record states it was translated by Kumārajīva; however, according to the sūtra colophon, it was produced by Saṃghayaśas, and thus it has been moved here and included within the *Śāriputra-abhidharma*.

The *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Tánlùn) consists of twenty-two fascicles—sometimes titled with the character "wú" (non-) instead of "tán," or appearing in versions of twenty or thirty fascicles—and was translated together with Dharmagupta at Shíyáng Temple.
The preface was composed by Shì Dàobiǎo. This is recorded in Sēngyòu’s *Cāojièlù*, Bǎochàng’s *Chóngjìnglù*, and the *Gāosēngzhuàn*.
These three works comprise thirty-four fascicles in total; of these, the first work is missing one fascicle, while the latter two remain complete.
The twenty-three fascicles currently extant were translated by the śramaṇa Dharmayaśas—
whose name means "Dharmakīrti" in the language of Qin— as the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks). [The name] "Faming" (Dharmaprabha) is a mistranslation of the meaning.
A native of Kaśmīra,
he was fond of learning from his youth.
At the age of fourteen, he came to the notice of Puṇyatāra.
As he grew, his physical frame was tall and robust, and he possessed a refined spiritual intelligence.
He had mastered the sutras and vinaya, his clear realization surpassing that of his peers;
he cultivated his thoughts within the eight dhyānas and let his mind roam through the seven factors of enlightenment.
People of the time compared him to Pūtimakṣika;
he traveled alone through mountains and marshes, avoiding neither tigers nor rhinoceroses,
dwelling in solitude with his contemplations shifting through the nights and days.
He once sat beneath a tree and reproached himself, saying:
"I am nearly thirty years old and have still not attained the fruit.
How negligent I have been!"
Thereupon, for several days he neither slept nor ate,
applying himself with single-minded intensity and extreme austerity to repent for his past transgressions.
He then saw the Deva King Vaicravana in a dream.
He said to him:
"A śramaṇa should contemplate observing the directions to propagate the transformation [of others], making vast salvation his concern.
Why do you cling to minor precepts and seek only your own perfection?"
The Way relies on manifold conditions and must await the ripening of the time;
to seek it by force beyond one's lot leads to death without realization.
He reflected within himself that he wished to travel abroad to transmit the Way.
Thereafter, he traveled through various countries, braving many hardships and dangers.
During the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty, he first arrived at Guangzhou and resided at Baisa Temple.
Guṇayashas was skilled at reciting the *Vibhāṣā-vinaya*.
People all called him Mahāvibhāṣā.
At that time, there was a laywoman named Zhang Puming who sought instruction in the Buddha-dharma;
Yaśas explained for her the *nidāna* of the Buddha’s birth.
He also translated one fascicle of the *Chaimo jing* (Sūtra on the Departure from the World).
Arriving in Chang’an during the Yixi era, he found that Yao Xing,
who had usurped the title of emperor, held the Buddha-dharma in extremely high esteem.
When Sengyai arrived, he treated him with profound courtesy and distinction.
It happened that the Indian śramaṇa Dharmagupta (translated into Chinese as Fǎzàng) came to Guāngzhōng.
Having a kindred spirit, they sought each other out as if they were old acquaintances, and together they translated the *Śāriputrābhidharma*.
The Sanskrit manuscript was brought out in the ninth year of the Hongshi era of the Qin dynasty, the year Dingwei;
it remained there until the sixteenth year, Jiayin.
Gradually, the masters of the scriptures became familiar with the Qin language and were able to proclaim the translations themselves.
It was finally completed in the seventeenth year, the year of Yimao (1720 CE).
It comprises twenty-two fascicles in total.
Prince Hong of the Qin personally oversaw its management and study.
The śramaṇa Daobiao composed a preface for it.
He also produced one fascicle of the *Lè yíngluò jīng* (Sūtra on the Joyful Necklace).
Later, Guṇabhadra traveled south to Jiangling and stayed at Xin Temple, where he widely propagated the methods of dhyāna.
Among those who came to visit him through the thicket were over three hundred guests of refined character.
As for the commoners and officials who visited him,
even those who previously lacked faith felt reverence and joy upon seeing him.
He himself stated that there was once a teacher and a disciple who,
through their joint cultivation of the path, both attained arhatship;
however, their names have been lost to tradition.
Furthermore, he once sat in meditation with the door closed at the outer gate when five śramaṇas suddenly entered his room.
On another occasion, he saw śramaṇas flying to the tops of trees.
These instances are often not isolated;
he constantly interfaced with the divine while remaining outwardly identical to the common folk.
Although his traces of the Way were not yet manifest, [he remained so].
The people of the time all believed that he had already attained the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*).
During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he took his leave to return to the Western Regions, though his ultimate destination remains unknown.

As for the West Qin, the Qifu clan established their capital at Yuanchuan; it is also said that the West Qin originated with Qifu Guoren, who was posthumously titled Emperor Xuanye. The first year of Jianyi was the *wuyou* year (the first year of the sexagenary cycle).
It reached the end of the Qifu dynasty in the fourth year of Yonghong, the Xinwei year;
in total, it passed through four rulers for forty-seven years,
with one śramaṇa.

The translated sūtras, as well as the new and old translations of the Vinaya and Śāstras from the Three Qin periods whose translators were lost, total fifty-six works in one hundred and ten fascicles;
among these, thirty-two works in seventy-nine fascicles are extant, while twenty-four works in thirty-one fascicles are missing.
The Qifu Qin dynasty: the śramaṇa Shi Shengjian translated fifteen works totaling twenty-four fascicles.

Regarding the newly and formerly untranslated scriptures of the Three Qin period, there are forty-one works totaling eighty-six fascicles; seven works totaling seven fascicles were collected from earlier sources, while thirty-four works totaling seventy-nine fascicles were newly appended.
The *Luo-mo-jia jing* (Rāmāyaṇa Sūtra) in three fascicles is a partial variant translation of the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Gandavyūha*) chapter of the *Avataṃsaka*, as noted in the *Neidian lu*.
The *Taizi xudanna jing* (Sūtra of Prince Viśvantara) in one fascicle is a variant translation from the second fascicle of the *Liudu ji*;
it was produced at Xin Monastery in Jiangling with Yu Shuang serving as the scribe. Some say it is titled *Xuda-na*; this is recorded in the *Shixing lu* and by Baochang.
Record of those that should have been included in the Jin [catalogue] but were found among the translations of the Qin:

one scroll of the *Śyāmaka-sūtra* (also known as the *Filial Son Śyāmaka Sūtra*, the *Bodhisattva Śyāmaka Sūtra*, the *Buddha-spoken Śyāmaka Sūtra*, the *Śyāmaka Original Sūtra*, and the *Filial Son Yin Sūtra*;
it has six titles in total). This fourth item is a variant translation appearing in the second volume of the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya* and is seen in the Shixing [catalogue].
Dharmottara’s record states that the *Mahāsthāmaprāpta-sūtra* in one fascicle is also titled *The Ritual for Bathing Buddha Images*, or simply *The Sūtra on Bathing the Buddha*.
This second edition is the same text as the *Ritual for Washing Buddha Images*.

It is noted in the *Shixing lu* that the *Anantadharmamukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in one fascicle—also known as the *Ananta-sūtra*—was first translated alongside the *Questions of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja*.

The *Jingdeng benjian xingxing lu* (Record of the Original Texts of the Sūtra Equivalents) and the *Fashang lu* (Record of Fashang) both state that the *Yandao suye jing* (Sūtra on the Practice of Lay and Clergy), one fascicle, is a second translation based on the same original as that translated by Zhi Qian;
this is recorded in the *Fashang lu*. The *Chukong zaihuang jing* (Sūtra on Removing Fear and Calamity), one fascicle, is a second translation based on the same original as that translated by Bo Yan;
this is recorded in the *Shixing baochang* and *Fashang* records. [This concludes] the section on "Xian" from the three records of Shixing, Baochang, and Fashang.

*Shou jing* (The Sutra of the Head), one fascicle; also known as *Xianshou furen jing* (Sutra of the Lady Xianshou); seen in the *Shixing lu*. *Anan fenbie jing* (The Sutra of Ānanda’s Analysis), one fascicle;
also known as *Anan wen shifo jixiong jing* (Sutra of Ānanda’s Questions on the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha);

third appearance, seen in the *Shixing lu* and the *Fashang lu*. *Furen yugu jing* (Sutra of the Woman Encountering Calamity), one fascicle; also known as *Fu yudui jing* (Sutra of the Wife Encountering Her Fate); seen in the *Shixing lu* and the *Fashang lu*.
The two preceding records above have already been seen; the following entries are missing.

The *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra* (or *Sūtra on the Questions of Ākāśagarbha*), also known as the *Sūtra Encouraging Bodhisattvas to Adorn Bodhi*, consists of eight fascicles—or alternatively five fascicles—and is a variant translation of the "Ākāśagarbha-parivarta" from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*.
This is recorded in the *Jin-shi-za-lu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) and the *Fa-shang-lu* (Record of Fashang), which state that it is [identical to]... [the previous text].

*The Sūtra of Rāmagrāma*, same text as [the previous], not [a duplicate]; *The Sūtra on the Place of Birth of the Bodhisattva*, one fascicle, also titled *The Sūtra of the Questions of Magadha*, second appearance in the *Xiaolu* (Record of Xia), its chronological order unknown;
appended according to the person [who translated it] during the Western Qin dynasty, appearing in the *Shixinglu* (Record of Shixing);
*The Paojing* (Bodhisattva Sūtra), one fascicle, third appearance in the *Fashanglu* (Record of Fashang); *The Sūtra of Kātyāyana the Child Resolving Difficulties*.
One fascicle; also called the *Tongjiaye jing* (Sūtra of Kaśyapa the Child), which is the same text as the *Jiumojiaye jing* (Sūtra of Kaśyapa Kumāra).

Sengyou states it was extracted from the *Dīrgha Āgama* and transcribed by Yu Shuang. It appears in the catalogs of Wang Zong, Baochang, Zhimin Du, and others. One fascicle of the *Qinnü benjing* (Sūtra of the Seven Daughters);
also titled the *Nüben xinming jing* (Sūtra of the Heart-Clarification of the Daughters) and the *Qinnü jing* (Sūtra of the Seven Daughters). Third extraction.
According to Zhi Mindu’s *Dulu* (General Catalog), the aforementioned fifteen works comprise twenty-four fascicles.
Of these, ten works totaling twelve fascicles concerning "Women Encountering Misfortune" are extant; five works totaling twelve fascicles from the section on the "Vaipulya Kings" are missing.
The śramaṇa Śākya Śrī-Sthira,
also known as Dharma-Sthira,
was likewise called Master Sthira.
It is not clear which of these is correct;
therefore, they have been listed in full.
His capacity was vast and universal, and his mind was set upon benefiting all beings.
During the Taichu era of the Qifu Qin dynasty,
he translated fifteen scriptures, including the *Rāmāyaṇa*, for Gan Gui while serving as the King of Henan, posthumously titled Wuyuanwang.
Investigating the holy Jian’s travels and transformations, he produced scriptures wherever he went;
having found no fixed place of residence, it is unknown to which era his records should be appended as authentic.
Now, following the account of Fashang, they are collectively entered into the records of the Qifu Qin period.

*Śrāmaṇera-sūtra*, one fascicle; secondly, the *Pañcamātṛputra-sūtra*, same text as above; *Sakrasaṃpramokṣa-rāja-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Adāsamaī-sūtra*, one fascicle (also titled *Adātta-xianwang-sūtra*); *Bhadrapāla-kṣamāpanā-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Vaipulya-nirṇaya-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Dvividha-bhikṣu-vastu-sūtra*, one fascicle. Sengyou’s Catalogue states: "The three matters above [refer to] these seven works. Sengyou’s Catalogue further notes: "Master Dao’an recorded that these were missing from the central collection among the miscellaneous scriptures. These seven works comprise seven fascicles. Regarding the first, the *Śrāmaṇera-sūtra*, there is a surviving manuscript, while the others are all missing. The Changfang Catalogue states: [as above].
These were all collected by the Tripiṭaka Master Sengyou from the records of the Śramaṇa Dao’an regarding variant versions of scriptures in Guanzhong;
they are now appended to the *Shilu* (Record of the Three Qin Dynasties) as works of lost translation.
The *Shidai chu* states:

"In the *Fanglu*, there is again a four-fascicle Hu-language version of the sutra, with a footnote at the end stating it appears to have been produced in Chang’an; it was already included in the *Hou Han shi yi lu*."
The entries contained herein were previously recorded;
as they have already been included above, they have been deleted and are no longer retained here.
The following are newly appended to this record.
*The Sūtra of the Crown Prince Virūḍhaka*, one fascicle (sometimes without the word "Crown Prince," also known as *The Sūtra of Prince Virūḍhaka*);
*The Sūtra on the Original Deeds of the Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Great Jewel Accumulation and the Sun*, one fascicle;
*The Sūtra on the Questions of Dhagala to the Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of Ānanda for the Sorcery of Malevolent Spirits*, one fascicle (the old catalog states: "Ānanda").
*The Sūtra on Being Cursed by Malevolent Sorcery*, which contains doubts; *The Sūtra of the Maiden Māndhātṛ* from among the [scriptures] in the Tripiṭaka;
*The Sūtra of Vulture Peak at Rājagṛha*, one fascicle (the old catalog states: *The Essential Direct Sūtra of Vulture Peak at Rājagṛha*);

*The Sūtra of Si Dao*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Buddha at Zhuyuan*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Dharma for Humans*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Meaning of the Path*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of A...* [text fragment].

*Yi Biqiu jing* (The Sutra of the Barbarian Bhikṣu), one fascicle; *Bade jing* (The Sutra of the Eight Virtues), one fascicle—these are now suspected to be the *Hai Bade jing* (The Sutra of the Eight Virtues of the Sea);

*Shande jing* (The Sutra of Good Virtue), one fascicle; *Mahāgandhavyūha Jin-xin Biqiu deng du jing* (The Sutra on the Mahāgandhavyūha and the Crossing by the Bhikṣu Jin-xin and Others), one fascicle—the old catalog calls it the *Jin-xin Biqiu jing*.
These fourteen works, totaling fourteen fascicles, begin with the "Parable of the Prince."
In the *Lüechù jīngdìng pǐn* (Catalogue of Determined Scriptures), all records of this [text] are missing.
Sengyou’s catalogue states:
"The *Guanzhong yijing* (Heterodox Scriptures of Guanzhong) by Master Dao'an, as well as the catalogues by Changfang and others, all omit it; only Sengyou has recorded it."
Master Dao’an’s *Collection of Extraordinary Scriptures from Guanzhong* consists of twenty-four fascicles in total.
Of these, seven fascicles are listed in the Fang Catalogue;
fourteen additional scriptures are now further presented here.
In total, there are twenty-one sections.
As for the remaining three sections, catalogs such as those by Changfang and others all specify the translators;
therefore, they have been omitted here.
*The Great Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, one fascicle; now included as the forty-third assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa*, renamed the "Assembly of the Bodhisattva Samantaprabhā," second edition.
This is a different translation of the same original text as the *Mahāratnavyūha-buddhāstamanasūtra* and the *Sūryamaṇiratna-sūtra*.
*The Sūtra on the Wisdom-Light Adornment of the Realm of All Buddhas*, one fascicle; first edition, which was the same original text as the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*.
Regarding the *Rulai Dezhi Buxiyi Jingjie Jing* (Sūtra on Entering the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata’s Virtue and Wisdom) and its counterparts,

the claim that they are identical to the *Yu Rulai Zhuangyan Zhihui Guangming Ru Yiqie Fojingjie Jing* (Sūtra on the Radiance of the Tathāgata’s Adorned Wisdom Entering the Realm of All Buddhas) is entirely incorrect. Furthermore,

the eight-fascicle *Dabei Fenali Jing* (Sūtra of the Great Compassion White Lotus) is also called the *Dasheng Beifenali Jing* (Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Great Compassion White Lotus), which is a second translation.
*The Sūtra of the Great Golden Peacock King Spell* (Dharmakṣema’s *Beihuajing* [Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samaya-sūtra] same text), one fascicle;
fifth appearance. *The Buddha-spoken Sūtra of the Great Golden Peacock King Spell*, one fascicle; sixth appearance.
These two sūtras are the same text as the *Mahāvaipulya Tathāgata-guhya-nidhi Sūtra* in two fascicles; the *Dazhou Catalogue* states it is the same as the *Mahāvaipulya-samantabhadra Sūtra*.
The claim that the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* is the same text [as this one] is incorrect.

The *Vajrasamādhi-prakṛti-viśuddhy-avināśy-anirodha-sūtra*, one fascicle—also titled the *Vajra-viśuddhi-sūtra*—is recorded by the *Chángfáng lù* and others as having been translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty;

however, it is also listed among the lost translations of the Later Han, so both versions are incorrect. Having now examined the phrasing and sentences, they appear to be a translation from the Qin period; therefore, it has been moved here for inclusion.
*The Sūtra on the Past Life of the Buddha Siṃhākṣa*, one fascicle. The *Chángfáng lù* and other catalogs state it was translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin;

however, upon examining the phrasing and sentences, this does not appear to have been produced by Master Dharmarakṣa, as it resembles translations from the Qin period. Therefore, it has been moved here.
*Sūtra on the One Fascicle of the Ten Auspiciousnesses*, one fascicle. *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Compassionate Heart of the Immortal Sarvajñāprabha and His Abstinence from Food*.
*Ekottarāgama-saṃgraha-śuddhakarmāvaraṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Saṃyuktāgama-vibhāga*, twenty fascicles;
*Pravrajyāguṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle (not extracted from the *Xianyu jing*); *Vinayamātṛkā*, eight fascicles (also called the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*);
*Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, nine fascicles; *Trimiḍi-bhūmi-śāstra*, three fascicles.
Either the *Abhidharmakośa* (or *Vibhāṣā*) is missing, or there is the *Pratyekabuddha-nidāna-śāstra* in four fascicles and the *Aṣṭādaśa-nikāya-śāstra* in one fascicle;

these were initially translated by Buddhabhadra, but they are identical in substance to the *Nikāyabheda-vibhaṅga-śāstra*. Master Huiyuan and others all claim these were translated by Paramārtha, which is incorrect.

There is also the *Maitreya-guhya-vajra-bala-anuśocana-sūtra* in one fascicle, concerning the Buddha’s entry into nirvāṇa. [The text continues with: *Wumingluo...* (The remainder of the title is illegible).
The *Rākṣasa-saṃgraha* (one fascicle), also known as the *Avidyā-rākṣasa-sūtra* (or two fascicles). The above twenty works comprise sixty-five fascicles;
all are included in the Canon.
It appears that several scriptures translated during the Qin dynasty contain words with the phonetic character "Qin.
Although these have never been recorded in any of the catalogs of lost translations,
they are now appended here to this catalog of the Qin period.
I hope this will avoid any omissions.
Together with the seven previously lost translations consisting of seven fascicles,
as well as the newly appended "Various Scriptures from Guanzhong" by Master An, [the total is now complete].
In total, there are forty-one sections comprising eighty-six fascicles.
These were all lost translations from the Three Qin period, according to the *Xinshang yulu*.

Regarding the dates: for the Former Liang, the Zhang clan ruled from Guzang; the years are based on the *Jiluan lu*, with most following the era names of the Jin dynasty. Following the posthumous title of Zhang Gui as Emperor Wuyong, these were newly translated in the first year of the Yongning era.
It reached the reign of Tianxi, the sixth year of Xian’an (the jingzi year), when the state of Qin conferred upon him the title of General of the Flying Cavalry, Grand Preceptor of Liangzhou.
In total, it passed through eight rulers for seventy-six years.
There was one foreign upāsaka.
Translated scriptures: four works totaling six fascicles; among these, one work in one fascicle currently exists, while three works totaling five fascicles are missing.
Former Liang: Upāsaka Zhi Shilun, four works totaling six fascicles of scripture.
*The Sūtra of Sūrata*, one fascicle. Third, translated by Bai Yan of the Cao Wei, Zhi Qian of the Wu, and Gongde Xian of the Song;
this is the same text as the *Sūtra of Sūrata*, as noted in its postscript, translated in the third year of the Xian’an era. *The Sūtra on the Samādhi Like an Illusion*, three fascicles.
Fourth, translated by An Fa-hu; this is the same text as the *Samādhi Like an Illusion* and the *Sūtra on the Assembly of the Good Intentions of Ratnakūṭa*.
Identical to the original *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, the *Jin guangshou jing* (Golden Light Sovereign Sūtra) in one fascicle was translated in the third year of the Xian’an era;

this second translation is identical in substance to the *Dajing famen jing* (Sūtra on the Great Pure Dharma Gate) by Dharmarakṣa of the Jin dynasty and the *Dazhuangyan famen jing* (Sūtra on the Great Adornment Dharma Gate) by Jñānayaśas of the Sui dynasty.
It was translated in the third year of the Xian’an era, as recorded in the postscript to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*. Śūraṅgama.

One fascicle; the eighth [translation] produced by Zhi Qian of the Han, Zhi Qian of the Wu, Bai Yan of the Wei, Dharmarakṣa of the Jin, and others, which shares the same original text as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*.
A postscript to the scripture states it was seen in the third year of Xian’an. Of these, four works totaling six fascicles are extant:
one fascicle of the *Sūryodgata-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (須賴經) is currently available, while three works totaling five fascicles, including the *Yathābhūta-māyopama-sūtra* (如幻經), are missing.
The Upāsaka Zhishilun was a person of the Yuezhi.
He had extensively studied various scriptures and was particularly proficient in the Vaipulya (fangdeng) texts.
His intention was to enlighten and transform those who had not yet heard [the Dharma].
Carrying the scriptures, he traveled to the land of Liang.
When Lord Zhang saw them, he held them in high esteem and requested that they be translated.
In the third year of the Xian’an era (the Guiyou year), according to the reign title of the Jin dynasty, he produced four sections of scriptures, including the *Sūrala*,
beneath the Zhānlù Pavilion behind the main hall within Liangzhou.
The Crown Prince of Kucha, Bo Yan, acted as interpreter;
the Palace Attendant Zhao Xiao of Xihai, the District Magistrate Ma Yi, and the Inner Attendant Lai Gongzheng were the three who took down the dictation in writing.
The śramaṇa Shi Huichang and Shi Jinxing were both present at the assembly for its verification.
This was transcribed by one from Liangzhou; no further literary embellishments have been added.

This postscript to the *Sūrala-sūtra* and the postscript to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* should have been produced during the era of Former Liang, yet they were encountered by later generations only now. It is fortunate that they have been appended here as supplementary additions.

The Northern Liang was established by the Juqu clan. Initially they were based in Zhangye, later moving to Guzang. From the first year of Yong’an (the *xinchou* year), during the reign of Juqu Mengxun—who posthumously received the title King Wuxuan—until the seventh year of Chenghe (the *jimao* year) of Juqu Mogaon, who was enfeoffed as the King of Hexi by the Wei dynasty.
In total, under two successive rulers, thirty-nine years passed. Nine individuals,
both monastics and laypeople,
produced various sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras, as well as newly translated works and previously untranslated sūtras from various collections.

In total, there are eighty-two sections comprising three hundred and ten fascicles; among these, twenty-five sections totaling two hundred and nine fascicles are extant, while fifty-seven sections totaling one hundred and two fascicles are missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Daogong translated twelve fascicles of sūtras from two sections; the śramaṇa Shi Fazhong translated four fascicles of sūtras from one section;
the śramaṇa Saṃghadeva translated two fascicles of sūtras from one section; the śramaṇa Dharmakṣema translated one hundred and thirty-one fascicles of sūtras and vinaya from nineteen sections;
and An-yang Hou Juqu Jingsheng compiled one section [of these works].
The *Śramaṇa-budhabhadra* collection, one work in sixty fascicles; the treatise by the *Śramaṇa Śākyamati*, one work in twenty fascicles;
the sutras by the *Śramaṇa Śākyamārgathāi*, two works in four fascicles; the treatise by the *Śramaṇa Śākyadharmaseng*, one work in one fascicle;
and fifty-three translated sutras from both old and new collections, totaling seventy-five fascicles. (5)

Volume 18: The old collection comprises forty-eight works in fifty-seven volumes; the newly appended *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (two volumes) is now included as the forty-fourth assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*.
This is seen in the *He-xi-lu* by Zhu Daozu and the *Seng-you-lu*. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (ten volumes):
the first edition was produced by Dharmarakṣa; it is also known as the *Khan-chü-ching* (Seclusion Sutra) and the *Ta-pei-ching* (Great Compassion Sutra).
The *Puṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Fen-tuo-li) and the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Bei-hua jing) by Dharmakṣema are of the same original text;

the Fang catalogue records that they were seen in the Yu-lu, suggesting they were earlier translations that were subsequently revised and edited by Gong. It is now suspected that these are indeed those produced by Dharmakṣema. Of the two works mentioned above, there are twelve fascicles in total:
the first, the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (Bao-liang jing), consists of two fascicles and is extant; the latter, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, consists of ten fascicles and is currently missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Daogong,
with a vacant mind and vast application, pursued the Way for the sake of broad benefit.
During the Yong’an era of Mengxun, the King of Hexi of Northern Liang, who had usurped the title [of emperor].
In Zhangye, he translated two scriptures for Mengsun:

the *Mahāvaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in four fascicles—also known as the *Vaipulya-tantra-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (without the character "da") or simply the *Tantra-dhāraṇī-sūtra*. This one work in four fascicles is extant; its existence is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty* and Sengyou’s catalog.
The śramaṇa Shi Fazhong was a native of Gaochang Commandery;
he also [translated] at Zhangye during the Yong'an era.
He translated one fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* for Mengsun, the King of Hexi.
Baochang’s record states that it was translated in Gaochang Commandery; it is unclear which account is correct.

The *Huishang pusa wen dashanquan jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Huishang Asking about Great Skillful Means), two fascicles; also known as the *Dashan jing*, the *Huishang pusa jing*, or the *Dacheng fangbian jing*. It has four titles, all of which refer to the same original work. This fifth edition is identical in text to the *Dashanquan jing* translated by An Shigao of the Han dynasty, the *Fobaoji dasheng fangbian jing* translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Jin dynasty, and other similar works. This one volume in two fascicles is currently missing.
The śramaṇa Saṃghadatta.
In the language of Liang, this means "Abounding in Goodness.
He was a man from the Western Regions.
With the intention of universal salvation and the transformation and guidance of others held in his heart,
he also translated the Mahāyāna sūtras at Zhangye during the Yong’an era for Juqu Mengxun.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Shànquán jīng), one fascicle, is recorded in the *Shìxīng lù* and the *Fǎshàng* [catalogue].

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, forty fascicles—or thirty-six fascicles—was the fifth translation; it was produced beginning in the third year of Xuánsì and completed on the twenty-third day of the tenth month in the tenth year.
The Sanskrit original is complete with thirty-five thousand gāthās; that which has been translated here amounts to only ten thousand or so.
The first part of the three sections of this verse begins with the preface composed by Dao Lang.
According to the *Liang lu* by Zhu Daozu and the *Sengyou lu*, there is a *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* in thirty fascicles, sometimes simply called the *Da ji jing*.

This third translation shares the same source text as those produced during the Han dynasty by Zhi Chen and during the Yao Qin dynasty by Kumārajīva; it consists of either twenty-nine or thirty-one fascicles.
The fact that it exists in either thirty-two or forty fascicles is due to the different ways the sections were divided when it was first translated.

This is seen in Zhu Daozu’s *Liang lu* and Sengyou’s *Lu*. The *Mahāvaipulya-tri-saṃvara-sūtra* in three fascicles was first translated; it is the same text as the "Three Codes of Discipline" (*Tri-vidhi-saṃvara*) section of the *Ratnakūṭa*.
This is seen in Fa Shang’s record. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in ten fascicles was the fourth translation; it is the same as the *Mahā*... [text truncated]
The *Karunapundarika Sutra* and others are seen to have the same original texts in the *He-xi-lu* by Zhu Daozu and the *Seng-you-lu*.

Sengyou states that they appear in the *Bie-lu* (Separate Catalog), or it is said they were brought out by Gong Shang; now I suspect that Dao, Gong, and Chen are the same person, and that these two versions of the same sutra were likely recorded in two places first—this is probably not the case.
The four-fascicle *Suvarnaprabhasa Sutra* first appeared with eighteen chapters, as seen in the records of Zhu [Daozu].
The *Dàozǔ Hésī Lù* (Record of the Ancestor of the Way from Hexi) and Sengyou’s catalog record that this work is identical to the newly translated *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
It is now included within the eight-fascicle *Combined Scripture* (*Héjīng*).

These four fascicles were [originally] in the *Shānfán Lù* (Record of the Elimination of Redundancies) as the six-fascicle *Mahāvaipulya-mahāmegha-sūtra*, also known as the *Mahāvaipulya-nirnimitta-mahāmegha-sūtra* or the *Mahāmegha-nirnimitta*.

The *Xiǎngjīng* (Sūtra on Perceptions), also known as the *Dà yún mì zàng jīng* (Great Cloud Secret Treasury Sūtra), or the *Fāngděng dà yún jīng* (Vaipulya Great Cloud Sūtra), exists in either four or five fascicles;
it was translated at Neiyuan Temple. This is the second appearance [of this text], recorded in the catalogs of Sengrui, Li Kuò, and Sengyòu.

The *Fùzhōng nǚ tīngjīng* (One Fascicle on a Woman Listening to the Sūtra from Her Womb), also known as the *Bùzhuāngjiào nǚ jīng* (Sūtra on the Unadorned Girl), is the third appearance, translated by Wúgòu xián.

The *Nü jing* (Sūtra on Women) and the *Zhuan nǚshēn jīng* (Sūtra on Transforming the Female Body) correspond to the original text as seen in the *Chángfáng lù*. The *Púsà dìchí jīng* (Bodhisattvabhūmi-śīla-sūtra) consists of ten fascicles;

sometimes the character "sūtra" (*jīng*) is omitted, and it is also called a *lùn* (treatise). It is further titled the *Púsà jiè jīng* (Bodhisattva Precepts Sūtra) or the *Púsà dì jīng* (Bodhisattva Ground Sūtra), or in eight fascicles.
It is found within the "Bodhisattva Ground" section of the *Yúqié shīlùn* (Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra), as recorded in Zhūdào zǔ’s *Héxī lù*.
The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* in seven fascicles (sometimes without the word "sūtra"), concerning the bodhisattva at home;

alternatively in five, six, or ten fascicles. Translated on the twenty-third day of the fourth month in the year Jǐyīn of the Xuānshí era (373 CE), completed on the twenty-third day of the seventh month.
Recorded by the śramaṇa Dàoyǎng as pen-receiver, as seen in the postscript to the sūtra.
Sengyou’s Catalog records one fascicle of the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, extracted from the *Dichi-jieben* (Śīlaparivarta).
This second extraction is identical to the *Śīla-sūtra* translated by the Great Tang Master Xuanzang; it is recorded separately as having been found at Dunhuang.
Sengyou’s Catalog also records one fascicle of the *King Māndhātṛ Sūtra*, extracted from the eleventh fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*; it is seen as a variant translation of the *Cang* [Sūtra].

The *Buddhacarita-saṃgraha* (or *Buddhacarita-avadāna*) in five fascicles—some editions omit the character "zhuan" (biography/record), while others omit the character "jing" (sūtra)—was composed by the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa;
it is also titled *Pūrva-yoga-sūtra*. It is recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*.
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* in one fascicle—also titled *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahopāya-sūtra*—first appeared in the *Chángfáng lù*.

The *Ramojia jing* (Lalitavistara Sūtra), one fascicle, which was translated by Song Gongde and Xian from the same source as the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* and the *Śrīmālā-devī-parivarta* section of the *Ratnakūṭa*, is the fourth translation;
it is the same text as that produced by An Faxian and others of the Cao Wei dynasty, differing only in its length and brevity.
It is a small portion of the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter (*dharmadhātupraveśa*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. This is recorded in the *Changfang lu* and the *Leng*.

The *Gā-sūtra* in four fascicles was first translated; it is the same text as those produced by Guṇabhadra of the Song dynasty, Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei, and Śikṣānanda, as seen in the *Chángfáng-lù*.
The *Suxuēntiānzǐ-jīng* in one fascicle is a second translation; it is the same text as that produced by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin.
Chángfáng states it is seen in the *Wù-lù*, and further notes that it appears to have been produced by Kumārajīva.
A re-translation of the *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra* in four fascicles, perhaps with newly added characters;
the second edition is identical in text to that translated by Dharmarakṣa, produced in the seventh year of the Xuanshi era, as recorded in the *Hexi lu* of Zhu Daozu and the *Sengyou lu*.
The *Guangde baoguang pusa jing* in one fascicle, as seen in the *Changfang lu*. Also, the *Pusa jitan wen* in one fascicle.
The *Upāsaka-śīla-maṇḍala-vinaya* (Text on the Ordination Platform for Upāsakas).
Sengyou states that the *Bodhisattva-śīla-upāsaka-śīla-maṇḍala-vinaya* is found in the two catalogs of Sengyou and Baochang. To the right, nineteen works in one hundred and thirty-one fascicles;
the *Buddhacarita* (Praise of the Buddha’s Deeds), thirteen works in one hundred and eighteen fascicles; currently extant; the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, seven works below, one [fascicle].
A twelve-fascicle incomplete manuscript.
Translated by the śramaṇa Dharmakṣema,
also known as Dharmakṣānta.
He is also called Tanmuchen;
this is likely due to differences in the transcription of the Sanskrit sound.
In the Liang dialect, he is called Fafeng.
A native of Central India of Brahmin descent;
his father died when he was six years old.
The mother supported Śāṇakavāsin by weaving for hire.
She saw the śramaṇa Dharmayaśas—translated as "Dharmakīrti"—who was revered by both the monastic and lay communities and received abundant offerings.
Because her mother envied him, she made Śāṇakavāsin his disciple.
At the age of ten, he recited mantras with several of his fellow students;
his intelligence surpassed his peers, and he could memorize over ten thousand words of scripture each day.
Initially, he studied the Hīnayāna while also surveying the various treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
His lectures and expositions were so refined and eloquent that none could match or oppose him.
Later, he encountered the Chan Master Baotou with whom he engaged in debate;
as their respective disciplines differed, they contended for a hundred days.
Although Ratnamati launched a series of sharp and difficult challenges, the Dhyāna Master remained resolutely unwilling to yield.
Convinced by his profound reasoning, Ratnamati said to the Master,
"Are there any scriptures that you might allow me to see?"
The Zen Master immediately gave him a copy of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* written on tree bark.
Upon reading it, Daomeng was struck with sudden realization;
he felt deep remorse, realizing that his knowledge—confined as it was to a narrow well—had long been lost to the Great Way.
Thereupon, he assembled the multitude to repent of his transgressions and subsequently devoted himself exclusively to the Mahāyāna.
By the age of twenty, he had recited more than two million words of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras.
Chen’s elder brother was skilled at training elephants for riding;
he killed the white-eared great elephant ridden by the king, who,
in his rage, had him executed.
The edict stated:
"Should anyone dare to look upon [the corpse], their three generations of kin shall be punished;
no relatives shall dare to go near it."
Chen wept as he buried him.
The King was enraged and wished to execute Chen,
but Chen said:
The king executed him for the sake of the law;
I buried him out of affection for my kin.
Neither of us has contravened the great principle of righteousness.
When he became enraged, those around him were struck with cold dread;
yet his countenance remained composed as before. The King, marveling at his spirit and resolve, subsequently retained him to provide for his needs.
He was clearly proficient in incantations and sorcery, such that his efforts were invariably successful;
thus, he was renowned throughout the Western Regions as a Great Master of Divine Incantations.
Later, he followed the King into the mountains.
The king was parched with thirst and required water, but could not obtain any.
Daśabala then secretly recited a mantra over a rock, causing water to gush forth.
He then praised it, saying:
Touched by the Great King’s benevolent grace,
a spring suddenly welled up from within a parched rock;
when neighboring kingdoms heard of this, they all marveled at the King’s virtue.
At that time, the rains were perfectly regulated, and the common people sang his praises.

The King delighted in his spiritual arts and treated him with profound favor and honor; however, after some time, the King’s interest gradually waned, and his treatment of him became increasingly perfunctory.
Chen said in anger,
"I shall take water from a jar to the pond and, through incantations, cause the dragon to enter the jar.
This will bring about a great drought across the land, and the King will surely request my incantations."
"Then, when you release the dragon to send down rain, how will it regard you?
Take a jar and go to the dragon.
Someone secretly informed him of this.
The king grew angry and arrested Dharmakṣema.

Fearing execution, Dharmakṣema took with him one fascicle of the first part of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*—the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, which is the *Bhūmi-vyavasthāna-sūtra*—and the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra-mūla*, and fled to Kucha.
In the kingdom of Kucha, there were many who studied the Hīnayāna and did not believe in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Consequently, [Faxian] went to Guzang and stayed at an inn;
fearing he might lose the original scripture, he used it as a pillow while he slept.
Someone dragged him to the ground;
the interpreter was startled and thought he was a thief.
This continued for three nights.
He heard a voice in the air saying,
"This is the treasury of liberation of the Tathāgata.
Why do you use it as a pillow?"
Daorong then felt ashamed and realized his error, so he moved it to a high place.
At night, there was a thief who tried to lift it but could not overcome its weight;
even after lifting it several times, he was ultimately unable to move it.
The next morning, Zhichen took the sutra and departed without regarding it as a heavy burden.
When the thieves saw this, they believed him to be a sage;
they all came forward to prostrate and offer their thanks.
When Juqu Mengxun, the King of Hexi, heard the name of the seer,
he summoned him for an audience and received him with great courtesy.
Mengxun had long been devoted to the Great Dharma, his aspiration being its widespread propagation.
He requested that the original manuscript of the scripture be brought forth.

However, because the *śāstra* master had not yet mastered the local dialects and there was no one to assist with the translation, he feared that the words might deviate from the principles; thus, he did not permit the immediate translation.
Thereupon, he studied the language for three years before finally translating the first ten fascicles.
At that time, the śramaṇas Huīsōng and Dàolǎng were peerless in Hexī.
When he [Bodhiruci] was expounding the Dharma-treasury,
[Xuanzang] deeply esteemed him and translated the Sanskrit texts,
with Master Song receiving them by dictation.
Several hundred monastics and laypeople raised doubts and questions from all sides;
as Dharmakṣema responded to each situation, he resolved their confusions without ever encountering an obstacle.
Sengsong, Senglao, and others further requested that he produce more of his remaining scriptures.
These include the Mahāsannipāta, the Mahāmegha, the Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka, and the Kṣitigarbha,
totaling nineteen sections including the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
