Because the number of chapters in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* was incomplete, Dharmakṣema returned to his home country to search for them.
Upon the death of his mother, he remained there for over a year.
Later, having obtained further manuscript copies of the scriptures in Khotan,
he returned to Guzang and continued the translation, completing four fascicles.

Dharmakṣema began his translations in the third year of Xuanshi, the Jia-yin year, and completed them entirely in the fifteenth year, the Jing-yin year; Faxiang states they were finished in the tenth year of Xuanshi, but this refers to the conclusion of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and not other scriptures. According to the postscript to the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, it says "translated in the Jing-yin year," which indicates that scriptures were still being produced during those fifteen years. Dharmakṣema did not pass away until the third month of the Gui-you year, the third year of Yihé; since he was active for six years in the interim, he must have produced further scriptures, though these are not mentioned in the catalogs and thus remain undetermined. Dharmakṣema once said to Xun:
Whenever a ghost enters a village, there will inevitably be much pestilence and calamity.
Sun did not believe this and wished to witness it for himself as proof.
Baoshan Chen immediately applied his esoteric arts upon Sun.
Xun was struck with terror upon seeing it.
Chen said,
"You should purify your sincerity and observe the fasts and abstinences, then drive it away with divine incantations."
He then recited the dhāraṇī for three days and said to Xun, "The ghosts have departed to the north.
Shortly thereafter, tens of thousands died of pestilence beyond the northern borders.
Xun’s reverence and awe increased, and his treatment of [the master] with courtesy and honor became even more profound.
At that time, Emperor Da Wu of the Wei dynasty, having heard of his spiritual arts, dispatched an envoy to invite him.
He further warned Xun, saying:
"If you do not send Chen, I shall immediately deploy troops against you."
Xun assessed his own situation and realized that his country was too weak to resist the command.
Furthermore, he feared that the many diviners might already be plotting for Wei on his behalf.
Confused and terrified regarding whether to advance or retreat, he secretly devised a plan to eliminate them.
Initially, when Baoyi Chǐn had finished translating the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the number of fascicles was already fixed;
however, the foreign śramaṇa Dharmaphala stated,
"The chapters of this sūtra are not yet complete."
Chen once sighed with regret and vowed that he must seek them out again.
Lü Mengxun, taking advantage of his resolve, provided him with the means for his journey and generously bestowed precious goods upon him.
However, within a few days of setting out, Chen wept and said to him:
The karmic retribution for his past deeds was about to arrive, and even the assembly of sages could not save him.
Because of his original vow, he could not remain [in hiding].
After traveling forty li, Sun secretly dispatched an assassin to kill him.
At that time he was forty-nine years old;
the assembly all mourned and lamented him deeply.
Shortly thereafter, his attendants frequently saw ghosts and spirits during the day striking Xu with swords.

In the fourth month, he fell ill and passed away. [The record] states that in the third month of the third year of Yìhé, Fǎchèn fell ill and died in the fourth month of that same year. Truly, retribution is not empty; it follows one’s form like a shadow. Fáng says that the claim [Fǎchèn] was in Màoqián and died in the fourth year of Chénghé is incorrect. That third year of Yìhé was the second year of Yánhé of the Wèi dynasty, with the year-stem being Gēi-yōu. Initially, Fǎchèn had been in Gūzāng.
There was a śramaṇa named Daojin from Zhangye who received the bodhisattva precepts from Dharmakṣema.
Dharmakṣema said:
Furthermore, he repented his transgressions and devoted himself with utmost sincerity for seven days and seven nights.
On the morning of the eighth day, he went to Baoyi to request ordination;
however, Baoyi suddenly became greatly enraged.
He further reflected, "It is simply that my karmic obstacles have not yet been extinguished.
Thereupon, he exerted himself for three years, practicing both meditation and repentance.
Then, within a state of meditative concentration, he beheld Śākyamuni Buddha and various great bodhisattvas bestowing the precepts upon him.
That evening, more than ten people staying together all had dreams identical to what Sengjin had seen.
Before Jin could reach Chan to tell him of it,
he was still ten paces away when Chan suddenly started up and cried out:
Excellent, excellent!
You have already received the precepts;
I shall bear witness for you.
He then proceeded to explain the characteristics of the precepts before the Buddha image.
At that time, the śramaṇa Daolang was renowned throughout Guansi;
on the very evening when Daojin received the precepts, Daolang also had a dream.
He then humbled himself by seeking to become his junior in the Dharma based on his seniority in the monastic order (*śīla-varṣa*).
Thereupon, more than a thousand people followed him to receive [the teachings].
The transmission of this Dharma has continued down to the present day.
These are all the remaining rules of the *Vyākaraṇa* (Prophecies).
A separate record states that the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (or *Bodhisattva-bhūmi-vidhi*) should have been transmitted to this land by the Bodhisattva Īṣādhara.

The *Póu-sà-jì jīng* (Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra) in eight fascicles, recorded by Sengyou, Fang, and others, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema; I now consider this to be the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*. It is suspected that Dharmakṣema may not have been an ordinary person. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* consists of ten fascicles. The *Dà-pí-pó-sà-lún* (Mahāyāna-bodhisattva-śāstra) in sixty fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. The *Shè-dà-shèng lùn* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra) in ten fascicles, recorded by Jingtai, states that it was translated by Paramārtha. This is likely the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. The *Jīngmíng zàng jīng* (Sūtra of the Treasury of the Pure Light) in one fascicle, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in one fascicle, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in two fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in three fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in four fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema.

This is likely the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in five fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in six fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in seven fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Gaṇḍavyūha-sūtra*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in eight fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in nine fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in ten fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in eleven fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in twelve fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in thirteen fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in fourteen fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in fifteen fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Triṃśikā-vijñapti*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in sixteen fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Viṃśatikā-vijñapti*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in seventeen fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in eighteen fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in nineteen fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-śāstra*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in twenty fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-upanibandhana*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in twenty-one fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in twenty-two fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-ṭīkā*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in twenty-three fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-vyākhyā*. The *Fóshuō dàfú jīng* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Great Fortune) in twenty-four fascicles, recorded by Daoxuan, states that it was translated by Dharmakṣema. This is likely the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha

Because it is an alternative title, it is not recorded twice. The *Xukongzang jing* (Ākāśagarbha Sūtra) in five fascicles—recorded in the catalogs of Dao You and Fang et al.—is also said to have been translated by Śikṣānanda.

It is now extracted from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, the "Ākāśagarbha" chapter, and circulated separately; it is therefore included here in the catalog of separate translations and is no longer extant elsewhere.
The *Upāsaka-śīla-mūla* (Sutra on the Precepts for Laymen) in one fascicle—recorded in the *Baoshang lu*—is also said to have been translated by Śikṣānanda. Furthermore...
The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* is now included in the *Biesheng lu* (Record of Separate Translations) and is not preserved separately.
The *Śraddhā-upāsikā Sūtra*, two fascicles; the *Wuwei dao jing*, two fascicles; the *Jushi qingseng fudian jing*, one fascicle;
and the *Jueding zui fu jing*, one fascicle—these four sūtras are all recorded by the *Changfang lu* and others as translations by Baosheng, and it is further noted that they were annotated by Shi.

Regarding these doubts, they are all appended here according to the old tradition; the *Chánfǎ yàojiě* (Essential Explanations of Dhyāna Methods) in two fascicles, the second translation which is the same text as that produced by Kumārajīva, is not recorded herein;
see the Chángfáng lù. This one work in two fascicles is missing from the current collection.
Jūqú Jīngshēng, Marquis of Ānyáng,
was the younger cousin of Móngxùn, King of Hēxī.
He was a man of strong will, open-minded, and quick-witted.
Possessing rare wisdom and discernment, he had perused various records and was skilled in discourse.
Having received the five precepts since childhood, he applied himself with keen intent to the inner scriptures;
whatever sutras he read, he was immediately able to recite them from memory.
I have always considered the diligent pursuit of learning and extensive erudition to be the preeminent undertaking of a great practitioner.
When I was young, I once crossed the flowing sands and reached the kingdom of Khotan;
there, at the Mahā-Gomati Monastery, I...
He encountered the Indian Dharma Master Buddhasena (translated as "Awakening Leader" in the Liang language), who was from Anyang; he followed him to inquire about the meaning of the Way.
Buddhasena had originally studied the Mahāyāna;
his natural talent was exceptionally outstanding, and he could recite fifty million verses and was thoroughly proficient in the methods of dhyāna.
Therefore, the various kingdoms of the West refer to him as the "Lion among Men.
Fǎ'ān received from him the various secret essential arts of the Dharma of Receiving the Mandate (Abhiseka), reciting the Sanskrit texts orally.
He then returned eastward to Liang.

During the Shunhe era of Emperor Muzhaoqian, he translated one work, the *Śamathavidhiparyāya*, and the sixty-fascicle *Abhidharmavibhāṣā-śāstra* (sometimes titled with the characters for "Aṣṭagrantha").

The original translation was the same text as the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* translated during the Tang dynasty, though it was sometimes divided into eighty-four fascicles or one hundred and nine fascicles. It was composed by five hundred arhats more than six hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. This is recorded in the two catalogs compiled by Sengyou and Baochang. This single work in sixty fascicles still exists today.
The śramaṇa Buddhavarman—
alternatively called Buddhabhadra;
in the language of Liang, this means "Awakening Armor."
He was a man from the Western Regions.
From his youth, his conduct was upright and straightforward, and his intelligence surpassed that of his peers.
He studied the Tripiṭaka and was particularly proficient in the Vibhāṣā.
He constantly recited and upheld this treatise as his essential core practice.
During the Shōwa era, he arrived at Guzang,
where there was previously a śramaṇa named Daotai.
Zhiyong was resolute and decisive; having traveled extensively throughout various countries, he obtained a Sanskrit manuscript of the *Vibhāṣā* consisting of ten thousand verses.
Upon arriving in Guzang, he sat with his robes arranged to one side and, with an open and humble heart, waited expectantly for a master of illumination.
Having heard that Guṇavarman was devoting his mind to this treatise, he requested him to translate it.
At that time, Juqu Mengxun had already passed away,
and his son Maoqian had succeeded to the throne.
In the fourth month of the middle spring of the Dingchou year of the fifth year of the Qiancheng era,
at the Xianyu Palace Temple in Liangzhou, Guṇavarman was invited to perform the translation,
while Sengtai acted as the scribe.
The śramaṇas Huìsōng and Dàolǎng, together with more than three hundred monks specializing in doctrinal studies, collated and verified the textual meanings;
this was completed only in the seventh month of the seventh year, the Jīmóu (jǐmǎo) year,
totaling one hundred fascicles.
The śramaṇa Daoting composed a preface for it.
Shortly thereafter, Emperor Taowu of the Wei dynasty launched a western campaign against Guzang;
the region of Liang fell into chaos and turmoil, and the scriptures and miscellaneous articles were all consumed by fire and swept away.
Consequently, forty fascicles were lost;
now only sixty remain extant.
Guṇavarman fled the chaos and returned to the west.

It is unknown where it ends; the preface states it was produced in the year Yichou, which is the fourteenth year of Meng Xun’s Xuanshi era, and completed in the year Dingmao, which is the sixteenth year of Xuanshi. This differs from the catalogue; the reason for this discrepancy remains unclear.

*The Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, twenty fascicles; recorded in the *Records of the Song and Qi Dynasties* and the *Monk You’s Records* as the sixth translation, which is the same text as Kumārajīva’s *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*. This one work in twenty fascicles is currently missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Zhimeng was a native of Xinfeng in Jingzhao.
By nature he was upright and intelligent, and he was diligent in his conduct and pure in his character.
At a young age, he inherited the dharma robes and applied himself to his studies with single-minded devotion;
the sound of his recitation continued from night until day.
Whenever he encountered non-Buddhist practitioners speaking of the traces left by Śākyamuni, [he would listen intently].
Furthermore, upon hearing that the Vaipulya sutras were circulating in the Western Regions,
he was constantly filled with profound emotion and directed his mind toward those distant lands.
He believed that ten thousand *li* were but a few inches away and that even a thousand years could be bridged.
Thereupon, in the sixth year of Hongshi during the Yao Qin dynasty— the year of Jiachen—
he summoned like-minded companions, numbering fifteen in all. Setting out from Chang’an,
they crossed rivers and traversed valleys thirty-six times before reaching the city of Liangzhou.
Thereafter, he traveled westward out of Yangguan Pass into the shifting sands for more than two thousand li.
The land was devoid of water and grass, and travelers were cut off from the road;
in winter it was bitterly cold and pestilential, while in summer it was miasmic and scorching.
When people die, their bones are gathered to mark the path.
Camels carry provisions through landscapes of extreme hardship and obstruction.
Thus, he traveled through the various kingdoms of Shanshan, Kucha, and Khotan, observing their customs in detail.
Traveling two thousand li southwest from Khotan, he first ascended the Pamir Mountains.
Of his nine companions, they all turned back;
only Faxian and his remaining associates proceeded for over one thousand seven hundred li to reach the kingdom of Bolor.
His fellow traveler, Zhu Daosong, also passed away.
Just as they were about to perform the cremation, the corpse suddenly vanished from its location.
Daomeng sighed in sorrow and marveled at this extraordinary event.
Thereupon, exerting his own strength, he moved forward;
together with four others, they crossed the Snowy Mountains three times.
The icy cliffs were vast and imposing, rising more than a hundred thousand *tan* high.
A flying rope served as a bridge for crossing through the void;
one could not see its bottom when looking down, nor the sky when looking up.
The cold air was cruel and biting, making the shadows tremble and the souls shudder with fear.
Traveling south again for one thousand *li*, he reached the kingdom of Kasmira.
He crossed the Indus River once more;
the snow mountains rose up with walls even steeper than before.
The lower regions are filled with miasmic vapors and malevolent spirits that block the roads; many travelers die there.
Only those with fierce sincerity and profound spiritual penetration can overcome these perils and reach their destination.
Upon arriving at the city of Kaśmīra, one always finds five hundred arhats there.
While dwelling in this country, [Vimalamati] constantly traveled back and forth to Lake Anavatapta.
A mahāśrāvaka of great virtue saw Māndhātṛ arrive and stop there; filled with joy, he praised him.
Māndhātṛ inquired about the region, and [the arhat] spoke to him concerning the affairs of the four devaputras.
The full account is contained in the *Foguo ji* (Record of Buddhist Kingdoms).
Faxian previously saw a stone spittoon inscribed with the Buddha’s writing in the country of Qiśa,
and he also saw the Buddha’s almsbowl in this same country.
Its radiance was deep purple-blue, vividly distinct at its four borders.
With fierce incense and flower offerings, he reverently upheld [the bowl] and made a vow.
If the bowl were to respond, it could become light or heavy at will.
Soon after, his strength shifted and he could no longer bear it;
yet when he lowered himself to press down, he again perceived no weight.
Such is the nature of what corresponds to his resolute mind.
Traveling further southwest for three hundred li, he reached the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
There he beheld the Buddha’s tooth, the bone of his *uṣṇīṣa*, and the Buddha’s shadow and footprints, all of which remained vividly and completely preserved.
Furthermore, he beheld the forest of the firm Nirvana and the Bodhi tree where Māra was subdued;
with a heart filled with fierce joy, he made offerings for one day,
using precious canopies and great robes to cover the image of the Subduer of Māra.
Wherever he traveled and stepped, he thoroughly investigated spiritual transformations;
the accounts of the Heavenly Ladder and the Dragon Pond are beyond counting.
Later, he arrived at the city of Pāṭaliputra.
This was the former capital of King Aśoka.
There lived a Brahmin of great wisdom named Rāhula,
whose entire clan was devoted to the propagation of the Dharma and whom the Dharmarāja held in high esteem.
A stupa made of pure silver, three *zhang* in height, was being constructed.
The śramaṇa Faxian had previously obtained six fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* from his family;
when he saw Faliang arrive, he asked him about it.
"Is there Mahayana study in the land of Qin?
He replied,
"All study the Mahayana."
Luo Yue was struck with wonder and exclaimed, "How rare!
How rare! Could it not be that a Bodhisattva has come to convert them?
He then went to their home and obtained a single copy of the *Nirvāṇa* in its original Sanskrit manuscript.
Furthermore, he sought out and obtained one copy of the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya in its Sanskrit original, as well as other sūtras in Sanskrit, vowing to circulate them.
Thereupon, he returned;
setting out from India in the year of the Jiazi cycle.
Four fellow monks passed away along the way;
only Fǎměng and Yúnmó returned together to Liangzhou.
During the Shunhe era of Emperor Miaoqian,
he translated the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* in twenty fascicles.
Daomeng passed away at the end of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
The Record of the Ascension and Travels of the Wandering Śramaṇa lists the routes with occasional discrepancies;
even the locations of the Buddha’s alms bowl and cranial bone differ.
One should know that traveling to India was not limited to a single route;
as his bowl and crown were miraculously transported when the time came for him to reach a foreign land,
the accounts of his traces and what has been seen and heard are difficult to generalize.

The *Mahāpuruṣa-śāstra* in two fascicles, composed by Bodhisattva Deva; see the *Fanjing tu*. The *Mahāyāna-avatāra-śāstra* in two fascicles, composed by Bodhisattva Sthiramati; see the *Tang jiulu* as well as the *Neidian lu* and the *Fanjing tu*. These two works, totaling four fascicles, their texts are currently extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Dao Tai possessed a talent bestowed by Heaven; his spirit was lofty and clear,
and his extensive learning led him to appreciate extraordinary interests and investigate distant foreign tongues.
In the past, although the various texts of the Han lands were already complete and the profound principles had been roughly elucidated,
I had not yet mastered the Three Piṭakas and the ninefold division of the scriptures.
Therefore, I took up my staff and braved the dangers, traveling as far as the west of the Pamirs.
Having comprehensively surveyed the Sanskrit texts and inherited their lofty intent,
he further obtained more than one hundred thousand verses of the original Sanskrit *Mahāvibhāṣā* as well as various sūtras and śāstras, which he brought back to Liang.
There, he encountered Buddhavarman and together they translated the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Tài later translated it himself.

Regarding the two sections of the *Mahāpuruṣa-śāstra*, both the *Chángfáng lù* and the *Nèidiǎn lù* state that during the Liáng dynasty, there was again the śramaṇa Tánjué, who translated the *Bhadra-kalpika-sūtra* (Xiányú jīng) in one fascicle at Gāochāng Guó; this corresponds to the twenty-second year of the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty. However, the current translation is not so; in the Jǐmǎo year, the sixteenth year of Yuánjiā, the Liáng state had already ceased to exist. How could there still have been a translation of scriptures in the Yǐyōu year, the twenty-second year? Thus, we know the two catalogs are in error. Now, Jìngmài’s *Jīngtú* places it in the period of the Northern Wèi. Although the Wèi and Sòng were contemporaneous, with the Sòng capital at Jiànyè and the Wèi capital at Héng'ān, when considered by geography, it belongs to the Wèi catalog.

*The Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Sacrifice of His Body to a Starving Tiger and the Circumstances of the Stupa’s Construction*, one fascicle. Monk You’s Catalog states it is titled *The Sutra on Giving One’s Body to a Starving Tiger*. This is seen in the postscript of the sutra. The aforementioned work consists of one volume; its manuscript currently exists.
The śramaṇa Shi Fasheng was a native of Gaochang.
During the Liang period,
he also translated the *Sūtra on Casting One’s Body to Feed a Starving Tiger* in one fascicle.
Therefore, at the end of the *Biography of the Former Eminent Monk Dharmakṣema*, it says:
"At that time, there was also the monk Fa-sheng of Gaochang who traveled abroad; he has a biography in four fascicles."
The *Postscript to the Sutra of the Bodhisattva’s Sacrifice of His Body to a Starving Tiger* states:
"At that time, having heard the Buddha's discourse, the king immediately erected a great stupa at this very spot,
which was named 'The Stupa of the Bodhisattva’s Sacrifice of His Body to a Starving Tiger.'"
It exists today.
On the mountain slope to the east of the stupa, there are monastic quarters, lecture halls, and viharas,
where a community of fifty monks is constantly provided with the four requisites of support.
At that time, Fa-sheng saw people in the kingdom suffering from leprosy, insanity, deafness, blindness, lameness, and various other ailments;
they all came to this stupa to burn incense and light lamps.
If one smears the ground with fragrant mud, cleanses and sweeps it,
and performs prostrations and repentance, all hundred ailments will be healed;
those who were previously afflicted shall depart immediately, and subsequently, such [ailments] shall never recur.
There are always more than a hundred people;
it is thus regardless of their status, whether noble or humble,
and there is never a time when they cease to come.
Now, examining the texts of the *Monastic Biographies* (*Sengzhuan*) and perusing the accounts in the scriptural records,
it is clear that this event— Fasheng’s journey to the Western Regions— is not unfounded.
It further states:
"Since I personally beheld the sacred reliquary, it must not be erroneous.
If it were not translated by Paramārtha himself, how could it be appended to the end of that sūtra?"
Since he was able to travel to the Western Regions himself, how could it be that he did not transmit the scriptural teachings?
Having examined the matter from beginning to end, the facts have become clear.
I have now compiled and recorded this account for the current flourishing translation project.

The *Anutpattika-dharmakṣānti-cakra-sūtra* in four fascicles (also known as the *Anutpattika-sūtra*), the second translation by Dharmarakṣa, identical to the *A-vui-yue-tche-tche-king*; the *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra* in two fascicles or one; the *Mahākṣānti-sūtra* in ten fascicles; the *Cakravartin-rāja-sūtra* in one fascicle; and the *Bhadrakalpa-pañcaśata-buddha-nāma-sūtra* in one fascicle—these five works comprise eighteen fascicles in total. Of these, the first two works totaling six fascicles are extant, while the latter three works totaling twelve fascicles are missing.

The records of Sengyou and others all state that these are the "Newly Compiled Heterodox Scriptures of the Liang Region by the Śramaṇa Sengyou," which were previously based on the works of Shi Dao’an. They have now been appended to the catalog of the Liang period as translations of unknown origin, so that the era, the presence or absence of explicit translators, the number of fascicles, and the provenance may be known. The following entries are newly appended to this catalog.
*Upāsikā-śīla-prakāśana-sūtra*, two fascicles; alternatively, without the word "sūtra," it is simply called the *Śīla-prakāśana-sūtra*.
*Gṛhapati-Dharmavatsa-patnī-sūtra*, one fascicle. *Mahāprajāpatī-bhikṣuṇī-sūtra*, two fascicles; also called the *Mahāprajāpatī-upasampadā-sūtra*;
the old catalog calls it the *Mahāprajāpatī-sūtra*. *Triprajñā-sūtra*, one fascicle. *Bodhisattva-ādi-sūtra*, etc. [one fascicle].
*Pratipadāsūtra*, one fascicle. The following titles are missing: *Catvāri-vaiśāradyasūtra*, one fascicle;
*Upāyakauśalyasūtra*, one fascicle—the old catalog states this is the *Mañjuśrī-upāyakauśalya-samādhisūtra* or simply the *Upāyakauśalya-samādhisūtra*;
*Daśa-udumbara-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Saptapada-dhyāna-lābha-sūtra*, one fascicle—the old catalog states this is the *Udumbara-saptapada-dhyāna*.

*Li jing pusa shi youhe jing* (The Sūtra on the Ten Oghas of the Bodhisattva), one fascicle; now suspected to be the same as the preceding *Shi youhe jing*. *Bingsha wang jing* (The Sūtra of King Bimbisāra), one fascicle.

*Youwu jing* (The Sūtra of Existence and Non-existence), one fascicle. *Wubai ge jing* (The Sūtra of Five Hundred Verses), one fascicle. *Suyue guo pinren jing* (The Sūtra of the Poor Man of the Country of Suyavya);

the old catalog states it is the *Suyue guo pinren lin ti tou jing* (The Sūtra of the Poor Man of the Country of Suyavya Hiring to Shave His Head). *Fu mu jing* (The Sūtra of Floating Wood), one fascicle.
*The Scripture of the Parable of the Cup*, one fascicle; *The Scripture of the Spirit-Demon*, one fascicle; *The Scripture of Anupama-nirvāṇa* (one version reads *Taoseji-nirvāṇa*), one fascicle;
*The Scripture of the Four Impermanences*, one fascicle; *The Scripture of the Five Losses and Coverings*, one fascicle;

*The Scripture of Essential Truth*, one fascicle; *The Scripture of Original Non-being*, one fascicle; *The Scripture of Exhorting Virtue*, one fascicle; *The Scripture of the Fifteen Virtues*, one fascicle.
*Fùmǔ yīnyuán jīng* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Parents), one fascicle; currently suspected to be the same as the *Fùzǐ yīnyuán jīng*. *Hùixíng jīng* (Sūtra on Wise Conduct), one fascicle.

*Wèishēngwáng jīng* (Sūtra of King Unborn), one fascicle; currently suspected to be the *Wèishēngyuàn jīng*. *Nèiwài wúwéi jīng* (Sūtra on Internal and External Unconditioned Phenomena), one fascicle.
*Dàojìng jīng* (Sūtra on the Purity of the Path), one fascicle. *Qīshì běnmò jīng* (Sūtra on the Origins and Endings of the Seven Matters), one fascicle; the old catalog states it is the *Qīshì*.
*Benxing jing* (Sūtra on Past Deeds), one fascicle; *Bao bao sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Hundred Jewels), one fascicle; *San cheng jing* (Sūtra of the Three Vehicles), one fascicle;

*Qi yu shu jing* (Sūtra on the Medical Arts of Jīvaka), one fascicle—the old catalog states it is the *Qi yu si shu jing* (Sūtra on the Four Medical Arts of Jīvaka); *Wu gai za yi jing* (Sūtra on the Miscellaneous Doubts of the Five Hindrances), one fascicle—this is now suspected to be the *Wu gai yi jing* (Sūtra on the Doubts of the Five Hindrances) with the character "xing" (practice) lost;
*Taizi zhizhi jing* (Sūtra on the Prince’s Cessation through Wisdom), one fascicle; *Daode zhang jing* (Sūtra on the Chapters of the Way and Virtue), one fascicle; *Ku...* [text fragment].

*Xiāng jīng* (Sūtra on Characteristics), one fascicle; *Xū fó dé dù jīng* (Sūtra on Receiving the Buddha’s Deliverance), one fascicle; *Yóu jīng* (Sūtra on Causes), one fascicle; *Fēn rán huán guó jiā luó yuè jīng* (Sūtra on the Householder Karo-vyaya of the City of Pūrṇa), one fascicle;

*Wǔ yīn shì jīng* (Sūtra on the Matters of the Five Aggregates), one fascicle; *Yì jué fǎ shì jīng* (Sūtra on Resolving the Meaning of Dharma Matters), one fascicle; *Shí sīwéi jīng* (Sūtra on the Ten Contemplations), one fascicle;

*Fēnbié liù qíng jīng* (Sūtra on the Discrimination of the Six Sense Faculties), one fascicle; *Sān shī gài jīng* (Sūtra on the Three Losses and the Veil), one fascicle; *Fó bǎo sān* (The Three Jewels of the Buddha), [one fascicle].
*Mei jing* (Sutra on Obscurity), one fascicle; *Fazhi nü jing* (Sutra of the Girl Fazhi), one fascicle.
These forty-seven works, totaling forty-nine fascicles—of which six fascicles comprising the first four works exist, while the remainder are missing—are listed as above.
Sengyou’s Catalogue states:
"Master Dao’an’s *Yijing* (Different Scripture) from the Liang region is missing and not recorded in the catalogues of Hui Changfang and others."
Now, these are appended to the Liang catalog as translations of unknown origin.
Sengyou records that Master Daoan listed fifty-nine distinct scriptures from the Liang region in total.
Among these, fifty-two works in total have already been recorded in the *Fanglü* (Catalogue of the Repository) of the five sections;
now forty-seven additional works are presented, bringing the total to fifty-two. There remain seven works comprising fourteen fascicles.
I have carefully examined the records of Sengchangfang and others, all of which have reliable sources; thus, these are certainly not lost translations.
For this reason, they were omitted from the present catalog and are not included here.
Now, I shall provide a detailed list of those missing works as follows.

*Subhūtiparivarta Sūtra*, seven fascicles; an alternative title for a *Prajñāpāramitā* excerpt, translated by Dharmaratna during the Qin dynasty. *Mañjuśrī-parinirmita-ratnagarbha Sūtra*, two fascicles; translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty. *Saptajñāna Sūtra*, one fascicle; also titled *Saptajñāna*; translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. *Durdharṣa-nāgarāja Sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *Durdharṣa Sūtra* or *Nāgarāja-bhrātṛ Sūtra*; an alternative title translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. *Ātā-samaya Sūtra*, one fascicle; an alternative title for the *Ātā-samādhi Sūtra*; recorded in the catalog of Master Dao’an as a missing text. *Mahā-pañca-kāluṣya Sūtra*, one fascicle; the old catalogs call it the *Mahā-pañca-kāluṣya-loka Sūtra*, while various records label it as spurious; it is now also included at the beginning [of this collection]. *Śrotā-viṃśati-prakaraṇa Sūtra*, one fascicle; the old catalogs call it the *Śrotā-viṃśati-prakaraṇa-buddha-caturdaśārtha Sūtra*, or the *Śrotā-viṃśati-prakaraṇa-caturdaśavastu Sūtra*; it is also called...

Translated by Zhi Yao of the Later Han; now included in the *Chao jing* (Extracted Scriptures) and recorded in the *Bie sheng lu* (Separate Record of Additional Translations). The *Dafangguang shilun jing* (Mahāvaipulya Daśacakrakṣitigarbha Sūtra) in eight fascicles was first produced as having the same text as the Tang translation of the *Dizang shilun jing*. It appears to be the thirteenth division of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* and seems to have been translated during the Liang dynasty, though it is not recorded in the various catalogs. It is now appended here at the end of the Liang period so that this lost compilation may not be overlooked. Including both new and old versions, there are fifty-three works in a total of seventy-five fascicles, all attributed to the "lost sources" of Northern Liang.

During the Song Dynasty, under the Liu clan, the capital was Jianye. From the first year of Emperor Wu’s Yongchu era, the Gengshen year, until the third year of Emperor Shun’s Shengming era, the Jiwu year.
In total, there were eight masters over a period of sixty years.
Including both monastics and laypeople, there were twenty-two individuals in all.
These included the various sūtras and śāstras they produced, as well as newly compiled scriptures whose translators had been lost.

In total, there are four hundred and sixty-five works comprising seven hundred and seventeen fascicles; among these, nine hundred and thirty works totaling two hundred and forty-three fascicles are extant, while three hundred and seventy-three works totaling four hundred and seventy-four fascicles are missing.
The Sramaṇa Buddhayaśas of the Song dynasty [translated] three sections totaling thirty-two fascicles of the Vinaya-karmavācanā;
the Sramaṇa Kuṃārajīva [translated] two sections totaling two fascicles of sūtras; the Sramaṇa Dharmamitra [translated] twelve sections totaling seventeen fascicles;
the Sramaṇa Śikṣānanda [translated] ten sections totaling thirty-one fascicles of sūtras; and the Sramaṇa Ratnamegha [translated] four...

ten collections totaling eighteen fascicles of vinaya compendia by the śramaṇa Saṃghavarman;
and fifty-two collections of vinaya treatise compendia by the śramaṇa Guṇabhadra.
A collection of one hundred and thirty-four volumes of sutras and śāstras by the śramaṇa Shi Tanwujie, comprising one volume;
twenty-eight collections of twenty-eight volumes of sutras and vinaya by the layman Juqu Jingsheng;
ten collections of ten volumes of sutras by the śramaṇa Shi Huijian; and two collections of seven volumes of sutras by the śramaṇa Gongdezhi.
*Men shi seng qu* (The Monk Sengqu’s Explanations of the Gates), one fascicle; *Jie mo* (Karmavācanā) by the Śramaṇa Shi Faying, one fascicle;
*Ni jie* (Nun Precepts) by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fajian, six works totaling twenty-nine fascicles; *Jing* (Scriptures) by the Śramaṇa Shi Xianggong, one work in two fascicles;
*Jing* (Scriptures) by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoyan, two works totaling three fascicles; and *Jing lü* (Scriptures and Vinaya) by the Śramaṇa Shi Yonggong, three [works].
Three fascicles of sutras by the śramaṇa Shi Fahaï; two fascicles of sutras and vinaya by the śramaṇa Shi Xiàngōng;
one fascicle of sutras by the śramaṇa Saṃghavarman; one fascicle of a vinaya compendium;

three hundred and seven works totaling three hundred and forty fascicles of various newly collected sutras of lost translation; and thirty fascicles of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, also known as the *Wufen lü*.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śīla* in thirty-four fascicles; the separate catalog states it is in twenty-four fascicles, which is likely an error (as seen in Daohui’s *Song Qi Lu* and Sengyou’s catalog).

The *Wufen Biqiu Jieben* (Five-Part Bhikṣu Precept Manual) in one fascicle, also called the *Mahīśāsaka Śīla-mūla*, is found in Zhu Daozu’s catalog and Sengyou’s catalog. The *Mahīśāsaka Karma* in one fascicle is also seen [in these records].
The catalog by Zhu Daozu and the catalog by Sengyou: these three sections comprise thirty-two fascicles;
the *Vinaya-śīla* currently exists, while the *Karmavācanā* is missing. [Compiled by] the Śramaṇa Buddhayaśas.
In the Song language, his name is Jue-shou (Jñānāyuṣa).
He was a native of Kaśmīra who,
in his youth, received his training in the Mahīśāsaka school.
He specialized in the Vinaya-piṭaka while simultaneously mastering the essentials of Dhyāna.
In the seventh month of the first year of the Jingping era (the *guihai* year) of the deposed Emperor Yifu, he arrived at the capital of Yangdu.
Previously, the śramaṇa Faxian had obtained a Sanskrit manuscript of the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya in the Kingdom of Siṃhala.
Before he had even completed the translation, he passed away.
When the monks in Jianye heard that Kumārajīva was well-versed in this field of study,
they requested him to produce a translation of it.
In the eleventh month of winter in that same year, he assembled at Longguang Temple to translate it;
it was titled the *Five-Part Vinaya* (*Wufen lü*),
and the responsibility for the Sanskrit manuscript was entrusted to him.
The śramaṇa Yú Tiánshān Zhìshèng acted as the oral transmitter;
the śramaṇa Zhú Dàoshēng of Lóngguāng and the śramaṇa Shì Huìyán of Dōng'ān held the brush together to revise and correct the text.
Wáng Liàn of Lángyá, Imperial Attendant of the Song dynasty, served as the patron (dānapati).
It was only completed in the twelfth month of the following year.
He then produced the *Śīlacitta* and the *Karmavācanā* texts,
both of which were circulated throughout the world.
His final whereabouts are unknown.

The *Sūtra on the Contemplation of Amitāyus* (one fascicle), also known as the *Amitāyus Contemplation Sūtra*, first appeared in the *Daohui lu* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. The *Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata* (one fascicle) was the second [work] to appear in the *Song Qi lu* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. These two works, totaling two fascicles, still exist today.
The śramaṇa Jiang Liangyeshe,
known in the Song dynasty as Chicheng,
was a native of the Western Regions.
By nature he was upright and had few desires.
He was skilled at reciting the Abhidharma and had extensively studied the Vinaya-piṭaka;
furthermore, he possessed a comprehensive mastery of most other sūtras.
Although he was well-versed in all three collections of the Tripiṭaka, he specialized professionally in the Chan school.
Whenever he engaged in contemplative observation, he would sometimes remain without rising for seven days.
He constantly used the correct reception of samādhi to transform and guide people throughout various kingdoms.
In the first year of the Yuanjia era, a *jiǎzǐ* year, he traveled far across the Shahe River and arrived at Jianye.
Emperor Wen, whose personal name was Yilong, deeply marveled at his extraordinary qualities and issued an edict for him to reside at Daolin Monastery on Mount Zhong.
The śramaṇa Baozhi revered his dhyāna methods.
The śramaṇa Senghan requested that he translate the *Contemplation of Immeasurable Life* and the *Medicine King and Medicine Superior [Sūtras]*;
Senghan himself served as the scribe for the transcription.
Since these two sutras are the great cause for the Pure Land and the secret art for transforming obstacles,
they were circulated in the Song state with deep reflection and reverent appreciation.
Meng Yi of Pingchang, responding to this influence with sincere devotion, provided them with abundant support.
When Zhiyi was appointed to govern Kuaiji, he firmly declined the post and did not go.
Later, he moved to rest at Jiangling.
In the nineteenth year of the Yuanjia era, he traveled west to the regions of Min and Shu.
Everywhere he propagated the Way, and his disciples of Chan studies gathered in great numbers.
Later, he returned and passed away in Jiangling at the age of sixty.

The śramaṇa Dharmamitra—
translated into the Song language as Fashou—
was a native of Jibin.
At the age of six or seven, his spiritual faculties were clear and upright;
whenever he witnessed a Dharma ceremony, he would spontaneously leap for joy.
His parents loved him and marveled at this, so they eventually allowed him to leave the household life.
In Kaśmīra, many sages and realized ones have appeared;
he repeatedly encountered enlightened masters,
extensively studied the various scriptures, and maintained profound methods of dhyāna.
The essentials he attained were extremely subtle and profound.
He was grave and sagacious, possessing deep wisdom and understanding; his ritual observances were meticulous and orderly.
Because he was born with joined eyebrows, he was known in the world as the Chan Master Lianmei (Joined-Brow).
From his youth, he delighted in traveling abroad and vowed to propagate the teachings.
After journeying through various kingdoms, he eventually reached Kucha.
One day before his arrival, the king dreamed.
The deity announced:
"A person of great merit shall enter the kingdom tomorrow; you should provide him with offerings.
At dawn, he immediately issued an edict to the external offices.
If any stranger entered the borders, they would invariably be dispatched to report it to the throne.
Shortly thereafter, Guṇamati indeed arrived;
the king personally went out to the outskirts to welcome him and invited him into the palace.
He subsequently received the precepts from him and provided him with the four requisites.
Guṇamati remained there yet was able to move on, not being detained by offerings and gain.
After several years, Guṇamati formed the intention to depart.
The deity again descended in a dream and said,
"A person of merit has abandoned the king and departed.
The king woke up in a state of startled alarm.
Subsequently, although the ruler and his ministers earnestly entreated him to remain, none could stop him.
He then crossed the shifting sands and proceeded to Dunhuang,
where he established a vihāra in the midst of the wilderness.
He planted a thousand peach trees and established a garden of one hundred mu;
its chambers, pavilions, ponds, and groves were exceedingly solemn and pure.
Shortly thereafter, he again traveled to Liangzhou.
He further renovated the halls and chambers within the old monastery on the public estate.
Students gathered there in great numbers, and their practice of dhyāna flourished most remarkably.
He constantly harbored the desire to transmit the Dharma to the many people of Jiangzuo.
In the first year of the Yuanjia era, he traveled by circuitous routes to Shu.
Shortly thereafter, he emerged from the gorges and stayed in Jingzhou,
where he established a meditation hall at Changsha Temple.
With sincere devotion and profound compassion, he prayed for a relic;
after more than ten days, he was moved by a response and obtained one.
It struck the vessel with a sound and emitted light that filled the room.
Among his disciples, both monastics and laypeople, there was none who did not redouble their vigor;
each person resolved to exert themselves a hundredfold.
After a short while, they traveled downstream eastward until they reached Jianye.
He first resided at Zhongxing Temple and later stayed at Jihuan Monastery.
His reputation for the sound of the Way was long established, such that the entire capital came to pay him homage;
this included Empress Yuan of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, as well as princes and princesses.
There were none who did not establish fasts at the Gui Palace and request the precepts from the椒掖 (Jiāoyè) [the inner quarters].
Envoys arriving to inquire after her health followed one another every ten days.
From the first year of the Yuánjiā era, the jiǎzǐ year, until the eighteenth year, the xīn sì year, she followed the imperial decree.
He translated twelve sections of scriptures, including the *Ākāśagarbha-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
He constantly instructed his disciples in the path of meditation (*dhyāna*).
Those who sought refuge with him traveled from as far as a thousand li.
The four classes of followers, both far and near, all hailed him as the Great Chan Master.
Meng Yi, the Governor of Kuaiji, had profound faith in the ultimate truth and took it upon himself to serve as the guardian of the Triple Gem.
He had long cherished a taste for the flavor of Chan and possessed a profound sense of reverence.
Upon reaching the banks of the Zhe River, he requested that [the Master] accompany him on a journey;
thereupon, they established a pagoda and a temple on the mountain of Mao County.
In the eastern regions, the ancient customs largely favored sorcery and divination;
however, through the transformative power of the wondrous teachings, every household has returned to the orthodox path.
From west to east, there is none who does not submit with sincerity.
Later, he returned to Jianye and stayed at the Lower Dinglin Monastery.
By nature, the Dhyāna Master was serene and tranquil, possessing a refined love for mountains and waters;
he considered Mount Zhong to be a presiding peak that rivaled the splendors of Mount Song and Mount Hua.
He often lamented that the foundation and structure of the Lower Temple had not yet fully realized its scenic excellence.
Thereupon, he ascended a high point to survey the terrain and deliberate upon the mountain's topography;
he cleared stones and felled trees to establish the Upper Temple.
The imperial halls and meditation chambers were solemn and profound;
they truly resembled, in their subtle likeness, the Vulture Peak and the Jetavana Grove.
Thereupon, the assembly of those who had stilled their minds gathered from ten thousand *li* away.
Reciting the scriptures with solemnity and harmony, he transformed others by his very presence.
From the Western Regions to the southern lands,
wherever he traveled, he established dāna assemblies and expounded the teachings without exception.
When Master Chūshin set out from Kāpiśī,
the deity Kapila escorted him;
they subsequently reached Kucha, though he intended to turn back midway.
Thereupon, he manifested his form and took his leave.
The Zen Master said,
"Your supernatural powers of transformation and change are truly sovereign."
"Let us go together to the south," he said,
and as soon as he finished speaking, his shadow vanished and was no longer seen.
Thereupon, [the Master] followed him from afar all the way to the capital of Yangdu.
Therefore, the images were subsequently painted upon the walls of the upper temple;
even to this day, there are still manifestations of sound and shadow.
Those who offer prayers with pure sincerity have none whose wishes are not fulfilled.
He passed away at Shangsi Temple on the sixth day of the seventh month in the nineteenth year of the Yuanjia era,
at the age of eighty-seven.
Monastics and laypeople of the fourfold assembly followed one another in a procession of wailing and weeping.
He was subsequently buried at Mount Zhong, in front of Songxi Temple.

The *Wujinyi pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati) consists of six fascicles; its initial title reads "The Thirty-second Chapter on the Inexhaustible Meaning Spoken by Akṣayamati within the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*.
It is also simply called the *Wujinyi jing* (Akṣayamati Sūtra) and is further known as the *Achapo* (Akṣayamati).
The *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra*, fascicle 4, translated by Dharmarakṣa; this is the same text as the *Aksayamati-sūtra*. See Li Kuò’s record.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi-sūtra*, one fascicle; a branch of the *Lotus Sūtra* tradition. See Zhìfáng’s record.

The *Vaipulya-prabhāsa-viśuddha-avaivartika-cakra-sūtra*, four fascicles (also in three or six fascicles, or simply called the *Vaipulya-prabhāsa-viśuddha-sūtra*). Third translation. Also simply [called the *Vaipulya-prabhāsa-viśuddha-sūtra*].
The *Avaivartika-dharmacakra-sūtra* and the *Dharmarakṣa-avaivartika-caryā-sūtra*, among others, were first translated in the fourth year of the Yuanjia era;
this is recorded in the *Song Qi lu* and the *Sengyou lu*. The one-fascicle *Caturmahārāja-sūtra* appears in the *Sengyou lu* and the *Gaoseng zhuan*.
The eight-fascicle *Lalitavistara-sūtra* is the third translation; it is also found in six or four fascicles. It is the same as [the previous versions].
The *Shu Puyao* (Shu Version of the Lalitavistara) by Zhu Fahu; the *Puyao* and the *Fangguang* (Vaipulya) versions recorded in the Tang catalogues;

these all share the same source as seen in the Song and Qi catalogs, Sengyou’s catalog, the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, and others. The one-fascicle *Jingdu sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Pure Deliverance) first appeared in the Changfang catalog.

The two-fascicle *Bodhisattva yingluo benye jing* (Sūtra on the Original Acts of the Bodhisattva’s Diadem) is the second appearance, according to the Fang catalog. The five-fascicle *Sheng jing* (Sūtra of Births)...
Scroll Two. Those translated by Zhu Fahu (Dharmarakṣa) are the same as those in the original collection. Fang says he saw them in the *Bielu* (Separate Record):
*Shan-de upāsaka jing* (Sūtra of the Layman Shan-de), one scroll; seen in the *Changfang lu* (Record of Zhangfang). *Anagāmi jing* (Sūtra on Non-returners), two scrolls;
seen in the *Changfang lu*. The above ten works comprise thirty-one scrolls. The first four works, totaling twelve scrolls, are currently extant at [Pu]... (e.g., Puji Temple).
The lower six sections of the *Yao jing* (Dhyāna Sūtra), totaling nineteen fascicles,
are missing. The śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan was a native of Xiliangzhou.
Having left home at the age of twenty, he was already renowned for his diligent application.
He wore patched robes, sat in meditation, and maintained a vegetarian diet for many years.
He frequently desired to serve famous masters and extensively seek out sūtras and śāstras.
He then traveled extensively through the Western Regions until he reached Kaśmīra.
Entering the Mahāvana Monastery, he received instruction in the methods of dhyāna from the bhikṣu Buddhasena.
He practiced for three years, yet his mastery exceeded that of ten years.
Buddhayaśas first observed that his meditative contemplation was systematic and that he possessed a profound and extraordinary vessel.
Upon hearing this, both the monastics and the laity marveled, saying,
"In the land of Qin, there is indeed a śramaṇa who seeks the Way."
At first, he did not slight the Qin people, treating foreigners with respect.
At that time, there was the bhikṣu Buddhabhadra,
who was also a master of dhyāna in that country.
Daoyan then earnestly requested him to return eastward so that he might transmit the Dharma to the Middle Kingdom.
Guṇabhadra, admiring his sincerity, eventually traveled east with him.
After more than a year had passed, they reached the interior of the Passes.
They constantly relied upon one another and resided together in Chang’an.
After some time, Guṇabhadra was unjustly expelled by the monks of the Qin,
and Huiguan, along with the assembly who had come from the West, were all dispersed.
After passing through the frontier pass, he stayed at the Shandong Monastery, where he sat in meditation, recited the sutras, and applied himself with diligence to his studies.
In the thirteenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, Song Wudi marched westward to replace Yao Hong.
Upon his victorious return, his banners passed through Shandong.
At that time, Wang Huai, the Duke of Shixing, accompanied the imperial carriage on a tour of the mountains and rivers until they reached the Yan Monastery.
There he saw three monks, his spiritual companions, each sitting upon a rope-bench, their meditative concentration profound and serene.
Hui then snapped his fingers, and the three men opened their eyes;
shortly thereafter, they closed them again and did not exchange a word with him.
Hui, inwardly admiring their extraordinary nature, inquired of the local elders, all of whom said: [they were the Three Immortals].
Having lived in seclusion for many years, he had never once ventured out lightly.
When Hui invited him to return to the capital at the request of Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty, he was unwilling to go.
After repeated entreaties, he finally arrived; of the three men, Yan was the one who accompanied him.
Huīhuī’s Way was expansive and his observance of the ancient rites was most thorough.
Upon returning to the capital, he resided at Shixing Temple.
By nature, he was serene and tranquil, his will set on avoiding the clamor and dust of the world.
Huī then constructed another vihāra on the outskirts of the eastern suburb;
this was the Jiyuan Monastery (Zhīyuán sì).
There, he brought back the Sanskrit manuscripts of various scriptures that he had previously obtained in the Western Regions, which he had not yet translated or transcribed.
In the fourth year of the Yuanjia era, the year Dingmao,
he together with the śramaṇa Baoyun translated ten scriptures, including the Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra.
Daoyan resided at the monastery and did not accept private invitations, supporting himself through alms-gathering.
The influence of his transformation through the Way reached both the hidden and the manifest, such that all submitted to him.
He maintained a strict purity and was of few desires; he gave away whatever he received as soon as it came to him.
From his youth, he traveled to various regions, remaining unattached to anything.
By nature he was profound and aloof, and would not speak of himself;
thus, although his virtuous deeds were many, none could be fully transmitted to the world.
In the past, before he had left the household life, Yan had received the five precepts, yet there were instances where he had committed transgressions against them.
Later, he entered the Way and received full ordination;
however, he constantly doubted whether he had attained the precepts and lived in perpetual fear of this.
Although he practiced meditative contemplation for many years, he could not resolve his uncertainty.
Thereupon, he again crossed the sea and returned to India to consult with those who were wise and erudite.
He encountered an arhat bhikṣu and related the matter in detail to him;
the arhat did not dare to provide a definitive judgment.
Thereupon, Yan entered meditative absorption and traveled to the Tuṣita Heaven to consult Maitreya.
Maitreya replied,
"You have obtained the precepts."
Yan Da was filled with great joy.
He then returned on foot and reached Jibin,
where he passed away without illness.
At that time, he was seventy-eight years old.
In that country, ordinary people and sages each had their own designated places for cremation.
Although Yan’s observance of the precepts and his moral integrity were lofty and brilliant, his actual practice had not yet reached full realization.
When they first moved the corpse toward the cemetery for ordinary monks, it was too heavy to lift;
when they turned it toward the cemetery for the saints, it became light and floated away of its own accord.
Yan’s disciples, Zhiyu and Zhiyuan, had followed him from the west.
Having received these auspicious signs, they both returned to their foreign lands.
By this we may infer that Daoxian was indeed a man who had attained the Way;
it is simply unknown whether his realization was deep or shallow along the path toward the fruit.

The *Tiaofu zhongsheng jing* (Sūtra on Taming Sentient Beings) is excerpted from the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*; the *Yiyin xian zhengfa jing* (Sūtra on Manifesting the True Dharma with a Single Sound), also known as the *Yiyin yan zhengfa jing*, is excerpted from the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; and the *Shande boluomen wen tipo datuo jing* (Sūtra on the Questions of the Brahmin Śubhavyūha regarding Devadatta) is excerpted from the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*. Regarding the two-fascicle *Vīrasamādhi-sūtra*, various catalogs such as those by Sengyou and others all note it as doubtful; however, it was included as authentic in the *Dazhou lu*. Now, upon examining its phrasing, it is found to be shallow and vulgar, and its principles are neglected; therefore, it is placed in the category of "doubtful" to weed out the chaff. These four works, including the *Tiaofu zhongsheng jing*, comprise five fascicles.
The catalogs compiled by Sengchang and others all state that these were translated by Yan Fotiao.
However, I now consider the first three to have been produced separately and the last one to be suspiciously spurious.
Since this is intended as a definitive record, I have deleted them all.

The *Buddhacarita-sūtra* (佛本行經) in seven fascicles—also known as the *Buddhacarita-praśasti* (佛本行讚)—was produced at Mount Liuhe (六合山) Monastery; some say it consists of five fascicles and is recorded in Sengyou’s and Baochang’s catalogs of Buddhist scriptures. The *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks) states that the *Buddhacarita-praśasti-sūtra* and the new *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* in two fascicles were produced at Daochang Monastery in the second year of the Yongchu era. One catalog records its production at Mount Liuhe Monastery. This ninth translation is identical in content to the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, the *Amitāyus-parivarta*, and others, according to the catalogs of Daohui, Sengyou, and others. The *Viśuddhi-samādhi-sūtra* (淨度三昧經) in two fascicles is the second edition, appearing in Zhu Daozu’s *Zalu* (Miscellaneous Records). The *Dharmapada-śāstra* (付法藏經) in six fascicles is the first edition, appearing in Li Kuò’s catalog. These four works comprise seventeen fascicles in total: the first work consists of seven fascicles and is extant; the remaining three works consist of ten fascicles, but their texts are missing.
The śramaṇa Śikṣānanda (Shi Baoyun) was a native of Liangzhou.
Having entered the monastic order in his youth, he was diligent and possessed both learning and virtuous conduct.
His character and temperament were firm and pure, setting him apart from the world;
thus, in his youth, he was renowned for his integrity, rectitude, and devotion to pure practice.
In his quest for the Dharma, he was earnest and sincere, forgetting his own person to devote himself to the Way.
Vowing to personally behold sacred traces and extensively seek out the scriptural teachings,
he traveled far to the Western Regions at the beginning of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty,
accompanying Faxian and Zhiyan in succession.
He traversed the shifting sands and ascended the snowy peaks of Mount Shu;
though his labors were arduous and his journey perilous, he did not consider them difficult.
Thus he passed through the various kingdoms of Yutian and India, where he witnessed numerous spiritual wonders in person.
He then traversed the wilderness of the rākṣasas and heard the sound of celestial drums.
He paid homage at many sites associated with the traces of Śākyamuni’s shadow.
While abroad in foreign lands, he studied Sanskrit scripts everywhere.
He was thoroughly proficient in the phonology, characters, and glossaries of all the kingdoms of India.
Later, upon returning to Chang’an, he followed the Dhyāna Master Buddhabhadra to receive instruction.
He devoted himself to the study of the Dhyāna gate with unremitting diligence.
Furthermore, when the Meditation Master was unjustly expelled by a monk from the Qin, Huiyun also fled.
Upon meeting Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu, who resolved the matter of his expulsion,
they returned together to the capital city of Yangdu and settled at Daochang Temple.
The monastic community, recognizing his cloud-like resolve and steadfast, fierce vigor in propagating the Way in remote regions, all opened their hearts to consult him; they revered and loved him.
Initially, he had traveled abroad together with Zhiyan to translate various scriptures.
After Yan had passed away, Daoyun alone continued the work of proclamation and translation.
During the Yuanjia era, he translated four works, including the *Buddhacarita-sūtra*.
Yun held the Sanskrit manuscripts in his hands while reciting and translating them himself.
He was proficient in both Chinese and non-Chinese languages, and his phonology and glossaries were fundamental and definitive.
Regarding the principles established by Yún, everyone was convinced and submitted to them.
Initially, the śramaṇa Zhú Fóniàn of Guānzhōng was skilled at oral translation.
During the two reigns of Fu Jian and Yao Xing, he translated numerous scriptures;
none in the region south of the Yangtze River surpassed Yun.
Thus, during the transition between the Jin and Song dynasties, he widely propagated the treasury of the Dharma.
The śramaṇas Huìguān and others all befriended him and esteemed his virtue.
Because Sengyún’s nature favored dwelling in seclusion to preserve tranquility and stillness,
he eventually retired to the monastery on Mount Liùhé.
The mountains are largely desolate and the local customs favor petty banditry;
however, after Yún preached the Dharma and exhorted them, many reformed their evil ways.
Nine out of ten households now perform rites and offer worship.
Recently, when Daochang Huiguan was approaching his end, he requested that Huiyun return to the capital to take overall charge of the temple administration.
Reluctantly, Huiyun returned to reside at Daochang Temple;
he subsequently consented to return once more to Liuhe.
He passed away at the mountain monastery in the twenty-sixth year of the Yuanjia era at the age of seventy-four.
There are separate records and biographies concerning his travels abroad.

The *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* in thirteen fascicles; the third edition appears in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) and the *Catalogue of Dharma Master Sengyou* (*Sengyou lu*). Alternatively, it exists in fourteen fascicles. This one work in thirteen fascicles is a missing text.
The śramaṇa Yebaluo (Ityapala),
translated as "Zizai" (Svatantra) in the Song language, was a man from the Western Regions.
He was profoundly versed in the Tripiṭaka and possessed clear understanding of the four Āgamas.
In the third year of the Yuanjia era, on a jing-chen day,
he traveled to Pengcheng and, for Wang Zhongde— the Governor of Beizhou and a native of Taiyuan— translated the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*.
The translation was interrupted before reaching the conclusion of the "Chapter on Discernment" (*Vibhaṅga*) due to obstacles;
consequently, it was left unfinished, resulting in only ten fascicles.
The Prefect personally acted as the scribe for the oral dictation.
In the eighth year, the *xinwei* (辛未) year, he further requested Guṇavarman to continue the translation,
completing a total of thirteen fascicles.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* in nine fascicles— also known as the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, or in ten fascicles— was produced at the Jetavana Monastery.

The two catalogs by Zhu Daozu and Sengyou, as well as the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) and the records of Changfang and others, all state that the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* consists of twenty fascicles;
they further claim that a disciple later produced two additional chapters to complete the twenty fascicles, but this is not correct.
There is only one fascicle of the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, titled *The Dharma of Bodhisattva Precepts Asked by Upāli*, as seen in Baochang’s catalog. If it were merely...
Yǒu’s record treats this as the first fascicle, combining it with the preceding nine fascicles to form ten in total;

however, as the Northern Dynasties manuscript has been intermingled with other texts for a long time, they cannot be merged. Thus, we shall follow the established tradition: the *Bodhisattva-neijie jing* (One Fascicle), seen in the *Baoshang lu*;
the *Upāsaka-wujie yi jing* (One Fascicle), seen in the *Baochang lu*; and the *Śrāmaṇera-weiyi* (One Fascicle).
One fascicle; alternatively, it is called the *Śrāmaṇera-Ācāra-sūtra* (Sāmmī Vīyi Jing), as seen in the Chángfáng Lù. One fascicle of the *Caturvarga-Bhikṣuṇī-Karman* (Sìfēn Bǐqiūní Jīmó Fǎ);
Sengyòu states it is the Dharmaguptaka Karman, also called the *Miśra-Karman*. It was translated at Qiyuan Temple in the eighth year of the Yuánjiā era.
It is found in Sengyòu’s and Bǎochàng’s catalogs, as well as the Gāosēng Zhuàn and other sources; some simply refer to it as the "Four."

*Fenjiemo Upāsaka Wujiexiang Jing* (Sūtra on the Analysis of the Ritual Procedures for the Five Precepts of a Lay Disciple), one fascicle; also known as *Upāsaka Wujie Luelun* (A Brief Treatise on the Five Precepts of a Lay Disciple).
Translated at Qihuan Temple in the eighth year of the Yuanjia era; recorded in the first translations in the *Sengyou Lu*, *Baochang Lu*, and the *Gaoseng Zhuan*.
*Longshu Pusa Wei Chanduojia Wang Shuofayaojie* (Verses on the Essential Dharma Spoken by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna for King Caṇḍotka), one fascicle; recorded in [the aforementioned catalogues].

The *Táng jiùlù* [Records of the Old Tang] contains one fascicle titled *Shànxìn èrshí'èr jiè* (Twenty-two Precepts for Good Faith), also called *Líyù ōubōyí jùxíng èrshí'èr jiè wén* (Text on the Twenty-two Precepts Fully Observed by a Laywoman Free from Desire).
It also mentions the *Ōubōsè jiè* (Precepts for Upāsakas). Sengyou states that these include the Three Refuges and the thirty-two precepts for upāsakas;
some also refer to them as the *Ōubōsè jiè*. These are seen in the *Gāosēng zhuàn* (Biographies of Eminent Monks) and Sengyou’s *Lùjīng lǜfēn* (Catalogue of Scriptures and Vinaya Classifications).
*Yiji* (Record of Differences), one fascicle; found in the *Changfang lu*. The above ten works comprise eighteen fascicles. [Works by] Nāgārjuna:

*Fayao jie shang* (Verses on the Essentials of the Dharma, Part One), eight works in sixteen fascicles, currently extant; *Shanxin ershi jie* (Twenty Precepts for Good Faith), two works in two fascicles, missing from the original.
The śramaṇa Guṇavarman—
translated into the Song language as "Armor of Merit"—
was originally of the kṣatriya caste.
For generations his family served as kings, and their domain was in the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
His grandfather, Haribhadra—translated here as "Lion-Worthy"—was exiled due to his upright and rigid character.
His paternal uncle, Saṃghananda—translated here as "Assembly-Admired"—thereupon withdrew into seclusion among the mountains and marshes.
At the age of fourteen, Guṇavarman was already exceptionally perceptive and possessed profound foresight.
He was magnanimous and broad-minded, honoring virtue and striving for goodness.
Once, his mother requested some wild meat and ordered Guṇavarman to procure it; Guṇavarman replied:
"Among all living beings, there are none that do not cherish life.
To take away another's life is not the act of a benevolent person.
His mother said in anger:
"Even if I were to commit a transgression, I would take your place.
Later, when Guṇavarman was boiling rice gruel, he mistakenly poured it over his finger.
He then said to his mother:
The mother said, "I can endure the pain on your behalf, my son,
but the pain is in your body; how could I possibly endure it for you?"
Guṇavarman said,
"If one cannot even substitute for the suffering before one's eyes, how much less so for the three miserable realms? Thereupon,
the mother repented and awakened, vowing to abstain from killing for the rest of her life.
When he reached the age of eighteen, a physiognomist saw him and said:
"At the age of thirty, you shall rule over a great kingdom and face south as its sovereign.
If you do not delight in worldly glory, you shall instead attain the fruit of sainthood."
At the age of twenty, he left the household life and received the precepts.
He thoroughly mastered the nine divisions of the scriptures and was extensively learned in the four Āgamas;
he could recite more than a million words of the sūtras.
He profoundly mastered the categories of the Vinaya and entered the essentials of dhyāna with subtle skill;
at that time, he was titled the Tripitaka Master.
When he reached the age of thirty, the King of Kaśmīra passed away, leaving no heir to the throne.
The assembly all deliberated, saying:
"Guṇavarman is a scion of the royal house;
moreover, he is talented, wise, and of profound virtue."
He requested that [the prince] be allowed to return to lay life so as to succeed to the throne;
though several hundred ministers repeatedly and earnestly entreated him, Guṇavarman would not accept.
He then took leave of his teacher, defied the multitude, and dwelt among the forests and drank from the mountain valleys.
He traveled alone through mountains and fields, withdrawing from the world of men.
Later, he arrived in the Kingdom of Siṃhala to observe the local conditions and propagate the teachings;
those who recognized the truth all declared that he had attained the first fruit of the path.
His dignified appearance moved all who beheld him, causing them to awaken the aspiration for enlightenment.
Later, he arrived at the kingdom of Śrīvijaya;
one day before his initial arrival there—
The mother of the King of Java dreamed that a Taoist priest arrived in the kingdom by flying ship.
The following morning, Guṇavarman indeed arrived.
The Queen Mother honored him with rites befitting a sage and received the five precepts from him.
The mother then exhorted the king, saying:
"Through the causal conditions of past lives, we have become mother and son.
I have already received the precepts, yet you do not believe."
Fearing that the causes for future lives might forever sever his connection to the present fruit,
the King, constrained by his mother’s command, immediately accepted the precepts at her behest.
As time passed, his habitual practice became long-established, and his single-minded devotion gradually grew more earnest.
Shortly thereafter, neighboring troops violated the borders.
The King said to Guṇavarman,
"The external enemies rely on their strength and wish to invade and insult us."
"If we engage in battle, there will surely be many casualties;
yet if we do not resist, our perilous destruction will soon be upon us. We can only take refuge in the Venerable Master; we know not what other plan to employ.
Guṇavarman said:
"When violent rebels attack one another, it is appropriate to provide defense and protection;
however, you should simply give rise to a mind of compassion and refrain from harboring thoughts of harm.
You, O King, should personally lead your troops to confront them."
As soon as the banners and drums crossed, the rebels retreated and dispersed.
King [Sudhanu] was struck by a stray arrow and wounded in his foot;
Guṇavarman performed a consecration with water to wash it, and after two nights, he was fully restored.
King Gongxin became increasingly earnest in his devotion and desired to leave the household life to cultivate the Way;
he therefore addressed his ministers, saying:
"I wish to personally dwell within the Dharma-gate; you, my ministers, must further select a wise sovereign.
The assembly of ministers all prostrated themselves and entreated him, saying, "If Your Majesty abandons the kingdom, the subjects will have no one to rely upon."
Furthermore, our enemy state is fierce and powerful, relying on its natural defenses as we face them.
If we lose Your Majesty’s compassionate protection, where will the common people find refuge?
Great King, with your heavenly kindness, how could you not pity their lives?
The King, unable to bear stubbornly refusing them, approached his ministers and requested three wishes;
if they were granted, he would remain to govern the kingdom.
His first wish was that all within the realm of his sovereignty should likewise serve the Upādhyāya.
Second, he vowed to completely eliminate all killing within his realm.
Third, he vowed to distribute all his accumulated wealth to relieve the poor and the sick.
The ministers were delighted and unanimously gave their respectful assent.
Thereupon, the entire kingdom followed his example and received the precepts.
Later, the king established a vihāra for Guṇavarman;
while personally leading him to the village, he injured his own big toe.
Guṇavarman further treated him with incantations, and after a short while, he was restored to health.
The fame of his spiritual transformation spread far and wide;
hearing of his reputation, neighboring kingdoms all dispatched envoys to invite him.
At that time, the eminent and virtuous śramaṇas of the capital city of Yangdu, such as Huiguan and Huicong,
held his character and conduct in high esteem from afar and desired to receive his instruction.
Thus, in the ninth month of the first year of the Yuanjia era, they [set out].
He personally petitioned Emperor Wen to invite Guṇavarman;
the Emperor immediately issued an edict to the Governor of Jiaozhou,
ordering him to dispatch a ship to welcome and escort Guṇavarman and his companions.
Furthermore, he dispatched the śramaṇas Fachang, Daochong, Daojun,
and others to that region to offer prayers and petitions, and sent letters to Guṇavarman as well as to King Bhadraka of Java.
He earnestly hoped that [the Master] would deign to visit the borders of Song to propagate the Way of the Buddha.
Guṇavarman, believing that the sacred transformation should be spread widely, did not shrink from traveling to distant lands.
Previously, he had already accompanied the merchant Zhu Nanti on a ship intending to head toward a small kingdom.
Encountering a favorable wind, he eventually arrived at Guangzhou;
thus his surviving writings state:
"Driven by the winds of my past karma, I have come to the borders of Song."
This is what is meant by that.
When Emperor Wen learned that Guṇavarman had already arrived at Nanhai,
he then issued another edict to the provincial and commandery authorities ordering them to provide the necessary provisions for his journey to the capital.
The route began at Shixing, where he stayed for nearly a year.
In Shixing there was Mount Huza;
its form was steep and precipitous, with peaks and ridges rising high and isolated.
Guṇavarman remarked that it resembled Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa),
and thus he renamed it Lingjiu (Vulture Peak).
He then established a separate meditation hall outside the mountain monastery.
The temple was several li away, yet the sound of the chime could not be heard;
whenever the mallet struck, Guṇabhadra had already arrived.
Or, when it rained, he remained untouched by the rain.
Sometimes he walked through mud without getting wet;
at that time, among the assembly of monastics and laypeople, there was none who did not feel solemn awe and increase their reverence.
In the monastery was the Baoyue Hall (Jewel Moon Hall).
On the northern wall of the hall,
Guṇavarman personally painted an image of Rāhula as well as the figure of the youth Megha offering his hair to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara;
after their completion, they emitted light every evening.
After a long time, he finally ceased [his practice].
Cai Muzhi, the Governor of Shixing, held him in profound reverence and admiration.
Later, when Muzhi was about to die, he said:
Guṇavarman went in person to see him, preaching the Dharma and offering consolation.
Later, his family members saw him in a dream,
residing within the monastery and expounding the Dharma to the assembly of monks.
This was truly due to the power of Guṇavarman’s transformative guidance.
This mountain had originally suffered many disasters from tigers;
however, since Guṇavarman resided there, people would travel by day and return at night.
On occasion, when he encountered a tiger, he would press its head with his staff, play with it, and depart.
Consequently, travelers by land and guests by water passed to and fro without obstruction.
Those who were moved by his virtue and returned to the path of transformation numbered seven or eight out of ten.
Guṇavarman once entered meditative absorption in a separate room and did not emerge for several days.
The monks of the monastery sent a novice to inquire after him;
there he saw a white lion standing upon a pillar, its gaze reaching out across the void, while blue lotuses grew profusely all around.
The śrāmaṇera, terrified and shouting, went to pursue the lion, but suddenly saw nothing at all.
Its spiritual manifestations were diverse and beyond measure; most were like this.
