Later, Emperor Wen issued a solemn decree once more, earnestly inviting [Hui]guan and the others.
He then took to the boat and traveled downstream to the capital, arriving at Jianye in the first month of the eighth year of the Yuanjia era.
Emperor Wen received him in audience, greeting him with great warmth and courtesy,
and further remarked:
"I, your disciple, have always desired to observe the fasts and refrain from killing;
however, constrained by the necessity of serving others with my person, I have been unable to follow this aspiration.
Now that the Dharma Master has traveled ten thousand li from afar to transform this land,"
"How will you instruct them?
Guṇavarman replied,
"The Way resides in the mind, not in external affairs."
The Dharma depends on oneself and not on others.
Furthermore, the cultivation practiced by a sovereign and that of a commoner differ; the commoner’s status is lowly and their name insignificant, so their words lack authority.
If they do not discipline themselves and subject their bodies to hardship, what purpose will they serve?
The Emperor takes the four seas as his home and the myriad people as his children.
When he utters a single virtuous word, both men and women rejoice;
when he implements a single benevolent policy, both humans and spirits attain harmony.
When punishments do not cut short life and labor does not exhaust strength,
then wind and rain will arrive at their proper times, cold and warmth will correspond to the seasons,
the hundred grains will flourish, and mulberry and hemp will grow luxuriantly.
If one observes the fast in this manner, the fast itself is truly great;
if one refrains from killing, the merit is likewise vast.
Must one wait until half a day’s meal is omitted and the life of a single bird is fully preserved before it can be considered a grand act of salvation?
The Emperor then leaned on his desk and sighed, saying:
"Ordinary people are deluded by distant principles,
while śramaṇas are hindered by proximate teachings."
Those who are deluded by profound principles treat the ultimate Way as empty talk;
those who are hindered by proximate teachings remain fettered by the literal words of the chapters.
This is just as the Dharma Master Guṇavarman has stated.
Zhen was truly one of awakened understanding and far-reaching insight;
he was worthy of being discussed as a peer in the realm between heaven and humanity.
Consequently, an imperial decree was issued for him to reside at Qihuan Temple, where he was provided with abundant and generous supplies.
Dukes, kings, and eminent scholars all revered and followed him.
Shortly thereafter, he opened a lecture series on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* at the monastery;
on the days of these dharma assemblies, carriages and canopies filled the streets.
As people watched him come and go, they followed one after another in a continuous stream.
Guṇavarman’s spiritual treasury was naturally profound, and his wondrous eloquence was transcendent;
at times, he would converse through an interpreter, yet his responses were intuitively and spontaneously realized.

Guṇavarman immediately translated ten works, including the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, at the Jetavana Monastery; the catalogs of Sengchang and others all state that the *Śīla-sūtra* consists of twenty fascicles. As for the note stating that later disciples produced two additional chapters at Dinglin Temple to form a thirty-fascicle version, this is incorrect.
At present, it consists of only nine fascicles;
some say there are ten.
This is due to an error in transcription, with two characters having been added.
In Sengyou’s catalogue, it is stated that there are only ten fascicles;
thus, we know that other catalogues contain errors in transcription.
Furthermore, according to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan):
When Huiyi of Jetavana requested the translation of the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, he initially obtained twenty-eight chapters.
Later, his disciples continued the work by producing two more chapters, completing the thirty-chapter version.
Fang and others claim that it was subsequently expanded into thirty fascicles, but this is a grave error.
Furthermore, the records of Sengchang and others state that Guṇavarman translated the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* in thirteen fascicles;
however, it is now [known that] it was translated in ten fascicles by Saṃghavarman.
Guṇavarman subsequently completed its twelve [chapters];
this does not mean that Guṇavarman produced a separate translation,
as it is recorded in both locations.
This is also not the case;
it has now been deleted and recorded in the preceding catalogue.
The phrasing and meaning were both detailed and accurate, with no discrepancies between the Sanskrit and the Chinese translation.
At that time, the nuns Huìguǒ, Jìngyīn, and others from Yǐngfú Temple collectively requested Guṇavarman, saying:
"Six years ago, eight nuns arrived from Siṃhala."
Zhi Du said:
"In the land of Song, there have previously never been bhikṣuṇīs.
How could the two assemblies have conferred the precepts? I fear that the categories of the precepts are incomplete."
Guṇavarman said:
"The dharma of the precepts fundamentally originates within the great assembly of monks.
Even if one does not personally attend the ceremony, there is no hindrance to obtaining the precepts."
As was the case with the story of Mahāprajāpatī,
the nuns were again fearful that their years [of ordination] would not be complete and wished to undergo the ceremony once more;
however, Guṇavarman declared:
Excellent! If you truly wish to increase its clarity, I shall most gladly assist you.
However, the nuns of the Western Regions have not yet reached the required seniority in years, nor do they number ten.
Furthermore, she was instructed to learn the Song language.
Subsequently, at the request of a lay devotee from the Western Regions, another foreign nun was invited to arrive so that the number of nuns would be completed to ten.
That summer, she observed the rains retreat at the Lower Dinglin Temple.
At that time, there were believers who gathered flowers to spread upon the seats;
however, the floral colors where Guṇavarman sat were even more brilliant.
The assembly all honored him with rites befitting a sage.

At the end of the summer retreat, he returned to the Jetavana Monastery. On the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month of that year, before his midday meal was finished, he rose first and returned to his chamber.
When his disciples arrived, they found that he had already passed away.
At sixty-five years of age,
before his passing, he composed thirty-six lines of a posthumous literary verse and gāthā,
in which he himself explained the causes and conditions as follows:
Having realized the second fruit [of the path],
he personally sealed the document and entrusted it to his disciple Āśvalāyana,
saying: "After my passing, you may present this text back to the monks of India."
He may also manifest this state to the assembly of monks.
After his passing, he is immediately assisted to sit upon a rope-cot; his countenance shows no change, appearing as if he had entered meditative absorption.
More than a thousand people, both monastics and laypeople, attended;
they all smelled a powerful, fragrant aroma and everyone saw a certain object.
In appearance they were like dragons or snakes, approximately one chi in length;
rising from the side of the corpse, they shot straight up toward the heavens,
such that no one could identify them.
Thereupon, before the ordination platform in the Southern Grove,
he was cremated according to the foreign rites;
the four assemblies gathered like scales, and they piled up fragrant wood to form a pyre.
He was bathed with fragrant oil and cremated;
five-colored flames rose up, their vapors swirling beautifully through the sky.
At that time, the heavens were clear and bright, while both monastics and laypeople lamented in sorrow.
A white stupa was subsequently erected at that site.
When the nuns who wished to receive the precepts again were on the verge of despair, weeping piteously and unable to restrain themselves,
Guṇavarman first arrived during the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, and the Emperor desired to receive the Bodhisattva precepts from him.
Before he had the opportunity to consult with me on these matters, he suddenly passed away.
Because his original intentions were not fulfilled, my grief and regret have become even deeper.

I have therefore ordered the assembly of monks to translate his surviving writings; however, as these writings already exist in circulation, I fear they would be too voluminous, and so I have desisted.
The *Vinayamātṛkā* in ten fascicles; its first fascicle states:

"The *Sarvāstivāda-vinayamātṛkā* was translated at Pínglè Monastery in Mólíng during the first month of the twelfth year of Yuánjiā (the year Yǐhài), and was completed on the twentieth day of the ninth month.
This is recorded in Dàohuì’s *Sòngqí lù* and Sēngyòu’s *Lù*, as well as in the *Zá āpítán xīn lùn*.
The eleven-fascicle version—or one that omits the character *lun*—is also called the *Za apitan jing* (Saṃyuktābhidharma-sūtra). Sengfang calls it the *Za apitan biposha*.

Alternatively, there is a fourteen-fascicle version; this was the fourth translation. It was produced at Changgan Temple in the ninth month of the Jiashu year, the eleventh year of the Yuanjia era, and was completed after one year.
This is seen in Sengyou’s catalogue and in the preface to the scripture, titled *Quanfa zhewang yao* (Essentials for Exhorting Various Kings).
*Gāthā*, one fascicle; composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna. Second appearance in Sengyou’s *Lu* (Catalogue) and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
*Pinfen Yebao Lueji* (A Brief Collection on the Differentiation of Karmic Retribution), one fascicle; composed by Bodhisattva Mahavīra. Also known as *Daiyū Bosatsu Pinfen Yebao Lueji*.
Appears in Sengyou’s *Lu* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. *Qingshengseng Yuwen* (Text for Inviting the Holy Sangha to Bathe), one fascicle; appears in [the aforementioned records].
According to Sengyou’s *Lu* (Catalogue) and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, these five works comprise twenty-four fascicles in total:
the first four works consist of twenty-three fascicles and are extant; the final work consists of one fascicle and is missing.
The śramaṇa Saṃghavarman—
whose name means "Armor of the Multitude" in the Song language—
was a native of India.
Having renounced worldly life in his youth, he was pure and austere, possessing the virtue of the precepts.
He clearly understood the Vinaya-piṭaka and was especially proficient in the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
In the tenth year of the Yuanjia era (the Guiyou year), he traveled on foot from Liusha and arrived at Jianye.
His presence inspired awe and solemnity, such that both monastics and laypeople revered him with wonder;
they all took him as their master and served him, calling him the Tripiṭaka Master. Initially, in the first year of the Jingping era, Xu Sang, the Magistrate of Pinglu, [invited him].
He donated his residence to establish a monastery, which was consequently named Pinglu Temple.
Later, Daochang Huiquan invited Guṇavarman— whose spiritual conduct was pure and complete— to reside at this temple,
providing him with the highest offerings to manifest his own reverence for his virtue.
Guṇavarman together with others supervised the construction of the three tiers of the stupa;
they practiced the Way and recited scriptures day and night without ceasing.
The monastic community gathered there, and the influence of the Dharma spread far and wide.
The Tripitaka Master, who possessed a profound understanding of the precepts,
was about to administer the full ordination again to the nun Huiguo and others at Yingfu Temple when the two assemblies were not yet complete;
at that time, the Tripitaka Master passed away.
Shortly thereafter, the Bhikṣuṇīs Tiṣyā and others arrived from Siṃhala.
The assembly then collectively requested Guṇavarman to serve as their preceptor and succeed the Tripiṭaka masters.
At that time, Huiyi of Jetavana was prominent in the capital, yet he was regarded as being pretentiously eccentric.
Their convictions differed, and Huiyi opposed Guṇavarman with repeated reversals of argument;
yet Guṇavarman established his thesis, elucidated the principles of the Dharma, and provided proofs that were clear and convincing.
Consequently, Huiyi turned from his rigid narrowness and submitted with total deference.
He then led his disciples to receive the teachings and accept the precepts;
several hundred monks and nuns received them.
Liu Yikang, the Prince of Pengcheng of the Song dynasty, honored him as a model of monastic discipline and extensively provided offerings for vegetarian feasts.

The fourfold assembly was so vast that it swelled the capital cities; at that time, renowned and virtuous great monks such as Hui-guan, noting that Guṇavarman had an exquisite understanding of the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* and could recite it with complete mastery, [invited him].
Although the Tripitaka Master had previously translated it, he had not yet had it transcribed.
In the ninth month of the eleventh year, at Changgan Temple,
he gathered scholars and requested that it be produced once more.
Ratnamegha translated the words,
while [the author] himself observed as he took them down in writing;
after a year of meticulous collation and refinement, the work was finally completed.
He subsequently produced five works in total, including the *Mātṛkā*.
With the propagation of the Dharma as his primary aim, Guṇavarman did not remain in any single location;
having completed his mission of transmitting the scriptures, he was about to return to his native land.
The multitude all entreated him, but none could detain him.
In the nineteenth year of the Yuanjia era,
he returned to his native country aboard a merchant ship from the Western Regions.
The end of this work is not detailed.
*The Scripture of the Lion’s Roar of Queen Śrīmālā on the Great Expedient Means of the One Vehicle*, one fascicle;
the second edition, identical in substance to the assembly with Queen Śrīmālā in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, produced on the fourteenth day of the eighth month in the thirteenth year of the Yuanjia era.
The *Ratnamegha-sūtra* (Great Vaipulya Jewel Casket Sutra) in three fascicles was translated by Baoyun of Danyang County; Huiquan transcribed it and also composed the preface.

It is recorded in the catalogs of Daohui, Sengyou, and Li Kuò. It is also found as a four-fascicle version, or sometimes as two fascicles, which is the same text as the *Mañjuśrī-vikurvāṇa-ratnakara-sūtra*, according to the record of Li Kuò. It corresponds to the *Anupūrva-vimokṣa-bhūmi-pāramitā*.

The *Liaoyi jing* (Sūtra on the Definitive Meaning), in one or two fascicles, also titled the *Jieliaoyi jing* (Sūtra Explaining the Definitive Meaning) or simply the *Xiangxu jietuo jing* (Sūtra on the Liberation of the Continuum), was produced at Dong’an Temple.
It comprises the final two chapters of the *Shenmi jing* (Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra).

According to the four catalogs by Jie Hui, Sengyou, Li Kuò, and Fashang, as well as the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks), it was produced in Jingzhou. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* [was likewise produced there].
The *Luo bao jing* (Sūtra of the Jewel Net), four fascicles; the second [version] produced at Daochang Monastery in the second year of the Yuanjia era, with Hui guan taking the dictation.
It is the same text as the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and the *Mahāyāna-laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.

According to the records of Sengyou, Fahu, and others in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, it was discovered in Danyang Commandery. It contains the "Chapter on the Divine Power of the Bodhisattva’s Practice of Skillful Means."

*The Sūtra on Pervasive Transformations*, three fascicles; first translated, it shares the same original text as the *Mahāsāṃghika-śākyaputrīya-nirgrantha-sūtra*, though some versions lack the word "realm" (*viṣaya*).
Recorded by Li Kuò. *The Sūtra of the Six Glories of the Old Mother*, one fascicle; also called the *Sūtra of the Old Mother*.
Third translation, sharing the same original text as the *Sūtra of the Old Woman*, etc. Fáng says it was seen in a separate record (*bielu*) as the version by Shēnrì.
One fascicle; alternatively called the *Śen-er-ben* (Shen'er Edition), it is the third appearance [of this text] and is the same version as that of Candraprabha Kumāra.
The Library records state that it was seen in the *Bie-lu* (Separate Record), which notes that the *Shen-dou-ben* (Shendou Edition) is erroneous.
One fascicle, the *Ānanda-mukha-nihārita-sūtra*; alternatively called the sixth translation of the *Anantamukha-parivarta*, it is the same text as the *Anantamukha-praveśa-rahasya*.

The claim that the *Dhāraṇī-sūtra* (Holding the Sūtra) is identical to the *Benfang* (Original Chamber) is an error; it appears in the *Bielu* (Separate Record) and is recorded separately in the *Fanglu* (Chamber Record).

Regarding the *Wuliangmen chijing* (Sūtra on the Holding of the Immeasurable Gate), it is stated in the *Daoci*, *Sengyou*, *Fashang*, and other records, as well as in the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks), that the four-fascicle *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* was produced at Daochang Temple.
Furthermore, the *Gaoseng zhuan* states that the two-fascicle *Mahābherī-hāraka-sūtra* (Great Drum Sūtra) was produced at Xin Temple in Jingzhou.
One fascicle of the *Dajiyijing* (Great Meaning Sutra), with a preface by Daohui; four catalogs [of this work] exist, including those by Sengyou and Li Kuō.
One fascicle of the *Shi'outouhuojing* (Sutra on Twelve Dhūtas), according to the catalog of Baochang.
One fascicle of the *Shutiqiejing* (Sutra of Jyotiṣka), according to the catalog of Baochang. Fifty fascicles of the *Za ahan jing* (Saṃyukta Āgama), translated at Waguan Temple.

The *Fǎngbě Fǎyuàn Jīláigāosēngzhuàn* (Biographies of Eminent Monks Compiled by Dharma Master Fǎyuàn of the Fǎngbǎ Temple) states that the *Yǒnghùjīng* (Śukarika-sūtra), one scroll, also known as the *Dōutiáojīng*, appeared at Qìhuán Temple;
it is an alternative translation of the forty-fourth sutra in the *Zhōngāhán* (Madhyama Āgama).
Fáng [Xuan] notes that it is found in the *Biélu* (Separate Catalog). Furthermore, the *Bīmósùjīng* (Vimāna-vastu-sūtra), one scroll, appears in the forty-fourth [sutra] of the *Zhōngāhán*.
Fifty-seventh: A different translation (yìyì) titled *The Scripture on the Appearance of Four Persons in the World* (Jiàn biélù sìrén chūxiàn shìjiān jīng), one fascicle;

found in the eighteenth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*. The section on different translations notes that it is seen in a separate record. Fifty-eighth: *The Scripture on Eleven Contemplations and Mindfulness of the Tathāgata* (Shíyī xiǎngsì niànrúlái jīng), one fascicle;
alternatively titled *The Scripture on Eleven Contemplations and Recollection of the Tathāgata* (Shíyī sīwéi niànrúlái jīng). It is found in the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

Forty-eighth: The first translation, the *Āśujāta-sūtra* (阿遬達經) in one fascicle, is recorded in the *Bie lu* (別錄); Changfang says he saw it there. The third translation is identical in text to the *Yujie jing* (玉耶經) and others;

Changfang says he saw it in the *Bie lu*. The fourth translation is the *Past and Present Cause and Effect Sūtra* (*Guoxi zaineng yinguo jing*) in four fascicles, produced at Xin Temple in Jingzhou; Changfang says he saw it there.
The sixth translation is the same as the *Xiuxing benqi jing* (修行本起經) and the *Ruixing benqi jing* (瑞應本起經).

Identical to the original cataloging by Shi Xing, Li Kuo, Sengyou, and others: *The Scripture on Mahākāśyapa Delivering a Poor Woman*, one fascicle; [Seng]fang says it is seen in the *Separate Catalog*.
*The Scripture on the Twelve Categories of Birth and Death*, one fascicle; [Seng]fang says it is seen in the *Separate Catalog*.

*The Scripture on the Retribution of Sin and Merit*, one fascicle—also known as the *Scripture on the Retribution of Sin and Merit through Transmigration in the Five Paths*; likewise [seen in the *Separate Catalog*].

The *Yun lun zhuan wudao jing* (Cloud Wheel Turning Five Realms Sutra), also known as the *Wudao lun jing* (Five Realms Wheel Sutra), was translated by [Dharmarakṣa] together with his disciple Buddhyayaśas.

According to Sengyou’s record, it is found in the *Bie lu* (Separate Record) and the twelve-fascicle *Zongshi fen apitan lun* (Saṃgītiparyāya-Abhidharma-śāstra)—some editions omit the character "lun" (treatise).

It was first produced as a text identical in content to the *Pinlei zu lun* (Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra) translated during the Tang dynasty. Sengyou’s catalog does not specify its place of origin. It consists of four chapters on the awakening of dharmas (*juefa*).
One fascicle; alternatively, it lacks the word "sūtra. Fang says he saw it in the *Bie lu* (Separate Record):
*The Sūtra Spoken by Piṇḍola-Bharadvāja for King Udayana*, one fascicle; also called *The Sūtra on Piṇḍola Preaching the Dharma for the King*.
Fang says he saw it in the *Bie lu*. [The preceding section] seen to the left is missing thereafter. *The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha*, one fascicle; this is the second edition.
The *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra* translated by Buddhayaśas during the Yao Qin dynasty has the same text as that found in the separate catalogues;
the *Anantārtha-sūtra*, one fascicle, first appeared with the version translated by Dharmagatayaśas during the Xiao Qi dynasty and is seen to have the same text according to Li Kuò’s record;
the *Sarvadharmācāra-sūtra*, one fascicle, is the second appearance of the text, identical to that produced by Kumārajīva.
The two-fascicle version and the *Dharmapada-mūla-abhāva-sūtra* share the same base text. Fang says he saw it in the *Bielu*.

There is also a one-fascicle *Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, sometimes without the word "smaller. This second translation is the same base text as Kumārajīva’s *Amitābha* and the Tang translation of the *Praise of the Pure Land*.
It was translated during the Xiaojian era; it is also known as the *Amitābha*, and Daohui and Sengyou both record its existence.
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) states that it was translated at Jingzhou; however, its separate appearance in the *Amitābha Sūtra* is an error.

One fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Eight Auspicious Ones* (*Ba jixiang jing*), the third translation, is identical in origin to Zhi Qian’s *Eight Auspicious Dhāraṇī* and Dharmarakṣa’s *Eight Yang Divine Dhāraṇī Sūtra*.
It was produced on the third day of the first month in the twenty-ninth year of the Yuanjia era at the city of Jingzhou.
Internally, Liu Yixuan, the Prince of Nanqiao and Minister of Works (Sikong) for Jingzhou, produced [this version] on the sixth day.
It is recorded that it is identical to the one-volume *Dharmadhātuparyantadhāraṇī-sūtra* found in the two catalogs compiled by Sengyou and Baochang;

it is the same text as the second edition produced by Shengjian and the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* requested by the Bodhisattva Uṣṇīṣa. Fáng states that he saw it in the *Bièlù* (Separate Record), noting that the poor man required it.
The *Rai jing* (Lai jing), one fascicle; the fourth translation, which is the same text as those translated by Bo Yan, Zhi Qian, and others, according to the Li Kuò lu.
The *Xiànzài fó míng jīng* (Sūtra of the Names of Present Buddhas), three fascicles, also titled *Huāfū xiànzài fó míng* (Flower-Spreading Sūtra of the Names of Present Buddhas);
the second translation, which is the same text as the *Chēngyáng zhū fó gōngdé jīng* (Sūtra of Praising the Merits of All Buddhas) and others. January 20th, the twenty-ninth year of Yuánjiā.
In the seventh month, at Jingzhou, he produced the *Shixing lu* (Record of the Beginning of Success) for the Prince of Nanqiao; the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks);
and the three-fascicle *Jingdu sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Pure Attainment), the third production, as recorded in the *Li kuolu lu* (Record of Li Kuoluo).

He also translated the one-fascicle *Wuyouwang jing* (Sūtra of King Aśoka) at Xin Temple in Jingzhou, as seen in the *Wu lu* (Record of Wu) and the *Sengyou lu* (Record of Sengyou). Furthermore, there is the one-fascicle *Benxing liuboluomi jing* (Sūtra of the Six Pāramitās of Original Conduct).

Fáng says he saw in the *Bielù* (Separate Catalog): *Qīchù sānguān jīng* (Sūtra on the Seven Places and Three Contemplations) in one fascicle—some versions lack the characters "yìchù" (different places)—a variant translation of the *Zá āhán jīng* (Saṃyukta Āgama).

Fáng says he saw in the *Bielù*: *Zá zàng jīng* (Saṃyukta Piṭaka Sūtra) in one fascicle; its fourth [section] appears as the same text as the *Guǐwèn mùlián jīng* (Sūtra of the Ghost’s Questioning of Maudgalyāyana).
Fáng says he saw in the *Bielù*: *Mùlián jiàng lóngwáng jīng* (Sūtra of Maudgalyāyana Subduing the Dragon King) in one fascicle.

Some versions lack the character "Wáng" (King), while others are titled *Jiànglóng jīng* (Sutra on Subduing Dragons) or *Jiànglóngwáng jīng* (Sutra on Subduing Dragon Kings). This second edition shares the same source as the *Lóngwáng xiongdi* (Dragon King Brothers).
Fáng says he saw it in the *Bièlù* (Separate Record); it is also called the *Nánjīng* (Sutra of Difficulties), one fascicle; another calls it the *Yuènánjīng* (Sutra of Overcoming Difficulties).
This third edition shares the same source as the *Niè Chéngyuǎn Yuènánjīng* (Nie Chengyuan’s Sutra of Overcoming Difficulties). Fáng says he saw it in the *Bièlù*; it explains the six [categories].
*The Sūtra on the Twelve Views*, four fascicles; Fang says it is seen in the *Bie lu*. *The Record of Dao Yu* says it is one fascicle.
*The Sūtra Requesting the Bhikṣu Paṇḍita*, one fascicle; sometimes written as *Paṇḍi* or also as *Paṇḍi*; Fang says it is seen in the *Bie lu*.

*The Sūtra on the Twelve Dhūtas*, two fascicles; Fang says it is seen in the *Bie lu*. *The Sūtra on Āniruddha’s Chapter on the Seven Mindfulnesses*, one fascicle; Fang says [it is seen in the *Bie lu*].
The *Jian bielu shibao fa san tong lue jing* (One fascicle), which Fang says is seen in the *Bieliu*;
the *Liu zhai bajie jing* (One fascicle), which Fang says is seen in the *Bieliu*;
the *Alanya xichan jing* (One fascicle), the third edition of which is the same text as Kumārajīva’s *Zuochan sanmei jing*, according to Li Kuò’s record; and the *Pusa heyu jing* (One fascicle).
Scroll Three. The first edition, which is the same text as that produced by Kumārajīva, is recorded in the *Fáng* (Chamber) catalog as being seen in the *Bièlù* (Separate Record);

it is the one-scroll *Nàxiān jīng* (Nagasena Sūtra). The second edition is the same text as the two-scroll version; the *Fáng* catalog records it as being seen in the *Bièlù*. The third edition is the one-scroll *Shí'èryóu jīng* (Sūtra of the Twelve Wanderings).

The *Fáng* catalog records it as being seen in the old records. Also included is the one-scroll *Dìyīyì wǔxiàng lüèjí* (Brief Collection of the Five Characteristics of the Primary Meaning), located in the East.
The *Sengyou lu* (Catalogue of Sengyou) and the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks) record that [these texts] were recovered from Xin Temple in Jingzhou:
fifty-two sections totaling one hundred thirty-four fascicles from the *Bin-tou-lu shang* (Upper Section on Piṇḍola), of which twenty-six sections totaling one hundred fascicles are currently extant,
while twenty-six sections totaling thirty-four fascicles from the *Xukongzang xia* (Lower Section on Ākāśagarbha) are missing.
The śramaṇa Guṇabhadra— translated into the Song language as Gōngdéxián (Merit-Worthy)—
was a native of Central India.
Because he studied the Mahāyāna, he was known in the world as Mahāyāna.
He was originally of Brahmin descent;
in his youth, he studied the various treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
He was extensively proficient in astronomy, mathematics, medicine, incantations,
and arts; later, upon encountering and reading the *Samyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*,
he was struck with realization and thereafter revered the Buddha-dharma deeply.
His family had followed the traditions of the world-renunciants and strictly prohibited [the presence of] śramaṇas;
consequently, he left his home and went into hiding to seek out a master from afar.
He then shaved his head, changed his attire, and devoted himself single-mindedly to his studies.
Having received full ordination, he became extensively versed in the Tripiṭaka.
He was compassionate, harmonious, respectful, and obedient, serving his teacher with utmost diligence.
After some time, he took leave of his teacher of the Hīnayāna to advance his studies in the Mahāyāna.
The Mahayana master tested him by having him reach into a case of scriptures;
he immediately retrieved the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
The master rejoiced and sighed in admiration, saying:
"You possess a profound karmic affinity for the Mahāyāna.
Consequently, none were able to challenge you when you read, recited, and expounded its meanings.
You have further received the Bodhisattva precepts."
He then presented a letter to his parents, urging them to return to the True Dharma, saying:
"If you persist solely in following external paths,
then even if I return, it will be of no benefit."
"If you take refuge in the Triple Gem,
we shall long behold one another.
His father, moved by these sincere words, subsequently abandoned heterodoxy and followed the Right Path.
Bhadra proceeded forward to the various kingdoms of Siṃhala,
where he was provided with travel provisions and offerings by all.
Having established a connection with the eastern regions, he continued his journey.
He then boarded a merchant vessel and sailed across the sea;
midway through the journey, the wind ceased,
and their supply of fresh water was later exhausted.
The entire ship was filled with anxiety and fear.
Guṇabhadra said,
"You should unite your minds and join your strength to recollect the Buddhas of the ten directions and invoke Avalokiteśvara."
There was nowhere he went that he did not move others to faith;
he then secretly recited dharani sutras and performed repentance rites with utmost sincerity.
Suddenly, a favorable wind blew in violently.
Dense clouds gathered and rain fell, so that the entire ship was saved;
such was the power of his sincere resonance.
On the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era, the year of Yihai, he arrived at Guangzhou.
At that time, the Provincial Governor Che Lang submitted a memorial to report the matter.
Emperor Wen dispatched an envoy to welcome him,
and he arrived at the capital, Yangdu.
The Emperor issued an edict for the eminent monks Huiyan and Huiguan to receive him with ceremonial hospitality at Xinting;
their spirits were so clear and penetrating that all were filled with reverent devotion, even though they had to communicate through interpreters.
He greeted him with such joy as if meeting an old friend under a roadside canopy.
He initially resided at Zhihuan Temple,
where Emperor Wen invited him and showed him the deepest reverence.
Yan Yanzhi of Langya,
a man of versatile talent and profound learning, girded his belt and arrived at the gate.
Thereupon, from near and far throughout the capital of Yangdu, carriages and capes followed one after another.
The Grand General, Prince of Pengcheng, Yikang,
and the Chancellor, Prince of Nanqiao, Yixuan,
both served him as their teacher.
Shortly thereafter, the community of monks collectively requested that he produce a translation of a sutra.
At the Jetavana Monastery, they assembled various monks specializing in the study of doctrine,
and he translated the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
The *Dharmadundubhi-sūtra* was brought forth at Dong’an Temple;
later, at Danyang Commandery, he translated the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
His disciples numbered more than seven hundred.
Baoyun transmitted the translation while Huiquan took up the brush;
through repeated consultation and inquiry, they perfectly captured the original intent.
Later, when Prince Xiao was stationed in Jingzhou, he invited [the Master] to accompany him.
He settled there at Xin Temple and further renovated its halls and chambers.

It was at Xin Temple that [the Master] produced translations of various sutras, including the *Sutra on the Causes and Effects of King Aśoka in the Past and Present*, the *Shorter Aparimitāyur-jñāna Sūtra*, the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*, the *Sutra on the Names of Buddhas of the Present*, the *Paramārtha-śūnyatā Sūtra*, and the *Aṣṭamaṅgalaka Sūtra*.
Including those previously mentioned, there were fifty-two works in total.
Most of these were transmitted and propagated by his disciple Fayong.
Prince Qiao wished to invite him to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other scriptures.
Bhadra, however, reflected that she was not yet proficient in the Song language and felt deep regret for many days.
She immediately performed prostrations and repentance morning and night, entreating for a response from the unseen realm.
One night, she dreamed of a person dressed in white, holding a sword and carrying a human head, who came before her and said:
"Why are you grieving?
Bhadra related the matter in full.
He replied:
Without much sorrow,
he immediately exchanged his head for a sword and replaced it with a new one.
He spoke to him, instructing him to turn back, saying,
"Are you not in pain?
He replied:
He was not in pain.
Suddenly, he felt his mind and spirit filled with joy.
When he arose at dawn, his understanding of the meanings of the teachings became thorough, and he fully mastered the Song language.
Thereupon, the lecture commenced.
The disciple Fayong served as the oral translator,
while Sengnian acted as the presiding lecturer (dugang).
Although the profound understanding was achieved through the mediation of translators,
toward the end of the Yuanjia era, Prince Xiao of Qiao had frequent strange dreams.
Guṇabhadra said:
Calamity and disorder were about to break out within the capital;
before a year had passed, two villains plotted rebellion.
Furthermore, at the beginning of the Xiaojian era, when Prince Qiao conspired in secret, Guṇabhadra’s countenance was filled with sorrow and distress, yet he did not speak a word.
The Prince of Qiao asked him the reason for this.
Guṇabhadra remonstrated with him earnestly and, shedding tears as he departed, said:
"I have no hope at all; I shall not accompany you as your retinue."
Because the Prince of Qiao was trusted by the people’s sentiments,
he coerced [Hui] to go down with him.
At the defeat at Liangshan, the fire ships closed in from all sides.
The shore was so far away that it seemed impossible to reach;
he could do nothing but single-mindedly invoke Avalokiteśvara,
grasping a bamboo staff in his hand as he threw himself into the river.
The water reached his knees; he prodded the water with a staff and found it to be deep and the current swift.
He saw a young boy following behind him and pulled him back by the hand.
Looking at the boy, he said:
"How can you, a mere child, cross over me?
In that moment of dazed confusion, he realized he had already walked some ten paces and had thus reached the shore.
He immediately removed his inner robe to reward the youth, but upon looking around, he could not find it;
his hair stood on end with horror as he finally realized it was due to supernatural power.
At that time, General Xuanmu was supervising the army at Liangshan.
Emperor Xiaowu (r. 373–396), whose personal name was Jun, issued an edict to the military command stating:
"Should you find any Mahāyāna [texts], treat them with special care and send them to the Palace by courier.
Shortly thereafter, they were found and transported to the capital on a fleet of boats.
Emperor Xiaowu immediately summoned him for an audience and questioned him in detail,
saying, "I have long looked forward to this, and only now do we meet.
Guṇabhadra replied:
Having already been defiled by transgressions and reduced to ashes and powder, I have now been granted the honor of an audience;
I am deeply grateful for this life-giving creation. I submit this in response to Your Majesty’s inquiry.
"And who is the thief?
He replied,
"A person who has left the household life does not participate in military affairs."
However, Zhang Chang, Zong Lingxiu, and others were all pressuring me;
what I have clarified is that I did not anticipate meeting such a situation due to past karmic conditions.
Emperor Xiaowu said:
He had nothing to fear.
On that day,
he was commanded to reside in the Rear Hall.
He provided clothing and offerings to those who came to him as human vehicles.
Initially, when Baotuo resided in Jingzhou for ten years,
every letter and correspondence he exchanged with Prince Qiao was recorded without exception.
When the army was defeated, a thorough investigation was conducted, yet not a single word concerning military affairs was found [in his records].
Emperor Xiaowu, recognizing his pure integrity, treated him with even greater courtesy and honor.
Later, during a casual conversation, the Emperor jokingly asked:
"Do you not think of the Chancellor?
He replied,
"Having received his offerings for ten years, how could I forget his virtue?"
"I now follow Your Majesty;
I beg you to grant me the wish to burn incense for the Chancellor for three years.
The Emperor’s countenance moved with sorrowful emotion, and he granted the request out of a sense of righteousness.
When Zhongxing Temple was completed,
an imperial decree ordered him to move there,
and three rooms were opened for his residence.
Later, at a banquet held in the Eastern Palace,
where princes and dukes had all assembled,
an imperial decree was issued for Guṇabhadra to have an audience.
At that time, his hair had not yet been cleansed, and his white head was brilliantly radiant.
Emperor Xiaowu gazed at him from afar and, turning to the Minister of the Interior, Xie Zhuang, said,
"Mahāyāna is intelligent and possesses keen understanding, yet the period of old age has already arrived."
"I shall test him;
he will surely perceive my intent.
When Guṇabhadra ascended the steps, [the Emperor] greeted him, saying:
Mahāyāna did not fail the purpose of his long journey;
however, there was still one thing remaining.
He immediately replied in response:
This poor monk has returned from afar to the imperial capital for nearly thirty years.
I feel boundless gratitude and shame for the Emperor’s gracious favor.
Although he was seventy years old and afflicted by illness, he remained solely focused on death.
The Emperor praised his eloquence and wit, issuing an imperial decree to invite him to sit in the presence of the throne.
The entire court turned their eyes toward him in admiration.
Later, he established a monastery west of the Phoenix Pavilion in the realm of Pāṭaliputra.
Every time it reached midnight, there would suddenly be someone knocking on the door and calling out;
though they looked for the person, no one was seen, and the assembly frequently suffered from nightmares.
Bhadra burned incense and made this prayer:
"By your karmic affinity from past lives, you dwell here;
I now erect this temple to practice the Way and perform rites of repentance."
I have always acted for your sake;
as for those who dwell here, they are the guardian deities of the monastery.
Since they cannot remain here, let each go wherever they find comfort.
Shortly thereafter, more than ten monastics and laypeople alike dreamed on the same night that thousands of ghosts and spirits were carrying the temple away upon their shoulders.
Consequently, the community of the monastery became peaceful.
In the seventh year of the Daming era, a severe drought occurred throughout the realm.
He had prayed to the mountains and rivers for months without effect.
The Emperor then requested that he pray for rain with the certainty that a response would be felt;
he added that if it proved ineffective, they need not meet again.
Bhadra replied,
"I rely upon the Three Jewels and the celestial majesty of Your Majesty."
I hope that grace will surely descend;
if there is no result, I shall not see you again.
He then went at once to the Fishing Terrace at Beihu to burn incense and offer prayers.
He no longer took food or drink;
silently reciting the sutras and secretly adding secret mantras,
at the hour of *bhu* (the afternoon) on the following day, clouds first arose from the northwest corner like a carriage canopy.
The sun was setting behind the mulberry trees as winds shook and clouds gathered, and it rained continuously for several days.
On the following morning, the high officials entered to offer congratulations and consolation.
By imperial decree, he was granted audiences for comfort and encouragement, with gifts and alms bestowed upon him in succession.
From his youth until the end of his life, Bhadra maintained a vegetarian diet;
he constantly held an incense burner, never letting it leave his hand,
and whenever he finished a meal, he would set aside a portion to feed the birds.
Birds would gather at his hands to take the food.
During the reign of Emperor Ming, the offerings and veneration became even more abundant.
In the first month of the fourth year of the Taishi era, he perceived that his physical condition was unwell.
He then took leave in advance of Emperor Ming and the high officials.
On the day of his passing, he gazed out into the distance with a lingering look and said:
He saw celestial flowers and sacred images,
and passed away at the hour of Youzhong (the fifth watch).
He was seventy-five years of age.
Emperor Ming was deeply grieved and lamented him, bestowing lavish funeral gifts.
The high officials assembled for the burial,
and both honor and mourning were fully observed.

The *Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* (or *Banniehuan jing*), one fascicle—sometimes without the character "ban"—was translated at Xin Temple in the first year of the Xiaojian era (454 CE) by Daohui; it appears in the *Song Qi Lu*. Upon examining the preceding and following passages of this single-fascicle *Nirvāṇa*, they do not seem to be the translation of Dharmabhadra, but rather appear to be the translation of Guṇavarman and others. Having now located a two-fascicle version, I have provisionally appended it to the catalog of the Eastern Jin. The *Śikhin-māṇava-mūla-sūtra*, one fascicle, was translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. The *Zi-shu-yu*, one fascicle, was composed by the Tripiṭaka Master himself and is not of Indic origin; therefore, it has also been deleted.
The *Sūtra on Choosing Among Evil Worlds in the Future* and the *Sūtra on Past Practice of the Dānapāramitā*—
these two sūtras are both derived from the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The *Sūtra on Killing a Dragon to Relieve a Nation* is derived from the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya*.
The *Sangoku enkyō* (Scripture on the Conditions of the Three Countries) is excerpted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
The *Sanshō kikyō* (Scripture on the Three Minor Kalpas) is excerpted from the *Loutan jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra).
The *Butsu nyū kanro chō shōi kyō* (Scripture on the Buddha Entering the Ambrosia to Regulate and Rectify the Mind) is excerpted from the *Da jūnimon kyō* (Mahādvāraśataka-sūtra).
The *Araṇavibhaṅga-sūtra* appears in the *Madhyama Āgama*; the *Śāriputrādi-bhikṣu-kāyāsākṣātkriyāprāpti-sūtra* appears in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
There are also the *Nārada-sūtra* and the *Sūtra on the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel Cast into the Ocean*.
The Sutra on Uncle and Nephew;
the Śāriputra-parinirvāṇa-sūtra;
and the Sutra on Becoming an Ox Due to Debt.
The *Ruler and Minister Sūtra* (Jūnshin kyō), the six sūtras on the simultaneous arising of the world (*Shusseikyō*),
the *Four Kinds of Food Sūtra* (*Shishikkyō*) from the *Miscellaneous Compilation of the Hīnayāna* (*Shōjō zasshō*),
and the *Ānanda Weeps at Seeing Music and Performance: The Sūtra on Impermanence* (*Anan kenkigaku teiku mujōkyō*).
The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Visit to Console Kāśyapa While He Was Ill;
the Sūtra on the Buddha Commanding Ānanda to Visit the Householder Jyeṣṭha;
and the Sūtra of the Two Arrogant Men.

The *Maudgalyāyana-bhrātṛ-dāna-āśā-pratyupakāra-sūtra* (目連弟布施望即報經) and the five preceding sūtras were all translated from the *Udānavarga* (出曜經), the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* (般泥洹經), and other texts, totaling twenty-three sections in twenty-three fascicles.
Alternatively, it may have been transcribed from a separate copy,
or perhaps it was not produced by Buddhabhadra;
now, this is recorded as it truly is.
Therefore, these have been deleted in their entirety. *Zhenyuan xinding shijiao mulu*, Volume Seven.
*Zhenyuan xinding shijiao mulu*, Volume Eight.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xīmíng Monastery in the Western Capital.
*General Catalogue of Collected Scriptures*, Volume One, Part Eight.

*The Scripture on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva* (one fascicle), also known as *The Scripture on the Vow of Avalokiteśvara*. This third edition is identical in text to that translated by Dharmarakṣa and Dàozhēn during the Western Jìn dynasty. It is recorded in the catalogues of Wángzōng, Sēngyòu, Lǐkuò, Fǎshàng, and others, as well as in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. This one work, consisting of one fascicle, is currently extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Fayong was named Dharmodgata;
his original surname was Li.
He was a native of Huanglong Commandery in Youzhou.
Having become a śrāmaṇera in his youth, he practiced asceticism;
because he observed the precepts and recited the sūtras, he was held in high esteem by his teacher.
I have heard that the monks Faxian and Baoyun personally traveled to the Buddha-lands; moved by their example,
they made a solemn vow to disregard their own lives, and thus,
at the beginning of the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty, they set forth.
He summoned twenty-five fellow śramaṇas, including Sengtan and Langzhi,
and they together brought along banners, canopies, and other articles for making offerings.
Setting out from the northern lands, he traveled far to the Western Regions.
Upon first arriving at the kingdom of Henan, he then departed for Haixi Commandery;
proceeding further into the shifting sands, he reached Gaochang Commandery.
Having traveled through the various kingdoms of Kucha and Kashgar,
he previously ascended the Pamir Mountains and the Snowy Mountains;
the plank paths were so perilous and treacherous that neither mules nor horses could pass.
Layered ice rises high and steep, utterly devoid of grass or trees;
the mountains abound with miasmic vapors.
Below flows a great river, deep and swift as an arrow.
Ropes were fastened between the flanks of the eastern and western mountains to form a bridge;
as they were extremely distant apart, ten people had to pass across at once.
Once they reached the opposite shore, they raised smoke as a signal.
Those who come later see the smoke and know that the previous person has already crossed over, so they can proceed further.
If they do not see smoke for a long time,
they know that a violent wind blew the rope away and the person fell into the river.
After traveling for three days across the Pamir Range, he finally crossed it and ascended the Snow Mountains.
There, precipitous cliffs rose sheer like walls, leaving no place to set foot;
on the stone faces, there were ancient arrow-holes facing one another at every turn.
Each person held four spears;
first they pulled out the lower spear and grasped the upper one with their hands, passing them along in succession as they waited for one another.
Only after three days had passed did they reach level ground.
While waiting for and searching for his companions, twelve people were lost.
He proceeded to the kingdom of Kaśmīra, where he paid homage to the Buddha’s alms bowl and stayed for over a year.
Having completed his study of the Brāhmī script, he then mastered the Sanskrit language.
He obtained one fascicle of the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* in Sanskrit.

Together with thirteen other fellow śramaṇas, including Wujie, they traveled west to the Sindhu River (translated here as "Lion’s Mouth"); following the river's course to the west, they entered the kingdom of Yuezhi.
He paid homage to the Buddha’s *uṣṇīṣa* bone and beheld his own wooden boat that had floated up by itself;
subsequently, he arrived at the Shiliu Monastery on the southern side of Mount Dantaka.
More than three hundred monks resided there, studying the various vehicles of the Three Vehicles.
Wujie then stayed at this monastery to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The Indian śramaṇa Buddhatāra—translated here as "Awakening Savior"—and the assembly of monks from that region said:
Once he had attained the fruits of the Path,
Wujie requested him to be his *upādhyāya*,
while the Chinese śramaṇa Zhiding served as his *ācārya*.
He spent the three-month summer retreat at the monastery;
then, traveling northward day by day, he reached Central India.
In these vast and desolate regions, he constantly carried rock honey as his provisions.
His eight companions perished on the road.
Five of them traveled together and repeatedly encountered perilous difficulties;
however, Bodhisattva Wujie maintained single-minded devotion to his recitation of the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra.
As he proceeded through the kingdom of Śrāvastī,
he encountered a herd of wild elephants in the wilderness;
Sudhana called out their names and took refuge in them.
Immediately, a lion emerged from the forest,
and the elephant fled in terror.
Later, while crossing the Ganges, he encountered a herd of wild oxen coming toward him with bellowing roars, intending to harm him.
Wujie took refuge [in the Buddha] as before; immediately, a large vulture flew down.
The wild oxen were startled and dispersed, and he thus escaped harm.
That his sincere heart moved [the divine] such that he was delivered from danger amidst perilous circumstances is always of this kind.
Later, he traveled by ship across the South Sea from South India and arrived at Guangzhou;
his deeds during these travels are recorded in a separate biography.
In the final years of the Yuanjia era, he reached the capital of Yangdu.
He personally translated the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* in one fascicle,
which is still transmitted in the world today.
His final whereabouts are unknown.
The *Sūtra on Maitreya’s Ascent to Tuṣita Heaven* (one fascicle), also known as the *Maitreya’s Ascent Sūtra*, is recorded in the *Records of Daohui* and the *Monastic Records of Song and Qi*.
According to the *Monastic Records*, it was first translated in Gaochang Commandery and subsequently brought back [to China].
The *Sūtra of King Mahāgovinda* (one fascicle); its initial title was also *Mahāgovinda and Govinda Sūtra*, which corresponds to the *Jayaśrī Sūtra* translated during the Tang dynasty.

The *Rājan-sūtra* and the *Sūryadevaputra-sūtra* share the same original text; the Fangyuan zhu jing mu (Catalogue of Scriptures Compiled by the Court) notes that they are seen in the *Bie lu* (Separate Record).

There is one fascicle of the *Zhanchanbing biyao jing* (Secret Essentials for Treating the Illnesses of Dhyāna), also called the *Zhanchanbing biyao fa* (Secret Methods for Treating the Illnesses of Dhyāna) without the character "jing" (sūtra), or the *Chan yao mimi zhilibing jing* (Sūtra on the Secret Treatment of Illnesses through the Essentials of Dhyāna);
it is either in two fascicles or appears in the *Za ahan jing* (Saṃyukta Āgama). It was [translated] on the eighth day of the ninth month in the second year of the Xiaojian era.
The *Śuddhodana-rāja-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* (one fascicle), also titled with the character "pán" (般) added to it;
translated by Zhu Fashou at Zhuyuan Temple on the twenty-fifth day of the second month, based on the records of Sengyou, Baochang, and others. Second translation, same text as that produced by Faju.
Recorded in the *Fanglüe*. The *Jinxue jing* (one fascicle), also called the *Quanjinxue dao jing*; second translation. Recorded in the *Bielu*.

The same text as that translated by Zhi Qian and others; the Fangyun catalogue states it is seen in the *Bie lu* (Separate Record) as one fascicle of the *Baguanzhai jing* (Sutra on the Eight Precepts Retreat). A different translation of the same text;

the Fangyun catalogue states it is seen in the *Bie lu* as one fascicle of the *Wu wanfufu jing* (Sutra on the Five Without Repentance), also titled the *Wu fanchufu dayi jing* (Sutra on the Great Meaning of the Five Reversals), or sometimes written with the character "fu" (attached).
The Fangyun catalogue states it is seen in the *Bie lu* as one fascicle of the *Fodasengda jing* (Sutra of the Great Assembly of Buddhas), concerning two children.
The *Yejijing* (Yaṣṭī-sūtra) in one fascicle; Sengfang says it was seen in the *Bielu*. The *Moluwangjing* (Mallarāja-sūtra) in one fascicle; Sengfang says it was seen in the *Bielu*.
The *Modaguo Wangjing* (King Mada-sūtra) in one fascicle; Sengfang says it was seen in the *Bielu*, though some versions lack the characters "King" (Wang).
The *Zhantayueguo Wangjing* (King Caṇḍāyudha-sūtra) in one fascicle; some versions lack the characters "King," and Sengfang says it was seen [in the *Bielu*].
*Bié lù* (Separate Record), fascicle 5: *Wǔ kǒngbù shì jīng* (Sūtra on the Five Terrors of the World), one fascicle; alternatively called *Wǔ kǒngbù jīng*. Fáng says it is seen in the *Bié lù*.
*Dìzǐ sǐ fù shēng jīng* (Sūtra on a Disciple’s Death and Rebirth), one fascicle; alternatively called *Sǐwáng gèngshēng jīng*. Fáng says it is seen in the *Bié lù*.
*Kāshē yìnjiè jīng* (Kāśyapa’s Sūtra on the Prohibitions), one fascicle; also named *Móhē bǐqīu jīng* (Mahābhikṣu Sūtra) and called *Zhēnwěi shā mén* (True and False Śramaṇas).
The second scripture, the *Bodhisattva-praṇidhāna-sūtra* (一卷), was recorded by the Master as having been seen in a separate catalog; the portion above exists while that below is missing.

The fifth scripture, the *Sūtra on the Instruction of the Elder’s Son* (一卷), shares the same text as [the previous entry]. The Master recorded that he saw the *Antarābhava-sūtra* (一卷) in a separate catalog.
The Master also recorded that he saw the *Avalokiteśvara-dhyāna-sūtra* (一卷), which was previously located in Gaochang Commandery.

Translated from a manuscript brought from abroad; listed in Sengyou’s *Chusanzangjiji* as one fascicle of the *Bōsiniwang Sangmu jing* (Sūtra on King Prasenajit Mourning His Mother), also called the *Bōsiniwang jing*, while Sengyou notes it as the *Poye-ni Wang jing*. Faxian notes it was found in a separate record.

It is an alternative translation of the first fascicle of the *Fomu Baniepan jing* (Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha’s Mother) from the eighteenth fascicle of the *Zengyi Ahan jing*, produced in the second year of the Xiaojian era.

In the [X]th year, at Jian-shan Dinglin Shang-si (Upper Monastery), he produced one work titled *Dà-ài-dào bānnièhán jīng* (The Sūtra on Mahāprajāpatī’s Parinirvāṇa), which appears in Sengyou’s Catalogue.

He also produced *Yìyì dìzǐ màn wéi qíyù shù jīng* (A Translation of the Disciple Māna’s Narration for Jīvaka, in One Fascicle), also called *Dìzǐ wéi qíyù shù mànjiè yǔ dìzǐ xìtàn jīng* (The Disciple’s Narration for Jīvaka on the Precepts of Arrogance and the Disciple’s Playful Exaggerations). It is the [X]th fascicle.

The fourth translation is identical to the *Wen shi fo jixiong jing* (Sūtra on Asking about the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha); Master Fang says it is seen in the *Bielu* (Separate Record).
The *Zhangzhe yinyue jing* (Sūtra of the Householder’s Melodious Joy), one fascicle; the second translation is identical to that produced by Zhi Qian; Master Fang says it is seen in the *Bielu*.
The *Wuku zhangju jing* (Sūtra of the Verses on the Five Sufferings), one fascicle; the second translation is identical to that produced by Dharmaratna; Master Fang [says it is seen in the *Bielu*].

Yun says he saw in the *Bie lu* (Separate Catalog): the *Fen hu dan wang jing* (Sūtra on King Bimbisāra), one fascicle; the second [entry] is the *Zhu lü yan san mo jie jing* (Sūtra of Dharmarakṣa and Samghavarman), same text as the former;

and the *Di zi shi fo ji xiong jing* (Sūtra on the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Disciples Serving the Buddha), one fascicle—You says it is the *Di zi wen shi fo ji xiong jing* (Sūtra of the Disciple’s Questions on the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha);
and the *Sheng si bian shi jing* (Sūtra on the Transformation of Consciousness in Birth and Death), one fascicle—now seen in the *Bie lu*.
It is suspected that these were seen among the Tripitaka as alternative titles for the *Sūtra*. Fang says he saw them in the *Bie lu* (Separate Record):

the *Upāsaka-pañcaśīla-sūtra*, one fascicle, also called the *Wuxiang jing* (Sūtra of the Five Characteristics), second edition; its text is identical to the *Wujiexiang jing* (Sūtra on the Characteristics of the Five Precepts). Fang says he saw it in the *Bie lu*:
the *Xianzhe luyi jing* (Sūtra on the Venerable One’s Discipline), one fascicle, also called the *Wei yi* (Dignified Conduct). These two [entries] are listed above.
The eighteen sections in twenty-eight fascicles of the *Kāśyapa-śīla-sūtra*, upper part: fifteen sections in fifteen fascicles currently extant;
lower part: thirteen sections in thirteen fascicles, missing from the original.
The lay devotee Juqu Jingsheng was the Marquis of Anyang and a younger cousin of Mengsun, the Prince of Hexi of Northern Liang.
After the Wei dynasty annexed Liang, he fled south to the Song.
He concealed his ambitions and humbled himself, refusing to involve himself in worldly affairs.
He frequently visited prominent monasteries, dedicating his life as a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*).
Meng Yi, the Governor of Danyang, saw him and held him in high regard.
I request an audience with you.
Once we have met face-to-face, I shall honor and cherish you most sincerely,
promptly preparing offerings and providing you with generous hospitality.
In the second year of the Xiaojian era of Emperor Xiaowu, the year of Yiwu (465 CE),
Huiguo translated twenty-eight scriptures, including the *Maitreya’s Ascent to Heaven Sūtra*, at Zhuyuan and Dinglin Shangsi on Mount Zhong in the capital of Yangdu.
Having practiced for a long time, his hand was unimpeded when he took up the brush.
His reputation was preeminent in the capital, yet he had no desire for wealth or status for himself or his family.
He lived at ease among his fellow practitioners, expounding and propagating the sutras and treatises.
Therefore, both the clergy and the laity in Jianye revered and praised him.
At the end of the Daming era, he fell ill and passed away.
The *Pumingwang jing* and the *Fanmo huang jing*—these two scriptures—were both translated from the *Liuyidu ji*, along with the *Shami biqiu jing*.

The *Upāsaka-pañca-dharma-sūtra* (upper volume) and the second sūtra are both from the *Madhyama Āgama*; the *Śākyaputrīya-upāsaka-paripṛcchā-sūtra* is from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*; the *Cīrṇaśuddha-upāsaka-āryasena-sūtra* is also called the *Āryasena-holding-father-sūtra*, the *Utpatti-sūtra*, the *Pañca-brāhmaṇa-śata-sūtra*, and the *Vimalaprabhā-rāja-ādi-saptasūtra*. The notes in the various catalogs express doubt regarding these seven sūtras.
Sixth is the separate production.
First is the suspicion of forgery;
now it is recorded as an authentic account.
Therefore, both have been deleted.
*The Scripture on the Five Heavenly Messengers of King Yama* (one fascicle), also known as the *Scripture on the Iron City Niraya*, is found in the *Chángfáng Lù*;
it is a different translation of the twelfth sutra of the *Madhyama Āgama*. *The Scripture on Gautamī’s Prediction of Her Fruit* (one fascicle) is from the *Madhyama Āgama*.
The *Sūtra on the Six Times a Householder’s Son Left Home to Practice*, one fascicle;
translated differently from the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*; listed in the Catalogue of Changfang. The *Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha’s Mother*, one fascicle;
translated differently from the fiftieth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*; listed in the Catalogue of Changfang.
*Record of the Sutra on the Poor Old Man*, one fascicle; also called *The Poor Old Man*, second appearance in the *Chángfáng Lù*.
*Sutra on the Lazy Plowman*, one fascicle; the old catalogs call it *The Lazy Plowman’s Son*; appears in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *Sutra on Inviting Piṇḍola*, one fascicle;
some add the word "sutra" (*jing*); appears in the *Chángfáng Lù*. Second appearance: *Sutra on the Son of a Good Family*.
One fascicle; also titled *The Sutra on the Six Directions of Prostration* (Yichu liuxiang bai jing), recorded in the Catalogue of Changfang.
One fascicle, *The Sutra on Various Bhikṣus after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha* (Foban niepan hou zhu biqiu jing), said to be from the *Madhyamāgama*, volume thirty-three, a variant translation;
recorded in the Catalogue of Changfang. One fascicle, *The Sutra of Similes* (Piyu jing); recorded in the Catalogue of Changfang. The above eleven works constitute one [set].
The eleven-fascicle *Qing Bintou* [in seven sections] consists of seven fascicles currently extant; the lower three sections, comprising three fascicles, are missing from the *Shanshengzi jing*.
Translated by the śramaṇa Shi Huijian.
His origins are unknown.
In the first year of the Daming era of Emperor Xiaowu, the Dingyou year, he translated ten sections of scriptures, including the *Sūtra of the Five Divine Messengers*, at Luye Monastery.

The *Zhenwei shamen fa jing* (Sutra on the True and False Dharmas of Śramaṇas) is identical in every word and phrase to the *Kāśyapa-jīngjiè jīng* (Sutra of Kāśyapa’s Prohibitions) produced by Jing-sheng; it is simply an alternative title for the *Shishi jing*. It is an error on the part of the cataloguers to list the *Yaoshi liuliguang jing* (Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabhāsa-sūtra)—also titled the *Guanding bachuzuogui shengsi dedu jing* (Consecration Sutra for Eradicating Transgressions and Attaining Deliverance from Birth and Death)—under the *Daguanding jing* as a "suspicious sutra" (yi jing). It is not the *Shijia bi zui jing* (Sutra on Śākyamuni’s Expiation of Sins).

*Sūtra on Sacrificing One’s Body to Rescue Merchants*, Part I; the above two sūtras both appear in the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya*. *Sūtra on Ānanda Seeing the Auspicious Omen of Water-Light*; also known as the *Sūtra on Wood-Light* or the *Excerpted Mahāyāna Sūtra on Merchants Seeking Wealth*.

The *Gautamī Sūtra*; the two aforementioned sūtras are both from the *Madhyama Āgama*: the *Sūtra on a Person of Śrāvastī Going Mad after the Death of a Son* and the *Sūtra on a Student with a Disturbed Mind*, also known as the *Sūtra on a Mother and Son Becoming a Bhikṣu and a Bhikṣuṇī with Disturbed Minds*. The two aforementioned sūtras are both from the *Ekottara Āgama*: the *Sūtra on a Great Malla Leaving Home and Attaining the Way*, also known as the *Bhadra Sūtra on the Malla*, and the *Sūtra on Two Old Men and Women Seeing the Buddha, Leaving Home, and Attaining the Way*. The two aforementioned sūtras are both from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*: the *Sūtra on Cañcāmatī’s Malicious Slander of the Buddha*, the *Sūtra on Birth*, and the *Sūtra on Secretly Becoming a Śramaṇa*.

The *Heshi shejia xue dao jing* (The Scripture on the Master of the Coarse Cloth Leaving Home to Study the Way), the aforementioned two scriptures, as well as the *Chuyao jing* (Scripture of Exalted Utterances) and the *Zhouyuan jing* (Scripture of Incantations and Vows)—these fifteen works, including the *Yuzai weilu* (Record of False Catalogues) and the *Zhenwei shamen deng* (True and False Śramaṇas), etc., were all produced.
The catalogs compiled by Sengchang and others all state that these were produced by Huijian;
however, as they consist mostly of apocryphal sutras and the like,
I have deleted them and do not retain them here.

The *Bodhisattva-nien-fo-san-mei-jing* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra) in six fascicles—also simply titled the *Nien-fo-san-mei-jing*—or in five fascicles; this first translation is the same text as that produced by Dharmagupta during the Sui dynasty. It is a separate division of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*. It is not found in the *Dao-hui* catalog of the Song and Qi dynasties or in the *Seng-you* catalog. The *Wu-liang-men-po-mo-tuo-luo-ni-jing* (Aparimitāyur-dhāraṇī-sūtra) in one fascicle—also simply titled the *Po-mo-tuo-luo-ni-jing*; this seventh translation is found in the *Seng-you* catalog. It is the same text as Zhi Qian’s *Wu-liang-men-wei-mi-chi-jing*. These two works, totaling seven fascicles, both exist in their original form.
Śramaṇa Gongdezhí was a man from the Western Regions.
His realization of the Way was vast, and his skillful guidance improved daily.
In the sixth year of the Daming era of Emperor Xiaowu, the year of Renyin,
he traveled to Jingzhou and stayed at Chanfang Temple. There,
the śramaṇa Xuanchang requested that he translate two scriptures, including the *Nianfo Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha).
Chang published the correct text, clarifying the meaning and intent with elegant and subtle phrasing;
yet when he extended his hand, fragrant water flowed from his palm, a phenomenon beyond anyone's comprehension.
Later, he traveled to Chengdu and stayed at Dashi Temple.
This is the stupa of King Aśoka.
It contains sixteen divine images, such as Vajrapāṇi and Guhyapada, which he fashioned with his own hands;
these have been handed down to the present day.
He remained in Jingzhou for several years;
his ultimate end is unknown.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-karmavācanā-bhikṣu-ayoga* (The Essential Karmavācanā for Bhikṣus) is in one fascicle—some say it is the *Lüyào jīemó fǎ* (Abridged Essential Karmavācanā Method), while Fáng says it is in two fascicles and Yòu says it is in one fascicle; this is found in Sēngyòu’s catalog. This one work in one fascicle is extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Sengqu, whose secular surname was Zhu,
was a native of Wu.
He left the household life as a disciple of Sengye.
He was preeminent among those who specialized in various sutras, with a particular mastery of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
Furthermore, he was proficient in historical records and composed literary works with considerable elegance.
He initially resided at Mount Huqiu in Wu.
Emperor Xiaowu admired his reputation and issued an imperial decree for him to go to Yangdu to serve as the *Sengzheng* (Director of Monks) and lead the assembly;
he resided at Zhongxing Temple.
In the seventh year of the Daming era (the Gui-mao year), Ju compiled one fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-karman*.

There is also one fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa-sūtra*, also called the *Daśabhāṇavāra-bhikṣuṇī-pārājika-śīla-sūtra* or the *Daśabhāṇavāra-bhikṣuṇī-mahāśīla*. These two works are recorded in the *Sengyou lu* and the *Baochang lu*. This one work in one fascicle still exists today.
The śramaṇa Shi Xuanying was of the Suo clan by secular surname;
he was a native of Dunhuang.
At thirteen, he left the household life as a disciple of Dharmagandha.
While at Gongfu Monastery in Liangzhou,
he and his fellow student Fali both became renowned for their mastery of the Vinaya-piṭaka.

After Huiying had humbly accepted [the teachings], his studies required no further requests as he committed everything to memory upon a single hearing; he refined his mastery of the Vinaya-piṭaka and extensively perused the sūtras and śāstras.
Toward the end of the Yuanjia era, he traveled to Jianye and resided at Xinting Temple.
Emperor Xiaowu, because Sengying’s learning and practice were both exceptionally clear,
issued an edict appointing him as the Sangha Rectifier (Sengzheng) of the capital.
Later, he resigned from his post and returned to Duobao Temple.
He constantly practiced meditation in a secluded room and occasionally held lectures on the Vinaya.
Later, he moved his residence to Changgan Temple.
During the first year of the Taishi era of Emperor Ming,
he compiled and produced one volume of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa*,
along with the *Karmavācanā*.

These circulated during that era. The *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra* in ten fascicles (fifth appearance): it is the same text as the *A-chamo jing*; see the catalogs of Shi-xing, Seng-you, Bao-chang, and others. The *Āśvaghosa-bodhisattva-sūtra* in one fascicle (fourth appearance): it is the same text as the *Ratnakūṭa-abhayaguṇa-parivarta*; translated in the Tai-shi era at Guangzhou; see the catalogs of Shi-xing, Bao-chang, and others. The *Sāgaramati-sūtra* in seven fascicles: see the catalogs of Shi-xing, Seng-you, Bao-chang, and others. The *Tathāgatānugraha-acintya-sūtra* in five fascicles: see the catalogs of Shi-xing, Seng-you, and others. The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* in five fascicles: see the catalogs of Shi-xing, Seng-you, Bao-chang, and others. The *Triguhyārtha-sūtra* in one fascicle—translated into Chinese as the *Xianren yonglü jing* (Sūtra on the Sage’s Use of Discipline)—see the catalogs of Shi-xing, Seng-you, Bao-chang, and others. These six works comprise twenty-nine fascicles, all of which are currently missing.
The śramaṇa Zhu Fajian was a native of India.
His character was exceptionally simple and straightforward,
and he was dedicated to the task of opening and benefiting others.
Furthermore, during the reign of Emperor Ming or in the Tai-shi period, he translated six scriptures at Guangzhou, including the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

His second translation of the *Rucidevaputra-anuttara-viśuddha-piṇḍapāta-sūtra* in two fascicles—also titled the *Sarvadharma-māyopama-samādhi-nirṇaya-sūtra*—is identical in its original text to the version translated by Yan Fotiao for Emperor Xian of the Han dynasty and the portion by Mahāprajñānāgaśrī; this is recorded in the *Shixing lu*. This one work in two fascicles currently exists.
The śramaṇa Shi Xianggong was also called Shuogong.
While in Nanhai, he translated one fascicle of the *Ruru Pusa Jing* (Lalita-vistara Sūtra).
Various catalogs simply state it belongs to the Song period, without specifying the year or his name.
It is unknown under which emperor this was translated.

*Buddhapiṭaka Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, one fascicle—also titled *Wenming Xianjing* (Sūtra of the Questions of Mingxian), with the "Chapter on Difficulties" as a separate translation—is recorded in the *Shixing lu* and the *Fashang lu*. *Yingluo Benye jing*, two fascicles—also known as the *Pusa Yingluo jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva’s Garland)—is the third edition, recorded in the *Shixing lu* and the *Fashang lu*. These two works, totaling three fascicles, are currently missing from the canon.
The śramaṇa Shi Daoyan translated two works, including the *Buddhapiṭaka Vaipulya Sūtra*, during the Song dynasty.
Various catalogs simply state "during the Song dynasty" without specifying the imperial reign year.

*The Scripture of the Brahma Maiden Śirīṣā*, one fascicle; second appearance in the *Shixing lu*, the *Zhao lu*, and the *Fashang lu*. *The Scripture of the Emptiness-Purity Samādhi*, one fascicle; also titled *The Scripture on the Responsive Manifestation of the Emptiness-Purity Deva’s Samādhi*; second appearance in the *Shixing lu*, the *Zhao lu*, and the *Fashang lu*. *The Scripture Encouraging the Study of the Path*, one fascicle; also named *The Encouragement Scripture*; co-transmitted with the *Liang shi*; third translation; appears in the *Shixing lu*, the *Zhao lu*, and the *Fashang lu*. The three sections comprising these three fascicles are all currently missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Yong translated three sūtras,
including the *Vimaladattā-paripṛcchā*, during the Song dynasty;
although various catalogs state they were produced in the Song period, [further investigation is required].
The imperial year is not specified.
The *Candana-sūtra* is also titled the *Candana-pūrvāparānta-sūtra*, which appears in the *Six Pāramitās Collection*. It is an alternative title for the *Śibiprabha-rāja-sūtra*;
although various catalogs state it was translated by Zhu Foyong, I have omitted it here as it is a separately produced apocryphal scripture.
*The Sūtra on the Question of Silent and Harmonious Sound* (一卷), also known as *The Sūtra on the Pure Subjugation Spoken by the Tathāgata*;
this is the same text as the *Mañjuśrī-vimala-vinaya-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Western Jin dynasty.

This is the fourth appearance [of this title], recorded in the *Shixing lu* and the *Fashang lu*. *The Sūtra on the Skillful Means of the Adornment of Joyful Garlands* (一卷), also known as the *Mahāyāna*.
The *Yingluo zhuangyan jing* (Sutra on the Adornment of Necklaces), also titled the *Zhuan nüshen pusa jing* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva Transforming the Female Body), fascicle four;
this is the same text as the *Shunquan fangbian jing* (Sutra on Skillful Means) translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Western Jin, as seen in the *Shixing lu* and Sengyou’s *Fashang lu*.
Of these two works in two fascicles, the former, the *Jiaotiao yin*, is extant, while the latter, the *Leyingluo jing*, is missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Fahaï translated two sūtras,
including the *Jiaotiyaoyin* (Sūtra of the Silent and Harmonious Sound), during the Song dynasty.
Various catalogs note that these were produced as translations during the Song period.
As neither the year nor the reigning emperor is specified, the details remain uncertain.

*Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra*, one fascicle—also known as *Mañjuśrī-bodhisattva-daśa-kriyā-sūtra* or *Jianhui-samādhi-sūtra*. This is a variant translation of the seventh fascicle of the *Mahā-candrapradīpa-sūtra*. It appears in the Zhao lu and the Fashang lu. This single work, consisting of one fascicle, is extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Xian translated one fascicle of the Candrapradīpa-sūtra during the Song dynasty;
various catalogs note that it was produced in the Song period.
The year of translation is not indicated, and it remains uncertain under which emperor it was produced.
One fascicle of an excerpt from the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya is found in Baochang’s catalogue; it is also titled *Tiāpótánán juànshǔ bínnì jīng*. This one work in one fascicle is missing.
The śramaṇa Saṃghavarman was a native of Siṃhala.
He translated one fascicle of an abridgment of the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya.
In the *Dazhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalog), it is recorded that Baochang’s catalog does not mention imperial reigns.
Having examined the original source of Baochang’s catalog,
I have provisionally appended it to the Song catalog.

This is merely to provide a documented basis; furthermore, according to Sengyou’s *Fayuan*, on the tenth day of the third month in the eighth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, at the Eastern Vihāra on Mount Lu’s Prajñā Terrace, he translated the *Śrāvakavinaya-saṃgraha* together with the Vinaya Master Saṃghavarman from Siṃhala. Having assembled one hundred and twenty monks, they had already compiled this catalogue, though they had not yet had the leisure to revise it.
The Newly Compiled Collection of Various Scriptures of Lost Translation: *The Tathāgata-jñāna-mudrā Sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *The Dharma-body of All Buddhas*.
Second edition; same text as the *Prajñā-mudrā-samādhi Sūtra*. *The Scripture of the Old Mother*, one fascicle; second edition;
same text as the *Scripture of the Old Woman* and others. *The Scripture on the Extinction of the Dharma*, one fascicle. *The Scripture of the Profound and Great Dedication*, one fascicle.
*The Sūtra on the Training Spoken by the Buddha for the Old Brahmin of Yellow Bamboo Garden*, one fascicle; translated from the fortieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.

*The Sūtra of Upatiṣya’s Fall from the Śākya Clan*, one fascicle; translated from the fifty-fifth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama* with a variant translation (some versions omit the character "jia" [迦]).
*The Sūtra on False Views*, one fascicle; translated from the sixth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama* with a variant translation.
*The One Hundred and One Karmavācanās of the Great Śramaṇa*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Karmavācanās of the Great Śramaṇa*.

Translated from the *Daśabhāṇaka-vinaya* by the Bhikṣu Kātyāyanīputra. *Sūtra on the Transformations of the Future*, one fascicle; alternatively simply titled *Sūtra of the Bhikṣu Kātyāyanīputra*. The text is missing after this point.
*Sūtra of the Names of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions*, one fascicle. *Pure Sūtra of the Avataṃsaka*, one fascicle. (30)

*Qīpǐn jīng* (Sūtra in Seven Chapters), one fascicle; Yǒu records two versions, both stating they are different recensions; for now, only one is retained. *Sìqī fó gèshuō jì jīng* (Sūtra of the Verses Spoken by Each of the Seven Buddhas), one fascicle.
*Rúlǎng rúlái jīng* (Sūtra of the Tathāgata Milk-King), one fascicle; some call it the *Rúlǎng jīng*. The current sūtra is the same text as the *Rúguāng jīng*.
*Xīnfàn shìfāng fó míng jīng* (Sūtra of the Names of the Buddhas Currently Present in the Ten Directions), one fascicle. *Guòqù zhū fó míng jīng* (Sūtra of the Names of the Buddhas of the Past).
*The Sūtra of the Names of One Thousand Five Hundred Buddhas*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Names of Five Hundred and Seven Hundred Buddhas*, one fascicle;
*The Sūtra of Avalokiteśvara’s Attainment of Buddhahood*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Mañjuśrī*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on the Original Vows of Mañjuśrī*, one fascicle;
*The Sūtra on the Contemplation of Mañjuśrī*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of Maitreya’s Exhortation*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Questions of the Guide to the Buddha*, one fascicle.
*The Sūtra of One Hundred and Twenty Difficult Questions by Bodhisattva Kuan-fa-t'o*, one scroll; *The Sūtra of Bodhisattva Ch’i-shen*, one scroll;
*The Sūtra of Two Hundred Questions by Bodhisattva Hsien-shou*, one scroll; *The Sūtra of Bodhisattva Vajra-Dārikā*, one scroll; *The Sūtra of Bodhisattva Shan-i*, one scroll;
*The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva’s Descent from Tuṣita Heaven through the Intermediate State*, one scroll; *The Joyful Practice of the Bodhisattva*.
*Sūtra* in one fascicle; *Bodhisattva-viśuddha-mūla-karma-sūtra* in one fascicle; *Bodhisattva-ādi-karma-sūtra* in one fascicle; *Bodhisattva-catur-artha-sūtra* in one fascicle;
*Bodhisattva-ṣoḍaśa-praṇidhāna-sūtra* in one fascicle; *Bodhisattva-pañcāśad-guṇa-caryā-sūtra* in one fascicle;
*Bodhisattva-śāsana-dharma-sūtra* in one fascicle; *Bodhisattva-samyak-caryā-sūtra* in one fascicle; *Bodhisattva-praveśa-niṣkramaṇa-sūtra*.

Of the three hundred and forty fascicles, only nine fascicles from the first nine sections exist; the remainder are all missing.
These are all scriptures whose translators were lost, newly compiled in the catalog of the Liang dynasty monk Sengyou.
However, according to Sengyou’s original catalog and the new collection compiled by Sengyou himself,
there were a total of one thousand three hundred and six works comprising one thousand five hundred and seventy fascicles.

Now, upon a detailed search and examination, it is found that among the remaining nine hundred and ninety-nine works totaling one thousand two hundred and thirty fascicles, most are various derivative sūtras,
or those already recorded in the catalogs of lost translations by Zhisheng and others.
