Furthermore, among those works for which the primary translators are recorded in the *Dai-lu* (Great Catalog),
there are three hundred and seven works in three hundred and forty fascicles that were never included in the searches of the *Chang-fang lu* and other catalogs.
Now, these have been newly collected here because they are considered to have lost their source.
However, in Sengyou’s catalogue, it is merely stated that they were of lost translation without specifying the date.
For now, they shall be appended to the end of the Song dynasty catalogue.
I hope this will avoid any omissions.

As for the Southern Qi of the Xiao clan, which was based in Jianye: it began from the first year of the Jianyuan era of Emperor Gao (Jiwei) until the second year of the Zhongxing era of Emperor He (Renwu).
In total, under seven successive rulers for twenty-four years,
seven śramaṇas translated various sūtras and vinayas.
In total, there are twelve sections comprising thirty-three fascicles; among these, seven sections totaling twenty-eight fascicles are extant, while five sections totaling five fascicles are missing.

*The Sūtra of the Śramaṇa Dharmagādayaśas*: one section, one fascicle. *The Vinaya of the Śramaṇa Mahāyāna*: two sections, two fascicles. *The Vinaya of the Śramaṇa Saṃghabhadra*: one section, eighteen fascicles. *The Sūtras of the Śramaṇa Dharmamati*: two sections, two fascicles. *The Collected Sūtras of the Śramaṇa Shi Tanying*: two sections, three fascicles. *The Sūtra of the Śramaṇa Shi Fahua*: one section, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, one fascicle, a second edition found in the *Sengyou Lu*; it contains a preface by Liu Qiu, a recluse of Jingzhou. This one section is currently extant.
The śramaṇa Dharmagatayaśas,
whose name in the Qi language means Fashengcheng,
was a native of Central India.
Awakening to the nature of things and abiding in the Way, he found no need to abandon worldly benefits.
In the second year of the Jianyuan era (the *xin-you* year), when Emperor Gao had achieved the Way,
he translated the *Anantārthasūtra* (*Wuliangyi jing*) in one fascicle at Chaoting Temple in Guangzhou.
Yeshé was skilled in the Li script and proficient in the Qi language; he transmitted the scriptures to others.
In the third year of the Yongming era, the śramaṇa Huìbiǎo of Wǔdāng Mountain brought [the texts] to the capital of Yáng.

Copied and circulated. One fascicle of the *Pañcajātaka-sūtra* is found in Sengyou’s catalogue; Sengyou states its number of fascicles is unknown, while Fazang records it as one fascicle. One fascicle of the *Tāpasa-vinaya* (in the Qi language, *Sude-lü*) is found in Sengyou’s catalogue; Sengyou states its number of fascicles is unknown, while Fazang records it as one fascicle. These two works, totaling two fascicles, are both currently missing.
The śramaṇa Mahāyāna was a native of the Western Regions.
He settled his mind upon the wondrous Way and resolved his will upon its broad propagation.
During the Yongming era of Emperor Wu’s reign, he translated two works, including the *Pañcaśata-jātaka-sūtra*, at Guangzhou.

The *Sudarsana-vinaya-vibhāṣā* in eighteen fascicles—also known as the *Vibhāṣā-vinaya* or simply the *Sudarsana-vinaya*—is recorded in the *Song Qi lu* by Jie Daohui and the *Sengyou lu*. This one work in eighteen fascicles still exists today.
The śramaṇa Saṃghabhadra, whose name means "Saṃgha-virtuous" (Zhòngxián) in the Qi language,
was a native of the Western Regions.
Embracing the Way with expansive freedom, his transformative grace was inexhaustible.
According to the tradition passed down from master to disciple:
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, once Upāli had completed the compilation of the Vinaya Piṭaka...
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month of that same year, having completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony,
he made offerings of incense and flowers to the Vinaya Piṭaka and placed a single dot before it.
Year after year it was thus.
Upāli, desiring to enter parinirvāṇa, entrusted [the teaching] to his disciple Dovaśika.
Dovaśika, desiring to enter parinirvāṇa, entrusted it to his disciple Susika.
Śuklodana entrusted it to his disciple Siggava;
Siggava entrusted it to his disciple Moggaliputtatissa;
and Moggaliputtatissa entrusted it to his disciple Candavajji.

In this manner, the masters transmitted [the teachings] to one another until the present day; however, the name of the Tripiṭaka Master has not been recorded. When the Tripiṭaka Master was about to take the Vinaya Piṭaka to Guangzhou, he turned back and departed before boarding the ship.

He entrusted the Vinaya Piṭaka to his disciple Saṃghabhadra; in the sixth year of Emperor Wu’s Yongming era (the Wucheng year, which Fang Yun identifies as Jisi), together with the śramaṇa Senghui, he [translated it].
It was translated at Zhulin Monastery in Guangzhou and titled the *Śāriputrābhidharma-vinaya-vibhāṣā*.
It was undertaken because [the translators] were in joint retreat.
In the seventh year of the Yongming era, the year of Jisi (489 CE), on the fifteenth day of the seventh month of the year of Gengwu, he completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
Following the methods of his former masters, he finished making offerings of incense and flowers to the Vinaya-piṭaka.
One immediately places a dot.
In that year, one calculates a total of nine hundred and seventy-five dots;
each dot represents one year.
In the first year of the Datong era of the Liang dynasty (537 CE),
Zhao Baxiu encountered the ascetic Vinaya Master Hongdu at Mount Lu and obtained this record of the dates and months marked by various sages following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
In the seventh year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty,
Boxiu visited Hongdu and asked,
"Since the seventh year of Yongming, why have you not been seen to receive the initiation [of the *dīna*]? Hongdu replied:
From this point onward, all [marks] were personally applied by the hands of sages who had attained the Way.
This poor monk, being but an ordinary person, can only receive them with reverence upon his head;
he does not dare to apply them himself.
Based on this calculation by Bo Xiu, tracing back from the ninth year of the Daming era of the Liang dynasty,
the year Guihai, one arrives at a total of one thousand twenty-eight years.
Following Bo Xiu’s reckoning, tracing forward from that point until the seventeenth year of the Kaiyuan era of the Great Tang, the year Gengwu, [the total remains consistent].
This results in a total of one thousand two hundred and sixteen years.

If this were the case, there would be a discrepancy in the dates of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, making it impossible to rely upon this ink-marked record; it differs entirely from the chronological account of the Buddha’s tooth relic shrine in Siṃhala transmitted by Faxian.

This concludes the Upāli Vinaya Piṭaka; having finished the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, he personally applied the dots [of punctuation], and thus it has been transmitted from year to year through successive handovers down to the present day.
This may not be the case;
upon examining this *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*,
it was not compiled by Upāli.
This is merely an abridged explanation of the tenets of one school from among the twenty sections that followed after the partial compilation;
it is not the complete Vinaya.
This very point was added later during the compilation;
this may well be so. However, if it is said that Upāli himself placed the dot with his own hand, [then...]

It cannot yet serve as a definitive guide. The *Devadatta-parivarta*, the twelfth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, in one fascicle, is now included at the beginning of the fifth fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The śramaṇa Faxian obtained a single-fascicle Sanskrit manuscript in the kingdom of Khotan. Daohui’s *Song Qi Lu* and Sengyou’s *Lu* state that it was translated from a Sanskrit manuscript by a group of translators in Gaochang; it is unclear which version is correct. The *Avalokiteśvara-kṣamāpaka-pāpa-vināśana-mantra-sūtra*, in one fascicle, was translated on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month in the eighth year of the Yongming era; this is recorded in Sengyou’s *Lu* and Baochang’s *Lu*. These two works comprise two fascicles. The *Devadatta-parivarta* currently exists, while the *Avalokiteśvara-mantra-sūtra* is missing.
The śramaṇa Dharmamati, whose name means "Fa-yi" (Dharma-intent) in the Qi language,
was a man from the Western Regions.
His realization of the nature of things was profound, and he provided illustrations according to the needs of his audience.
In the eighth year of Emperor Wu’s Yongming era (the Gengwu year),
he translated two works, including the *Devadatta-varga*, for the śramaṇa Faxian at Waguan Monastery in the capital of Yangdu.
At the time of his offering,
he served as the Sangha Chief (Sengzheng). Initially, in the third year of the Yuanhui era of the Song dynasty,
he traveled through the Western Regions and obtained Sanskrit manuscripts of the scriptures, along with a Buddha’s tooth, in the kingdom of Khotan.
There was a Kāpila deity who escorted it back to Song. When the scripture arrived during the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, it was translated together with the śramaṇa Fayi.

The Buddha’s tooth relic was enshrined at Zhongshan Shangdinglin Temple; it is approximately three cun long, with a circumference of the same measure. Its color is yellowish-white, and its surface is marked with auspicious patterns that protrude like modern seal characters. It is smooth, lustrous, and pure, much resembling jade or precious gems. According to the internal scriptures, the Buddha has four teeth: one is in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, one is in the palace of the Dragon King, one is in Siṃhala, and one is in Udyāna. This is the tooth from Udyāna. Later, it was suddenly lost, but then appeared in Khotan and was offered there. Upon the request for its return, in the first month of the third year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, several people suddenly appeared.
Carrying weapons, they knocked on the door at the first watch of the night,
crying out, "A slave of His Highness the Prince of Linchuan has rebelled!
Someone reported this, saying:
He requested that the gate of the Buddha-tooth pavilion be opened so he might look inside.
The temple monks complied with his words.
The Master approached the seat of the Buddha-tooth relic.
He opened the casket, took out the tooth relic, and after performing three prostrations,
he placed the relic in a silk cloth and traveled eastward toward Mount Song.
Later, he sought it out again and returned it to the forest of Anding.
When Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty annexed the Chen, he remained at Mount Zhong.
In the third year of the Renshou era,
the Inner Envoy sent Prince Yuzhang, Xian.
It was brought from Yangzhou to be presented to Emperor Wen.
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month of that year, an imperial decree ordered it to be sent to Dongchan Ding Temple for veneration.
The miraculous manifestations of the Buddha’s tooth relic are fully detailed in Sengyou’s *Record of the Buddha’s Tooth Relic*.
This shall not be elaborated upon further.
The Eastern Chan Temple is none other than the present-day Dazhuangyan Temple.

*The Sūtra of Sudatta* (one fascicle), also titled *The Sūtra of the Elder Sudatta*; translated from the thirty-ninth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*. A different translation seen in the *Chángfáng Lù* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. Sengyou states it was translated in the second year of the Jianwu era. *The Sūtra of One Hundred Parables* (four fascicles), also titled *The Sūtra of One Hundred Sentences of Similes*; five fascicles according to some accounts. Compiled by the Indian monk Saṃghasena; translated on the tenth day of the ninth month of the tenth year of the Yongming era. Seen in the records of Sengyou and others, all of whom state it was completed in ten fascicles; these four fascicles contain a hundred matters, which is sufficient. *The Sūtra of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* (one fascicle); the fifth appearance, identical in text to the *Sūtra of the Pei-tuo Tree*. Sengyou states it was translated in the second year of the Jianwu era; seen in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* and the *Chángfáng Lù*. Of the three sections totaling six fascicles above, the first two sections of five fascicles each are extant; the latter section of one fascicle is missing.
The śramaṇa Guṇavidi,
whose name in the Qi language means "Virtuous Progress," was a native of Central India.
In his youth, he followed the Way and served the Indian Mahayana Dharma Master Saṃghasena as his teacher.
Intelligent and possessing a powerful memory, he was diligent in recitation and study;
the Mahayana and Hinayana sutras he had mastered numbered over one hundred thousand words.
He studied secular classics concurrently and was clearly versed in the principles of yin and yang.
His prognostications regarding seasonal signs and his divinations were frequently verified by results;
thus, his reputation for mastery of esoteric arts became renowned throughout the Western Regions.
At the beginning of the Jianyuan era, he arrived at the Jianghuai region and stayed at the Vaiśālī Monastery.
Carrying his *khakkhara* staff and followed by his disciples, his demeanor was dignified and solemn;
from the princes and dukes downward, they all vied with one another to pay him their respects.
Initially, Saṃghasena, in the kingdom of India,
excerpted essential parables from the twelve divisions of the Sūtra-piṭaka and compiled them into a single work.
In all matters,
he instructed the new students;
they were able to recite the *Vibhāṣā* in its entirety and also clearly understood its underlying meanings.
In the ninth month of the autumn of the tenth year of Emperor Wu’s Yongming era, the year of Renshen (492 CE), it was translated into the Qi language;
this is the *Śatapañcāśatkathā* (The Sutra of One Hundred Parables).
Furthermore, he produced the *Sudatta-sūtra* and the *Dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.
Since the Daming era of the Song dynasty, the translation of scriptures had almost ceased.
When he propagated the Jewel of the Dharma, everyone praised him.
Vidya was a man of broad magnanimity and great discernment.
He was skilled at welcoming and guiding others,
diligently practicing the Way with tireless devotion day and night;
consequently, monastics from foreign lands gathered there from ten thousand miles away.
The merchants of the South Sea all revered and served him together;
offerings and gifts came and went without ceasing throughout the year.
By nature, he was quite prone to accumulation and was wealthy in riches and treasures.
Nevertheless, he had no private interests in the construction of religious edifices.
On the banks of the Huai River in Jianye, he built Zhengguan Temple,
where the multi-storied pavilions, tiered gates, halls, and chambers were all magnificently adorned.
He nurtured disciples and propagated the teachings, his virtuous deeds being highly renowned.
He passed away in the winter of the second year of the Zhongxing era.

One fascicle of the *Mahāmāyā-sūtra*, the second translation, also known as the *Sūtra on the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*, or simply the *Māyā-sūtra*, consists of two fascicles; it is found in the three catalogs of Wang Zongbao, Chang, Fashang, and others. Two fascicles of the *Adbhutadharmaparyāya-sūtra* (The Sūtra of Unprecedented Causes and Conditions), including the preface by the novice Rāhula, also known simply as the *Adbhuta-sūtra*, constitute the second translation and is found in the Shixing catalog. These two works, totaling three fascicles, all have their original texts extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Tanying was a man of unknown origins.
During the Qi dynasty, he translated two works, including the *Māyā-sūtra*.
The *Qunlu* states directly that it was translated during the Qi dynasty;
since the specific year is not revealed,
it remains unclear which emperor’s reign it belongs to.

*Fuzhong nü ting jing* (The Scripture on the Woman in the Womb Listening to the Dharma), one fascicle. Fifth appearance; same text as the *Wugou xian nü jing* (The Scripture on the Immaculate Virtuous Woman). The library records state that it was seen in an ancient catalog. This one work, in one fascicle, is missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Fahu,
during the Yongyuan era of the deposed Emperor Baojuan,
recited the *Tāizhongnǚ tīngjīng* (The Scripture Heard by the Girl in the Womb) in its entirety.
The various catalogs transmitted through successive generations all state that these were recited [from memory], yet the intent behind the recitation remains unclear.
I have listed them here as they exist in earlier translations to avoid the error of doubt; the *Chángfáng nèidiǎn lù* states:
During the Qi dynasty, the śramaṇa Daozheng of Jiangzhou revised and abridged the *Mile chengfo jing* (Sūtra on Maitreya’s Attainment of Buddhahood) in one fascicle.
This is not correct, as will be explained in detail later in the Mahāyāna Catalogue.
Fang et al. further state:
"During the Qi dynasty, the śramaṇa Fadu produced at Yangdu one fascicle of the *Huīhé jīng* (Ash River Sūtra) and one fascicle of the *Pípó lǜ* (Vibhāṣā-vinaya)."
Now, the *Kṣāranadī-sūtra* appears in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
Regarding the *Vibhaṅga-vinaya*, the *Sui Fajing lu* states:
"Fadu forged this work and falsely used the name of the Vinaya to mislead others."
Now it has been discarded and not established.
Fang and others also state that during the Qi dynasty,
there were two śramaṇas, Shi Fani and Shi Yiyi, who [translated] one fascicle each of the *Jing* (Sūtra).
This present scripture is that which the nun Sengfani recited from memory with her eyes closed during the Qi dynasty and at the beginning of the Liang dynasty;
however, as it is currently seen, its wording and structure are erroneous and corrupted, making it unfit for circulation.
If it is said that [this work] appeared at the end of the Qi dynasty,
why was it not included in Sengyou’s catalogue?
It is now compiled in the section on Doubtful Works.
The authentic records do not preserve them.
Sengfang and others further state that during the Qi dynasty,
the śramaṇa Daobei produced five scriptures in five fascicles, including the *Jiushang jing* (Scripture on the Nine Wounds).
The *Qunlu* (Collection of Records) contains doubts regarding its annotations;
for now, we follow the old version as the definitive text. *Zhenyuan Xinding Shijiao Mulü*, Volume Eight.
The Catalogue of the Newly Established Buddhist Teachings of the Zhenyuan Era, Volume Nine.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xìmíng Monastery in the Western Capital.
General Collection of Records of the Multitude of Scriptures, Part One, Number Nine.

The Later Liang of the Xiao clan was based in Jianye; it is also called the Former Liang. It lasted from the first year of the Tianjian era of Emperor Wu, the *wumao* year (470 CE), until the second year of the Daping era of Emperor Jing, the *dingchou* year (549 CE).
In total, under four successive rulers, for a period of fifty-six years,
nine individuals— both monastics and laypeople—
produced various translations of the sūtras, vinayas, śāstras, and biographical records.
Together with the newly compiled scriptures of unknown translators, there are a total of forty-seven works comprising two hundred and seventeen fascicles.
Among these, forty-one works totaling two hundred and seven fascicles are extant; six works totaling ten fascicles are missing. [Compiled by] the Śramaṇa of Liang...
*Men She Sengyou Sanbu Sanjiushi Juan Zhulu Ji* (The Collection of Various Records in Three Sections and Thirty-nine Volumes by the Gatekeeper Śramaṇa Sengyou);

*Sha Men Mantuoluo Xian Sanbu Shiyi Juan Jing* (The Scriptures in Three Sections and Eleven Volumes by the Śramaṇa Mandaraka); *Sha Men Sengqiepoluo Yibu Sanshier Juan Jing Lun Zhuan* (The Scriptures, Treatises, and Biographies in One Section and Thirty-two Volumes by the Śramaṇa Saṃghabara);
*Sha Men Shi Baochang Erbu Wushi'er Juan Jing Ji Nizhuan* (The Collection of Scriptures and Biographies of Nuns in Two Sections and Fifty-four Volumes by the Śramaṇa Shi Baochang).
*The Bright Praise* (Mínghuī), one fascicle; one fascicle on the *Nikāya* of Prince Candraprabha (Yuèpóshǒunà);
eleven sūtras and śāstras by the śramaṇa Paramārtha, totaling twenty-four fascicles; one work by the śramaṇa Shi Huìjiǎo, fourteen fascicles;
one anonymous collection of *Biographies of Monks*, sixteen fascicles; and the *Sūtra of the Names of Buddhas*.
The newly collected translations of various scriptures by unknown translators consist of fourteen works in twenty-five fascicles.

Among them, the *Śākyaputra-vaṃśa* (Sūtra on the Genealogy of Śākyamuni) in ten fascicles was compiled during the Qi dynasty; there is also a separate five-fascicle version, which differs in length from this one. Fazang says that the four-fascicle version is likely an error.
According to the records of Sengyou and Changfang’s *Neidian lu*, these should be included in the Qi catalog according to their respective sources.
The *Liang chu sanzang ji ji* (Collection of Records Concerning the Tripitaka Master of the Liang) in fifteen fascicles was compiled by Sengyou;
he himself stated it consisted of ten fascicles, yet both extant versions contain fifteen. Both the *Changfang lu* and the *Neidian lu* state it has fourteen fascicles.

Furthermore, the *Hongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of Buddhism) in fourteen fascicles—also compiled during the Qi dynasty by Sengyou and others—is recorded as having ten fascicles in all three catalogs, including those of Sengyou, Changfang, and the *Neidian lu*.

Volume [X]: Currently fourteen volumes are extant. According to the catalogs of Sengyou, Changfang, the Neidian lu, and others, these three works comprise thirty-nine volumes, all of which are currently extant.
Compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Sengyou.
He was a monk at Jianchu Monastery in Yangdu.
His original surname was Yu,
and his ancestors were from Xiapo in Pengcheng.
His father had lived in Jianye for generations.
When Sengyou was several years old, he entered Jianchu Temple to pay his respects;
thereupon, he leaped for joy at the Way and refused to return home.
His parents, pitying his resolve, permitted him to enter the religious life, and he served the practitioner Sengfan as his teacher.
When he was fourteen years old, his family members secretly sought a marriage for him; Huiyou learned of this.
He then withdrew to Dinglin Temple to seek refuge with Dharma Master Fada.
Fada was also one whose preceptual virtue was refined and strict, serving as a pillar for the Dharma gate;
Master Sengyou served him with the utmost sincerity.
When he reached the age for full ordination, his conduct was firm and his understanding clear.
Initially, he received instruction from the śramaṇa Faying;
since Faying was a renowned master of his time, he was the preeminent authority for the study of the Vinaya.
Fayou then exhausted his thoughts in his diligent pursuit [of the Vinaya] without ceasing day or night;
he subsequently achieved great mastery in the Vinaya section, surpassing the sages of antiquity.
Emperor Wu (Yan) treated him with profound courtesy and esteem.
Regarding all matters concerning the Sangha that were subject to great doubt,
the Emperor would issue decrees to examine and resolve them.
As he grew old and suffered from foot ailments, the Emperor issued a decree permitting him to enter the inner palace by carriage.
He conferred the precepts upon the ladies of the six palaces;
such was the esteem in which he was held.
He also [conferred them] upon Prince Wenxuan of Jingling of the Qi dynasty, Xiao Ziliang.
Liang Prince of Linchuan Hong;
Nanping Prince Wei, a Grand Master of Ceremonial;
and Yuan Ao of Chenjun, Duke of Yongkangding.
Noble Consort Ding and the others all revered his precepts and models,
exhausting every mark of respect due to a teacher.
His lay and monastic disciples numbered more than ten thousand in total.
Yòu was profoundly versed in the Vinaya-piṭaka and possessed great skill in literary composition.
He collected and recorded [the material] to compile it into volumes,
so that those who seek and examine it may achieve their purpose with little effort yet gain broad understanding.
This is the essential outline of the gateway to the true Dharma and the fundamental source of the Śākya lineage.
From the end of the Xiao-Qi period through the Liang dynasty,
he composed three works, including the *Śākyaputravaṃśa*.
As for other works such as the *Fayuan zaji*, the *Shijie ji*, and the *Sizichuan*,
they are omitted from discussion here because they were not included in the canon;
these are all fully elucidated in the *Sanzang ji* and other such records.
The *Mañjuśrī-bhāṣita-mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* in two fascicles (or one fascicle), also simply titled the *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Its initial translation was identical to that produced by Saṃghavarman;
it corresponds to the seventh assembly, the "Mañjuśrī Section," of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and is included in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* as the fourth [assembly].

The *Dharmadhātusvabhāva-avikalpa-sūtra* in two fascicles, as recorded in the *Li Kuò Lù* (Record of Li Kuò) and the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Xu Gāosēng Zhuàn*), is the second appearance;
it is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa* collection as the eighth assembly, according to the records of Li Kuò and Bǎo Chàng and the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
The *Bǎoyún Jīng* (Sūtra of the Jewel Cloud) in seven fascicles was first translated during the Chen dynasty by Subhūti and others.

The *Ratnamegha-sūtra* and the *Ratnavarṣa-sūtra* translated by Dharmaruci during the Tang dynasty, among others, appear as different translations under the same title in the Chen-dynasty catalog and the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
These three works, totaling eleven fascicles, all still exist today.
The śramaṇa Mandaraka (仙),
which in the Liang language means "Weak Voice" (弱聲) and is also called "Greatly Weak" (弘弱), was a native of Funan.
With divine understanding and transcendent awakening, he perceives both the hidden and the manifest;
undaunted by either ease or peril, his resolve is set upon enlightening and transforming others.
Bringing a great collection of Sanskrit scriptures, he has come from afar to present them as tribute.
In the second year of Emperor Wu’s Tianjian era, the year of Guiwei, he arrived at the capital of Yangdu.
By imperial decree, Saṃghavarman was ordered to collaborate with him on the translation,
and they subsequently produced three scriptures, including the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā*.
Although his work as a translator was not yet proficient in the Liang language, the phrasing of the sūtras he produced remained obscure and substantial.
The *Mañjuśrī-bhāṣita-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, one fascicle, is the second translation; it is similar to the previous [translation of the] *Māṇ*.

Regarding the *Dhāraṇī-sūtra* and the *Mañjuśrī-parivarta* from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the same edition kept at Fangyuan states that these two fascicles produced from the mandala are slightly superior to the previous ones.

The *Daśadharma-mahāyāna-sūtra* (一卷), first translated during the Putong era, is the same text as the *Daśadharma-sūtra* translated by Jueding of the Northern Wei; it is titled *The Range of All Buddhas*.
*Jiyan jing* (Sūtra of Wisdom Adornment), one fascicle; second edition, same text as the *Rufojingjie jing* (Sūtra on Entering the Buddha’s Realm) translated by Dharmaruci during the Northern Wei.
*Bajixiang jing* (Sūtra of the Eight Auspicious Ones), one fascicle; if a person hears the names of these eight Buddhas, they shall not be harmed by any demons or spirits.
Fourth edition, same text as the *Bajixiang zhou* (Spell of the Eight Auspicious Ones) and the *Baliang shenzhou* (Spell of the Eight Yang Spirits).
The *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra* (two fascicles), also known as the *Mahāmāyūrī-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, the tenth translation;
it is identical to the *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra* translated by Yijing of the Tang dynasty.
The *Śāriputra-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (one fascicle): this dhāraṇī possesses divine power; if one can maintain it, there are eight yakṣas on Mount Himavat.

The King constantly came to provide protection, fulfilling his desires according to his heart's wish. This first translation is identical in its original text to the *Amoghapāśa-hṛdaya-sūtra* (or *Anantamukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī*) translated by Zhi Qian.
It is the same as the two-fascicle *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, which is also simply titled the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.
It was translated at the Zhanyun Hall in the seventeenth year of the Tianjian era; Yuan Tanyun served as the scribe, and it was produced at Guangzhai Temple.
*Śramaṇa Fǎyún’s Detailed Determination of the Bodhisattvapitaka-sūtra*, one fascicle;
*Vimuktimārga-śāstra*, twelve fascicles (also said to be thirteen fascicles), translated at Zhānyún Guǎn in the fourteenth year of the Tiānjīn era;

*Aśokarāja-sūtra*, ten fascicles (sometimes titled with the character "Dà" [Great] added), the second translation, which shares the same source text as the *Jìn Ānqīn Yùwáng Zhuàn* but is a different translation, translated during the Tiānjīn era.
On the second day of the sixth month in the eleventh year, [this was] translated at the Shouguang Hall in Yangdu. This is recorded in the *Jianbao chang lu*.

The aforementioned ten works comprise thirty-two fascicles; their texts are all extant and are also found in the *Changfang lu* and the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*, though the number of sections and titles therein are not fully listed here.
The śramaṇa Saṃghavarman— “Saṃgha” meaning “army” (in the Liang language) and “varman” meaning “armor”—
is also called Saṃgyang.
He was a native of the kingdom of Funan.
From childhood, he was exceptionally brilliant and early on devoted himself to the Vinaya.
Although he investigated both the Sūtras and the Śāstras thoroughly, he specialized in the Abhidharma.
The Śrāvakas gradually spread their fame throughout the lands south of the sea; after they were fully established, they extensively refined the Vinaya-piṭaka.
With courageous resolve, they surveyed the various regions, delighting in the principles of conversion and edification.
Hearing that the Dharma was being propagated in the Qi kingdom, he traveled by ship to the capital.
He resided at Zhengguan Monastery as a disciple of the Indian śramaṇa Guṇabhadra,
and further studied the Vaipulya sūtras under Guṇabhadra with great diligence.
Before he had even reached maturity, he was already extensively learned and versatile,
coming to understand the scripts and languages of several countries.
It happened that the Qi calendar had fallen into ruin.
As Daoism declined,
Bo Luo consequently purified his body and mind and severed external ties; thus,
he occupied a chamber to dwell in leisure, cultivating his essential nature as his primary pursuit.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Great Liang, a search was conducted for those possessing skill and ability in the arts.
In the fifth year of the Tianjian era, he was summoned by imperial decree to the five locations of Yangdu:
Shouguang Hall, Hualin Garden, Zhengguan Monastery, Zhanyun Hall, and Funan Hall, where he engaged in the transmission and translation of scriptures.

From the *jǐng* year of the fifth year of the Tianjian era (506 CE) to the *gēngzǐ* year of the first year of the Putong era (520 CE), he translated ten works, including the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra*, all of which were based on Sanskrit manuscripts provided by Manlu Xian.

Furthermore, the *Chángfáng-lù* states that Puṇyatrāta additionally produced a five-fascicle *Aśoka-avadāna*; however, this is incorrect, as the previously mentioned *Aśoka-rāja-sūtra* is itself its biography and should not be recorded twice.
On the first day of the translation,
Emperor Wu personally attended the Dharma seat at Shouguang Hall to receive the text by pen.
Only then did he entrust the complete manuscript of the sutra to the translators.
By imperial decree, the śramaṇas Baochang, Huichao, Sengzhi, Fayun, Yuan Tanyun, and others were assembled to transcribe and edit [the text].
Their work was elegant yet substantial and well-ordered, ensuring that the tradition of translation would not fall into decline.
The Son of Heaven received him with great courtesy and honor, inviting him to serve as his personal preceptor.
The relevant authorities provided him with all necessary provisions, leading both monastics and laypeople to change their views.
Vajrabodhi did not maintain private wealth; he used the offerings he received to establish monasteries.
The Grand Marshal, Prince Hong of Linchuan, treated him with great honor and respect.
In the fifth year of the Putong era, he passed away at Zhengguan Temple due to illness at the age of sixty-five.

The *Jīnglù yìxiàng* (Diverse Phenomena of Sūtras and Vinaya) in fifty fascicles was compiled by imperial decree in the fifteenth year of the Tiānjiān era; it is said that this included a catalog in five additional fascicles, making fifty-five in total. At present, the catalog is missing, leaving only the fifty fascicles. As for the titles of its compiled sections, there appears to be no other matter [to note]. This is recorded in the *Bǎochàng lù* and the *Chángfáng lù*. The *Bǐqūní zhuàn* (Biographies of Bhikṣuṇīs) in four fascicles, containing newly compiled records of the conduct of bhikṣuṇīs from the four dynasties of Jìn, Sòng, Qí, and Liáng, has also been added to the catalog. These two works, totaling fifty-four fascicles, both have their original texts extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Baochang was a monk of Zhuangyan Monastery in the capital of Yangdu.
His secular surname was Feng, and he was a native of Wu Commandery.
He was a preeminent disciple of the Vinaya Master Sengyou.
Possessing broad learning and extensive literary talent, he had few equals;
Emperor Wu held him in the highest esteem and veneration.
During the Tianjian era, he was repeatedly commissioned by imperial edict to compile and collect [texts], all of which met with the Emperor's approval.
In the year Jingshen of the fifteenth year, he once again...
The imperial compilation *Jīnglù yìxiàng* (A Collection of Extraordinary Phenomena from the Sūtras and Vinaya) in one fascicle;
furthermore, among the catalogues of Fang [Xuanling], there are seven works including the *Nǐzhuàn* (Biographies of Nuns) in four fascicles and the *Míngsēngzhuàn* (Biographies of Eminent Monks).
It was not included here because it is missing from the canon and thus not discussed.
All other [texts] are fully contained in the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks).

The *Wufen biquni jieben* (Five-Part Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra), one fascicle, also called the *Mishasai lü* (Mahīśāsaka Vinaya) or the *Shami ni jieben* (Śrāmaṇerī Prātimokṣa Sūtra), is recorded in the *Baoshang lu*. This one work, in one fascicle, its manuscript currently exists.
The śramaṇa Shi Minghui was a monk of Jianchu Monastery in the capital of Yangdu.
He was rigorous and austere in his observance of the precepts and studied the Mahīśāsaka school.
During the Song dynasty, Huiguo translated the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya;
however, it only produced the Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra and lacked the Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa.
Consequently, in the third year of the Putong era of Emperor Wu, the Renyin year, [he undertook the task].
From within the *Mahāvinaya*, one fascicle of the Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa was extracted; this is the version currently in use. The compiler stated:

"Upon examining these precepts, following the *saṃvara-śikṣāpada* (rules of training), there are no *saptadharmāḥ saṃghāvaśeṣa* (seven methods for settling disputes). Although the original text is brief, according to the meaning, they ought to be inserted. How could it be that when the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha has a dispute, it is not settled? For the formal text of those rules is identical to that of the Bhikṣus. Thus, the fortieth [section] of that Vinaya states: "Among the *śaikṣa-dharmas*, with the sole exception of 'not trampling grass or water,' the seven methods for settling disputes and the *anuvartana-dharmas* (rules of conformity) are all the same as those of the Bhikṣus. It is illogical and unreasonable for that master not to insert them.

*Mahāyāna-śikhara-rāja-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Vimala-putra-sūtra*. This third edition was translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty. It is said that the *Cunda-bhadra-pāpa-dāraka-sūtra* and others are the same text as this. See the *Chángfáng-lù* and the *Xù gāosēng-zhuàn*. This one work in one fascicle currently exists.
Prince Candraprabha was the son of the King of Ujjayinī in Central India.

This country of Ujjayinī is sometimes said to be in Southern India and at other times in Western India; it has not yet been definitively settled. Alternatively, as this kingdom lies on the southwestern border of Central India, close to the south, the traditional accounts have become confused and uncertain. From birth, he was brilliant and gifted, intuitively grasping the most profound and subtle truths.
He specialized in the study of Buddhist scriptures and was particularly adept at their doctrinal principles.
He had a profound understanding of phonology and was also skilled in local dialects.
Previously, during the Xinghe era of the Eastern Wei dynasty, he translated three sections of scripture.
During the Daming era of the Liang dynasty, he traveled from Wei to the Liang capital, where Emperor Wu invited him to remain.
By imperial decree, he was appointed to oversee all foreign diplomatic missions.
Thereupon, he translated the *Cūḍāmaṇi-rāja-sūtra* in one fascicle.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* consists of seven fascicles (or six) and twenty-two chapters.

It was translated during the first year of the Chengsheng era at Zhengguan Temple and at the residence of Yang Xiong. The four-fascicle version produced by An Shigao during the Liuliang period contained eighteen chapters;

Paramārtha subsequently translated four additional chapters to bring the total to twenty-two, forming seven fascicles. This version is currently included in the *Shanfan yulu*. No [other] version exists.

The above is based on two fascicles of the sutra. On the eighth day of the ninth month of the third year of the Shaotai era of the Liang dynasty (the Dingchou year), at the request of Liu Wentai, the Interior Historian of Nan-kang in Pingguo County, this translation was produced.
Regarding the postscript to the currently extant sutra, Master Fang states that the version appearing to have been produced during the Chen dynasty is incorrect;
for in none of the various dynastic calendars is there a "third year of Shaotai," as found in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* manuscript within the *Bielu*.

*Jinwu jielun* (Discourse on the Absence of Verses), one fascicle; Sengfang states it was translated in the fourth year of the Taiching era. Upon examining various chronological records, the Taiching era does not reach a fourth year;

all entries below this point are consistent with the *Deciding Treasury Treatise* (*Niśchaya-arthabhidharma-śāstra*). Among its three fascicles, there are characters written in the Liang script, indicating it was translated during the Liang dynasty;
its phrasing and sentences were produced by Paramārtha. *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna), one fascicle; its initial appearance is [as follows].
The version translated by Śikṣānanda of the Tang dynasty is based on the same original text.

On the tenth day of the ninth month of the second year of the Chengsheng era (the Guiyou year), it was first produced at Jianxing Temple in Hengzhou, with Upaśūnya and others serving as oral translators, while the śramaṇas Zhizheng and others took up their pens and composed the preface.
As seen in the preface to the *Yathārtha-śāstra*, there is one fascicle of the *Yathārtha-śāstra*, the original title of which is given as the *Yathārtha-śāstra*. And...

From the *Zhinanpin* (Chapter on Refutation): It is recorded that in the fourth year of the Taicheng era, he produced one fascicle of the *Renwang Banruo Jing* (Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra).

In the third year of the Chengsheng era, at Baotian Temple in Yuzhang, he translated it; this third edition is identical in its original text to those produced by Dharmarakṣa and others during the Western Jin dynasty.

He also translated one fascicle of the *Mile Xiasheng Jing* (Sūtra of Maitreya’s Descent), which was translated in the third year of the Chengsheng era at Baotian Temple in Yuzhang. This is the third [edition].
The five fascicles of the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Five-Volume Treatise on the Stages) translated by [Paramārtha] share the same original text as those translated by Kumārajīva;

they correspond to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* translated during the Tang dynasty. Having obtained five fascicles, his work was interrupted due to the upheavals of the times, as recorded in the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
In the fourth year of the Tàiqīng era, he translated for twenty virtuous śramaṇas, including Bǎojióng, at the residence of Lù Yuánzhé, the Magistrate of Fùchūn.
*Zhonglun* (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā), one fascicle; Fang states it was produced in the fourth year of the Taicheng era. *Shishen fenshilun* (Traiśatika-vibhaṅga-śāstra), one fascicle;
Fang states it was produced in the fourth year of the Taicheng era. The above, totaling eleven works in twenty-four fascicles, are all recorded in the *Changfang Neidian Lu* and other catalogs.
As for the *Rushi lun* (Tattvasiddhi-śāstra), the first six sections comprising fifteen fascicles are currently extant within the *Renwang jing*.
The final five sections, totaling nine fascicles, are missing.
[Translated by] the śramaṇa Paramārtha,
which in the Liang language means "True Meaning."
Some call him Kulanātha;
this means "Reliance on Kin.
Both are names in the Sanskrit language.
He was originally a native of Ujjayinī in Western India,
of Brahmin lineage.
His conduct was exceptionally clear and bright, and his character was pure and dignified.
His spirit was as fresh and transcendent as the wind god, naturally detached from the mundane;
there were no sections of the vast Tripitaka that he did not hold dear in his heart.
In various arts and extraordinary skills, he was particularly well-versed and practiced.
Although he followed the harmonious principles of the Buddha and was renowned for his mastery of the Way,
he traveled far across hardships, undaunted by either level ground or perilous terrain.
Having journeyed through various kingdoms, he finally settled in Central India.
During the Datong era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, he issued an imperial decree for Zhang Si and others of the Zhisheng Office to escort the envoys from Funan back to their country,
while simultaneously dispatching a mission of its own to establish diplomatic relations.
In the kingdom of Magadha in Central India,
he invited a virtuous Tripiṭaka master and sought Mahāyāna treatises, the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra*, and other works.
Paramārtha had long heard of his conduct, his methods of transformation, and his observance of the rites of sages and worthies.
He sought out and selected renowned masters to benefit the common people.
Thereupon, that kingdom sent Zhendi (Paramārtha) along with various sūtras and śāstras to respectfully receive the imperial decree;
having long harbored this intention in his heart, he was filled with joy upon hearing the command.
He arrived at the South Sea on the fifteenth day of the eighth month in the twelfth year of the Datong era.
Traveling along perilous and vast waters, he remained delayed for two springs.
It was not until the intercalary eighth month of the second year of the Taicheng era that he finally reached the capital city.
Emperor Wu personally expressed his reverence and enshrined [the scriptures] in the Baoyun Hall, making offerings with utmost sincerity.
The Emperor desired to transmit and translate the teachings of the Dharma, having no envy for the era of Qin;
he produced new texts that surpassed those of the Qi period.
During the Qi dynasty, as the Way declined and the barbarian invaders from the Jie tribe took advantage of the chaos to oppress the land, the Dharma fell into ruin.
Unable to fulfill his mission of propagation and exposition, he traveled eastward to China.
He then went to Fuchun, where he was received by the Magistrate Lu Yuanzhe, who established a center for him to inquire into and transmit the Vinaya.
He invited more than twenty eminent śramaṇas, including Baojing,
to translate the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; however, having completed only five fascicles,
the national crisis remained unresolved, so he temporarily set aside the work to focus on the *Tongzhuan*.
In the first year of the Dàbǎo era, he was requested by Hóu Jǐng to return to the imperial palace for veneration.
At that time, military conflict and famine were rampant, and the Dharma was on the verge of collapse.
Fortunately, Emperor Yuán ascended the throne, and the world became peaceful and prosperous under his reign.
He then stayed at Zhengguan Temple in Jinling,
where he translated the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* together with more than twenty people, including Master Yuan.
In the second month of the third year, he returned to Yuzhang.
He then traveled to Xinwu and Shixing.
Later, he followed Xiao Dabaodao across the mountain passes to Nankang;
in each place, he engaged in translation according to local needs, remaining restless and without a fixed residence.
The scriptures and treatises translated by Paramārtha during the Liang dynasty total eleven works.
At the end of the Liang dynasty, he entered the Chen dynasty and further produced scriptures and treatises as described below.
The *Chángfáng nèidiǎn lù* and other catalogs record eighteen treatises in one fascicle, also attributed to the translation of Paramārtha.
Now, upon examining the wording, this is not a literal translation.
Since it is identical in substance to the original text of the school's tenets (nikāyabheda), it ought not to be reproduced here.
Therefore, I have deleted it, as is described in the separate record.
Furthermore, there are six works totaling twenty-six fascicles, including the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-śāstra* and others, all of which were composed by Paramārtha.
These have likewise been deleted [from the canon].

The *Chángfáng nèidiǎn lù* and other catalogs further state that in the fifteenth year of the Tiānjiān era, Zhūdàoxián presented one fascicle of the *Uruvilvā-sūtra*, simply recording it as "presented to the Emperor" without clarifying the details; thus, it has been compiled in the *Yílù* (Record of Doubtful Works) and is not included here in this deletion.

The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) consists of fourteen volumes: one volume for the preface and catalog, and thirteen volumes for the biographies, totaling fourteen volumes. It was compiled in the eighteenth year of the Tianjian era. It is recorded in the *Changfang lu* and the *Neidian lu*. This single work comprises fourteen volumes, and its manuscript is currently extant. The śramaṇa Shi Huijiao, whose clan and lineage are unknown, was a native of Shangyu in Kuaiji.
His learning encompassed both Buddhist and secular texts, and he was extensively trained in the sutras and vinaya.
Residing at Jiaxiang Temple, he propagated the Dharma during the spring and summer and engaged in composition during the autumn and winter.
He authored commentaries on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
Furthermore, because the eminent monks compiled by Master Chōng were largely redundant and superfluous,
he consequently established a precedent and composed the *Guǎngzhù Gāosēng Zhuàn* (Extended Biographies of Eminent Monks) in one volume.
It begins from the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Míng of the Hàn dynasty and concludes with the eighteenth year of the Tiānjiān era of the Liáng dynasty.
In total, there were four hundred and fifty-three years and two hundred and fifty-seven individuals;
additionally, there were two hundred and thirty-nine persons recorded as collateral or supplementary entries.
In total, there were four hundred and ninety-six individuals.
Their virtuous deeds and achievements were categorized into ten major sections;
the preface briefly states:
Previous authors, perhaps finding the account too voluminous, have pruned it of its details;
consequently, many of the wondrous traces of his journey have been omitted and excised.
This is because they regarded him merely as a renunciant who visited kings while residing in their realms.
One ought to be haughty and keep oneself at a distance, soaring aloft and standing alone in excellence, seeking to decline honors and renounce attachments;
it was originally with the intent of inspiring the world that one is deemed a worthy man.
If such as these are not discussed, what on earth is there to record?
Furthermore, it is said that the compilations of previous generations mostly refer to them as "famous monks.
I humbly believe there is a distinction between being "famous" and being "exalted.
As for those whose true practice remains hidden, they are exalted but not famous; whereas those with meager virtue who merely adapt to the times are famous but not exalted.
Those who are renowned but not eminent were originally not recorded;
those who are eminent but not renowned are now fully included in this record.
Therefore, I have omitted their names and sounds, substituting them with the character "eminent" (gāo).
I have carefully examined the principles and examples of this biography; its literary style is elegant and refined.
It is truly worthy of being transmitted for eternity as an enduring model.

Within the *Mahābuddhanāma-sūtra* in sixteen fascicles, the title is simply given as the *Buddhanāma-sūtra*, or in thirty-two fascicles, or in fourteen fascicles. This latter version is commonly known among the people of the time as the *Mārīcī-rākṣasa-buddhanāma-avadāna*.
It appeared during the Liang dynasty, though the name and lineage of its compiler remain unknown.

The *Kaiyuan lu* states that it appears to have been compiled recently by taking the twelve-fascicle version translated by Dharmarakṣa and reorganizing it through a process of selection and synthesis.
From among these, one takes the titles of various sūtras;
subsequently, one takes the names of pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats from various sūtras,
thereby establishing the sequence of the Three Jewels.
In total there are thirty-two items.
Following the worship of the Three Jewels, there is always a confession.
Following the confession, the *Mātaraharākṣasa* apocryphal scripture is further cited and placed therein.
Later, however, vulgar and worldly language was mixed with the sacred words.
Although the original scripture was authentic, because it had been corrupted by such false interpolations,
this comparative analysis was compiled within the "Record of Forged Works that Confuse the Authentic," and it was not permitted to enter the canon.
From this point on, for several hundred years, the sagely Emperor Wen,
with his brilliant intelligence, inherited the sacred entrustment;
he venerated and propagated the teachings of Śākyamuni, extolling the True Vehicle.
Having personally verified the text, it was permitted to be included in the Imperial Canon.
On the twenty-third day of the tenth month in the fifteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, an imperial decree was issued stating:
"The *Mahābuddhanāmasūtra*, one volume consisting of sixteen fascicles."
Ma Chengqian, General of the Left and Right Gate Guards and Director of the Office of Palace Attendants, memorialized:
"The aforementioned scripture has not yet been included in the catalog of the Tripitaka.
By Imperial Decree, it is appropriate that the relevant authorities be ordered to append it to the catalog."
Furthermore, the old catalog states:
"Upon examining those who compiled [this work], they were entirely mediocre and ignorant.
For instance, the *Biography of Faxian* from the fourth fascicle is listed here among the 'Dharma Treasures' (*Fǎbǎo*) despite not being a sutra."
This work is originally not a sūtra;
its inclusion among the treasures of the Dharma is a most egregious error.
An ancient proverb says:
Although they were conversant with the Tripitaka, they remained confused when confronted with specific matters, treating biographies as if they were scriptures; such was the case.
Therefore, I request that these compiled biographies be excluded from the canon.
Furthermore, the old catalog states that as it says in the ninth fascicle: "Namo Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.

*Namo* is translated into Chinese as "homage" (*namu*). *Pūrṇa* is translated as "fully complete" (*juman*). *Maitrāyaṇī* is translated as "Compassionate Mother" (*cizi*). The son of this [mother] is called "Full-Compassion-Son" (*man-cizi*) in the translation by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang, the Great Sage of the Great Tang.
In the sutra, these two are divided; I now request that they be addressed together.
Furthermore, "Namo Ānanda Rāhula" refers to two individuals;
in the sutra, they are combined as one; I now request that they be separated into two.
What fault could there be in this?
We humbly request that those of such a kind be corrected,
so as to accord with the expectations of the people below and fulfill the will of Heaven above.

Included in the *Zhenyuan xinding shijiao mulu* (Newly Compiled Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings of the Zhenyuan Era), it is recorded as having been transmitted during the Liang dynasty and appended to the Liang period.

The *Xinji shituo zhujing* (New Collection of Translated Scriptures of Unknown Origin) contains one fascicle of the *Molizhitian jing* (Sūtra of Mārīcī), also known as the *Xiaomolizhitian jing* (Minor Sūtra of Mārīcī).
This is a partial variant translation of the *Mārīcī-sūtra* found at the beginning of the tenth fascicle of the *Tuoluoni ji jing* (Collection of Dhāraṇī Sūtras).
*The Scripture of the Word-Spell King*, one fascicle; second edition, identical in substance to the *Scripture of the Six Spell Kings*.

*The Scripture of the Questions of Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva to the Buddha*, one fascicle; also titled *The Scripture of the Dhāraṇī Spells of the Seven Buddhas Asked by Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva*, and also titled *The Scripture of the Divine Spells of the Seven Buddhas*.
Its first edition was identical to the Sui dynasty translation of the *Tathāgata-upāya-kauśalya*.
The *Dhāraṇī-sūtra* (same original text as the *Sūtra of the Names of Three Thousand Buddhas of the Three Kalpas*, three fascicles):
the *Sūtra of the Names of One Thousand Buddhas of the Past Adornment Kalpa*, Fascicle I; the *Sūtra of the Names of One Thousand Buddhas of the Present Auspicious Kalpa*, Fascicle II;

and the *Sūtra of the Names of One Thousand Buddhas of the Future Constellation Kalpa*, Fascicle III. According to the *Chángfáng Rùzànglù*, these were originally three separate texts, but they have now been combined into one.
*The Sūtra of the Bhumili-mantra* (one fascicle), or alternatively without the word "sūtra";
*The Āṭavaka-dhāraṇī of the Great General of Ghosts and Spirits to be Recited for the Buddha* (one fascicle), also simply called the *Āṭavaka-mantra-sūtra*;
*The Amitābha-dundubhisvara-rāja-dhāraṇī* (one fascicle); *The Mahāsamantabhadra-dhāraṇī* (one fascicle).
*Mahāsaptaratnadhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Ṣaḍakṣarī-mahādhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle;
*Upāsikā-āntiśā-siṃhanāda-nītārtha-sūtra*, one fascicle;
*Bodhisattva-pañcadharma-pratideśana*, one fascicle—also titled *Bodhisattva-pañcadharma-pratideśana-sūtra*; *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha*, one fascicle; Mahāyāna.
*Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*, one fascicle, composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; seen in the catalog of the Mahāyāna Temple during the Chen dynasty.

Its initial publication was identical to the *Mahāyāna-pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* translated in the Tang dynasty. Of the fourteen works totaling twenty-five fascicles listed above, the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* is excluded [from this count].
The remainder were all included in the canon; however, they are missing from the catalogs of the Changfang school and others that record works of unknown translators.
Upon examining their phrasing and terminology, it is clear they are not from a remote antiquity.
Therefore, they are compiled here as belonging to the late Liang period, noted as works of the Liang era whose origins are lost.

The Northern Wei dynasty, of the Yuan clan, initially established its capital at Heng’an, later moved south to Luoyang, and subsequently to Ye; it is also called the Later Wei. It began in the first year of Huangshi of Emperor Daowu, the Jingshen year (the twenty-first year of the Taiyuan era of the Eastern Jin), and ended in the eighth year of Wuding of Emperor Xiaojing of the Liang, the Gengwu year.

In total, there were thirteen emperors over a period of one hundred and fifty-five years. Five emperors resided at Heng'an until the eighteenth year of the Dàhé era of Emperor Wénxìng; seven emperors resided at Luoyang; and two sovereigns resided at Yè.
A total of eighty-three works in two hundred and seventy-four fascicles were translated by twelve individuals, both monastics and laypeople;
among these, seventy-three works in two hundred and fifty-five fascicles are extant, while ten works in nineteen fascicles are missing.
The Śramaṇa Shi Huijiao: one collection in thirteen fascicles, consisting of compiled scriptures; the Śramaṇa Shi Tanyao:

three collections in seven fascicles, consisting of scriptural commentaries and biographies; the Śramaṇa Jikaya: five collections in nineteen fascicles, consisting of a compilation of scriptures, treatises, and biographies;
the Śramaṇa Tanmaliuzhi: three collections in eight fascicles, consisting of scriptures; the Śramaṇa Shi Fachang: one collection in one fascicle, consisting of a scripture.
The śramaṇa Ratnamati translated nine volumes of treatises from three schools;
the śramaṇa Bodhiruci translated one hundred and one volumes of sutras and treatises from thirty schools; the śramaṇa Buddhasanta translated eleven volumes of sutras and treatises from ten schools;
and the brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci translated ninety-two volumes of precepts and treatises from eighteen schools.
The *Prince Candraprabha Tripiṭaka* in seven fascicles; the *Śramaṇa Vimokṣaprajñā*’s five treatises in five fascicles;
the *Śramaṇa Dharmaprajñā*’s one treatise in one fascicle;

and the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* in thirteen, fifteen, sixteen, or seventeen fascicles—also known as the *Sūtra of the Causes and Conditions of the Wise and the Foolish*—are seen in the Canon.
The *Hui-sòng-qí-lù* (Record of the Song and Qi Dynasties) and the *Sēng-yòu-lù* (Record of Sēngyòu), comprising one collection in thirteen fascicles,
are extant. [Compiled by] the śramaṇa Śākya Huìjué—
also known as Tánjué.
Yao said:
"Tanjiao was a native of Liangzhou.
His stature reached the heavens, and his spirit and character were clear and enlightened."
His observance of the precepts was pure and resolute, and his wisdom was so penetrating that it discerned the subtle mysteries.
He obtained a Sanskrit manuscript of the sutra in the kingdom of Khotan.
This was during the sixth year of the Taiping Zhenjun era of Emperor Taiwu, the year of Yiyou (485 CE).
Returning from Khotan to the Kingdom of Gaochang, he translated the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Xiányújīng*) in one fascicle together with the śramaṇa Wéidé.

I have consulted Jingmài’s *Jīngtú* (Illustrations of the Scriptures), which cites the record by the Liang dynasty śramaṇa Sēngyòu regarding the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, stating: [text follows].
There were eight monks in total, including the śramaṇa Shi Tande from Hexi,
who resolved to travel abroad to seek out the scriptures at the Great Monastery in Khotan.
There they encountered those observing the Pañcavārṣika festival.
In the language of Han, this refers to the "Assemblies of All the Great Multitudes" occurring every five years.
The various scholars of the Tripiṭaka each propagate the jewel of the Dharma;

they expound the sūtras and lecture on the vinaya according to their respective duties. The eight classes of saṃgha, such as those of virtue, listen to the teachings in accordance with their conditions.
Thereupon, they vied with one another in practicing the foreign sounds and interpreting them according to Chinese meanings;
through diligent reflection, they mastered the translations and each recorded their inquiries.
He returned to Gaochang and compiled [the texts] into a single collection. Subsequently,
he crossed the shifting sands and brought them to Liangzhou.
At that time, the śramaṇa Shi Huiming was a master of the Hexi school;
his spiritual practice was profound and vast,
and he fully mastered the Vaipulya scriptures.

I believe that the source recorded in this sutra lies in the *avadāna* (parables); what is elucidated by these parables concurrently presents good and evil in contrast, which is precisely the distinction between the wise and the foolish.
In previous generations, many such parables were already transmitted within the scriptures.
Therefore, based on these events, the title was changed to *The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Xianyu jing*).

Two fascicles (or four fascicles) of the *Daji yi shenzhou jing* are found in the *Fashang lu*; one fascicle of the *Jingdu sanmei jing* is the fourth edition found in the *Zhu Daozu lu* and the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*; and four fascicles of the *Fofa zang zhuan* are the second edition found in the *Bodhiruci lu* and the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*. The above three works comprise seven fascicles. One work, the two-fascicle *Jiyi zhujing*, is extant; two works comprising five fascicles, including the *Jingtu jing*, are missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Tanyao was a man of unknown origin.
Having left home in his youth, he was firm and steadfast in his practice; his character was refined and his conduct was simple and restrained.
During the Huiping era of the Wei dynasty, he served as the Northern Tai Zhaohuantong.
He pacified and gathered the monastic community, skillfully winning their hearts.
He resided at Tongle Monastery within the Heng'an Stone Caves.
This was constructed by the Emperor of Wei.
Located thirty li northwest of Heng’an, it was carved into a stone cliff on the northern face of Mount Wuzhou, where a Buddhist temple was established.
It is named Lingyan.
Its largest grottoes are over twenty zhang in height and can accommodate approximately three thousand people;
the images carved upon their facades exhaust every artistry and splendor.
The niches vary in shape, striking both humans and spirits with awe;
they are arranged side by side for more than thirty li.
At the eastern end, a monastery constantly provides sustenance for a thousand monks.
The inscriptions on the steles currently extant have not yet been fully set forth in detail.
Previously, during the tenth year of the Taiping Zhenjun era of Emperor Taiwu, the Minister of Education Cui Hao used wicked, sycophantic, and flattering words.
He caused Emperor Taiwu to honor and revere the Daoist Kou Qianzhi, who was appointed as the Celestial Master (Tianshi).
The Emperor held the followers of Laozi in high esteem while treating the Śākyas with contempt, destroying monasteries and pagodas.
It was not until the gengyin year that Emperor Taiwu was stricken by a pestilential illness, at which point he finally attained awakening.
Furthermore, the Chan Master Bazu came to provide him with spiritual exhortation.
Feeling remorse and shame, he immediately executed Cui Hao,
burying him in a public marketplace and using his mouth as a latrine to defile him before the multitude.
In the year of Renchen, when Great Wu passed away and his grandson Wen Cheng ascended the throne,
he immediately established monasteries and searched for the scriptures;
after seven years during which the Dharma had been suppressed, the Triple Gem was restored.
Yao was filled with regret for the former decline and joy at the renewed prosperity of later times.
In the third year of the Pinghe era (the Renyin year), he gathered a community of virtuous monks at the stone cave of the Northern Terrace and,
together with the Indian śramaṇa Jñānagupta and others, translated three sections of scriptures.
The intention of later worthies was that this should circulate so as not to be interrupted.
One fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Bodhisattva-daśabhūmi-sūtra*, the fifth [translation] produced, is identical in text to Kumārajīva’s *Bodhicittotpāda-alaṃkāra-sūtra*;
this is seen in the *Shixing lu* and the *Daohui Songqi lu*. It extols the merits of all Buddhas.

The *Dejing* (Sūtra on Virtue) in three fascicles, also titled *Jizhufuhua jing* (Sūtra Collecting the Flowers of All Buddhas), also simply titled *Jihua jing* (Sūtra of Collected Flowers), or alternatively titled *Xianzai ming jing* (Sūtra of Present Names);
sometimes in four fascicles. The third edition, produced by Kumārajīva and others, is the same text as that seen in Daohui’s *Song Qi lu*.
The *Fangbian xin lun* (Treatise on the Expedient Mind), in one or two fascicles, comprising four chapters; the second edition, produced during the Eastern Jin.
The *Juechuzhe tongben jian dao hui* (The Wisdom of the Path of Seeing Shared by the Awakened) was translated during the Song and Qi dynasties;

according to the *Song Qi lu*, the *Sengyou lu*, and the *Fufa zang yinyuan zhuan*, it consists of six fascicles—though some versions omit the characters "yinyuan" (causal conditions)—and is also referred to as the *Zangjing*. It may also appear in four or two fascicles.
This third edition, found in the *Song Qi lu*, shares the same original text as the version translated by Zhiyan of the Song and Tan Yao of the Wei, and is likewise recorded therein.
Sengyou’s Record states that the *Saṃyukta-ratnapiṭaka-sūtra* was originally thirteen fascicles, though this is not yet clear;
currently, only eight fascicles remain, or perhaps these were divided into thirteen. This is seen in Daohui’s *Records of the Song and Qi Dynasties* and Sengyou’s *Record*.
The above comprises five works totaling nineteen fascicles.
The śramaṇa Jikaya (also known as He-shi in the Wei language) was a man from the Western Regions.
Wandering to transform others was his concern, and guiding sentient beings was his heart’s purpose.
In the second year of the Yanxing era of Emperor Xiaowen (the Renzi year),
he translated five scriptures, including the *Mahāvaipulya Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, together with the śramaṇas Zhaoxuan and Tanyao.

Liu Xiaobiao recorded the dictation. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-saṃnipāta-mudrā-praveśa-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* in five fascicles was translated in the first year of the Zhengshi era. The *Avataṃsaka-parivāra-sūtra* and the *Tathāgata-vyūha-jñāna-āloka-sarva-buddha-viṣaya-praveśa-sūtra* in two fascicles—also known as the *Tathāgata-sarva-buddha-viṣaya-praveśa-sūtra*—were translated at the Baima Monastery in the second year of the Jingming era; this is the first translation, identical in content to the *Sarva-buddha-viṣaya-jñāna-vyūha-sūtra* by Saṃghavarman of the Liang dynasty. The *Suvarṇahariṇa-rāja-sūtra* in one fascicle was initially translated by Gautama Dharmakṣema; it was re-examined later by Bodhiruci. According to Fashang’s catalog, these three works comprise eight fascicles in total: the first two consist of seven fascicles and are extant, while the latter one consists of one fascicle and is missing.
The śramaṇa Dharmaruci;
in Wei it is translated as Fǎxī (Dharma-Desire),
also called Fǎlè (Dharma-Joy).
A native of South India,
he left his home to enter the monastic path and became particularly renowned for his transmission of the Vinaya-piṭaka.
Devoted to the propagation of the Way, he moved others through his spiritual resonance.
During the reign of Emperor Xuanwu, he traveled to Luoyang to propagate the Dharma.
From the second year of Jingming (Xinsi) until the fourth year of Zhengshi (Dinghai),
he translated three scriptures, including the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra*, for Emperor Xuanwu.
Śramaṇa Dàobǎo recorded it in writing.
It is seen in the *Chángfáng lù* and other records.

The *Biànyì zhǎngzhězǐ jīng*, one fascicle—also called the *Biànyì zhǎngzhězǐ suǒwèn jīng* or simply the *Zhǎngzhě Biànyì jīng*—is seen in the *Fǎshàng lù*. This one work, consisting of one fascicle, its original manuscript currently exists.
The śramaṇa Shi Fanchang was a man of unknown origins.

He also translated the *Bianyi jing* (Sūtra of the Meaningful Discourse) in one fascicle during the reign of Emperor Xuanwu of the Northern Wei dynasty at Luoyang. The compiler of the scripture states: "I have carefully consulted the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) and other records, all of which state that when Dao’an went forth as a monk during the Jin dynasty, after several years he requested scriptures from his teacher. His teacher first bestowed upon him the *Bianyi jing* in one fascicle, consisting of approximately five thousand words, which Dao’an recited from memory upon a single reading. Furthermore, since the lost translations of Master Dao’an also include its title, based on this, the *Bianyi jing* had already been circulating in the world during the Eastern Jin; how could it be said that it was only produced by Fanchang during the reign of Emperor Xuanwu of the Wei?"
*The Treatise on the Lotus Sutra*, one fascicle, composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; also known as the *Dharma-puṣpa-sūtra-śāstra*.
Transmitted by the Palace Attendant Cui Guang, Senglang, and others, who recorded it by dictation. It appears in the *Changfang lu*.
Its initial publication was largely identical to the translation by Bodhiruci, with only minor differences. It is titled: *The Upadeśa of the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma*.

The *Jing yicheng baoxing lun* (Treatise on the Ultimate One Vehicle Nature of the Jewel), four fascicles—also known as the *Baoxing fenbie qicheng sengshang lun* (Treatise on the Analysis of the Seven Vehicles and the Superiority of the Sangha according to the Jewel Nature)—appears in two or five fascicles;
it was produced at the residence of Zhao Xin and is recorded in the second section of the *Baochang lu*.

Its translation is the same text as that produced by Bodhiruci. The *Baoji jing lun* (Treatise on the Ratnakūṭa Sūtra), four fascicles, is the second production, identical to that produced by Bodhiruci.
The *Mahāyāna-ratnakūṭa-sūtra-śāstra* by [Vasubandhu] is recorded as being of the same text in Baochang’s catalogue.
Of the three sections totaling nine fascicles mentioned above, the first two sections comprising five fascicles are extant, while the third section of four fascicles is missing.
The śramaṇa Ratnamati, also called Bati;
in the Wei language, this means "Precious Intention."
A native of Central India,
he was exceptionally learned and proficient in both principle and practice;
he could recite approximately one hundred million verses from the scriptures of the Tripiṭaka.
The verses consist of thirty-two characters.
He was particularly clear regarding the intent of Chan meditation, which lies in traveling to convert others.
In the fifth year of the Zhengshi era of Emperor Xuanwu, the Wuzi year, he first arrived at the capital of Luoyang and subsequently translated three works, including the *Dharmapada-śāstra*.
The śramaṇa Saṅgharāta, Jueyi, Cui Guang, and others acted as scribes.
On the day the scripture was being translated in the Inner Palace of Luoyang,
Bodhiruci transmitted the original text.
Ratnaśānti assisted him. Subsequently,
these three virtuous masters followed rumors and each transmitted their teacher’s practices without consulting one another.
The Emperor, considering the grandeur of the propagation of the Dharma, briefly outlined the details and issued an edict for the three locations to each complete their translations;
these were then compared and collated.
Among them, there were omissions and mutual discrepancies.
As for the textual sources and their underlying principles, they were originally composed by different authors; later generations compiled them together to form a complete collection.

This is why works such as the *Fahua lun*, the *Baoji lun*, and the *Baoxing lun* each exist in two versions, as seen in the records of Baochang and others. Initially, the śramaṇa Baoyi was distinguished by his profound grasp of the divine principle; he mastered the Wei terminology and propagated it throughout every corner of the land.
The Emperor frequently ordered him to lecture on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
As he expounded and interpreted it, profound meanings were constantly brought forth.
One day, while he was seated upon the high throne,
Suddenly, there appeared a figure holding a ceremonial tablet and bearing a name-list, appearing like a high official.
He said,
"I have come by the command of the Heavenly Emperor to invite the Dharma Master to lecture on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra."
The Master said,
"Since this Dharma assembly has not yet concluded,
please wait until the sutra text is finished; then I shall comply with your command."

"Although the Dharma assembly cannot be established by the patron alone, it also requires the *dougao*, the incense-burner, the *weina*, and the chanting of *fanbai*; you may request that these be settled.
The messenger then acted according to these instructions.
He saw that the monks were preaching, and as the religious service was about to conclude,
he again saw the former messenger say,
"I have come down by the command of the Heavenly Emperor to welcome you."
Thereupon, with a smile and a serene countenance, he addressed the assembly to bid them farewell.
Suddenly, he passed away while seated upon his Dharma throne;
four monks, including the *Dujiang*, also died at that same moment.
Whatever he heard or saw, he marveled at as something unprecedented.

Regarding the *Viyāsaparipṛcchā-sūtra* in two fascicles, the catalogs of Sengchang and others all state that it was translated by Baoyi in Luoyang; however, examining the preface to the sutra now, it states that it was translated by Gautama Prajñāruci in the capital of Ye in the fourth year of the Taihe era, and it has therefore been moved here into the catalog of Gautama [Prajñāruci]. Regarding the twelve-fascicle commentary on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the note states: "The initial translation was not yet refined; the Wei term for 'receptacle world' (*bhājana-loka*) was translated as 'cup-like world.'"

Later, while entering the hall, he saw various venerable elders and disciples all requesting vessels; when they were given alms bowls and bags in turn, he realized that "vessel" (*bhājana*) was a collective term.
He subsequently changed [the name] to the "Vessel World" (*bhājanaloka*).
This *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* is recorded by both the Chángfáng and other catalogs as having been translated by Ratnamati at two separate locations.
However, according to Cúi Guāng’s preface to the treatise, it states that Bodhiruci and Ratnamati were together in the palace halls of Luoyang when the two of them translated it jointly.
Buddhasanta transmitted these words, which the Emperor personally recorded in two catalogs; however, their titles appear to be logically untenable.

Now, they have been merged into a single volume within the catalog of Bodhiruci. There is one scroll titled *The Incense Formula of Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva*, containing fifty methods in total; as these do not belong to the Tripiṭaka teachings, they have not been included here. The three sections mentioned above have all been deleted.
*Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated in the Hu kingdom in the second year of the Yongping era;

this is the second translation. Recorded by Senglang. It is identical in text to the *Nengduan Jingang Fen* (The Section on the Diamond that Can Cut), the ninth assembly of Kumārajīva’s translation during the Qin dynasty;
as seen in the records of Fashang. *Maitreyaparipṛcchā Sūtra*, one fascicle. Second [translation].

The *Chūyō daijō hōtō yōe kyō* (Sutra on the Essential Wisdom of the Vaipulya Mahāyāna) shares the same original text as this; it was translated at the residence of Zhao Xin, with Jueyi serving as the scribe.
It is now included in the forty-first assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, where it has been renamed the "Assembly on the Eight Dharmas Asked by Maitreya Bodhisattva.

The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* (or *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*) in six fascicles was translated in Luoyang in the first year of the Shenggui era. This is the [first]... [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a bibliographic record for several sutras. The final sentence is incomplete, but based on the context of such records, it likely refers to the sequence of translations.]
The third translation, titled *Hùchí xīn* (Protecting the Mind), is identical in substance to Kumārajīva’s *Sìyì jīng* (Sūtra on Increasing Thought) though differing in its title;

this is recorded in Fǎshàng’s catalog and the *Xù gāosēng zhuàn* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks). The five-fascicle complete version of the *Shēnmì jiětuō jīng* (Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra) was first translated in Luoyang in the third year of the Yánchāng era.
Sēngbiàn acted as the scribe for the oral transmission, and it corresponds to the *Jiě shēnmì jīng* and the *Xiāngxù jiětuō jīng* translated during the Táng dynasty.
The *Jiejing* (Excerpted Sūtra) and others are all identical to the original versions seen in Fǎshàng’s record and the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*.

The ten-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, translated in the second year of the Yánchāng era, is the second translation; it is identical to the four-fascicle *Laṅkā* by Guǒdéxián of the Song dynasty and the *Mahāyāna-laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* translated during the Táng.
According to the *Continued [Biographies]*, the scribe for this translation was the monk Lǎng of Pǔmíng Temple and Dào Zhàn.

The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* records that the *Sūtra Spoken by the Great Śākyan Son of the Nirgrantha* consists of ten fascicles—alternatively titled the *Sūtra of the Prediction of What Was Not Spoken* or the *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Range of Vigorous Dharma-Gates*—and consists of eight fascicles.

It was translated for the second time at Luoyang in the first year of the Zhengguang era (520 CE) by the Prince of Runan, who served as the Governor of Sizhou; it is also known as the *Sūtra of Supernatural Powers and Transformations*.

*The Sutra of the Jewel Casket of Letterless Wisdom*, one fascicle; first translation, transcribed by Senglang; identical in content to the Tang translation of the *Mahāyāna-sūtra on Departing from Words*.
*The Sutra of the Summit of Gayā*, one fascicle; also known as the *Sutra of the Peak of Gayā*; second translation;
identical in content to Kumārajīva’s *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra*. *Sutra on Slandering the Buddha*, one fascicle; third [translation].
2. *The Sūtra of the Decisive Dhāraṇī* (translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin), one fascicle;
same text as the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra King*. 3. *The Sūtra on the Turning of Enlightenment* (first translated), one fascicle; same text as the *Sūtra of the Buddha’s Words* translated by Zhu Fahu.
