4. *The Sūtra of the Names of Buddhas*, twelve fascicles; also known as [the version] translated by Saṃghavarman and others, with Senglang receiving the transcription. Or it is said: [same text as the previous].
The *Thirteen-Volume [Sutra]* was translated at the residence of the Marquis Hu during the Zhengguang era; it is also recorded in the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*.

The *Dhāraṇī Sūtra for Protecting All Children* (one volume), also known as the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra for Requesting Sons and Daughters for the Protection of All Children*, and the *Dharma-saṃgraha Sūtra* (six, seven, or eight volumes) were translated during the Yanchang era.
In the fourth year [of the Zhengguang era], he translated the *Mopodi shouji jing* (Sūtra on the Prophecy of Māyādevī) in one fascicle at Luoyang.
In the sixth year of the Zhengguang era, he translated the *Buzeng bujian jing* (Sūtra on Neither Increasing nor Decreasing) in one fascicle at Luoyang;

the mention of it being "two fascicles" on seven sheets is an error. He also translated the *Shidi jing lun* (Treatise on the Ten Stages Sūtra) in twelve or fifteen fascicles by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
The Commentary on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* was translated at the Daji Ziting Pavilion in the fourth month of the first year of the Yongping era.

The Emperor personally received the dictation and subsequently entrusted it to the śramaṇa Sengbian and others to record. The entire treatise was completed by the beginning of summer. See the preface by Cui Guang.
The *Maitreyaparipṛcchā-sūtra-śāstra* consists of five, six, seven, or ten fascicles; it is a commentary on the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā*.
That which was asked by Puṇyālaṃkāra is the forty-first assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa*, produced at the residence of Zhao Xin in Luoyang;
it is the first translation of the four-fascicle *Mahāyāna-ratnakūṭa-sūtra-śāstra*, which shares the same original text as the *Ratnākara* but is a different translation.
The single-fascicle *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* is the fortieth assembly, the "Assembly of the Bodhisattva Samantaprabhā. The *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* [is also included therein].
*Treatise in Three Volumes*, composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; translated at the residence of the State Councilor Hu in the second year of the Yongping era, with Senglang serving as scribe.
This first translation is identical in text to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Śāstra* produced by Yi Jing of the Tang dynasty.
*Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry into the Sūtra on Bodhi*, in two volumes; also known as the *Gayāśīrṣa Śāstra*; composed by Vasubandhu.

In the second year of the Tiānpíng era, the Bodhisattva Pándòu produced at Yechéng (Yecheng) in Yíntóng Monastery the *Fǎhuájīng Lùn* (Treatise on the Lotus Sūtra) in two fascicles, with Sēngbiàn and Dàokān serving as scribes. It is titled *Miaofa lianhua jing yōubótíshē* (Upadeśa on the Lotus Sūtra of the Wondrous Dharma); alternatively, it is in one fascicle. Tánlín served as the scribe and composed the preface. This is the second production; it is the same text as that previously produced by Bǎoyì. Initial Note: The first production was made by Zhú Fódì in the fourth year of the Yǒngxiāng era of the Qi dynasty. It was translated in the capital at Zhèngshān Monastery, with Sēngyún and others serving as scribes. It consists of four fascicles and is titled *Fǎhuájīng Lùn*. It is also known as the *Fǎhuájīng Yōubótíshē*. It is also called the *Fǎhuájīng Shìyì Lùn*. It is also called the *Fǎhuájīng Shìfēn Lùn*. It is also called the *Fǎhuájīng Shìfēn Shìyì Lùn*. It is also called the *Fǎhuájīng Shìfēn Shìfēn Lùn*. It is also called the *Fǎhuájīng Shìfēn Shìfēn Shìyì Lùn*. It is also called the *Fǎhuájīng Shìfēn Shìfēn Shìfēn Lùn*. It is also called the *Fǎhuájīng Shìfēn Shìfēn Shìfēn Shìfēn Shìfēn Shìfēn Shìfēn Shìfēn Shìyì Lùn*. It is also called the *Fǎhuájīng Shìfēn Shìfēn Shìfēn Shìfēn Shìfēn Shìfēn Shìfēn Shìfēn Shìfēn Lùn*. The śramaṇa Bodhiruci, whose name was translated into Wei as Daoxi.
He was a native of North India.
He was thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka and had attained profound mastery of dhāraṇīs; his resolve was set upon propagating the Dharma so that it might flow widely to all who hear it.
Consequently, he traveled by night across the heavens on the path of the Way, arriving far away at the left of the Pamir Mountains.
In the Yongping era of the Wei dynasty, he arrived at Donghua.
Emperor Xuanwu issued an edict expressing his earnest courtesy and concern for his well-being.
Subsequently, he was stationed at the Great Yongning Monastery, where his provisions and service were most abundant.
Seven hundred Brahman monks were all provided for with complete support.
By imperial decree, Paramārtha was appointed as the primary master for the translation of the scriptures.
That monastery was originally established by Empress Dowager Hu during the first year of the Xiping era of Emperor Xiaoming.
It is located to the east of the imperial road south of the Changhe Gate in front of the palace.
In its center stands a nine-story pagoda constructed upon a raised platform of water,
reaching a height of over ninety zhang.
Above it stood a golden spire, ten zhang high;
rising a thousand chi from the ground, it could be seen from as far as a hundred li away from the terrace.
On the day the foundation was first laid, they dug down to the Yellow Springs and obtained thirty-two golden images.
The Empress Dowager considered this an auspicious omen and a sign of the faithful transmission of the Dharma.
Therefore, she commissioned a stupa of exquisite craftsmanship, exhausting the world’s finest beauty.
At the summit of the spire, a golden jeweled vase was placed, with a capacity of twenty-five hu.
The dew-receiving golden basins are arranged in eleven tiers, secured by iron chains extending from the corners.
Both the basins and the chains are adorned with golden bells as large as stone jars;
at each of the nine levels, large bells are suspended from every corner.
In total, there are one hundred and thirty such [images] from top to bottom.
On the four sides of the stupa, there are nine bays with six windows and three doors;
all have vermilion-lacquered panels and doors from which various golden bells hang.
The tiers consist of five thousand four hundred pieces.
Furthermore, golden bells and door-knobs are provided;
the Buddhist works are exquisite and refined, surpassing the craftsmanship of ordinary wood and earth.
The embroidered pillars and golden door-ornaments startle the eyes and mind;
when the high winds blow through the long nights, the bells and chimes resonate in harmony,
their tinkling sound heard for more than ten li.
To the north is the main hall, modeled after the Taiji Palace;
within it, the various images and decorations are crafted from gold, jade, pearls, and embroidery,
their exquisite workmanship being peerless in the world.
The monastic quarters extend in all directions for more than a thousand rooms;
its towers and pavilions are scattered like stars, emerging at varying heights.
They are adorned with vermilion and purple, and painted with cinnabar and azure.
Cypress, juniper, *zheng* trees, and pines were gathered together with various other plants.
The courtyard and terrace were surrounded on all sides by eaves and tiles.
To the due south stood a three-gated tower, opening in three passages and consisting of three stories.
It rises more than two hundred chi above the ground;
its appearance is like that of a celestial gate, magnificent and resplendent.
Flanking the gate stand four mighty warriors and four lions.
Adorned with gold and jade, it was magnificent and resplendent;
both the eastern and western gates were likewise decorated in this manner.
The only difference was that the north gate, which served as the main thoroughfare, was situated along a path between two double-storied pavilions.
Outside its four gates, green locust trees were planted and emerald waters flowed.
Travelers from the capital often took shelter beneath them;
the roads were cleared of flying dust, not by the moisture of lingering clouds, but as cool breezes delivered refreshing chill.
It was certainly not merely for the sake of celebrating a festive occasion that he commanded the Palace Secretary (Zhongshu Sheren) Chang Jing to compose the inscription for the temple stele;
thus it was said: "Neither the precious palaces of Mount Sumeru nor the pure abodes of Tuṣita surpass this."
The scriptures and images presented by foreign lands were all kept in this temple.
When the temple was first completed, Emperor Ming and the Empress Dowager ascended the pagoda together and viewed the palace from within as clearly as if it were in the palm of their hands.
Below it, clouds and rain gathered, while above, the sky was clear and bright.
Because one could see the affairs within the palace from there, the people were forbidden from ascending it.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa from the Western Regions named Bodhidharma.
He was a man from the kingdom of Persia who traveled from the Western Regions to visit the capital of Luoyang.
There he beheld golden platters dazzling in the sun, their radiance shining beyond the clouds, and precious bells catching the breeze, their resonance drifting out beyond the heavens.
Her songs and praises were such that they seemed the work of a divine artisan.
She claimed to be one hundred and fifty years of age and stated that she had traveled throughout various countries without exception.
Such a monastic retreat as this temple is without peer in Jambudvīpa;
even throughout the entire realm of the Buddha, there is nothing to compare with it.
Day after day, he would chant "Namo" and join his palms in reverence.
In the second year of the Xiaochang era, a great wind arose that tore off roofs and uprooted trees.
The precious vase atop the stupa was blown down by the wind and buried in the earth more than one zhang deep.
The Emperor again ordered artisans to install a new one.
In the second month of the third year of the Yongxi era, the palace was struck by a lightning bolt from heaven.
The Emperor ascended the Lingyun Terrace to observe the fire and dispatched Prince Baoru of Nanyang,
along with the Minister of the Secretariat Sun Zhi, leading one thousand men of the Feathered Forest Guard to come to his rescue.
At that time, thunder and rain brought darkness and gloom as sleet and snow fell in torrents.
At dawn, fire broke out on the eighth level;
two practitioners of the Way, unable to bear being consumed by the flames, threw themselves into the fire and died.
The flames continued in succession for another three months;
even after the pillar had entered the earth and a full year had passed, there was still a lingering scent of smoke.
In the fifth month of that year, a person arrived from Donglai Commandery and reported this.
He saw a stupa in the midst of the sea, its radiance solemn and majestic;
looking around, he beheld many such forms.
Suddenly, clouds and mist rose in confusion, and it vanished from sight.
In the seventh month, Prince Pingyang was coerced by the court attendant Huisun Chun and fled westward to Chang’an.
By the tenth month, the capital at Luoyang had been moved to Zhangye.
Previously, Paramārtha was commissioned by imperial decree to begin the translation of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra*.
At its inception, Emperor Xuanwu personally acted as the scribe for the oral transmission of the text.
Thereafter, he entrusted it to the śramaṇas Sengbian and others until the entire treatise was completed.
The Buddha-dharma flourished and thrived, with eminent and talented individuals flourishing in abundance;
they followed one another in transmitting the teachings with such diligent devotion.
Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha arrived at the capital of Ye from Luoyang in the first year of the Yongping era (the Wuzi year) of Emperor Xuancheng,
and remained there until the second year of the Tianping era (the Yimao year) of Emperor Xiaojing.
Over the course of thirty years, he successively translated thirty works in total, including sutras such as the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* and treatises such as the *Daśabhūmika*.
The Emperor further commanded the lay devotee Li Kuò to compile a catalog of these various scriptures.
Kuo’s learning permeated the profound and the fundamental; his mastery of the sūtras and śāstras was systematic and elegant, possessing a clear standard of comparison.
Thus, his record states:
"Within the quarters of the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha..."
The Sanskrit manuscripts of the sūtras and śāstras may number ten thousand fascicles;
the newly translated texts and the transcribed originals fill an entire room.
Nevertheless, his wisdom and understanding are nearly equal to those of Ratnamati.
He possessed divine insight and keen intelligence, thoroughly mastering local dialects;
moreover, he was so skilled in incantations that none could rival him.
Once, he sat at the mouth of a well, his ritual pitcher suspended in mid-air within it.
The disciple would have no one to draw water for him in the future;
thus, Guṇavīra took a willow branch and lightly stirred it within the well,
while secretly reciting a mantra only a few times.
The spring water surged upward until it reached the level of the well-railing;
he then used his bowl to draw some for washing.
The monks nearby witnessed this entirely, yet none could fathom its divine nature.
Everyone together praised him, exclaiming, "A truly great sage!
Puṇyatrāta said, "Do not praise him recklessly; this is merely a matter of skillful methods."
These [teachings] were practiced together in foreign lands but were not studied here in this region; they were merely called "holy" (ārya).

"One who retreats from an army is not of my clan.

The four Śibi and Cili kings each ruled over a single kingdom;

Braving the perils of the desert sands, my resolve was set upon benefiting sentient beings.

How tragic, how lamentable—this is truly deeply to be sighed over!

"Qi" (齊) is a respectful term of address.
He was a native of Uḍḍiyāna in North India;
in its original pronunciation, it should be rendered as "Ūcchaya," with the "ū" sounding like "chu" (荼) and the "ya" as a retroflex "zhē" (持耶反).
Master Xuanzang said:
"Udyāna is translated in the Tang language as 'Garden' (Yuan),
referring to what was formerly the pleasure garden of a Cakravartin King."
That king shared the same clan as the Buddha, also being of the Śākya lineage;
he was of the Kṣatriya caste,
which in the language of Qi means "lord of the land."
At the beginning of the kalpa, he first became the lord who divided the land and was thus named accordingly;
he is the one currently known as the King.
At the age of seventeen, Śākyamuni resolved to leave the household life.
Soon he encountered a renowned master and heard the complete teachings of the True Dharma.
At the age of twenty-one, he received the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Hearing the elder monks praise the traces of the Buddha’s legacy, he was moved by their words.
Some say that in such-and-such a country there is a bowl, and in such-and-such a country there are robes, a cranial bone,
and tooth relics; their miraculous transformations are manifold.
He immediately gave rise to the aspiration to attend upon and serve [the Master].
Since one must understand the characteristics of the Vinaya at the time of first receiving the precepts,
he waited until five summer retreats were complete before setting out on his travels.
Thus, regarding the traces of the Celestial Ladder and the Stone Terrace,
as well as the sites of the Dragon Temple and the Jewel Stupa,
he traveled extensively throughout various countries, personally prostrating at each one without leaving anything out.
He once resided at Zhuyuan Temple for ten years;
throughout his travels among the monasteries, he frequently encountered men of great virtue.
Among them was one venerable elder.
Having deeply discerned the person's capacity for awakening,
he said to his wife,
"If you can practice in stillness, you shall surely attain the fruits of sainthood."
I fear that as you wander about, you will ultimately achieve nothing.
Although you heard [the teachings] on that day, your mind failed to grasp them;
if you wish to repent later, how can it be of any avail?
Yaśas turned his back on the Snow Mountains to the north and traveled as far south as Siṃhala;
having toured the sacred sites, he returned to his former residence and beheld the ruler of the kingdom of Wu-chang, who was truly a Mahāsattva.
Among what I have personally witnessed and observed, few can be compared to this.
Allow me to briefly describe it:
he pacifies the people through principle, and the people love him as if he were their own kin.
During the fifth watch of the night, he first pays homage to the Triple Gem with incense, flowers, and music, making offerings with utmost sincerity.
At sunrise, he ascends the hall to attend to the myriad affairs of state.
Next, at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), he bathes the images with fragrant water.
A vegetarian feast for one hundred monks was regularly provided within the palace.
The King and his consort personally served the food with their own hands.
After the meal, they practiced various martial arts to aid digestion.
When the sun’s shadow was about to fall past the meridian,
he would transcribe ten lines of scripture and discuss the principles of the Dharma with the various monks;
thereafter, he would deliberate on matters of governance with his ministers.
At dusk, he would enter the Buddha hall to personally offer lamps and candles;
his prostrations, recitations, and readings each followed a constant routine.
Having completed these regular duties, he would then retire to a place of quietude.
For over thirty years, this meritorious work has continued without cessation.
The king has one hundred sons who dwell in sincerity and filial piety;
the lingering influence of the Śākya clan flows on through their lineage in this land.
However, because their monastery was situated on a mountain ridge and consumed by a wildfire,
they each sent word to one another,
and six men traveled together as companions to spread the teachings north of the Snow Mountains, seeking refuge and lodging along the way.
Upon reaching the steep summit, one sees two paths: one for humans and one for ghosts.
The human path is desolate and perilous, while the ghost path is smooth and passable.
A traveler, their mind confused, mistakenly seeks the path of the ghosts.
Upon gradually entering its territory, one will meet with slaughter.
In the past, there was a holy king who erected a stone image of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa at the head of the road to point out the path to people.
One of his companions, a monk, had mistakenly entered the realm of ghosts.
Having realized this, Yeśa recited the divine mantra of Avalokiteśvara;
he caught up with him at a distance of a hundred paces, but the companion had already been harmed by the ghost.
Relying on the power of his incantations, he escaped this calamity and proceeded further.
Again he encountered mountain bandits; by single-mindedly reciting the previous incantation, he was protected by its spiritual power.
When the bandits came to attack him, they could not even see him as they faced one another.
Following the road eastward, he reached the kingdom of Rouran; however, encountering the turmoil of the Turks, the western route was impassable.
His original intention having been frustrated, he followed the current northward until he arrived at the vicinity of the Ni-hai (the Sea of Mud).
It was located more than seventy *li* south of the Turks.
Having found no peace there, he fled far away to the borders of Qi,
arriving at the capital city of Ye in the seventh year of the Tianbao era.
Emperor Wenxuan Yang treated him with exceptional courtesy, setting him apart from his peers;
at that time, Yaśas was forty years old,
and his stern and elegant character drew criticism from public opinion.
Consequently, Emperor Wenxuan accorded him a most grand reception,
installing him at Tianting Temple and inviting him to serve as a Tripiṭaka Master for the translation of scriptures.
Within the palace hall were more than one thousand fascicles of Sanskrit manuscripts.
By imperial decree, [the image] was sent to the temple and installed in an upper chamber;
a ritual arena (*dharmapūjā-śālā*) was established there with offerings of the most exquisite and precious materials,
and a separate kitchen and storehouse were constructed to manifest its veneration.

From the eighth year of the Tianbao era of Emperor Wenxuan (Dingchou) until the fourth year of the Tiantong era of Gao Wei (Wushi)— a period during which Gao Wei had not yet received a posthumous title—
Śikṣānanda translated seven works, including the *Bodhisattvadarśanabhūtanirdeśasūtra*, at Tiānpíng Monastery in Yecheng.
By imperial decree, more than twenty individuals, including the Great Master (Mahāsaṃghī) Śramaṇa Faxiang and others, were appointed to supervise and oversee the translation.
Śramaṇa Dharmajñāna—the eldest son of Gautama Prajñāruci from Central India, whose name means "Dharma-Wisdom" in the language of Qi—and the layman Wan Yi served as the interpreters.
During the period of Emperor Xiaowen’s reign, he greatly promoted the True Dharma, causing it to flourish and broaden the minds of the masses.
Emperor Wenxuan, who held the Dharma in high esteem, personally showed him exceptional reverence.
Such was the sincerity with which he offered his faith and devotion.
Whenever Yaśas had leisure from his duties of preaching and translating, he would recite divine mantras;
thus, through both secret salvation and manifest assistance, he performed many meritorious deeds.
Before long, he was appointed as the Metropolitan Superintendent of the Office of Buddhist Affairs (Zhaoxuan Du), and soon thereafter was promoted to the position of Chief Administrator (Tong).
The stipends and offerings he received were not used solely for his own sustenance;
rather, he delighted in giving rise to compassion and kindness, and took pleasure in performing meritorious deeds.
He provided meals for the Sangha and bestowed alms upon the poor and destitute.
He rescued those imprisoned in jails and those kept as livestock.
In busy marketplaces and bustling thoroughfares, he constructed many charitable wells;
he personally filtered the water to provide it to sentient beings.
Furthermore, he established three monasteries on the western mountains of Jijun;
built upon springs and beside valleys, they were fashioned with the utmost mountain beauty.
He also established separate quarters to provide care for men and women afflicted by leprosy.
She provided for him with the four types of offerings, attending to his needs so that they were fully supplied.
Furthermore, she went to the guesthouse of the Turks and exhorted them to observe the six fast days, to release animals for their food, and to practice vegetarianism.
She also once fell ill and was unable to rise for a hundred days.
The Son of Heaven and the Empress personally inquired after his well-being.
Yaśas sighed and said, "I was originally but a foreign guest; my virtuous conduct has not yet flourished."
The imperial carriage has now lowered its status to honor this profound Dharma;
thus it is so. Internally, he touched his heart, where shame and fear converged.
Later, during the Sui dynasty, Yaśas further translated various sutras.

This sutra was translated during the late spring of the second year [of the reign].

*Mahāyāna Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one fascicle (alternatively titled *Wucheng* [Without the word "Vehicle"]); translated in the seventh month of the second year of the Kaihuang era; this second translation is the same text as the *Ji zhufangdengxue jing* by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin, as recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. *Elephant Head Vihāra Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated in the second month of the second year of the Kaihuang era; this third translation is the same text as the *Wenshushili wen puti jing* by Kumārajīva and others, as recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. The śramaṇa Vinītadeva, whose name means "Extinction of Joy" in the Sui language,

From no great distance, he traveled five hundred *yojanas*, shaking his mendicant’s staff as he toured the monasteries to witness this flourishing transformation.

He translated two sections of scriptures, including the Vaipulya and the Dhāraṇī.
Li Daobao, a court attendant, and Tanpi, the younger son of Prajñāruci, served as oral interpreters.
The śramaṇa Shi Fazuan of Chang’an received the text in writing and rendered it into the Sui language.

The śramaṇa Yancong composed prefaces for both [versions], and the *Chángfáng lù* (Record of Chángfáng) also states that this was produced at Xingshansi; however, this is likewise incorrect, as the errors have been described above.

titled "The Mahāyāna Vaipulya Division on the Sun-Treasury," which shares the same original text as the "Secret Division" of the *Mahāsannipāta*. This is the fourth edition.
Translation commenced in the fifth month of the fourth year of the Kaihuang era and completed in the second month of the fifth year. Translated by the śramaṇa Zhixuan; Fei Changfang acted as scribe.

It is identical in its original text to the *Mahāmegha-varṣaṇa-sūtra* translated during the Zhou dynasty by Jñānayaśas, as well as the *Vajrapāṇi-mahāvidyā-varṣaṇa-sūtra* translated during the Sui dynasty. [This concludes] the *Mahāvyūha*.
*Dharmamukha-sūtra*, two fascicles; also titled *Mañjuśrī-ṛddhibala-sūtra* and *Śrīpuṣpadattā-bhadradevī-sūtra*.

He was a native of Ujjayinī in North India.
Previously, during the Qi dynasty, he served as the Director of the Office for Buddhist Affairs (Zhaoxuantong).
Together with the śramaṇa Fazhi of the Zhuangyan Monastery, he translated seven works of the sūtras,
all of which are recorded in the Qi Catalogue.
Toward the end of the Jiande era, Emperor Wu of Zhou conquered the Qi dynasty.
At that time, Buddhism was being suppressed by the state.
Guṇabhadra outwardly assumed the attire of a layman while inwardly donning the three robes of a monk;
he fled from place to place, east and west, finding no rest.
When the five aggregates were withered and distressed, leaving them nowhere to turn for refuge,
he reduced his own food to give to those starving in the ditches and ravines;
to the elderly and the infirm, he provided aid and benefit according to their needs.
Although his resources were meager and he persisted in acting despite being rebuffed by those who offered counsel,
his spirit remained robust and tireless in his exhortations and guidance.
Thus, he endured hardships and obstacles for as many as four years.
When the Sui dynasty ruled the realm, the Three Jewels were restored;
at the beginning of the Kaihuang era, Sanskrit scriptures responded from afar.
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued requesting that they be brought to China for wide propagation and translation.
In the seventh month of the second year, his disciples Daomi and others escorted him into the capital,
where he resided at Daxingshan Temple.
In the final winter of that same year, they began the preliminary work of translating his treatises.

By imperial decree, more than thirty individuals, including the Śramaṇa Tanyan, the Director of the Office for the Propagation of the Mysteries (Zhaoxuantong), were commissioned to translate [the texts] together.
The Sovereign showed him profound courtesy and frequent inquiry, providing him with lavish and abundant support.
Although his years were advanced, his practice became increasingly diligent.
Having relied upon the Śāriputra-dhāraṇī and fully practiced its cultivation,
he dreamed of attaining the state of a Buddha;
such auspicious omens occurred in great numbers, not just once.
Later, he moved his residence to Guangji; because Emperor Yang had named it Guang, it was changed to Hongji, and now, to avoid the imperial taboo, it is called Chongji.
He served as the presiding master for foreign monks, providing comfort and care to those who were strangers, and skillfully won their hearts.
Suddenly, one day, he informed his disciples:
"I am old and my strength is failing; I shall not remain long in this world.
Now, while I am still clear-headed, I exhort you, my followers."
"The Buddha-dharma is difficult to encounter; one should diligently practice and study it.
A human body is difficult to obtain; take care not to let it pass in vain.
Having spoken these words, he lay upon his pillow and passed away suddenly.
When the hundred years were complete—
specifically on the twenty-ninth day of the eighth month in the ninth year of the Kaihuang era—
Yaśas first encountered a master of physiognomy who said:
"He was certain to reach a hundred years of age and would have ascended as an immortal.
That his life ended at middle age proves his words true."
The principles of ascending to transcendence remain difficult to fathom;
nevertheless, his physical appearance was extraordinary and marvelous,
with hair-like flesh atop his head.
His ears were long and upright;
his eyes were positioned perfectly in the center.
These features differed from those of ordinary beings and constituted extraordinary marks of distinction.
He was truly a man of eminent virtue who transmitted the Dharma.
Once the Master of the Dharma had passed away, both monastics and laypeople were overcome with grief and alarm;
the task of upholding and flourishing the teachings was on the verge of falling into decline.

The country is over fifty li [in circumference] and has a population of one hundred and fifty thousand.
