*Fǎjù tuóluóní jīng* (Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Dharma Torch), twenty fascicles; produced in the fourth month of the twelfth year of the Kāiyuáng era and completed in the sixth month of the fourteenth year.
Transcribed by the śramaṇa Dàosuí and others; recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. *Dàwéidé tuóluóní jīng* (Dhāraṇī Sūtra of Great Majestic Virtue), twenty fascicles;
produced in the seventh month of the fifteenth year of the Kāiyuáng era and completed in the twelfth month of the sixteenth year. Transcribed by the śramaṇa... [text ends].
The *Sūtra of the Names of Five Thousand Five Hundred Buddhas* in eight fascicles was transcribed by the scribe Sengkun and others;
it was produced in the eighth month of the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era and completed in the ninth month of the fourteenth year; this is recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*.

The *Sūtra on Observing the Practice of All Dharmas* in four fascicles was [begun] on the second day of the fourth month of the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era; the scribes were the śramaṇa Sengtán and others; this is recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*.
Translated from the 14th day [of the month] until the 25th day of the fifth month; recorded by the scholars Fei Changfang and others.
[This is] seen in Changfang’s Record as the *Amoghadarśin-bodhisattva-sūtra* in four fascicles. [Also] seen in the *Neidian lu* as the *Candrottarā-dārikā-sūtra* in two fascicles.
Translated in the fourth month of the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era, completed in the sixth month; recorded by the scholar Liu Ping. Recorded by the śramaṇa...

Yanzong composed the preface; it is recorded in the *Chángfáng lù* that the *Boshìxīn jīng* (Sūtra on the Arising of the Bodhicitta) was produced in the tenth month of the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era, and completed in that same month;
the scholar Liu Péng received the dictation, as recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*.

The *Shāngzhǔtiānzǐ suowèn jīng* (Sūtra of the Questions of the Merchant Lord Devaputra), one fascicle—sometimes lacking the characters "suowèn" (questions)—was produced in the eighth month of the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era and completed in the ninth month.
The scholar Fei Changfang and others transcribed [the text], as recorded in Changfang’s catalogue: *The Sūtra of the King Supreme Among All Dharmas*, one fascicle;
translated in the fifth month of the third year of the Kaihuang era, completed in the seventh month; transcribed by the śramaṇa Mingfen and others, as recorded in Changfang’s catalogue:
*The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Three Aggregates of Repentance*, one fascicle; as recorded in the Neidian lu: *The Sūtra on the Origin of the World*, one fascicle, number...
Record of the Five Translations of the *Ji shijie jing* (Sūtra on the World-Ages) from the *Dīrgha Āgama*, appearing as a separate edition at the head of the sūtra’s title:
"The Dharma Masters Guṇabhadra and Jñānagupta together produced this new compilation, which was incorporated into the sixty-fascicle *Buddhacarita-saṃgraha-sūtra*.

It was begun in the seventh month of the seventh year of the Kaihuang era and completed in the second month of the eleventh year. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Sengtan, the Academician Fei Changfang, Liu Ping, and others."

The scribe was the śramaṇa Yancong; the preface was composed by him and is recorded in the Chángfáng lù. *The Sūtra on the Questions of the Devaputra Śrī-Suvikrānta* (Shèng shànzhùyì tiānzǐ suowèn jīng), four fascicles.
This sixth translation is the same text as the *Rúhuàn sānmèi jīng* and the *Bǎojí shànzhùyì huì*.
It was translated in the fourth month of the fifteenth year of the Kāiyuáng era; the scribes were the śramaṇa Dàosuì and others, as recorded in the Chángfáng lù.
*Record of the Sūtra on the Buddhas’ Protective Mindfulness*, ten fascicles. Translated in the tenth month of the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era, completed in the twelfth month.
Transcribed by the śramaṇas Sengtan and others. Recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. The above thirty-nine works comprise one hundred and ninety-two fascicles.
The *Bénxíng jí* (Collection of Past Deeds), upper volume, contains thirty-seven works totaling one hundred and seventy-eight fascicles, currently extant at Shèngshàn Monastery.
The fourteen fascicles of the first two sections of the *Zhùxià* (Staying Below) are missing from the original text.
Translated by the śramaṇa Jñānagupta,
whose name means "Will-Virtue" in the Sui language.

Beidu (北賢豆) and Xiandu (賢豆) are the original pronunciations of *Indraprastha*, which is translated here as "The Place Reached" (*zhichu*), meaning it is protected by Śakra, the Lord of Devas; the sound *Xiandu* is merely a corruption and abbreviation of that country's name. *Shendu* (身毒) and *Tianzhu* (天竺) are corruptions of the names used in this region [of China]. However, the people of that land generally refer to it as *Xiandu*, and they categorize it into five regions.
The *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions* states:

"The correct pronunciation for 'Indu' is *Indra*; in the language of Tang, it is translated as 'Sun and Moon. It has many names, of which this is one. It is said that all sentient beings, circling in saṃsāra, cannot do so without ignorance; in the long night, there is none to preside over the dawn."
It is like when the white sun has already set and the night lamp must follow;
there is only the illumination of the starlight,
yet how can it compare to the brilliance of the bright moon?
If one follows this reasoning and uses the moon as a metaphor,
it is truly because the sages and worthies have succeeded one another in that land, guiding the common people and governing all things like the moon’s shining descent.
For this reason, it is called India.
In India, the social classes are divided into castes, among which the Brahmins are particularly pure and noble.

Following their traditional designation, this has become a custom such that, regardless of regional boundaries, the entire land is collectively called the Kingdom of the Brahmins; it is the land of the people of Gandhāra.
In the language of the Sui, it means "Country of Fragrant Conduct. It is situated in the city of Pūṣapura (Sui: *Zhàngfū Gōng*, meaning "Palace of the Hero").

The king belongs to the Kṣatriya caste and his clan name is Kauṇḍinya (Sui: *Dǐng*, meaning "Crest"), signifying that he is like the crest of a peacock, which is considered a noble lineage in that country. His father’s name was Vajrasena (Sui: *Jīngāng Jiān*, meaning "Vajra-Firm"). From youth, he possessed far-reaching capacity, and as he grew, he established pure standards of conduct. Holding the position of prime minister, he governed with established principles.
Among the five brothers of the Kuñjara clan, he was the youngest.
Having planted the roots of virtue in past lives, he had early developed the aspiration for the Way;
even while still in his childhood, he sought liberation, and his parents, seeing his discernment and capacity, supported him.
He immediately entered the Mahāvana Monastery and was thereby granted liberation.

His *upādhyāya*—translated in the Sui period as "Constantly Near" (*chángjìn*) and referring to one who receives and maintains [the precepts]—is what is now called the *heshang*; this is a phonetic corruption and abbreviation of the name used in Khotan. Master Xuanzang states that the Middle Indic pronunciation is *upādhyāya*, which in the Tang language means "Personal Teacher" (*qīnjiào*) and is also translated as "One upon Whom One Relies for Study" (*yīxué*).
His name was Śīlanāśa (Sui: Shèngmíng), who specialized in meditative seclusion and reached the profound mastery of the practices of dhyāna.

His ācārya (Sui: Chuánshòu, or alternatively Zhèngxíng)—which refers to what is known as an ācārya—is also a phonetic abbreviation of the local [Central Asian] term; Master Xuanzang states that *ācārya* in the Tang language means "model" (*guǐfàn*) or "instruction" (*jiàoshòu*).
His name was Śrīñānavardhana (translated into the Sui language as Zhixian), who was thoroughly versed in the three studies and specialized in the Vinaya-piṭaka.
Since his ordination, Jñānagupta had been exceptionally filial and sincere in his devotion.
Although I have spent many years receiving instruction and have attained a comprehensive understanding of the ultimate goal,
since sacred sites and miraculous traces still remain in the holy land of India,
I have followed my master there to pay full homage to them all.
At that time, he was twenty-seven years old.
Having observed the precepts for three summers,
he and his teacher resolved to travel abroad to propagate the Dharma.
Initially, ten men made a pact to travel abroad.
On their route, they stayed for years in the kingdom of Kāpiśī.
The king earnestly invited their master to serve as his Dharma-lord, benefiting him extensively.
As he was about to proceed on his travels,
he crossed the western foot of the Great Snowy Mountains;
it was truly a place of extreme and formidable natural peril.
Upon arriving in the kingdom of Yantala, the land was vast and sparsely populated;
there was no one to provide the food and drink he required.

Consequently, Ratnagupta relinquished his full ordination and devoted himself with all his strength to serving [his companion]. After enduring many hardships over time, they were fortunately spared from calamities through the protection of the numinous spirits.
Furthermore, he visited the kingdoms of Lopamanda and Khotan,
where he was forced to halt for brief periods due to summer rains and cold snow;
since there were no conditions for extensive propagation of the Dharma, he did not reside in those places for long.
He then reached the kingdom of Tuyuhun and gradually arrived at Shanzhou;
this was the first year of the Later Yuan era of the Western Wei.
Although he encountered many hardships and perils, his resolve became even more fierce and resolute.
I have followed his tracks and traversed the mountains for three years now;
of my ten companions, only four remain.
This was in the year of Chengwu of the Zhou Ming Emperor.
Upon first arriving in Chang’an, he stayed at Caotang Temple;
having fulfilled his original intention through the journey of teaching and transforming others with his disciples,
he ascended the pure altar once more to receive full ordination.
His sincerity in following the Way was even more profound than that of his predecessors.
Having resided in the capital, he gradually became proficient in the Sui language;
his reputation spread somewhat afar, and he was held in high esteem by his contemporaries.
Having been summoned by imperial decree to enter the rear garden to discuss the Buddha-dharma together,
he was provided with exceptional honors and special offerings throughout the palace.
Desiring to transmit the Dharma, he found no means to manifest his purpose himself, and thus submitted a formal petition expressing his full intentions.
He was immediately granted a special imperial edict permitting him to reside at the newly constructed Four Heavenly Kings Temple (Sìtiānwáng Sì).
From that time forward, he revised and updated the new translations and supplemented the missing portions of the earlier ones;
since these were no longer merely perfunctory tasks, his work was neither extensive nor grand, but rather a matter of formal maintenance.
When Prince Xiao of Qiao, Yuwen Jian, was stationed in Shu,
he again invited [Huiyuan] to go with him;
there for three years, he constantly served as the Monastic Head (Sengzhu) of Yizhou and resided at Longyuan Temple.
During the Jian-de era, the times were in decline and the teachings of the Image Period were not widespread;
the five groups of monastics for a time all wore the same secular clothing.
Emperor Wu issued an edict summoning him to the imperial capital.
The Emperor repeatedly conferred upon him ranks and emoluments, pressuring him to adopt the rituals of the Confucian tradition;
yet he maintained his integrity with resolute firmness, remaining fearless even unto death.
The Emperor, moved by his steadfast sincerity, pitied him and permitted him to return home.
The route departed from north of Ganzhou via the Turks,
where he encountered Zhongmian Tabgach Khan,
who earnestly invited him to remain.
In response to our correspondence, I say:
In the case of the secular world, there is formation and destruction, and armies toil in going and returning;
here, however, there is neither decline nor prosperity, so you may rest assured and remain at ease.
He provided for his needs and made offerings so that [the master] was fully satisfied.
Consequently, [the master] remained there for more than ten years.
Then, the Ācārya Zhixian returned to the West and passed away.
Not long after, the Upādhyāya passed away.
Left alone with only his solitary shadow, he had no one to rely upon and knew not where to find peace.
Fortunately, the ruler and people of the Northern Di tribes extensively provided him with spiritual benefits and material support.
Consequently, he wandered as a sojourner, benefiting sentient beings wherever he went.
There were ten men who followed him: the Qi monks Baoxian, Daosui, Zhiyou, Sengwei, Fabao, Sengtanzhi, Zhao, Senglü, and others.
In the sixth year of the Wuping era, they formed an alliance to travel together to the Western Regions to collect scriptures.
After seven years of travel, as they were about to return eastward,
they obtained a total of two hundred and sixty Sanskrit texts before reaching the territory of the Turks.
Hearing that the Zhou had destroyed Qi and had utterly demolished the Buddha-dharma,
he felt he could not retreat, yet had nowhere to advance.
While lingering there, he eventually encountered one of supreme virtue.
Like one who encounters a drink when thirsty or meets with light in the darkness,
he resided together with [the Master] to discuss and enjoy the Way.
He took the newly brought scriptures and, together with him, examined them, requesting that their titles be translated.
Upon examining the old catalog, I find it even more skillfully arranged than that of my predecessors.
Within the Vinaya and other texts, we each feel sincere joy;
having obtained this treasure and encountered such a master, our practice has not been in vain.
In accordance with our shared vow, we have burned incense together to proclaim this covenant.
Now that the Great Sui has received the mandate to rule and the Buddha-dharma has flourished, I,
Xian, and others have brought these scriptures here first to respond to the times.
In the final month of winter in the first year of the Kaihuang era,
an imperial edict was issued entrusting the matter to the relevant authorities to seek out a person to perform the translation.
In the second month of spring in the second year, the work of transmission and narration commenced.
In the seventh month of summer, the Emperor issued an edict, saying:
"The five migrations of the Yin dynasty resulted in the fear that the people would all perish;
this was because the lands of fortune and misfortune determined the length of their lives."
To plan for the new while discarding the old is like a farmer looking toward the autumn harvest.
The mountains, rivers, plains, and valleys of Longshou are magnificent and beautiful, with flourishing vegetation and abundant growth;
it is a fitting site to establish a capital and lay the foundation for the state’s enduring power.
The karma that ensures eternal and inexhaustible stability is established here;
thus, the palace is named Daxing Dian (Palace of Great Prosperity) and the gate is named Daxing (Great Prosperity).
The commandery was named Daxing;
its gardens, groves, ponds, and marshes all bore the same name.
The monastery was named Daxingshan.
The fundamental texts of the Dharma were transmitted within this monastery.
At that time, Xuemati was still residing among the Northern Di.
In the fourth year of the Kaihuang era, more than thirty people, including the śramaṇa Tanyan and others from Daxingshan Monastery, [arrived].
Because he had personally undertaken the translations, the phonology and meaning were inconsistent and erroneous.
Upon learning that Paramārtha was in the north, he submitted a petition to return to the capital.
The Emperor then issued a separate edict to summon him back.
Since returning from Mount Kukkutapāda, ten years have passed without interruption.
I have reflected deeply upon this bright age and the fortunate reunion with the Triple Gem.
To be suddenly visited by you from afar fills me with both joy and profound aspiration.
He then arrived in the country together with the envoy.
At that time, Emperor Wen was on an inspection tour of Luoyang, where [Bodhidharma] paid his respects to him.
The Son of Heaven was greatly pleased and repeatedly bestowed inquiries upon him.
Before he had yet returned to the imperial capital, an edict was issued for him to propagate and translate [the scriptures].
The newly arrived Sanskrit manuscripts were exceedingly numerous across various sections;
whether they were sūtras or treatises, and whether they pertained to the inner or outer teachings, they were all present.
In all instances of translations and transmissions, Kumārajīva was invariably the primary authority.
Everyone agreed that because Kumārajīva’s linguistic insight encompassed the scripts of foreign lands and he understood their diverse customs,
he was able to expound and debate with such spontaneity that he required no assistance from intermediary translators.
Having understood the principles of the categories of meaning and the structure of the phrases,
the textual intent is roughly settled and the critical edition is thus completed;
those who take up the pen will not need to expend great effort.
I shall attempt to emulate the predecessors and continue their work.
In the fifth year, by imperial decree,
I was joined by the Brahmin Śramaṇa Jñānagupta and [the monk] Ratnabhadra.
Gaofu Gao Gong’s sons were the Commander-in-Chief Tiannu and Horen.

Together with six people—both monastics and laypeople, including the Brahmin Viśada—they were ordered to work within the Inner History (Neishi) and the Inner Inspection (Neisheng) on the translation of Sanskrit ancient texts and the *Gāndhārī* script; at that time, at Guangji Temple, Yashas alone was translating the scriptures.
By a special imperial edict, Paramārtha was commissioned to concurrently oversee the translation of scriptures.
Traveling back and forth between the two locations for twelve years,
he completed the translation and recordation of over two hundred fascicles and submitted them.
At that time, Yaśas had already passed away; consequently,
he commanded Guṇabhadra to take sole charge of the translations,
moving the dharma seat to Daxingshan Temple.
Furthermore, he summoned the Brahmin and śramaṇa Dharmagupta, along with Gao Tiannu and Gao Heren—brothers who were proficient in the Sanskrit language—and commanded them to serve as co-translators.
He also increased the number of eminent śramaṇas by appointing ten virtuous monks: Sengxiu, Fachan, Fajing, Huizang, Hongzun, Huiyuan, Fazuan, Senghui, Mingmu, and Tanqian.
The Supervisors of Translation were responsible for determining the fundamental principles;
the śramaṇas Mingmu and Yancong re-translated against the Sanskrit manuscripts,
conducting a second round of critical examination to refine the phrasing and meaning.
Jñānagupta once related that more than two thousand *li* to the southeast of Udyāna lies the kingdom of Cakuka.
Its king possesses pure faith and holds the Mahāyāna in profound reverence.
Within the palace itself were the three great sūtras—the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, the Mahāsannipāta, and the Avataṃsaka—each consisting of one hundred thousand verses;
the King personally upheld them and kept their locks and keys himself.
While reciting, they opened the incense and flowers for offering.
Furthermore, the interior of the ritual arena was adorned with various ornaments to entice the minor kings to enter and pay their respects.
More than twenty li to the southeast of this country, there is a mountain that is extremely precipitous and rugged,

containing a deep and pure cave. Within it are placed twelve sections of scriptures, including the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, *Avataṃsaka*, *Vaipulya*, *Ratnakūṭa*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, *Vaiśālīpradeśa*, the two *Śāriputra-dhāraṇīs*, the *Puṣpasaṃcaya*, the *Dharmasaṃgraha*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the eight sections of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*.
It consists of one hundred thousand verses.
According to the laws of the kingdom, it has been traditionally handed down and guarded with great care.
Furthermore, there are three arhats who have entered the meditative absorption of extinction, dwelling in silent meditation within a cave.
Every half-month, the monks would go to the mountain to shave his head.
This was the very basis upon which the person and the Dharma were maintained, providing reliance for all living beings.
Guṇabhadra’s nature was pure and profound, and his spirit and will were firm and upright.
He cherished virtue without weariness and sought the Dharma without slackening.
He was widely learned in the Tripiṭaka and investigated the True Doctrine to its furthest reaches;
he studied all five sciences and was equally proficient in worldly treatises.
Through walking meditation, one attains the merit of the site of enlightenment;
through dhāraṇīs, one penetrates the principle of divine mantras.
Wearing the three robes and eating but one meal, one ultimately solidifies their sincerity.
His benevolence and compassion were vast and all-encompassing, not merely resulting from formal exhortations.
He diligently recited Buddhist scriptures, becoming even more devoted as he grew old;
his powerful memory of antiquity remained ever more profound as time passed.
Scholars and commoners alike revered him, and both monastics and laypeople venerated him with deep respect.
Prince Xuan of Teng of the Sui dynasty looked up to his moral example and followed him as his teacher.
However, due to certain affairs involving worldly defilement, he was exiled to Dongyue.
Furthermore, his reputation spread widely throughout the regions of Wuyue and Min.

He benefited beings immensely by providing salvation for both body and mind. He passed away in the twentieth year of the Kaihuang era at the age of seventy-eight, leaving behind only the "Preface to the Expanded Version of the Lotus Sutra."

In the first year of the Renshou era (the Xin-you year), the two Dharma Masters Kumārajīva and Guptadatta re-examined the Sanskrit manuscripts at Daxingshan Temple; they supplemented the missing portions and produced a revised translation.
Since this was produced in the first year of the Renshou era, it is known as the "Supplemented Version."
Thus, it was not that he passed away in the twentieth year of the Kaihuang era.

Furthermore, the *Neidian lu* (Record of Inner Scriptures) states that at the end of the Renshou era, Guṇabhadra was exiled to Dongyue due to other circumstances; however, the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks) states that he passed away in the twentieth year of the Kaihuang era.
Both the *Lù* (Catalog) and the *Chuán* (Biographies) were compiled by Xuansu, yet why do they contradict one another?
From his arrival at the Eastern Capital from the Western Regions, Kumārajīva traveled through various locations translating and transmitting scriptures;
from the fifth year of the Kaihuang era until the end of the Renshou era, he produced the *Huguo jing* and other texts.
In total, there are thirty-nine sections comprising one hundred and ninety-two fascicles.
These have all been meticulously examined for their thorough integration of governance and the teachings;
their clarity and the synthesis of their meanings circulate widely throughout the world.
I have seen the *Buddha-sūtra of the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara* in the two catalogs of the Sui and Tang dynasties,
as well as the *Huayan ruruilai dezhijing* (Avataṃsaka-sūtra on Entering the Tathāgata’s Virtue and Wisdom) and the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāmegha-varṣaprārthanā-sūtra*.
The *Sūtra of the Tathāgata Supreme Lamp King of the East*,
the *Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Nothingness*,
and the *Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Three Aggregates of Repentance*.
The aforementioned six sections are recorded in the *Neidian lu* as translations by Jñānagupta;
the *Jingmai jingtu* states they were produced by Dharmagupta.
For now, we follow the *Neidian lu* as authoritative.
The Mahāsannipāta-ratna-kūṭa-sūtra (The Great Collection Sutra of Similes and Kings),
the Saṃkrānti-vijñāna-sūtra (The Sutra on the Transference of Consciousness), and the Dharmolkā-dhāraṇī-sūtra (The Sutra of the Dharma-Torch Dhāraṇī).
Regarding the three sections above,
it was an error for both the catalogs of Jñānagupta and Dharmagupta to include them within the *Jingtu* (Scripture and Diagram) section.
Now, they are all included in the remainder of Jñānagupta’s catalog, while they have been removed from Dharmagupta’s catalog.

The *Zhong jing mulu* (Catalogue of All Scriptures) in seven fascicles was compiled by order of the Emperor at the Translation Office of Xingshan Monastery on the tenth day of the fifth month in the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era; it was completed on the fourteenth day of the tenth month, consisting of a separate catalogue in six fascicles and a general catalogue in one fascicle, totaling seven. This is recorded in the *Changfang lu*. The *Zhong jing mulu* in five fascicles was compiled by order of the Emperor in the second year of the Renshou era, with the assistance of śramaṇas and scholars from the Translation Office of Xingshan Monastery; this is recorded in the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*. These two works comprise twelve fascicles in total, and their manuscripts are all extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Fa-jing and others were all eminent masters of the translation bureau at Daxingshan Monastery.
In the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era (the Jia-yin year), they compiled the *Catalogue of All Scriptures*.
The twenty great virtuous ones, including Fa-jing and others, compiled and completed it.
They established a general framework consisting of nine catalogs (lu) and categorized the contents into forty-two sections (fen).
In total, there are two thousand two hundred and fifty-seven sections comprising five thousand three hundred and ten fascicles;
the śramaṇa Mingmu of Yanghua Monastery has categorized them by region and divided them into sections, tracing their origins and mapping out their vast connections.
The śramaṇa Yancong of Riyang Monastery meticulously examined the structural framework and collated the similarities and differences,
as seen in the Record of Changfang.
Furthermore, in the second year of the Renshou era, an imperial edict was issued to the relevant authorities,
requesting that the virtuous masters of Xingshan Monastery, along with the śramaṇas and scholars engaged in translating the scriptures,
examine the treasury of the Dharma and carefully determine the catalog of the sutras.
Categorized according to their types, they are divided into five sections:
the first is the single original version;
the second is the second round of separate translations.
Third, the Collection of Biographies of Worthies and Sages;
fourth, those of Doubtful Authenticity;
fifth, those with Missing Sections.
In total, there are two thousand one hundred and nine sections comprising five thousand fifty-eight fascicles.
Those separately identified as suspicious or spurious need not be transcribed; the remaining three parts have been included in the canon and are recorded in the catalog.
The śramaṇa Yancong oversaw and finalized the compilation.
This is recorded in the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks).

It combines the eight fascicles and twenty-four chapters of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*; its compilation corresponds to the fourth version from the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era, as noted in the *Changfang lu*. The śramaṇa Yancong composed the preface for this work. This one section, consisting of eight fascicles, is currently extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Baogui,
a monk of Daxingshan Monastery,
in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era (the Ding-si year), compiled a single volume of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
The Venerable [Daoan] was the spiritual disciple of Daosheng, the master of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* during the Zhou dynasty.

While perusing various scriptures, he observed that in the Jin dynasty, the śramaṇa Zhi Mindu had combined the works of two Zhis, two Zhus, and one Bai—five masters in total—into a single volume of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, consisting of eight fascicles. Now, according to the *Fajing lu* and the *Hejing ji*, four versions have been synthesized; this excludes the version by Bai Yan. Furthermore, the works of one Zhi and two Zhus—three masters in total—have been combined into a single volume of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, consisting of five fascicles.
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Sengjù compiled four families of texts into sixty fascicles.
In these combined scriptures, both the phrasing and the meaning are complete and precise.
Since these are the bequeathed works of former sages, they should be preserved.
The Master Gui subsequently relied upon this as his standard.

Thus, the sixteen chapters in four fascicles of the *Liang* edition of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (or *Abhidharma-dharmapada*)—which the Zhou dynasty referred to as the *Zang-xu*—were divided into five fascicles. During the Liang dynasty, Paramārtha further translated four additional chapters: the "Distinction of the Three Bodies," the "Extinguishing Karmic Obstacles," the "Dhāraṇī of the Most Pure Ground," and the "Fulfilling Vows by Relying on Emptiness. Including these, the eighteen chapters became twenty-four, forming seven fascicles. During the Sui dynasty, Zhìdé further translated the "Dhāraṇī of the Silver Lord" chapter and the "Entrustment" chapter; these were the additions made throughout the preceding and succeeding periods.
In twenty-four fascicles, it was divided into eight volumes.
The śramaṇa Yancong carefully re-examined and collated the chapters and sections until they were complete.
It was from this point that the title of this text was designated as the "King of Sutras."
The meaning is profound and subtle; I pray that it may be protected and upheld by both the hidden and the manifest.

Furthermore, Changfang states that the śramaṇa Sengjiu of Zhaoti Monastery compiled the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* into sixty fascicles during the sixth year of the Kaihuang era. Having now examined the sutra as compiled by Jiù, it is difficult to rely upon as it contains discrepancies, such as those fully described in the *Dacheng lu* and the *Shanfan lu*. Therefore, in this catalog, I have retained its separate version and deleted the one that was incorporated into the combined collection.

The *Zhan cha shan e ye bao jing* (Sūtra on Divining the Retribution of Good and Evil Karma), two fascicles; also titled the *Liu gen ju jing* (Sūtra on the Collection of the Six Sense Bases), the *Da cheng shi yi jing* (Mahāyāna Sūtra on the True Meaning), the *Di zang pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha), simply the *Zhan cha jing*, or the *Di zang pusa ye bao jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha on Karma and Retribution). This one work in two fascicles is extant.
The śramaṇa Bodhiden was a man from foreign lands;
it is unknown in which era he translated [this work].
One fascicle of the *Zhan cha jing*.
Changfang’s catalogue states:
"This scripture was searched for in the records but no entry was found."
However, the title at the beginning of the sutra states that it was translated by Bodhideng in a foreign country;
this suggests it appeared in more recent times.
Currently, these [texts] are all transcribed and circulated within the various Tripitakas.
However, there was once a monk in Guangzhou who practiced the *tāpó* (stūpa-penance) ritual;
he made two slips of paper out of leather.
Write the word "good" on one slip and the word "evil" on another,
and have the person cast them.
Obtaining good is desirable;
obtaining evil is undesirable.
Furthermore, they practice the method of prostrating themselves to the ground as a means to extinguish their transgressions.
There was also a lay practitioner in Qingzhou who practiced this same method.
In the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era, someone reported to the local authorities in Guangzhou that he was a sorcerer.
The authorities then investigated the man.
The citation states:
"The method for repentance at a stupa is based on the *Zhancha jing*;
the method of prostrating oneself is based on various sutras."
He prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground like the collapsing of Mount Tai.
Guo Yi, the Commandant of Guangzhou, came to the capital and submitted a formal petition to Qizhou for presentation to the throne.
An imperial edict was issued stating that the principles of the *Zhanchara Sūtra* were not to be believed.
The Palace Secretary and Gentleman-in-Waiting Li Yuancao, together with Guo Yi, visited Baochang Monastery to inquire of the various virtuous ones.
The śramaṇa Fajing and others replied that the name and the place of translation do not appear in the catalog of the *Zancha jing*.
The method for repentance at the stupa differs from that of other scriptures;
it cannot be followed as practiced [therein].
The Imperial Edict states:
Such views as these need not be circulated.
Now, I say this is not so.
How can one, like someone peering through a tube, refuse to acknowledge those who possess broad vision?
The eighty-four thousand dharma-gates possess manifold principles;
were it not for that which was proclaimed by the Golden Mouth, how could such profound teachings be revealed?
In the first year of the Tiace Wansui era of the Great Tang Empress Dowager.
An imperial decree to the śramaṇas Mingquan and others of Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital:
The cataloging and definitive arrangement of the entire collection of scriptures have now been completed and incorporated into the canon.
May all future readers be free from doubt.

The *Kaihuang Sanbao Lu* (Catalogue of the Three Jewels of the Kaihuang Era), fifteen fascicles, was presented on the twenty-third day of the twelfth month of the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era. The internal title states: *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Record of the Three Jewels Through the Successive Dynasties). This one work in fifteen fascicles is extant, as seen in the *Neidian Lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue) and the *Xu Gaoseng Zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks).
Fei Changfang, a scholar who translated the scriptures,
was a native of Chengdu.
Originally, Changfang had entered the monastic order.
During the Zhou dynasty, the privileges of the monastic were abolished and they followed the Confucian dress code.
Upon the rise of the Sui, these practices were restored and they again wore lay clothing.
At that time, [the author] participated in the transmission of the teachings, receiving and recording the words and meanings with his own hand.

Since the various catalogs of successive dynasties mostly compiled only the scriptures, while records concerning the Buddha and the monastic community were scarce, he composed the *Sanbao Lili* (Chronicles of the Three Jewels).
He dated the imperial era from the reigns of Kings Zhuang of Zhou and Lu up until the final year of the Kaihuang period.
The *Kaihuang Sanbao Lu* (Catalogue of the Three Jewels of the Kaihuang Era) lists the *Jiazi* [year] at the head and arranges various scriptures alongside it,
with the dates of their translation appended as a comprehensive synthesis.
It was compiled and presented for imperial review;
an edict was issued for its implementation.
Its preface states briefly:
The present compilation is roughly modeled upon three scriptures to serve as a guide for manifesting these Three Jewels:
the auspicious signs of the Buddha’s birth follow the "Night-Brightness" (Yayuming) of the Zhou dynasty,
while the auspicious omens of the sūtra’s translation date are received from the dream at night during the Han dynasty.
He was the foundational pillar and structural beam for the Sangha’s origins,
his brilliant contributions surpassing those of Huijiao.

Furthermore, he extensively consulted dozens of sources, including records of recluses, dynastic annals, the *Chū-sō-ki* (Biographies of Eminent Monks), various historical chronicles, and the collected records of Sengyou.
Plucking those azure feathers, he fashioned these inscribed wings;
with them, he fans the wind of a thousand ages across the reigns of a hundred kings.
Together they uphold the compass of wisdom, illuminating the darkness of the times.
Together, they spread the moisture of the Dharma-transmission to quench the parching witheredness of the world,
and expounded our Imperial Way so that its path might open at its inception.
In the past, at the beginning of the councils, it was recorded that [the teachings] were all pointed to as being in such-and-such a country and such-and-such a city.
Now, as for the merit of this proclamation and translation, it is necessary that each be categorized according to its respective era;
therefore, the structure of this record generally cites the titles [of the dynasties], designating them as the Records of Han, Wei, Wu, and the Great Sui.
Those translations whose translators are lost or which are suspected of being apocryphal are annotated according to their traditional records.
The scriptures are arranged in chronological order based on the dates of their translation;
where there are duplicate listings, they are likewise categorized according to their respective eras.
In total, there were one hundred and ninety-seven individuals, comprising both Chinese and foreigners, monastics and laypeople, and those of both genders.
They produced a total of two thousand one hundred and forty-six works, consisting of six thousand two hundred and thirty-five fascicles, including sutras, vinayas, śāstras, and biographies.
Categorized by their positions, they comprise fifteen fascicles: one fascicle for the general catalog,
two fascicles for the collection in the imperial repository,
and three fascicles for the imperial chronology.
The *Jiujuan dailu* (Nine-Scroll Supplementary Record) compiles and examines the quantity of sutras translated during successive reigns,
and records the imperial year in which the Buddha lived and the duration of his presence in the world.

The *Dafangdeng Shanzhuyitianzi Suowen Jing* (Mahāvaipulya-suvikrāntavikrami-paripṛcchā-sūtra) in four fascicles, the second edition, is the same text as the *Pusa Nianfo Sanmei Jing* (Bodhisattva-bhadracaryā-smṛtyupasthāna-samādhi-sūtra) translated by Guṇabhadra during the Song dynasty. It is a separate division of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*.

This is recorded in the *Neidian Lu* (Catalogue of Inner Scriptures). Regarding its depth and shallowness, it distinguishes the teachings of the Śrāvaka and Mahāyāna within the Tripiṭaka. It was produced at the Great Square Hall (*Dafangdeng*). [End of entry].

*The Sūtra on the Dharma-Root of the Supreme Portion at Birth*, two fascicles. Its initial translation was the same text as the *Sūtra on the Analysis of Dependent Origination* translated during the Tang dynasty;

it is also simply titled the *Sūtra on Dependent Arising*. It appears in the *Neidian lu*; it was produced in the tenth month of the twelfth year of Daye, and both the sūtra and its commentary were completed in the ninth month of the thirteenth year.
See the preface to the sūtra. *The Sūtra on the Original Vows of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru*, one fascicle.
Volume Two. Extracted for the Consecration [Rite], Volume Twelve. This is identical to the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabhāsa-pūrvapraṇidhāna-guṇa-sūtra* translated during the Tang dynasty;
see the *Neidian lu*. Completed on the eighth day of the twelfth month in the eleventh year of the Daye era at the Translation Hall.
Preface composed by the Śramaṇa Xingju. *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, three volumes, by Bodhisattva Asaṅga.
The *Bodhicaryāvatāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Equipment for Enlightenment) in six fascicles, authored by the Noble Nāgārjuna and translated by the Bhikṣu Guṇavarman;
see the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue) for the commentary. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* (Commentary on the Compendium of the Great Vehicle) in ten fascicles, the second translation;

it is identical in text to the translation by Paramārtha and the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (or *Mahāyānasaṃgrahopanibandhana*) by Vasubandhu translated during the Tang dynasty. See the *Neidian lu* for the commentary by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
*Record of the Treatise on Dependent Origination*, one fascicle, composed by the Noble Ullangha; it is the same text as the *Sūtra on Dependent Origination*, as noted in the *Neidian lu*.
*The Sūtra on the Causes and Origins of the World*, ten fascicles; the sixth [translation] among those produced.

It is the same text as the fourth division of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the *Lokadhātu-vibhāga-sūtra*, as well as the *Loutan jing* (Vaiśeṣika-sūtra), etc., though it is also simply titled the *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Origin of the World), as seen in the *Neidian lu*. Right.
The nine divisions in forty-six fascicles are extant;
they were translated by the śramaṇa Dharmagupta (translated as Fami in the Sui period).
He is also called Dharmatāla.

He was originally a native of the country of Roruka in South India; it is incorrect for the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Inner Scriptures) and the *Fanying tu* (Diagram of Translated Scriptures) to state that he was a native of Uḍḍiyāna in North India. He belonged to the Kṣatriya caste.
His surname was Piyaka (translated in the Sui language as "Tiger Clan"). He had three younger brothers, and he himself was the eldest son.
Although his parents were deeply attached to him and would not permit him to leave the household life, he possessed a profound love for the Dharma and a deep aspiration to renounce worldly life.

At the age of twenty-three, he went to the city of Kaṇauj (Sui: Erchu) in the region of Central India, located within the district of Kōmudī (Sui: Huanghua). There, at the monastery called Saṃghārāma (Sui: Zhongyuan; the old translation "Yugalam" is an abbreviation and corruption), Guptaka finally received the tonsure.
He changed his name to Fa-mi (Dharmamitra).
It was not until he was twenty-five years old that he received full ordination (*upasampadā*).

His *upādhyāya* was named Buddhapālita (translated into Chinese as Jué-mì, "Awakened Secret"); his *ācārya* was named Guṇadatta (translated into Chinese as Dé-shī, "Attained Giving"); and there was another *ācārya* named Puzhào (Samantaprabha).
He was able to recite and expound upon the sūtras and śāstras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

He practiced the *piṇḍapāta* dharma—what was formerly called *fenwei*, a corruption and abbreviation of the term—he entered *dhyāna* (translated in the Sui period as "contemplative cultivation," whereas the former term *chan-na* and the term *chih-ho-na* are both erroneous and deviant), constantly entering this meditative observation as his regular practice.
After Guptā had received full ordination (*upasampadā*), she remained for three years studying under her teacher,
gaining a general insight into the master’s attainments.
Later, the teacher Puzhao was invited by the King of Taka.
The Master traveled with him to that place and stayed for one year; when the Master returned to his own country, Guptaka remained there for another four years.

He resided at Devabhāra (translated in the Sui language as Tiányóu [Heavenly Travel]; "Tiān" refers to the king and "yóu" refers to the monastic quarters; it was so named because the king established it, hence "Heavenly Travel"). Formerly, the term "si" (temple) was used as a substitute, but this is merely the name for a government office or bureau in this land—meaning a "commission" or "extension. Furthermore, the term "zhāotí" (招提) is also a corruption and abbreviation. To explain it character by character generation after generation is erroneous: "zhāo" means to invite and "tí" means to support—these are all idle words. This is actually a Western (Indic) term; its correct pronunciation is *cātusala*, which means "the four directions," referring to a place where the Sangha from the four directions relies.
Thereupon, as he traveled through various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna countries and monasteries, his见闻 (what he heard and saw) increased manifold.

Merchants from the northern routes frequently visited those lands, and from afar it was transmitted that there existed a Great Country of Zhina in the eastern region. Its former names, Zhendan and Zhandan, were neither correct phonetics nor possessed translatable meanings; one only knew they were general names for this divine continent.
At first, although he had heard the accounts, he did not yet believe them with full clarity nor resolve to come;
however, as his aspiration lay in traveling abroad and his mind was free from attachments,
he eventually set out for the kingdom of Kāpiśī accompanied by six companions.
She remained in this country, staying at the Royal Monastery.
Gupta then took four companions and stayed within the city for two years,
visiting various monasteries to fully observe and study what they had learned.
The heart’s desire for distant travel has not yet found rest.
That country is a crossroads of the northern route, situated in the northern shadow of the Snow Mountains;
merchants from all quarters flock to its borders.
Furthermore, from the merchants, we heard that the Triple Gem flourishes in the great nation of China;
thus, our companions have come here with one mind and focused intent,
not merely to observe its customs and culture.
Vowing to benefit sentient beings and propagate the sutras,
he then crossed the western foot of the Snow Mountains and reached the kingdoms of Bāhlika and Sāṭakani.
In the kingdom of Dharmasīla and these various kingdoms, he did not reside for long; thus,
he was able to fully understand the local customs and the ritual protocols of the monasteries.
He then traveled to the kingdom of Kharapandha and stayed there for one year;
having not yet extensively guided others, he proceeded to the kingdom of Shache,
where one of his companions returned to his native city.
The remaining three men stayed at the King’s Temple—
so called because it was built by the King of Śākala—
and remained there for two years.
He further expounded the *Vigrahavyāvartanī* (Treatise on Dispelling Disputes) in two thousand stanzas for those monks;
its purport clarifies the three seals and extensively refutes non-Buddhists.
He also expounded the *Tattvasiddhi* (Treatise on Reality) in two thousand stanzas for them.
Judging by its literary style and principles,
it is a treatise on worldly scholastic debate.
Furthermore, he also stayed at Wang Temple in the kingdom of Kucha.
He remained there for another two years,
continuing to lecture on and explain the aforementioned treatise to that community of monks.
The king was a devoted admirer of the Mahāyāna and attained great enlightenment through his teachings.
With a lingering heart, he visited [the master] morning and evening;
yet Guptā fixed her mind on the Eastern Lands (China) and had no intention of remaining in concealment.
She secretly took a monk along and traveled by circuitous routes until they reached the kingdom of Kucha.
At the Āraṇya Monastery, he lectured on the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* for another two years; subsequently,
he gradually traveled to various monasteries in Gaochang.
The monks in that country were mostly learned in the Chinese language;
although he stayed there for two years, he produced no translations.
He then proceeded to Yiwu, where he remained for one year.
Encountering a place of hardship where one must flee,
the road to the southwest was entirely sandy and stony, with both water and grass utterly lacking;
companions were forced to rely on one another as there was no refuge for their lives.
He then temporarily set aside the scriptures and treatises he had brought with him by the side of the road;
crossing the mountains in search of water, he hoped thereby to sustain his life.
But as his search proved fruitless, his exhaustion and distress increased all the more.
While he was intently reciting the Avalokiteśvara mantra, rain suddenly fell during the night.
His body and mind were filled with joy, and he soon returned to his original path;
however, looking around in bewilderment, he found himself lost as to the way.
Hesitating between advancing and retreating,
he eventually proceeded forward and reached Guazhou;
there he finally realized that he had taken the northern route by circuitous means.
Guptā had long yearned for the Great Kingdom and had traveled there on foot for many years;
when she first joined her fellow disciples,
some had already remained behind or passed away.
Turning my gaze alone toward this solitary landscape at this sublime site, I reflected in silence;
grief and joy welled up within me simultaneously.
Soon thereafter, by imperial decree, I was invited into the capital.
He was provided with abundant supplies at the famous temple of that location;
this was in the tenth month of winter in the tenth year of the Kaihuang era.
Not long after his arrival, he had mastered the Chinese language in its essentials.
Furthermore, by imperial decree, he was ordered to proceed with the translation of scriptures;
he moved his residence to Xingshan Monastery, where he took up the original texts to perform the translation,
ensuring accuracy and resolving complexities.
The Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna treatises you have recited are all profoundly essential;
as for their exposition and elucidation, they extensively propagate subtle and profound meanings.
Those who study here in this land have frequently sent forth their accumulated doubts.
Nevertheless, he established himself through compassion and forbearance, and cultivated a nature of gentleness.
His mind did not stray outside the Way, and his conduct preceded his words.
The ground of his precepts was level and tranquil; the waters of his wisdom were profound and pure.
The *Xiǎngzìyuánlùn* (Discourse on the Source of Characters) exhaustively investigates sounds and meanings;
furthermore, its majestic appearance is detailed and correct, its diligent discipline lofty and fierce.
Its chanting resounds through the day and night, and its Dharma words penetrate both internal and external traditions.
Furthermore, his family was fond of dwelling in tranquility and maintaining simplicity, severing ties with worldly affairs.
They were frugal and had few desires, putting an end to all seeking.
They never grew weary of instructing others, prioritizing the benefit of others over their own self-interest.
He never showed a countenance of displeasure toward those of lowly status, nor did he harbor contempt for those of humble kind.
Consequently, those who had not yet seen him were drawn by his reputation, and those who visited him briefly felt deep reverence.
Standing at the forefront of translators, he remained solely devoted to the faithful transmission of the teachings.
In all matters of governance and administration, the primary focus was on maintaining the fundamental principles.
Emperor Yang established his capital at the Eastern Metropolis (Luoyang) with profound reverence and generous patronage;
as for the Buddha-dharma, he increased its veneration and further promoted its flourishing.
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued to establish a Translation Hall within the Shanglin Garden on the southern bank of the Luo River.
Talented and eminent individuals were sought out to permanently reside there and transmit the Dharma.
Immediately thereafter, Dharmagupta and various scholars were summoned by imperial decree and assembled together.
He provided the fourfold service with constant devotion,
ensuring that the translators did not lose their momentum and that the records were completed without interruption throughout his time.
When the imperial framework of the Sui dynasty collapsed, he continued his efforts, building upon the foundations like smoke rising from a stack of wood.
The new translation of the Sanskrit text was abruptly interrupted at that time.
Guptā, having stored away her profound understanding, consequently failed to transmit it further.
It was not until the Kaihuang era that she arrived in the capital.
He immediately joined with Ratnamati in the work of consultation and translation;
at that time, Ratnamati presided over the proceedings, and they together transmitted the Sanskrit texts into the Sui language.
At that time, he was universally praised for his excellence;
yet regarding profound meanings, there were none who did not turn to him for instruction.
His dignified bearing was vast and serene, remaining entirely untouched by the mundane paths of the world.
Consequently, the reputation of the translator was eclipsed as he suppressed his own merits to exalt others.
Toward the end of the Renshou era, Xuanzang was exiled to Dongyue due to other matters;
seizing this opportunity, Jñānagupta took sole charge of the translation work.
From the first year of the Daye era until the final year of that same era,
he translated nine sections of the *Mahāvaipulya-suvikrāntavikrami-paripṛcchā-sūtra* and other scriptures; in all cases,
both the phrasing and the meaning were lucid and pure, with the elegant and the plain clearly and fluently expressed.
The śramaṇa Yanzong [was] brilliant, with Xingju and others serving as scribes.
He passed away at Luonan in the third year of the Wude era of the Great Tang;
the śramaṇa Yanzong composed his biography.
Initially, Guṇabhadra translated the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in one fascicle and the *Sarvasukhāvaha Sūtra* in fifteen fascicles.
Before he had time to verify and revise them, he encountered the collapse of the state under the illegitimate Zheng dynasty; thus, he lacked the leisure to undertake further revisions.
The present fascicle contains matters such as the "Eight Manifestations" (Aṣṭamahāprātihārya) found in the *Capital* edition.
It is now said that the Tripitaka Master Daizhou Rizhao has translated the *Vaipulya-puṇyālaṃkāra-sūtra* (Fangguang dazhuangyan jing) in twelve fascicles.
It is identical to the old *Lalitavistara-sūtra* (Puyao jing) in its Sanskrit original;
therein it also clarifies matters such as the eight signs [of a great man].
It should likewise be identical to the Sanskrit original of this *Sarvasukha-saṃpāda-sūtra* (Pule jing).
