Ziliang was a preeminent leader in literature; he upheld Confucianism and venerated Buddhism, encouraging others to achieve the Way, so that his followers were as numerous as clouds.

At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, Emperor Wen abandoned the old palace of Dahuang at Mount Zhongnan to establish Longtian Monastery. This Longtian Monastery was the main courtyard of the Dahuang Palace; it is now located south of Cuiwei. The main court of the palace became Dahua Monastery, which has since been merged into Cuiwei Monastery. As for Huilin, by nature he delighted in seclusion and tranquility.
He took up residence there;
esteemed by the assembly, he was appointed to oversee the affairs of the monastery.
Clad in mountain robes, he lived with ease among the peaks, chanting and singing amidst the forests and wilds.
In the third year,
an imperial edict was issued for the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñāvarman to translate the Ratnolkā-sūtra and the Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra.
He summoned Huilin and ordered him to take up the brush;
Huilin received his instructions and also carefully examined the meanings of the names.
In the winter of the thirteenth year, there was one Qin Shiying, who wore the yellow turban.
Exploiting his mastery of esoteric arts to seek honor,
he subsequently presented his talents for evaluation before the Crown Prince;
harboring a long-standing animosity toward the Śākya clan, he secretly laid out his schemes.
Failing to recognize that Lin’s polemical writings slandered the imperial clan,
the Emperor deemed his crime equivalent to treason.
He issued a sudden edict to purge the monastic community of both monks and nuns.
Seeing that there was a group of associates,
he followed the Bequeathed Teachings and sought out Senglin’s person to investigate the matter according to the Dharma.
Senglin clenched his fists in indignation and rose up with vigor, not waiting for further summons.
He went alone to the public court, disregarding his lord to pursue what he deemed right;
consequently, he was bound in fetters,
and an imperial edict was issued to inquire:
In the feudal alliances of the Zhou, those of different surnames were placed last;
this honoring of ancestors and valuing of kinship truly originated from antiquity.
Why then do you pursue their shortcomings?
He wavers like a rat between two ends, extensively citing analogies based on superficial resemblance and presenting a full array of insolent metaphors;
he seeks to tear down my ancestors and defiles my forebears with slander.
"In such a case, the crime of pressuring the sovereign would be unforgivable.
Senglin replied,
"King Wen was a great sage and the Duke of Zhou were great worthies."
In honoring the distant past and being cautious at the end of life, the vast heavens offer no response;
yet the ultimate expression of filial piety and fraternal duty penetrates even to the divine spirits.
Although the House of Zhou was the ancestral dynasty, in principle one should not strive for precedence.
Why is this? The August Heaven shows no favoritism; it ultimately relies upon the support of virtue.
The ancients sided with principle rather than with kinship.
He does not place himself before others nor after them;
though a close relative may have committed a crime, he must surely punish them,
and though a distant person may have performed a service, he must surely reward them.
Because rewards and punishments accorded with principle, the world was at peace.
Laozi cultivated human instruction and took virtue as his model, extending it to the common people;
through self-reflection and humble radiance, the breeze of benevolence manifested throughout the four seas.
It is further said:
"My teacher is named Buddha.
'Buddha' means one who awakens all people."
The Ancient Sovereign of Gandhāra ascended to the West and passed away;
yet the origins and end of the Laoist teaching may still be traced.
He personally bestowed the *Zhongjing* (Central Scripture) upon me, instructing his disciples, saying: [text continues].
"My Master was skilled at entering nirvana; he exists perpetually and eternally.
I am now departing.
As for what Liu and Li have written, they slanderously claim that the Master of Laozi has been extinguished."
The world was unable to understand this.
He composed the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on the Rectification of Arguments) in eight fascicles,
providing a brief rebuttal to the Daoists.
There are more than sixty articles,
all citing historical records;
it is truly not the case that these previous words slander or defame the state and its family.
Thereafter, more than sixty points of debate were addressed entirely based on Senglin’s statements;
a formal petition was prepared and submitted to the throne.
The imperial edict stated:
In the "Chapter on the Reciprocal Retribution of Faith and Slander" in his *Discourse on the Rectification of Orthodoxy*, he states:
"There are those who, by recollecting Avalokiteśvara, are not wounded even when facing the blade.
Furthermore, I have granted you a seven-day reprieve so that you may recollect him yourself."
When the trial and sentencing arrived, could he avoid being harmed?
Lin was externally bound by shackles and internally oppressed by the approaching date of his execution;
fire and water were intermingled within his breast.
Having no way to appeal for succor,
he then recorded the scriptures and teachings he had heard since birth, as well as the names of the Three Holy Ones, and engraved them within the treasury of his heart,
intending them to manifest a divine response.
When the term of confinement expired, his spirit suddenly became bold and unrestrained, and a sense of joy and celebration arose within his breast,
causing him to momentarily forget all fear of death;
he stood waiting for the interrogation.
A short while later, an imperial decree arrived, saying:
"The period of grace has now expired; you are about to face execution.
What do you have on your mind? Is there any spiritual efficacy [in your practice]?"
Lín took up his brush and replied:
"Since the chaos at the end of the Sui dynasty, the four seas have been in turmoil;
pestilence has spread and the clash of arms has arisen in competition."
They raise armies to strike one another, each monopolizing military power.
Ministers are sycophantic and their sovereigns are dissolute, failing to govern with rectitude.
They block the roads and obstinately cling to a single corner of the realm.
Since the imperial kings have conducted punitive expeditions to bring peace to both land and sea,
this is truly due to the power of Avalokiteśvara and entirely thanks to the grace of Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Their virtue was comparable and their footsteps followed in tandem with those of the supreme sages;
they rescued those facing untimely deaths within the imperial court and spared those condemned by licentious punishments in the marketplace.
For seven days past, Ling has not been mindful of Avalokiteśvara, but has been mindful only of Your Majesty.
An imperial edict was issued to Wei Zong, the Director of the Secretariat for Scrutiny of Documents, ordering him to inquire with Ling:
"There is an imperial decree commanding you to be mindful of Avalokiteśvara."
"By what cause do you not recite [the name], yet say that you only recite it?
Your Majesty," Lin replied.
I humbly acknowledge that you, O Holy Avalokiteśvara, have observed my physical form throughout the six realms;
from the heavens above to the earth below, you serve as a model for all.
Throughout the Great Tang, your influence pervades the four seas.
The nine tribes of Yi submit to their duties and the eight regions of the world are serene.
With a sage ruler and worthy ministers, there shall be no injustice or excess.
Now...
Your Majesty nurtures all beings as if they were your own children, just as described in the sutras;
this is none other than Avalokiteśvara.
Since your spiritual discernment thus accords with his, [the response is manifest].
Therefore, I venture to think that Your Majesty should consider this:
as for the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Discerning the Correct) composed by Senglin, it states:
This is comparable to the conventions of calligraphy and history:
if a single phrase deviates slightly, one must be prepared for the axe and the hatchet.
If Your Majesty follows what is loyal and upright, [the merit shall be yours].
As for Lin, not even a single hair of his will be harmed;
yet if Your Majesty inflicts punishment upon the innocent,
Lin shall suffer the pain of prostrate corpses.
He reported the matter in its entirety to the Emperor,
who consequently did not impose any punishment upon him. There was [a case where]...
By imperial decree, he was transferred to a monastery for monks in Yibu.
While traveling to Bodhi Monastery at Bailao Pass, he passed away due to illness.
He was sixty-nine years old at the time.
The śramaṇa Huixu attended to his master’s ailments with diligent care;
their bond was as firm as severed metal, and they shared a single quilt from dawn until dusk, offering comfort and support.
When his life was drawing to a close, he rested upon Xu’s knees.
He wailed in grief until his body collapsed, his tears falling like torrential rain.
He then summoned the monastics and laypeople from the surrounding passes and buried him on the summit of the mountain east of the city.
A white stupa was erected upon a high tree,
and an inscription was engraved upon it.
Those passing by who had forgotten [the Buddha] would know [of his presence] and shed tears.

The poems, fu, petitions, eulogies, inscriptions, prefaces, memorial tablets, dirges, Mahāyāna teachings, as well as various treatises, records, and biographies composed by Lin total more than thirty fascicles.
All of them strike the very essence of poetic resonance, like the clashing of metal and stone.
The patterns of his literary thought were richly embroidered and brilliantly painted;
his style flowed with grace and elegance, its soaring brilliance ever more profound and solemn.
Furthermore, he was adept at responding to the capacities of his audience, guiding them through discourse that followed the immediate circumstances of each occasion.
His speech harmonized with the musical notes of Gong and Shang, and its meaning accorded with the profound scriptures.
Yet, Ying of the Qin era was executed for hiding his madness;
both public and private opinion marveled that his death had come so late.
The Liu, Li, and Chuan clans followed one another in conversion;
thus, their surviving writings and past deeds may serve as a guiding model for ten thousand generations.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* in six hundred fascicles appears in the *Fanying tu*; the Buddha [taught it] in four locations. Ten...

The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one fascicle, was translated at the Yu-hua Hall of Yu-hua Monastery on the first day of the first month in the fifth year of the Xianqing era (660 CE) across six assemblies, completed on the twentieth day of the tenth month in the third year of the Longshuo era (663 CE).
The śramaṇas Dashengguang, Dashengqin, Jia Shang, and others acted as scribes. It is recorded in the *Neidian lu*.
The fourth edition is identical in its original text to those translated by Kumārajīva and others of the Yao Qin dynasty.
On the first day of the tenth month in the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era, it was translated at the Hongfa Terrace of the Yuhua Palace in Yijun County, Fangzhou;
Du Xingyi, Director of the Secretariat, acted as the scribe. This one fascicle of the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* is recorded in the second volume of the *Neidian lu*.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitāmahāvidyāmantra-sūtra* (摩訶般若大明呪經), etc., was translated on the twenty-fourth day of the fifth month in the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era at the Cuiwei Palace on Mount Zhongnan. The śramaṇa Zhirin acted as the scribe.
The *Mahābodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* in twenty fascicles is recorded in the *Neidian lu*; it is now compiled into the *Ratnakūṭa*, constituting the twelfth assembly. Recorded by the monk Jingtai.

The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-kṣitigarbha-daśacakra-sūtra* in ten fascicles was translated at the Sūtra Translation Hall of Hongfu Monastery in the Western Capital, beginning on the second day of the fifth month of the nineteenth year [of the Zhenguan era] and completed on the second day of the ninth month.
The śramaṇa Zhizheng acted as the scribe (*bishou*), and Daoxuan verified the text.
It is recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalog) that this constitutes the thirteenth division of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, corresponding to the former *Vaipulya* section.

The *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* (Ten Wheels Sutra), translated from the original Sanskrit at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery in the Western Capital on the twenty-third day of the first month in the second year of the Yonghui era, was completed on the twenty-ninth day of the sixth month. Transcribed by the śramaṇa Mahāyānaprabha and others.

One fascicle of the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-viśvabuddhakṣetraguṇavyūha-sūtra* (Sutra on the Manifestation of the Merits of Boundless Buddha-fields) is recorded in the *Neidian lu*; this is the "Life" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

A different translation of the *Pramāṇa-pariccheda* (Chapter on Valid Cognition). Translated on the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month in the fifth year of the Yonghui era at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery.
Scribe: the Śramaṇa Dashengyun. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, six fascicles. Recorded in the *Neidian lu* as the seventh translation;
it is identical in text to Kumārajīva’s *Vimalakīrti-sūtra*. Translated on the eighth day of the second month in the first year of the Yonghui era.

On the first day of the eighth month, the translation of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* in five fascicles was completed at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery by the Śramaṇa Mahāyānaprabha, who acted as the scribe.

According to the second record in the *Neidian lu*, this version is identical in its original text to the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, the *Saṃdhivyākaraṇa*, the *Saṃdhinirmocanavibhaṅga*, and the *Anupūrvasamudgata-parivarta*.
[The work was begun] on the tenth day of the fifth month of the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era.
On the eighth day [of the month], the translation was begun at Hongfu Monastery and completed on the thirteenth day of the seventh month.

The *Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśa-sūtra* (Fenbie yuanqi chusheng famen jing), in two fascicles, was transcribed by the śramaṇa Mahāyānaprabha. This is recorded as the second appearance in the *Neidian lu*.

It is the same text as the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* translated by Guṇabhadra during the Sui dynasty. On the third day of the second month of the first year of the Yonghui era, [the work was finalized] at the Great Ci'en Monastery.

The translation at the Translation Institute of the Monastery was completed in the eighth month. The *Bhaisajyaguru-vaidūryaprabhāsa-tathāgata-pūrvapraṇidhāna-guṇa-dharma-sūtra*, one fascicle, was transcribed by the śramaṇa Damaxian (Dacheng Xun).
It appears in the third volume of the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue) as being the same text as that produced by Dharmagupta and others during the Sui dynasty.
It was translated on the fifth day of the fifth month of the first year of the Yonghui era at the Great Ci’en Monastery.
*The Sūtra on Praising the Pure Land and Being Received by the Buddha*, one fascicle; recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Inner Classics), section three.
Translated at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery on the first day of the first month of the first year of the Yonghui era (650 CE);
received by the śramaṇa Dasheng Xun. This text is identical in substance to the *Amitābha Sūtra* translated by Kumārajīva.
*The Rare Sūtra*, one fascicle; listed in the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Inner Scriptures), third entry.
Translated on the eighteenth day of the fifth month in the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era at Cuiwei Palace in Zhongnan Mountain. Transcribed by the śramaṇa Daming Qin.
*The Sūtra of the Most Peerless*, one fascicle; listed in the *Neidian lu*, second entry. A translation from the Sui dynasty.
The *Sūtra on the Rare Merit of Comparative Measurement* (希有校量功德經), same text as the *Sūtra Praising the Merit of the Mahāyāna* (稱讚大乘功德經), one fascicle;
translated at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery on the nineteenth day of the seventh month in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era. Transcribed by the śramaṇa Dàchéngguāng.
Recorded in the *Nèidiǎnlù*. Initially produced as the same text as the *Sūtra on Definitive Karmic Obstructions* (決定業障經). Permanently [established].

On the fifth day of the sixth month in the fifth year of the Huichang era, at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery, the *Tathāgata-śāsanopadeśa-rājñaḥ-senajit-sūtra* (一卷) was translated, with the śramaṇa Dashengguang serving as the scribe. It is recorded in the second volume of the *Neidian lu*.

This version is identical in substance to the *Jianwang jing* (Sūtra on Admonishing the King), having been produced on the sixth day of the second month in the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era at the Great Ci’en Monastery.
One fascicle of the *Āryamārga-utpatti-sūtra*, translated by the śramaṇa Mahāyāna-prabha of the Translation Institute and received in writing;

recorded in the sixth volume of the *Neidian lu*. This text was translated on the first day of the first month of the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era at the Zihui Palace within the Northern Gate of the Western Capital (Xi’jing).
It is a śramaṇa of the Right Hongfa Court. It is identical in substance to the *Paitāla-vṛkṣa-mūla-sūtra* and other related texts.
*The Heart Sūtra of the Amoghapāśa Divine Mantra*, one fascicle, transcribed by the śramaṇa Mahāyānaprabha; recorded in the second volume of the *Neidian lu*.
This edition is identical to those translated by Jñānagupta and others during the Sui dynasty.

Translated on the nineteenth day of the fourth month in the fourth year of the Xianqing era at the Translation Hall of Daci’en Monastery, with the śramaṇa Mahāyānaprabha serving as the scribe. [The Eleven-faced Divine...]
*Zhòuxīn jīng* (Dhāraṇī-hṛdaya Sūtra), one fascicle; listed in the *Nèidiǎn lù* (Record of Buddhist Scriptures) as the second edition, identical in text to those translated by Yaśogupta and others.
Translated on the twenty-eighth day of the third month in the first year of the Xiǎnqìng era at the Fàn-jīng Yuàn (Translation Institute) of Dàcí'ēn Sī (Great Ci'en Monastery);

the śramaṇa Xuánzé recorded the oral transmission. *Zhòu wǔshǒu jīng* (Sūtra of Five Dhāraṇīs), one fascicle; listed in the *Fàn-jīng tú* (Illustrated Record of Translations) as having been produced in the first year of the LínDé era.

On the first day of the first month of the year, at the Yu-hua Hall of the Yu-hua Monastery, the *Sheng-dang-bi-yin tuoluo-ni jing* (One Scroll of the Arm-Seal Banner Dhāraṇī Sūtra) was translated, with the śramaṇa Da-sheng-guang serving as scribe.
It is recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue). Its initial publication shared the same text as the *Miao-bi-yin-chuang tuoluo-ni* (Arm-Seal Banner Dhāraṇī).
On the twenty-ninth day of the ninth month of the fifth year of Yonghui, [it was further revised] at the Great Ci-en Monastery.
One fascicle of the *Sarvabuddhahṛdaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, translated at the Translation Hall of the Monastery by the śramaṇa Mahāyāna-yun as scribe; recorded in the *Neidian lu*.
Translated on the twenty-sixth day of the ninth month of the first year of the Yonghui era at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery, with the śramaṇa Mahāyāna-yun serving as scribe.
One [fascicle] of the *Duḥkhaparitrāṇa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, translated at the Translation Hall of the Monastery by the śramaṇa Mahāyāna-yun as scribe.
One fascicle, seen in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue). Translated on the tenth day of the ninth month in the fifth year of the Yonghui era at the Translation Hall of Da Ci’en Monastery;
received by brush from the śramaṇa Dashengguang. Title: *Pumidi Dharani Sutra*, one fascicle. Seen in the *Neidian lu*.
Translated on the twenty-seventh day of the ninth month in the fifth year of the Yonghui era at the Translation Hall of Da Ci’en Monastery.
*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of Holding the World*, one fascicle;
translated at the Translation Court of the Great Ci’en Monastery on the tenth day of the tenth month in the fifth year of the Yonghui era by the śramaṇa Dashengyun, with Shencha serving as scribe;
recorded in the *Neidian lu*. *The Six-Gate Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era; recorded in the *Neidian lu*.
On the fourteenth day of the seventh month of the [X] year, at the Translation Hall of Hongfu Monastery, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* in one fascicle was translated;

the śramaṇa Bianji received it by dictation. This is recorded in the *Neidian lu*. On the fifth day of the seventh month of the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, at the Translation Hall of Hongfu Monastery, the *Shouchi qifo minghao suosheng* (The Merits Arising from Upholding the Names of the Seven Buddhas) was translated; the śramaṇa Bianji received it by dictation.

*Gongde jing* (Sūtra on Merit), one fascicle; recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Translated at the Translation Hall of Daci’en Monastery on the ninth day of the first month in the second year of the Yonghui era.
Scribe for the oral transmission: the śramaṇa Dashengguang. *Folinnanipanjiji fazhu jing* (Sūtra on the Buddha’s Record of the Duration of the Dharma at the Time of His Nirvāṇa), one fascicle;
recorded in the *Fanying tu*. Translated at Daci’en Monastery on the fourth day of the fourth month in the third year of the Yonghui era.
*The Sūtra on the Miraculous Transformation of Samādhi*, one fascicle; translated by the śramaṇa Mahāyāna-Prabha at the Translation Institute, with Daśaśrī as scribe.

Recorded in the *Tuanjing tu* (Diagram of the Translation Halls). Translated on the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month of the second year of the Longshuo era at the Yu Hua Palace in Yu Hua Monastery;
the śramaṇa Mahāyāna-Prabha served as scribe. *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, one fascicle; recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue).
Record of the third translation: The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which is the same text as that translated by Dharmakṣema and others.
Translated on the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery;
the Mahāyāna Master Guǎng received the dictation. One fascicle of the *Bodhisattva-śīla-karman* (Ritual for the Bodhisattva Precepts) is seen within [the canon].

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, "Bodhisattvabhūmi" section from the *Maulībhūmi*, translated on the fifteenth day of the seventh month in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era at the Translation Hall of Da Ci’en Temple; received by the śramaṇa Mahāyāna-guang as scribe.
The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* in seven fascicles, composed by the Bodhisattvas Sthiramati and others, as recorded in the *Neidian lu*; translated in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era.

On the second day of the twelfth month of the third year, the translation was commenced at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery; it was completed on the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* in one hundred fascicles, spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva, was received in writing by the Śramaṇa Mahāyāna-prabhāsa.
It is recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures) that this took place on the fifteenth day of the fifth month of the twelfth year of the Zhenguan era.
The translation at the Translation Hall of Hongfu Monastery was completed on the fifteenth day of the fifth month in the twentieth year. The śramaṇas Linghui, Mingyao, and others acted as scribes.

The *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (Treatise on the Manifestation of the Holy Teaching) in twenty fascicles, composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga, was translated on the eleventh day of the tenth month in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era at the Translation Hall of Hongfu Monastery; it is recorded in the *Neidian lu*.
The translation was completed on the fifth day of the first month of the twentieth year. The śramaṇas Zhizheng and others recorded it by pen.

One fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra), composed by Bodhisattva Jinzishizi (Jin-zhi-zi), was translated on the first day of the second month of the ninth year of Yonghui at the Translation Hall of Da Cien Monastery;
the śramaṇa Dashenghui recorded it by pen. It appears in the *Fanying tu* (Illustrated Record of Translations).
*Yang shengjiao lun song* (Verses on the Propagation of the Holy Teachings), one fascicle; listed in the *Neidian lu*. Composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga.
Translated at the Fanyingyuan of Hongfu Monastery on the eleventh day of the tenth month in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era. Transcribed by the śramaṇa Bianji.

*Wangfa zhengli lun* (Treatise on the Correct Principles of the King’s Dharma), one fascicle; listed in the *Neidian lu*. Composed by Bodhisattva Maitreya. [Translated] in the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era...

On the eighteenth day of the seventh month of the third year [of the Yonghui era], at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci'en Monastery, the *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra* in seven fascicles was translated;
the śramaṇa Damashenglín acted as the scribe. It is recorded in the *Neidian lu* that it was composed by Bodhisattva Asanga.
On the sixteenth day of the first month of the third year of Yonghui, it was translated at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci'en Monastery.
On the twenty-eighth day of the third month, the *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* in sixteen fascicles was completed,
with Piśama, Dashengguang, Dashengyun, and others serving as scribes. As recorded in the *Neidian lu*,

this commentary by the Bodhisattva Sthiramati was translated at the Translation Hall of Hongfu Monastery on the seventeenth day of the first month of the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era, through the intercalary month.
On the twenty-ninth day of the third month, the *Bai lun ben* (Root Text of the *Śataśāstra*) in one fascicle was transcribed by the śramaṇas Xuanzé and others;
it is recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalog) as composed by the Bodhisattva Āryadeva.

On the sixth day of the sixth month of the first year of the Yonghui era, the *Dacheng guang bai lun shi lun* (Commentary on the *Mahāyāna-śataśāstra*) in ten [fascicles] was translated at the Translation Hall of Daci’en Monastery, with the śramaṇa Damoyu serving as the scribe.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* by Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, in three fascicles, as recorded in the *Neidian lu*.

Translated at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery on the twenty-seventh day of the sixth month in the first year of the Yonghui era, completed on the twenty-third day of the twelfth month.
Scribe: Śramaṇa Jingming and others. The original text of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* in three fascicles, by Bodhisattva Asaṅga, as recorded in the *Neidian lu*.
The third production was undertaken on the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month of the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era at the Hongfa Monastery west of the Ziwai Hall in the Northern Palace;
it was completed at Cien Monastery on the seventeenth day of the sixth month of the twenty-third year.

The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* (Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃparigraha), translated by Paramārtha, with Vasubandhu’s commentary in ten fascicles, was received by Wei as the scribe. This is recorded in the *Neidian lu*.

The śramaṇa Śikṣānanda (Shi Xuanzang),
whose original name was Hui, [translated them].
His secular surname was Chen;
he was a native of Chenliu.
He was a descendant of Chen Zhonggong, the Grand Master of Taichou during the Han dynasty.
His great-great-grandfather, Qin, was the Governor of Shangdang during the Northern Wei.
His grandfather, Kang, was a State Doctor at the Guozijian during the Northern Qi;
as his fief was located in Zhounan, his descendants took up residence there due to their official posts.
Furthermore, he was a native of Guoshi.
His father, Huīyīng, was pure and possessed refined integrity;
he mastered the classical arts at an early age.
He was eight chi tall, with beautiful eyebrows and clear eyes.
During the Daye era, he was appointed as the Magistrate of Jiangling,
but he returned his ceremonial sash and resigned.
Those who understood him believed this was because it marked the time for his final departure into reclusion.
He had four sons, of whom Xuanzang was the youngest;
from childhood, he possessed exceptional character and intelligence that set him apart from his peers.
When he was eight years old, his father sat beside a desk and orally transmitted the *Xiaojing* (Classic of Filial Piety) to him.
Upon reaching the passage where Zengzi left his seat, [the boy] suddenly adjusted his robes and rose.
His father asked him the reason for this.
He replied,
"When Zengzi heard his teacher's command, he still rose from his mat;
how much more so do I now receive your compassionate instruction?"
"How could he remain sitting idly?
His father was greatly pleased and, knowing that his son would surely achieve success,
summoned his kinsmen and spoke to them.
Everyone congratulated him, saying,
"This is the 'Yangwu' (the parrot) of this gentleman;
such was his precocious wisdom."
Thereafter, he thoroughly mastered the profound depths of the scriptures.
His elder brother, Changjie, had previously left the household life at Jingtu Monastery in the Eastern Capital;
because Xuanzang had suffered extreme hardship in his youth, his brother took him along with him.
Jishou was granted the essential principles of the teachings and supplemented them with skillful discourses.
At the age of eleven, he could recite the *Vimalakīrti* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras;
at the Eastern Capital, Hengdu immediately placed him among his peers.
From that time on, he stood out as exceptionally upright and did not associate with his peers.
He recited the catalogues from memory without the slightest omission.
When he saw the novices engaged in boisterous talk and playful antics, [he would look upon them with disapproval].
Xuanzang said to him,
"Does the Sūtra not say that those who have left the household life practice the dharma of non-action?"
How could one continue to indulge in mere child's play?
It can be said that such a person has squandered their hundred years in vain.
At that time, there was Dharma Master Jing at the monastery who was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Holding the scrolls and humbly receiving them into his heart, he eventually forgot both sleep and food. Furthermore,
when studying Master Yan’s *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*,
he mastered it upon the first hearing, and after a second reading, there was nothing left unretained.
At that time he was thirteen years old.
Subsequently, as the Sui dynasty lost its mandate over the empire and the world fell into turmoil,
the brothers took each other's hands and traveled to the capital city, where they resided at Zhuangyan Temple.
This was the first year of the Wude era.
As the foundations of the state were still being laid and military affairs remained active,
there were no lecture halls in the capital.
However, within the regions of Mian and Shu, Buddhist activities were extremely flourishing.
Consequently, he and his elder brother followed the path through the Zimugou Valley into Hanchuan,
where they encountered the two Dharma Masters Kong and Jing.
After staying for over a month, he followed him to receive instruction.
Together they proceeded toward Chengdu,
where various virtuous masters had already gathered to establish a great Dharma assembly.
Thereupon, he was further permitted to study Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Mārgavibhāga-śāstra*, and the *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra*.
Reverently valuing every moment, he applied himself with untiring diligence.
Within two or three years, he had thoroughly mastered all these various treatises.
Having reached the age of twenty,
he received full ordination in Chengdu in the fifth year of the Wude era.
During the summer retreat, he studied the Vinaya, focusing on the essential principles of the seven groups of offenses.
By reciting it once, one attains this.
Xuanzang reflected to himself:
"In study, what is prized is enduring depth; in meaning, what is valued is broad comprehension."
Admiring [the teachings] from one direction alone, he had not yet succeeded in fathoming their depths;
he therefore traveled from Shu to Jing to seek out the former masters,
eventually reaching Xiangzhou.

After composing the *Huixiu Fashi Zhijwen Yiai* (Questions on Doubts and Obstructions to Dharma Master Huixiu), he traveled next to Zhaozhou to visit Dharma Master Daoshen and study the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
He subsequently entered Chang’an and resided at Dajue Temple.
He studied the Abhidharmakośa-śāstra under Master Jue;
he mastered its essential meaning after reading it only once,
committing everything to memory upon merely seeing it with his eyes.
Even those of long-standing learning and advanced age were unable to surpass him;
as for his ability to probe the profound, reach the distant, and illuminate the subtle and the hidden—
matters beyond the reach of the common crowd— he was unsurpassed.
That those who have attained solitary awakening into the profound and abstruse do not, of course, constitute a single school of thought.
At that time, there were the two Dharma Masters Chang and Bian in Chang’an,
who served as preeminent masters of the Dharma in the capital.
Xuanzang again consulted them, and they found that all their profound insights were likewise fully contained therein.
Both masters deeply sighed in admiration and said to Xuanzang:
[The rest of the passage follows].
"You may truly be called a 'thousand-li steed' of the Śākya gate.
