he paid particular attention to the gateway of dhāraṇī.
It is generally recorded that Tong left the household life during the Daye era of the Sui dynasty.
He resided at Dazongchi Monastery in the capital and harbored the aspiration to travel abroad.
He subsequently studied the Sanskrit script and language at the Translation Hall in the capital of Luoyang,
where he quickly mastered its profound subtleties.
During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, there was a monk from North India.

He brought a Sanskrit manuscript of the *Qianbi Qianyanshou Guanshiyin Pusa Mimi Dajiaowang Jing* (The Sutra of the Secret Great Teaching King of the Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva) to present to Emperor Wen.
By imperial decree, it was translated in collaboration with a Sanskrit monk,
resulting in two fascicles.
Later, in the fourth year of Emperor Gaozong’s Yonghui era (the Gui-chou year), three additional scriptures, including the *Qianzhuan* [Thousand Verses], were produced at Zongchi Monastery.

The *Qianshou Qianyan Guanshiyin Pusa Guangda Yuanman Wuai Dabeixin Duoaloni Jing* (The Scripture on the Greatly Vast, Perfect, and Unobstructed Heart-Dhāraṇī of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with a Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes), one fascicle: this single work in one fascicle still exists today.
The śramaṇa Gaovendharma—
here translated as "Venerable Dharma"—
was a native of Western India.
A single fascicle of the *Qianshou Qianyan Dabeixin Jing* was translated.
However, its title states it was translated by Gāvadharma of Western India, without specifying the date.
Judging from its provenance and characteristics, it appears to be a recent translation produced during the Imperial Dynasty (the Song).
However, as those who transmit the Dharma appear according to conditions to benefit beings,
and as the translated scriptures are circulated further to other regions,
since the reign titles are not recorded, it is impossible to know whether they are recent or distant.
Shengqin asked a Brahman monk about it, who replied that there was a Sanskrit manuscript;
as it was neither erroneous nor spurious, he included it in this record.
According to the preface to the *Qianbi jing* (Sūtra of a Thousand Arms), it also states that Zhitong [and others] produced it together.

The *Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha-sūtra*, twelve fascicles; recorded in the *Da Zhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalogue). Translated at Huiri Monastery on the fourteenth day of the third month in the fourth year of the Yonghui era, completed on the fifteenth day of the fourth month in the fifth year. Sramana Xuan Kai acted as the scribe and recipient of the oral transmission. This one work in twelve fascicles is extant.
The śramaṇa Ajitaghosa (in the language of Tang,
Wujige) was a native of Central India.
His learning exhausted the full range of the written word and his conduct was as pure as a perfect pearl;
he was refined in the five sciences and possessed a subtle mastery of the Tripitaka.
Furthermore, this Great Being, in benefiting living beings, showed no stinginess regarding his native land.
With a vast resolve to propagate the Buddha’s teachings, he feared no hardships or perils;
thus he crossed the Snowy Mountains to the west and traversed the Desert River to the east.
Having endured numerous dangers and perils, he has now arrived at the Imperial Palace.
In the first month of the third year of the Yonghui era of the Heavenly Emperor (the Renzi year), he brought many Sanskrit manuscripts to Chang’an;
by imperial decree, they were to be housed at Ci’en Monastery.
The śramaṇas Daśamahāyāna Zōng and others, sixteen in number,
along with the Dukes Ying and Ē and others, twelve in number,
invited Hǎo to the pagoda courtyard of Huìrì Temple.
He constructed a maṇḍala for the universal assembly of dhāraṇīs;
all that was required was fully prepared and provided.
On the day the rite was completed, spiritual wonders descended repeatedly.
The monastics and laypeople throughout the capital all marveled at such a rare encounter.
The śramaṇas Xuankai and others then earnestly requested that he translate the original text of this dharma.
This was subsequently carried out from the fourth year, Gui-chou, to the fifth year, Jia-yin.
At Huiri Temple, he compiled an essential abridgment from the *Vajramahāmaṇḍala-sūtra* in twelve fascicles.
The śramaṇa Xuankai and others acted as scribes.
At that time, the monks Ānanda-vinaya-ācārya and Kāśyapa-ācārya from the Mahābodhi Monastery in Central India were translating the *Dharmatārā-dhāraṇī* at a monastery for walking meditation.
It is compiled within the tenth fascicle of the *Saṃyuktāgama*, and therefore is not preserved separately.
The *Zhu jing yao ji* (Essentials of Various Scriptures) in twenty fascicles was compiled at Ximing Temple in the fourth year of the Xianqing era. This one work in twenty fascicles currently exists.
The śramaṇa Shi Xuanwen,
whose original name was Shidao,
was highly renowned for his mastery of the Vinaya and esteemed as a paragon of former worthies.
He made it his primary task to compile and edit works;
he also produced transcriptions, commentaries, and sub-commentaries on various sutras.
When the Ximing Monastery was first established, he was summoned to serve as a Mahādeba (Great Virtue).
During the Xianqing era, he read through the entire canon of scriptures.
He excerpted various essential matters and compiled them into a single work titled *Zhujing yaoji* (A Compendium of Essential Passages from All Scriptures).
The remainder is as recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Inner Scriptures).

The six-fascicle *Ji shamen buyaisu yi* (Collected Discourses on the Argument that Śramaṇas Should Not Bow to Laypeople) is listed in the *Neidian lu*; this one work in six fascicles currently exists.
The śramaṇa Shi Yancong was of keen intelligence and vast learning;

he was well-versed in the various scriptures and excelled at literary composition, being particularly skilled in authorship. In the second year of the Longshuo era (Renxu), the Heavenly Emperor issued an edict ordering him to pay homage to his sovereign and his parents.
Fearing that this might harm the state's transformation, he ordered the various officials to deliberate on the matter extensively. At that time,
the śramaṇa Daoxuan and others collectively submitted a memorial to inform the imperial court, as the public discourse had become divided by differing opinions.
The officials presented it for the Emperor’s personal inspection,
whereupon an imperial edict was issued to abolish it.
Because Zong feared that future generations would have no record of these events, he [composed this account].
I have compiled these matters along with historical precedents from previous dynasties and the responses of past sages,
titling it "A Collection of Discourses on Why Śramaṇas Do Not Bow to Laypeople," to be transmitted to future generations as an eternal model.
The laws of walls and moats protect the city so that the profound tradition does not fall. He also compiled the *Record of Temples in the Capital of the Great Tang*, which is circulated in the world.

*The Sūtra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍita-rāja*, one fascicle; also titled *The Sūtra of the Eight Maṇḍalas*. Translated at Ci’en Monastery in the third year of the Longshuo era. Recorded in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. *The Sūtra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Vimalamati regarding the Rites for the Buddha-dharma*, one fascicle. Translated at Ci’en Monastery in the third year of the Longshuo era. Recorded in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. *The Āṭānāṭiya Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated at Ci’en Monastery in the third year of the Longshuo era. Recorded in the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*. The above three works comprise three fascicles in total. Of these, the first two works comprise two fascicles and are extant; the latter work comprises one fascicle and is missing.
The śramaṇa Nādi; in the language of Tang, this means "Born of Merit" (Fúshēng).
According to the full Sanskrit expression, it is called Pūrṇodaya.
Because the original account was wordy,
this version is merely an abbreviated corruption that says "Nadi.
He was originally a person from Central India.
He left home to become a monk at a young age; his name was Shikai, and his aspirations were noble and far-reaching.
With the propagation of the Way as his primary concern, he traveled extensively through various regions, primarily devoted to enlightening sentient beings.
He was highly proficient in the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*) and thoroughly mastered all systems of interpretation and exegesis.
Daya summoned him to serve as a literary scholar, modeling him after those scholars who composed works at the Lantai Academy.
He was broadly affectionate and possessed a curious disposition;
hearing of those who had attained spiritual awakening, he did not hesitate to travel even to distant barbarian lands.
He once traveled to the Kingdom of Siṃhala;
furthermore, he ascended Mount Laṅkā to the southeast and propagated the teachings far and wide throughout the various kingdoms of the Southern Sea according to the conditions of his time.
It was heard that in the Eastern Land of Zhina (China), the Mahāyāna Buddhist Dharma was flourishing so greatly that it was renowned throughout Jambudvīpa as being preeminent.
Consequently, [he] collected over five hundred bundles of sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, totaling more than one thousand five hundred works.
In the sixth year of the Yonghui era of the Heavenly Emperor, it first arrived at the capital.
By imperial decree, it was to be enshrined at Ci'en Monastery, with its maintenance provided by the relevant authorities.
At that time, Dharma Master Xuanzang was engaged in translation work, his reputation flourishing and spreading far and wide.
There is no means by which [the truth] can be fully manifested; our reverent admiration remains desolate.
It is truly difficult for a name to reach its reality.
Since Nādi cannot receive guidance, there is no way for him to unfold [the teaching] on his own.
In the first year of the Xianqing era,
he was commanded by imperial decree to travel to the various kingdoms of Kunlun to collect rare medicinal herbs.
Upon arriving in the lands of the South Sea, the local kings paid him their respects and veneration, establishing a separate monastery for him, ordaining individuals, and transmitting the Dharma.
The breadth of his propagation of the teachings was twice as great as before.
Having previously received an imperial edict to go and manage affairs, he was required to return and report to Ci’en Monastery to once again seek out and study Sanskrit manuscripts.
In the third year of the Longshuo era, he returned to his former monastery.
The various scriptures he had brought were all intended to be translated by Xuanzang;
however, as there was no one to rely upon for the purpose of translating them,
he translated only three texts, including the *Aṣṭamaṇḍala-sūtra*.
The Essential Summary of the *Sāratama*: To be constantly practiced and studied.
Translated by the śramaṇa Huìzé of Cínlín Monastery;
compiled and with preface composed by the śramaṇa Dàoxuān of Fēngdé Monastery.
In that year, those in the kingdom of Chenla in the South Sea who had been converted by Natīsu paid him boundless reverence;
longing to see him, they urged one another to join in a distant invitation, taking a circuitous route to reach him.
He then said,
"In our country there is a fine medicine that only you, O Ti-shih, recognize.
I request that you go and gather it yourself."
It was unprecedented that an imperial edict was issued permitting him to travel back and forth.
Upon extensive inquiry, he learned from a traveler from Da-xia (Bactria) that the Tripitaka Master Nadi was a disciple of Nāgārjuna.
Regarding his understanding of the signless (animitta), he was equal to Xuanzang;
conversely, the Western Indian monks said,
"After the Great Master’s passing, this man is the foremost."
He deeply understood the true nature of reality and was well-versed in skillful means;
he was proficient in the Vinaya of the five divisions of the Hīnayāna and the four Vedas of the non-Buddhists.
There was none whom he did not penetrate to the very source and bottom; he thoroughly elucidated both words and meanings.
His expressions were linked like pearls, and his principles soared like clouds.
He composed approximately forty volumes of the *Mahāyāna-jī-yì-lùn* (Treatise on the Collected Meanings of the Mahāyāna).
When the matter was translated, the one sent [to verify it] subsequently failed to arrive.
Indeed, sighs over the discovery of the *Lunyu* have occurred throughout the ages;
how difficult it is to truly know another!
A thousand years rarely produce such a person; how could Nadi have traveled so far to bring the Way?
Having cast himself into the northern abyss, he had nothing left to wait for;
thus, he was poisoned three times and sent south on military service twice.
Traversing tens of thousands of miles over rugged terrain, he repeatedly encountered the miasma of pestilence.
To entrust one’s life and to meet one’s fate—this was the lot of this man.
Alas! How lamentable!

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, later translation, "Section on the Cremation" (Cháwī fēn), in two fascicles; also called the "Section on the Funeral Pyre" (Shāwéi fēn) or the "Later Section. The preface was composed by the Śramaṇa Huìlì. It is recorded in the *Dàzhōu lù*. This one work in two fascicles is currently extant.
The śramaṇa Yanabadhara— translated into Chinese as Zhixian (Wise and Virtuous)—
was a native of the kingdom of Po-ling, also called He-ling, in the South Sea.
He was well-versed in the Tripitaka.
Formerly, during the Linde era, the śramaṇa Huining of Chengdu in Yizhou traveled to India to pay homage to the sacred sites.
Faxian boarded a merchant vessel and sailed westward; his route passed through the kingdom of Pāraṅga (Bolin).
There, he collaborated with Zhixian to translate the latter two fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
He then sent these scriptures by ship to Jiaozhou.
Regarding Hui-ning’s journey to India:
later, at the beginning of the Yifeng era, Liang Nan-di, the Governor of Jiaozhou, dispatched an envoy with scriptures to the capital.
In the third year, the Wuyin year, the śramaṇa Linghui of the Great Ci’en Monastery—
Petitioned for implementation at the Eastern Palace.
*Mahāyāna-viṣayavibhāga-sūtra*, two fascicles; the second translation, identical in text to the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* and the *Bhadrapāla-śreṣṭhī-parivarta*.
Recorded in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. Translated in the first year of the Yonglong era at Taiyuan Temple in the Eastern Capital. *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*.

*The Avataṃsaka Sūtra: Continued Entry into the Dharmadhātu Chapter*, one fascicle; alternatively, without the word "Continued" (*xu*). This supplements missing passages from the old *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as recorded in the *Dazhou Catalogue*.
Translated at the Guining Hall of Xitaiyuan Temple in the first year of the Chuigong era (685 CE).
*The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, twelve fascicles; also known as the *Divyāvadāna* (Play of Supernatural Powers), the fourth part translated alongside those by Zhu Fahu.
The *Dīpa-śāstra* (or *Yao jing*) and other texts of the same root were recorded in the *Da Zhou Lu*.

On the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the second year of Yongchun, the translation was completed at the Guining Yuan of Xitaiyuan Si. The śramaṇa Fuli acted as the scribe and received the oral transmission.
The *Mahāyāna-saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* in two fascicles, also titled *Ruzhuyiqiefojingjie zhipeiluozhe nazang*, is the second edition produced alongside the *Mahāvairocana-abhisambodhi-tantra*.
The *Mahāyāna-sarva-akṣara-vigata-samantaprabhā-garbha-sūtra* (大乘離文字普光明藏經), one fascicle;
the third translation of this same text as found in the *Dazhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalogue), translated at Taiyuan Temple in the first year of the Yonglong era.

It is the same text as the *Anakṣara-ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* (無字寶篋經) produced by Bodhiruci during the Northern Wei dynasty, as recorded in the *Dazhou lu*, translated in the second year of the Yongchun era.
One fascicle of the *Mahāyāna Sarvāvabhāsa-prakāśagarbha-anakṣara-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*, translated at Guīníng-yuàn in Tàiyuán Temple;
the fourth appearance, which is the same text as the previously mentioned *Líwén-jīng*. One fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Siṃhanāda-sūtra*, re-translated by Rìzhào;
the second appearance, which is the same text as the *Tathāgata-siṃhanāda-sūtra*. Seen in the *Jiàn dà* [catalogue].
The *Mahāyāna Sūtra on the One Hundred Auspicious Marks* (Dacheng baifu xiang jing), one fascicle, was translated at Dong Taishan Temple during the first year of the Yonglong era of the Zhou dynasty;

its initial appearance is recorded in the *Dazhou lu*. The *Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Adorned Marks of the One Hundred Auspicious Features* (Dacheng baifu zhuangyan xiang jing), one fascicle, was translated at Guining Yuan in Xitaiyuan Temple during the second year of the Yongchun era of the Zhou dynasty;
this second version is identical to the aforementioned *Baifu xiang jing*.
*The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Four Dharmas*, one fascicle, translated again by Tánwénrìzhào based on the same original text; its first appearance is recorded in the *Dàzhōu Lù*.

It was translated at Dōngtáiyuán Temple in the first year of the Yǒnglóng era. *The Sūtra on the Four Dharmas for the Practice of Bodhisattvas*, one fascicle, translated at Hóngfú Temple in the capital during the first month of the second year of the Yǒnglóng era;
the śramaṇa Yànzōng composed the preface. This is the second appearance [of this text].

The aforementioned *Mahāyāna Four Dharmas* shares the same original text as the *Saptakoṭi-buddha-mahācitta-śūcinī-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle, which was retranslated in the capital based on the same original as that produced by Vajrabodhi; this is recorded in the *Dazhou lu*.
In the first year of the Chuigong era, at the Guining Monastery of the West Taiyuan Temple, he translated the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-parama-vijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
One fascicle; the second edition is identical to that produced by Du Yi and others.

On the twentieth day of the fifth month of the first year of the Yongchun era, it was translated together with the śramaṇa Yancong at Hongfu Monastery in the capital, and he also composed the preface, which appears before the scripture.
*The Sūtra of the Most Victorious Uṣṇīṣa Dhāraṇī for Eliminating Karmic Obstructions*, one fascicle; the fourth edition is identical to the aforementioned scripture.
The same original manuscript, *The Sun Shining Upon the World*, was later translated at the Great Eastern Capital (Dàdōngdū) together with the śramaṇa Huìzhì.
The two texts, "Previous Conditions" (*Qiányuán*) and "Subsequent Dharmas" (*Hòufǎ*), were both expanded; the *Mahāyāna-Ghanavyūha-sūtra* in three fascicles is recorded in the *Dàzhōu Lù*.

The *Stūpa-karaṇa-puṇya-sūtra* in one fascicle is also recorded in the *Dàzhōu Lù*. It was translated at the Eastern Tàiyuán Temple in the first year of the Yǒnglóng era. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*... [text ends].
*The Treatise on Breaking Attachment to Grasping and Not Destroying Provisional Names* (*Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra-bhāṣya-nāma-grahaṇa-anupaccheda-prajñapti-śāstra*), two fascicles;

composed by Bodhisattva Guṇaprabha (also known as Guṇadatta), according to the *Da Zhou Catalogue*; translated on the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the second year of Yongchun at the Guining Hall of the West Taiyuan Monastery.
*The Mahāyāna Extensive Treatise on the Five Aggregates* (*Mahāyāna-pañcaskandha-śāstra*), one fascicle; composed by Ācārya Vasubandhu; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Huì, this was translated on the fifteenth day of the sixth month in the first year of the Chuǐgǒng era at the Guīníngyuan of the West Taiyuán Monastery,
as recorded in the Great Zhou Catalogue. The eighteen sections comprising thirty-four fascicles are all extant.
The śramaṇa Divākara— translated into Chinese as Rìzhào (Sunlight)—
was a native of Central India who had a profound mastery of the Tripiṭaka.
He was extensively learned in the four Āgamas;
his observance of the precepts was pure and lofty, and his scholarly achievements were abundant.
He was especially skilled in incantations and arts, while also penetratingly mastering the five sciences (pañcavidyā).
His resolve was to benefit living beings, and so he traveled to this country.
He arrived at the beginning of the Yifeng era of the Tianhuang period and remained until the end of the Chuihong era of the Tianhou period.

During these years, he resided at the East and West Taiyuan Temples in the two capitals—the West Taiyuan Temple being the present-day Xichongfu Temple, and the East Taiyuan Temple being the present-day Taifuxian Temple.
At Hongfu Monastery in the Western Capital,
he translated eighteen works, including the *Mahāyāna-vijñapti-prakāśana-sūtra*,
with the śramaṇa Śuddhaprajñādeva serving as the oral interpreter.
The śramaṇa Huizhi realized the Sanskrit language; by imperial decree, ten men of renowned virtue were summoned to assist in his propagation of the Dharma:
the śramaṇas Daocheng, Bocen, Jia Shang, Yuance, Lingbian, Mingxun, Huaidu, and Zhengyi.
The śramaṇas Sīxuán, Fùlǐ, and others compiled the text and recorded it by pen.
Empress Wu personally composed the preface with her own sagely brushwork and placed it at the beginning.
Thus, the teachings of the Buddha were glorified and transmitted for eternity.

*The Sūtra of the Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī*, one fascicle. This initial translation is the same text as that produced by Jiryo and others. It was translated on the fifth day of the first month in the fourth year of the Yifeng era. This one work in one fascicle is extant.
The lay devotee Du Xingyi was a native of Jingzhao.
During the Yifeng era, he served as the Acting Director of the Dianke Bureau of the Honglu Temple.
Xingyi was proficient in the languages of various foreign tribes and possessed literary talent; he also mastered the subtleties of Indian scripts and the Indian language.
At that time, a monk from the kingdom of Kaśmīra named Buddhapāli arrived at the imperial palace carrying a bundle of Sanskrit scriptures to present as an offering.
The Emperor issued an edict commanding Zhiyi to translate them.
Entitled *The Buddha-uṣṇīṣavijaya Dhāraṇī*.
Translated and verified by the General of the Far Reaches, Dupo, and the Tripiṭaka Master from Central India, Divākara.
This was the first month of the fourth year of the Yifeng era.
Regarding this translation by Du [Shunzhi], he concealed and avoided all temple names and national taboos;
thus, for example, he rendered "World-Honored One" (Śāstṛ) as "Holy Honored One."
The world is the realm of sentient beings;
great power is the great destination;
healing and protection are the means of deliverance.
Upon completing the translation, he presented it for imperial inspection.
After the Emperor had read it, he looked toward Zhiyi and said,
"Since these are the words of a Sage, there is no need to avoid taboo characters."
Du Shi, having received the imperial decree, set it aside because his own lineage was involved;
in the course of time, Master Du passed away,
and before he could have the text corrected, it was put into circulation as it was.
Later, the Tripiṭaka Master Huizhao translated it again by imperial decree;
it was titled the *Buddhōṣṇīṣa-sūtra-vijaya-dhāraṇī*.
The *Dazhou Catalogue* states:
The *Buddhoṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī* was wrongly attributed to the Tripiṭaka Master Sūryavarman as its translator.

The *Shimen bianhuo lun* (Treatise on the Elucidation of Doubts in Ten Gates) in two fascicles; the *Dadai wenxue quan wuer shidian ji yi* (Answers to the Literary Scholar Quan Wuer’s Questions Regarding Doubts Concerning the Buddhist Canon), also known as the *Ji yi*, in three fascicles. This one work exists in a two-fascicle version.
The śramaṇa Shi Fuli was a native of Jingzhao;
his secular surname was Huangfu.
He left home at a young age and resided at Xingshan Monastery.
His nature was serene and his desires few;
he directed his mind toward the Inner Canon while also extensively studying the profound teachings of both Daoism and Confucianism.
He was particularly skilled in poetic composition and excelled at literary authorship.
The worldly elite and renowned scholars all admired and looked up to him.
When the Tripiṭaka masters Śīladharma (Dipāṃkara), Śikṣānanda, and others were translating the *Mahāvyūha*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and other sūtras,
the Emperor issued an imperial decree summoning [the Master] to pay his respects and participate in the translations alongside them.
The composition of texts and the determination of their meaning truly belong to this man.
In the second year of the Yonglong era (the *xin-si* year), the Emperor,

based on the ten points of doubt regarding the interpretation of the Buddhist scriptures submitted by the Court Gentleman for Literary Studies, Quan Wuer, posed questions concerning ritual propriety and requested that these obscurities be resolved.
He then composed a response in two fascicles,
titled *The Ten Gates for Dispelling Delusions and Ignorance* (*Shimen bianhuomeng*).
In it, he engaged in a dialogue between host and guest, analyzing and resolving doubts.
The phrasing issues forth from the treasury of wisdom;
the meaning resides beyond the mind.
If one asks who else but this person could provide such a response?
One may truly say that Nāgārjuna has been reborn and Aśvaghoṣa has appeared once more.
Upon seeing this wheel, the scholar Quan had his many doubts instantly dispelled; he received it upon the crown of his head and followed its teachings with reverence.
Although this was but a single response given on the occasion, [it was of profound significance].
This truly serves as a mirror for ten thousand generations.
The Dharma Master also possessed a collection of literary works that circulated during his time.
The "Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Ci'en Monastery of the Great Tang," in ten fascicles—this one work in ten fascicles is currently extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Hui-li:
his original name was Li;
the Emperor changed it to Hui-li.
Her secular surname was Zhao;
she was a native of Tianshui.
Her distant ancestors had migrated and settled in Xingping due to official service.
Thus, what was formerly called Bīn has now been changed to Bīn.
His grandfather and father both enjoyed high reputations;
he was the third son of Yìzhī, a Secretariat Drafter (Bìshūláng) under the Sui dynasty.
From birth, he was precocious and possessed the resolve to renounce worldly life.
At the age of fifteen, in the third year of the Zhenguan era, he left home to become a monk at Zhaoren Temple in Bingzhou;
this temple had been the battlefield where Xue Ju was defeated.
Established in wisdom with keen talent and refined spirit, his path was vast and far-reaching;
he emulated the lofty character of Lin Yuan and surpassed the intellectual capacity of Sengzhao and Daorong.
His reputation spread far and wide,
and by imperial decree he was summoned to serve as a Great Virtuous Master (Mahāśramaṇa) for translating scriptures at Da Ci’en Monastery.
Subsequently, he was appointed as the Chief Steward (Karmadāna) of Ximing Monastery.
Later, he was appointed as the head of Taiyuan Temple;
on both occasions, imperial edicts were issued ordering him to remain in residence at the temple.
During the reign of the Emperor, he was summoned to the inner palace on several occasions.
His debates with the Daoist priests (wearing yellow caps) were entirely to the Emperor's satisfaction;
the details of these matters are recorded in a separate biography.
Li [Yuan] noted that since the time Master Xuanzang sought out scriptures in India, there had been no systematic records and little was heard of such matters in recent times;
he therefore composed the *Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Cien*,
but passed away before it was completed.
Later, the śramaṇa Yancong of Hongfu Monastery continued and completed it, totaling ten fascicles.
Therefore, the original title reads: "Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huili, with annotations by the Śramaṇa Yancong."

*The Dharmaguptaka Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, one fascicle; the title reads *The Dharmaguptaka Prātimokṣa with Preface*, compiled by the Śramaṇa Huaisu of the Western Taiyuan Monastery. *The Dharmaguptaka Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, one fascicle; the title is augmented with the character "Ni" (尼), while the rest is identical to the preceding work. *The Dharmaguptaka Saṃgha Karma*, three fascicles; the title reads *Karma, Fascicle One, with Preface*, produced from the Dharmaguptaka school by the Śramaṇa Huaisu of the Western Taiyuan Monastery. *The Dharmaguptaka Bhikṣuṇī Karma*, three fascicles; the title is augmented with the character "Ni," while the rest is identical to the preceding work. The above four works comprise eight fascicles, and their texts are all extant.
The śramaṇa Huaisu was of the secular surname Fan;
he was a native of Jingzhao.
He inherited his father’s official cap as a hereditary title.
In the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he left the household life and took the Dharma Master Xuanzang as his teacher.
By nature, he was intelligent and quick-witted, devoting himself exclusively to the study of sutras and treatises.
After receiving full ordination, he devoted himself exclusively to the Vinaya;
following the teachings of Master Chengdao, he studied the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and,
before long, became a preeminent leader among his peers.
He first resided at Hongji and later stayed at Taiyuan.
Disciples flocked to him like clouds, and his teaching never ceased.
He observed that much of what had been compiled by previous masters did not rely upon the original texts, but instead followed their own private views, arbitrarily adding or subtracting material.
He then searched through the Vinaya-piṭaka and extracted the *Śīlacitta-karman*.
He took only those passages that were established texts, avoiding any arbitrary fabrication;
it may truly be said that he succeeded to the excellence of Kāśyapa and followed in the footsteps of Upāli.

Furthermore, he separately compiled more than fifty fascicles of the *Commentary on the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* (Sifen ji chao), including exegeses on sutras and śāstras, which circulated during his era.
The *Dafangguang yuanjue xingduo liao yi jing* (The Sutra of the Great Vaipulya Perfect Enlightenment’s Definitive Meaning), one fascicle: this single work in one fascicle still exists today.
The śramaṇa Buddhavarman, translated into Chinese as Juejiu (Awakening Rescue),
was a native of Jibin in Northern India.
At the Baima Monastery in the Eastern Capital, he translated one fascicle of the *Nirvana-artha-bodhicitta-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Perfect Enlightenment of Ultimate Meaning).
This was produced recently, though the exact year is not certain;
his primary concern was to propagate the Way and to distinguish between the genuine and the fraudulent.
Since the true exposition is unerring, how could it depend on the number of years one has known it?

The *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-vijayā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle, the third edition, is identical in text to that produced by Du Yi and others; this is seen in the *Da Zhou Catalogue* and the preface to the scripture. This one work, in one fascicle, its manuscript currently exists.
The śramaṇa Buddhapālita— translated into Chinese as Juéhù (Awakened Protector)—
was a native of Jibin in North India.
Forgetting his own body, he pursued the Way and traveled extensively to visit sacred sites.
Hearing that Mañjuśrī resided on Mount Qingliang,
he journeyed far across the shifting sands to pay his respects in person.
In the *jingzi* year of the first year of the Yifeng era of the Heavenly Emperor’s reign, he took up his monk’s staff at Mount Wutai and performed prostrations with profound sincerity;
weeping bitterly with tears falling like rain, he gazed in hope for a vision of the Holy Countenance.
Suddenly, an old man was seen emerging from the mountains.
Speaking in the language of a Brahmin,
he said to Pāli:
The Master asked with sincere earnestness,
"What is it that you seek? Pāli replied,
"I have heard that the Great Being Mañjuśrī has hidden his traces upon this mountain."
He came from India wishing to pay homage [to the Master].
The Master asked, "Did you bring the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* from that country?
The sentient beings of this land commit many transgressions."
Even among those who have left the household life, there are many who commit transgressions.
This secret method for removing sins through the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa Dhāraṇī—
if you do not bring the scripture, what benefit would it be for you to come here in vain?
Even if you were to see Mañjuśrī, how could you necessarily recognize him?
You should return to the Western Land to retrieve that scripture and circulate it here in this land;
this would be equivalent to making offerings to all the sages.
To extensively benefit all sentient beings and rescue those in the dark realms is to repay the kindness of all Buddhas.
The Master took the scripture and came here, saying, "Disciple, you shall show me where the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī resides.
Upon hearing these words, Pāli was overcome with such joy that he could not contain himself.
He then restrained his tears and prostrated once more toward the mountain.
In the brief moment he raised his head, the old man had suddenly vanished.
Pāli was struck with even greater astonishment and his devotion increased all the more.
He then returned to his own country and obtained the scriptures;
having arrived at the imperial capital, he immediately requested an audience with the Emperor.
The officials prepared a formal report and presented it to the throne.
The Emperor, appreciating their sincere devotion, honored this esoteric scripture.
Thereupon, an imperial decree was issued for Du Xingyi, the Director of the Guest Office at the Honglu Si, and the Tripitaka Master of Rizhao to translate [the text] together within the palace.
Once the translation was completed, thirty rolls of silk were bestowed as a reward,
and the scripture was retained within the palace.
Pāliyin then shed tears and addressed the Emperor, saying:
"I have cast aside my own life with the sole intent of benefiting others.
I pray that you permit this teaching to be spread and circulated; this is my sincere hope."
The Emperor, moved by his single-minded devotion, retained the translated scriptures and returned the Sanskrit originals to him, allowing him to circulate them as he saw fit.
Pāli was overjoyed at having obtained the scriptures;
he proceeded to Ximing Monastery to seek out a monk proficient in Sanskrit, and upon finding Śunzheng, he petitioned the Emperor to translate them together.
The Emperor granted his request;
he then, together with the great virtuous master Yuan Ce, who was engaged in translating scriptures, and [the monk] Zhen, translated it.
It is titled the *Buddhoṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī*.
Compared with the version previously translated by Prefect Du,
the phonology and scriptural text are largely the same with minor differences.
Having fulfilled his aspirations, Wopoli took the Sanskrit manuscript of the sutra to Mount Wutai and has not emerged from there until this day.
It is unknown where it has gone;
compared with various other translations, this one is the most widely disseminated.

According to the preface of the sutra, it states that in the second year of the Yongchun era, [the manuscript] was returned to the Western Capital (Xi'ang), where a formal report was submitted to the throne.
In that same year, he [Du Xingyi] translated it again together with Shunzhen under the title *Buddhoṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
Now, upon examining this account, the dates are somewhat inconsistent.

The translation by Du Ling (Du Xingyi) took place on the fifth day of the first month of the fourth year of the Yifeng era, whereas the re-translation by Rizhao occurred on the thirteenth day of the fifth month of the first year of the Yongchun era.
Since it is stated that he only reached the borders of Tang in the second year of Yongchun,
from where did he obtain the previous two versions?
Furthermore, by the second year of Yongchun, the Heavenly Emperor had already traveled to the Eastern Capital.
How can it then be said that it was translated in the capital?
Furthermore, its preface was recorded by someone after the Yongchang era who confusedly recounted past events,
resulting in these discrepancies.
The dates for these translations by Bo-li cannot be fixed according to their sequence.
*Zhenyuan xinding shijiao mulu*, Scroll 12;
*Zhenyuan xinding shijiao mulu*, Scroll 13.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xīmíng Monastery in the Western Capital.
*Zǒngjí qījīng lù* (General Catalogue of Collected Scriptures), Volume Upper, Number Thirteen.
*Dàfāngguǎng fó huá yán jīng bù sīyì fó jìngjiè fēn* (The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya, Chapter on the Inconceivable Realm of the Buddha), one fascicle, or two fascicles. Number Ten.
Two scrolls. Translated at the Dongsi Monastery in the Wei Kingdom in the first year of the Yongchang era (689 CE); recorded in the *Dazhou lu*.
Originally translated together with the later *Acintyaviṣayāvatāra-nirdeśa-sūtra* by Śikṣānanda. One scroll of the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra-karuṇāparivarta*.
Translated at the Dongsi Monastery in the Dazhou period in the second year of the Tianguo era (691 CE); recorded in the *Dazhou lu*. Mahāyāna.
*Sūtra on the Merit of Casting Images*, two fascicles (or one fascicle), translated at the Eastern Monastery of the Great Zhou in the second year of the Tianshou era;
recorded in the *Great Zhou Catalog*. *Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Wisdom Torch*, one fascicle, translated at the Eastern Monastery of the Great Zhou in the second year of the Tianshou era;
recorded in the *Great Zhou Catalog*. *Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Assembly of All Buddhas*, one fascicle, translated in the second year of the Tianshou era.
Translated at the Eastern Monastery during the Dazhou period; recorded in the Dazhou Catalogue. *Mahāyāna-dharmadhātu-aviśeṣa-śāstra*, one fascicle.
Translated on the fourteenth day of the [third] month in the second year of Tiangshou at the Eastern Monastery during the Dazhou period; recorded in the Dazhou Catalogue.
These six works, totaling seven fascicles, all have their original texts extant.
The śramaṇa Divākara-prajñā,
also called Divākara-jñāna; translated into Chinese as Tiānzhì (Heavenly Wisdom).
A native of Khotan,
his learning encompassed both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and his wisdom spanned both the ultimate and conventional truths;
he was thoroughly proficient in both incantations and the gates of dhyāna.
In the first year of the Yongchang era of Empress Wu, he arrived here;
that very same year, he had an audience with the Emperor in Luoyang.
By imperial decree, the Eastern Temple of the Wei State was subsequently renamed the Eastern Temple of the Great Zhou for the purpose of translating scriptures.
This took place from the Jichou year of the first Yongchang era (689) to the Xinnao year of the second Tiangshou era (691).
In total, six sections of the sutra were produced.
The śramaṇas Vidyā and Huizhi and others acted as translators,
while the śramaṇa Chuyi and others served as scribes.
The śramaṇas Fuli and others composed the text;
the śramaṇas Dewei, Huiyan, Faming, and Hongjing and others verified the meaning.
One fascicle of the *Praise in Verse to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*, found in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. This one work in one fascicle currently exists.
The śramaṇa Shi Hui-zhi was of Brahmin descent;
his father was a native of Central India.
It was through being sent on this journey that he gave rise to wisdom.
From his youth, he was diligent and possessed the aspiration to transcend the mundane world.
During the reign of the Heavenly Sovereign, due to an elderly Brahman monk...
By imperial decree, he was ordained as a disciple.
Being originally an Indian,
he was well-versed in the scripts and languages of India.
Furthermore, he was born in the land of Tang and subsequently mastered the spoken language of this soil.
He is the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara.
All translations by Ratnacintā and others were made by summoning Jñāna to certify the meaning and facilitate the crossing over of the language;
thus did Jñāna [act].
In the second year of the Changshou era (Gui-si) of Empress Wu,
at Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital,
he personally translated one fascicle of the *Praise in Verse to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*.
The *Dazhou kan ding zhong jing mulu* (Great Zhou Catalogue of Determined Scriptures), fifteen fascicles. This one work in fifteen fascicles is extant.
It was compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Mingquan, a monk of Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital.
He was particularly proficient in the Vinaya and was also well-versed in the sūtras and śāstras.
In the first year of the Tiāncè Wànsuì era (the year of Yǐwèi), during the reign of Empress Wu,
he was commanded by imperial edict to compile and finalize the catalog of the scriptures.
The sequence for compiling these records from beginning to end was jointly determined by me and more than twenty virtuous masters (bhadanta) who were translating the scriptures.
Although it is said that the text has been edited and finalized, there are still many redundancies and impurities.
Although these circulating versions are seen, they are truly difficult to rely upon as authoritative;
there are discrepancies among them, as described elsewhere.
This is identical to the eighty-fascicle *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, fascicle two, translated by Buddhabhadra during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
On the fourteenth day of the third month of the first year of the Shōshō era, this was translated within the Great Palace at the Daibenzūkyō-ji in the Eastern Capital;
Empress Tenshō personally oversaw the revisions. On the eighth day of the tenth month of the second year of the Jōreki era, the work was completed at the Busshukuki-ji.
The *Mañjuśrī-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* in three fascicles was translated at the Seizen-ji; this is the third edition.
The *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-vyūha-sūtra* and others, identical to the extant versions, are now compiled as the fifteenth assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa*.
The *Mahāvaipulya-tathāgata-jñānaguṇa-acintya-praveśa-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated at the Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital;
this is the fourth appearance, identical to the *Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatāra-jñānālokalaṃkāra-sūtra*. The Great... [text ends]
*The Vaipulya Sūtra on the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata*, one fascicle; the third translation, identical in text to the *Bhūmi-vibhaṅga* translated by Ti-yun-banya.
*The Vaipulya Sūtra Spoken by Samantabhadra*, one fascicle; the fourth translation, identical in text to that produced by Gong-de-xian and others during the Song dynasty.
On the fifth day of the fifth month of the first year of the Jiushi era, at the East...

The *Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* in seven fascicles and the *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-guhyakośa-mantra-sūtra* in one fascicle were first brought out within the Doushangong Palace and completed on the fifth day of the first month of the fourth year of the Chang’an era.
These were the same texts as those previously brought out by Baosiwei and others. Also included is the *Subāhu-dharaṇī-mudrā-dhvaja-sūtra* in one fascicle.
Scroll Two: The *Śatasahasramudrā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle (same text as the *Jaya-dhvaja-mudrā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*);
the *Dhāraṇī-mantra Sūtra for Saving the Face-Burning Hungry Ghosts*, one fascicle;

the *Sūtra on the Merit of Circumambulating a Buddha Stūpa*, one fascicle (also called the *Sūtra on the Merit of Circumambulating a Stūpa*); and the *Mahāyāna Caturdharma-sūtra*, one fascicle. Together with these...

On the previous day, the Tripiṭaka Master translated the *Sūtra on the Ten Wholesome Paths of Action* (one fascicle), which, although sharing the same title as another work, differs entirely in its textual substance;
the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (two fascicles); the second [work] translated is the same text as that by Paramārtha;
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-anuparivarta-sūtra* (one fascicle); the *Mahāvaipulya-ajāty-aniruddha-sūtra* (one fascicle); and the *Mahāvaipulya-*.

*The Tathāgata’s Inconceivable Realm Sūtra*, one fascicle; *The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of Stainless Pure Light*, one fascicle (the first appearance [of these texts] shares the same translators as those for the Amitābha sūtras);
*The Sūtra on the Four Dharmas for the Birth of Bodhisattvas*, one fascicle.
The above consists of nineteen works totaling one hundred and seven fascicles. From the *Awakening of Faith Treatise* upward, there are fourteen works totaling one hundred and two fascicles.
The following five sections in five fascicles of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-anuparivarta-sūtra* (The Sutra Following the Mind) are currently missing.
[Translated by] the śramaṇa Śikṣānanda,
which in the language of Tang means "Delighting in Learning."
A native of Khotan,
his wisdom was vast and expansive, and he took the benefit of sentient beings as his primary concern.
He was proficient in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings, as well as the treatises of other schools.
Empress Wu, who illuminated the sun of the Buddha and revered the Mahāyāna,
heard from afar that a Sanskrit manuscript of the *Avataṃsaka* existed in Khotan;
as the existing Chinese translations were incomplete in their assemblies, she dispatched envoys to seek it out.
He also requested that the translator,
Śikṣānanda, arrive at the imperial palace together with the scripture;
this was in the first year of the Zhengsheng era of Empress Wu, the year of Yiwei (695 CE).
At Dàbiànhóngkōng Temple within the Imperial Palace in the Eastern Capital, he translated the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Empress Wu personally attended the Dharma seat and composed the preface;
she herself wielded her immortal brush to inscribe the title at the head of the work.
The Sanskrit original was proclaimed by the śramaṇa Bodhiruci from South India and the śramaṇa Yijing;
it was subsequently translated at Foshouji Monastery by the śramaṇas Fuli, Fazang, and others.
It was completed in the second year of the Shengli era, the Jihai year.
Furthermore, in the first year of the Jiushi era, the Gengzi year, he translated the *Mahāyāna-laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* within the Sanyang Palace.
Furthermore, at Qingchan Temple in the Western Capital and Shouji Temple in the Eastern Capital,
he translated the *Mañjuśrīvyākaraṇa* and other sutras, totaling nineteen works in all.
The śramaṇas Bolun and Xuanguan served as scribes for these translations.
The śramaṇas Fuli and others composed the text;
the śramaṇas Fabao and Hongjing and others verified the meaning;
and Jia Yingfu, Court Attendant of the Crown Prince, supervised the project.
In the fourth year of the Chang’an era, Śikṣānanda requested to return home to visit his aged mother;
after submitting his petition twice, he finally received permission.
By imperial decree, the Censor Huo Siguang escorted him to Khotan.
Later, when Emperor Huidi ascended the throne, he caused the sun of the Buddha’s teachings to shine once more with renewed brilliance.
By imperial decree, he was summoned again and arrived at the imperial capital;
in the second year of the Jinglong era, he reached this land.
The Emperor, humbling himself despite the dignity of his imperial carriage, personally went to meet him outside the Kaiyuan Gate.
The monastics of the capital, equipped with various banners and streamers, lined the road to escort him;
he was then placed upon a decorated blue elephant and led into the city, where by imperial decree he was installed at the Great Jianfu Monastery.
Before he had yet found the leisure to translate [the texts], he encountered a terminal illness.
On the twelfth day of the tenth month of the first year of the Jingyun era,
he passed away at Dajianfu Monastery, lying on his right side with his feet stacked one upon the other.
The *Chunqiu* has fifty-nine sections;
the assembly of black-robed monks wept with choked sobs,
sighing that the Dharma-beam had suddenly collapsed.
The lay followers wailed in grief,
lamenting that all living beings had lost their guide. There was...
An imperial edict was issued permitting burial according to foreign customs.
On the twelfth day of the eleventh month,
he was cremated outside the Kaiyuan Gate at the site of the ancient Lamp-Kindling Terrace.
When the firewood was exhausted and the flames extinguished, his tongue remained intact;
this was a sublime auspicious sign of his propagation of the Dharma.
On the twenty-third day of the twelfth month, it reached [its destination].
The disciples of our own country,
Bei and Zhi, were commissioned by imperial decree to send back his remains along with this miraculous tongue.
He returned to Khotan and erected a stūpa there to make offerings.
Later, people again erected a seven-story stūpa at the site where his body had been cremated.

The *Amoghapāśa Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Samantamukha*. This consists of sixteen chapters and is an excerpt from the Sanskrit original, with a preface composed by the śramaṇa Bolun. This second edition is the same text as the three-fascicle version translated by Baosiwei. This single work, comprising one fascicle, is currently extant.
The Brahmin Li Wuchan was a native of Lampāka in North India;
he possessed keen intelligence and vast learning,
being thoroughly versed in both Buddhist and non-Buddhist doctrines.
He was thoroughly proficient in both the Chinese and Sanskrit languages without impediment.
When the Tripiṭaka masters Ān-chen-na and Bodhiruci and others translated various scriptures,
they were free from any words of flattery or distortion.
In the third month of the gengzi year, the third year of the Shengli era during the reign of Empress Wu,
there was a monk from the kingdom of Silla named Mingxiao.
Observing from afar that the influence of the Tang dynasty was about to turn its course,
he first turned his attention toward the gateway of *dhāraṇī*.
He then earnestly and insistently requested that this mantra be translated.
He caused those in the remote borderlands to likewise hear this secret teaching;
consequently, at the Translation Institute of the Buddhadatta Monastery,
he translated one fascicle of the *Amoghapāśa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
The śramaṇa Polun served as scribe.
In the eighth month of the first year of the Jiushi era,
he took the translated scriptures and re-examined them against the Sanskrit originals once more in Kaśmīra.
Now being transcribed and circulated:

*The Sutra of the Vimalaprabhāsa-mahādhāraṇī*, one fascicle; the second edition, which is the same text as the *Vimalaprabhāsa-dhāraṇī* translated by Śikṣānanda. This one work in one fascicle is currently extant.
The śramaṇa Mīdushan (彌陀山),
whose name means "Virtuous Friend" (淑友) in the language of Tang,
was a native of the country of Tukhāra.
He left home as a youth and traveled throughout India, studying the sūtras and śāstras extensively;
he was most proficient in the *Laṅkāvatāra* and the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Resolving to propagate the Semblance Dharma, he had no regard for his own native land.
Carrying his staff and alms bowl, he traveled on foot until he arrived at the Imperial Palace.
During the reign of Emperor Tianhuang, he translated the *Mahāyāna-laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* together with Śikṣānanda.
Later, during the final years of Empress Wu’s reign, he translated the *Vimalaprabhā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in one fascicle together with the śramaṇa Fazang and others.
Having completed the translation, he entered the inner palace to take leave of the Emperor and return to his own country.
Empress Wu bestowed generous gifts upon him as he departed for his native land.
*Jiǎnzhènglùn* (Discourse on Distinguishing the Authentic), three fascicles; one volume in total.
Three fascicles of its original text still exist.
The śramaṇa Shi Xuanyi’s secular surname was Du.
His name was Yi.
He wore the yellow cap and served as the abbot of Dàhóngdào Guàn in the Eastern Capital.
He roamed his mind through the Seven Classics and excelled in the subtleties of the Three Mysteries;
within the Yellow School, this served as its guiding principle.
Empress Wu revered the Great Dharma and extensively propagated the teachings of the Śākya lineage.
Furthermore, he subsequently turned his heart toward the Dharma and requested ordination.
An imperial edict granted permission for his admission into the monastic order.
He resided at Fo-shou-ji Monastery.
Later, he served as the administrative head of the monastery and participated in the work of translation;
he thoroughly understood the empty pretenses of that school and realized that the authentic teaching could be relied upon.
He subsequently composed the *Zhengzhilun* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Authentic) in one fascicle.
It exposes falsehoods and employs a dialogue between host and guest that is exceedingly concise and essential.

The *Amoghapāśa-dhāraṇī-īśvararāja-sūtra* in three fascicles, also titled the *Amoghapāśa-hṛdaya-mantra-rāja-sūtra*, translated at the Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital in the tenth month of the second year of the Changshou era; received by the śramaṇa Degan.
This initial edition is the same text as the one-fascicle version produced by Li Wuchan, concerning the merit of bathing the Buddha image.
One fascicle. Translated on the twenty-third day of the first month in the first year of the Shénlóng era at Dàfúxiān Monastery in the Eastern Capital.
Li Wúchǎn, a Brāhmaṇa, served as the oral interpreter. This initial translation was collated with the later version produced by Yìjìng and found to be the same text.
*Jiǔshù Gōngdé Jīng* (Sūtra on the Merit of Rosaries), one fascicle. Translated on the twenty-third day of the first month in the first year of the Shénlóng era at [Dàfúxiān Monastery].
*The Sūtra of the Cintāmaṇi Dhāraṇī of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; translated at Fuxian Temple by Li Wuchan as the first rendition, corresponding to the version produced by Yijing.
*The Sūtra of the Fundamental One-Syllable Dhāraṇī of Mañjuśrī*, one fascicle; the second rendition, corresponding to the version produced by Śikṣānanda and others.

In the second year of the Chang’an era, at Tiangong Monastery, the *Ekākṣara-hṛdaya-mantra-sūtra* (The Sūtra of the One-Syllable Heart Mantra for the Dharma-Age of Decline) was translated in one fascicle.
The śramaṇa Huizhi and others verified the Sanskrit text; the Brahmin Li Wuchan provided the oral interpretation; and Li Wu’ai, Director of the Secretariat, received the text in writing.
This initial translation is identical in its original source to the version later produced by Yi Jing. In the first year of the Shenlong era.

In the first year of the [Dazhong] era, at Dafuxian Temple, he translated the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-mahā-īśvara-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (also known as the *Siddhārtha-mahā-īśvara-dhāraṇī-sūtra*), one fascicle, with Li Wuchan serving as the oral interpreter; this is also recorded in the *Da Zhou Lu*.

In the second year of the Changshou era, at Dongtianguan Temple, he translated [the text], with the Kapiśa śramaṇas Śrīnanda and others verifying the Sanskrit text, and Li Wuchan serving as the oral interpreter.
Translated by the interpreter Li Wuchu and orally received by Li Wuchu; the seven sections comprising nine fascicles of these texts are currently extant.
The śramaṇa A-ni-zhen-na—translated into Chinese as Baosiyi (Ratnasmṛti)—[is the translator].
He was a native of Kaśmīra in North India,
of the Kṣatriya caste,
and a descendant of that king’s noble lineage.
Having left home in his youth, he made meditation and recitation his primary practice.
After receiving full ordination, he specialized in the Vinaya-piṭaka;
furthermore, his wisdom and understanding surpassed those of his peers, and his learning encompassed both the ultimate and conventional truths.
His mastery of the *qianwen* incantations and esoteric arts was particularly profound and marvelous.
Furthermore, he took the transformation and guidance of others as his primary concern, having no lingering attachment to his native land.
In the second year of the Changshou era of Empress Wu (the Gui-si year), it arrived at the capital of Luoyang.
By imperial decree, it was enshrined at Tianguan Temple.
Immediately, thereupon—
From the second year of the Changshou era of Empress Wu (Gui-si) to the second year of the Shenlong era of Emperor Zhongzong (Jing-wu),
[this was established] at Fuxian Temple in the Shouji Celestial Palace.
He translated seven works, including the *Amoghapāśa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
Later, in the fourth month of the Renzi year, the first year of the Taicheng era of Emperor Ruizong,
Zhang Qixian, the Attendant Cavalier to the Crown Prince, and others transcribed them and presented them to the palace.
In the sixth month of the first year of the Yanyang era,

an imperial edict was issued ordering the Minister of Rites, the Duke of Jin Xue Ji, the Right Attendant, the Marquis of Gaoping Xu Yanbo, and others to carefully determine the contents for inclusion in the catalogue and to put them into practice.
From the second year of the Shenlong era onward, the Tripitaka Master no longer translated sutras;
he devoted himself solely to diligent prostrations, recitations, and the cultivation of various meritorious deeds.
Every morning, he would grind incense into water and use it to bathe the Buddha images.
He took his meals only after [the meal offering was finished].
From beginning to end, this was his constant practice.
Aside from his robes and alms bowl, he gave away whatever he obtained as soon as he received it.
Later, he requested that a monastery be established at Longmen Mountain,
constructed according to foreign architectural styles,
which was called "Tianzhu" (India).
He and his disciples lived together in this temple;
moved by their refined sincerity, those who attained such longevity were truly numerous,
living for over a hundred years.
He passed away at the temple in the ninth year of the Kaiyuan era.

The śramaṇa Śikṣānanda was a native of Qízhōu.
His secular surname was Zhang and his courtesy name was Wenming.
In his early childhood, he renounced worldly glory and cast off the finery of the mundane world.
Thereupon, he consulted renowned masters everywhere and extensively gathered from a wide range of texts;
becoming proficient in both Buddhist and secular learning, and thoroughly acquainted with matters of both the present and the past,
he resolved at the age of fifteen to travel to the Western Regions.
He admired the refined integrity of Faxian and yearned for the lofty character of Xuanzang; furthermore,
he was diligent without wasting a moment, never letting his hands leave the volumes of scripture.
Having attained maturity in his early twenties, he redoubled his efforts to remain steadfast and pure.
In the second year of the Xianheng era, at the age of thirty-seven, he finally realized his long-held aspiration and proceeded to Guangzhou.
There, he first made a vow with like-minded companions until their number reached ten.
When the ships set sail, everyone else withdrew and desisted;
only Jingjian’s resolve grew even more fervent.
He then traveled alone, enduring numerous hardships until he gradually reached India.
In every place he reached, his words and sounds were clearly understood;
wherever he encountered kings or ministers, all received him with profound respect.
He personally ascended both Vulture Peak and Chicken Foot Mountain.
He traveled extensively throughout Jeta Grove and the Deer Park;
he rested at Nālandā, paid homage to the Bodhi tree, and studied both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna under various masters and learned teachers.
Having completed his travels, he returned to his native village.
In all, he traveled through more than thirty countries,
spending over twenty years traveling back and forth to seek the Way.
In the second month of summer in the year of Yiwei, the first year of the Zhengsheng era of Empress Wu Zetian, he returned to the region of the Yellow and Luo Rivers.
He brought approximately four hundred Sanskrit texts of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras, totaling five hundred thousand stanzas;
one set of the true likeness of the Vajrāsana;
and three hundred śarīra relics.
The Empress Dowager revered the Dharma and honored its practitioners;
she personally went out to meet [the Master] outside the Upper East Gate.
The monastics of Luoyang prepared banners and streamers and arranged drums and music to lead the way in front.
The Buddha-shouji Monastery was established as a repository for the Sanskrit manuscripts he had brought, and he ordered them all to be translated.
Initially, he worked together with the Khotanese Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda to translate the Avataṃsaka Sūtra; it was only after the Jiushi era that he began translating [the scriptures] himself.
From the first year of Jiushi, the gengzi year,
until the third year of Chang’an, the guiyou year,
[he resided] at Fuxian Monastery in the Eastern Capital and Ximing Monastery in the Western Capital.

Subsequently, when Emperor Zhongzong ascended the throne, in the first year of the Shenglong era, the year of Yisi (705 CE).
Within the Inner Chamber of the Eastern Capital, he translated the *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra*.
Furthermore, at Dafuxian Temple, he translated the *Sūryadevaputra-gandharāja-bodhisattva-mantra* and the *Sarvaguṇavyūharāja-sūtra*, among others.

Emperor He held the Buddhist scriptures in high esteem and composed a preface to praise them, titled "The Sacred Teaching Preface of the Tripitaka of the Dragon-Rising Great Tang.
The Emperor personally went to the West Gate of Luocheng and proclaimed to the multitude the newly translated texts from the Pure Land.
He was also ordered to compile a catalog of the texts.
In the second year, the Jǐwǔ year (659), he accompanied the Emperor back to the capital.
By imperial decree, a separate Translation Institute (Fānyīngyuàn) was established within Dà Jiànfú Sī, where he was stationed.
In the third year, the Year of Dingwei,
the Emperor summoned him into the palace to sit out the summer retreat (*varṣā*) for ninety days together with nine other śramaṇas translating the scriptures.
The Emperor remarked that in the past, when he resided in the remote and perilous regions of Fangbu, he had been without refuge.
Through his prayers, Bhaisajyaguru responded by bestowing blessings;
thus, these past benefits were celebrated as he once again expounded the grand tradition.
Consequently, he commanded his disciples to undertake a further translation.
It was translated into two fascicles at the Buddha Light Hall within the Imperial Palace and titled the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha-saptabuddha-pūrvapraṇidhāna-guṇa-dhāraṇī Sūtra*.
The Emperor personally presided over the Dharma assembly and transcribed the text by hand.
Furthermore, in the fourth year of the Jinglong era (the gengxu year),
at Dajianfu Monastery, he translated the *Bath Image Merit Sūtra* and the *Rosary Merit Sūtra*.

Epitaph and Preface for the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Flourishing Dragon Era of the Great Tang The Master’s name was Wenming; his courtesy name was Yijing.
His secular surname was Zhang.
He was a native of Mount Zhuang in Qi Commandery.
His spiritual brilliance was exceptionally outstanding, and he possessed innate wisdom and insight.
Having received full ordination at the age of twenty, he immediately began lecturing on the Vinaya.
Regretting that his literary cultivation was incomplete at the age of seven,
and sighing that he had not yet mastered the five branches of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*),
he packed his provisions, took up his book-case, and set out with sandals upon his feet and a staff over his shoulder.
In the second year of the Xianheng era, he set out from the region of Quanqi and reached Guangzhou.
He boarded a ship for the South Sea and headed toward the Central Kingdom (India).
He traveled through more than thirty countries over a total period of twenty-five years.
He explored over four hundred sections of the subtle words on palm leaves and obtained more than three hundred grains of the True Form’s relics.
Having fulfilled his vow to transmit the lamp of the Dharma, he returned, shaking his mendicant’s staff.
In the first year of the Zhengsheng era, [the Emperor] arrived at Dongluo.

His intelligence was peerless and his spirit exceptionally refined; at the age of twelve, he left home to join the non-Buddhist sects.

His teacher, Parśva, instructed him in their scriptures and arts, whereupon he thoroughly mastered the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*) and became particularly proficient in the Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika systems.

He possessed a thorough command of the principles of yin and yang, calendrical calculations, celestial patterns, astrology, incantations, and medical prescriptions, as if they were held in the palm of his hand.
Having reached the age of sixty, he considered himself capable of acting alone;

Before long, his arguments and reasoning were both exhausted;
he finally realized that the sun of the Buddha’s wisdom is so lofty and brilliant that it cannot be matched by the light of a firefly,
and that the flow of the Dharma is so deep and vast that it cannot be equaled by the moisture of a single drop.
He devoted himself to reverent service, specializing in the study of the Buddha-vehicle, and upheld the precepts without flaw.
His resolve and character were lofty and austere, and his devotion to wisdom was profound.

It was polished by Xu Jian (Duke of Donghai Commandery and Grand Master for Palace Affairs), Lu Can (Viscount of Gu'an), Lu Zangyong (Right Attendant of the Department of State Affairs and Viscount of Donghai), Su Jing (Son of the Prince of Shu and Secretary of the Secretariat), Peng Jingzhi (Minister of the Ministry of Rites), Wang Jing (Viscount of Qi County and Assistant in the Left Office), Yan Wenzhi (Vice Director of the Grand Court of Justice), He Zhizhang (Doctor of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices), and others.
The translation was supervised by Lu Xiangxian, Minister of the Court of Imperial Secretaries and Marquis of Pingyu, and Wei Zhigu, Palace Attendant and Duke of Julu.
It was protected by Xue Chongyin, former Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and Yang Zhongsu, Gentleman of the Court of Ceremonial and Baron of Hongnong.
Once the transcription was completed, the original manuscript was presented to the Inner Palace.
Emperor Wu, who externally governed the myriad regions and internally venerated the Triple Gem,
composed a preface by imperial brush to be placed at the beginning of the scripture.
In total, fifty-two works comprising one hundred and eleven fascicles were translated before and after this period.
Once the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* had been completed by Tripiṭaka-translator Ratnarakṣita himself, he no longer translated further scriptures.
He delighted his spirit through Zen contemplation and nurtured his will through the Golden Elixir.
Although his lifespan exceeded one hundred years, his progress in the Way remained unimpaired.
He maintained the recitation of scriptures and circumambulation without fail from morning until night.
In the twelfth year of the Kaiyuan era,
he followed the imperial entourage into Luoyang and was ordered by imperial decree to reside at Changshou Temple.
Because Liu Zhi’s place of residence was designated as Kaiyuan, [the temple] received that name.
In the ninth month of the fifteenth year, he looked toward his disciples and said,
"This illusory body of mine is daily approaching decay and ruin."
Even if one dwells for a long time, in the end all things must perish.
Though I have maintained my health since birth, hoping to avoid decay, I am now gradually approaching old age;
it is in vain that I further prolong my time.
Consequently, for twenty days he neither drank nor ate, severing all use of medicine and food.
Although nearly fifty days had passed, his countenance remained as usual.
On the third day of the eleventh month, he then requested scented water to bathe and changed into fresh, clean clothes.
On the morning of the fourth day, he took up the various sūtras in the Sanskrit original, holding them aloft upon his head and offering praise to each one.
On the fifth day, at the time for the midday meal, he commanded all his attendants to disperse in the four directions.
"I shall now briefly retire to the purification chamber; do not make any noise.
Thereupon, within the purification chamber, he lay down on his right side and passed away suddenly at the age of one hundred and fifty-six.
Were it not for the accumulation of superior karma through cultivation and the casting off of worldly toil,
how could one preserve such a long life?
To decide upon departure or remaining is a matter of personal resolve alone.
Having heard this,
the Emperor listened with deep sorrow and grief, sighing in lamentation for a long time.
He subsequently posthumously conferred upon him the title of Grand Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.
His posthumous title was "Kaiyuan Yiqie Bianzhi Sanzang. By imperial decree, the inner attendant Du Huaijing was dispatched to the Eastern Capital to supervise the funeral.
An edict ordered the Inner Treasury to provide all necessary items for the burial expenses.
He caused them to be provided in infinite numbers.
Thereupon, the ceremonial retinue, with its feathered insignia, banners, standards,
and flower-canopies, filled the streets and alleys beyond counting.
He subsequently moved the burial site to Longmen and erected a stupa there to offer worship.
One fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-karman*, titled *Mīśāsaka-karmapada*, constitutes one work in one fascicle; its manuscript currently exists.
The śramaṇa Shi Ai-tong was of the secular surname Zhao;
he was originally a native of Tianshui.
He inherited the family’s ceremonial cap and crown.
Like [his predecessor], he left home to become a monk at a tender age;
later, he became renowned for his mastery of the Vinaya studies.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* was lectured upon by masters both near and far.
Formerly, during the Song dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Jue-shou of Kaśmīra translated the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*,
from which he subsequently produced one fascicle of the *Karmavācanā*.
As the times shifted and its original text fell into decay,
scholars sought it in vain and were left without support; thus,
they subsequently extracted one fascicle of the *Karmavācanā* from within the *Mahāvinaya*.
The doctrines of that school were widely propagated and disseminated.
Regarding the two fascicles of the *Yinyi* (Phonetics and Meanings) of the newly translated *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*: this one work in two fascicles is extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Huiyuan was a native of Jingzhao and a preeminent disciple of Dharma Master Huayan Zang.
He studied diligently without indolence, attaining mastery in both Buddhist and secular learning.
He was particularly proficient in the Huayan school.
Since there were no phonetic glosses for the newly translated scriptures,

He then extensively consulted various character dictionaries and compiled them into two fascicles, so that those who study and enjoy them need not seek a teacher from afar to understand the meanings of the characters.

*The Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, ten fascicles; also known as the *Record of the Consecration Section from the Great Maṇḍala Site of Nālandā in Central India*, circulated separately. This one work in ten fascicles is currently extant.
The śramaṇa Paramiti (translated into Chinese as Jízhòng) was a native of Central India.
Embracing the Way and observing the regions, he traveled and converted others according to conditions.
Through successive journeys of propagation, he reached my China; for the customs of India call this land "Zhina," and they refer to the imperial capital as "Mahāzhina."

the assembly, knowing him to be profoundly learned, offered many prayers to him.

On the twenty-third day of the fifth month in the year of the Dragon, the *yisi* (jia-zi) cycle— specifically the *xinchou* day—

This refers precisely to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, the foremost among the ten thousand practices.

Translated at the Lanruo of Lao Yin in Shibi Valley, Zhongnan Mountains, on the second day of the sixth month in the ninth year of the Kaiyuan era. The śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan was the hostage son of the King of Khotan.
By nature steadfast and renowned for his upholding of the Dharma, he arrived in the Great Tang in his youth and early on came to occupy a position of honor and emolument.
He was appointed as General of the Left Guard of the Imperial Army (Zuo Lingjun Wei Dajiangjun), Grand Marshal of the State (Shangzhuguo), and enfeoffed as Duke of Jinman Commandery.
By nature he was pure, simple, upright, and sincere, possessing these virtues within his heart;
he requested to donate his residence to establish a monastery in honor of the state.
On the eleventh day of the fifth month in the second year of the Shenlong era, an imperial edict granted his request.
Furthermore, he reflected upon himself: "Though born in a foreign land, I have grown up within the Middle Kingdom."
Fortunate have I been to serve four successive reigns, reaching the pinnacle of honor and favor. Yet,
fearing that I might still be unworthily receiving these abundant emoluments and immoderately basking in this extraordinary grace,
I have therefore requested to leave the household life, hoping thereby to repay the profound bounty of the Emperor.
On the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month in the second year of the Shenglong era,
an imperial edict stated:
"In the nature of human beings, there are none who do not covet and cherish rank and emolument."
Your aspiration is to renounce worldly desires and leave the household life, following the path of the *araṇya* and undertaking the practice of *dhyāna*.
Having suddenly reviewed your recent memorial, I both admire it and feel deep affection for you.
Having fulfilled his prayers and realized his lofty aspiration,
on the fifth day of the eleventh month in the first year of the Jinglong era—
the birthday of the Emperor— he left the household life and underwent tonsure.
His dharma name was Zhiyan.
He was further invited to reside at the Lanruo Hermitage of Zhongnanshan Zhixiang Temple to cultivate the Way.
Thereupon, with a vacant mind and tranquil contemplation, he engaged in seated meditation and walking practice.
With diligent austerity dwelling in his heart and profound contemplation accumulated through secluded seclusion,
he was further endowed with a mastery of both Chinese and Sanskrit scriptures that illuminated the most subtle and hidden truths.
Thus, he attained the true exegesis of the *Ratnakūṭa* and the secret verses of the Tathāgata.
There is none who has not repeatedly received [his] assistance;
for a long time he has been entrusted with the task of translating and scrutinizing the imperial edicts,
and he has frequently received [them].
Siyin was also commissioned to assist with the translation.
He resided in an āraṇya at Shibi Valley, where he practiced the dhūta austerities.
In the ninth year of the Kaiyuan era, at the Shibi Āraṇya and Feng’en Monastery, he...
He translated four works, including the *Sutra on the Definitive Karmic Obstructions*,
all of which combined literary elegance with substantive depth, thereby capturing their profound significance.
Furthermore, he translated one dhāraṇī incantation, the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī*, and six incantations from the *Lotus Sūtra*, such as those of Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva.
At this time, there was a manuscript of the sutra into which a newly transcribed mantra had been inserted;

The *Mahāvairocana-buddhābhisambodhi-vikurvāṇa-adhiṣṭhāna-sūtra* consists of seven fascicles; the seventh is the first [of these]. This is the recitation.
In the thirteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, Bukong recited the *Subāhuparipṛcchā-tantra* (three fascicles; in Chinese:
