This is called the *Sādhanavidhi* (Method of Wondrous Accomplishment). It is identical to the *Subāhu*, both being mantras of the *Vinaya*. One who has not entered a great maṇḍala is not permitted to read them at will;
it is the same as the offense of stealing when one listens surreptitiously to the *Prātimokṣa* while seeking full ordination—it constitutes the sin of theft.
Translated in the fourteenth year of the Kaiyuan era: the *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sarvāśāparipūraka-paramahṛdaya-dhāraṇī*.

*The Scripture on the Bhikṣuṇī’s Quest for the Dhāraṇī of Hearing and Retention*, one fascicle; translated from the Sanskrit original of the *Vajraśekhara-sūtra*, Chapter on the Accomplishment of All Meanings, as a brief abridgment.
A small portion was translated at the Pútíyuan of Xìmíng Temple in the fifth year of the Kaiyuán era.
The above four works comprise fourteen fascicles; their manuscripts are extant.
The śramaṇa Śubhakarasiṃha— his name,
when rendered in full with the Brahma-sound, should be pronounced *Śubhakarasimha* (with the "xian" and "zheng" tones);
in the Tang pronunciation, it is correctly translated as "Pure Lion."
Translated according to its meaning, his name was Śīlabhadra.
He was a native of Mahāsthāna in Central India and resided at Nālandā Monastery in Rājagṛha.
He was originally of the kṣatriya caste,
belonging to the Śākya clan;
having renounced worldly glory and nobility, he left the household life to follow the Buddha.
His spirit was pure and void, and his accomplishments in the Way were vast and eminent.
He was profoundly versed in dhyāna and wisdom, and attained marvelous mastery of the dhāraṇīs.
He entered with single-minded devotion into the gates of the Tripiṭaka teachings.
The fame of the Five Indian Kingdoms has long been spread abroad;
through great compassion for the benefit of living beings, its influence gradually extended eastward until it reached the borders of Northern India.
Its fame resounded throughout Mahācīna.
Our Sovereign, having gathered together men of virtue and talent, dispatched envoys to welcome him.
In the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era, on the Jǐchén day, he brought a vast collection of Sanskrit manuscripts and arrived at Chang’an.
Initially, it was placed in the Southern Courtyard of Kōfuku-ji;
subsequently, in the fifth year (the Ding-si year), at Bodai-in,
he translated the *Ākāśagarbha-śravaṇadhāraṇī-dharmaparyāya*, one fascicle.
The śramaṇa Siddha translated the words;
the śramaṇa Asanga composed the text and received it by dictation.
By imperial decree, the Sanskrit manuscripts brought by Venerable Wuwei were all ordered to be sent to the palace.
For this reason, I have not yet been able to translate the various sutras extensively.
Formerly, the śramaṇa Wuxing traveled west to India;
having completed his studies, he spoke of returning home.
Upon returning to Northern India, he unfortunately passed away;
the Sanskrit manuscripts he had brought with him were subsequently ordered by imperial decree to be welcomed back [to China].
Previously, while at Huayan Temple in the Western Capital,
Amoghavajra and the śramaṇa Yi-xing retrieved several copies of Sanskrit sūtras from there;
these were all profound gateways of dhāraṇī that had never before been translated.
In the twelfth year, he accompanied the imperial entourage to Luoyang and was stationed at Dafuxian Temple; thereupon,
he served as the śramaṇa Yixing’s assistant in translating the Mahāvairocana Sūtra.
The complete Sanskrit version of this sutra consists of one hundred thousand stanzas;
what is now presented is merely an abridgment of its essentials.
The śramaṇa Ratnacandra translated the words.
The śramaṇa Yixing transcribed the oral instructions and also revised and supplemented the phrasing and logic;
the style was a blend of the refined and the plain, perfectly harmonizing with the profound meaning.
He also produced the two sūtras, the Subāhu and the Susiddhi.
Possessing a fearless nature, he cherished tranquility and simplicity, using meditative concentration to delight his spirit.
From time to time, he engaged in Chan contemplation and encouraged those who were beginners.
With compassion in mind, he guided and received others without fail.
When people asked him about doubts, he analyzed them with unimpeded fluency.

*The Sūtra of the Great Dhāraṇī of the Mother of Seven Koṭis of Buddhas, Cundī*, one fascicle; the second edition, translated by Tripiṭaka Master Jñānabhadra (Nichiō), identical to the original text, translated at Zisheng Temple in the eleventh year of the Kaiyuan era. *The Method of Recitation Briefly Extracted from the Yoga of the Vajraśekhara*, four fascicles; also called a *sūtra*, translated at Zisheng Temple in the eleventh year of the Kaiyuan era. *The Chapter on the Five-Syllable Heart Dhāraṇī of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva from the Vajraśekhara Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated at Dajianfu Temple in the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era. *The Essential Methods of the Yoga of Avalokiteśvara Cintāmaṇicakra Bodhisattva*, one fascicle. The above three sūtras were all produced from Sanskrit originals; they are abridged excerpts from the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra* and do not comprise the complete texts. Translated at Dajianfu Temple in the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era. These four works, totaling seven fascicles, are all extant.

The śramaṇa Vajrabodhi (in the Tang language, "Vajra Wisdom") was a native of Mālaya in South India—a country known as "Land of Light"—which is near Mount Potalaka, the palace of Avalokiteśvara; he was of Brahmin descent.
Leaving home in his youth, he traveled throughout India.
Although he was widely proficient in both Buddhist and non-Buddhist teachings, he was particularly adept at *dhāraṇī*;
in this specific field, he had few equals.
Wandering and teaching according to conditions, he benefited sentient beings wherever he went.
Hearing that the Buddha-dharma was flourishing in Great China,
he eventually set sail eastward and reached the coastal region.
In the eighth year thereafter, he finally arrived at the capital.
Thereupon, he widely propagated the secret teachings and constructed mandalas;
as they were fashioned according to the Dharma, all were moved by auspicious spiritual omens.
The śramaṇa Yixing deeply revered this secret dharma and frequently approached him for consultation.

Each time, the Master pointed out the details one by one and further established a maṇḍala to confer empowerment upon him. Yixing reverently received this dharma and requested its translation for circulation.
In the eleventh year, the Guihai year (723 CE), at Zisheng Monastery,
he translated the *Yogacaryābhūmi-bhāṣya-vidhi* and the *Saptakoṭi-dhāraṇī*.
The translation was interpreted by Īśvara, a chief Brahmin from Eastern India serving in the Secretariat.
Scribe: the śramaṇa Wengu of Mount Song.
In the eighteenth year, the Gengwu year, at Dajianfu Monastery, he brought forth the Five-Syllable Heart Mantra of Mañjuśrī and the Essentials of the Yoga of Avalokiteśvara.
The śramaṇa Zhizang translated the terminology.
Furthermore, he appended new mantras to the existing *Sūtra of the Heart of the Dhāraṇī for Deliverance from All Fears*.
He firmly grasped the seals (*mudrā*) of the dhāraṇīs, and wherever he went, his practices were efficacious.
It was indeed this man through whom the secret teachings were transmitted.

Furthermore, there was his consecrated disciple, Lü Xiang—Grand Master for Rectifying Counsel, Acting Secretary of the Central Secretariat, Attendant to the Crown Prince and the Princes, and Academician of the Institute for the Collection of Writings—who served the Imperial Heir.
Out of reverence for the Tripitaka Master, I have thus recorded this:
The Upādhyāya was originally the third son of King Īśānavarman of the Kṣatriya caste in Central India.
Later, because King Mi-jun-na of South India recommended him,
he was subsequently known as a man from South India.
At the age of ten, he entered the monastic order at Nālandā Monastery.
Having studied the treatises on grammar under the master Śāntijñāna,
he traveled to Western India at the age of fifteen and studied the Dharmakīrti-śāstra for four years.
He returned to Nālandā Monastery and received full ordination at the age of twenty. For six years,
he studied the Vinaya of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions.
Furthermore, he studied the *Prajñāpradīpa*, the *Śataśāstra*, and the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* of the Southern School.
At the age of twenty-eight, in the city of Kapilavastu,
he studied the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, and the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra* under the master Śubhamitra.
After three years, at the age of thirty-one, he traveled to South India.
There he met Nāgabodhi, a disciple of the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna who was seven hundred years old and was still living.
Having served and made offerings for seven years,
he studied the *Vajraśekhara-yoga-sūtra*, the *Vairocana-dhāraṇī-dharmaparyāya*, various Mahāyāna sūtras, and the treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
Having received the secret treasury of the essential teachings of the Buddhas of the five families, he attained complete mastery of them all.
He then took leave of his teacher, Nāgabodhi, and returned to Central India,
where he visited the sacred stupas commemorating the eight manifestations of the Tathāgata.
Subsequently, there was a severe drought in South India for three years.
King Narasimhapotavarman dispatched an envoy to invite the Master;
he established an empowerment mandala within his own palace and requested rain.
At that time, sweet rain fell in profusion, and the king and his ministers rejoiced;
they subsequently constructed a monastery for the Upādhyāya and settled him there.
More than three years passed.
To the south of the kingdom, near the sea, there is a temple of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Beside its gate stands a nyagrodha tree that had previously withered and become decrepit.
The Upādhyāya fasted for seven days and practiced the Way;
the tree flourished once more.
The Bodhisattva manifested himself and spoke these words:
"What you have studied is now perfected.
You may go to the Kingdom of Siṃhala to pay homage to the Buddha’s tooth relic,
and ascend Mount Laṅkā to worship the Buddha’s footprints."
"Return and proceed to China to pay homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
That land has a karmic affinity with you;
you should go there to transmit the teachings and deliver all sentient beings."
Upon hearing these words, they were overcome with joy and consolation.
When the monks heard his speech,
the assembly of the monastery said:
If a Bodhisattva descends, the branches and leaves of the nyagrodha tree flourish;
when he departs, they immediately wither and fade.
Taking this as a sign, one observes for three times seven days.
He then took his leave of the king of that country and,
leading eight disciples— both monastics and laypeople—
proceeded to the kingdom of Siṃhala, arriving at Laṅkāpura.
The king, his ministers, and the fourfold assembly welcomed and paid homage to the Upādhyāya with various fragrant flowers.
Upon reaching the side of the palace, they proceeded to the Vairāṭya-rāja Monastery to prostrate before the Buddha’s tooth relic,
making offerings of fragrant flowers with sincere devotion.
Thereupon, the Buddha’s tooth emitted light that formed a canopy in the air,
manifesting everywhere for all the great assembly to behold this auspicious omen.
He then remained at that monastery for half a year, receiving offerings, before proceeding southeast to Mount Laṅkā.
He proceeded directly to the middle road to pay homage at the Fuyan Stūpa.
At that time, he practiced the Way for one day and one night;
there was no wish that was not fulfilled.
Next, he arrived at the city of Saptaratnaparvata.
Continuing on his journey, he reached the kingdom of Rohana, which governed over Mount Ratnagiri;
the land of that mountain abounded in tāla trees.
The king had previously followed the Hinayana;
upon hearing that the Upādhyāya had arrived, he went out of the city to welcome him from afar and,
within the royal palace, prepared extensive offerings for him.
After more than a month, the Upādhyāya expounded for him the principles of the Mahāyāna nature;
he was immediately able to penetrate this teaching, receiving it with faith and joy.
He then offered a wide variety of precious gems, but the Upādhyāya would not accept them, saying:
The original intention was to pay homage at the Buddha’s footprint, not for the sake of the precious jewel.
Having traveled from afar to this place, he wished to be shown the way.
The King immediately dispatched attendants with a palanquin, ordering them to carry him upon it.
He escorted him as far as the foot of the mountain.
That mountain abounded in fierce beasts, lions, venomous dragons, wild men, and rākṣasas;
black winds and bitter mists constantly guarded the precious treasures upon this mountain.
"One who has not paid homage to the sacred traces of the Sage cannot ascend and enter this mountain. Therefore,
the Upādhyāya burned incense at the foot of the mountain, prostrated himself, and made a great vow."
He wished to see the mountain deity from when the former Buddha was in the world preaching the Dharma.
Once the vow had been fulfilled, the heavens opened and the mists dispersed, while the fierce beasts retreated into hiding.
Thereupon, together with his disciples, he crossed the water on the northern side of the mountain, near the east.
Then he turned back toward the northwest and then southwest again, following the valley, climbing over vines and climbing plants.
Amidst various species of flora, he reached a precarious height at the midpoint of the mountain.
Nearby, to the north, there was a spring flowing out.
Within it were always red crystal, *śarkara*, gold, silver, and various other jewels;
there were also many plants of precious nature, as well as *māndārava* flowers and *utpala* flowers.
At that time, Gṛdhrakūṭa was entirely a place where the spirits of former sages had practiced the Way.
The fragrant flowers, grasses, trees, and shrubs within the mountains were beyond counting.
Without resting or lingering, he followed his mental traces for seven days until he reached the mountain summit.
There, seeking sacred traces, he beheld a round stone.
It is approximately four or five feet high and about twenty feet square in extent.
The Buddha’s right foot is partially embedded in the stone, showing signs of wear and damage;
seeing this, a doubt immediately arose in his mind, and he thought it could not be the Buddha’s footprint.
Gazing toward heaven and wailing in lamentation, he recalled the Tathāgata;
thereupon, five-colored clouds appeared, and a halo, a Buddha’s footprint, and a *cakra* (wheel) became clearly manifest.
A voice was heard saying:
"This is the true footprint of the Buddha;
it was left merely because the karma of sentient beings in past generations and those yet to come was heavy.
Having heard this, they rejoiced and made offerings of incense and flowers.
He entered meditative absorption for one day;
having emerged from concentration, he circumambulated for seven days,
carrying a stone and seeking the conditions for practicing the Way.
Outside the Buddha’s footprint, there are several stone cups upon the rock,
in which lamps were also lit. At times,
wild men would come to offer the Venerable Master sugarcane seeds, coconuts, plantains, and medicinal herbs.
At that time, the disciples saw him and scattered in all directions, fleeing away.
The Upādhyāya said, "He has come to make offerings; he will not harm you."
He then took what was offered and conferred the Three Refuges upon him.
That rustic man took a small stone, placed it upon the Buddha’s footprint, smashed it to pieces, and ate it.
Why is it said that he thus damaged his own mind?
It is said that this cures heart pain.
From this, one may verify that the Buddha’s footprint gradually diminishes;
there is much wind upon it, making it impossible to remain for long. Looking four directions from the top:
Fifty or sixty *li* outside the foot of this mountain, it is surrounded on all sides by a range of mountains that resemble a fortified wall;
the summits of these mountains are entirely covered in white clouds.
The people of the country call it Mount Laṅkāpura.
To the northwest of the mountain, it borders the kingdom of Siṃhala;
the remainder is the great ocean.
While looking about,
the Master unconsciously lost his footing and fell onto the steps down to the edge of a cliff, where he came to a halt;
not even a hair’s breadth of him was harmed.
One should know that this is the inconceivable power of the Buddha;
his disciples were filled with boundless wonder and joy,

presented above by the Great Auspicious Heavenly Son of the Great Tang Empire of Mahācīna, the Great Sovereign Lion King, the Middle King, who personally transcribed this with his own hand.

The Chapter on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra, Entering the Sphere of Inconceivable Liberation, concerning the fifty-five noble spiritual friends whom the youth Sudhana approached and served within his practice of attending upon as many spiritual friends as there are atoms in a Buddha-field, as taught in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in One Hundred Thousand Verses.
I respectfully present this for Your Majesty’s acceptance.
I humbly pray that the merit and blessings of the Sage-King of the Great Nation shall rise higher than Mount Sumeru,
and that His wisdom shall be deeper and vaster than the four great oceans.
May the lands of the ten directions become one single family.
By recording the merit of this sutra,
may that immeasurable mass of blessings be gathered.
May all beings throughout the infinite oceans of worlds, as vast as the realm of space, become just like the youth Sudhana—
attaining the correct view of the Buddhas and being fully endowed with wisdom.
Upon seeing these inconceivable and truly virtuous spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), they all gave rise to joy;
they attained the vast and universal radiance of the Buddhas, became free from all greedy attachments,
and accomplished the supreme practices and vows of the stainless Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
I humbly pray that through the merit of transcribing this Mahāyāna sūtra and offering it,
I may early behold the Compassionate One, Tathāgata Maitreya,
within the Dragon Flower Assembly when he attains Buddhahood.
The Great Holy Heavenly King attained the knowledge of past lives;
upon beholding them, he recognized those who had likewise received the Buddha’s prophecy,
as far as the limits of space and throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
May all sentient beings of the future be extensively delivered and swiftly attain Buddhahood.
This is verified by the tenth fascicle of the *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions*, which states:
"The kingdom of Uḍra is over seven thousand *li* in circuit."
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit.
The soil is rich and fertile, and the crops grow in abundance.
All manner of fruits are notably large.
The various countries have diverse grasses and famous flowers that are difficult to describe exhaustively.
The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are fierce and violent.
The people are of robust stature, and their complexions are dark.
The local dialects and customs differ from those of Central India.
The people are fond of learning without weariness and have great faith in the Buddha-dharma.
There are over one hundred monasteries with more than ten thousand monks.
All of them study and practice the teachings of the Mahāyāna.
There are fifty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
There are generally more than ten stūpas.
These are all places where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma and were established by King Aśoka.
On the southeastern border of the kingdom, bordering the great ocean, lies the city of Caritra (translated into Chinese as Dengxing), which is over twenty li in circuit.
It is a road where merchants traveling by sea and travelers from distant lands halt on their journeys to and fro.
Its city walls are firm and lofty, and it abounds in many rare treasures.
Outside the city, there are five monasteries situated one after another;
their towers and pavilions are lofty, and their sacred images are exquisitely crafted.
To the south, it is more than twenty thousand *li* to the country of Saṃkāśya (translated into Chinese as Shiziguo, "Lion-Holding Country").

On a tranquil night, gazing from afar, I beheld the radiance of the precious jewels atop the stūpa housing the Buddha’s tooth relic in that country, shimmering like the light of bright torches suspended on high.
Now, this Flower Garland (Avataṃsaka) sūtra has come from the hand of the King of Oḍḍiyāna.
He personally wrote out [this scripture] and sent it across the seas by dispatching an envoy to present it.
From this, we know that the Dharma King, in his reign, does not prize exotic goods or precious jewels;
rather, he places great faith in the Mahāyāna, regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha as his supreme treasures.
This is indeed a means to rescue those submerged in suffering and enable them to realize Bodhi.
On the eighth day of the eleventh month in the year of Yihai, the tenth year of the Zhenyuan era,
it arrived in Chang’an to be presented to the Enlightened Sovereign.
When the Emperor reviewed the petition, he conceived deep faith in it.
Since the script was different, it was necessary to have it translated;
Tripitaka Master Prajñā was the very person for this task.
The Tripitaka Master was styled Prajñā.
He was a native of Kaśmīra; the transcription "Fan-shou" (梵首) is an abbreviation, and the correct name is Kaśmīra.
As stated in the first fascicle of the *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions*: [text follows].
The country of Kāpiśī is over four thousand li in circuit.
To the north it backs upon the Snow Mountains, and on three sides it borders the Black Ranges.
The capital city of the country is over ten li in circuit.
It is suitable for growing grain, wheat, and many fruit trees;
it produces fine horses and saffron.
Exotic goods from various regions are gathered in great abundance in this country.
The climate is windy and cold, and the people are violent and fierce by nature.
Their speech is vulgar and coarse, and their marriage customs are promiscuous;
in these respects, they are largely similar to those of the Tukhāra kingdom.
Their customs, language, and social mores differ considerably [from those of other regions].
They wear cotton garments as well as furs and coarse woolens.
Their currency consists of gold coins, silver coins, and small copper coins.
Their customs and appearance differ from those of China.
Their king is of the Kṣatriya caste;
he possesses strategic insight and is by nature courageous and fierce.
He exercised military authority over neighboring regions and governed more than ten kingdoms.
He cherished and nurtured his people and venerated the Triple Gem.
Every year, he commissioned the creation of a Buddha image eighteen feet in height.
They also established the Unrestricted Great Assembly (Amogha-mahā-pariṣad),
providing universal relief to the poor and destitute and bestowing alms upon widowers and widows.
There are more than one hundred monasteries with over six thousand monks.
Furthermore, many there study and practice the teachings of the Mahāyāna.
The Sthūpa Monastery is lofty, vast, expansive, and pure.
There are several dozen deva temples with more than a thousand followers of heterodox paths.
Some go naked, while others smear themselves with ashes;
they string human skulls together to form crowns and garlands.
The Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā was born in this country;
his secular surname was Gautama,
or perhaps Lāṭa according to his maternal lineage.
Favored by Heaven with intelligence and acumen, at fourteen he left his hometown.
He followed a teacher in the Northern Celestial Crown (Beitianguan) and received full ordination.
There he studied the Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, as well as the Abhidharmakośa and Vibhāṣā.
Next, he traveled to Central India to study the five branches of knowledge (*pañcavidyā*) and Mahāyāna teachings.
He resided at Nālandā Monastery and frequently visited and paid homage to the eight sacred sites and stupas.
Having studied in this manner for eighteen years,
he next proceeded to the Udāya-rāja Monastery in South India,
where he practiced the Yoga teachings and ascended the consecration altar (*abhiṣeka-maṇḍala*).
He received and studied all the mantras of the five families.
From afar, he heard that the Great Holy One Mañjuśrī was the Five-Crested Youth (Pañcacīra-kumārabhūta).
Dwelling upon the five peaks of Cool Serenity,
they extinguish the scorching heat of afflictions;
together with a multitude of ten thousand bodhisattvas, they protect the Great Tang.
Thereupon, he crossed the seas and climbed over mountains carrying the Sanskrit scriptures;
sacrificing his body and entrusting his life,
he traversed Java and arrived at the Central Kingdom during the final years of the Zhongzhong era.
In the fourth year of the Zhenyuan era, he received an imperial decree to translate the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*;
this is the matter detailed in his separate record.
By the sixth year, he was appointed as an envoy to Northern India.
In the eighth year of the Zhenyuan era, he returned to Qi Xia.
He reflected that his long-cherished vow had not yet been fulfilled,
as he had not yet had the opportunity to pay homage to the Great Sage Mañjuśrī.
Reflecting on his original vow, his heart burned with fervor;
if his gracious command were not contradicted, he vowed that he would personally go there.
In the third month of the tenth year, he set out for Mount Qingliang to pay homage at the Five Terraces, arriving at the beginning of autumn.
In the fourth month of the eleventh year, he returned to the capital.
Then, on the eighteenth day of the eleventh month,
from King Uḍra of South India...
Two fascicles of Sanskrit scriptures were presented to the Great Tang.
On the final day of the month, an imperial edict was issued to the relevant office,
ordering the Tripiṭaka Master, together with the various Mahā-satpuruṣas, to examine the titles and submit the translated names for approval.
The Tripitaka Master then transcribed it from Sanskrit into the Hu (Central Asian) language,
which the śramaṇa Zhizhen then translated into the Chinese language.
He submitted this re-translation to the Imperial Secretariat.
The Sanskrit original of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* consists of six bundles in total, comprising one hundred thousand verses.
Of these, the eighty fascicles already translated during the Great Tang dynasty constitute the second bundle.
The present offering from the King of South India constitutes the third fascicle.
It contains sixteen thousand seven hundred verses.
The aforementioned scripture corresponds to the ninth assembly of the old translation of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* in eighty fascicles, which was preached at Śrāvastī.
The Tripitaka Śramaṇa Prajña of Kaśmīra proclaimed the Sanskrit text;
the Śramaṇa Zhizhen of Guangzhai Temple, a court attendant of the Hanlin Academy, translated the words;
and the Śramaṇa Yuanzhao, a translator at Ximing Monastery, received the dictation by pen.
The Commissioner received the petition and reported it in full to the Emperor.
Upon reviewing the circumstances, the Emperor issued an edict ordering its translation.
Although successive envoys repeatedly urged him, there was no one capable of interpreting the language.
Having learned through inquiry that there was one of virtuous speech in the Eastern Capital,
the Tripitaka Master submitted a formal petition requesting that he be presented to the Emperor.
The Imperial Secretariat received the petition and recorded it in detail for submission to the throne.
By the grace of Heaven, his request was granted.
He was issued a pass by Du Ya, the Imperial Resident of Henan Commandery, to proceed to the court.
Departing from East Luo on the twelfth day of the third month, he set out.
On the twenty-seventh day, he arrived at the Capital and reached Ximing Monastery.
The Imperial Secretariat reported this to the throne.
On the second day of the fourth month, the Palace Eunuch Zhang Chaojin delivered an imperial edict of consolation to the monk Guangji, conveying the Emperor’s words: [text follows].
Having traveled so far to the imperial court,
I imagine your journey has been most fatiguing.
I trust you have remained in good health and peace amidst the summer heat.
On this day, I respectfully entrust this memorial to the Imperial Messenger Zhang Chao to express my gratitude.
Having humbly received the Imperial decree, I am moved by a sense of awe and trepidation beyond measure.
As the Imperial Messenger returns, I respectfully submit this reply with him.
I, your servant, respectfully submit this memorial accompanying the imperial decree of consolation addressed to the translator-monk Guangji. That I,
a humble monk, have been specially favored with the Sage’s compassionate inquiry leaves me deeply moved and filled with gratitude beyond measure.
I respectfully submit this letter of thanks for your information.
At that time, the virtuous ones gathered like clouds and deliberated together on the translation of the scriptures.
Having already identified the appropriate person, it was necessary to secure a suitable location.
The Ximing Monastery is located far away, making travel there difficult and arduous.
It would therefore be appropriate to take possession of Chongfu Monastery instead;
please prepare a formal petition and submit it to the Office of the Commissioner for reporting to the Emperor.
By the grace of Heaven, the Imperial Messenger has delivered this decree.
On the fourth day of the sixth month of the twelfth year, the Imperial Messenger Zhang Tingxuan proclaimed and received the imperial edict:
"The Sanskrit scriptures contained in these cases should be translated immediately, and the completed work shall be presented for submission."
Thirty-five and a half taels of incense and fifty catties of tea are granted for the offerings at the Translation Institute.
With respect, I inquire after you during the summer heat:
may each of the Great Virtuous Ones be well and at peace?
The commentary states:
Tracing back the Great Sage’s establishment of the teachings in the Western Land, they were spread throughout the Eastern Realm according to the capacities and needs of those to be transformed.
Formerly, when the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he turned the Wheel of Dharma at the Deer Park; later, he entered parinirvāṇa beneath the twin śāla trees.
The assembly at the Piṇḍola Cave was concluded.
From the time Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty took up the reins of governance and the Dharma’s transformation spread to this land,
through the Jin, Wei, Zhou, and Sui dynasties, down to the present day.
The sun and moon have passed and are approaching their thousandth year;
yet the achievements of our Emperor are even more magnificent than those.
During the Later Qin Yao dynasty, the translations were transmitted at the Caotang Monastery.
The Sage Emperor honors the translation of scriptures at Chongfu Monastery;
throughout the ages, past and present, his orthodox lineage remains uniquely supreme.
The four nations admire his influence, and the myriad regions look up to his virtue.

On this day, the title of the scripture was first established as: *The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll One: The Chapter on Entering the Sphere of Inconceivable Liberation and the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra*.
It was presented for imperial inspection on the twenty-fourth day of the second month in the fourteenth year.
The Tripiṭaka Master from Kaśmīra, the purple-robed Śramaṇa Prajña, proclaimed the Sanskrit text;
the Śramaṇa Guangji of Tiangong Monastery in the Eastern Capital provided the oral translation.
Recorded by the Imperial Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xìmíng Monastery;
compiled and edited by the Śramaṇas Zhīróu and Zhītōng of Bǎoshòu Monastery;
and refined by the Śramaṇa Dàohóng of Zhèngjué Monastery and the Śramaṇa Jiànlíng of Zhāngjìng Monastery in Chéngdū Prefecture.
Śramaṇa Dào zhāng of Dàjué Monastery verified the meanings;
Śramaṇa Dàtōng of Qiānfú Monastery verified the meditative meanings;
and Śramaṇa Chéngguān of Chóngfú Monastery in Dàyuán Prefecture and Śramaṇa Língsuì of Qiānfú Monastery collated and finalized the text.

Presented by Your Majesty’s subject Nánzhēn, a Special Advance Rank Officer, Commandant of the Right Shen-ce Army Cavalry, Senior Officer of the Palace Guard, and Acting Deputy Commander, concurrently serving as Judicial Assistant of Dēng Prefecture.

I, the subject Huo Xianming—General of the Cloud Banner (Yunhui Jiangjun) of the Original Retinue of Xingyuan, General of the Right Gate Guard (You Jianmenwei Jiangjun), Concurrent Commissioner for Merit of the Right Street (Youjie Gongde Shi), and Director of the Affairs of the Palace Eunuchs (Zhi Neishisheng Shi)—who holds the rank of Shangzhuguo, is a Marquis of Jiaocheng County with an appanage of three hundred households, and serves as the Commander-in-Chief (Hujun Zhongwei) of the Shence Army—[hereby submit this memorial].

A memorial from the subject Dou Wenchang, Palace Attendant for the Protection of the Left Shen-ce Army, concurrently Commissioner of Merit for the Left Ward, former attendant at the start of the Xingyuan campaign, General of the Household of the Flying Cavalry, acting Grand General of the Left Gate Guard, Marquis of Bin with the rank of Shangzhu-guo, enjoying an estate of three thousand households, and others.
I, the subject Xianming,
humbly submit this report. I have observed that the King of Uḍra in South India has presented a Sanskrit manuscript of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
and by imperial decree, I and others have been charged with overseeing the translation alongside the Tripiṭaka Master Prajña of Kapiśa and the Great Virtuous Monk Ling sui of the capital.
It has now been translated into forty fascicles as a single work.
It is the same translation as the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" chapter, the ninth assembly, of the old *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The language of that country is rendered here in this vernacular dialect;
the profound pivot and subtle key are thus revealed with vast clarity.
Monastics and laypeople alike gaze upon him in reverence and offer praise, as if they were present within the assembly.
Your servant Xianming and others, with utmost sincerity and reverence, prostrate themselves repeatedly.
Your servant has heard that the Ultimate Teaching is wordless.
There is no way to communicate its essential meaning except through speech;
speech serves only to guide practice,
and when practice is perfected, one establishes words.
Thus, having attained mastery in both meditative concentration and wisdom, he transforms beings through both speech and silence.
We humbly submit that Your Majesty, the Emperor, possesses the vast grace of heaven and earth, and your Way extends to the boundless horizons.
Your sagely reflections illuminate and manifest the profound virtue of the Dark Mystery.
This truly demonstrates that though the myriad phenomena differ, they are unified by a single thread; the three teachings converge upon the same goal.
Beholding the sentiments of those distant lands who yearn for transformation through the Middle Kingdom, they have profoundly explored the treasury of liberation.
Gathering palm leaves in the Zen grove,
he personally transcribed them once more to manifest his utmost devotion;
those who have come from afar by boat and ladder have not yet been recorded in the annals.
Had I not previously heard of this as a profound and mysterious resonance between us,
how could I have ventured across the unfathomable perils of the blue waves or escaped the calamity of being swallowed by a giant whale?
From its distant origins through the nine assemblies, it is surely that which is perfectly luminous;
tracing its beginning, the Bodhisattva Juexian transmitted it to the Jin dynasty,
and examining its end, the kings of Fan have upheld it to this day.
The seven luminaries thereby increase in brilliance;
all things revere its supreme principle.
It is difficult to express adequately through the capacity of intellectual knowledge.
As for establishing models and leaving instructions, governing the state and bringing peace to the people—
though his reign has been long-lasting and his virtuous influence profound,
there has never been a period of such flourishing restoration as this.
The Hua and the Rong submit to his rule;
he establishes the foundation of ritual and music and reveals the omens of spiritual sageliness.
The rivers are clear and the seas are calm;
this was not solely for the sake of the Qin dynasty’s translations.
[This was also the case for] the monks Ling-sui and others.
Delving into the refined subtleties and profound mysteries, I reverently uphold the sacred teachings.
For the purpose of this glossary on the *Lishu*, I have now drawn upon Sanskrit to verify ancient forms;
having exhaustively sought out their subtle meanings, I have taken the precedents of past masters as my testimony.
How could it be that only the nine scrolls of the *Geyi* have monopolized its fame? We have carefully placed them within a precious casket, adorned with solemn reverence.
Incense and flowers surround them as devas and humans receive and welcome them;
together we proceed to the Right Silver Terrace Gate to present them.
We humbly reflect that the Celestial Spirit’s vast operation takes the nurturing of all beings as its heart;
thus, mindful of the multitude of people, it has sought the ferry and bridge upon the path to enlightenment.
We, the ministers Xianming and others, have by chance encountered this flourishing era and been permitted to protect the True Doctrine.
As a supervisor, I am incompetent;
yet I have mistakenly received the offerings of the Southern Palace.
Your grace is so profound that it is difficult to repay.
I further increase my sincerity in this endeavor.
I humbly hope that this scripture may be promulgated both within and without the realm,
so that its blessings may, above, support the imperial succession and, below, bestow protection upon all living beings.
Unable to restrain our utmost earnestness and sincerity,
we respectfully present this memorial for Your Majesty’s perusal. We,
your subjects, Xianming and others.
With utmost reverence and trepidation, we prostrate ourselves repeatedly and respectfully submit this.
On the twenty-fourth day of the second month in the fourteenth year of the Zhenyuan era,

presented by the subjects Huo Xianming and others— Right Commander-in-Chief of the Shen-ce Army, concurrently Commissioner of Merit for the Right Ward, Former Attendant of Xingyuan, Yun-hui General, Right General of the Palace Gate Guard, Overseer of Affairs for the Inner Eunuch Service, Marquis of Jiaocheng County with a fief of three hundred households, and Grand Master of the Household.

Submitted together by Your Servant Dou Wenchang, Commander-in-Chief of the Shen-ce Army, Protector-General of the Army, concurrently Director of Merit for the Left Ward, Original Attendant from Xingyuan, General of the Flying Cavalry, acting Grand General of the Right Gate Guard, Marquis of Bin with the rank of Shangzhu-guo, enjoying an appanage of three thousand households.
The commentary states:
On this day, as the Emperor was reviewing the memorial and the newly translated sutra were being presented,
suddenly the clouds dispersed and the mist cleared away.
The Sun of the Sage shines with equal brilliance to the bright sun;
as soon as the scroll of the sutra is opened,
the imperial wind and the wind of the Way blow forth together.
The springtime radiates auspicious energy, and the beautiful scenery is warm and harmonious.
A joyful countenance floats across the sky as the common people share in this celebration.
Thereupon, the Imperial Messenger of High Rank, Ma Shiquan, was dispatched.
Announcement for the Buddhist Community:
By Imperial Decree, I address the Tripiṭaka Masters and others.
I wish to relieve you of your fatigue regarding the recent translation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (The Flower Ornament Scripture of the Buddha).
Now that these have been fully presented, they deeply satisfy the Emperor’s wishes.
With the arrival of spring, may each of you, Master and disciples, be well and at peace.
Tripitaka Master Prajñā has submitted this memorial to offer his congratulations.
The Tripiṭaka Master from Kaśmīra, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Prajñā, residing at Liquan Temple in the Capital,

humbly submits this in accordance with the gracious imperial decree to translate the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* presented by the King of Uḍḍiyāna in Southern India, together with the Great Virtuous Ones of the capital, including Liṅsuì and others.
Now translated into forty fascicles as a single work,
its subtle principles are illuminated and its refined meanings extensively expounded.
Monastics gather like clouds, and the common people assemble like stars.
As the recollections fill the streets and the praises are beyond recording,
Śramaṇa Prajña is truly joyful and celebrant.
We humbly pray that Your Majesty, the Emperor, possesses a celestial nature from within and softens distant realms through your sacred instructions.
Distant lands and diverse customs have all returned to the source of transformation;
the supreme teaching has spread everywhere, and its profound virtue shines brilliantly.
Consequently, King Uḍa personally inscribed the Sanskrit manuscripts and respectfully presented them to the Central Court.
It was not that sagely resonance was triggered by the ultimate principle;
for how could those dwelling beyond the blue seas and shifting sands have been able to reach such a state, such that the chariots and books were unified?
Since the Eastern Jin, none has equaled the present Sage Tang.
How magnificent and how splendid!
Although Emperor Ming of the Han sought the scriptures of the Yuezhi, they were not his equal.
The translations he produced exhaustively elucidate the meaning of the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter across the nine assemblies of the old *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The words are subtle and the meaning profound;
by grasping the essential principles, one opens the gate of the secret and exhaustively explores the treasury of liberation.
With my meager and inferior practice, it is difficult to fathom the source of the Way;
as for translating the teachings, how could I possibly succeed?
I can only feel empty shame before the imperial power.
I humbly reflect that, while the auspicious era is one of non-action,
we are pained by delusion; may you propagate the true scriptures of the Maitreya Lord and rescue all classes of beings upon the bridge of salvation.
In my devout and celebratory sincerity, I am deeply moved by awe and trepidation.
I respectfully entrust this to Huo Xianming, Military Protector of the Right Strategy and concurrently Emissary for Merit of the Right Street.
I respectfully present this memorial to express my congratulations for your perusal.
The *śramaṇa* Prajñā, with utmost reverence and trepidation, speaks thus.
The Emperor’s decree stated:
The profound and mysterious intent of the Buddha’s teachings relies upon translation for its transmission.
The Dharma Master, having mastered his studies with leisure and refinement, possesses a refined intellect that penetrates the obscure;
he thoroughly understands the subtle words of the palm-leaf manuscripts.
I rejoice to know that you have extensively cultivated the pure precepts of the Lotus and,
by harmonizing them with the True Teaching, have truly fulfilled my own aspirations.
Congratulations!

When the scriptures had been presented and he received the imperial decree to be released and return home, on the twenty-sixth day, a celestial messenger of high rank, Gao Zhongliang, arrived and again proclaimed the imperial instructions, delivering the edict to the Tripiṭaka Master and the others:
"By Imperial Order, it is said to the Tripiṭaka Mahāsattvas and others: [The rest of the message follows].
You have labored long in the translation hall at the site of enlightenment.
I now bestow upon you, the masters, Dharma robes, silk, and tea; please accept them.
With the warmth of spring approaching, may each of you remain in safety and well-being.

He bestowed upon the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā one set of six items consisting of a purple single-layered lined robe, an official *shī* silk robe, and a *líng* silk robe, along with twenty strings of tea and one hundred bolts of silk.
He also bestowed upon the monk Yuánzhào one set of six items consisting of a purple single-layered lined robe, an official *shī* silk robe, and a *líng* silk robe.
The other nine persons each received one set of garments consisting of a coarse brown robe, a single-layered garment, an official *shici* silk robe, and a brocade silk robe—six items in total.
Each of the ten persons also received ten strings of tea and fifty rolls of silk.
The monks submitted a memorial to express their gratitude.
The Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Prajñā and others state:
We have reverently received the proclamation delivered on the twenty-sixth day of this month by the Right Street Commissioner for Merit, Huo Xianming, and his officials, Gaopin Zhongliang.
Regarding the bestowal of an imperial edict, as well as dharma robes, tea, silk, and other gifts:
Heaven has bestowed extraordinary grace, and its radiant favor descends upon us in this crooked world.
Once again spreading the clouds of Yao, the teachings of Śākyamuni are restored to prosperity.
All those within the monastic community prostrate themselves in profound celebration and joy.
We humbly beseech Your Majesty, the Emperor:
Heaven has bestowed upon you sagely virtue, and you nobly esteem the Way of Non-action.
With his mind wandering through the sagely statutes, he forgot the immortals as the sun set;
when the bells and drums resounded at the imperial pinnacle,
the entire realm came to know that the Buddhist scriptures had arrived and that the civilizing influence of culture had found its true home.
The Prajñāpāramitā and other consciousnesses are not clear to me; my principles are obscure and my life is in decline.
Yet, having been uniquely favored by Your Imperial Grace, I have falsely undertaken this translation.
While Your Sacred Virtue remains hidden, the volumes of the canon are now complete.
Your Majesty has bestowed upon me exceptional favors to encourage and inspire me;
I am so overcome with joy that I have no place to stand, holding the gift with trembling hands in awe.
I respectfully entrust this memorial of thanks to Huo Xianming, Commissioner of Merit for the Right Ward, to present to Your Majesty.
The śramaṇas Prajñā and others, with utmost reverence and trepidation, and with sincere joy and awe, respectfully submit this statement.
On this day, the memorial of gratitude was presented;
the assembly of monks withdrew, rejoicing that the Great Teaching is now spreading.
"Excellently composed and beautifully written.
By imperial decree on the eighth day of the ninth month of the fifteenth year of the Yuanhe era,
it was incorporated into the *Zhenyuan xinding shijiao mulu* (The Newly Compiled Catalogue of Śākyamuni’s Teachings of the Zhenyuan Era).

The *Buddhabhāṣita-daśabala-sūtra*, one fascicle. This work, consisting of one fascicle, was translated at the Lotus Temple west of the city of Anxi by the Tripiṭaka Master from Kucha, the Śramaṇa Mudritaśiṣya (whose name means "Lotus-Vīrya" in the language of Tang).

*The Sūtra on the Wheel of Dedication Spoken by the Buddha*, one fascicle, three and a half sheets. *The Sūtra on the Ten Stages Spoken by the Buddha*, nine fascicles, one hundred twenty-one sheets. These two works, totaling ten fascicles, were [translated] by the Tripiṭaka Master from Khotan, the Śramaṇa Śīladharma (whose name means "Precept-Dharma" in the language of Tang), at Longxing Monastery in Beiting Prefecture.
He translated from the Sanskrit while simultaneously rendering them into Chinese.
These three sections comprise eleven fascicles in total, and their original texts are extant.
As for the aforementioned newly translated *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, *Pariṇāmacakra-sūtra*, *Daśabala-sūtra*, and others:
This was the śramaṇa Wukong of Zhangjing Monastery in the Capital,
whose original name was Fajie;
he obtained it while on an embassy to Central India from Kapiśī.
In the tenth year of the Tianbao era, the year of Ximao (751 CE), the Master was commissioned as an envoy to Kapiśa.
It was not until the year of Guisi (753 CE) that he finally arrived in that country.
On his return journey, he contracted an illness that did not abate.
Thereafter, he eventually resolved to leave the household life and receive the precepts.
He traveled on pilgrimage to the Eight Stūpas, reaching Central India;
after many years had passed, he made a vow to return to his own country.
Having received the Sanskrit originals of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and other scriptures from the Tripiṭaka Master Śīlādharma, he returned to Anxi and resided at the Lotus Temple.
There was a Tripiṭaka Master, the śramaṇa Muditaśrī.
He requested that the *Daśabala-sūtra* in one fascicle be translated.
Furthermore, while at Beiting, he was joined by Yang Xigu, the Regional Commander and Censor-in-Chief, along with the śramaṇa Dazhen of Longxing Monastery and others.
He requested the Khotanese Tripiṭaka Master Śīladharma to translate the *Pratideśanā-cakra-sūtra* in one fascicle and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* in nine fascicles.
He arrived at the capital in the second month of the sixth year of the Zhenyuan era.
The Memorial for Merit Commissioner of the Left Ward, Dou Wenchang, has completed the transcription and presented it for imperial inspection;
the original manuscript remains extant.
This is in accordance with the Imperial Decree issued on the twenty-third day of the tenth month of the fifteenth year.
It has been incorporated into the *Zhenyuan xinding shijiao mulu*.

*Jiujinglu* (Old Catalogue of Scriptures), one fascicle: The above [entry] appears to be the catalogue compiled by Liu Xiang of the Former Han dynasty while he was collating the books.

these are what are called the ancient catalogs of the Tripitaka,

Alternatively, when the King of Qin burned the books, those preserved among the people [remained].

In the various catalogs of the past, only the titles of the sūtras were listed;
as for their categories and the eras in which they appeared,
these were generally omitted and not recorded.
Subsequent readers might otherwise fail to discern the origins; therefore,
Dao’an has here compiled the titles to indicate their respective eras, categorized them as new or old,
and determined their authorship.
The various scriptures have their sources;
from this point onward they become clear.
Later, the numerous catalogs drew upon these to expand and broaden them.
Thus we know that his lofty aspirations and solitary awakening were sufficient to serve as a model for future generations;
such are the writings he composed.

Sengrui was a disciple of Dao’an.

He participated in the translations at the school of Kumārajīva and compiled many works.

The *Collection of Records Concerning the Tripitaka Translated during the Liang Dynasty* consists of fifteen fascicles; its preface states briefly:
"Sengyou, though of mediocre and shallow capacity, has long relied upon the Dharma-gate.
Gazing up with devotion at the profound breeze [of the teachings], he vows to propagate the Great Transformation."
Every time from dusk until dawn he would recite and uphold [the scriptures];
throughout the autumns and summers of his lectures,
his mind never failed to race toward the Garden of Amrāvatī and his spirit to leap upon Vulture Peak.
Thereupon, I have exerted my feeble will to follow the current and traced the source to compile what I have heard,
naming this work *The Collection of Records for the Translation of the Tripiṭaka*.
1. A Record of the Compilation of Circumstances;
2. A Catalogue of Explanatory Titles;
3. General Prefaces to the Sutras.
Fourth, the "Chronicle of Biographies" (Lichuan Yuanji):
its composition clarifies the original sources of the catalogs,
and its arrangement ensures that the chronological records do not fall into oblivion.
In the general preface, the excellence of their assembly is amply evidenced by the biographies;
in the accounts, the character of these individuals may be discerned.
Together they delved into the inner scriptures and scrutinized external teachings.

Volume Fifteen: The Biography of Bai Fazhu and others, ten entries. The compiler states:
The regulations compiled by Youlu are worthy of observation;
yet, if one seeks them closely, they are not without errors. For instance, as stated in the first fascicle, in the "Record of Differences in Scriptures" (*Chujing yiji*):
The term *tathāgata-arhat-samyaksaṃbuddha* in the old translation and *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the new translation are one and the same;
[the former] is merely an error.
If we contrast the old and new translations,
one should say that the old sūtras use *tathāgata arhat samyaksaṃbuddha*,
while the new sūtras use *tathāgata arhat samyaksaṃbuddha*.
In the old translation, it is rendered as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
in the new translation, it is rendered as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The two meanings differ entirely.
They cannot be interchanged.
Furthermore, Dharmarakṣa and Zhu Fahu were actually one and the same person.
"Dharmā" means "Dharma."
The rākṣasa said, "I shall protect you," and he divided himself into two persons;
both were mistaken.
In the catalogs of various translated scriptures and treatises,
works that merely share similar titles are simply labeled as "retranslations" without careful examination or detailed analysis.
The third error is the confusion of large and small texts,
whereby the *Jiuguanting Yaoshi* (Old Consecration Medicine Master) was included in the *Bianwei Lu* (Record of Compiled Forgeries) by Huijian of the Song dynasty.
The fourth error:
furthermore, within the introductory section (*nidāna*) of the collection, there are occasional discrepancies with the previous translation; they were not carefully compared.
This is the fifth error.
Compared to the various works produced by the multitude, this [present work] is entirely deficient; it is but a single flaw upon a precious jade.

It contains the *Mahāyāna-sūtra-piṭaka-lu* in six sections, totaling seven [volumes].
The section on various sūtras translated by a single person comprises 184 works totaling 1,718 fascicles;
the section on various sūtras with different translations comprises 195 works totaling 532 fascicles;
and the section on various sūtras of unknown translators comprises 134 works.

Section Four: Doubtful Scriptures, totaling twenty-one works in thirty fascicles. Section Five:
Spurious and False Scriptures, totaling eighty works in one hundred and ninety-six fascicles. This concludes the Catalogue of the Sūtra Piṭaka of the Hīnayāna.
The second division, consisting of six sections, comprises eight hundred and forty-two works, totaling four hundred and fifty works in one thousand three hundred and one fascicles;
this amounts to three hundred and four fascicles. The section on various translations of the same scriptures comprises seventy-two works in two hundred and ninety-two fascicles.
The section on different translations of the same scriptures comprises one hundred works in three hundred and seventy fascicles. These constitute the various scriptures.
The section on works of Lost Translation comprises 250 works in 272 fascicles;
the section on derivative works of various scriptures comprises 341 works in 346 fascicles; the section on scriptures of Doubtful Authenticity comprises 29 works in 31 fascicles;

compiled after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, seven divisions totaling one hundred forty-four works and six hundred twenty-seven fascicles. *Xīyù xiánshèng chāojí fēn hé* (The Collection of Transcripts by Sages and Holy Ones from the Western Regions), four divisions totaling forty-eight works and one hundred nineteen fascicles.

however, when calculated, they amount to 2,254 works in 5,191 fascicles. Upon detailed examination, the number of works and fascicles in the *Bieyuan* (Separate Sources) section differs from that in the general catalog.

The compiler stated:
"In my examination of these remaining texts, there were not a few errors."
This refers to Dharmarakṣa (translated into Chinese as Fahu),
who is in fact a single person;
he is divided into two entries within this catalog.
The *Yun chū xūzhēn tiānzǐ jīng* in two fascicles is compiled as a re-translation;
yet it does not distinguish between Indic and Chinese terminology—
this is the first error.
The *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Vinaya-viṃśati-prakaraṇa-vibhāṣā-śāstra*), consisting of twenty-two fascicles,
is generally treated as a single work within the catalog of scriptures, yet it is divided into two parts;
the twenty-two fascicles of the Vinaya are compiled among the Vinaya texts.
The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī-śāstra* (Mingliao lun), in one fascicle, is listed in the catalog of śāstras.
Regarding the title of this single sūtra, it appears twice in the two catalogs;
the second instance is an error.
The statement that "its vinaya consists of twenty-two [chapters]" refers to the abbreviated title of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*;
to now say it is "twenty-two fascicles" is a grave error.
As for the twelve-fascicle version translated by Paramārtha:
The two versions are not different;
they both belong to the same two schools,
yet you speak of them as "retranslations."
The third is an error.
To include such works as the *Renwang jing* and the *Qixin lun* among the "doubtful" scriptures is the fourth error.
I am unable to present these in full detail; they are briefly described here as such.

It was compiled by Fei Changfang of Chengdu, a scholar-translator at Xingshan Monastery in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era. The first volume of the *Lidai Sanbao Ji* covers the reigns from the Zhou through the Qin dynasties.
From the tenth year of the reign of King Zhuang of Zhou, the Jiamu year,
until the Jiamu year of Zi Ying, the son of the First Emperor of Qin,
there were twenty-six sovereigns for a total of four hundred and eighty-one years.
The Second Volume of the Record of the Three Jewels Through the Successive Dynasties: From the Former Han Xinshi period to the Latter Han.

the *Abhidharma* of lost translation consists of six works totaling ten works and twenty-seven fascicles. The *General Catalogue of the Three Jewels of the Kaihuang Era* contains one fascicle.
The *Catalogue of Inner Scriptures* states that the total number of sutras, vinayas, śāstras, and biographies produced according to the Fang catalogue is two thousand one hundred forty-six.
The six thousand two hundred and thirty-five fascicles do not count toward the canon; they comprise seventy-four sections and thirty-seven fascicles, differing from the internal scriptures (Āgama).
Together with the general catalog, these form fifteen volumes in total.

Regarding the thirteenth and fourteenth [volumes], the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna works included in the canon number one thousand seven hundred and sixty sections and three thousand three hundred and twenty fascicles.
The statement that the number of volumes recorded in the Fifteen-Volume Catalogue is three thousand two hundred and ninety-two is a calculation error.
The *Neidian lu* states:
Among those works compiled by Fang that have been included in the Canon,
there are generally mutual errors,
yet they remain abundant and extensive.
It cannot be dismissed as unfounded;
it is not without basis.
To those who would unilaterally edit and abridge [the texts], it is said:
I have examined Changfang’s *Catalogue of Works Included in the Canon*,
and its factual content is muddled and erroneous;
even those texts with missing portions or suspected apocryphal origins are all compiled therein.
I humbly consider this to be incorrect.
Furthermore, for example, in the *Mahāyāna Catalogue*, there are the *Bhadrakalpika Sūtra* and the *Bhadrakalpika-samādhi Sūtra*.
This is a single sūtra with two titles;
currently, two versions exist,
one of which is erroneous.
The *Subhūti-parivarta* and the *Dīrgha-devaputra-sūtra*—also known as the *Sujāta-devaputra-catuṣpraśna-sūtra*—are two names for the same scripture recorded twice in two sections;
this is a third error.
The *Hastipadopama-sūtra* is an alternate title for the *Aśokasena-sūtra*, each containing four errors.
The *Bodhicaryāvatāra-sūtra* is the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra*.
The variant titles preserve two original versions and contain five errors,
including the inclusion of the Sāṃkhya non-Buddhist school within the Mahāyāna.
Sixth Error:
Among the records of the Hīnayāna, the *Dharmatrāta-dhyāna-sūtra* and the *Aśubha-bhāvanā-dhyāna-guṇa* are in fact one and the same scripture;
the title *Dharmatrāta* was applied based on its subject matter, namely the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Regarding the establishment of titles based on persons, both divisions exist;
this is the seventh error.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), sixty-one fascicles.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* consists of fifty-nine fascicles;
the two versions do not differ.
As for the sixty-first fascicle, it was added by Vimalākṣa as a preface to the *Vinaya* and placed at the end.
There are no other differences whatsoever.
As for the present mention of a "retranslation," both versions exist together.
The eighth error:
The *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* (Twenty-two) is contained within the Vinaya,
while the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* is recorded among the treatises (*śāstra*).
The title is divided into two parts.
There are nine errors;
the "twenty-two" in that Vinaya text is actually half of the title of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
The twenty-two fascicles currently extant as the *Vinaya* are a "double error within errors.
Among the catalogs of successive dynasties, the *Saṅghabheda-vibhaṅga-śāstra* (Zhòngshìfēn Āpítán lùn) states that it was translated during the Song dynasty by Guṇabhadra together with Buddhabhadra.
Regarding those included within the Canon, it is said that they have lost their source;
there are ten errors due to discrepancies between the preceding and following sections.
The remainder has been preserved in records;
it cannot be described in detail here.

The *Sui Zhong jing mulu* (Catalogue of All Scriptures of the Sui Dynasty) in five fascicles was compiled by imperial decree in the second year of the Renshou era (602 CE), by the Great Virtuous One of Xingshan Monastery together with śramaṇas translating the scriptures and scholars. In total, it comprises two thousand one hundred and nine works in five thousand fifty-nine fascicles.
The original single volume contains no other separate translations; it comprises three hundred and seventy works in one thousand seven hundred and eighty-six fascicles.
This is the first fascicle of the aforementioned collection.
The works translated multiple times—including those with one revision, up to as many as six revisions—total two hundred and seventy-seven sections comprising five hundred and eighty-three fascicles.

The *Xian sheng ji zhuan* (Collected Biographies of Worthies and Sages) was compiled by worthies and sages; its translations have an established origin, comprising forty-one works in one hundred and sixty-four fascicles.

The aforementioned two and a half fascicles from the second volume onward comprise six hundred and eighty-eight works in two thousand five hundred and thirty-three fascicles, which are recorded as being included in the Canon.
Separate works extracted from within the main collections and circulated independently total eight hundred ten sections and one thousand two hundred eighty-eight fascicles.
This is the third volume of the above.

The section on Doubtful and Spurious Works, though its titles resemble those of authentic scriptures, consists of human compositions; it comprises two hundred and nine sections totaling four hundred and ninety-one fascicles.

The right-hand column, the fourth volume, contains works for which the original texts are missing; although these were listed in ancient catalogs, the actual scriptures are not extant. Altogether, there are four hundred and two sections totaling seven hundred and forty-seven fascicles, which one should seek out.
This concludes the fifth fascicle.
Its preface states briefly:
"If a text is suspected of being spurious, there is no need to transcribe it."
Those outside of these three categories that are included in the Tripitaka—
such as works like the *Fǎbǎo jí* (Collection of Dharma Treasures) and the *Jìngzhù zǐ* (Disciple of Pure Abiding)—
are likewise treated according to the precedent of the *Lüchāo* (Abridged Extracts) and placed in a separate section.
Other works, such as the *Biographies of Monks* (*Sengzhuan*), incorporate literary prose and historical styles; their diction is not pure or orthodox.
Although the events may be investigated, their meaning is not worth recording.
The *Neidian lu* states:
At present, the practice of transcribing [the titles] throughout the capital is widespread.
While the names of the sūtras are listed directly, they are further categorized according to their translators;
since more than half have been omitted, it is insufficient for study. Thus, the compiler says:
I have examined this catalogue and found it is not without errors; for instance,
the *Sūtra on the Samādhi of Extensively Manifesting the Propagation of the Way* and the *Sūtra of the Dragon King Anavatapta* [are listed as one].
These are two titles for a single sūtra,
both attributed to Zhu Fahu as the translator;
both versions have been preserved.
The first is an error.
Furthermore, the eight-fascicle *Puyao jing* (Lalitavistara-sūtra) states it was translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin;
yet, within the catalog of missing texts, it is again stated that the eight-fascicle *Puyao jing* was also translated by Zhu Fahu.
The two catalogues both record this omission as an error.
Furthermore, the eight-fascicle *Puyao jing* included in the canon is designated as a "single-text" edition.
In the *Lüzhong quēběn* (Record of Missing Texts), it is stated that this is a retranslation.
The missing text contains three errors resulting from discrepancies between its earlier and later portions.
Regarding the twelve-fascicle and fifteen-fascicle versions of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* translated by Paramārtha,
although the number of fascicles differs, the text itself is no different.
Both editions currently exist.
The fourth error:
the *Mīśāsaka-karmavācanā* is recorded redundantly, both before and after, within the *Qiūběn lù*.
The fifth error.
The *Suixuanwangsheng jing* (Sūtra on Rebirth According to One’s Vows), the *Yiwei lun* (Treatise on the Bequeathed Intent), and others are compiled among the "Doubtful and Spurious" works.
This is the sixth error;
the remainder are listed in the catalog.
It cannot be fully recorded here.

The *Dàtáng nèishuànlù* (Record of the Inner Transmission of the Great Tang), ten fascicles, was compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery in the first year of the Línḍé era (the Jiǎzǐ year). Its first section, titled "A Record of the Origins of the Translation of Various Scriptures Throughout Successive Dynasties," states that the various scriptures produced in different eras and the works composed by individuals are all without exception the universal Dharma; as they are all subsumed within the category of scripture, they are recorded according to the appearance of each specific scripture.

During the Later Han dynasty, twelve monastics and laypeople transmitted and translated scriptures and vinayas, totaling three hundred and thirty-four works in four hundred and sixteen fascicles; additionally, there are one hundred and two works in one hundred and forty-eight fascicles whose translators are lost.

During the Later Han dynasty, six monk-translators produced thirteen scriptures and vinaya texts totaling twenty-five fascicles. Regarding the fifth record, titled "A Catalogue of Various Scriptures Through Successive Dynasties with Missing Texts": this refers to a comprehensive examination of various editions of the scriptures; however, as they were produced separately according to different regions, they have not been universally clarified. Section Six: A Record of Works and Commentaries Composed by Monastics and Laypeople Throughout Successive Dynasties. This refers to the commentaries on the sacred words [of the Buddha] intended to facilitate the understanding of those who have not yet awakened; as these works clarify what was previously implicit and provide further elucidation where the explicit teachings were insufficient, they are now recorded under this separate heading.

The seventh section of the *Lìdài zhūjīng zhīliú chénhuà lù* (Record of the Successive Branches and Transformations of Various Scriptures Through the Ages) states that various scriptures produced separately were composed in accordance with the customs of their times; they do not transmit the extensive versions and are intended merely to guide beginners. Therefore, even a single four-line verse must not be lightly excised.

Section Eight: A Catalogue of Suspected and Spurious Scriptures and Treatises Produced in Successive Dynasties. This refers to the fact that because the conditions for the True Dharma are remote, ordinary and ignorant people have not yet attained realization; thus, in order to transform beings according to worldly conventions, there are instances where the sublime True Doctrine has become obscured. If these were not clearly distinguished, then jade and stone would be confused.

Chapter Nine: Preface to the Successive Catalogues of the Scriptures of All Dynasties. This states that as scriptural catalogues have appeared throughout the ages, one must recognize their origins. Chapter Ten:

A Record of the Miraculous Responses and Veneration Regarding the Translation of the Scriptures in the Eastern Land. The patriarchs who established the teachings and the wise models of conduct encountered these scriptures and interrogated them on their merits and capacities, examining them with their own eyes and paying them personal homage.

Consequently, from the Wei and Jin dynasties onward, translations by Dharmarakṣa and others flourished;

some are sought by name;
and some rely on historical period.
Some were entrusted with the task of translation;
each recorded their own perspective,

"In all these cases, they were men of their time who had investigated antiquity and possessed refined discernment and wisdom;
yet that their compositions and editorial revisions did not reach the level of perfect precision was neither due to a lack of talent nor an insufficiency of intelligence."
I have collated and carefully verified the texts from the *Qunmu* (Clustered Eyes) and the *Sengzhuan* (Biographies of Monks),
and then compared them with the records of Baoyou and others.
Baoyou’s record is worthy of examination, as its citations and textual meanings are well-observed.

Now, regarding this compilation of mine, I hope it will rectify the former defects. The compiler states:

There is indeed much to be admired;
the author’s stylistic flair is evident herein.
Nevertheless, there are a few instances of inconsistency and confusion.
It has not yet reached perfection.
Truly, the task of composing such works is difficult indeed.
I now briefly outline several points to clarify their errors;
this is not intended to pass judgment on their merits or faults,

In works such as the *Dai-zōkenroku* (Record of the Existence and Extinction of the Tripitaka), it is stated that the new *Pǔxiǎopǐn* (Shorter Prajñāpāramitā) and five other sutras are all the same original text as the *Dàpǐn* (Large Prajñāpāramitā); however, this is not the case.
Although their principles and meanings are generally consistent, they differ entirely in terms of their structural organization; therefore, to say they share the same original text is incorrect.
The first error:
both the *Bodhisattva-ūrdhvagāmi-sūtra* and the *Ratnacūḍa-bodhisattva-sūtra* state that they were translated by Zhu Fahu;
these are two names for the same sūtra.
Two original manuscripts have been preserved.
There are two errors:
the *Sūtra on the Samādhi of Extensively Manifesting the Propagation of the Way* and the *Sūtra of the Dragon King Anavatapta* are also one and the same sūtra with two different titles.
Two versions both exist;
three are erroneous.
*Sumerugarbha-sūtra*, two fascicles.
This was translated by Yaśas during the Gao Qi dynasty;
there are four errors resulting from repeated submissions at different times.
Regarding the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* translated by Paramārtha,

both editions exist.
The fifth error.

The sixth error.

The old *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* is taken as a single edition while the new *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* is taken as a retranslation—this is the eighth error. The *Lokotpāda-sūtra* is taken as a single edition while the *Loutan-jing* is taken as its retranslation—this is the ninth error. Instances such as these are not limited to these alone and cannot be fully enumerated.

For example, as recorded in the *Juyao zhuan du lu* (Record of Essential Translations), although the *Xinli ruyin famen jing* (Sūtra on the Dharma-gate of Entering the Seal through Faith) is a branch of the *Avataṃsaka*, it is not included within the main body of that collection, being similar instead to sūtras such as the *Dushi jianbei jing* (Sūtra on Gradual Preparation for Deliverance).

Human natures differ, and what each finds pleasing is distinct.
How could one, based on their own personal preferences, compel others to conform to their own views?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* has been recited by an immense number of people.
The Buddha’s prophecy states that its widespread propagation will occur in the northeast;
yet, to say it is difficult to practice constantly seems,
in my humble opinion, premature.
Furthermore, as for the *Pǐnxiǎo* (Shorter Version) and the *Dàpǐn* (Larger Version), their underlying principles are entirely different;
one is discarded while the other is promoted.
This second point is not so.

It is not reasonable to claim that although the *Sumerugarbha-sūtra* and others are separate sections of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, they do not circulate because they are not included within its main body;

If one lacks them due to lack of leisure, such as the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*, which was composed by the non-Buddhists..."
These are not the Buddha-dharma;
it is appropriate to exclude them.
The four schools of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* agree with that deletion.
This will not be feasible;
for this is an internal treatise that refutes external doctrines.

Seventh, it is not so.

Furthermore, as seen in the *Ren-da cunwang lu* (Record of Substituting for the Living and the Dead), the *Juyao zhuan-du lu* (Record of Essential Recitations), and the *Dacheng lu* (Record of the Mahāyāna).

it includes the sūtras they produced as well as those of unknown translators.
