The First Threefold Samvara Assembly, in three fascicles. Newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. Second Translation. The aforementioned new translation, being a re-edition, is a different translation of the same text as the old *Mahāvaipulya Trisamvara Sūtra*.
From the first fascicle to the third fascicle. Fascicle Four:
The Second Assembly on Infinite Adornments. Newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. The above is a newly translated single-text edition.
From the fourth fascicle to the seventh fascicle:

*The Third Assembly of the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada*, seven fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty; verified for accuracy and included here as a single ancient translation. From the eighth fascicle to the fourteenth fascicle.

The Fourth Assembly of the Śuddhāvāsa Devaputras, in two fascicles; translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa; recorded in the *Fashang lu*; verified and included herein. This old translation, originally titled the *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Dream*, has been newly renamed the *Assembly of the Śuddhāvāsa Devaputras*. It constitutes volumes fifteen and sixteen. Upon careful examination of the phrasing and syntax, it is found to differ slightly from other translations by Dharmarakṣa. Catalogs such as those by Changfang and others all state that this work was of unknown translation; however, within the *Fashang lu*, it is attributed to Dharmarakṣa. For the time being, I have recorded it here according to the *Fashang lu*.

The Fifth: The Assembly of the Tathāgata Amitāyus, in two fascicles; newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. This new translation, a revised version, is identical in content to the old translations such as the *Wuliang qingjing pingdengjue jing*, the *Amituo jing*, and the *Wuliangshou jing*, though differing in wording; it corresponds to the eighteenth fascicle [of the *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*].

The Sixth Assembly of Akṣobhya Tathāgata, in two fascicles; newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang Dynasty; the second translation. Note: This new translation, being a re-edition, is the same text as the *Akṣobhyavyūha Sūtra* (Old Translation), though differing in its rendering.
Volumes nineteen and twenty. The seventh section, the *Kavaca-vyūha-parivarta*, in five volumes;
newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. The aforementioned newly translated single-volume texts comprise volumes twenty-one through twenty-five.

The Eighth Assembly on the Non-differentiation of the Essential Nature of the Dharma-realm, in two fascicles; translated by the Liang Dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Mandaravaśa; Second Translation; included here as a revised edition collated with the previous translation.
This is a different translation from the *Dharmadhātuprakṛti-sūtra* translated by Kumārajīva during the Yao Qin dynasty;
it corresponds to volumes twenty-six and twenty-seven of the Qin translation.

The Ninth Assembly on the Ten Dharmas of the Mahāyāna, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of the Northern Wei; second translation; included here as a revised edition collated with the previous translation.

This is a different translation of the same text as the *Mahāyāna-daśadharmaka-sūtra* translated by Liang Zhongkai; it is the one that begins with "Bhagavān. It was an error for the title of the twenty-eighth fascicle to have been recorded as *Saṃghavarman*.

The Tenth: The Mañjuśrī-Pūrvamukha-parivarta, in one fascicle. Newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. Second Translation. The aforementioned new translation, being a re-translation, is identical in substance to the old *Pūrvamukha-parivarta Sūtra* and other such texts, though differing in its translation; it corresponds to the twenty-ninth fascicle.

The eleventh, the *Prabhāsa-samudgama-parivarta*, in five fascicles; newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. The aforementioned new translations consist of single texts from fascicle thirty to fascicle thirty-four.

The Twelfth Assembly on the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, twenty fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures) and included here after verification. Regarding the aforementioned old Tang translations listed as single texts from fascicle thirty-five to fifty-four: the inclusion of the *Bodhisattva-piṭaka Assembly* among the "re-translations" according to the *Dazhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalogue)—where it is treated as a different translation of the same text as the three-fascicle *Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtra*—is a grave error. Although the titles are identical, their length differs entirely, and upon examining the textual meaning, they are further divergent. Furthermore, the three-fascicle *Bodhisattva-piṭaka* has also been included herein; it is the *Pūrṇa Assembly*, which I have now corrected from its former status as a single translation.

The Thirteenth Buddha’s Discourse on the Assembly Concerning Abiding in the Womb, One Scroll. Newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. Second Translation. The above new translation, being a re-translation, is the same text as the old *Bao tai jing* (Sūtra of the Embryo) but with different wording; it constitutes volume fifty-five.

The Fourteenth: *The Buddha’s Discourse on Entering the Womb*, in three fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang. This text was collated and incorporated [into the canon]. It corresponds to the fifth and sixth volumes of the old Tang translations of single-text editions. This version of the *Discourse on Entering the Womb* is originally titled *The Sutra on the Buddha Preaching to Nanda Concerning Leaving Home and Entering the Womb*.
In the eleventh and twelfth fascicles of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*,
Tripiṭaka Master Yijing extracted this portion to circulate separately.

Now, as Bodhiruci has collated it against the Sanskrit original and included it within the sequential order of the assembly, and since it was not translated anew, it is presented here as a standalone text.

Furthermore, the account in the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-vyūha-sūtra* regarding the circumstances of Nanda’s forced ordination by the Buddha shares some minor similarities at the beginning but differs entirely thereafter;
thus, it should not be considered a duplicate translation.
These assemblies and the preceding ones, according to their textual principles, should have been included within the Śrāvaka Piṭaka;
however, they are now compiled and categorized generally within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka as part of the *Ratnakūṭa*.

Fifteenth: The Assembly on Mañjuśrī’s Prophecy, in three fascicles. Translated during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan. Third translation. Verified for accuracy and included here as a re-edition of an earlier Tang translation.
This is a different translation of the same original text as the *Sūtra on the Adornment and Purity of the Buddha-land of the Original Mañjuśrī*, spanning from volume fifty-eight to sixty.

*The Sixteenth Assembly: The Bodhisattva’s Vision of Reality*, sixteen fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of the Gao Qi dynasty. Verified for accuracy and included here. The preceding is the single-fascicle old translation. From volume sixty-one to seventy-six:

Seventeenth: The Assembly of Pūrṇa, in three fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; second translation; included here as a revised edition collated with the previous translation.
It is titled the *Bodhisattvapitaka-sūtra* and is also titled the *Mahākaruṇācitta-sūtra*.
It is a different translation from the same original text as the *Bodhisattvapitaka-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Western Jin dynasty.
From Volume 77 to Volume 79 [is missing from the Jin translation].

The eighteenth section, the *Rāṣṭrapāla-bodhisattva-parivarta*, in two volumes, translated by the Sui Dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta; it appears in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalog). Having been verified and collated, these previously translated single-volume texts are now included as Volumes 80 and 81.

The nineteenth is the *Ugra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kang Seng Kai of the Cao Wei dynasty; the third translation; included here after collation. This is an earlier translation and a duplicate version that is identical in substance to the *Dharmādarśa-sūtra* and the *Ugraparipṛcchā-bodhisattvacaryā-sūtra*, though differing in their translations.
The attribution of the eighty-second fascicle to Kang Sengyi is an error. Fascicles Twenty-one and Twenty-two:

The Assembly on the Inexhaustible Treasure-Trove. Newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. The above constitutes the eighty-third and eighty-fourth fascicles as newly translated single-text editions.

The Twenty-first Assembly: The Bestowal of the Prophecy upon the Illusionist Bhadra. One fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang Dynasty. Second Translation. The above new translation, being a reissued version, is a different translation of the same text as the old *Renxian Jing* (Sūtra of the Illusionist Renxian).
Volume Eighty-five.

The Twenty-second Assembly on Great Supernatural Transformations, two fascicles. Newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. The above newly translated single-fascicle version constitutes Volume Eighty-six and Volume Eighty-seven.

The twenty-third assembly, *Mahākāśyapa*, in two fascicles; translated by Prince Śaśiketu of the kingdom of Ujjayinī during the Northern Wei dynasty; verified and included as the eighty-eighth and eighty-ninth fascicles of the right-hand section, among the old translations consisting of single texts.

The Twenty-fourth Assembly: Upāli, in one fascicle. Newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang; the second translation. Note: This new translation, being a re-rendering, is the same text as the previously existing *Vinayaviniścaya-sūtra* (Jueding pini jing), though differing in translation; it corresponds to the ninety-first fascicle [of the original collection].

The Twenty-fifth Assembly: The Exposition of the Superior Aspiration and Joy, in two fascicles. Newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang Dynasty; the second translation. Note: This newly translated re-edition is the same text as the *Sūtra on the Awakening of the Pure Mind*, though it is a different translation.
Volumes Ninety-one and Ninety-two.

The twenty-sixth assembly, the Two Volumes on the Bodhisattva Subāhu, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; recorded in the Fashang Catalogue and included here after verification. The aforementioned old translations as single volumes correspond to Volumes Ninety-three and Ninety-four.

The *Dazhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalogue) states that this *Shanbi jing* (Sūtra of the Good Arm) is a different translation of the same text as the *Chiren pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Holding People), the *Chishi jing* (Sūtra of Holding the World), and the *Shanjian pin jing* (Sūtra of the Good Shoulder Chapter). However, upon examining its literary style and principles, it differs significantly in meaning from the *Chiren jing* and others. Furthermore, the *Shanjian jing* was excerpted from the *Shanbi jing* and is of the same category as the "Universal Gateway" chapter (*Pumen pin*) of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Since these are distinct [from the aforementioned], it is considered a single, independent translation.

The Twenty-seventh Assembly: The Good and Obedient Bodhisattva, one fascicle. Newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. Note: This newly translated single-fascicle version corresponds to the ninety-fifth fascicle [of the current edition].

The Twenty-eighth Assembly: The Discourse on the Householder Ātīraṇa, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. The aforementioned newly translated single-text version corresponds to fascicle ninety-six [of the Taishō Canon].

The Twenty-ninth: The Assembly of King Udayana, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. Second Translation. The above new translation, a re-edited version, is the same text as the old *Udayana-rāja-sūtra* but differs in its translation; it corresponds to fascicle ninety-seven. The two versions, new and old, each contain varying degrees of detail and brevity.

The Thirtieth Assembly: The Chapter on the Girl Sumati, including one subsequent fascicle; newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. This is the fourth translation. Note: This new translation, the revised edition, shares the same source text as the two previous translations—the *Sūmāgadhā-sūtra* and the *Sūtra of the Girl Sumati* previously translated by Bodhiruci—though they differ in their specific renderings.
From the beginning up to the midpoint of the ninety-eighth fascicle, the previously translated version of the *Sūtra of Sublime Wisdom* was sought for in the Eastern Capital but could not be found.

The thirty-first assembly, "The Assembly of the Female Lay Devotee Gaṅgottarā," is contained in the same volume as the preceding [text]. This newly translated single-text edition by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang Dynasty constitutes the portion from the midpoint to the end of the ninety-eighth fascicle.

The Thirty-second Assembly: The Bodhisattva Fearless Virtue, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of the Northern Wei. Fifth translation; included here after collation. This is a re-translation of an old version that is a different translation of the same text as the *Aśokarājadhītṛ-aśokadattā-bodhisattva-sūtra*, and it corresponds to the ninety-ninth fascicle.

The Thirty-third [Sutra]: *The Bodhisattva Vimaladatta-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Western Jin layman Nie Daozhen. Second translation. Verified and included herein. This re-translation of the old version is a different translation of the same text as the *Vimaladattā-dārikā-paripṛcchā-sūtra* and the *Vimalā-dārikā-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.
It is an error to attribute the title of the hundredth fascicle to Zhu Fahu; as will be shown below, the *Vimaladattāparipṛcchā-sūtra* was translated by Zhu Fahu.

The Thirty-Fourth Assembly: The Bodhisattva Puṣpadhvaja-ratna-vyūha, together with the subsequent fascicle. Newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. The aforementioned newly translated single-fascicle version constitutes the first hundred and first fascicle, from the beginning up to its midpoint.

The Thirty-fifth Assembly: The Good Virtue Devaputra. Same volume as the preceding. Newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. Second Translation. The above new translation and the revised version should be compared with the earlier translation by Bodhiruci.
The *Mañjuśrī-buddhaviṣaya-acintya-sūtra* (文殊師利所說不思議佛境界經), a different translation of the same original text.
It constitutes fascicle 101, from the middle to the end. 36.

*Suvikrāntavikrami-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (善住意天子會), four fascicles. Translated by the Sui Dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta. Recorded in the *Neidian lu* (內典錄). This is the seventh translation. It has been collated and included here; it is a re-translation of an old version that shares the same original text as the *Māyopama-samādhi-sūtra* (如幻三昧經) and the *Āryasuvikrāntavikrami-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (聖善住意經).
From Fascicle 102 to Fascicle 115. The Thirty-Seventh Assembly:

The Prince Ajātaśatru, together with the final three fascicles. Newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. Third Translation. Note: This new translation, a re-circulated version, shares the same original text as the previous translations by Daizi Shuhu and Daishi Xiuhui, though they differ in their renderings.
From the beginning up to the midpoint of the one hundred and sixth fascicle.

The Thirty-eighth Assembly on Mahāyāna Expedients, together with the preceding three fascicles. Translated by the Indian lay practitioner Zhu Nanti during the Eastern Jin dynasty. Third translation. Verified and included herein. The aforementioned re-edited version of the old translation is the same text as a different translation of the *Bodhisattva Huishang’s Inquiry into the Great Skillful Means Sūtra*.
From the middle of fascicle 106 to the end of fascicle 108, the title of the scripture states "Translated during the Western Jin," which is an error.
Fascicle 39: *The Assembly of the Elder Bhadrapāla*, two fascicles; translated by the Sui Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta; first translation. Verified and included as a duplicate of an old translation.
The original title was *Yishijing* (Sutra on the Transference of Consciousness).

It has been newly renamed *Xianhu Zhangzhehui* (The Assembly of the Elder Bhadrapāla). The "Certification of Faith" (*zhengxinxu*) at the beginning is a later addition from the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*. This text shares the same source as the *Xianshijing* (Sutra on the Manifestation of Consciousness) but is a different translation.

Regarding the fact that the *Bhadrapāla-parivarta* in volumes one hundred and nine and one hundred and ten lacks a section on the non-transmigration of consciousness, while other versions of the sutra have rearranged the text to clarify this point: although the Sanskrit originals of these two versions do not differ, such arbitrary alterations are, in my humble opinion, inadmissible.

The Fortieth Assembly on the Pure-Faith Maiden, combined with the final three assemblies in one volume; newly translated by Bodhiruci during the Great Tang Dynasty. The above new translation constitutes the beginning of the one hundred and eleventh fascicle.

The Forty-first Assembly: Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Questions on the Eight Dharmas. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty. Second Translation. Verified and included herein; this is a re-edited version of the earlier translation, titled the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsaṃnipāta-uttaratantra-prajñā-sūtra*.

It corresponds to the one hundred eleventh fascicle of that work; among these eight assemblies, there are five fascicles of translated treatises, while the text of the *Prajñā-sūtra* itself is somewhat abridged and contains minor corruptions.

The Forty-second Assembly: Questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva, combined with the preceding three assemblies in a single volume. Newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang Dynasty; the third translation. Note: This newly translated re-edition is the same text as the earlier translation, the *Maitreyavyākaraṇa-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Original Vows of Maitreya Bodhisattva), though it is a different recension.

The colophon at the end of the one hundred and eleventh fascicle stating that it was translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin is an error; the original manuscript of this *Pranidhāna-sūtra* was indeed translated by Zhu Fahu, as will be demonstrated below.

The Forty-third Assembly: The Universal Radiance Bodhisattva, one fascicle. An old translation now appended to the Qin Records; verified and included in the canon. Third translation. Note: This re-translated version of the old text was originally a single-fascicle edition.
The *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*, newly renamed the *Puming pusa hui* (Assembly of the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha),
is a different translation of the same original text as the *Mahāyāna-ratnavyūha-buddhāstamgata-maṇiratna-sūtra*.
This corresponds to fascicle 112.
This old *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* has a commentary in four fascicles.

The forty-fourth section, the *Ratnarāśi-parivarta*, consists of two fascicles; translated by the Śramaṇa Dao-gong of Beiliang. Having been verified and compared, it is included here. The aforementioned old translations as single texts correspond to fascicles 113 and 114.

The Forty-fifth Assembly on the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, together with the final two fascicles, translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by imperial decree. The above newly translated single-text version constitutes the beginning of the one hundred and fifteenth fascicle.

The Forty-sixth Assembly on the Prajñāpāramitā Spoken by Mañjuśrī, together with the preceding [sections]. Translated by the Liang Dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Mandarasa. First Translation. Compiled through collation and included here. The aforementioned old translation is a re-edited version that is identical in substance to the *Mañjuśrī-parivarta* of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā* translated by Zhu Fashang; these are different translations of the same original text.
From scroll 115 through the end of scroll 116, the titles of the sūtras were erroneously attributed to Saṃghavarman as the translator.

The Forty-Seventh Assembly: The Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin, in two fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty. The aforementioned old translation is a re-edition, also titled the *Bodhisattva-viśuddha-caryā-sūtra*.
This is a different translation of the same text as the "Mahāsannipāta-ratna-keśa-parivarta" and the *Bodhisattva-viśuddha-caryā-sūtra* translated by Kang Senghui.
It corresponds to fascicles 117 and 118 [of the Mahāsannipāta], and there is one fascicle of commentary on the Ratna-keśa assembly.

The Forty-Eighth Assembly: The Lady Śrīmālā, in one fascicle. Newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. This third translation is a re-translation of the same text as the previously existing *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahā-upāya-sūtra*, though differing in its wording.
Volume 119. The Forty-ninth: The Assembly of the Vast Sage (Vaiśvānara), one fascicle.

Newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang Dynasty. Second Translation. Note: This new translation, being a re-edition, is the same original text as the *Viyasapraśna-sūtra* (The Sūtra of the Questions of Vaiśvānara), though it is a different translation.

Regarding the one hundred and twentieth fascicle, when compared with the old translation, the new version lacks slightly less than one page of text from the latter part; this was because some had appended the old translation to it in order to ensure that the meaning was complete and perfect.

*Mahāvaipulya Triśaraṇa Sūtra*, three fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty; recorded in the *Fashang lu*; first translation. The above sutra is a different translation of the same text as the "First Assembly on the Three Codes of Discipline" (*Tri-vidhi-saṃvara-parivarta*) in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*.

*The Sutra on the Immeasurable Pure Equal Enlightenment*, two fascicles; also simply called *The Sutra of Immeasurable Purity*. Translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Loujiachen of the Later Han. Second translation: *The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Amitābha of All Buddhas, the Sarvārthasiddha Tathāgata, Who Transcends the Human Path*, two fascicles; the internal title states this. Translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian (style name Gongming) of the Wu dynasty. Third translation: *The Sutra of Immeasurable Life*, two fascicles. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Kang Sengkai of the Cao Wei. Fourth translation: [Title omitted]. These three sutras are alternative translations of the same text as the "Immeasurable Life Assembly," the fifth assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*. This fifth assembly has eleven old and new translations, seven of which are missing. The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed one fascicle of a commentary based on the meaning of these sutras.
The four aforementioned scriptures comprise nine fascicles in one volume. *The Sūtra on the Land of Akṣobhya Buddha*, two fascicles;

also titled *The Sūtra on the Attainment of Training by Bodhisattvas in the Buddha-field of Akṣobhya*. Translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Loujiachen of the Later Han. First translation. Of three translations, one is missing. Note: This scripture is a different translation of the same text as the "Akṣobhya Tathāgata Assembly" from the sixth section of the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*.

*The Ritual for the Recitation of Akṣobhya Tathāgata*, one fascicle. The internal title of this scripture reads: *The Ritual for Recitation and Offering*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery by imperial decree. *The Scripture on the Ten Mahāyāna Dharmas*, one fascicle. The first part states: "The Buddha was dwelling in Rājagṛha. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of Funan during the Liang dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). [Note: The above scripture is a different translation of the same text as the ninth chapter of the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, the "Mahāyāna Chapter on the Ten Dharmas."

*Fummon-hon-kyō* (Sutra on the Universal Gate Chapter), one fascicle; also known as *Fumon-kyō*. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. First translation. The aforementioned single sutra is identical in substance to the "Mañjuśrī Universal Gate Assembly" (the tenth assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*), though it is a different translation. It is a grave error to consider this, as recorded in the Zhou catalog, a branch of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Of the three translations—old and new—one translation is missing.

*The Sūtra on the Womb* (one fascicle), also titled *The Sūtra on Receiving a Body in the Womb*. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. First translation. The above sūtra is a different translation of the same text as the "Chapter on the Buddha Speaking of the Dwelling in the Womb for Ānanda" in the thirteenth assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*. According to the old catalogs, this *Sūtra on the Womb* was classified as a single-text work of the Hīnayāna; it is now appended here according to its thematic category.

*The Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-vyūha-pariśuddhi-sūtra*, three fascicles; alternatively titled simply *The Sūtra on the Adornment and Purity of the Buddha-field* or *The Sūtra on the Adornment of the Buddha-field*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty. First translation. Of the three translations, one is missing. (Note: This sūtra is a different translation of the same text as the "Mañjuśrī-vyākaraṇa-parivarta," the fifteenth chapter of the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*.)

*The Scripture on the Meritorious Adornments of the Buddha-field of the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva*, three fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery by imperial decree. *The Dharma-mirror Scripture*, two fascicles (or one fascicle); newly entered into the catalog during the Zhenyuan era; translated by the Anxi lay devotee An Xuan of the Later Han together with the Śramaṇa Yan Fotiao. First Translation: The above eight scriptures comprise thirteen fascicles in one volume.

*The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Practice as Asked by Ugra* (one fascicle); alternatively titled *The Sūtra of the Householder Ugra* (two fascicles). Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. Fourth translation. Of the six translations, three are missing. These two sūtras are alternative translations of the same text as the "Assembly of the Householder Ugra," the nineteenth chapter of the *Ratnakūṭa*.

*The Scripture of the Illusionist Renxian*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Scripture of the Illusionist Renxian*. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. First Translation. The above scripture is a different translation of the same text as the "Chapter on the Prediction for the Illusionist" (the twenty-first chapter) of the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*.
*Deciding Vinaya Sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *Destroying All Consciousness*. All catalogs state it was translated at Dunhuang, yet neither the translator’s name nor the date remains evident.

Now appended to the Record of the Eastern Jin: First Translation. The above one sutra is a different translation of the same text as the Upāli-parivarta, the twenty-fourth assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa*.

*Prakṛtyabhisamaya-citta-viśuddhi-sūtra*, two fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty. First Translation. The above one sutra is a different translation of the same text as the *Abhijña-śraddhā-prasthāna-parivarta*, the twenty-fifth assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa*.

*The Sūtra of King Udayana*, one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Faju of the Western Jin dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement). First translation. *Sumati-sūtra*, one fascicle; also simply called *Sumati-sūtra*. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. First translation. *Sumati-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Aśokadatta, Daughter of King Aśoka* (one fascicle). Also simply titled *The Sūtra of the Daughter of King Aśoka*, and also simply titled *The Sūtra of Aśokadatta*. *The Sūtra of the Girl Vimaladattā*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin—this is the first translation. [The above nine sūtras comprise ten fascicles in one volume.

The *Mañjuśrī-bhāṣita-acintya-buddha-viṣaya-sūtra* in two fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang. Included in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. First translation. The above sutra is the same text as the "Assembly of the Good Virtue Devaputra" (Sudatta-devaputra-parivarta), the thirty-fifth chapter of the *Ratnakūṭa*, though it is a different translation.

*The Sūtra on the Illusion-like Samādhi*, in two, three, or four fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. *Maitreyabodhisattvapṛcchā-pūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa; first translation; three translations, one missing. *Śrīmālādevīsiṃhanādanirdeśa-ekayānamahopāya-vaipulyasūtra*, one fascicle; also simply known as the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. The Vyāsaparipṛcchāsūtra, in two fascicles;

preface and record.

First Translation: This sutra is a different translation of the same text as the "Assembly of the Venerable Seer Vaiśravaṇa" (Chapter 49) of the *Ratnakūṭa*. Its preface records: "In the fourth year of the Xinghe era of the Wei dynasty, the cyclical year being Renxu, the moon positioned in Shen, the first day of the month being Yichou, the Brahmin guest Gautama Dharmaruci and the śramaṇa Tánlín translated it at the residence of the Duke Gāo, Minister of the Secretariat and Commander-in-Chief. It was completed on the Jiawu day of the Xin-si year of the Jianchu era. The total number of characters, produced by the labor of a single person, is fourteen thousand four hundred and fifty-seven. All catalogs state that it was translated by Ratnamati or Bodhiruci; both claims are erroneous. We now follow the preface as authoritative. Regarding this *Vaiśvāsika-sūtra*, while old catalogs classified it as a single-text work of the Hīnayāna, our examination has determined it to be a Mahāyāna re-translation.
The eight preceding scriptures comprise eleven fascicles in one volume.

As for the Mahāsaṃnipāta section, all works that are categories or sub-types of the Mahāsaṃnipāta are compiled here; in total, there are twenty-four sections comprising one hundred and forty-two fascicles across fourteen volumes.

The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, thirty fascicles (or forty fascicles), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty at Guzang; three bundles; third translation; three translations compared with three missing versions, respectfully examined.
The Record of the Mahāsannipāta by the Liang Dynasty śramaṇa Sengyou states:

Chapter One: The Necklace;

Chapter Three: The Precious Woman.

the fifth is the Chapter on Sāgaramati;
the sixth is the Chapter on Silence.
Chapter Seven: The Ineffable;
Chapter Eight: The Treasury of Space;
Chapter Nine: The Section on the Jewel Banner.
The tenth chapter, "The Section on the Eye of Space";
the eleventh chapter, "The Chapter on the Jewel Garland"; and the twelfth chapter, "The Chapter on Akṣayamati.
Now, having examined the manuscript of the sutra:
This differs from Yǒu’s record.

Furthermore, as for the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Dhāraṇīs," there are some editions of the sutra that divide it into the "Chapter on the Necklace" (Yíngluò pǐn), but this is not the case; these two should not be divided, as they constitute a single section. The subsequent "Great Decline Sutra" (Dàshuāi jīng) is precisely the second chapter of this work, the "Chapter on the Precious Woman" (Bǎonǚ pǐn).
Chapter Three: The Bodhisattva Animiṣa;
Chapter Four: The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati;
Chapter Five: The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja.
Chapter Six: The Bodhisattva Without Speech;
Chapter Seven: The Ineffable Bodhisattva; Chapter Eight:
The Section on the Jewel Banner.
The ninth is the *Ākāśanetra-parivarta*; the tenth is the *Ratnamālā-bodhisattva-parivarta*.

Regarding the eleventh, the *Sūryaguhya-parivarta*, I have searched through various catalogs and found that this *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* lacks a fixed standard for its volume count: some say twenty-nine, some ten, thirty-one, thirty-two, or forty fascicles. At present, most versions of the *Mahāsannipāta* consist of thirty fascicles; however, the text of the *Sūryaguhya-parivarta* is incomplete, lacking approximately one fascicle. The version in thirty-one fascicles should be complete, yet despite my search, I have not obtained it. Furthermore, in Sengyou’s records, the *Sūryaguhya-parivarta* does not appear.
It is not the case that there is no "Akṣayamati-parivarta" chapter.
Although the *Akṣayamati-sūtra* is a separate division of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*,
it was not without a translation by Kumārajīva.
Furthermore, it is not sequential;
it does not appropriately belong within the *Gaganagañja-parivarta*.
[The section on] Yu follows after the *Avaktavya-parivarta*.
The reason for this is not yet clear.
From the "Chapter on the Sovereign King of Dhāraṇīs" to the "Section on Solar Secrets," there are eleven sections in total.
This *Sūryagarbha-sūtra* is a different translation of the same text as the *Sūryaguhya-parivarta*.

Furthermore, both the eleventh chapter of the *Sūryaguhya-parivarta* and the beginning of this *Sūryagarbha-sūtra* state that after the "Gate of the Ambrosia of Ānāpāna with the Eye of Space" has been taught, this sūtra is subsequently expounded.

Furthermore, since the "Section on the Sun's Secret" (*Sūryaguhya*) is mentioned after the "Chapter on the Eyes" (*Netra*) in the void, it would not be logical for it to be separated from the "Chapter on Ratnaśikhin" (*Ratnaśikhinparivarta*) according to the underlying meaning;
yet, the reason why this chapter is interspersed in the current edition of the sutra remains unclear.

Furthermore, although the *Sūryagarbha* and *Sūryaguhya* share the same root text, the textual divisions of the *Sūryagarbha* are extremely concise and its latter sections are missing, such that it could be further abridged.

The *Candragarbha-sūtra* is the twelfth division; some manuscript titles refer to it as the "Twelfth Division of the Mahāsaṃnipāta-mahāyāna-sūtra," and the beginning of the scripture states: "Having taught the *Sūryagarbha-sūtra* to the various hosts of nāgas, he next taught this sūtra."

The *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* states at the beginning of its thirteenth fascicle: "Having already expounded the *Candragarbha-sūtra*, I shall next expound this *Daśacakra-sūtra*. Furthermore, the fourteenth fascicle originally existed in the Western Regions but has not yet circulated here [in China].
The *Sumerugarbha-sūtra* is the fifteenth division of the sūtra; its initial title reads: *Mahāyāna Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Sumerugarbha Division, Number Fifteen*.

The sixteenth division is combined with the *Gaganagañja-sūtra*. Its beginning states that after the Dharma for bestowing the prophecy upon Goddess Puṇyavatī has been taught, this sūtra is subsequently expounded. Since the *Sumerugarbha-sūtra* is spoken by the Tathāgata specifically because of Goddess Puṇyavatī, it is known that this sūtra ought to occupy the position immediately following it.
This *Sūtra of the Sun Treasury* was first preached at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove;
next, he ascended to the summit of Mount Sumeru;
and finally, at the request of the nāgas, he went to Mount Khadiraka.
The *Candragarbha-sūtra* and the other three sūtras were all preached on Mount Kālaparvata;
their sequence is as follows.
Furthermore, there are the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*, the *Bhadrapāla-sūtra*, the *Bāhuyakṣa-rāja-sūtra*, the *Akṣayamati-sūtra*, and others.
Although this is a specific portion of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*,
since its sequential order is unknown,
it is difficult to compile and record.
However, the Sui dynasty monk Jiu combined the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* and took the title of the *Pañcāśat-prajñāpāramitā-gaṇanā-sūtra*,
designating it as the "Chapter on the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Directions."
It is incorrect to claim that after the compilation of the *Candragarbha-parivarta*, the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra* was completed in fifty-eight fascicles;
for there is no authoritative basis for such a claim.

Therefore, it does not rely on that [version]. There is also a compilation of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* consisting of sixty fascicles; however, because fascicles thirty-one and thirty-two both contain the *Ratnacūḍa-parivarta*, these two fascicles together complete the count of sixty. This *Ratnacūḍa-parivarta* appears before the *Sūryagarbha* in fascicles twenty-six and twenty-seven; it is unclear for what reason this was re-edited again. Furthermore, since the Sanskrit originals for the *Sūryagarbha* and *Sūryakośa* do not differ, such a redundant inclusion is a grave error. If one wishes to merge them [into a single version]:
Excluding the *Dinakarsha* (Day Secret) section from the previously mentioned *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, there are twenty-seven fascicles.

This replaces the *Dinakārsha* section with the *Sūryagarbha* (Sun Treasury) section and continues with the *Dinakārsha*. Although the Sanskrit original for the *Dinakārsha* is the same as that for the *Sūryagarbha*, because the Chinese translation is somewhat deficient, the *Sūryagarbha* is substituted for it. Following this are the *Candragarbha* (Moon Treasury), the *Kṣitigarbha-daśacakraka*, the ten-fascicle *Daśacakraka* translated during the Tang dynasty, the *Sumerugarbha*, and the *Gaganagañja*; these are the four sutras that follow.
Although the sequence of their exposition is not known, if one aligns them according to their internal logic, there will likely be no error.

Following the *Ākāśagarbha*, the *Buddhānusmṛti*—using the six-fascicle version translated during the Song dynasty to supplement the latter portion of the ten-fascicle version from the Sui dynasty, which lacks two chapters—is followed by the *Bhadrapāla*, the *Dṛṣṭāntamālā-rāja*, and finally the *Akṣayamati*; these together constitute eighty fascicles.

This also accords with the fact that the initial title of the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra* reads: "The Thirty-second Chapter on the Inexhaustible Meaning of the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati within the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*"; it is indeed the thirty-second division (*bhāga*). Thus, the claim in Sengyou’s records that it follows the *Ratnacūḍa-parivarta*, and his inclusion of it at the end of the compiled *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, is clearly erroneous. Furthermore, regarding the *Susthitamati-devaputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, a detailed examination of its textual meaning shows it should be a separate division of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*; it ought to be incorporated into the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra* rather than being recorded alongside it. For this reason, it is omitted here.

The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra: The Division on the Sun-Treasury (Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra sūryagarbha-parivarta), ten fascicles (or fifteen fascicles), eleventh division; one volume; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Sui Dynasty; identical to the *Sūryaguhya* [Division]; the fourth translation. The above sutra is the same text as the preceding *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, the *Sūryaguhya-parivarta*, though it is a different translation.
The *Sūtra on the Sun-Honey* (Rimik) is abbreviated here; this [text] is somewhat more extensive.

*Mahāsaṃnipāta-candragarbha-sūtra*, ten fascicles—or fifteen fascicles—twelfth division, one bundle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master from India, Narendrayaśas, during the Gao Qi dynasty. *Sūtra on the Praise of the Dharmakāya Requested by Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva*, one fascicle. The title within the sūtra reads: *The Praise of the Dharmakāya Requested by Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva from the Hundred Thousand Verses Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*. Translated by the Tripitaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery by imperial decree. *Mahāyāna Mahāsaṃnipāta Kṣitigarbha-daśacakra Sūtra*, ten fascicles, twelfth division. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Divided into one bundle. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. [Note: These two aforementioned sūtras, totaling eleven fascicles, are combined into a single bundle as the second translation.

*Mahāvaipulya Daśacakra Sūtra*, eight fascicles; translator lost. Currently appended to the Northern Liang catalogue; this is the first translation. The two aforementioned sūtras are translations of the same original text with different versions. Regarding the old *Daśacakra Sūtra*, the Great Zhou Catalogue states it was translated by Dharmakṣema. *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sumerugarbha Sūtra*, two fascicles; the fifteenth division. Translated by the Tripitaka Master from India, Narendrayaśas, together with Fazhi, during the Northern Qi dynasty. These two single-text sūtras comprise ten fascicles and are bound in the same volume.

*Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle (sometimes lacking the word "bodhisattva"). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty; brought from Kapiśī to the kingdom of Qin. First translation. *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-divyamantra-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Kapiśī during the Song dynasty. Second translation. *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sūtra*, two fascicles. Combined, these constitute the eighteenth division. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India and others during the Sui dynasty. Fourth translation. The above three sūtras are translations of the same text with different versions. Of the four successive translations, one version is missing.

*Guān xūkōngzàng púsà jīng* (Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha), one fascicle; also titled *Xūkōngzàng guān jīng* (Sūtra on the Contemplation of Ākāśagarbha) or without the character "guān" (contemplation). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Kapiśa during the Song dynasty. *Dānběn xīnyì dàxūkōngzàng púsà suowèn jīng* (New Translation of the Single-Volume Sūtra on the Questions of the Great Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha), eight fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Mahāvajrabodhi of Daxingshan Temple by imperial decree. [Recorded in] the *Zhenyuan xīnrù mùlù* (New Catalogue of Works Entered During the Zhenyuan Era). *Bodhisattva Nianfo Sanmei Jing* (Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha Sūtra), six fascicles; sometimes without the word "Bodhisattva. In the fourth year of the Xinghe era of the Wei dynasty, the cyclical year being Renxu, the moon positioned in Shen, the first day of the month being Yichou, on the day of Jiamu, the śramaṇa Tanlin and Gautama Liuzhi began the work at the residence of the Duke Gao, the Minister of State and Grand Marshal (Yitong). The total number of characters is eighteen thousand three hundred and forty-one.
The statement in various catalogs that "Bodhizhi" was the translator is an error;
the *Xujiji* (Record of the Succession) is correct.

Furthermore, the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue) states that the aforementioned two sutras are abridgments of the "Dhāraṇī-īśvara-rāja-bodhisattva-parivarta" chapter of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* translated separately; however, this is not the case.
Upon examining their literary style and principles, they differ vastly and are entirely distinct.
However, it may simply not be a separate division of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*;

or perhaps these two sutras are not parts of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* at all, but are merely different translations of the "Chapter on the Sovereign King of Dhāraṇīs" (*Dhāraṇīśvararāja-parivarta*), as all catalogues from previous dynasties state.
Although the catalogues differ,
they are recorded here at the end of the *Mahāsannipāta* collection.
The four aforementioned scriptures comprise nine fascicles and are contained within the same volume.

*The Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, ten fascicles (or eight fascicles), translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty. It appears in the *Neidian lu*. This single work is noted in the *Neidian lu* as follows:
This is a separate section extracted from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, specifically seeking out the "Ratnaketu" chapter within that earlier *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*.
In the Great Jewel Enclosure between the realms of desire and form, the Buddha again preached this *Ratnajyoti Dhāraṇī Sūtra*.
Therefore, the first section of the *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī* states: "The Buddha was staying in the Great Enclosure between the desire realm and the form realm, and addressed the great assembly, saying:
'In the past, when I first attained bodhi, I resided at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.'"
At that time, there were two wise men:
one named Upatiṣya and the other named Kolita, and so on in succession until the end.
The meaning of the text is identical in both cases.
This scripture may be considered a reiteration,
but it cannot be considered a redundant translation.
In the old catalogues, there was a *Sūtra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin*, which is an alternative translation of the "Ratnaśikhin Chapter.
It is now included as the forty-seventh assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa*.
Once one has entered therein,
there is no further burdening.
Furthermore, there is the *Ākāśagarbha Sūtra* in eight fascicles.
I have examined various copies and found no distinct original text;
it is simply an excerpt from the *Ākāśagarbha-parivarta* circulated separately.
Furthermore, there is the *Ākāśagarbha-paripṛcchā-sūtra on the Merit of Upholding this Sūtra*, which is likewise an excerpt of a separate passage from the *Ākāśagarbha-parivarta*.
Since it has been separately issued,
it is excluded and not recorded here.
Furthermore, within the *Neidian lu* and the *Dazhou lu*, there is additionally an eight-fascicle version of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*.
Examining its textual passages, it is precisely the sixth fascicle of the *Compendium of the Great Collection Sūtra* (*Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*).
The first two scrolls are titled "Chapter on the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Directions.
This is none other than the *Sūtra of Fifty Methods of Calculation for the Perfection of Wisdom*.
For some unknown reason, it has been included herein.
The subsequent six fascicles, however, are the Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra;
as they are already voluminous, [they should not be added].
Also excluded and not recorded.

Part Two of the First Separate Record, compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xīmíng Monastery in the Western Capital. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra and others during the Eastern Jin dynasty. This is the initial translation of the large version. First, the Assembly at the Site of Enlightenment (Dharmacakra-pravartana-parivarta), comprising two chapters in four fascicles;
second, the Assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance (Samantaprabhā-dharmasabhā-parivarta), comprising six chapters in three fascicles; third, the Assembly in the Palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Volume Eighty:
Translated during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan and others;
newly compiled and entered into the canon.

The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (Dàběn jīng) translated again: the two aforementioned sūtras are translations of the same original text with different versions. In total, the translated scriptures of this section comprise seven locations and nine assemblies, comprising thirty-nine chapters, listed below.

The first assembly, spoken at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), comprises six chapters in eleven fascicles; the second assembly, spoken in the Hall of Universal Radiance (Samantaprabhā-vimāna), comprises six chapters in four fascicles;
the third assembly was spoken in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven Palace.
Combined six chapters in three fascicles; the Fourth Assembly, spoken in the Yāma Heaven Palace, combined four chapters in three fascicles;
the Fifth Assembly, spoken in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace, combined three chapters in twelve fascicles;
the Sixth Assembly, spoken in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven Palace.
The first assembly, consisting of six fascicles, was preached at the Universal Radiance Hall;
together they comprise eleven assemblies and thirteen fascicles. The second assembly, consisting of seven fascicles, was preached at the Universal Radiance Hall.
The third assembly was preached at the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden.
*The Flower Ornament Sutra of the Buddha’s Great Extensive Teachings*, 40 fascicles, translated by the Tripitaka Master Prajña of Kaśmīra, a purple-robed śramaṇa, by imperial decree;

new entry in the Zhenyuan Catalogue, four cases. *Puxian Xingyuan Zan* (Hymn to the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra), 1 fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master of Daxingshan Monastery, the śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Great Wisdom, by imperial decree;
new entry in the Zhenyuan Catalogue. *Miaoshan Wenzhu Wen Zimu Pin Jing* (Sutra on the Chapter of Mañjuśrī Asking about the Alphabet), 1 fascicle.

*The Chapter on the Explanation of the Alphabet from the Yoga Vajraśekhara Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Temple by imperial decree. Included in the *New Catalogue of the Zhenyuan Era*.

*The Gate of Contemplation on the Forty-two Characters for Entering the Dharma Realm of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, one fascicle; inner title: *The Mahāvaipulya Buddha-avatamsaka Sūtra*; translated by the Tripitaka Śramaṇa Mahājñāna Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Temple by imperial decree. Included in the *New Catalogue of the Zhenyuan Era*.

*The Ritual for the Worship of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva according to the Yoga of the Vajraśekhara Sūtra*, first chapter, together with the Sanskrit characters; also titled *The Method of Reciting the Five Syllables of Mañjuśrī*. Included in the *New Catalogue of the Zhenyuan Era*.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa of Daxingshan Monastery, the Great Widely Wise Amoghavajra, by Imperial Decree. *New Catalogue of the Zhenyuan Era*: *The Vajraśekhara Yoga Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Sūtra*, one fascicle. The title within the sūtra reads:

*Dharma Chapter One*, also known as the *Five-Syllable Mantra Method*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa of Daxingshan Monastery, the Great Widely Wise Amoghavajra, by Imperial Decree. *New Catalogue of the Zhenyuan Era*: *The Five-Syllable Yoga Method of the Youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī*, one fascicle, including Sanskrit characters.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa of Daxingshan Monastery, the Great Widely Wise Amoghavajra, by Imperial Decree. *New Catalogue of the Zhenyuan Era*: *Verses on the Five-Syllable Dhāraṇī*, one fascicle, including Sanskrit characters.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa of Daxingshan Monastery, the Great Widespread Wisdom Amoghavajra, by Imperial Decree. *The Sūtra on the Superior Characteristics of the Five-Syllable Mantra of Mañjuśrī Spoken in the Vajraśekhara Sūtra that Transcends the Three Worlds*, one fascicle.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa of Daxingshan Monastery, the Great Widespread Wisdom Amoghavajra, by Imperial Decree. Recorded in the *New Catalogue of the Zhenyuan Era*. *The Liturgy for Paying Homage to the Dharmakāya of the Buddha as Praised by Mañjuśrī*, one fascicle. The title within the scripture reads: *The Liturgy for Paying Homage to the Dharmakāya Praised by the Great Sage Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, Together with its Preface*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa of Daxingshan Monastery, the Great Widespread Wisdom Amoghavajra, by Imperial Decree.
Recorded in the *New Catalogue of the Zhenyuan Era*. *Sūtra on the Dharma-Gate of Entering the Seal through the Power of Faith*, five fascicles.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmaruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty; eleven sūtras in eleven volumes from the single-text edition, bound together in one fascicle.

*The Sūtra on the Adornment of the Light of Wisdom that Transcends the Realms of All Buddhas*, one volume; translator lost, now appended to the Qin Records as the first translation. Regarding this one sūtra, the Great Zhou Record states it was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei. However, according to the records of Liangfang and others, there is no sūtra by this name among the translations of Bodhiruci. It is therefore treated as a lost translation and appended here to the Qin Records.
Furthermore, the claim that this is a different translation of the same original text as the *Tathāgata-vyūha-jñāna-prabhā-sarva-buddha-viṣaya-praveśa-jñānālaṃkāra-sūtra* is erroneous;
upon examining the phrasing and the underlying principles, the two differ significantly.
Although the titles appear similar,
their expressed meanings differ;

upon examining their essential purport, they are found to be a different translation of the same original text as the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*, "Entering the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata’s Virtue and Wisdom."
Therefore, this has been moved and cataloged here as the *Buddhāvatamsaka-praveśa-tathāgata-dharmaguṇa-acintyaviṣaya-sūtra* in two fascicles,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty,
according to the *Neidian lu*.
The Third Translation: *Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatajñānaguṇavaipulyasūtra*, one fascicle;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the reign of the Empress of the Great Tang, newly included in the canon as the Fourth Translation.
The three aforementioned sūtras are different translations of the same original text; among the four old and new translations, one version is missing.

The *Buddhāvataṃsaka-mahāvaipulya-sūtra, Chapter on the Inconceivable Realm of the Buddha*, in one or two fascicles, was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara of Khotan during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang, as recorded in the *Dazhou lu*.
First Translation: *The Mahāvaipulya Sūtra on the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata*, one fascicle.
Translated during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan;
newly included in the canon.
Second Translation: The two sutras on the right are different translations of the same original text.

*Mahāyāna-vajra-śikhā-maṇi-bodhisattva-caryā-prakaraṇa*, one fascicle; also known as the *Vajramālā-bodhisattva-prayoga-parivarta*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the reign of the Empress of the Great Tang. Included in the *Dazhou Catalogue* as a separate text. *Mahāvaipulya-buddha-avadāna-sūtra-maitrī-bhāvanā-prakaraṇa*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Tiyun Bore of Khotan during the reign of the Empress of the Great Tang. Newly included in the catalog. *Mahāvaipulya-samantabhadra-bodhisattva-bhāṣita-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the reign of the Empress of the Great Tang. Newly included in the catalog. *Bodhicitta-alaṃkāra-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. The above nine scriptures, totaling ten fascicles, are bound together in one volume.

*The Mahāvaipulya Bodhisattva Ten Grounds Sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kiṅkara of the Western Regions during the Northern Wei, together with Tanyao. This is the fifth translation. Regarding the two sūtras mentioned above, they share the same original text but differ in their translations; among the five successive translations, three are missing. As for this *Bodhisattva Ten Grounds Sūtra*, the *Dazhou Catalogue* claims it is an alternative translation of the "Ten Abodes Chapter" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; this is an error. Upon examining the phrasing and the essential meaning, they are vastly different; it can only be considered an affiliated text of the *Avataṃsaka*.

The eleven sutras beginning with the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-dharmaparyāya* all share similarities with portions of the *Avataṃsaka*; they are categorized as its affiliated branches rather than the primary division itself, because their adornments of the three kinds of worlds are inferior.

*The Scripture on the Ten Powers Spoken by the Buddha*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Muditaśrī of Anxi at Lianhua Monastery during the Zhenyuan era; included in the new catalog of the Zhenyuan period. *The Scripture on the Wheel of Dedication Spoken by the Buddha*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śīladharma of Khotan at Longxing Monastery in Beiting during the Zhenyuan era; included in the new catalog of the Zhenyuan period. *The Scripture on the Ten Stages Spoken by the Buddha*, nine fascicles. Translated by the Khotanese Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa Śīladharma at Longxing Monastery in Beiting; presented to the court from Anxi and Beiting during the Zhenyuan era; included in the new catalog of the Zhenyuan period. The above four scriptures, totaling twelve fascicles, constitute one bundle.

*Duṣa jīng* (The Scripture on the Tuṣita Heaven), one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi during the Later Han Dynasty. The above scripture is an alternative translation of the "Chapter on the Names of the Tathāgatas" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The old translation is in the fifth fascicle, while the new translation is in the twelfth; compared to the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra], this scripture is somewhat abbreviated.

The *Bodhisattvabhūmividyā-sūtra* (one fascicle), also simply called the *Benye jing*, or the *Jingxing pin jing*, was translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. The *Sarvabodhisattvabuddhabhūmividyā-sūtra* (one fascicle), or sometimes without the word "all" (*sarva*), was translated by the lay follower Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin. These two scriptures above are alternative translations of the "Pure Conduct Chapter" (*Śīlaparivarta*) from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

The old translation is in the sixth fascicle, while the new translation is in the fourteenth; the version translated by Zhi Qian includes the "Ten Stages Chapter" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) but lacks the verses. Furthermore, according to the *Dazhou xu zang lu*, there was also a one-fascicle *Bodhisattva-mūla-karma-sūtra* which was another translation of the "Pure Conduct Chapter" (*Śuddhacaryā-parivarta*); however, as its original could not be found, it has been omitted here.

*The Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Practice of the Ten Abodes*, one fascicle; also simply titled *The Bodhisattva’s Ten Abodes*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty. Recorded in the *Fajing lu*. Later supplemented and included as the second fascicle of the *Bodhisattva Ten Abodes Sūtra*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of the Eastern Jin dynasty from the Western Regions. These two sūtras are alternative translations of the "Ten Abodes" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka*. The older version is in the ninth fascicle [of the *Avataṃsaka*], while the newer version is in the sixteenth fascicle; the latter lacks the verses.

*Jianbei yiqiezhide jing* (Sūtra on Gradually Preparing for All-Wisdom Virtue), five fascicles or ten fascicles; also known as *Shizhu* (Ten Stages) or *Dahui guang sanmei* (Great Wisdom Light Samādhi). Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. The above six sūtras comprise eleven fascicles in a single volume.

*Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, four fascicles (or five fascicles), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva together with Buddhayaśas during the Yao Qin dynasty. The two sūtras above are alternative translations of the "Ten Stages" chapter (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

The old translation spans from the twenty-fifth to the twenty-ninth fascicle, while the new translation spans from the thirty-fourth to the thirty-ninth fascicle. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* in twelve fascicles was composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.

The Samādhi Enquired of by the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin, also known as the Universal Worthy’s Meditative Intent; alternatively, three fascicles. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty. The above sutra is an alternative translation of the "Ten Samādhis" chapter from the new *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

From the fortieth to the forty-third fascicle, the old *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* lacks the "Ten Samādhis" chapter; these titles were recorded as a separate single volume in the *Zhou lu*, but upon examination, they are now identified as a retranslation.

*The Scripture on Manifesting the Merits of Boundless Buddha-lands*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. The above scripture is an alternative translation of the "Chapter on the Lifespan" (*Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*) from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
The old translation is found in the thirtieth [fascicle] and the new translation in the forty-fifth.

The *Tathāgata-udaya-vibhūti-sūtra* (Ruruixian jing) in four fascicles—also known as the *Xingxian ruyuan jing*—is a different translation of the "Jewel King" (*Ratnarāja*) and "Arising of the Tathāgata’s Nature" (*Tathāgatagarbha*) chapters, as well as the "Ten Patiences" (*Daśakṣānti*) chapter, from the old *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

From the middle of the thirty-fifth fascicle to the end of the thirty-seventh, the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences" (Daśakṣānti-parivarta) is located within the thirtieth fascicle; it is omitted here without verses, and the reason for this discrepancy between the earlier and later versions is unknown.
The title of the new scripture is *The Appearance of the Tathāgata*. From the fiftieth to the fifty-second fascicle, the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences" is contained therein.

Furthermore, in the old catalog under the fortieth fascicle, there is the two-fascicle *Tathāgatagotra-udbhava-saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. This is simply an excerpt from the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" (*Gotra-udbhava*) of the old scripture, circulated separately; its text does not differ. It merely takes the initial prologue of the second assembly and places it at the head of the scripture, adding the *śraddhā-prasāda* (testimony of faith) sequence. Since this is not a separate translation, it is not recorded here again.
The four aforementioned scriptures comprise eleven fascicles in one volume.

*Dushi pin jing* (Sūtra on the Chapter on Transcending the World), six fascicles (or five), translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. This single scripture is an earlier translation of the "Lishi jian pin" (Chapter on Transcending the World) from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; it corresponds to fascicles 38 through 44 of the new [translation], and fascicles 53 through 59 of the old [translation].

*Lokakṣema Sūtra* (Luo-mo-jia jing), three fascicles; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Shengjian of the Qifu Qin dynasty. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. The above one sūtra is an alternative translation of the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" chapter (*dharmadhātupraveśa*) of the *Avataṃsaka*.

Compared to the text of this chapter, the *Rāmāyaṇa-sūtra* is incomplete; within it, only a small portion has been translated from the old version, spanning from the fifty-first fascicle, "The Elder Anuttara-jaya," to the beginning of the fifty-second fascicle, "The Night Goddess Viśeṣavatī Who Protects Sentient Beings. This concludes the text [of the old version], which corresponds to the sixty-seventh fascicle and a half through the beginning of the seventieth fascicle of the new version.

The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, the Great Vaipulya, Continued: The Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm, one fascicle (sometimes without the word "Continued"). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śīlabhadra of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty. Recorded in the Catalogue of the Great Zhou. The aforementioned scripture continues the previous *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm; alternatively, some versions of the scripture have been incorporated into the main body of the *Avataṃsaka* within its fifty-seventh fascicle.
The three preceding sutras comprise ten fascicles in one volume.
From the *Dousha* (Śūraṅgama) downward, twenty-three sutras are all alternative translations of individual sections from the *Mahāvaipulya* [Buddhāvataṃsaka].
The *Nirvāṇa* section, along with its subsidiary sutras, are all compiled here, totaling six divisions and fifty-eight fascicles in six volumes.

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, forty fascicles (or thirty-six fascicles) in four volumes. Translated at Guzang by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema from India during the Northern Liang dynasty; the fifth volume was translated by Danrehe. When this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* reached Jianye during the Yuanjia era of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, the śramaṇa Fan Huishen of Yizhou, the śramaṇa Cui Huiguan of Qinghe, and the retired scholar Xie Lingyun of Chenjun, finding that the number of chapters in Dharmakṣema’s earlier translation was sparse and concise, added chapter titles based on the old *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. As the text was somewhat coarse, they also revised the compilation into thirty fascicles for circulation in the region south of the Yangtze River. This version differs slightly from the previous translation. There is one fascicle of a treatise providing a brief explanation of the Great Sūtra, and another fascicle of a treatise explaining the single verse concerning "existence in the past and non-existence in the present."

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, Later Translation: *Cremation Section* (two fascicles), also titled *Jhāva Section* or *Later Section*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Jñānabhadra of P'o-ling in the South Sea of the Great Tang, together with the Śramaṇa Hui-ning of the Tang, at that country. Recorded as a single volume in the *Catalogue of the Great Zhou*. This aforementioned scripture is a supplement to the previous *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
At the end of the *Kauṇḍinya-parivarta*,

there is also an account of the events following his parinirvāṇa, such as the cremation and so forth. According to the *Xuanzang Sanzang Qufa Zhuan* (Biography of Master Xuanzang’s Quest for the Dharma),
the śramaṇa Huining of Chengdu in Yizhou traveled to India during the Linde era.
He arrived at the kingdom of Pālaṅga in South India,
where he met the Tripiṭaka Master of that country, Jayabhadra—
translated into Chinese as Zhixian (Wisdom-Worthy).
This is an excerpt from the Āgama sūtras concerning the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa and cremation;
it is not the Mahāyāna *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
It was sent as a messenger-delivery to be compared with the Indian versions.
Now, upon examining this sutra, it bears some resemblance to a portion of the *Cankī Sūtra* (or *Parivrajaka Sūtra*) at the beginning of the *Dīrgha Āgama*,
yet they are not entirely identical.
Furthermore, the sutra states that the Dharma-body is eternally present.
The eternal, blissful, self,
and pure are the realm of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, not something known by the followers of the Two Vehicles;
they are consistent with the principles of the Great Nirvana.
The title at the beginning of the sutra is again "Cundabhadrī-varga"; as the textual flow connects with the end of that section, it has been compiled here.
Let those of broad learning examine it closely and determine its place.

*Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, six fascicles (or ten fascicles). Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faxian of Pingyang, together with Buddhabhadra, during the Eastern Jin dynasty. This is the fourth translation; the aforementioned scripture constitutes the preliminary section of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
The *Jin Dàzhòng Wèn Pǐn* (Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly) is a variant translation of the same original text.
Furthermore, regarding the *Chāpí Fēn* (Section on the Cremation), there are seven translations in total, four of which are missing.
The two aforementioned scriptures comprise eight fascicles and are bound together in one volume.
The *Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* in two fascicles, also titled the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, or in three fascicles,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin;
the first translation is the *Catuḥkumāra-samādhi Sūtra* in three fascicles, or simply titled the *Catuḥkumāra Sūtra*.
Translated by the Sui Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others. Second Translation. The above two sutras are different translations of the same original text.

According to various catalogs, there is also a *Aiqi jing* (Sutra of Lamentation) in two fascicles—or perhaps one fascicle—which is said to be a different translation of the same original as the *Vaipulya Nirvāṇa*, though its translation history is not recorded. Upon examining its phrasing and sentences, it is nothing other than the *Vaipulya Nirvāṇa*; there is no difference between them. The first chapter of the *Vaipulya Nirvāṇa* is titled "Lamentation" (*Aiqi*); this [text] simply takes the title of that chapter to serve as its own name. Compared to the *Vaipulya Nirvāṇa*, it lacks three chapters, while the rest is identical with no differences. As it is redundant and cumbersome, it has been omitted and not included here.

*Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, five fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India together with Fazhi during the Northern Qi dynasty. This single volume contains the three aforementioned sūtras totaling ten fascicles in one bundle. The three *Vaipulya-parinirvāṇa* sūtras and others are branches of the *Nirvāṇa* tradition.
Various Re-translated Scriptures Outside the Five Great Collections: 373 works in 588 fascicles, arranged in 51 bundles.

*Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*, twelve fascicles; also known as *Abhijñā-vikrīḍita*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty. Recorded in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. This is the fourth translation. *Puyao jing* (Sūtra of Universal Radiance), eight fascicles; also known as *Vaipulya-mūla-utpatti*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty. This is the second translation. Regarding these two translations, although they are different versions of the same original text, the *Dazhuangyan jing wenlu* (Catalogue of Questions on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra) classifies them as independent translations. Furthermore, there are those who include the *Puyao jing* within the Hīnayāna Piṭaka; both of these views are erroneous.
The two aforementioned sutras comprise twenty fascicles in two volumes.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi Sūtra* in one fascicle is a branch of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The Single-Volume *Anantārthasūtra*, translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan of Jingzhou during the Song Dynasty;
preached prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Dharmagatayaśas during the Xiao Qi dynasty;
this is the second translation.

There is one missing volume of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which consists of partial portions of the "Devadatta" and "Stūpa" chapters from a different recension. Sengyou’s Record states that it was lost among the records of Master Dao’an and is now appended to the "Missing Translations" of the Western Jin records. It is included in the eight-volume *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* consisting of twenty-eight chapters, or alternatively in the seven-volume edition.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. Fifth Translation. The above four sutras constitute the first part of the fifth fascicle of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, beginning with the "Devadatta Chapter. During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, the foreign Tripiṭaka Master Mātṛceṭa, together with the Śramaṇa Fǎxiàn, the Sangha Rectifier of Yangdu, translated it at Waguan Monastery. Fǎxiàn had brought the Sanskrit manuscript from Khotan. The eighth fascicle, beginning with the "Universal Gate Chapter," contains verses in the *gāthā* style of repeated recitation. These were translated during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou dynasty by the Northern Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta at Longyuan Monastery in Yizhou. Both the Qin and Zhou versions lacked the subsequent sections, which have been appended here. Furthermore, the six spells of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and others within the eighth fascicle were retranslated by the Great Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang; they are included in the *Yinyi* (Explanations of Pronunciations and Meanings) and are not reproduced separately here.

*The Ritual Manual for the Yoga Contemplation Wisdom of the King of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of Daxingshan Monastery, the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra, by Imperial Decree. This work, along with five other scriptures totaling twelve fascicles, constitutes the first volume of the *New Catalogue of the Zhenyuan Era*.

*Zhengfahua jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra), ten fascicles; alternatively known as *Fangdeng Zhengfahua*, or seven fascicles in one volume. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. Third translation: *Miaofa lianhua jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra), seven fascicles and twenty-seven chapters, or eight fascicles. Translated by the two Dharma Masters Kumārajīva and Jñānagupta, Tripiṭaka Masters from India of the Sui dynasty, with supplementary chapters added. Regarding the preface to these scriptures and the *Neidian lu*: the brief preface to the supplementary version states that these two scriptures are the same text translated differently.
The *Zhengfafa hu* (Correct Dharma Dharma-protecting) was translated by Baoyun;
the *Miaofa* (Wondrous Dharma) was translated by Kumārajīva.
Upon examining the two texts, both contain omissions.
The portions missing from the *Hugu* (Guarding) version are the verses of the "Universal Gate" (*Pumen pin*) chapter;

those missing from Kumārajīva’s version are the latter half of the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" (*Yaocao yu pin*), the beginning of the two chapters on Pūrṇa and the Dharma Master, and the "Devadatta" (*Tiduoboda pin*) chapter.
The *Samantamukha-gāthā* was moved by Kumārajīva to appear before the *Bhaiṣajyarāja* chapter;
furthermore, the two *dhāraṇīs* were placed after the *Samantamukha*.
The differences and similarities between these versions are such that words cannot fully express them.
I have humbly observed that the verses from the "Devadatta Chapter" and the "Universal Gate Chapter" were subsequently produced by former sages to supplement the missing portions for circulation.
I, [the author], look up to their spiritual influence and take their established models as my standard.
In the first year of the Renshou era of the Great Sui dynasty, the year of Xinyou (701 CE),
at the request of the śramaṇa Shangxing of Puyao Monastery,

[the translators] together with the two Dharma Masters Kumārajīva and Jñānagupta at Daxingshan Monastery re-examined the Indian palm-leaf manuscript. At the beginning of the two chapters, "Pūrṇa" and "The Dharma Master," they found that the manuscript was still missing the "Simile of the Medicinal Herbs."

Furthermore, I have added half [a chapter] to the "Devadatta’s Penetration of People’s Stūpas" (Devadattaprativedha-stūpa) dhāraṇī; following the section on supernatural powers, I have appended the final words of the entrustment (parindanā), and I have also corrected many discrepancies in the phrasing of the concluding verses.
Should you happen to consult this,
I hope you will not harbor any doubts;
furthermore, this supplementary version has been added.
In total, there are six translations;
three of these are extant while three are missing.

The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* in two fascicles—also titled *Acintyavimokṣa* or *Vimalakīrti-sūtra*—was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. This is the sixth translation. The aforementioned two sūtras comprise ten fascicles and are contained in the same volume.

*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, two fascicles (or three fascicles), translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty]. Second translation: *Lalita-vistara-nāma-vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, six fascicles, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Seventh translation. The above three sūtras are translations of the same text with different versions; across seven successive translations, four of them are missing.

*Mahāvaipulya-śīrṣarāja-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Vimalakīrti-putra-praśna-sūtra* or the *Susīma-kumāra-sūtra*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. First translation. *Mahāyāna-śīrṣarāja-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Vimalakīrti-putra-sūtra*. Translated by Prince Upaśūna of the Kingdom of Ujjayinī during the Liang dynasty. Second translation. The above four sūtras comprise ten fascicles and are contained in the same volume.

*The Scripture of the Youth Subāhu*, two fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty, etc.; the fourth translation. The above three scriptures are different translations of the same original text. It was an error for the *Scripture of the Youth Subāhu* to be listed as a single independent work in the Zhou catalog. Of the four translations, the second version is missing.
*Mahākaruṇāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, eight fascicles; also titled *Mahākaruṇā*. Attached to the Qin Records. Second translation; translator lost. The above two sūtras comprise ten fascicles in one volume.

*The Sutra of the Compassionate Flower*, ten fascicles, one volume. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty at Guzang. This is the fourth translation. The two aforementioned sutras are different translations of the same original; among the four successive translations, two are missing.

*Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra-rāja*, ten fascicles, one set; translated by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang; newly included in the canon.
