Fifth Translation: *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, eight fascicles, twenty-four chapters; compiled and produced by the Śramaṇa Baogui of Daxingshan Temple during the Sui dynasty; this constitutes the fourth version. The preface to these two sutras—which are the same text with different translations—states briefly: [text follows].
Furthermore, there are three versions of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
The first was translated by Dharmakṣema during the Liang dynasty in four fascicles, consisting of eighteen chapters.
The second was translated by Śīladharma (Jñānagupta) during the Great Zhou dynasty in five fascicles, comprising twenty chapters.

Later, during the Liang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha translated at Jiankang four chapters—the "Distinction of the Three Bodies," "Extinguishing Karmic Obstacles," "Dhāraṇī," and "The Most Quiescent Ground Fulfilling Wishes by Relying on Emptiness"—to supplement the previously mentioned [text], resulting in twenty-four chapters in total.
Baogui frequently marveled at the profound mysteries of this sutra,
wondering why its latter portion lacked any final entrustment.
Although there were previously three translations, he suspected they were not yet complete.
I have long cherished the aspiration to encounter this Sanskrit text.
During a brief interval in the Dharma assembly in the seventeenth year of the Great Sui dynasty,
I accordingly requested the Tripiṭaka Master from the country of Gandhāra in Northern India.
This was translated by Zhìdé.
Upon re-examining a later edition, it was found that there is indeed a "Chapter on Entrustment" (Zhūlèi pǐn),
and furthermore, a "Chapter on the Silver-Lord Dhāraṇī" (Yínzhǔ tuóluóní pǐn) has been obtained.
He translated it immediately at Daxingshan Temple in the capital;
together with those previously produced,
they comprise twenty-four chapters in eight fascicles.
The transcription was performed by the Academician Fei Changfang of Chengdu.
The proofreading and collation were conducted by the Sanskrit scholar and śramaṇa Shi Yanzong of Riyen Temple.
The compiler states:
The textual meaning of this combined version is complete;
as for the four-fascicle version by Kumārajīva and the seven-fascicle authentic translation, [they are included herein].
The five fascicles translated by Jueta are all incomplete; therefore,
these three scriptures are not recorded here with redundant duplication.
I have carefully consulted the records of Master Changfang and others.

During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou dynasty, the Indian Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta translated one version titled the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, which was further expanded into five fascicles as the *Mahāprajñā-dhāraṇī-sūtra on the Vastness of Life Span*. This formed a complete section of the canon.
Now, upon careful examination, it appears that this title is not a complete translation;
rather, it merely continues with two additional chapters from the four-fascicle version of the sutra translated by Dharmakṣema.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Lifespan" (Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta) extends the text even further.
Within the "Chapter on Great Eloquence" (Mahāpratisarā), the dhāraṇī methods are further expanded;
there are also continuations within other chapters.
Therefore, it is called the *Further Expansion of the Mahāpratisarā Dhāraṇī Sūtra on the Measure of Longevity*.
Therefore, the preface to the combined six-fascicle version states that "Śūra, the Great Debater, further supplemented its deficiencies.
By this evidence, it is known that these [versions] merely continued where the text was missing.
This is not a separate translation.
Furthermore, the preface to the sutra states that it was translated by Jñānagupta in five fascicles;
yet the catalogues of Fang and others state it was translated by Yaśogupta. These two Tripiṭaka masters were, in fact, disciples of the same teacher.

At that time, we translated them together and cross-referenced them, ensuring they were all in accord. Regarding the six-fascicle version of this scripture and these eight fascicles, to clarify their similarities and differences:
in the six-fascicle version, one chapter is transposed.
Regarding the comparison with the eight-fascicle new version of the sutra:
furthermore, the intent of the entrustment (*parīndanā*) sections in these two versions is entirely different;
the entrustment in the six-fascicle version is largely similar to the great entrustment in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The reason for this is not yet clear.
Now, upon examining the version in eight fascicles,
it likewise accords with the new scripture.
The two versions differ slightly;
they cannot both be recorded.
Therefore, the eight-fascicle edition is preserved as the definitive version.
It has been compiled and entered into the Tripiṭaka;
may those who seek and examine it hereafter be free from confusion.
Combined with this, the scriptures total five translations;
two versions remain in the canon,
while three have been included in the *Shanfan lu* (Record of the Elimination of Redundancies).

*The Sūtra of the Questions of Candraprabha*, two fascicles (or three fascicles), translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Loujiachen of the Later Han; first translation. The above two sūtras, totaling ten fascicles, are bound together in one volume.

*Mahādruma-kinnara-rāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, four fascicles; also titled *Acintya-vyākhyāna-parivarta*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. Second translation. The two sūtras above are the same text with different translations.

*The Sūtra on the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*, two fascicles; also titled *The Chapter on the Buddha’s Ascent to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven*, or three fascicles. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. *The Sūtra on the Infinite Transformations of the Divine Footsteps of the Way*, four fascicles; also known as *The Sūtra on the Divine Footsteps of the Way*, or in two or three fascicles. Translated by the Tripitaka Master An Faqin of Parthia during the Western Jin. [Second Translation] The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.
The three preceding scriptures comprise ten fascicles in one volume. *Ratnamegha-sūtra* (Jewel Rain Scripture), ten fascicles, one volume;

translated during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmaruci from South India and others. Recorded in the Zhou Catalogue. Third translation. *Ratnamegha-sūtra*, seven fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mandrasena of Funan together with Saṃghavarman during the Liang dynasty. First translation. The above two scriptures are different translations of the same original text; there are three translations in total, both new and old, though the second version is missing.

*The Avyavartaniya Sūtra*, three fascicles (sometimes without the character "遮" [zhē], or four fascicles); translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty. First Translation. The above two sūtras, totaling ten fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

*The Sūtra on the Non-retrogressive Wheel of Dharma*, four fascicles. Sengyou’s catalogue states that it was among the "Different Scriptures" from the Liang region attributed to Master Dao’an; it was translated during the Northern Liang dynasty. Second translation: *The Extensive and Majestic Pure Non-retrogressive Wheel Sūtra*, four fascicles (or six fascicles). Translated by the śramaṇa Zhìyán of Liangzhou together with Bǎoyún during the Song dynasty. Third translation: [Title missing]. These three sūtras are translations of the same original text with different versions. Their inclusion in the Āwéiyuèzhìzhā (Avaivartika-śāstra) catalogue as separate individual works is an error.

*The Scripture on the Seal of Entering and Not Entering Samādhi*, one fascicle. Translated by the Indian Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei dynasty. First Translation, with Preface and Record. The preface and record at the beginning of this scripture state: On the day of Renwu, the month of Janglǒu (the seventh lunar month), the year Xinghe 4 of the Wei dynasty (corresponding to the sexagenary cycle), when the moon was in the mansion of Shù and the calendar marked Jiǎzǐ, the śramaṇa Gautama Prajñāruci and the śramaṇa Tánlín translated [this text] consisting of 9,193 characters at the residence of the Duke Gāo, who served as Minister of the Secretariat and Grand Marshal. All other catalogs claim it was translated by Bodhiruci; this is an error. Now, following the preface and record, this is established as the correct version. *The Scripture on the Seal of Entering and Not Entering Samādhi*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yìjìng during the reign of Empress Wǔ of the Great Táng dynasty. Newly included in the catalog. Second Translation. These two scriptures are translations of the same original text. The older translation was recorded in the *Zhōu Lù* (Catalogue of the Zhou Dynasty) as a single independent work, whereas the new edition has been verified as a re-translation.
The four aforementioned scriptures comprise ten fascicles in one volume. *Samādhi of the Collection of All Virtues Sūtra*, three fascicles (or two fascicles).

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. First Translation. *Samādhi of the Collection of All Meritorious Virtues Sūtra*, three fascicles. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin. Recorded in the Catalogue of the Zhenji Monastery. Second Translation. The above two scriptures are the same text with different translations; there have been three translations in total, one of which is missing.

*The Scripture on the Brahma-deva Sustaining the Mind* (4 fascicles; also titled *The Scripture on Adorning the Buddha-Dharma*, or alternatively *The Scripture on Equally Governing All Dharmas*). Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty; alternatively in six fascicles and seventy chapters. The first translation [of the following three scriptures] comprised ten fascicles in a single volume. In the preface to the *Siyi jing* (Suvikrāntavikrāmī-paripṛcchā) by Shi Sengrui of the Yao Qin dynasty, it states: "I respectfully examine the previous translation; while its phrasing is quite elegant, its essential meaning is lost. Now, consulting various catalogs, we find that during the Wu dynasty, the lay devotee Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi country—whose courtesy name was Gongming—translated numerous scriptures, yet there is no version of the *Siyi jing* among them that shares the same text as this one. The *Chixin jing* (Dharmacakra-sūtra) which shares the same content as the *Siyi jing* is actually the translation by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. Thus, Sengrui’s claim that "Gongming previously translated [it] but lost its essential meaning" is an error.

*The Sūtra on the Questions of the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin*, four fascicles; also simply called *The Sūtra on the Increase of Thought* (or *The Sūtra on the Meaning of the Increase of Thought*), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. Second translation: *The Sūtra on the Questions of the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin*, two fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei dynasty. The above three sūtras are translations of the same original text with different versions. Regarding the *Sūtra on the Questions of the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin*, there is a commentary in four fascicles.
The first two sutras comprise six fascicles in one volume.

*Dharanidhara-bodhisattva-sūtra*, four fascicles (sometimes with the characters "Qisuo-wen" [Questioned by Jie] added, or three fascicles); translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin—First Translation. *Dharanindhara-sūtra*, four fascicles (also known as *Dharmamudrā-sūtra*, or three fascicles); translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin—Third Translation. The above two sutras are different translations of the same text; there have been three translations in total, of which the second version is missing.

*Ji zhū fāngděng xué jīng* (Sūtra on the Universal Learning of All Vehicles), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Wú xué* (Without Learning). Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. First Translation. *Dàchéng fāngguǎng zǒngchí jīng* (Mahāyāna Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Wú chéng* (Without Vehicle). Translated by the Sui Indian Tripiṭaka Master Vinītāruci. Second Translation. The above two sūtras are translations of the same original text with different versions. They were recorded as single texts in the Zhou catalog, but have been identified as duplicate translations through recent examination.
The four aforementioned scriptures comprise ten fascicles in one volume.

*Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra*, three fascicles (alternatively titled simply *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* or in two fascicles). Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. First translation. *Mahāvaipulya-ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra*, two fascicles (alternatively in three fascicles). Translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. Fourth translation. The above two scriptures are different translations of the same original text. Among the four successive translations, two are missing.

*The Sūtra of the Precious Casket*, one fascicle. The title within the sūtra reads: *The Dhāraṇī of the Seal of the Precious Casket Containing the Whole-Body Śarīras of the Secrets of the Hearts of All Tathāgatas*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery by Imperial Decree. *The Mahāyāna Sūtra of Common Nature*, two fascicles (also in four fascicles). Also titled: *The Sūtra Spoken from the Vairocana Treasury Entering the Wisdom of the Conduct of All Buddhas*. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñāyaśas during the Northern Zhou dynasty of the Yuwen clan. Appears in the *Da Zhou Catalogue*. Second Translation: *The Sūtra on Realizing the Mahāyāna*, two fascicles. Also titled: *Entering the Realm of Wisdom of All Buddhas, the Vairocana Treasury*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara of Central India during the Great Tang. Appears in the *Da Zhou Catalogue* as the second translation. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations.
The above five scriptures comprise ten fascicles in one volume. *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (Shenmi jietuo jing), five fascicles.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei dynasty. Complete edition, first translation of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, five fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang dynasty. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Complete edition, second translation. The above two scriptures comprise ten fascicles in one volume.

*Jiejie jing* (Sūtra on the Explanation of the Sections), one fascicle; translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Chen Dynasty. The above-mentioned sūtra is an alternative translation of the first five chapters of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*; it appears in the first fascicle [of this collection].

*The Sūtra on the Definitive Meaning of the Perfection of the Stage of Continuous Liberation*, one fascicle; also titled *The Sūtra on the Definitive Meaning of Liberation* or *The Sūtra on Continuous Liberation*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇarata from India during the Song dynasty. This aforementioned sūtra is an alternative translation of the final two chapters of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. It appears in fascicles 45 and 52.
The four scriptures above are translations of the same original text, two being complete versions and two being abridgments.

*Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśa-sūtra*, two fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. First translation. *Bhava-saṃkrānti-sūtra* (also known as *Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅga-sūtra*), two fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Second translation. The two scriptures above are translations of the same original text.

The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra in Four Volumes, translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty; the second translation. The aforementioned five sūtras in ten volumes are contained in the same fascicle.

*Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, ten fascicles, one volume. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei dynasty. Third translation: *Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, seven fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang. Newly included in the catalog. Fourth translation. The above three sūtras are the same text with different translations; among the four new and old versions, one translation is missing.

*Bodhisattvayogācārabhūmi-vikurvaṇa-ṛddhi-prātihārya-sūtra*, three fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. This is the fourth translation. The above two sūtras comprise ten fascicles and are contained in the same volume.

*Mahāsāṃghika-śāṭhyaputra-nirgrantha-bhāṣita-sūtra*, ten fascicles, one volume; alternatively, seven or eight fascicles. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei. This is the third translation. The two aforementioned sūtras are translations of the same original text.

The *Mahāvaipulya-mahāmegha-sūtra* in six fascicles, also titled the *Mahāvaipulya-animitta-sūtra*, in either four or five fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty;
this is the second translation. The *Mahāmegha-varṣaprārthana-sūtra* in one fascicle, whose internal title reads: *The Mahāmegha-sūtra, Chapter Sixty-four: The Request for Rain*.
Translated during the Northern Zhou Yuwen period by the Tripiṭaka Master from India, Jñāyasa, and others;
first translation. *Mahāmegha-cakra-varṣa-prārthana-sūtra*, two fascicles;
translated during the Sui dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master from India, Narendrayaśas.

The second translation is the *Dafangdeng Dayun Qingyu Jing* (Mahāvaipulya Mahāmegha Vṛṣṭy-ārthika Sūtra), one fascicle; its internal title reads *Dafangdeng Dayun Jing Qingyu* (Mahāvaipulya Mahāmegha Sūtra: Requesting Rain), the sixty-fourth [fascicle].
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others during the Sui dynasty.
Recorded in the *Neidian Lu*.
Second Translation: The three sutras on the right are different translations of the same original text.

*The Great Cloud Sutra on Requesting Rain*, two fascicles; the title within the text reads *The Great Cloud Wheel Sutra on Requesting Rain*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of Daxingshan Monastery, the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra, by Imperial Decree. The five sutras above, totaling twelve fascicles, are contained in the same volume according to the *New Catalogue of the Zhenyuan Era*.

*The Scripture on the Non-Activity of All Dharmas*, two fascicles (or one fascicle), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; the first translation. *The Scripture on the Original Non-existence of All Dharmas*, three fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta et al. of India during the Sui dynasty; the third translation. The above two scriptures are the same text with different translations; of the former and latter two translations, one translation is missing.

*Wújí bǎo sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Ultimate Treasure), one fascicle; alternatively titled simply *Wújí bǎo jīng*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. First translation. *Bǎo rúlái sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Treasure Tathāgata), two fascicles; also known as *Wújí bǎo sānmèi jīng*, or in one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Jñātāmitra of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin. Second translation. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

*The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom*, one fascicle; also known as *The Scripture on the Buddha’s Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom in the Field of Jewels*. Translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. First translation. *The Scripture on the Tathāgata’s Seal of Wisdom*, one fascicle; also known as *The Scripture on the Dharma-body of All Buddhas*. In Sengyou’s catalogue, this was listed among scriptures of unknown translation; it is now appended to the Song dynasty catalogue. Second translation. The above two scriptures are the same text with different translations.
The *Shangliujing* (Six Upper Scriptures), ten fascicles, in one bundle.

The *Daguandingjing* (Great Consecration Scripture), twelve fascicles—or, according to some catalogs, nine fascicles without the character "Da" (Great); details are unknown. One bundle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bo Shili Miltuo from the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty; also translated by Dan Chong. The following individual fascicles are each separate scriptures, listed in full as follows:

Volume One: The Sūtra of the Consecrated Three Refuges and Five Precepts with the Protective Amulets and Mantras Volume Two: The Sūtra of the Consecrated Mantras of the Seventy-two Thousand Divine Kings Who Protect Bhikṣus Volume Three:

The Sūtra of the Consecrated Mantras of the One Hundred and Twenty Thousand Divine Kings Who Protect Bhikṣus Volume Four: The Sūtra of the Consecrated Mantras of the Hundred-knot Divine Kings for Protecting the Body Volume Five:

The Sūtra of the Consecrated Mantras of the Divine Kings of Palaces and Residences for Guarding and Stabilizing the Left and Right Volume Six: The Sūtra of the Consecrated Mantras of the Deities of the Four Directions Concerning the Causes and Conditions of Tombs Volume Seven: [Title missing]
Scroll Eight: The Great Divine Spell of the Consecration for Subduing Māras and Sealing [Evil] Scroll Nine: The Great Divine Spell of the Consecration of the Maṇirohaṇa Scroll Ten:

The Divine Spell of the Consecration for Summoning the Dragons of the Five Directions and Controlling Pestilence and Toxicity Scroll Eleven: The Consecration Sūtra of the Brahman’s Celestial Edict Scroll Eleven (Alternative):

The Consecration Sūtra of Rebirth in the Pure Lands of the Ten Directions According to One’s Wishes, also known as the Separate Circulation of the Sūtra of Rebirth According to Wishes Scroll Twelve: The Consecration Sūtra for Eradicating Transgressions and Sins

The *Sūtra on Deliverance from Birth and Death* is the same as the old *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra*; "The Buddha Travels to Vaiśālī" is its first translation. The *One-Scroll Sūtra on the Original Vows of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru* has been newly included in the catalog.

Fourth Translation: The three scriptures above are different translations of the same original text as the *Sūtra on the Eradication of Transgressions and the Attainment of Liberation from Birth and Death*, the twelfth fascicle of the *Abhiṣeka* collection.
As for the three-fascicle version translated by Tripiṭaka Yijing, it further includes the original vows and mantras of six Buddhas;
otherwise, the text is largely identical to that translated by Master Xuanzang.
As for the older *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra*:
Various catalogs all state that it was translated by the śramaṇa Huìjiǎn of Lùnyě Monastery during the Song dynasty;
however, upon examining the text, it is found to be a separate circulation extracted from the twelfth fascicle of the *Guǎndǐng*.
There is no other original version.
Regarding the *Sūtra on Rebirth According to One’s Vows*,
various catalogs sometimes refer to it as follows:
It was translated during the Wu dynasty by Zhi Qian,
or alternatively, it is said to have been translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin.
The version currently in circulation is the "Puguang Chapter" from the twelfth fascicle of the *Mahābhiṣeka-sūtra* (*Daguanding jing*), and there is no separate edition of this text.
Since these two sūtras are already contained within the great collections (mahānikāya),
those versions that circulated separately have been omitted and not recorded here.

*Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra*, two fascicles; translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Later Han—first translation. *Puchao sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Universal Transcendence), two fascicles (sometimes titled *Wenshushili puchao sanmei jing* with the addition of the word "Mañjuśrī," or four fascicles); translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa—second translation. *Bofang jing* (Sūtra on the Alms Bowl), one fascicle; a separate translation of the "Chapter on Raising the Bowl" from the first fascicle of the *Puchao jing*. According to Sengyou’s catalogue:
Regarding the scriptures of lost translators recorded by Master Dao’an:
Master Dao’an stated that these were derived from the Vaipulya (fangděng) class.

They are now appended to the Catalogue of the Western Jin. The three aforementioned scriptures are the same original work with different translations; across six successive translations, three of them are currently missing.
The first six scriptures comprise ten fascicles in one volume. *Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra*, ten fascicles (or eleven fascicles), one volume.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master from India, Narendrayaśas, during the Northern Qi dynasty. This complete version was produced later; there is also a single-fascicle re-translation of the *Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra*, also titled *Mañjuśrī-bodhisattva-daśakriyā-sūtra*. Translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Xiangu. Second, separate translations: Of the above, the single-fascicle version of the first translation is missing from the original [canon].

*The Sūtra on Having No Expectations*, one fascicle; also known as the *Sūtra on the Elephant’s Stride*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. Second translation: *The Sūtra on the Elephant’s Armpit*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dhamamitra of Kaśmīra during the Song dynasty. Fourth translation. The above two sūtras are translations of the same original text with different versions; among the four successive translations, two versions are missing.

*Mahāśuddhadharmamukha Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin—First Translation. *Mahāvyūhadharmamukha Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Sui Dynasty—Third Translation. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations; among the three successive translations, one version is missing.
*The Tathāgata’s Adorned Wisdom Radiance Entering the Realm of All Buddhas Sūtra*, two fascicles,
translated by Dharmaruci (First Translation).
*The Sūtra on the Wisdom Adornment Entering the Realm of All Buddhas*, one fascicle.
Translated by the Liang dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman and others.
Second Translation: *The Sūtra of Verses on Amitābha Buddha* (one fascicle), a different version from the subsequent sūtra;
translated during the Later Han dynasty, author unknown.
The second translation, or perhaps lacking the word "sūtra," consists of two versions of which one is missing;
it is titled *One Scroll of the Sūtra on the Contemplation of Amitāyus*, also called the *Sūtra on the Contemplation of Amitāyus*. It is a different recension from the preceding and following sūtras.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Jñānayaśas of the Western Regions during the Song Dynasty;
one of two translations, the other being missing.

First Translation: *The Ritual Manual for the Recitation of the Tathāgata Amitāyus*, one fascicle. Within the scripture it says: "The Ritual Manual for Cultivating Contemplative Practice and Making Offerings."
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa of Daxingshan Monastery, the Great Widespread Wisdom Amoghavajra, by Imperial Decree.
*The New Catalogue of the Zhenyuan Era*: One fascicle of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, also known as the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty;
First Translation, Second Copy. Missing from the *Chengzan jingtu fo sheyoushou jing*, one fascicle; also directly titled *Chengzan jingtu jing*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang Dynasty; recorded in the *Neidian lu*.

Third Translation: The two sutras mentioned above are different translations of the same original text. As for the *Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* translated by Guṇabhadra, its original has not been recovered; furthermore, although there may be versions in the various collections that accord with the text of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, they do not differ from it.
The twelve preceding sutras, totaling thirteen fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

*The Scripture on Avalokana of Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Rebirth in Tuṣita Heaven*, one fascicle; also titled *The Scripture on Maitreya’s Rebirth Above*. Translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng. This single-text edition of the *Scripture on Rebirth Above*, although a standalone translation, [is included here].
This has been compiled following the sequence of the *Sūtra on the Attainment of Buddhahood*.
The *Maitreya-buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, one fascicle, is a different version from the subsequent sūtra;
it was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
The second translation consists of two versions; one lacks the *Maitreya-āgama-sūtra* (one fascicle),
and its translator is lost.
From the *Fǎshàng lù* (Record of Dharmottara), now appended to the third section of the *Dōngjìn lù* (Record of the Eastern Jin).
The *Mílè xiàshēng jīng* (Sūtra on Maitreya’s Descent) in one fascicle, also known as the *Mílè shòu jué jīng* (Sūtra on Maitreya Receiving the Prediction), begins with the words:
"The Great Wise Śāriputra," translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yaoqin period.

Regarding the fourth translation, both the *Chángfáng lù* and the *Nèidiǎn lù* state that the *Mílè xiàshēng jīng* (Sūtra on Maitreya’s Descent) begins with "The Greatly Wise Śāriputra. This sūtra was previously edited and revised by the Śramaṇa Shi Daobiao of Cháng’ān and the Śramaṇa Daozheng of Jiangzhou during the Qi dynasty. Now, examining this account, some may say it is not so. That Shi Daobiao was a monk who expounded the meaning under the guidance of Master Kumārajīva and was not the primary translator. Even if it were Daobiao who produced the text, what would be incomplete about its phrasing and meaning? As for Daozheng’s revisions during the Qi period, the dates are widely separated and the accounts are inconsistent; thus, Daozheng’s deletions are difficult to take as authoritative. The sub-commentary within the sūtra itself states, "In the language of Qin," which confirms it was translated in the Qin era and leaves no room for further confusion. Since it was already recorded in Kumārajīva’s catalog, it is clear that this is its source. *Mílè xiàshēng chéngfó jīng*, one fascicle.
Translated during the reign of the Empress of the Great Tang by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing;
newly compiled and included in the canon, sixth translation.
The three aforementioned sūtras share the same original text but differ in their translations; there have been six translations in total, of which three original versions are now missing.
*The Sūtra of the King of Valiantness of All Dharmas*, one fascicle;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dhamamitra of Kasmīra during the Song dynasty;
second translation. *The Sūtra of the High King of All Dharmas*, one fascicle; also known as the *Sūtra of the Meaning-King of All Dharmas*.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei; Third Translation Record of the Preface. The aforementioned preface to the scripture states:

"In the fourth year of the Xinghe era of the Wei dynasty, the cyclical year being Renxu, on the twenty-third day of the sixth month of late summer, the day Dingsi, following the first day of the month (Yiwei), the foreign Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci and the śramaṇa Tanlin began the initial translation at Dingchang Temple in the presence of the Grand Comforter Dou. It consists of eight thousand four hundred and forty-nine characters. All catalogs stating that this was translated by Bodhiruci are erroneous. Now, I rely on this preface record as the correct authority. Furthermore, the entry in the Zhou catalog listing the *Sarvadharma-gāndhārī-rāja-sūtra* as a standalone text is also erroneous."
The two scriptures above are translations of the same original text with different versions; of the three translations spanning the earlier and later periods, one version is missing.

*Paramārtha-dharmavijaya-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei. First Translation. [Extracted from] the Preface Record. The preface record at the beginning of this scripture states: "On the first day of the ninth month of the year Renxu (the fourth year of the Xinghe era of the Wei dynasty), a Monday, Gautama Prajñāruci and the śramaṇa Tanlin translated [this text], totaling 5,576 characters, at the residence of Duke Gao, the Minister of the Secretariat and Grand Marshal. All other catalogs claim it was translated by Bodhiruci; this is an error. Now, I rely on the preface record as the correct authority.

*The Scripture on the Questions of the Doubts of the Rishi Mahātejo’rcis*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty, etc.; this is the second translation. The two scriptures to the right are the same original text with different translations.

*Shunquan fangbian jing* (Sūtra on Accordance with Expedient Means), two fascicles; also known as *Zhuan nüshen pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Who Transforms the Female Body), or one fascicle. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. Second translation: *Leyingluo zhuangyan fangbian pin jing* (Sūtra on the Chapter of the Ornamentation of Joyful Garlands and Expedient Means), one fascicle; also called *Zhuan nüshen pusa wenda jing* (Sūtra of the Questions and Answers of the Bodhisattva Who Transforms the Female Body). Translated by the Yao Qin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kaśmīra. Third translation. [Record from the Later Sūtra Catalogue. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text. Regarding the *Leyingluo zhuangyan*: [End of entry]
Consulting various records, some say it was translated by Kumārajīva during the Yao Qin dynasty,
while others claim it was translated by Fǎhǎi during the Song dynasty.
Now, according to the postscript to the sutra, the bhikṣu Huìfǎ requested Vimalākṣa (Pípóshātánmóyéshī) to translate it out at the Qín Monastery in Jibin.
Therefore, there should be no error.
Some collections state that because Dharmayaśas was proficient in the *Vibhāṣā*, his contemporaries collectively referred to him as "Vibhāṣā.
Thus, Sengyou’s catalog states:
The person who translated the *Śāriputrābhidharma-vibhāṣā* was precisely this individual.
"She" (Śā) and "shi" (Śī) are merely phonetic approximations of one another.
Now, among the records compiled by Kumārajīva, we exclude the four previous translations associated with the record of Saṃghayaśas.
The two translations for these are missing. The eleven sutras above, totaling twelve fascicles, are contained in one volume.

*Ṣaḍpāramitā-saṃgraha-sūtra*, eight fascicles (also titled *Ṣaḍpāramitā-ananta-sūtra* or nine fascicles), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kāṅ Sēnghuì of India during the Wù dynasty. [This is a] re-translation of a single original. *Sudāna-jātaka-sūtra*, one fascicle (also called *Dāna*), translated by the Śramaṇa Shèng Jiàn of the Qífú-Qìn. Recorded as a single translation in the Zhōu catalog; here it is classified as a re-translation. The above one sutra is a different translation from within the "Dānapāramitā" section of the second fascicle of the *Ṣaḍpāramitā-sūtra*.

*The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Śyāma*, one fascicle; also titled *The Sūtra of the Filial Son Śyāma*. It was lost among the translations attributed to Master An in Sengyou’s catalogue and is now appended to the Western Jin catalogue. Second translation: *The Sūtra of Śyāma*, one fascicle, translated by the Qifu Qin śramaṇa Shi Shengjian. Fourth translation: The two sūtras above are the same text as those appearing in the second fascicle of the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*, within the section on the Perfection of Giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), though they are different translations.

*The Sūtra of the Crown Prince Mupò*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty; the first translation. *The Sūtra of the Crown Prince Mupò*, one fascicle (also written as *Mubò*). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty; the third translation. These two sūtras above are included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). They are the same text as the fourth fascicle of the *Six Pāramitās Sūtra* (*Liùdù jīng*), specifically from the section on the *Śīla-pāramitā* (Perfection of Morality), and are alternative translations thereof.

*The Sūtra of the Nine-Colored Deer*, one fascicle; translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty]; recorded in the *Fashang lu*. The above sūtra is an alternative translation from the "Perfection of Vigor" section within the sixth fascicle of the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*.
The seven preceding scriptures comprise fourteen fascicles in one volume; as for the *Sūtra of the Nine-Colored Deer*, its inclusion in the Zhou catalog as a separate work is an error.

*The Sūtra of the Jewel Casket Without Letters*, one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei—First Translation. *The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Universal Radiance Treasury Free from Words and Letters*, one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Divākara at the Western Taiyuan Temple during the Great Tang—Appears in the *Dazhou Catalogue*—Third Translation. *The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Unlettered Dharma-Gate of the All-Illuminating Radiance Treasury*, one fascicle; retranslated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Divākara of the Great Tang—Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). Fourth Translation. The above three sūtras are different translations of the same original text. The statement in the *Dazhou Catalogue* that they are different translations of the same original as the *Mahāvaipulya Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra* is erroneous. Of these four successive translations, one is missing.

*The Sūtra of the Old Woman*, one fascicle; also titled *The Sūtra of the Old Mother* or *The Sūtra of the Old Girl*. Translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu period. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement). First translation: *The Sūtra of the Old Mother*, one fascicle. Recorded in Sengyou’s catalog as a translation of unknown origin; now appended to the Song catalog. Second translation: *The Sūtra of the Old Mother and Her Six Daughters*, one fascicle; also titled *The Sūtra of the Old Mother*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song period. Third translation. The above three sūtras are translations of the same original text.
*The Scripture of the Youth Candraprabha* (Candraprabhakumāra-sūtra), one fascicle; also known as *The Scripture of the Youth Candrasūrya* or *The Scripture of Śunika*.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
First Translation: *The Scripture of Śunika’s Son*, one fascicle. Recorded as "Douben" (兜本) in catalogs, which is an error; the character "ri" (日) is missing.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty;
compiled as a supplement to the third translation, the *Śrīgupta-gṛhapati-sūtra* in two fascicles, also known as the *Śrīkūṭa-gṛhapati-sūtra*.
Translated by the Sui Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas; appended as a supplement, this is the fourth translation.

These three sūtras above share the same original text but differ in their translations; while they are of the same root, they vary significantly in length and detail, with mutual additions and subtractions. Furthermore, among the translations by Zhi Qian, there is a one-fascicle *Śunirjīva-sūtra* which states it is a different translation of the same root as the *Candraprabha-kumāra-sūtra*. Upon examining the phrasing and sentences, the two sūtras do not differ. Since the father’s name is Śunirjīva and the son’s name is Candraprabha, the two volumes were divided based on these paternal and filial names. As both versions are identical, they are not listed twice here. Alternatively, the *Śunirjīva-sūtra* may belong to the Hīnayāna Piṭaka, as "Śun" indicates it originates from the Āgamas. Within the *Ekottarika-āgama*, there is the account of the householder Śrīgupta, yet it lacks the matter concerning the youth Candraprabha; its inclusion therein is likely an error.
*The Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Bodhi-apracāra-sūtra* or simply the *Bodhi-sūtra*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
First translation. *The Gayāśīrṣa-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Gayāśīrṣa-sūtra*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. First translation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty;
the second translation is the *Hastikṣaṇa-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* (One Scroll),
translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Vinitaruci during the Sui Dynasty.
The Third Translation of the *Mahāyāna-gayāśīrṣa-sūtra*, one fascicle;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang,
recorded in the *Dazhou lu*.

Regarding the fourth translation: the four scriptures to the right are different translations of the same original text. In Sramana Jingmai’s *Catalogue of Translated Scriptures*, a separate *Bodhi Sūtra* in one fascicle is recorded; furthermore, in the *Record of the Great Zhou*, there is another *Bodhi-apracāra Sūtra* in one fascicle. These two sūtras were both translated by Master Kumārajīva and are merely alternative titles for the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhi*; thus, they have not been recorded here again to avoid redundancy.

*Jiāzhǎngzǐ zhì jīng* (The Scripture on the Elder’s Son’s Resolve), one fascicle; also known as *Zhì jīng*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han. First translation. *Bōsà shì jīng* (The Scripture on the Bodhisattva’s Departure), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Shì tóngzǐ jīng* (The Scripture on the Vowed Youth) or simply *Shì jīng*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Bái Fǎzǔ of the Western Jin. Third translation. *Shì tóngzǐ jīng* (The Scripture on the Departing Youth), one fascicle. Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhī Fǎdù of the Western Jin. Fifth translation. Two omissions. Fourth translation. The above three scriptures are translations of the same original text with different versions. Furthermore, the *Dàwèn lù* separately records one fascicle of this scripture translated by An Shigao; this is a single version with a different title and should not be recorded again here.

*Vatsa-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian. Recorded in the *Fashang lu*. First translation. *Milk-Light Buddha Sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Milk-Light Sūtra*; translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. Second translation. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations, differing slightly in length and detail. Of the four translations in total, two are missing.

*The Sutra of the Stainless Virtuous Woman*, one fascicle; also known as the *Womb Treasury Sutra*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. Recorded in the catalogue of Nie Daozhen. Second Translation. The aforementioned sutra states that it shares the same original text as the *Womb Treasury Sutra*, both being attributed to the translation of Zhu Fahu. Upon collating the two texts, the wording is entirely identical, differing only in their titles. Therefore, only one version is retained here.

*The Scripture on the Woman in the Womb Listening to the Sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *The Scripture on the Unadorned Woman*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty. Third translation: *The Scripture on Transforming the Female Body*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dhamamitra of Kaśmīra during the Song dynasty. Fourth translation. The above three scriptures are the same text with different translations; the first two are somewhat abbreviated. In total there are five translations, two of which are missing.
The twenty-one sūtras above, totaling twenty-two fascicles, are contained in one volume. *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra*, two fascicles;

translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Liang Dynasty. This is the second complete translation. [From] the Postscript to the Sūtra. Regarding this *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra*, I have carefully consulted the records of Fa-chang and others, all of which state:
In the second year of the Yongding era of the Chen dynasty (the Dingchou year), the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha produced this sūtra at Jingtu Monastery in Nanjiang Commandery.

The postscript states: "On the eighth day of the ninth month in the Dingchou year, the third year of the Shaotai era of the Liang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha was requested by Liu Wentai, the Interior Historian of Nanjiang in Pinggu County, to translate it."
Now, upon examining the chronological records of various schools,
they differ and contradict one another.
The *Nianli* of Baochang ends only with the fifth year of the Chengsheng era (the Jingsi year), at which point the Liang dynasty is recorded as having ceased.
The years of Zhen Luan and Wang Dao-gui reached the Jǐngzǐ year of the second year of Shàotài, which was changed to the first year of Tàipíng.
The second year of Tàipíng, Dīngchū, was changed to the first year of Wǒngdìng.
Chen Shouxian first established the title of the Chen Kingdom.
There is also a chronological record (nianji) of unknown authorship which states:

"In the third year of Chengsheng, the Jiaxu year, it was changed to the first year of Dading; it was established under the Later Liang for a total of eight years before the era name was finally changed."
However, none of the four calendrical systems includes the third year of the Shaotai era.
Since all four versions differ from one another,
I do not know which represents the correct account.
It may be that the third year of the Shaotai era of the Liang dynasty, the Dingchou year, was precisely the first year of Yongding at the beginning of the Chen dynasty.
In calendars, only the later reign titles are recorded, while the former names are not included.
For now, these are provisionally classified as translations from the Liang dynasty according to their catalogs.

*The Sutra of Unprecedented Events*, one fascicle. Translator lost during the Later Han. This was erroneously placed among the single-text works of the Hīnayāna in older catalogs. *The Extremely Rare Translation*, first version, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. *The Third Translation*: The above two sutras are different translations of the same text; they are the first chapter of the aforementioned *Anuttara-śraya-sūtra* (Sutra on the Supreme Reliance), appearing in its first fascicle.

*The Sūtra of the Decisive Compendium* (or alternatively titled *The Sūtra of the Decisive Dhāraṇī*, also known as *The Decisive Dhāraṇī Sūtra*), one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. First translation. *Sūtra on the Slander of the Buddha*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei. Second translation. The above two sūtras are translations of the same original text with different versions.

*The Scripture on Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry into the Dharmakāya within the Ratnakūṭa Samādhi*, one fascicle; translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han—First Translation. *The Scripture on the Essential Nature of Entering the Dharmadhātu*, one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of the Sui dynasty; included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection)—Second Translation. The above two scriptures are different translations of the same original text.

*The Scripture on Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry into the Dharmakāya within the Ratnakūṭa Samādhi*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han—First Translation. *The Mahāvaipulya Siṃhanāda Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Jīvaka of Central India during the Great Tang—Second Translation. Recorded in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. The above two scriptures are the same text with different translations.

*Mahāyāna-bhadrakalakṣaṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty. Recorded in the *Dazhou Catalog*. First Translation. *Mahāyāna-bhadrakalakṣaṇa-vyūha-sūtra*, one fascicle; retranslated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). Second Translation. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*Mahāyānacaturdharmasūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śīlabhadra of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty at Dongtaiyuan Temple. Recorded in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. First Translation. *Bodhisattvacaryācaturdharmasūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śīlabhadra of Central India at Hongfu Temple during the Great Tang Dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). First Translation. The two sūtras above are the same text with different translations.

*The Sūtra on the Measurement of Rare and Wondrous Merits*, one fascicle; also simply titled *The Sūtra on the Measurement of Rare and Wondrous Merits*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty. First translation. *The Sūtra of the Peerless Excellence*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Second translation. The two sūtras above are translations of the same original text with slight differences in length and detail.

*The Scripture on the Three Turnings of the Previous Life*, one fascicle; translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju—First Translation. *The Scripture on the Silver-Colored Woman*, one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of the Northern Wei—Second Translation. The above two scriptures are different translations of the same original text.

*The Sūtra on King Ajātaśatru Receiving the Prediction*, one fascicle; translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju—First Translation. *The Sūtra on King Utpalavaktra Receiving the Buddha’s Prediction and Being Named Subhūṣita*, one fascicle, also simply titled *The Sūtra on King Utpalavaktra*; translated by the Eastern Jin śramaṇa Dharmaruci from the Western Regions—Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement). Second Translation. These two sūtras are the same text with different translations. From the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra* (Sūtra on the Supreme Basis) down to these nineteen sūtras, they were previously listed as independent works in the *Dazhou Catalogue*; however, upon examination, they are now classified as retranslations.

*The Sūtra on Reverence for the Correct* (one fascicle), also titled *The Sūtra on Reverence for the True Dharma*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of India during the Northern Wei dynasty. First translation. *The Sūtra on Good Reverence* (one fascicle), also titled *The Sūtra on Good Reverence* or *The Sūtra on the Teacher of Good Reverence*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta et al. of India during the Sui dynasty. Second translation. The above two sūtras are translations of the same original text with minor differences in length.

*The Sūtra on Praising the Merits of the Mahāyāna*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. *Neidian lu* (Record of Inner Scriptures), first translation. *Sūtra on the Definitive Karmic Obstructions of the Sublime Dharma*, one fascicle. Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan of Zhixiang Monastery during the Great Tang. Newly included in the catalog; second translation. The two sūtras above are the same text with different translations. The *Sūtra on Praising the Mahāyāna* was previously a single independent work, but now constitutes a re-translation [of the same text].

The twenty-three aforementioned sūtras comprise twenty-four fascicles in one volume. *Sūtra on Admonishing the King* (1 scroll), also titled *Sūtra on Greatly Admonishing the King*. Translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng. First translation.

*Sūtra on the Tathāgata Teaching King Śatrujit* (1 scroll), also simply titled *Sūtra on King Śatrujit*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Second translation. *Sūtra on the Buddha Expounding the Royal Law to Devānampriya* (1 scroll), also simply titled *Sūtra on Devānampriya*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang. Newly included in the catalog. Third translation. The three sūtras above are the same text translated differently. These three sūtras are all listed in the Hīnayāna section, whereas the *Śatrujit-sūtra* is listed in the Mahāyāna section; both instances are errors, as they are single-text [versions].

*Mahāvaipulya Sūtra-rāja Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei dynasty—First Translation. *Parivarta-sattva Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of the Northern Wei dynasty—Second Translation. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

*Mañjuśrīparipṛcchāsūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci during the Northern Wei dynasty. First translation. *Mañjuśrīcaritrasūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others during the Sui dynasty. Second translation. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text. Second translation.
The Mañjuśrī-bodhisattva-mūla-tantra-rāja-kinnara-rāja-parivarta, one fascicle.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery,
by Imperial Decree.

*The Sūtra on Auspicious and Inauspicious Times and Days and the Good and Evil Nakṣatras and Planets Spoken by Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and Various Sages*, two fascicles; the lower fascicle contains a preface.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daixingshan Temple, by Imperial Decree. During the Zhenyuan era.
*The Sūtra on Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination under the Pāṭala Tree*, one fascicle;
translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty (second translation).
*The Sūtra on the Noble Path of Dependent Origination*, one fascicle.
Record of the Translation of the Inner Scriptures by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, Part Two:

Translations. The two aforementioned sutras are different translations of the same text. There have been six translations in total; four of these are missing. It is an error that the *Qiyuan shengdao jing* (Sutra on the Noble Path of Origination) is listed as a separate volume in the *Zhou lu* (Zhou Catalogue). Furthermore, there is the *Wencheng shier yinyuan jing* (Sutra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination Heard in the City), one fascicle, which is identical in text to the *Beidu shuxia siwei shier yinyuan jing* (Sutra on Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination under the Peepal Tree) without any difference; it is merely a different title. Only one version is currently preserved.

*Śālistamba Sūtra*, one fascicle; translator lost, now appended to the Eastern Jin catalog. *Śālistamba-parikathā Sūtra*, one fascicle; the internal title states: *Mahāyāna-śālistamba-parikathā Sūtra Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery by imperial decree during the Zhenyuan era. *Jñānaprasthāna Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty. Zhi Qian himself provided the commentary. Three translations exist, one of which is missing. [Note: This single sūtra is the same text as the aforementioned *Śālistamba Sūtra*, though it is a different translation; it is impossible to determine which came first.

*The Scripture on the Samādhi of Self-Vow* (Zishì sānmèijīng), one fascicle. A note beneath the title states: "From the 'Chapter on Sole Realization' (Dúzhèng pǐn) No. 4, excerpted from the *Bhikṣu’s Pure Conduct* (Bǐqiū jìngxíng). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han; included in the *Shiyi*. First Translation: *The Scripture on the Tathāgata’s Sole Realization of the Samādhi of Self-Vow* (Rúlái dúzhèng zìshì sānmèijīng), one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. Third Translation: The above two scriptures are the same text with different translations. Of the three successive translations, one translation is missing its original manuscript.

*The Sūtra on the Ablution of the Buddha’s Image*, one fascicle; also called *The Sūtra of the Eighth Day of the Fourth Month for Ablution*, or simply *The Consecration*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin Dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). First Translation. *The Mahāsthāman-sūtra*, one fascicle; also titled *The Sūtra on the Ablution of the Buddha’s Image*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Shengjian of the Qifu Qin Dynasty. Second Translation. The above two sūtras are translations of the same original text with different translations.

*Jiaozhilixiang fubao jing* (Sutra on the Meritorious Retribution of Casting Images), one fascicle; translator lost. Currently appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin. *Zuofoxingxiang jing* (Sutra on Making Buddha Images), also called *Youdianwang zuofoxingxiang jing* (Sutra on King Udayana Making Buddha Images), one fascicle; translator lost. Currently in the Han-Zhou catalogue among the single-text works of the Hīnayāna, where it states it was translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Dharmakṣema. This is an error. The two sutras above are the same text with different translations; it cannot be determined which was lost later.

*Longshi nü jing* (The Scripture of the Daughter Nāgadattā), one fascicle; alternatively, without the character "nü" (daughter). Translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian. First translation. *Longshi pusa benqi jing* (The Scripture on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Nāgadatta), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Longshi nü jing* or *Longshi ben jing*. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. Second translation. The above two scriptures are translations of the same original text with different renderings; they differ slightly in their degree of detail.
*The Catalogue of Dhāraṇī Sections*, one fascicle. The title within the scripture reads: *The Essential Catalogue of the Various Sections of the Dhāraṇī Gates*.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master and Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Temple, by imperial decree.

The *Catalogue of New Entries from the Zhenyuan Era* lists one fascicle of the *Bāshijixiang shenzhou jing* (Scripture of the Divine Incantation of the Eight Auspicious Ones), sometimes omitting the character "shen" (divine).
It was translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty.

Second, there is one fascicle of the *Bāyang shenzhou jing* (Scripture of the Divine Incantation of the Eight Yangs), also simply titled the *Bāyang jing*. A recent examination has determined this to be a single-text edition.
The *Sūtra of the Eight Auspicious Ones*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin (the third translation); one fascicle;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghavarman of Funan during the Liang dynasty.

The fourth translation is the *Sūtra on the Names of the Eight Buddhas*, one fascicle, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of the Sui dynasty. The fifth translation follows.

These four sūtras share the same original text but differ in their translations; while their introductory narratives (*nidāna*) are largely identical, the names of the Buddhas vary slightly from those in the previous five translations. One of these translations is missing its original manuscript.

*The Maṇḍala Sūtra of the Eight Great Bodhisattvas*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Temple by imperial decree. Recorded in the *New Catalogue of the Zhenyuan Era*. *The Ullambana Sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Ullambana Sūtra*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. *The Sūtra on Repaying Kindness by Offering the Alms Bowl*, one fascicle. Translator lost. Currently appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin. The above two sūtras are translations of the same original text with different versions; it cannot be determined which came first, nor do they differ significantly in length or detail.

*The Scripture on the Merit of Bathing the Image*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of India during the Great Tang Dynasty. Newly included in the canon. First translation. *The Scripture on the Merit of Bathing the Image*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang Dynasty. Newly included in the canon. Second translation. The above two scriptures are translations of the same original text with different renditions; the latter version is slightly more extensive.

*Jiaoliang shuzhu gongde jing* (Sūtra on Comparing the Merit of Rosaries), one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śubhākarasiṃha of India during the Great Tang Dynasty. Newly included in the canon. First translation. *Suzhu gongde jing* (Sūtra on the Merit of Rosaries), one fascicle. States within the text: "From the *Mañjuśrī-mantra-piṭaka*, comparing the merit of rosaries. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang Dynasty. Newly included in the canon. Second translation. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*The Yoga Rosary Sūtra*, one fascicle. The title within the sūtra reads: *The Vajraśekhara Yoga Rosary Sūtra, Extracted in Brief from the One Hundred Thousand Extensive Recitations*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master of Daxingshan Monastery, the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra, by Imperial Decree. *The New Catalogue of the Zhenyuan Era*: Newly translated, *The Wood-Bead Sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master of Daxingshan Monastery, the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra, by Imperial Decree. The thirty-six sūtras and thirty-seven fascicles listed above in the *New Catalogue of the Zhenyuan Era* are contained in the same volume.

*Amoghapāśakalparāja-sūtra*, thirty fascicles; three volumes. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of South India. Newly entered into the canon. Fourth translation. *Amoghapāśa-mantra-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui dynasty. First translation. *Amoghapāśahṛdaya-mantra-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Second translation. The two aforementioned sūtras are translations of the same original text with different versions. This is the introductory chapter of the aforementioned large sūtra, previously translated by the Tripitaka Master [Bodhi]ruci under the title *Amoghapāśahṛdaya-mantra-sūtra*; however, the original manuscript has not yet been obtained.

*Amoghapāśa-dhāraṇī-īśvararāja-sūtra*, three fascicles; also titled *Amoghapāśa-hṛdaya-mantra-sūtra*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha during the reign of the Empress of the Great Tang. Newly included in the canon. First Translation. *Amoghapāśa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle; also titled *Samantamukha*. Translated by the Brahmin Li Wuchan of Northern India during the reign of the Empress of the Great Tang. Newly included in the canon. Second Translation. The two sūtras above are translations of the same original text with different renditions. These are excerpts from the Sanskrit manuscript and do not constitute the complete work. They share the same title as the previous three sūtras but are distinct versions.

*The Dhāraṇī Divine Spell Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with a Thousand Eyes and a Thousand Arms*, two fascicles (or three fascicles). Translated by the Da Tang śramaṇa Śākya Jñānagupta. First translation. *Sūtra on the Body of the Mūla-dhāraṇī of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with a Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes*, one fascicle (also known as *The Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Eyed*). Translated by the Da Tang Tripiṭaka Master from South India, Bodhiruci. Newly included in the catalog. Second translation. The above two sūtras are the same original text translated differently. In the first translation, the palm-leaf manuscripts were intermingled, resulting in some loss of textual order.

*The Original Text of the Great Body Dharani of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi of South India. Included in the *Zhenyuan New Catalogue*. *The Sūtra of the Great, Vast, Perfect, and Unobstructed Heart of Great Compassion of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*, translated by the Śramaṇa Gāvadharma of West India during the Tang Dynasty. Compiled as a supplement (*shiyi*). [Single Volume] Although this Heart Sūtra exists as a standalone text, it is included here following the previous sūtras.

*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Heart of Vast, Perfect, and Unobstructed Great Compassion of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with a Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi, a Śramaṇa from South India. Recorded in the *Zhenyuan New Catalogue*. *The Sūtra of the Secret Treasury of the Divine Dhāraṇīs of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara*, one fascicle. Translated during the reign of the Empress of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda from Khotan. Newly included in the catalogue. *The Sūtra of the Wish-Fulfilling Maṇi Dhāraṇī of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñādeva (Baosiwei) of the Great Tang. Newly included in the catalogue. The two aforementioned sūtras are the same text translated differently. Although these two versions vary in length, even according to their Sanskrit originals, they do not fully exhaust the meaning. The translation by Yijing is the most concise of these methods.

*The Ritual for the Recitation of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara according to the Yoga of the Vajraśekhara*, one fascicle. The scripture states: "The Ritual Manual for the Bodhisattva’s Cultivation. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery by Imperial Decree. This is included in the *Zhenyuan New Catalogue* as part of twelve scriptures in fifteen fascicles within the same volume.

*The Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī-Mantra of the Wish-Fulfilling Heart of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Yi Jing of the Great Tang; newly included in the canon; the third translation. *The Sūtra of the Cintāmaṇicakra Dhāraṇī*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Great Tang; newly included in the canon; the fourth translation. The two aforementioned sūtras are the same text as the preceding two, though translated differently. Although these four versions of the sūtra vary in length—ranging from detailed to abbreviated—they all remain incomplete translations based on their Sanskrit originals. Among those produced by Yi Jing, the ritual methods are the most concise.

*The Sūtra on the Universal Worthy Dhāraṇī Spoken by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery by imperial decree during the Zhenyuan era. *The Sūtra of the One-Syllable Root Dhāraṇī of Mañjuśrī*, also known as the *One-Syllable King of Spells*, one fascicle. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Prajñādeva during the reign of the Empress of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog. First Translation: *The One-Syllable King of Spells from the Dhāraṇī Collection of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the reign of the Empress of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog. Second Translation. The two sūtras above are the same text with different translations.

*The Sūtra of the Divine Mantra of the Names of the Twelve Buddhas*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty; the first translation. *The Sūtra of the Divine Mantra Praising the Merits of the Tathāgata*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yi Jing of the Great Tang; included in the *New Catalogue of the Kaiyuan Era*; the second translation. These two sūtras are the same text with different translations. Regarding the *Sūtra of the Names of Five Thousand Five Hundred Buddhas*, the twelve Buddha names at the beginning of the first fascicle are identical to those in the aforementioned *Sūtra of the Names of the Twelve Buddhas* and are not distinct from them. In older catalogs, the *Sūtra of the Names of the Twelve Buddhas* was recorded as a single, independent work, but according to the new examination, it is identified as a duplicate translation.

*The Scripture on the Names of the Thirty-five Buddhas Spoken by the Buddha*, one fascicle. The internal title states: *The Liturgical Text for Repentance before the Thirty-five Buddhas Spoken by the Buddha*, extracted from the *Sūtra of the Questions of Upāli*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of Daxingshan Monastery, the Śramaṇa Mahāprajña Amoghavajra, by imperial decree.

*Zhengyuan xinyu mulu*: *The Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī Sūtra*, one fascicle; also titled *The Great Golden-Colored Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī Sūtra* and including the *Dharmaparyāya for Binding the Ritual Site*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty;
this is the fourth translation. *The Great Golden-Colored Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī Sūtra*, one fascicle.

*The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Great Golden-Colored Peacock King Mantra*, one fascicle; translator lost, now appended to the Qin Records as part of the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection), included in the fifth translation group. *The [Sutra] Spoken by the Buddha on the [Great Golden-Colored Peacock King]*, one fascicle;
translator lost, also appended to the Qin Records as part of the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection), included.
The sixth translation is the *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra* in two fascicles,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghabara of Funan during the Liang Dynasty.
The seventh translation is the *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra* in three fascicles.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang at the Inner Sanctuary in the Eastern Capital and newly included in the canon, Eighth Translation.

The above five sūtras are different translations of the same original; among the eight translations—both old and new—five survive and three are missing. The first six texts are brief, while the latter two are somewhat more extensive.

*The Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī Sūtra*, three fascicles. The title within the scripture reads *The Buddha-mātṛ Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī Sūtra*. At the beginning, before the first fascicle, there is the *Dharmaprārthanā* (Method of Invocation). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery by Imperial Decree. Included in the *New Catalogue of the Zhenyuan Era*. *The Ritual Manual for the Altar and Image of the Buddha-spoken Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery by Imperial Decree. Included in the *New Catalogue of the Zhenyuan Era*. The above fifteen scriptures, totaling twenty fascicles, are bound together in one volume.

*The Compendium of Dhāraṇīs*, twelve fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ajita from Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty; recorded in the *Dazhou Catalogue*; a single combined translation. The following is excerpted from the *Vajramahāmaṇḍala-sūtra*.
This is but a small portion of the Great Bright Dharani Treasury (*Mahāvidyā-kośa*).

Having extracted the essentials, I have translated this collection; however, among the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-mantra-sūtras* and others, there are those that were recorded separately by practitioners and not fully revealed here. Furthermore, many harbor doubts, fearing these may not be authentic scriptures. Now, in order to dispel such doubts, I have separately categorized them as follows.
Volume One, Buddha Section, Upper: The Great Power Dhāraṇī Sūtra Commentary, Chapter on the Śākyabuddha-uṣṇīṣa Samādhi Dhāraṇī. Volume Two, Buddha Section, Lower:

From the beginning of the Ritual Methods for All Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Images, followed by the two sets of seven, six seals and mantras, and the ritual methods for the mantras and seals of all Buddhas. Volume Three: The Preface to the Mahācintya-sūtra of Amitābha Buddha, including the ritual methods for mantras and seals, an exposition on the attainment of rebirth through recitation, and the ritual methods for rosaries. Volume Four: The Great Golden Wheel Dhāraṇī. Volume Five: The Chapter on the Characteristics of the Efficacy of the Extraction Method.

The third fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*. When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, he preached the mantras within the *Mahāprajñā-naya*; both the mantra and the *Prajñā-hṛdaya-mantra* are contained herein. Among these, the twelfth seal and its mantra are named the "Inexhaustible Treasury of Prajñā" (*Prajñā-akṣaya-kośa*). The commentary notes: "This is a single-seal mantra. Translated by the Dharma Master Varjya-siṅga. At the end of the fascicle, there is further the *Mahācakra-vajra-dhāraṇī*. If one recites this mantra, one shall immediately enter the maṇḍala and be permitted to employ the seals; it shall not constitute a transgression of the dharma.
Volume Four: *The Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara Divine Mantra Sūtra*, Upper Scroll. Volume Five: *Avalokiteśvara*, Middle Scroll.

First, there are two seals and mantras for the Thousand-Turned Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Mantra; next, there are six seals and mantras for the Miscellaneous Avalokiteśvara Mantra Seals; third, the seal and mantra of the Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; fourth, the four seals and mantras of the Amoghapāśa Avalokiteśvara; fifth, the method for painting images of Avalokiteśvara; sixth, the Dhyāna-Seal Mantra of the Avalokiteśvara-Bhṛkuṭī Bodhisattva.

Volume Six: The Latter Part of the Scroll on Avalokiteśvara and Other Bodhisattvas. First, the Dharma Seal and Mantra of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara Ajagarbha (translated into Chinese as Maitou). Second, the Chapter on the Seals and Mantras of the Assembly of Great Bodhisattvas. The Bodhisattvas Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, Kṣitigarbha, Samantabhadra, Gaganagañja, and others all possess their respective methods of seals and mantras.

Volume Seven, Vajra Section, Upper Part. Chapter Two: The Dharma-Seal Mantra of the Great Majestic Power Samādhi of Vajragarbha; and the Dharma-Seal Mantras of the Vajra Retinue. Herein are the mantras and seals spoken by the various retinue vajras.

Volume Eight, Vajra Section, Middle Part, First: Chapter Two on the Mantra-Seals of the Sovereign Supernatural Powers of the Bodhisattva Vajramṛta-Kuṇḍalī; the Vidyā-Mantra of the Vajratāḥpabha Seal. (In the Tang language: *Daji* [Great Secret] Vajra.)

The Ninth Fascicle, Vajra Section, Part Two: Chapter One on the Dharma-Seals and Mantras of Vajra-Ucchuṣma; in the Tang language, the Impure Vajra-Seal of the Fire-Headed Vajra. This is the second: the Dharma of the Mantra of Mahānīla-Vajra.

Volume Ten, Upper Section of the *Sūtra on the Goddess Mārīcī*, Second: The Dharma-Goddess Puṇyavatī. Translated at the Bodhi Monastery in Central India by the monk Ānanda, the Vinaya Master, and the Mūlasarvāstivāda Master Kāśyapa, et al., during their itinerant travels, and circulated in the land of Tang.
Volume Eleven, Part Two of the *Sūtra on the Various Devas*. Chapter on the Dharanis and Seals for the Rites of Offering by the Various Devas to Assist in the Accomplishment of Samādhi.

[This includes] the dharanis and seals of Mahābrahmā, Śakra Devendra, Maheśvara, the Four Heavenly Kings, the Sun Deity, the Moon Deity, the Constellations, the Earth Deity, the Fire Deity, Yama, and all the Dragon Kings.
And the ritual for praying for rain: the methods of the deity Nārāyaṇa,

the Gandharvas, the Kiṃnaras, the Mahoragas, the Peacock King, the Lion King, the Garuḍa, the Great Accomplishing Heavenly King, the Fire Deity, the Water Deity, the Wind Deity, the Asura King Cāmunda, and the Dharma.
All the rites of the vināyakas,
all the rites of the yakṣas,
and all the rites of the rākṣasas.
The above are the mantra-seals (*mudrā*) offered by Mahābrahmā, the Lord of Heaven, and others.

The twelfth fascicle, "The Chapter on the Mantra-Seals of the Universal Assembly of All Buddha-Dhāraṇīs at the Site of Enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*), is the consecration altar-pool for the Universal Assembly (*samāja*).

*Ekādaśamukha-avalokiteśvara-vidyā-mantra-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yaśogupta of India during the Northern Zhou Yuwen dynasty; the first translation. *Ekādaśamukha-vidyā-mantra-hṛdaya-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; the second translation. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. The above two sūtras are alternative translations of the same text as the *Ekādaśamukha-vidyā-sūtra* found in the fourth fascicle of the *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha*; however, the ritual methods (*vidhi*) therein are somewhat more extensive.

*The Scripture on the Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*, three fascicles. The internal title of this scripture reads: *The Scripture on the Ritual Manual for the Heart Mantra of the Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master, Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Great Xingshan Monastery, by imperial decree. Included in the *Zhenyuan New Catalogue*. *Mārīcī Devī Scripture*, one fascicle. A small character is added above the title. Translator lost. Now appended to the Liang dynasty catalogue. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). The above one scripture is a partial alternative translation of the *Mārīcī Devī Scripture* found at the beginning of the tenth fascicle of the *Collected Scriptures*.
*The Scripture on the Goddess Mārīcī Spoken by the Buddha*, one fascicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Temple by Imperial Decree.
