translator lost, now appended to the Qin records. The *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra*, two fascicles, or one fascicle.
One fascicle of the *Dharmakṣaya-nirdeśa-sūtra* (or *Dharmakṣaya-kṣaya-sūtra*), translated during the Northern Liang dynasty with the translator lost;
included in the "Supplementary Collection" (*Shiyi*) and listed among the works of unknown translators in Sengyou’s catalogue.
Now appended to the Song Record (Song lu): *The Sūtra of the Profound and Great Dedication* (Shen-shen da-hui-xiang jing), one fascicle;
lost in the record of Sengyou, now appended to the Song Record.

*The Sūtra of the Crown Prince Piluo* (Tian-wang taizi Biluo jing), one fascicle; sometimes lacking the words "Crown Prince" (Tianwang). Also called *Piluo*. Sengyou’s record states it is an alternative translation by Master Dao’an from Guanzhong.

The *Upāsikā-śīla-prakāśana-sūtra* in two fascicles, which was included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection), is now appended to the Qin Records; it is also simply called the *Jingxing jing* (Sūtra on Pure Conduct) or lacks the word "sūtra. Sengyou’s Catalog states that this is a different sūtra from the one by Master Dao’an found in the Liang region;
it is now appended to the Liang Records. The *Bhadramahāpuruṣa-vihāra-sūtra* in one fascicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty;
recorded in Baochang’s catalogue as the *Śrāvakatrimandala-sūtra* (one fascicle),
also known as the *Sūtra on the Three Grades of Disciples’ Training*.
The *Sūtra on the Four Classes*, translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Wu;
also known as the *Sūtra on the Four Classes of Disciples* or the *Sūtra on the Training of the Four Classes*.
*The Scripture on the Transformations of the Future*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty;
recorded in the catalog of Fa Shang, also known as *The Scripture on the Consciousness of the Transformations of the Future*. One fascicle.
*Past Buddhas’ Almsround Sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin;
also known as *The Sūtra of the Past World*.
*Twelve Dhūta Sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin.

*The Sutra on the Dhūtas of a Śramaṇa*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty; *The Sutra of Jyotiṣka*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty;
*The Sutra of King Dīrghāyu*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
Sengyou’s Catalogue states that Master Dao’an lost the translation of this work and has now appended it to the Western Jin catalogue.

Regarding the *Rājan Dīrghāyus Sūtra* and others mentioned here as being extracted from the *Āgama*, I have carefully examined the four *Āgamas* and found that none of these sūtras exist within them. Although the *Dīrghāyus-rāja-avadāna* appears in the sixteenth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*, its textual content and meaning differ entirely; since that is a Mahāyāna text, I have included this [work] here.

*Fǎchángzhù jīng* (Sūtra on the Permanence of the Dharma), one fascicle. Sengyou’s Catalogue states that this was a translation by Master An whose translator was lost. It is now appended to the twenty-four sūtras in twenty-six fascicles contained in the Western Jin catalogue within the same volume. Upon examining its literary style and principles, it largely pertains to the Mahāyāna; however, as it had been classified among the Hīnayāna, it has now been moved here according to its ultimate meaning.
The *Bodhisattva-vinaya-piṭaka* (The Bodhisattva’s Treasury of Discipline) consists of twenty-seven sections in fifty-five fascicles, arranged in five bundles.
Now, as for "precepts" (*śīla*), it is a general term for the prevention of transgressions.
The pure precepts of a bodhisattva restrain only the mind;

since the śrāvaka discipline prevents transgressions of body and speech, there are occasions where faults arise due to external conditions, leading to the accumulation of errors and the subsequent reprimands and formal resolutions of the assembly.
For a bodhisattva mahāsattva, none of these things exist.
The Buddha directly taught [the precepts] so that they might be followed and practiced;
since there was no occasion for violating the regulations,
he omitted the matter of reprimand and formal conclusion.
Regarding those Mahāyāna sūtras that clarify the points of training (*śikṣāpada*), I have extracted them here as the *Bodhisattva-vinaya-piṭaka*.

The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-vidhi-sūtra* (or *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*) in ten fascicles—also known as the *Dichilun* or in eight fascicles, one volume—was translated at Guzang by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema during the Northern Liang dynasty. The aforementioned sūtra begins with a verse of homage, which is excerpted from the "Bodhisattvabhūmi" within the *Maulī Bhūmi* section of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Formerly, the Śramaṇa Fashang, the Chief Administrator (Zhaoxuantong) of the Gao Qi dynasty, replied to a Śramaṇa from Goguryeo, saying:
"The *Dichizhi* was received from Maitreya by the Bhikṣu Aśvaghoṣa."
Asaṅga was none other than the Bodhisattva Asaṅga. Furthermore,
according to the *Dichiji* (Record of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*) by the Liang dynasty śramaṇa Sengyou,
the eight-fascicle *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* consists of twenty-seven chapters and is divided into three sections.
The first section consists of eighteen chapters;
the second section, four chapters;
and the third section, five chapters.
The text does not explicitly state that there are alternative titles; however, this current edition is sometimes titled *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*.
Upon examining the end of the scripture, one finds that it has many names.
Furthermore, the text itself states: "It is named the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*."
It is called the Bodhisattvapiṭaka-mātṛkā;
it is designated as the Mahāyāna-saṃgraha;
it is named the Unbreakable Manifestation.
It is called the "Root of Unobstructed Pure Wisdom.
Master Yu stated that it is not the case that no other names appear;
furthermore, this has been verified by consulting various catalogs.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* translated by Dharmakṣema exists separately;
it is an error to call it the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*.

The *Bodhisattva-kuśala-śīla-sūtra* in nine fascicles—also known as the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, or in ten fascicles—was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kaśmīra during the Song dynasty and others. Regarding this sutra, all catalogs state that it is a different translation of the same original text as the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*.
Now, upon careful examination of the textual principles, it is clear that they are not without their differences.
The *Śīlasūtra* has a "Preface Chapter" at the beginning and a "Practice and Adherence" section at the end.
Neither the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* nor the *Śīlapaṭala* of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* contains the text for receiving the bodhisattva precepts or the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*; indeed,
these are entirely absent from the *Bhadraśīla-sūtra*.
Aside from these, the textual meaning is largely the same;
furthermore, the *Bhūmivastu* (Dichizhi) emerges from the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Various catalogs have either included it among the treatises;
as there are such discrepancies,
I do not yet dare to establish a definitive classification.
Furthermore, according to the *Record of the Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* by the Liang dynasty śramaṇa Sengyou, it is stated:
"This is named the *Śīla-sūtra*;
it is also named the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*."
It is called the Bodhisattva-vinaya-mātṛkā;
it is called the Tathāgatagarbha;
it is called the root of all wholesome dharmas.
It is named the Land of Peace and Bliss;
it is named the Collection of All Pāramitās.
In total, there are seven names.
In the first fascicle, the *Upāliparipṛcchā-śīlasaṃvara-dharma* (The Questions of Upāli on the Method for Receiving the Precepts) appears first.
Only at the beginning of the second fascicle does the title "Thus have I heard" appear.
The chapters are then listed in sequence, totaling thirty.
Furthermore, there is another edition titled the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*.
Upon examining this sūtra manuscript, it is found to differ from the record of Sengyou;
at the very beginning of the sūtra, it reads: "Thus have I heard."
However, there is no *Upāliparipṛcchā-śīla-saṃvara-vidhi* (The Questions of Upāli on the Method of Receiving Precepts);
there is only the nine-fascicle [text], which is precisely the later single-fascicle *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* (Bodhisattva-śīla-saṃvara-sūtra).
If one takes this as the first fascicle,
it accords with the record of [Dao]you;
however, the original manuscript of this *Dichizhi jing* has been separated from it for a long time.
If these were newly compiled into ten fascicles, one might perhaps harbor doubts;
this *Śīlasūtra* is likewise divided into three sections like the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
The first section is titled the "Bodhisattvabhūmi" and contains twenty chapters.
The second section is titled "The Four Categories of Abiding as Suchness" (*yathā-sthita*).
The third section is titled "The Ground of Ultimate Perfection" (*atyanta-bhūmi*) and contains six categories.
Sengyou states that these categories are listed in sequential order.
I fear that my search for its provenance has not been definitive.

*Jingyezhang jing* (Sūtra on Purifying Karmic Obstructions), one fascicle; translator lost. Now appended to the Qin catalog. This single-fascicle work and the two preceding sūtras (totaling ten fascicles) share one volume. Regarding the *Jingyezhang jing*, the Fashang Catalog states it was translated by Zhu Fahu. However, upon examining its phrasing and syntax, it differs entirely from the style and intent of the scriptures translated by Master Fahu; therefore, it is classified as a work of lost translation.

*Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, seven fascicles; the *Upāsaka-bodhisattva-śīla* [contained therein] consists of either five, six, or seven [precepts]. Translated at Guzang by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty. *Singale Folio Brahmajāla Sūtra*, two fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; this is a second translation, as the previous version lacked the section on receiving the ten wholesome precepts. *Jie shi shan jie jing* (Sūtra on Receiving the Ten Wholesome Precepts), one fascicle. Translator lost during the Later Han; included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). *Shou puti xin jie yi* (Ritual for Receiving the Bodhicitta Precepts), one fascicle. The title within the text reads: *Worst Vehicle Teaching: Text for Receiving Precepts and Repentance*, compiled by the Ācārya Samantabhadra-yoga. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Great Xingshan Monastery by imperial decree. The above four sūtras, totaling eleven fascicles, are contained in the same volume according to the *Zhenyuan xinding shijiao mulu*.

*Bodhisattvapiṭaka-mūla-karman-sūtra*, two fascicles; alternatively titled *Bodhisattva* [Sūtra], newly compiled as a Vinaya text, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
First Translation.

The *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* (佛藏經) exists in three translations; two of these are missing. It consists of four fascicles, also known as the *Sarvadharmavibhaṅga-sūtra* (選擇諸法經), and is alternatively found in two or three fascicles.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty, it is a standalone text.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* (菩薩戒本) in one fascicle is extracted from the "Chapter on the Maintenance of Precepts" (*Dichijie pin*) and was spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated at Guzang by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema from India during the Northern Liang dynasty;

this supplementary version is incorporated here as the second translation of the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* (Pusa jieben), one fascicle, extracted from the "Bodhisattvabhūmi" section of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Record of the Translation of Inner Scriptures by Tripitaka Master Xuanzang, Volume Three: Translations.

The two aforementioned sūtras are different translations of the same text; there are three translations in total, of which one lacks the *Bodhisattva-śīla-karman* (Ritual for the Bodhisattva Precepts) in one fascicle. This was extracted from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; listed in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalog). *The Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* (Single Volume), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Jibin during the Song dynasty; listed in the *Fachang lu* (Dharma-Chant Catalog). The above six single-volume scriptures comprise ten fascicles and are contained in the same case.

*Bodhisattva-antar-śīla-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kaśmīra during the Song dynasty. Recorded in the *Fashang lu*. *Upāsaka-pañca-śīla-vidhi-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kaśmīra during the Song dynasty. Note: It is an error for various catalogs to include this *Upāsaka-pañca-śīla-vidhi-sūtra* among the Hīnayāna Vinaya texts. Since the former is the root text of the Bodhisattva precepts and the latter contains the ritual for receiving the Bodhisattva precepts, as well as the methods for relinquishing them and performing repentance (*pratikramaṇa*), they do not belong to the Hīnayāna tradition and have therefore been moved here and included in this collection.

*Mañjuśrī-viśuddha-vinaya-sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively titled simply *Viśuddha-vinaya-sūtra*. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. First translation. *Vimala-vinaya-vaipulya-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Yao Qin Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva. Recorded in the *Fashang lu*. Third translation. *Prasāda-ghoṣa-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *Tathāgata-bhāṣita-viśuddha-vinaya-sūtra*. Translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Śikṣānanda (Shi Fahai). Fourth translation. The above three sūtras share the same original text but differ in their translations. Of these four successive translations, one translation is missing.
*Mahāyāna Tri-saṃvara-pāpadeśanā Sūtra*, one fascicle;
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others during the Sui Dynasty,
as recorded in the *Neidian lu*.

*The Single-Volume Ritual for the Fivefold Repentance of Bodhisattvas*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Sūtra on the Fivefold Repentance of Bodhisattvas*. Translator lost; now appended to the Liang dynasty records.
*The Single-Volume Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtra*, one fascicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of Funan during the Liang dynasty.
*Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle;
translated by the lay devotee Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin dynasty.
*Bodhisattva-śīla-upavāsa-sūtra*, one fascicle.
The Sutra of Mañjuśrī’s Repentance, translated by the lay devotee Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin Dynasty;
second translation, third translation, with three missing passages; one fascicle.
The Mañjuśrī-pañcāṅga-pratikramaṇa-sūtra,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty;
the first translation.
One of the two translations is missing; there is also the *Śāriputra-parivarta-sūtra* (or simply *Parivarta-sūtra*), one fascicle,
translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han dynasty.
The first translation;

three translations [in total], two of which are missing: *Fǎlǜ sānmèijīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Dharma and Discipline), one fascicle, also simply titled *Fǎlǜjīng* (Sūtra on the Dharma and Discipline), translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu kingdom.
The second translation;
one of the two translations is missing. *Daśakuśalakarmapathasūtra*, one fascicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang.
The fourteen scriptures in fourteen fascicles newly included in this record are contained in the same volume.

I have carefully examined the old records and find that among the Mahāyāna Vinaya texts, the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* and the *Kāśyapa-sūtra* are now included within the *Ratnakūṭa-parivarta*, and thus are not listed here again. Furthermore, the *Mahāvaipulya-triśikṣā-sūtra* shares the same original text as the *Trisamvara-parivarta* of the *Ratnakūṭa*, and the *Viniścaya-vinaya-sūtra* shares the same original text as the *Upāli-parivarta* of the *Ratnakūṭa*; these are now all compiled into the *Ratnakūṭa* section, and therefore they are not recorded here.
The Bodhisattva Abhidharma Pitaka consists of ninety-nine works totaling five hundred and twenty fascicles in fifty bundles; this Bodhisattva Abhidharma has two categories.
The first explains the sūtras;
the second elucidates the essential nature and characteristics of phenomena.
These two categories, as recorded in the old catalogues, are intermingled and pervasive throughout.
The collection presented here is divided into two categories:
those explaining the sūtras are listed first,
while those elucidating the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) are compiled afterward.
May there be no confusion or intermixture, so that readers may understand with ease.

**Mahāyāna Commentaries on Sūtras:** Twenty-two works in one hundred and fifty-five fascicles, arranged in fifteen bundles. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom): One hundred fascicles, or one hundred and ten fascicles, or seventy fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. [Single Volume] Right: Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna as a commentary on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. Master Kumārajīva stated: "If translated in its entirety, it should comprise one thousand fascicles; however, because the intellectual capacity of the people of the Qin was weak, he abridged it, retaining only one-tenth."

*Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra*, twelve fascicles (or fifteen fascicles), one set; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci and others during the Northern Wei dynasty. Single volume; the above [treatise] was composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
The *Śikṣāsamuccaya* (Explanation of the Ten Stages Sūtra) is precisely the "Ten Stages Chapter" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka*. The preface to the treatise states:

"Bodhiruci and Ratnamati were at the palace in Luoyang; the three of them translated together, with Buddhabhadra serving as the oral interpreter and the Emperor personally receiving the text by pen. This is not so, for while both the *Liu* and *Mati* catalogs record it as being transmitted, they do not both list it as such. Now, these have been combined into a single volume and are included in the Bodhiruci catalog.

*Maitreyaparipṛcchāsūtra-śāstra*, five fascicles, or six, seven, or ten fascicles. Translated by the Indian Bodhiruci during the Northern Wei dynasty. Single-text edition. The above commentary on the *Maitreyaparipṛcchāsūtra* is the forty-first assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*.

*Mahāyāna Ratnakūṭa Sūtra Śāstra*, four fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei dynasty. This is the first translation; of two translations, one is missing. The above is an explanation of the old single-fascicle *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*.
This is the forty-third assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa*.

The *Sūtra on the Four Dharmas of the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin*, one fascicle; composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Vimokṣaprajña and others of the Northern Wei dynasty. [This concludes] the preface and record; this is a single-text edition. The above is the commentary on the "Ratnaśikhin Chapter" of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*.
This is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa* collection, appearing as the forty-seventh assembly. The preface to the commentary records:

"On the day of Gengwu, the first day of the ninth month in the year of Xinyou, the third year of the Xinghe era of the Wei dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Vimalamitra, a Kṣatriya of royal lineage from the country of Udyāna, and the Dharma-protector Gopadatta, a Brāhmaṇa from the country of Central India, translated [this text] at Jinhua Temple within the city of Ye. They were assisted by the layman and monk Hengming, who was a cavalry general of the rank of Kai-fu Yitong-si, Imperial Censor, and a native of Bohai named Zhongmi, a person who cherished the Dharma. The text consists of 4,997 characters. All other catalogs state that this was translated by Bodhiruci; this is an error. We now follow the preface for the correct record."
The three aforementioned treatises, totaling ten fascicles, are contained in the same volume. *Commentary on the Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra* (7 fascicles), composed by Bodhisattvas such as Bandhuprabha;

translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; recorded in the *Neidian lu*. *Sole Text: Commentary on the Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (2 fascicles), composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga; translated by the Indian Tripitaka Master Dharmagupta of the Sui dynasty; recorded in the *Neidian lu*. *Sole Text: Verses of the Commentary on the Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (1 fascicle), composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga; translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog. The three aforementioned treatises, totaling ten fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

*Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Śāstra*, three fascicles. Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei dynasty. First Translation. *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Śāstra*, three fascicles. Verses composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga; commentary by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang dynasty. Second Translation. Newly included in the catalog. The two aforementioned śāstras and verses are the same text with different translations.

*The Treatise on Breaking Attachment to Grasping and Not Destroying Provisional Names* (*Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra-bhaṅgopādānābhedaprajñapti-śāstra*), two fascicles. Composed by Bodhisattva Guṇadatta; also known as the *Guṇadatta-śāstra*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Divākara of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty. Recorded in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. This is a standalone work. Regarding the four treatises and the verse commentary above, although their authors differ, they all comment upon the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. Furthermore, there is the *Vajrasena-śāstra* in ten fascicles. Upon examining its literary style and principles, it was composed by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei dynasty as a commentary on Vasubandhu’s treatise. Since it was not translated from a Sanskrit original, it is not included here.

*The Treatise on the Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *The Treatise on the Gayāśīrṣa-sūtra*. Composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei. *The Treatise on the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one fascicle; a single-text commentary. Composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati of Central India together with Senglang and others of the Northern Wei. The aforementioned five treatises, totaling ten fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

The *Dharmapada-śāstra* (or *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra*), two fascicles; the first contains a verse of homage. Alternatively, it exists in one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of North India during the Northern Wei dynasty, together with Tanlin and others. It was included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). This is the second translation. The above two treatises are different translations of the same original text.
Regarding the *Dharmapada-śāstra* in five fascicles, newly translated by Tripiṭaka Master Yi Jing: the original manuscript has not yet been obtained.
The *Suvikrāntavikrami-paripṛcchā-sūtra-śāstra* in four fascicles—or three fascicles—explains the *Suvikrāntavikrami-sūtra*;
it was translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci during the Northern Wei dynasty.
The *Nirvāṇa-śāstra* in one fascicle,
composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
a brief commentary translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmaprajñā.
An unknown date; appended within the Inner Scriptures following the first translation of the Northern Wei dynasty,
this is one fascicle of the *Treatise on Verses of "Originally Existing, Now Non-existent"* from the missing portion of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, explaining a single verse of the *Nirvāṇa*.
*The Treatise on the Single-Volume Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching*, translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Liang Dynasty, in one fascicle;
*The Commentary on the Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching*, translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Chen Dynasty.
One fascicle of the *Treatise on the Single-Volume Sutra of Immeasurable Life*, compiled from the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection),
composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
*Tri-samaya-sūtra-śāstra*, one fascicle, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty;
composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu. [This version] contains the commentary but lacks the sūtra text.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Masters Vimokṣaprajña and others of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
The Preface and Record of the Single Volume Edition:

The aforementioned treatise begins by stating that the Tripiṭaka Master Viśuddhasimha, a Brahmin from India, and the Dharma-loving śramaṇa Gautama Ruci, together with the śramaṇa Tánlín, translated [this work] at Jinhua Monastery within the city of Yecheng during the third year of the Xinghe era of the Wei dynasty—the year being Xinyou, the month being Jiashu, and the day being Gengwu, the thirteenth day of the month—amounting to one thousand ten words. It was requested for offering, protection, and circulation by Gāo Zhòngmì of Bohai, who held the rank of General of the Household, Grand Commandant, and Censor-in-Chief. All other catalogs state that this was translated by Bodhiruci; however, this is an error. Now, based on the Preface and Record, the above is established as correct.

*The Commentary on the Dharmacakra-pravartana-sūtra*, one fascicle. Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; includes the commentary but lacks the original sūtra text. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Vimokṣasena and others of the Northern Wei dynasty. Extracted from the *Preface Record*. Single volume. The initial record of this treatise states: "Gao Zhongmi of Bohai, General of the Flying Cavalry, Grand Marshal, and Censor-in-Chief, was skilled at seeking the principles of righteousness and selecting the true while rejecting the false. Therefore, he invited the Dharma Master Vimokṣasena along with his disciple Gautama Ratnākara to the Jinhua Temple within the city of Ye. On the eleventh day of the month of You (the eighth lunar month) in the year of Daliang, the third year of the Xinghe era, under the cyclical sign Gengzi, they translated [this work] consisting of three thousand nine hundred and forty-two words. The Śramaṇa Tanlin acted as the oral interpreter. All other records state that it was translated by Bodhiruci; this is an error. Now, I rely on the Preface Record to establish the correct version.

The eight preceding treatises comprise twelve fascicles in one bundle. The *Mahāyāna-saṃgraha-artha-śāstra* consists of seventy-eight works totaling three hundred and sixty-five fascicles in thirty-five bundles.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, one hundred fascicles, spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, occupies ten bundles. It appears in the *Neidian lu*. Regarding the single and combined translations: the *Yogācāra-śāstra* translated during the Liang dynasty by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha was titled the *Shiqidi lun* (Seventeen Stages Treatise), which reached only five fascicles before being interrupted due to obstacles. The *Dichichi lun* (Bodhisattvabhūmi) translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang consists of only ten fascicles; this is the "Bodhisattvabhūmi" within the "Maulī Bhūmi" section of this *Yogācāra-śāstra*. This *Yogācāra-śāstra* represents the third translation; whereas the previous two versions were incomplete in their main sections and bundles, the translator of the Great Tang has now rendered it fully complete.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Exposition of the Noble Teachings), twenty fascicles, composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, in two volumes.
Record of the Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures:
A Single-Volume Commentary on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,
composed by Bodhisattvas such as Jinaputra.
A Single Volume of the Chart for Translating Scriptures, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang:
The Verses of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Manifestation of the Holy Teachings), Volume One.
Compiled by Bodhisattva Asaṅga;
translated by the Great Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang;
recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Inner Scriptures).
*The Treatise on the Correct Principle of the King’s Law Alone*, one fascicle;
composed by Maitreya Bodhisattva and translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang.
Catalog of Inner and Outer Scriptures: Single-Volume Mahāyāna Abhidharmasamuccaya, seven fascicles;
composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga, translated by the Great Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang.
The single volumes of the Inner and Outer Scriptural Catalogues: the four treatises above, totaling ten fascicles, are in one bundle.

The *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* in sixteen fascicles, a commentary by the Bodhisattva Sthiramati on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; from the Inner and Outer Scriptural Catalogues. The single volume of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* in four fascicles, the original work of the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, with the commentary of the Brahmin Candrakīrti, translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin; these two treatises above, totaling twenty fascicles, are in two bundles.

*Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*, fifteen fascicles. Original by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, commentary by Bodhisattva Bhāviveka. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Prabhākaramitra of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Single volume. The above is identical in its root text to the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, though the commentaries differ.

*The Treatise on the Twelve Gates*, one fascicle; composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. *The Treatise on the Eighteen Emptinesses*, single volume, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of India during the Chen dynasty. [Recorded in] the *Catalogue of Translated Scriptures*. *The Hundred Treatises*, two fascicles; composed by Bodhisattva Āryadeva, explained by the Bodhisattva Vasu, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. Single volume. *The Extensive Hundred Treatises*, one fascicle; composed by Bodhisattva Āryadeva, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. [Recorded in] the *Catalogue of Inner Scriptures*. The above five treatises comprise twenty fascicles in two bundles, as single volumes.

*Mahāyāna-śataka-vṛtti* (Commentary on the Hundred Verses on the Mahāyāna), ten fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, based on the original text by Āryadeva and the commentary by Dharmapāla. *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Exposition of the Ten Stages), fourteen fascicles; composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; alternatively recorded as twelve or fifteen fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin, according to the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Inner Scriptures). *Bodhicaryāvatāra-prajñāpāramitā-upadeśa-śāstra* (Treatise on the Path to Enlightenment), six fascicles; based on the original text by the Venerable Nāgārjuna and the commentary by the Bhikṣu Vinitadeva; translated by the Indian Tripitaka Master Dharmagupta of the Sui dynasty, according to the *Neidian lu*. The above two treatises, totaling twenty fascicles in two volumes, constitute single-text editions.
The Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra, in thirteen fascicles,
composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga;
alternatively, in fifteen fascicles.
One fascicle:
A Catalogue of Inner Scriptures Translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
The Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra, fifteen fascicles (or ten fascicles), composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
The Madhyamaka-śāstra-anuvyākhyāna, two fascicles.
Preface and Record by Bodhisattva Asaṅga,
translated by the Brahamana Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.

The *Preface and Record* (xu ji) to the standalone edition of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states: "The High Duke Gao [Yan], Director of the Imperial Secretariat and General of the Same Rank, hosted the venerable guest Gautama Dharmaruci at his residence to provide offerings. While the Dharma was being correctly transmitted and the Buddha-dharma elucidated, he [Dharmaruci] faced off against Shi Tanlin to produce this treatise on the meaning [of the Middle Way]. On the tenth day of the eighth month of the first year of Wuding, the year being Guihai, he set down his brush; the cyclical sign was Jingtin. In total, there are thirteen thousand seven hundred twenty-seven characters. All catalogs claim that Bodhiruci translated it, but this is an error; according to the *Preface and Record*, the former is correct."

*Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra*, three fascicles; composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga; translated by the Chen Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha. This is the second translation. [The above three treatises comprise twenty fascicles in two volumes.]

*Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra*, two fascicles; composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Buddhanta of the Northern Wei. First translation. *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, three fascicles; composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Third translation. The above three versions of the treatise are the same original text with different translations.

*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, fifteen fascicles; composed by Vasubandhu Bodhisattva, or twelve fascicles; translated by the Chen dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha. This constitutes the first translation of the aforementioned three treatises, totaling twenty fascicles in two volumes.

According to the *Renshou lu*, the *Dazhou lu*, and other catalogs, there was also one version of the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) in twelve fascicles; its formation and contents were likewise said to have been translated by Paramārtha. Having compared it with this [text], they are found to be identical; thus, only this single version remains today.

*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, ten fascicles; commentary by Vasubandhu Bodhisattva; one set; translated by the Chen dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta; recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Third Translation: *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, ten fascicles; composed by Vasubandhu Bodhisattva; one set; translated by the Great Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang; recorded in the *Neidian lu*. The above three commentaries are translations of the same original text with different translations.

*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, ten fascicles; composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; one set; recorded in the *Neidian lu*. This single volume is the same work as the three preceding treatises, though translated differently.

*Buddhadhātu-śāstra* (Treatise on Buddha-nature), four fascicles; composed by Vasubandhu Bodhisattva; translated by the Chen Dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha from India. *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (Decisive Compendium), three fascicles; translated by the Liang Dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha from India. [Single Text] Regarding the above *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, the catalog of the Great Zhou dynasty states that it was a work of lost translation, without specifying the era in which it was rendered. Upon careful examination, the general consensus is that this treatise was indeed translated by Paramārtha. Furthermore, a sub-commentary within the treatises translated by Paramārtha states: "The catalogers of previous dynasties omitted it and did not include it [in their records]; it is now classified as a translation by Paramārtha and appended to the Liang dynasty catalogs."

*Madhyāntavibhāga-kārikā*, one fascicle. Composed by Maitreya Bodhisattva; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*, two fascicles (or three fascicles). Composed by Vasubandhu; translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen dynasty. The first translations of these four treatises comprise ten fascicles in a single volume.

*Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*, three fascicles. Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. This is the second translation. The two aforementioned commentaries are translations of the same original text with different versions.
*Mahāyānottaratantraśāstra*, in four fascicles, or three fascicles, or five fascicles;
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati during the Northern Wei dynasty.
Second translation.

Regarding the omission in one of the two translations: the preface to the treatise records that on the twenty-fifth day of the seventh month of the year Daliang (the third year of the Xinghe era of the Wei dynasty), corresponding to the cyclical sign Xinwei, the General of the Flying Cavalry, Grand Marshal, and Palace Aide-de-camp Gao Zhongmi of Bohai respectfully invited the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra from Udyāna and the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci from Central India, along with the Śramaṇa Tanlin and others, to translate [this work] at Jinhua Monastery within the city of Ye. The total word count was 4,872. Although the preface does not explicitly name the translators, according to established precedent, this refers to Vimalākṣa; it is an error for various catalogs to state simply that it was translated by Gautama Prajñāruci. Now, I have relied upon the preface for the correct attribution.

*Mahāyāna-karmasiddhi-śāstra*, one fascicle. Composed by Vasubandhu Bodhisattva; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang Dynasty. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. This is the second translation. The two treatises above are the same original text with different translations.

*Hetuvidyānyāyamukhaśāstra*, one fascicle. Composed by Bodhisattva Śīlabhadra; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. This is the first translation. The aforementioned five treatises in ten fascicles are contained in the same volume.

*Hetuvidyānyāyamukhaśāstra*, one fascicle. Composed by Bodhisattva Dharmapāla; translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang. Newly included in the canon. Second translation. The two treatises above are the same text with different translations. The old *Nyāyamukha-śāstra* was recorded in the Zhou catalog as a single work, but a new examination has determined it to be a duplicate translation.
*Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra*, one fascicle.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Śaṅkarasvāmin;
translated by the Great Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang.
The *Xiǎnshí lùn* (Treatise on Manifesting Consciousness), one fascicle, listed in the catalog of Buddhist and non-Buddhist scriptures;
its internal title reads "Chapter on Manifesting Consciousness," extracted from the *Wúxiàng lùn* (Treatise on Signlessness).
The Title of the Treatise Translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from Central India,
in a Single Volume.

Attached: A supplementary record of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Transformation of Consciousness), one fascicle, which is the same work as the previously issued *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha from India;
this is the single-text edition of the treatise’s title.
Attached: A Supplementary Record of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), one fascicle;
also known as the *Bheda-rūpacitta-śāstra*. It begins with: "Consciousness-only has no external objects.
Translated by the Indian Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei dynasty.
First Translation: *Mahāyāna-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, one fascicle.

The beginning states: "The Path of Cultivation Not Shared with Others. The above two treatises were both composed by Vasubandhu and translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen dynasty.

Second Translation. The three treatises above are of the same original text but different translations; the *Zhou lu* (Catalogue of Zhou) does not mention them as being the same text, but a new examination has determined they are retranslations.

Part 2: Catalogue of the Tripiṭaka of the Śrāvakas. Section on Works with Translations and Existing Texts. Catalogue of the Tripiṭaka of the Śrāvakas, Number Four. Regarding the Śrāvaka Piṭaka: it is the teaching elucidated by the Hīnayāna.
The Teacher who is able to preach demonstrates birth and extinction, responding to things according to conditions;
the teachings he expounds consist of the nine divisions of scripture, the four Āgamas, the Abhidharma, and the Vinaya.
Virtuous men and women who receive these teachings cast off the dust and toil of worldly existence.
Pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas revere it and thereby ascend to the other shore;
it is indeed the minor vehicle of the True Vehicle,
a transformation-city on the path to Bodhi.
To entice and advance those of initial resolve, nothing is more excellent than this.
Beginning at the Garden of Immortals and extending to the Golden River, the texts expounded therein consist of the "half-syllable" script; these are known as the Piṭaka of the Śrāvakas.
When the hundred rivers converge and the three vehicles reach their common destination,
all ascend together to wondrous enlightenment and collectively realize nirvana;
how could there be any distinction between "small" and "great" names?
Faith was the gradual guide for my venerable master.
Beginning from the year of Dingmao during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty and ending in the year of Gengchen of my own Kaiyuan era,
these were the practitioners of the Tripitaka of the Hīnayāna.
In total, there are three hundred and thirty-seven works comprising one thousand eight hundred and nine scrolls, arranged in one hundred and seventy fascicles, which constitute the Śrāvaka Piṭaka.
Their specific categories and divisions are clearly set forth,
as detailed in the list below.

The Śrāvaka Piṭaka of Sūtras: 240 sections in 618 fascicles. The Śrāvaka Piṭaka of Vinaya: 61 sections in 493 fascicles, arranged in 45 bundles. The Śrāvaka Piṭaka of Abhidharma: 36 sections in 698 fascicles, arranged in 72 bundles. Regarding the Śrāvaka Piṭaka of Sūtras: these are the Mahāyāna sūtras translated both in duplicate and as single texts. There are 153 sections in 394 fascicles, arranged in 31 bundles. As the four Āgamas constitute the fundamental sūtras of the Śrāvaka tradition, they are listed at the beginning, followed by the remaining sūtras.

*The Dīrgha Āgama*, twenty-two fascicles, in two volumes; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśā and Zhu Fonian during the Yao Qin dynasty, with supplementary translations by Dan Chong. This collection consists of four divisions totaling thirty sūtras. Sengzhao’s preface states: "The *Dīrgha Āgama* comprises four divisions and four recitations, totaling thirty sūtras, which together constitute one section."

*Madhyama Āgama*, sixty fascicles (or fifty-eight fascicles), six bundles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kasmīra during the Eastern Jin dynasty. This is the second translation; one of the two translations is missing. [Note: This collection of sūtras consists of five recitations (*saṃgīti*), totaling eighteen chapters and two hundred twenty-two sūtras. Separately, Sengzhao’s *Preface to the Long Āgama* states that the *Madhyama Āgama* comprises four divisions and five recitations.

*Ekottarika-āgama*, fifty-one fascicles (or fifty, or forty, or thirty-two), in five bundles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kapiśī during the Eastern Jin dynasty. This is the second translation; one of the two translations is missing. To the right, this section of the canon contains fifty chapters in total, comprising four hundred and seventy-two sūtras. As the preface to the *Dīrgha-āgama* by Sengzhao states: "The *Ekottarika-āgama* consists of four divisions and eight recitations."

*Saṃyukta Āgama*, fifty fascicles, five bundles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty, with supplementary translations by Dānapāla. Regarding this collection of sūtras, as the matters discussed are diverse, there is no differentiation into chapters, sections, or recitations. Sengzhao’s *Preface to the Long Āgama* states: "The *Saṃyukta Āgama* consists of four divisions and ten recitations."

The *Separate Translation of the Saṃyukta Āgama* in twenty fascicles, arranged in two volumes, consists of scriptures whose translators are lost. Although the inclusion of Chinese characters within the commentary by Zhizhu does not allow for certain knowledge of the translators' names, they must have been translated during the Three Qin periods; I have now appended them to the Qin records. Regarding this collection, although its textual content differs from that of the aforementioned scripture and its sequence is not consistent, [it is nonetheless included].
Upon careful investigation, it was found that these do not exceed the scope of the aforementioned sūtras;

rather, they are merely abridgments compiled as separate sections. Furthermore, the various sūtras following the *Buddha-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* are all alternative translations of individual sūtras contained within the *Catur-aṅga-nikāya*.

*The Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha*, two fascicles (alternatively titled simply *The Nirvāṇa Sūtra*), translated by the Śramaṇa Bai Fazang of Henan during the Western Jin dynasty; *The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, three fascicles (alternatively two fascicles), translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faxian of Pingyang during the Eastern Jin dynasty—now recorded as translated by Faxian, as described in the General Catalogue; *The Sūtra on Parinirvāṇa*, two fascicles (alternatively without the character "Parinirvāṇa"), now recorded as of lost translation and appended to the Eastern Jin catalogue. These three sūtras are extracted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
Volumes two through four are alternative translations of the same original text as the *Caturvargika-vinaya* (or *Prathama-bhāga-caryā-sūtra*).

Regarding the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, all catalogs state that it was translated by Guṇabhadra during the Song dynasty; however, this is incorrect. Upon examining its phrasing, it is mostly an ancient translation and bears no resemblance at all to the version translated by Guṇavarman. Among the various Tripitakas, only the upper volume exists while the lower volume is missing. Having lost its source, it has been included in the Jin-dynasty catalogs. Furthermore, there are some manuscript versions where the upper volume of the *Buddha-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* is identical in wording to the upper volume of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*; these are simply errors in the original texts.

*Renben yusheng jing* (Sūtra on the Fundamental Desire for Birth), one fascicle; translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. The above is extracted from the tenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

It is the same text as the *Mahā-upāya Sūtra* in the second division [of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*], though translated differently. That various catalogs of former generations all classified this *Renben yusheng jing* among the Mahāyāna sūtras was an error.

*Śīkṣānanda-vatsa-ṣaḍdig-namaskāra-sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *Śīkṣānanda-vatsa-ṣaḍdig-praṇāma-sūtra*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty. The above is extracted from the eleventh fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*; it is the same text as the *Sujāta-sūtra* in the second division [of the *Madhyama Āgama*], though a different translation. Compared to the original text, this version is somewhat abbreviated. This sūtra is also found within the thirty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.

The *Brahmajāla-ṣaṣṭidṛṣṭi Sūtra*, one fascicle—also known as the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*—translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. The above appears in the fourteenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
A different translation of the same text as the third part of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*.

One fascicle of the *Śramaṇaphala-sūtra*, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. The above is extracted from the seventeenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
This is a different translation of the same original text as the *Sāmaññaphala-sutta* (The Discourse on the Fruits of the Ascetic Life), the third part.
The eight preceding sūtras comprise twelve fascicles in one volume. *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World), ten fascicles, one volume.

Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of the Sui Dynasty. [Title appears at the beginning of the text. *Qishi yinben jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Origins of the Arising of the World), ten fascicles. Fearing confusion with the previous version, the title is specifically noted below as *Qishi yinben jing*, one volume. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of the Sui Dynasty. [Appears in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue). This is the sixth translation. It has been included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). According to the *Tang Neidian lu* and Jingmai’s *Jingtu*, the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta translated the ten-fascicle *Qishi jing* at the Translation Hall in the Shanglin Garden in the Eastern Capital during the Daye era.
Now, upon searching through the various Tripitakas, two versions have been found;
while their general meaning is the same, the wording differs slightly,
and as for the chapter titles, there are occasional discrepancies.
The first sūtra states that the Bhagavān was in the city of Śrāvastī,
whereas the latter sūtra states that the Bhagavān was in the city of Śālāvasitī.
According to the Sanskrit terminology:
The later version of the sutra is the correct one.
Now it is said that Guṇabhadra and Jñānagupta each translated a separate version;
furthermore, at the beginning of the former sutra, the title states that the two masters Guṇabhadra and Jñānagupta produced it together.
The former was translated by Jñānagupta,
while the latter is a re-translation by Dharmagupta;
since the texts of these two sūtras differ, [the distinction is clear].
For this reason, both recensions have been preserved here.
Thus, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* also states that the Bhagavat was in the city of Śrāvastī;
from this, we know that both were translated by Guṇabhadra.
Fearing that the two texts might be confused with one another, the title is specifically noted as *Qishi yinben* (The Origin of the World).

The *Lou tan jing* (Lokānuvartana-sūtra) consists of six fascicles—sometimes called the *Da lou tan jing* (Great Lokānuvartana-sūtra)—or five, or eight fascicles. This is a different translation from the same original text as the second part of the *Daśottara-sūtra*, differing slightly in its degree of detail.

The *Zhongbenqi jing* (Sūtra of the Middle Origination) is in two fascicles; it is also called the *Taizi zhongqi jing* (Sūtra of the Prince’s Middle Origination). Its initial title states that it is excerpted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*. It was translated by the Western Region śramaṇa Dharmaphala and Kang Mengxiang during the Later Han dynasty. These two aforementioned sūtras comprise ten fascicles and are contained in the same volume. The title of the *Zhongbenqi jing* therein states that it is excerpted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*. Upon searching the original *Dīrgha Āgama*, this particular sūtra is not found. One suspects that perhaps the Sanskrit text was not fully translated. Since it is stated to have been excerpted from that [Āgama], it has been appended at the end. The *Dazhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalogue) claims that it is a different translation of the same text as the *Guoqu xianzai yinguo jing*, the *Xiuxing benqi jing*, and the *Ruixiang benqi jing*; this is an error. Translated by the Northern Liang Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema. These two sūtras above share the same original text with different translations; they are extracted from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume Eleven, and share the same original text as the *Caturdvīpa Sūtra*.

*The Sūtra of the Five Divine Messengers of King Yama*, one fascicle; also known as the *Sūtra of the Iron City Niraya*. Translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Huijian. *The Sūtra of the Iron City Niraya*, one fascicle. Translated by the Eastern Jin dynasty śramaṇa from the Western Regions, Zhu Tanwulan. These two sūtras, included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection), are the same text with different translations.
Extracted from the *Madhyama Āgama*, fascicle twelve.
It shares the same source as the *Devadūta Sūtra*;
compared to that original sūtra, this version is somewhat abbreviated.

*Gǔlái shìshí jīng* (Sūtra on the Times of Ancient Ages), one fascicle. Translator lost; currently appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin. The above is extracted from the thirteenth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*;
it is a different translation of the same text as the *Shuōběn jīng*.
Compared to the original sūtra, this text is somewhat abbreviated.

*The Sūtra on Āniruddha’s Eight Recollections* (one fascicle), also known as *The Sūtra on the Concentration of the Mind through Dhyāna Practice*, or simply *The Sūtra on the Eight Recollections*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhi Yao of the Western Regions during the Later Han Dynasty. The above is extracted from the eighteenth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
A different translation of the same text as the *Āṣṭānusmṛti-sūtra*.

One fascicle of the *Vigata-nidrā-sūtra*, translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa; included in the Supplementary Collection (*Shiyi*). The above appears in the twentieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
A different translation of the same text as the *Sūtra on Sleeping with an Elder and Venerable One*.

*The Sūtra on What is Dharma and What is Not Dharma*, one fascicle; translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. The above is from the twenty-first fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Zhēnrén jīng* (Sūtra on the True Person).

One fascicle of the *Qiúyù jīng* (Sūtra on Seeking Desires), translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju. The above is extracted from the twenty-second fascicle of the *Zhōngāhán jīng* (Madhyama Āgama).
A different translation from the same original text as the *Sūtra on Impurity*.

One fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. Included in the *Supplement* (*Shiyi*). The above appears at the beginning of the twenty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation of the same text as the *Bhikṣu-āmantraṇa-sūtra*.

*The Sūtra on the Brahmin’s Calculation of Water Purity*, one fascicle; translator lost. Now appended to the *Dongjin lu* (Catalogue of the Eastern Jin) in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). The above appears in the twenty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Sūtra on the Brahmin Udāyin* (Yu shui jing).

*The Sūtra on the Aggregate of Suffering* (*Kuyin jing*), one fascicle; translator lost; listed in the Later Han records and included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement) section. The above appears in the twenty-fifth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation of the same original text as the *Duḥkhaskandha-sūtra*.

*Śāriputra-māṇava-sūtra*, one fascicle—also known as the *Pañcaskandha-hetuvastu-sūtra*—translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. *Duḥkhaskandha-hetuvastu-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin dynasty. The two aforementioned sūtras are included here as supplementary texts; they are translations of the same original work.
Extracted from the Madhyama Āgama, Volume 25.
This is the same original text as the subsequent *Duḥkhaskandha-sūtra*.
*Saṃjñā-sukha-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa; included here as a supplementary addition. The above is extracted from the Madhyama Āgama, Volume 26.
A different translation from the same original as the *Sañjñā-sūtra*.
One fascicle of the *Āsrava-vibhaṅga-sūtra*, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. The above is extracted from the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation of the same text as the *Sūtra on the Accomplishment of the Holy Life* (*Brahmacaryasamādāna-sūtra*).

One fascicle, titled *The Sūtra of the Anavatapta Wind*, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty; it was included in the *Supplemental Collection*. The following [text] appears in the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
A different translation of the same text as the *Anupada-sūtra*.
*Dharmapada-mūla-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. The above is extracted from the beginning of the twenty-eighth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
A different translation of the same text as the *Dharmamūla-sūtra*.

*The Sūtra on the Prediction of the Fruit for Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī*, one fascicle; translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Huìjiǎn. The above is extracted from the twenty-eighth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Gautamī-sūtra*.

*The Sūtra of the Bhikṣu of Campā*, one fascicle; also called *Campā*. Translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Śīladhvaja (Shi Faju). Included in the *Supplement* (*Shiyi*). The above appears in the twenty-ninth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
A different translation from the same original as the *Campa Sūtra*.

One fascicle of the *Fu yin jing* (Sūtra on Subduing Lust), translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju; included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). The above is a different translation from the same original as the *Xingyu jing* (Sūtra on Practicing Desire) in the thirtieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.

*Māraparidrava Sūtra* (one fascicle), also titled *Pimāra-parīkṣā-Maudgalyāyana Sūtra*, or *Mārarāja-Maudgalyāyana-vidruta-udara Sūtra*. Translator lost; included in the Later Han record. *Bimāra-parīkṣā-Maudgalyāyana Sūtra* (one fascicle), also titled *Māraparidrava Sūtra*. Translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty; appended to the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations, appearing in the thirtieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is the same text as the *Dānava-sūtra*.
The thirty preceding sūtras comprise thirty fascicles in one volume.

The *Ratthapāla-sūtra*, one fascicle—also known as the *Arhat Ratthapāla-sūtra*—was translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. The above is extracted from the thirty-first fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Ratthapāla Sūtra*.

*The Sūtra on the Son of the Good Man*, one fascicle; translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Zhi Fadu. This was included in the *Supplement* (*Shiyi*). The above is extracted from the thirty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
A different translation of the same text as the *Sujāta-sūtra*.

One fascicle of the *Śu-jing* (Numerical Sūtras), translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju; included in the *Shi-yi* (Supplementary Collection) and appearing in the thirty-fifth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
A different translation of the same original as the *Saṃkhyā-Maudgalyāyana Sūtra*.

*The Sūtra on the Questions of the Brahmin Aśvalāyana Regarding the Lineage of the Honored One*, one fascicle. Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). The above is a different translation of the same original as the *Āṣāḍha Sūtra* from the thirty-seventh fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.

*The Sūtra on the Merit of the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, Compassion, and Renunciation*, one fascicle; translator lost, now appended to the *Dongjin lu* (Catalogue of the Eastern Jin) as part of the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). *The Sūtra of Sudatta*, one fascicle—also known as the *Sūtra of the Elder Sudatta*; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavidi of India during the Tianqi era of the Xiao Qi dynasty. The two sūtras above are the same text with different translations.
Extracted from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume 39.

It shares the same original text as the *Sudatta Sūtra*. The wording of the *Maitracitta-vidvega-guṇa Sūtra* is largely identical; however, there are some titles that state it is "extracted from the twelfth [chapter] of the *Ekottara Āgama*," which is incorrect.

*The Sūtra on Training Spoken by the Buddha for the Old Brahmin of the Yellow Bamboo Garden*, one fascicle. Lost among the translations in Sengyou’s Catalogue; now appended to the Song Catalogue and included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement). The above is extracted from the fortieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Huanglu yuan jing* (Sūtra on the Yellow Reed Garden).
*Fanmoyu jing*, one fascicle; translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. The above is excerpted from the forty-first fascicle of the *Zhong ahan jing*.
This is a different translation of the same text as the *Brahmāyu Sūtra*; compared to that original, this version is somewhat abbreviated.

One fascicle of the *Āyuṣmān* Sūtra, translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa and included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). The above is extracted from the forty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation of the same text as the *Zhongchan shi zun jing* (Sūtra on the Venerable of the Central Meditation Chamber) translated by Śikṣānanda.

The *Yingwu jing* (Śuka-sūtra), one fascicle, also titled the *Douzhao jing*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. The *Douzhao jing*, one fascicle. Sengyou’s catalogue states that it was lost in translation under Master Dao’an; it is now appended to the Western Jin catalogue. These two sūtras listed above are included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) as different translations of the same original text.
This is identical in substance to the *Śuka-sūtra* (The Parrot Sutra) in the forty-fourth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.

*I-ching* (The Meaning Sutra), one fascicle; translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa and included here as a supplement. The above is from the forty-fifth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
A different translation from the same original text as the *Heart Sūtra*.

One fascicle of the *Ānanda-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*, translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa; included in the *Supplement* (*Shiyi*). The above appears in the forty-fifth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Yǔ hòu shòu fǎ jīng* (Sūtra on Receiving the Dharma Afterwards).

One fascicle of the *Nílí jīng* (Niraya Sūtra), also known as the *Zhōng āhán nílí jīng* (Madhyama Āgama Niraya Sūtra), translated by the Śramaṇa Zhú Tánwúlán of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. The above is extracted from the fifty-third fascicle of the *Zhōng āhán jīng*.
These are different translations of the same text as the *Dichihui di jing* (Sūtra on the Stages of Delusion and Wisdom).

*Upāśikā Duōshèjiā jīng* (The Sūtra of the Upāsikā Śakrā), one fascicle. This was among the scriptures of unknown translators in Sengyou’s catalogue; it is now appended to the Song catalogue. *Zhāijīng* (The Sūtra on Fasting), one fascicle; also known as the *Chízhāi*. Translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement) collection. The two sūtras above are different translations of the same text.
Extracted from the Madhyama Āgama, Volume 55.
It is the same text as the *Upoṣadha-sūtra*.
*Vimāsa-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song Dynasty; appended to the Supplements. The above is extracted from the Madhyama Āgama, Volume 57.
A different translation of the same text as the *Vimānāvadāna-sūtra*. One fascicle:

*The Sūtra on the Death of a Brahmin’s Son and the Unceasing Love and Remembrance*. Translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). The above appears in the sixtieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation of the same original text as the *Āditta-sutta* (The Discourse on Being Kindled by Lust).

The *Daśa-aṅga-gṛhapati-aṣṭapura-puruṣa-sūtra*, one fascicle—also simply titled *Aṅga*—was translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. The above is extracted from the sixtieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Yubachi jing* (Sūtra on the Eight Cities).

*Xiejian jing* (Sūtra on False Views), one fascicle; listed among the "Translated Scriptures of Lost Translators" in Sengyou’s Catalogue and included here as a supplement to the Song Catalogue. The above is extracted from the sixtieth fascicle of the *Zhong ahan jing*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Dṛṣṭasūtra*.
*Śalyopamasūtra*, one fascicle; translator lost; included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement); now appended to the Jin Catalogue. The above is extracted from the sixtieth fascicle of the *Madhyamāgama*.
A different translation from the same original text as the *Sūtra of the Simile of the Arrow*.

*The Sūtra on the Meaning of the Universal Dharma* (one fascicle), also known as the *Sūtra on the Practice Endowed with the Dharma* or the *Sūtra of Universal Meaning*. Translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. First translation: *The Sūtra of the Extensive Gate of Meaning* (one fascicle). Translated by the Central India Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty. Third translation: one is missing. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text. Regarding the *Sūtra of the Extensive Gate of Meaning*, its initial title states:
Among these, one chapter from the Madhyama Āgama was translated separately.
Upon examining the original Sanskrit version of the *Madhyama Āgama*, this particular sutra is not found;
it is possible that the translation from the Sanskrit text was incomplete.
Since it is stated that this was extracted from that [text], it should be appended at the end;
its inclusion among the single-text Mahāyāna works in the *Dazhou Zanglu* (Great Zhou Catalogue) is an error.
Furthermore, it is possible that this single scripture, the *Fǎpǔ* (Universal Dharma), has not been fully translated from the Sanskrit original.
Since it is stated that these were extracted from those [other texts] and appended to the end,
their inclusion as independent Mahāyāna works in the *Dàzhōu Rùzàng Lù* (Great Zhou Catalogue of Works Included in the Canon) is an error.

Furthermore, the *Fǎpǔyì Jīng* (Sūtra on the Meaning of the Universal Dharma) should read *Shèrìjù Fǎxíng Jīng* (Sūtra on the Dharma Practice of Śāriputra), with "舍日具" being a corruption of "舍利弗" (Śāriputra).
Only these two characters differ;
the rest of the text is without variation.
This applies from the *Saptajñāna-sūtra* down to the fifty-third sūtra.
Both are extracted from the *Madhyama Āgama*, being separate sūtras with different translations:

*Jièdéxiāng jīng* (Sutra on the Fragrance of Moral Virtue), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Jièdé jīng* (Sutra on Moral Virtue). Translated by the Western Region Śramaṇa Zhú Tánwúlán during the Eastern Jin dynasty. The above is extracted from the thirteenth fascicle of the *Ekottara Āgama*.

*The Sūtra on the Appearance of Four Persons in the World*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. This was included as a supplement. The above is a variant translation of the "Chapter on the Four Right Efforts" from the eighteenth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

*The Sūtra on King Prasenajit’s Empress’s Death and Her Body Being Covered in Dust*, one fascicle; translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju. The above is an alternative translation of the "Chapter on the Four Right Exertions" (*Caturdharmaprahāṇavarga*) from the eighteenth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

*The Sūtra of the Girl Sumati*, one fascicle; translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). The above is extracted from the twentieth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
The *Sūtra on the Brāhmaṇa Avoiding Death* (one fascicle), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty.
The above is an alternative translation of the "Sudatta Chapter" from the twenty-third fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the "Chapter on the Superior."

*Sūtra on the Five Kinds of Auspicious Rewards for Giving Food* (one fascicle). Also known as *Sūtra on Bestowing Physical Strength* or *Sūtra on Merit*. Translator lost; currently appended to the Eastern Jin catalogue. The above is extracted from the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

*The Sūtra on King Bimbisāra Visiting the Buddha to Make Offerings*, translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju; also known as *The Sūtra on King Bimbisāra*. This was extracted from the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the "Chapter on Equal Views. Compared to the original sūtra, this version is somewhat more concise in its phrasing. Its inclusion in the Mahāyāna canon in various catalogs is an error.

*The Sūtra on the Six Times the Son of a Householder Leaves Home*, one fascicle; translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Huìjiǎn. The above is an alternative translation of the "Chapter on Assemblies" (Pūga-varga) from the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*; this sūtra is somewhat more extensive.

*The Aṅgulimāla Sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Sūtra of the One Named Māra* or *The Sūtra of the Finger-Crest*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection), fascicle thirty-two among the thirty-two fascicles of the same volume.
*The Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin. The two sūtras above are the same text with different translations.
They appear in the thirty-first fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*, in the "Chapter on Power" (*Bala-varga*); this version is somewhat more extensive.

*The Scripture on the Malla Shifting Mountains*, one fascicle; alternatively titled simply *The Scripture on Shifting Mountains*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. *The Scripture on the Four Unprecedented Dharmas*, one fascicle; also called *The Scripture on the Four Unprecedented [Events]*, or sometimes omitting the character "fa" (dharma). Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. The above two scriptures are alternative translations of the "Chapter on the Eight Difficulties" in the thirty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*. They are separate translations of a single scripture, divided into two versions. These are somewhat more extensive than what appears here, as this [present collection] does not contain them in their entirety.

*Śāriputra-mahāmaudgalyāyana-catuṣpatha-saṃcāra-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Meng Xiang of the Western Regions during the Later Han dynasty. The above [text] appears as a variant translation of the "Horse King Chapter" (Aśvavarga) in the forty-first fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*. Its inclusion in the Zhou catalog among the Mahāyāna re-translations is an error.

*Saptabuddhapitṛmātṛnāman-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Names of the Parents of the Seven Buddhas), one fascicle; also known as *Saptabuddhanāman-sūtra*. Translator unknown during the Cao Wei dynasty. The above is an alternative translation of the "Chapter on the Unwholesome" in the forty-fifth fascicle of the *Ekottarika-āgama*.

*Fàngniú jīng* (Sūtra on Letting Cattle Loose), one fascicle; also known as *Mùniú jīng* (Sūtra on Tending Cattle). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yaoqin period. The above is an alternative translation of the "Fàngniú pǐn" (Chapter on Letting Cattle Loose) from the forty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*; this version is somewhat more extensive.

*Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *Dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. According to the *Fanying tu* (Catalogue of Translated Scriptures), this is a variant translation of the "Cowherd Chapter" (*Gopālaka-varga*) from the forty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika-āgama*. It is an error to include this in the catalog of Mahāyāna single-text scriptures, as the text here is somewhat more abbreviated than that in the original [Āgama] scripture.

*The Scripture on Eleven Contemplations and Mindfulness of the Tathāgata*, one scroll; alternatively titled *Eleven Contemplations*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). The above is an alternative translation of the beginning of the "Chapter on Paying Homage to the Triple Gem" in the forty-eighth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*. Of these eleven [chapters], two scriptures are connected: the first eleven items have identical text and meaning when compared, while the latter eleven items have not yet been found upon investigation.

*The Sutra of the Four Nirayas*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Four Great Nirayas*. Translated by the Western Region Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Eastern Jin dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). The above is a variant translation of the "Chapter on Paying Homage to the Three Jewels" from the forty-eighth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*; this version is somewhat more extensive.

*The Sūtra on Anāthapiṇḍada Converting His Seven Sons*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty. The above is an alternative translation of the "Chapter on Impermanence" (Asaṃskṛtavarga) in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, fascicle 49. This sūtra contains accounts of only four sons, though the general meaning is largely the same [as the other version].

*The Scripture on the Parinirvāṇa of Maitrāyaṇī*, one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Bai Fazang of Henei during the Western Jin dynasty. *The Scripture on the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha-Mother*, one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Huijian of the Song dynasty. These two scriptures, listed as supplementary additions, are the same text with different translations.
From the *Ekottarika Āgama*, Volume 50, the Chapter on the Parinirvāṇa of Mahāprajāpatī.

*The Scripture of King Bimbisāra’s Ten Dreams*, one fascicle. Translated by the Western Region Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Eastern Jin. *The Scripture of the King of Śrāvastī Dreaming Ten Matters*, one fascicle. Sengyou’s Catalogue states that it was lost during the time of Master Dao’an; it is now appended to the supplementary records of the Western Jin. These two scriptures above are the same text with different translations, appearing in the Chapter on the Parinirvāṇa of Mahāprajāpatī in the fifth volume of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

The *Ānanda-sahāya-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty. Regarding the aforementioned *Ānanda-sahāya-sūtra*, its initial title states that it is extracted from the *Ekottarika Āgama*. Upon examining the original version of that [Āgama], this sūtra is not found therein. Since it is stated to have been extracted from that source, it has been appended here at the end.
The twenty-four sutras from the *Jièdéxiāng jīng* (Sutra on the Fragrance of Precepts) onward are all alternative translations of separate sutras from the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

*Sūtra on the Emptiness of the Five Aggregates*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang. Newly included in the catalog. The above is an alternative translation of the second fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. Although this *Sūtra on the Emptiness of the Five Aggregates* appears within the thirty-ninth fascicle of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, it is not treated as a separate production [of a standalone sutra]. Therefore, it is preserved without being discarded; for this is a Vinaya citation of a sūtra, rather than a sūtra originating from the Vinaya.

*The Sūtra on the Seven Stations and Three Contemplations*, one fascicle (or two fascicles), translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. The above was excerpted from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*; it is an alternative translation of this sūtra. From beginning to end, there are thirty sūtras: the first is "The Seven Stations and Three Contemplations," and the last is titled "Accumulated Bones. It is named after its opening title. The initial *Sūtra on the Seven Stations and Three Contemplations* appears in fascicle two, while the subsequent *Sūtra on Accumulated Bones* appears in fascicle thirty-four; the remaining sūtras are scattered throughout various texts without following a fixed order.

*The Sūtra on the Seal of the Noble Dharma* (Ārya-dharmamudrā-sūtra), one fascicle; also known as *The Sūtra on the Direct Seal of the Noble* or *The Sūtra on the Seal of Wisdom*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty. The above is an alternative translation from the third fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

*Saṃyukta Āgama*, one fascicle. Translator unknown. [Appears] in the *Wei and Wu Records*. The following is an alternative translation from within the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
