This scripture contains twenty-seven sūtras from beginning to end; the first three sūtras appear in the fourth fascicle, though their sequence is not in order. The *Saptasthāna-triparīkṣā-sūtra* stands at the end of this fascicle; its wording is largely identical to the preceding sūtras, though it is somewhat more extensive. The *Asthisaṃcaya-sūtra* is also included therein, though it is unclear why these two sūtras overlap. The remaining sūtras are scattered throughout the expanded text. Various ancient catalogs all state that the translator is lost. Upon examining the wording and phrasing, they are somewhat similar in style and reasoning to the *Saptasthāna-triparīkṣā-sūtra*; thus, they likely originated from An Shigao. However, as no authentic record has been seen, I have provisionally maintained the traditional designation of "translator unknown."

*The Parable of the Five Aggregates* (Wǔyīn pìyù jīng), one fascicle; also titled *The Sūtra on Being Drifted by Water Froth* (Shuǐmò suǒpiāo jīng) or *The Parable of the Five Aggregates* (Wǔyīn yù jīng). Translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master Ān Shìgāo of the Later Han. *The Sūtra on Being Drifted by Water Froth* (Shuǐmò suǒpiāo jīng), one fascicle; also titled *The Sūtra on the Great Mass of Froth in the River Equal to an Arm* (Hézhōng dàjù mòbì jīng). Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhú Tánwúlán of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin. These two sūtras above are of the same original text as the tenth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, being alternative translations thereof. They have been included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection).

*The Scripture on Not Guarding One’s Own Mind* (or *The Scripture on No Mind*), one fascicle; translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty. The above is an alternative translation of the eleventh fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

*Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra-sūtra*, one fascicle; translator lost during the Jin dynasty, now appended to the *Dongjin lu* (Catalogue of the Eastern Jin) as part of the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Omissions). The above is a variant translation of the thirteenth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

*The Sūtra on Turning the Wheel of Dharma*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Sūtra on the Revolution of the Wheel*. Translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. *The Sūtra on the Three Turnings of the Wheel of Dharma*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yi Jing of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog. The above two sūtras are the same text, translated differently from the fifteenth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. Although this *Sūtra on the Three Turnings of the Wheel of Dharma* appears within the nineteenth fascicle of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, it is not treated as a separate independent work. Therefore, it is preserved here without being discarded. This is a citation of a sūtra within the Vinaya; while its latter portion is identical to the original sūtra, the former portion differs. The reason for this remains unclear.

*The Sūtra on the Eightfold Noble Path*, one fascicle; translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty. The above is a variant translation from the twenty-eighth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

*Nandika-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin. The above is an alternative translation from the thirtieth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. There are two sūtras in the larger version [of this text], which are here combined into one; its text is somewhat more extensive. It was previously listed among the single-fascicle works in old catalogs, but it is now included here.

*The Scripture on the Three Characteristics of Horses*, one fascicle; also titled *The Good Have Three Characteristics*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhi Yao of the Western Regions during the Later Han. *The Scripture on the Eight States of Horses Compared to Humans*, one fascicle; also simply titled *The Eight States*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhi Yao of the Western Regions during the Later Han. The above two scriptures both appear as alternative translations of the thirty-third fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

*Xiāngyìngxiàngkě jīng* (Sūtra on the Characteristics of Correspondence), one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Omissions) section as a variant translation from among the previously mentioned single-fascicle *Zá Āhán Jīng*.

*Treatise on the Secret Essentials for Healing the Diseases of Dhyāna*, one fascicle (alternatively titled *Dharma-Abhāva*; or two fascicles). Translated by the lay devotee Juqu Jingsheng of the Song dynasty. Regarding the above scripture, its initial title reads: "Questioned by the Venerable Śāriputra; excerpted from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, within the section on miscellaneous matters concerning araṇya-dwellers. Now, upon searching the extant large edition of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, these texts are not found. It is possible that the Sanskrit manuscript was not fully translated. Since it is stated to have been extracted from that source, I have appended it here at the end. However, upon examining the literary style, it slightly overlaps with Mahāyāna sūtras; as it was previously compiled among the collected transmissions (*ji zhuan*), I fear it may be somewhat deviant. The thirty-one scriptures above comprise thirty-one fascicles in a single volume. From the *Sūtra on the Emptiness of the Five Aggregates* onwards, the sixteen scriptures are all variant translations of sūtras from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

*Māndhātṛ-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *Ānanda-huodao-nü-huo-jing*. Translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Parthia during the Later Han. First translation. *Māndhātṛ-sūtra Explaining Six Matters Within the Body*, one fascicle. Translator lost; currently appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin. Fifth translation. *Māndhātṛ-sūtra*, three fascicles (or two fascicles). Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Zhu Lüyan and Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. Recorded in the *Fashang-lu*. Third translation. *Śatruñjaya-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *Taizi-ershiba-xiu-jing* or *Hu’er-jing*. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu. Fourth translation. The above four sūtras are different translations of the same original text. Of these, the first sūtra consists only of one chapter from the latter [text]. Thus, there are five translations in total, though one translation is missing.

*The Scripture on the Ghosts’ Questions to Maudgalyāyana*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han—First Translation. *The Scripture on the Miscellaneous Collection*, one fascicle; its textual principles differ slightly from the preceding and following scriptures; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faxian of Pingyang during the Eastern Jin—Second Translation. *The Scripture on the Retribution of Hungry Ghosts*, one fascicle; also titled *The Scripture on the Causes and Conditions of Hells and Hungry Ghosts Spoken by Maudgalyāyana*; translator lost, now appended to the Eastern Jin catalog—Third Translation. The above three scriptures are different translations of the same original text. Of the four translations listed in sequence, one translation is missing.

*Ānanda-questions-on-the-auspicious-and-inauspicious-of-servicing-the-Buddha Sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *Ānanda-questions-Sūtra* or *Sūtra on the Auspicious and Inauspicious of Servicing the Buddha*. Translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. First Translation. *Daman-fa Sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin; included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). Second Translation. *Ānanda-pinfen Sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Shengjian of the Qifu Qin. Third Translation. The above three sūtras are different translations of the same original text. Regarding the *Daman-fa Sūtra*, it has been newly retranslated. Thus, there are four translations in total, one of which is missing.

*The Sūtra of the Five Mothers and Sons*, one fascicle; translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty]; first translation. *The Śamīra Sūtra*, one fascicle; according to Sengyou’s Catalogue, it was among the "Alternative Translations from Guanzhong by Master Dao'an" and is recorded in the *Sanqin Lu*; second translation. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text. Regarding the *Śamīra Sūtra*, the *Dazhou Lu* states it was translated by Dharmakṣema; however, the *Changfang Lu* notes that upon searching the catalogues, this is not found there—the entry in the *Dazhou Lu* is an error.

*Yujie nü jing* (The Scripture of the Girl Yujie), one fascicle; alternatively called *Yuye jing*. Sengyou’s catalogue states it was a scripture of unknown translator from the period of Master Dao’an. It is now appended to the records of the Western Jin dynasty as its initial appearance. *Shiyi bian*: *Yujie jing*, one fascicle, also titled *Zhangzhe yi fo shuo zi fu wu jing jing* (The Scripture of the Elder Visiting the Buddha to Speak of His Daughter-in-law’s Lack of Reverence). Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. Second translation: *Asuda jing*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. Third translation: [Title missing]. The above three scriptures are translations of the same original text with different versions.

*Xiūxíng běnqǐ jīng* (Sūtra on the Original Deeds of Practice), two fascicles; also known as *Sùxíng běnqǐ* (Original Deeds of Past Conduct). Translated by the Western Region śramaṇa Zhú Dàlì and Kāng Mèngxiáng during the Later Han dynasty. The second translation [of this work] is included in the same volume as the sixteen preceding sūtras, totaling nineteen fascicles.

*The Sūtra on the Auspicious Response of the Prince’s Original Enlightenment*, two fascicles; also titled *The Original Enlightenment and Auspicious Response*, or simply *The Auspicious Original Enlightenment*. Translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty]. Fourth translation. *The Sūtra on Cause and Effect in Past and Present*, four fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song [Dynasty]. Sixth translation. The three sūtras listed above are the same text translated differently. Of the first two sūtras, the texts are brief and incomplete. Among the six translations, three are missing from the record.

*Fǎhǎi jīng* (Sūtra on the Ocean of Dharma), one fascicle; translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Fǎjù. Included in the *Shíyí* (Supplementary Collection). Second translation: *Hǎibādé jīng* (Sūtra on the Eight Virtues of the Ocean), one fascicle; translated by the Yao Qin Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva. Recorded in the catalog of Fǎshàng and included in the *Shíyí*. Third translation: The two sūtras above are translations of the same text with different versions. Of the three translations from the Later Han, one is missing.
*The Sutra in Forty-two Sections*, one fascicle.

Translated by the Indian śramaṇa Kāśyapa Mātanga and Zhu Fahu during the Later Han dynasty. This is the first of two translations; one version is missing. *The Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of the Maiden Amrapālī and Jīvaka*, one fascicle. Sometimes the word "causes and conditions" is omitted, or it is simply titled *The Sutra of the Maiden Amrapālī*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty.

The first translation consists of two versions; one is missing. *Zuìyè bàoyìng jiàohuà dìyù jīng* (Sūtra on the Teaching of Hellish Retribution for Karmic Offenses), one fascicle; also known as *Dìyù bàoyìng jīng* (Sūtra on Hellish Retribution).
Translated by An Shigao, Tripitaka Master of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty.
The first translation;
the second translation is missing: *Nāgarājaputrabhrātṛ-sūtra*, one fascicle—also titled *Nanda-nāgarāja-sūtra* or *Nāgarāja-vinaya-sūtra*.
Translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian.

The first translation consists of two versions; one is missing. *Jiāzhǎng Yīnyuè Jīng* (Sūtra on the Elder Yīnyuè), also known as *Jiāzhǎng Yīnyuè Bùlánjiāshè Jīng* (Sūtra on the Elder Yīnyuè and Pūraṇa Kāśyapa), translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty.

Of the two translations for the first [work], one is missing; the nine preceding scriptures, totaling thirteen fascicles, were previously included in the same volume. Among them, the *Dīrgha-āgama-sūtra* (Chángzhě yīnyuè jīng) was recorded in the *Zhōu lù* and categorized within the Mahāyāna Piṭaka; however, upon examining its literary structure and principles, it has now been moved here.
*The Sūtra on the Secret Essentials of Dhyāna*, three fascicles (alternatively titled *The Secret Essentials of the Dharma of Dhyāna*); four fascicles;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty;
second translation.

Regarding the three translations, two are missing. To the right: this *Dhyāna-guhyārtha-sūtra* was included among the ancient catalogs within the section on "Biographies" (*Avadāna*). Now, having examined the beginning, middle, and end of this sūtra, its three parts are extremely clear; the text throughout largely elucidates dhyāna-contemplation. Regarding the contemplation of the Buddha and other such practices, it clarifies the matter of repentance for extinguishing grave offenses. However, as it slightly overlaps with Mahāyāna teachings and is not a work of human composition, it has been moved here. Furthermore, among the various catalogs there is another work titled the *Dhyānārtha-sūtra* in five fascicles, said to have been translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of the Song dynasty; its text is highly disordered and cannot be circulated.

As described in detail in the *Shanfan-lu*, the *Saptakanyā-sūtra* in one fascicle—also known as the *Saptakanyā-pūrva-vṛttaka-sūtra*—was translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty (the first translation); of the three translations, two are missing. The *Aṣṭācārya-sūtra* in one fascicle was also translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty.
*Yue-nan jing* (Sūtra on Overcoming Difficulties), one fascicle; also known as *Ri-nan chang-zhe jing* (Sūtra of the Elder Sunakṣatra) or simply *Nan jing* (Sūtra of Difficulties).
Translated by the lay devotee Nie Chengyuan of the Western Jin dynasty.
[First Translation]
*Yùsuǒzhìhuàn jīng* (Sūtra on the Sufferings Resulting from Desires), one fascicle;
translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa.

First translation; second translation missing. *Aśeshewáng wèn wǔnì jīng* (Sūtra on King Ajātaśatru’s Inquiry into the Five Heinous Offenses), one fascicle. First translation; second translation missing.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin Dynasty;
collected as a supplement and included in the second translation.

One of the two translations lacks it; *Wǔkǔ zhāngjù jīng* (Sūtra on the Verses of the Five Sufferings), also known as *Wǔdào zhāngjù jīng* (Sūtra on the Verses of the Five Paths), translated by the Śramaṇa Zhú Tánwúlán of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
This is the first translation.

In one of the two translations, the *Jiānyì jīng* (Sūtra on Firm Resolve), one fascicle— also known as the *Jiānxīn zhèngyì jīng* (Sūtra on Firm Mind and Right Resolve) or the *Jiānxīn jīng* (Sūtra on Firm Mind)—
translated by An Shigao, the Tripiṭaka Master from Parthia during the Later Han dynasty, is missing.
The first translation is the *Jìngfàn wáng nièpán jīng* (Sūtra on the Nirvāṇa of King Śuddhodana), one fascicle.

Translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng. Second translation; one of the two translations is missing. *Dedao ti Deng xizhang jing* (The Scripture on the Monk Deng’s Staff for Attaining the Way), one fascicle; also simply titled *Xizhang jing* (Scripture on the Staff); lost translation, now appended to the Eastern Jin catalogue. Regarding this *Xizhang jing*, the *Dazhou lu* states it was extracted from the *Za puyi jing* (Miscellaneous Parable Scripture). Since it is not found in the current major collections, it is difficult to establish a definitive standard, and thus it is included here. *Pinqiong laoweng jing* (Scripture of the Poor Old Man), one fascicle; also known as *Pinlao jing* (Scripture of the Poor Old Man);

translated by the Song śramaṇa Shi Huijian. Second translation; one of the two translations is missing. *Sammajia jing* (Scripture of Samma-jia), one fascicle; also known as *Nuhe dan wang jing* (Scripture of King Nohandan) or *Nanguo wang jing* (Scripture of King Nanguo); translated by the Wu Indian śramaṇa Zhu Lüyian.

Regarding the first and second translations, one is missing. To the right: this *Samyukta-māgadhika-sūtra* (or *Māgadhika-sūtra*), according to the *Catalogue of the Great Zhou*, is said to have been extracted from the *Ekottarika-āgama*. However, upon examining that [Āgama], it is not found there; thus, it is included here. One fascicle, titled *The Sūtra of King Piṅgala’s Five Vows*, also known as the *Sūtra of King Puṣya*, translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty.

Regarding the first and second translations, one is missing. To the right: these records of the *Pañcaśikha-rāja-pañcāśa-praṇidhāna-sūtra* from the *Dazhou Catalogue* and others all state that it was extracted from the *Madhyama Āgama*. However, upon examining the text of that [Āgama], it is not found there; thus, it is included here.
One fascicle of the *Vaiḍūryarāja-sūtra*, translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa.

Regarding the second translation, one of the two is missing. According to the *Dazhou* and other catalogs, this *Sūtra of King Vimalacitra* belongs to the *Ekottarika Āgama*; however, although the narrative concerning King Vimalacitra exists within the thirty-sixth section of that collection, the meaning and intent differ entirely. Therefore, it has been compiled here. The fifteen preceding sūtras comprise seventy fascicles and are contained in the same volume.

The *Sheng jing* (Birth Sūtras), five fascicles, containing fifty sūtras, or [alternatively] four fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. First translation; two translations exist, one being missing. The *Yizu jing* (Sūtra on the Fulfillment of Meaning), two fascicles, containing sixteen sūtras; translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty. First translation; two translations exist, one being missing. The above two works comprise seven fascicles in a single volume. Although these twenty-two sūtras, from the *Sishier zhang jing* (Sūtra in Forty-two Sections) downwards, are retranslations, they are currently extant in circulation, though only in a single copy each; the others have all been lost and cannot be found despite diligent search.

Small Vehicle Sūtras Translated Individually: Eighty-seven works in two hundred twenty-four fascicles, arranged in seventeen bundles. *The Sūtra on the Stations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma* (Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra), seventy fascicles, seven bundles.

Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei. Note: This *Sūtra on the Stations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma* is listed as a "re-translation" in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. To claim it is an alternative translation of the same original text as the *Sūtra of the Goose King Kāla* is an error. The *Sūtra of the Goose King Kāla* was excerpted from this very scripture; the former is a derivative work, while the latter is the original independent text. *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds* (Buddhacarita-saṃgraha), sixty fascicles.

Six fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty, etc. Note: This *Buddhacarita-sūtra* is listed in the catalog of the Great Zhou as a Mahāyāna re-translation. To claim it is the same text as the seven-fascicle *Buddhacarita-sūtra* but a different translation is an error. That [seven-fascicle version] consists of verses of praise and differs vastly from this one. Various catalogs place it either among the Mahāyāna sūtras or within the *Xiuzheng zhuan* (Biographies of Cultivation and Correction). Fearing that such classifications may be erroneous, I have now moved it here to be included with the seven-fascicle *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang.
From the *Chūn-tien-lu* (Catalogue of Inner and Outer Scriptures): *Xingqixing jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of Deeds), two fascicles; also titled *Yanjie suyuan* (Admonition on Past Causes).

The title states it was translated by the foreign Tripiṭaka Master Kang Mengxiang of the Later Han dynasty from the *Zazang* (Miscellaneous Piṭaka). Commentary: Regarding this *Xingqixing jing*, the *Dazhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalogue) states that the sūtra is a re-translation and claims it is a different translation of the same original text as the *Mushuang cizuo yinyuan jing* (Sūtra on the Cause and Condition of Being Pierced in the Foot by a Wooden Spear). This is an error. Upon examining the original text, there are ten causes and conditions in total; the *Mushuang jiao jing* is simply one of these ten causes. It has been excerpted and circulated separately, similar to the case of Avalokiteśvara and others. Since it is not a second translation, it stands as a single-text edition. *Ye bao chabie jing* (Sūtra on the Differentiation of Karmic Retribution), one fascicle.

Translated by Dharmanandin of Yangchuan Commandery during the Sui Dynasty. The three aforementioned sūtras comprise ten fascicles in one volume. Regarding the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra*, it is incorrect for the *Dazhou Catalogue* to claim that it is a different translation of the same original text as the *Pāpapunyavipāka-sūtra*. Upon examining its phrasing and doctrinal intent, they are vastly different; thus, it stands as a separate, independent work.

*The Scripture on Guarding the Mind through the Great Ānāpāna*, two fascicles (also simply titled *The Scripture on the Great Ānāpāna*). Master Dao’an states that it may also be called the *Small Ānāpāna*, or it may consist of one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty.

[According to] the catalog of the Great Zhou and others, there is also a version of the *Great Ānāpāna* in one fascicle, likewise attributed to An Shigao; however, upon collating its phrases and sentences, it is identical to the first fascicle of the *Ānāpāna-shouyi*. Since the text is entirely the same, it is not recorded here again. *The Scripture on the Bases, Elements, and Entrances* (*Yin-chi-ru jing*), two fascicles (the character "chu" may be an error for "yin," or it may consist of one fascicle).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han dynasty. *The Scripture on Various Places* (*Chu-chu jing*), one fascicle.
*The Sūtra on Rebuking the Mind*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han;

included in the *Supplemental Collection*. *The Sūtra on the Arising of Good and Evil*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han; included in the *Supplemental Collection*.

*The Sūtra on the Conditions for Leaving Home*, one fascicle—also titled *The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Leaving Home*—translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han; included in the *Supplemental Collection*.
*The Sūtra on Right Practice of Aṅga*, one fascicle—also titled *The Sūtra on Right Intention*—translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty.
*The Sūtra on the Eighteen Nirayas*, one fascicle—also called *The Sūtra on the Eighteen Hells*—translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty.
*The Sūtra on the Reception of Dharmas and Dust*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty.
*The Sūtra on the Contemplation of Dharma in the Practice of Dhyāna*, one fascicle, translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Parthia during the Later Han.

*The Sūtra on the Elder’s Son’s Lamentation over Three States*, one fascicle, translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Parthia during the Later Han; also known as *The Sūtra on the Elder’s Premature Death and Lamentation*, or *The Sūtra on the Three States of Lamentation*.
*The Sūtra of King Khandha*, one fascicle, translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Parthia during the Later Han; sometimes the character for "king" (國) is omitted.
*The Sūtra of the Householder Sumati*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty;
*The Sūtra on the Four Matters of Ānanda*, one fascicle, translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty; *The Sūtra of Ajātaśatru*, one fascicle.
*The Sūtra of the Four Vows*, one fascicle, translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty].
*The Sūtra of the Black Brahmin*, one fascicle, translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty].
*The Sūtra of the Mad Dog*, one fascicle, included as a supplement; Sengyou states it is identical to the *Lüegou jing*.

*Fenbie jing* (Sūtra on the Analysis), one fascicle, translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian; it was previously claimed to be the same text as the *Ahan fenbie jing*, but this is incorrect.
*Baguanzhai jing* (Sūtra on the Eight Precepts of the Fast), one fascicle, translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa.

*Ajiuliu jing* (Āgama Sūtra), one fascicle, translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng. Sengyou’s catalogue states: "An Gong’s *Gudian jing* (Classical Sūtras); now appended to the Han catalogue. *Xiaozijing* (Sūtra on Filial Sons), one fascicle; also called the *Xiao baoen jing* (Sūtra on Filial Piety and Repaying Kindness). Sengyou’s catalogue states: "An Gong’s *Shiyi jing* (Lost Translations)."
Now appended to the Western Jin Record, these twenty-two scriptures in twenty-four fascicles are collected together in this single volume as supplementary additions.

*The Sutra on the Self-Exposition of the Origins of the Five Hundred Disciples*, one fascicle; some editions omit the character "explanation" (shuō), and it is also called *The Sutra of the Beginning and End*.
Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. *The Mahākāśyapa Sūtra*, one fascicle; some editions omit the character "root" (běn).
*The Scripture on the Four Self-Inflicted Injuries*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin.
*The Scripture on Rāhula’s Patience*, one fascicle; also simply titled *The Scripture on Patience*; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin.
*The Scripture on the Buddha Teaching the Young Bhikṣus Concerning Proper Matters*, one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin.
*Śāgha Bhikṣu-guṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju. *Time and Non-time Sūtra* (*Kāla-akāla-sūtra*), one fascicle, translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju;
alternatively titled simply *Time Sūtra*, translated by the foreign Dharma Master Yeluo Yan (Yarodhana), the imperial era of its production being unknown.

*Sūtra Postscript*: Regarding the *Time and Non-time Sūtra*, all catalogs state it was translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Faju. However, the colophon at the end of the sūtra states: "The foreign Dharma Master Yeluo Yan held the Hu (foreign) manuscript in his hand and orally proclaimed the translation; the Daoist Zhong of Liangzhou transcribed it within the city for memorization. Based on this record in the sūtra itself, it is considered authoritative. Since the imperial era remains unknown, it is provisionally appended to the Western Jin records. *Self-Love Sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *Self-Love and Non-Self-Love*.

*Zhongxin jing* (Sūtra on the Central Mind), one fascicle; also titled *Zhongxin zhengxing jing* (Sūtra on the Correct Practice of the Central Mind). Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. *Jianzheng jing* (Sūtra on Seeing the Correct), one fascicle;

also known as *Shengsi bianshi jing* (Sūtra on the Transformation of Consciousness through Birth and Death). Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
*Dayu shi jing* (Sūtra on the Matter of the Great Fish), one fascicle. Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
*Ānanda’s Seven Dreams Sūtra*, one fascicle—also simply titled *Seven Dreams Sūtra*—translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
*The Sūtra on the Hārītī Anāgāmin*, one fascicle—also known as *Hārītī* (sometimes written as *Kē*)—translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
*Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Lamp-Finger*, one fascicle.
*The Scripture on a Woman Meeting with Calamity*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin;
also known as *The Scripture on a Woman Meeting with Adversity*, translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Shengjian of the Qifu Qin.

*The Scripture of the Four Heavenly Kings*, one fascicle, translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhijian of Liangzhou together with Baoyun of the Song dynasty. *The Scripture on Mahākāśyapa Saving a Poor Mother*, one fascicle.
*The Scripture on the Twelve Stages of Birth and Death*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty.

*The Scripture on the Retribution of Sin and Merit*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty; also titled *The Scripture on the Retribution of Sin and Merit in the Revolving of the Five Paths*. [Note: In the catalog of the Great Zhou, there is additionally a *Scripture on the Retribution of Sin and Merit in the Revolving of the Five Paths*, one fascicle. Upon examining its phrasing, it is no different from this [present text]; only the titles differ in their brevity or detail. Since the text itself contains no variation, only one version is retained. *The Scripture on the Five Things Without Return*, one fascicle;

also titled *The Scripture on the Great Meaning of the Five Things Without Return*. Translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng. *The Scripture of the Buddha’s Greatness and the Sangha’s Greatness*, one fascicle.
*The Sūtra of Yajña*, one fascicle, translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng.
*The Sūtra of King Malla*, one fascicle, translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng.
*The Sūtra of King Madaka*, one fascicle, translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng.
*The Sūtra of King Candrāvatī*, one fascicle; translated by the lay devotee Juqu Jingsheng of the Song dynasty (some editions omit the word "King").
*The Sūtra of the Five Terrors of the World*, one fascicle; translated by the lay devotee Juqu Jingsheng of the Song dynasty (some editions omit the word "World").
*The Sūtra of the Disciple Who Died and Was Reborn*, one fascicle; translated by the lay devotee Juqu Jingsheng of the Song dynasty (also titled *The Sūtra of Death and Rebirth*).
*The Sutra on the Lazy Plowman*, one fascicle, translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng; alternatively titled *The Sutra on the Plow Boy*, translated by the Song śramaṇa Shi Huijian;
alternatively titled *The Sutra on the Elder Bianyi*, or with the words "Questioned by" (*suowen*) added [at the beginning].
*The Sutra of the Questioning of the Upright Laywoman*, one fascicle, translated by the Northern Wei śramaṇa Shi Fanchang.
Translated by the Bāṇa Ghoṭamka Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei: thirty fascicles comprising the first thirty sūtras in one volume.
*The Sūtra on the Five Blessings of the Worthy*, one fascicle, translated by the śramaṇa Bai Fazhu of Henei during the Western Jin. *The Sūtra of Questions from Heaven*, one fascicle.
Record of the Inner Scriptures Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang.

The aforementioned *Five Blessings* and *Heavenly Questions* Sūtras were both included among the Mahāyāna sūtras in the catalogs of the Great Zhou and other dynasties. However, upon examining their literary style and principles, they appear to involve elements of the Hīnayāna; therefore, they have been moved here. *Senghu jing* (Senghu Sūtra), one fascicle. Also known as the *Yinyuanyuan* (Causes and Conditions); the translator is lost.
Now appended to the Eastern Jin Record: *The Scripture on Protecting Purity*, one fascicle, translator lost;
now appended to the Eastern Jin Record: *The Scripture on the Wood Bead*, one fascicle—sometimes written with the character 患 (huàn) or 擐 (huàn).
Now appended to the Eastern Jin Records: *The Sutra on the Unsurpassed Place*, one fascicle, translator lost;
now appended to the Eastern Jin Records: *The Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of the Elder Lu Zhi*, one fascicle.
*Wangjing* (Sūtra of the Five Kings), one fascicle; translator lost, now appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin.
Now appended to the Eastern Jin Record: *The Sūtra on the Merit of Leaving Home*, one fascicle;
translator lost, now appended to the Eastern Jin Record.

The *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) includes the following: The *Chujia Gongde Jing* (Sutra on the Merit of Leaving Home) exists in three circulating versions. Although the other two differ in length—being either expanded or abbreviated—they are both said to have been extracted from the *Xianyu Jing* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish). This version records that the Buddha was preaching at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha; it is now included in the *Biesheng Lu* (Separate Record of Additional Translations). Another version records that the Buddha was in the country of Vaiśālī, preaching for the son of Licchavi, Vīrasena. It further states that "Vīrasena" means "Brave Army" (*yǒngjūn*) in the language of Qin. Although the translator’s surname is unknown, this must be a translation from the Qin dynasty. *Zhantan Shu Jing* (Sutra of the Sandalwood Tree), one fascicle. Sengyou’s catalogue states it is among the "Ancient Classics" of Master Dao’an.

Fashang’s catalogue attributes it to Kumārajīva; this is incorrect. It is now appended to the Han dynasty catalogues. *Adouhuo Duoji Jing* (Sutra of Ātuma and Dhṛtaka), one fascicle. Sengyou’s catalogue states it is a work of unknown translatorship by Master Dao’an.

Now appended to the Western Jin Catalogue: *Pudawang jing* (Sūtra of King Puda), one fascicle. Sengyou’s Catalogue states that this was a sūtra whose translator was lost during the time of Master Dao’an; it is now appended to the Western Jin Catalogue.

*Fomiehu hou guanlian zangsong jing* (Sūtra on the Enshrouding and Burial after the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa), one fascicle—also titled *Biqiu shi jing* (Sūtra of the Bhikṣu Teacher) and alternatively titled *Shiseng* (Teacher-Saṃgha). Sengyou’s Catalogue states that this was a sūtra whose translator was lost during the time of Master Dao’an;

it is now appended to the Western Jin Catalogue. *Guizimujing* (Sūtra of Hārītī), one fascicle. Sengyou’s Catalogue states that this was a sūtra whose translator was lost during the time of Master Dao’an.

Now appended to the "Supplementary Records" (*Shiyi*) of the Western Jin catalog, one fascicle of the *Brahmadatta-rāja-sūtra* is included; Sengyou’s catalog states it was a translation by Master Dao’an of unknown provenance, now appended to the Western Jin *Shiyi*.
One fascicle of the *Mātṛ-pitṛ-ṛṇa-duṣpratiniḥsaraṇa-sūtra* is also included;

it is also called the *Qinbao* (Diligently Repaying), translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han, and is appended to the *Shiyi*. One fascicle of the *Sundarī-sūtra* is included; sometimes the word "Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*) is added at the beginning of the title.
*The Scripture on the New Year*, one fascicle, translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Wu;

translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin. The aforementioned three scriptures, including *The Difficulty of Repaying Parental Kindness*, are all stated in the *Dazhou Catalogue* and other records to have been extracted from the *Madhyama Āgama*. However, upon examining the extant versions of the *Madhyama Āgama*, these scriptures are not found therein. Furthermore, although the general purport of the "occasion for the observance of the new year" (varṣā) in the twenty-fourth chapter of the *Ekottara Āgama* is entirely different [from these texts], they are therefore compiled here.

*Qun niu pi jing* (Sutra of the Parable of the Herd of Cows), one fascicle; translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju. Regarding the above *Qun niu pi jing*, the *Dazhou lu* states that it is extracted from the *Ekottarika Āgama*; however, as it is not found therein, it has been included here.
*Jiuheng jing* (Sūtra on the Nine Premature Deaths), one fascicle;

translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Parthia during the Later Han. *Cixing san shiqi jing* (Sūtra on the Thirty-seven Factors of Practice in Meditation), one fascicle; alternatively titled with the word "pin" (chapter) added;

translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Parthia during the Later Han. *Biqiu bi nü ewei zisha jing* (Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Who Commits Suicide to Avoid the Evil Reputation of a Woman), one fascicle.
*The Sutra on the Bhikṣu Hearing of Almsgiving*, one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin; also known as *The Sutra on the Bhikṣu Hearing of Almsgiving*;
translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin. *The Sutra on the Contemplation of the Body*, one fascicle;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin.

These are appended as supplements to the four scriptures on the "Nine Kinds of Cruelty" and others. The *Dazhou lu* states that they originate from the *Saṃyukta Āgama* and are alternative translations. The *Śarīra-vipaśyanā Sūtra* states that they are separately produced, yet upon examining the texts, neither exists; therefore, they are compiled here. *Anityatā Sūtra*, one fascicle, also titled *Tri-saṃdhi Sūtra*.
Translated by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog. *Aṣṭākṣaṇa-sakṣaṇa Sūtra*, one fascicle.
Translated by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog. *Dīrghanakha-brāhmaṇa-paripṛcchā Sūtra*, one fascicle.
*The Sūtra of Parables Newly Compiled and Included in the Catalogue*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang;
one fascicle. *The Sūtra of Brief Exhortations Newly Compiled and Included in the Catalogue*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; one fascicle.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang Dynasty;

newly included in the catalog. Regarding the statement in this *Brief Discourse on Instruction* (*Lü jiaojie jing*) that it is "extracted from the nineteenth fascicle of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*," this is an error. Although there is a brief text on instruction within that [vinaya], its meaning differs vastly from this one; as they were produced separately, this has been compiled here.

*The Sūtra on the Treatment of Hemorrhoids*, one fascicle; also titled *The Treatment of Fistulas*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang. Newly included in the catalogue. Note: This *Sūtra on the Treatment of Hemorrhoids* also contains this mantra within the second fascicle of the *Vinayavastu-nidāna* of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school. Some have classified it as a duplicate translation, but I maintain that this is not the case. That text states: "O Bhikṣus, this *Sūtra on the Treatment of Hemorrhoids* was already preached by me in another place, yet the purpose for which it was taught differs, and the location is also different. Thus, this is a reiteration of the same teaching, not a duplicate translation. The thirty sūtras above comprise thirty fascicles and are contained in the same volume.
Regarding the Śrāvaka Vinaya Piṭaka, consisting of sixty-one works in four hundred and ninety-three fascicles arranged in fifty bundles:
as for the Vinaya Piṭaka, a sutra states:
Because it is supreme, because it is secret, and because the Buddha alone prescribed its prohibition;
as stated in the sūtras,
when the disciples preach the Dharma...
The Dharma and Vinaya taught by various devas are not like this;
they are all the teachings of the Buddhas.
Since ancient times, the various catalogs have consistently included the *Mātṛkā*, the *Sārmavidhi-vinaya-śāstra*, and other such works.
These have been compiled as the *Vinayapiṭaka*.
Now, upon reflection, I fear this may not be entirely appropriate;
for these works were all composed by various noble sages after the division of the schools, based on their own respective traditions.
It was not proclaimed by the golden mouth of the Buddha,
nor was it compiled by the thousand sages;
what has now been composed and recorded is divided into two categories.
First, the five classes of the authentic Vinaya-piṭaka are clarified;
next, the various Śāstras and their affiliated Abhidharma works are elucidated.
In this way, the roots and branches shall not be confused, and the beginning and end shall be clearly distinguished.
I hope that those who have attained mastery will kindly provide further corrections.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, forty fascicles (or thirty fascicles), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
Single-volume edition, four fascicles. The aforementioned scripture is the *Mūla-vinaya-piṭaka*, which is the *Vinaya* of the Mahāsāṃghika school.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Venerable Kāśyapa convened one thousand arhats.
Compiled at the Stone Chamber in the Bamboo Grove near Rājagṛha. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, sixty-one fascicles;

the first five fascicles of the sixth bundle (fascicles 51–60) were translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra and others of the Yao Qin dynasty. The subsequent *Vinayottaragrantha* in three fascicles was continued in translation by the Tripiṭaka Master Vimalākṣa of the Eastern Jin dynasty. This aforementioned scripture belongs to the Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-piṭaka, which emerged from the Sthavira school approximately three hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

Regarding these three fascicles of the *Vinayamātṛkā* (Vini-xu) from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which are sometimes found appended after the ninth recitation and before the tenth—spanning from fascicle 55 to 57—that is an error. Now, having examined ancient manuscripts, they are all found at the very end. Therefore, I follow the ancient versions as the correct standard. Furthermore, according to the Tripitaka Master Yijing’s *Nanhai Jiguigui Zhuan*, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is not included within the Sarvāstivāda Vinaya; since their textual content and meanings differ, there is no cause for surprise.

*The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, fifty fascicles, in five bundles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the reign of the Empress of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog. *The Mūlasarvāstivāda-bhikṣu-vinaya*, twenty fascicles, in two bundles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog. *The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, forty fascicles, in four bundles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog. *The Mūlasarvāstivāda-nidāna-mātṛkā*, ten fascicles (or eight fascicles), in one bundle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the reign of the Empress of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog. The above four scriptures, together with the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, all belong to the Sarvāstivāda school.
Nevertheless, its literary style and principles are not without differences from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*;
the reason for this remains unclear.
Furthermore, it has been traditionally said:
However, as for the fact that the literary style and principles [of these texts] are not without differences, and the reason for this remains unclear,
I have carefully consulted the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas) by the Tripitaka Master Yijing. According to it,
the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is not a fundamental Vinaya collection.
There are differences [between these versions], as explained at length therein.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Wǔfēn lǜ) consists of thirty fascicles—or thirty-four fascicles according to some accounts—and is divided into three volumes. It was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśa from Jibin, together with Zhu Daosheng and others, during the Song dynasty. This single-text edition is the *Vinaya-piṭaka* of the Mahīśāsaka school, which emerged from the Sarvāstivāda school approximately three hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

*The Four-Part Vinaya*, sixty fascicles (alternatively recorded as forty-five or seventy), in six bundles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kaśmīra and Zhu Fonian during the Yao Qin dynasty. This single text belongs to the Dharmaguptaka school’s *Vinayapiṭaka*. It was produced from within the Mahīśāsaka school during the three hundred years following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. As for the Kāśyapīya school, they possess only the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*; their *Vinayapiṭaka* has not yet been translated.
*Mahāsāṃghika Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, one fascicle; also called *Mā-A-seng-qi Jieben*.
Second translation by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
One of the two translations is missing. *Mahāsāṃghika Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, one fascicle; also called *Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya Sūtra*.

*The Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Ten Recitations*, one fascicle (also known as the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Ten Recitations*), translated by the śramaṇa Faxian of Pingyang during the Eastern Jin dynasty together with Buddhabhadra;
and the [same] translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
The third translation [of the *Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa-sūtra*] consists of two translations, while the other two are missing.

There is also one fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa-sūtra*, also titled *Daśabhāṇavāra-bhikṣuṇī-pāramitā-mokṣa-śīla*, compiled and produced by the Śramaṇa Shi Faying of Changgan Temple during the Song dynasty. Furthermore, there is one fascicle of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-śīla-sūtra*.
*The Bhikṣuṇī-Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Mūlasarvāstivāda*, newly compiled and included in the catalog, translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; one fascicle.
*The Bhikṣu-Prātimokṣa of the Five-Part Vinaya*, also known as the *Mahīśāsaka Prātimokṣa*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; one fascicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Song Dynasty, et al.:
Seven fascicles containing seven individual sūtras in one volume. Also included:
*The Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra* of the Mahīśāsaka school, one fascicle; also known as the *Mīshāsè Níjièběn*.
The *Four-Part Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, one fascicle, compiled by the Liang dynasty śramaṇa Shi Mingyi at Jianchu Monastery based on the *Baoshang Lu* and the *Shiyi*, was titled the *Sifen Jieben*.
It was later recompiled according to the Vinaya by the Tang dynasty śramaṇa Huaisu of Xitaiyuan Monastery.
A newly compiled entry: *The Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Dharmaguptaka School*, one fascicle;
the title reads *The Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Dharmaguptaka School*, compiled according to the Vinaya by the Śramaṇa Huaisu of Xitaiyuan Temple during the Great Tang.

A newly compiled entry: *The Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Dharmaguptaka School*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Mahīśāsaka School* (Tánwúdé), or omitting the character "Bhikṣu" (Sēng).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Qin Dynasty; Single Text. Regarding this *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*:

at the beginning, some versions lack the verse of prostration, while others contain verses such as those concerning the "Hall" (maṇḍapa). These are the *Prātimokṣa* for monks and nuns according to the *Dharmaguptaka* school, of which several circulating versions exist. However, they all deviate from the original text, arbitrarily adding or omitting portions. Herein, I have retained only the version translated by Yaśas of the Yao Qin dynasty and that compiled by the Grand Master of Taiyuan based on the original text; all other versions have been omitted and not included in this record.

*Vimuktimārga-śīla-mūla* (The Root of the Precepts for Liberation), one fascicle; translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei, belonging to the Kāśyapīya school. *Sāmaṇera-daśa-śīla-dharma-sahita-vinaya* (The Ten Precepts for Sāmaṇeras Together with Ritual Decorum), one fascicle; also titled *Sāmaṇera-vinaya*. Translator lost; currently appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin. *Sāmaṇera-vinaya*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *Sūtra on Ritual Decorum*, which is largely identical to the preceding work with minor differences. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kaśmīra during the Song dynasty. *Sāmaṇerī-prakīrṇa-śīla-pāṭha* (The Text on Miscellaneous Precepts for Sāmaṇerīs), one fascicle. Translator lost; currently appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin. *Sāmaṇerī-śīla-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translator lost; originally included in the catalogue of the Later Han. *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translator lost; currently appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin. The above ten single-fascicle scriptures comprise ten volumes in a single bundle.
The Hundred and One Karmas of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, ten fascicles,
one volume;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang.
*Newly Compiled Record of the One Hundred and One Karmavācanās of the Great Śramaṇa*, one fascicle;

excerpted from the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, listed in Sengyou’s catalogue as a translation of unknown authorship, now appended to the Song dynasty catalogues. *The Essential Use of the Bhikṣu Karmavācanās of the Sarvāstivāda*, one fascicle (or two fascicles); excerpted from the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

The Sòng dynasty śramaṇa Shi Sengqu compiled the *Upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra* (one fascicle) at Zhongxing Temple in Yangdu according to the Vinaya; alternatively, it is said that the *Upāli-vinaya* was translated anonymously and is listed among the records of the Later Hàn period.
The *Wufen jieben* (Single Volume of the Five-Part Karmavācanā), one fascicle, is titled *Miśāsaka-karmavācanā*;
it was compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Aitong of Dàkāiyè Monastery during the Great Tang and newly entered into the canon.

The *Sifen zajiemo* (Single Volume of Miscellaneous Karmavācanā of the Four-Part [Vinaya]), one fascicle, is titled *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-bhāga-miśra-karmavācanā*; it begins with the formalization of the precepts (*pratimokṣa-saṃvara*).
One fascicle, titled *The Supplemental Compilation of the Dharmaguptaka Karmavācanā*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kang Senghai of India during the Cao Wei dynasty;
it begins with the "Binding of the Great Boundary" (Mahā-sīmā-bandha) and may consist of two fascicles.

It was translated by the Anxi śramaṇa Tandi of the Cao Wei dynasty. One fascicle, titled *The Dharmaguptaka Bhikṣuṇī Karmavācanā*, translated by [Tandi]. Daoxuan states that the *Dharmaguptaka Karmavācanā* is also called the *Miscellaneous Karmavācanā*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kapiśī during the Song Dynasty; the seven preceding scriptures comprise seven fascicles in one volume.

*Chisonglü shanbu suiji jiemó* (Abridged and Supplemented *Suiji Jiemó* of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*), one fascicle. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Chongyi Temple during the Great Tang. Newly included in the catalog. *Sifen seng jiemó* (The *Bhikṣu-karman* of the Four-Part Vinaya), three fascicles. Titled *Karman, Fascicle One*; excerpted from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huaisu of Taiyuan Temple during the Great Tang based on the Vinaya. Newly included in the catalog. *Sifen ni jiemó* (The *Bhikṣuṇī-karman* of the Four-Part Vinaya), three fascicles. Titled *Bhikṣuṇī-karman, Fascicle One*; excerpted from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huaisu of West Taiyuan Temple during the Great Tang based on the Vinaya. Newly included in the catalog. The aforementioned three scriptures comprise seven fascicles in one volume. The six preceding works concerning *karman* are all derived from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*; however, they differ in their degree of detail and the sequence of their contents.
*Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī Sūtra*, two fascicles; also called *Mahāprajāpatī’s Exhortation to Love* or simply *Mahāprajāpatī Sūtra*. The translator is lost.
Sengyou’s catalog states it was a different scripture from the Liang territory;
it is now appended to the Northern Liang catalog.
*The Single-Volume Scripture on the Prohibitions of Kāśyapa*, one fascicle; also titled *The Mahābhikṣu Scripture* and *The Scripture on Genuine and Spurious Śramaṇas*.
Translated by the Song dynasty layman Juqu Jingsheng;
this is the second translation.

Of the two translations, one is missing. Furthermore, among the various catalogs, there is another work titled *The Scripture on the True and False Śramaṇas* in one fascicle, translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Huìjiǎn. It shares the same source as the *Kāśyapa Precepts*. Upon examining its phrasing, it is identical from beginning to end with the *Scripture on the Prohibitions and Precepts*; since there are no differing passages, it is not recorded here twice. There is also the *Scripture on the Gravity of Retribution for Violating Precepts* in one fascicle, which appears in the *Maudgalyāyana’s Inquiry into the Vinaya* (or simply the *Maudgalyāyana’s Inquiry Scripture*), translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master Ān Shìgāo of the Later Han.
This was included in the *Supplement to the Omissions*.
*The Sutra on the Single Volume of the Precepts for Eliminating Calamities*, one scroll;

also titled *The Sutra on the Precepts for Subduing and Eliminating Calamities*, translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. *The Single Volume on the Characteristics of the Five Lay Precepts*, one scroll;
also titled *A Brief Treatise on the Five Lay Precepts*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kapiśī during the Song dynasty.
Of the first and second translations, one is missing. The above constitutes the Basket of the Subduing of Discipline (Vinaya-piṭaka) according to the Sūtras and Vinayas;
the following, such as the Śāstras, are termed "retinues" (parivāra) because they accord with the preceding tenets.
Regarding the *Śīlacitta-karman*, as it merely follows the essential compilation of the text without any additions or omissions, it is listed here first;
whereas the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* and other works rely upon their original source texts.
As additions or deletions occurred, they were immediately appended at the end. *Vinayakārikā of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, five fascicles. Composed by the Venerable Viśākha;

translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog. *Vinayakṣudrakavastu-saṃgraha-gāthā of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog. *Vinayanidāna-mātṛkā-saṃgraha-gāthā of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog. *Pañcaśata-praśna-vastu-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translator lost; now appended to the Eastern Jin record. These nine supplementary works, totaling fourteen fascicles, are placed together in one volume.
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, compiled by the Venerable Jayagupta, in twenty fascicles (or fourteen fascicles in two volumes);
translated during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing;
newly included in the canon.
*The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu (Medicine Chapter) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda*, twenty fascicles in two volumes,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; *The Saṃghabheda-vastu (Schism Chapter) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda*, twenty fascicles.

Within the two bundles, two fascicles are missing: one fascicle from the five-fascicle *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-pravrajyā-vastu*; one fascicle from the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-varṣā-vastu*; one fascicle from the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-pravāraṇā-vastu*; two fascicles from the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-carmavastu*; and one fascicle from the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kaṭhina-vastu*. These five sections, totaling nine fascicles within the same bundle, lack one fascicle.
The above seven sections, from the *Bhaiṣajyavastu* downwards, comprise fifty fascicles in total.

These were all translated at the two capitals by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Yijing, from the first year of the Zhengsheng era of the Dazhou period down to the second year of the Jingyun era of the Great Tang.
Not included in the *Kaiyuan shijiao lu*, they have now been sought out and entered into the *Zhenyuan shijiao lu*. Three volumes are missing from the beginning;
although copies have not yet been obtained, the Vinaya and other sections therein have already been recovered from the capital and the Wei Prefecture.
These are both included in the *Zhenyuan lu* (Zhenyuan Era Catalogue) among the missing texts.
The *Vinayamātṛkā* in ten fascicles, one set, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of the Song Dynasty;
and the *Piṇaiye lü* (Vinaya of the Piṇaiye School) in ten fascicles, also known as the *Ji yinyuan jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Precepts), one set.
The *Sūtra-vibhāṣā on the Sūtra of Good Vision* (Śīla-sūtra-vibhāṣā),
eighteen fascicles, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Fu dynasty of the Yao Qin; also known as the *Vibhāṣā-śīla* or simply the *Sūtra of Good Vision*,
translated by the foreign Śramaṇa Saṃghabhadra during the Xiao Qi dynasty.

The *Dabanfo apitan jing* (Singular Volume Buddha Abhidharma Sūtra), two fascicles; also called the *Fotu apitan lun* (Buddha Abhidharma Śāstra), translated by the Chen dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha. These two singular volumes comprise twenty fascicles in two bundles.

Regarding the *Fotu apitan lun*, various catalogs all state it consists of nine fascicles, though the reason for this remains unclear. At present, only two fascicles exist. Previously, these were compiled among the Mahāyāna treatises; however, upon examining their literary style and principles, they mostly discuss matters such as the salvation of people and the conferral of precepts, which correspond with the works in this section. Therefore, they have been moved here and compiled accordingly.

*Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra*, eight fascicles; also called *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*. Translator lost; currently appended to the Qin Records. *Sambahula-bhikṣu-vinaya-saṃvara-sūtra*, two fascicles; also called *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-saṃvara-sūtra* or four fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han. The above two single-text sūtras comprise ten fascicles in one volume. Regarding the *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra*, the Great Zhou Catalogue states:
Translated by Fulan during the Taian era of the Eastern Jin.
Jingan of the Fashang Record carefully examined the successive reigns of the emperors and found that there was no Taian era during the Eastern Jin period.
That Taian era actually belonged to the reign of Emperor Hui of the Western Jin; Jingan of the Fashang Record searched for it but did not find it [in his own records].
Since the dates are already confused and cannot be relied upon as a standard,
and furthermore, because examining the text reveals that wherever Sanskrit terms were translated,
they were all referred to as "the language of Qin," it is therefore a translation from the Qin period.
Now, because it has lost its original colophon, it is included in the Qin Records.
As for the *Sānqiānwēiyí jīng* (Sūtra on the Three Thousand Dignified Manners),
Sengyou divided it into two sections within his *Shīyì lù* (Record of Lost Translations).
Each consists of two fascicles.
The catalogues of Sengfang and others all state that there were two separate versions, each comprising two fascicles, thus totaling four fascicles;
however, at present, only two remain.

The other two [versions] do not exist. *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, nine fascicles; translator lost; currently appended to the Qin catalog. *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-śāstra* (also simply called the *Viniścaya-śāstra*), one fascicle; translated by the Chen dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of India. These two single-fascicle scriptures above comprise ten fascicles in the same volume. This *Viniścaya-śāstra* was extracted from the *Prātimokṣa-śāstra* of the Saṃmitīya school.
That great treatise has not yet been translated and consists of approximately six thousand stanzas.

A Dharma master of that school, an Anāgāmin named Guṇaprabha, based upon the Vinaya-vibhāṣā, the Jñānaprasthāna, and other texts, composed a work therein; that portion corresponding to the Vinaya has been briefly condensed into one fascicle.
This refers to the *Vibhaṅga-śāstra*.
This treatise explains twenty-two essential points of truth within the Vinaya Piṭaka,
capable of dispelling the deluded darkness of mind in those who follow the True Dharma.
Because it thoroughly penetrates the meaning of the Vinaya, it is called "Liaoming" (Clear Understanding).

In the *Fajing lu* (Catalogue of Dharma Master Jing) by the Sui dynasty monk and the *Changfang ruzang lu* (Longfang’s Catalogue of Works Included in the Canon), it is both classified as two separate sections of the Vinaya, totaling twenty-two fascicles, and compiled within the Vinaya section.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Mingliao lun) in one fascicle is recorded in the catalogs of treatises.
Furthermore, the "twenty-two [fascicles]" refers to half of the title of the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
It is a grave error to claim that twenty-two fascicles of it still exist.

The Abhidharma-piṭaka of the Śrāvakas consists of thirty-six treatises totaling six hundred and ninety-eight fascicles in seventy-two bundles; these various sections of the Abhidharma-piṭaka differ from one another.
Regarding the dissemination of these [teachings] here in this region for the sake of the assembly,
we shall now rely upon the Sarvāstivāda school,
beginning with its fundamental treatise (*mūla-śāstra*).
The *Pāda-śāstra* occupies the second position;
the branches such as the *Vibhāṣā* are compiled at the end.
Since the remaining schools are numerous, they are difficult to categorize systematically.
To await future [readers]. This [work] has no priority or sequence.

*Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra*, thirty fascicles; composed by Kātyāyanīputra, or twenty fascicles. Three bundles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīr in collaboration with Zhu Fonian during the Fu Qin dynasty. First translation. *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, twenty fascicles; composed by Kātyāyanīputra. Two bundles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Second translation. The two treatises above are the same original text with different translations.
This is the root of the Abhidharma-piṭaka of the Sarvāstivāda school;
it was composed by the master Kātyāyanīputra three hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
In later generations, the transmitters of the tradition possessed both extensive and abbreviated versions.
This *Jñānaprasthāna* (Treatise on the Establishment of Knowledge) is complete in both its textual expression and its meaning;
those who transmit and study it call it the "Body Treatise" (*Śarīra-śāstra*).
Since the remaining six treatises each expound upon one branch,
they are called "feet" because they differ from the body [of the main work].
These are subsequently compiled at the end, followed by the various sections.

1. *Abhidharma-dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra*, twelve fascicles, composed by the Venerable Mahakausthila; one bundle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; listed in the *Neidian lu* as a single work. 2. *Abhidharma-sangītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra*, twenty fascicles, spoken by the Venerable Śāriputra; two bundles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; listed in the *Neidian lu* as a single work. 3. *Prajñapti-pāda-śāstra*, consisting of eighteen thousand stanzas.

Composed by the Venerable Mahākātyāyana—*Kātyā* meaning "shearer" (*kātya*) and *yanana* meaning "lineage" (*yanana*), with *kātyā* being masculine; he was a member of a certain Brahmin clan. This treatise has not yet been translated. The aforementioned three *Pādasūtras* were all composed during the lifetime of the Buddha.

*Catuḥśata-abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, sixteen fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; recorded in the *Neidian lu*. This single work was composed by the Venerable Devaśarman (translated into Chinese as Tianji) after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, during the hundredth year [following his passing]; he was an Arhat.

*Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, eighteen fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; recorded in the *Neidian lu*; second translation. The aforementioned treatise was composed by the Venerable Vasumitra (translated into Chinese as Shiyou) during the three hundred years following the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha.

*Saṃgītiparyāya-Abhidharma-śāstra*, twelve fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇadatta of India together with Bodhiśe during the Song dynasty. First translation. (The two treatises above are the same original text with different translations.)
The two aforementioned treatises comprise twenty fascicles in three bundles.

*Ṣaḍ-abhidharma-dhātu-paryāya-pāda-śāstra* (Six Abhidharma Treatises on the Categories of Elements), three fascicles. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Appears in the *Fanying tu* (Diagram of Translated Scriptures). Single volume. To the right: This one treatise was composed by the Venerable Vasumitra during the third century after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. Together with the aforementioned *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra*, they comprise nineteen fascicles in two bundles.

*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, sixty fascicles, or eighty-four fascicles, or one hundred and nine fascicles. Translated by the Indian śramaṇa Buddhavarman together with Daotai and others during the Northern Liang dynasty. First translation. Note: This treatise was originally composed in one hundred fascicles as a complete collection.
The śramaṇa Daoting composed the preface.
During the annexation of Liang by Wei, forty fascicles were lost;
today, only sixty fascicles remain.
However, when the third *khandhaka* was completed, the latter five *khandhakas* were missing from their original [translation].
Those who translated it anew have fully restored all eight *skandhas*.
As for the versions consisting of eighty-four fascicles and one hundred and nine fascicles:
Later generations divided it into sixty fascicles;

it was not that it was originally incomplete. Furthermore, according to Sengyou’s *Fayuan* of the Liang dynasty, in the second month of the eleventh year of the Tianjian era, an imperial edict ordered Saṃghavarman to retranslate the remaining five *skandhas* of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*. Although this account exists, the original manuscript has still not been seen.

*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, 200 fascicles, 20 bundles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. The two treatises above are the same work with different translations.
This concludes the explanation of the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.
Four hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
five hundred great arhats and others composed it in the kingdom of Kaśmīra.

*Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, twenty-two fascicles, composed by Vasubandhu; translated by the Chen Dynasty Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India. First translation. *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā*, one fascicle (or three fascicles), composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu; translated by the Great Tang Tripitaka Master Xuanzang. Recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalog). Second translation. The above two treatises, totaling twenty-three fascicles in three bundles, are missing from the original texts of the Paramārtha translation.

*Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, thirty fascicles. Composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu. Three volumes. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. This is the second translation. The two treatises and their verses above are the same original text with different translations.

*Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, eighty fascicles; composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra; eight bundles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; recorded in the *Neidian lu*. *Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, forty fascicles; composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra; four bundles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; recorded in the *Neidian lu*. The two treatises listed above are single volumes whose commentary on the verses is identical to that of the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā*, though their explanations differ.

Saṃghabhadra composed the *Nyāyānusāra* (Following Reason); because the text of the Venerable Saṃghabhadra’s earlier work was extensive and difficult to consult, he later composed the *Abhidharmasamaya* (Exposition of Tenets), which is concise and easy to understand;

therefore, it has been retranslated. *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* (Treatise on the Heart of Abhidharma), four fascicles. Composed by the Venerable Dharmottara (or including the word "Vādin"). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kapiśī during the Eastern Jin dynasty. *Sarvāstivāda-abhidharmahṛdaya-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Heart of Abhidharma according to the Sarvāstivāda), six fascicles (or seven). Composed by the Mahābhadanta Revataśānta. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India together with Fazhi during the Northern Qi dynasty. The two aforementioned single-text treatises comprise ten fascicles in one volume.

The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* in eleven fascicles (also known as the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-vibhāṣā*), composed by the Venerable Dharmatrāta; alternatively in fourteen fascicles. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of the Song Dynasty. This is the fourth translation. Of the three translations, three are missing. The three treatises mentioned above are all titled *Abhidharmahṛdaya*.
However, there are differences in the extent of their respective commentaries; the introductory note to the first fascicle of the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states:
"The explanations of the Dharma by the various masters are brief.
Upaśānta has a commentary of eight thousand verses."
Furthermore, there is another master who has provided an exposition of twelve thousand verses;
these two treatises are known as the "Extensive" (Vistara).
Upānanda, moreover, has provided an exposition of six thousand verses. Furthermore, the opening verse of that treatise states:
I pay homage to the Venerable Dharmottara;
what he has spoken, I receive upon the crown of my head,
for I, Dharmatrāta, shall expound that which he has not yet explained.
Regarding the aforementioned *Śāstra-trayam*, the first four fascicles constitute Vasubandhu’s original treatise (*mūla-śāstra*),
while the subsequent six fascicles are the commentary by Upaśānta.
As stated at the end of that treatise:
The Venerable Upaśānta composed this *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* for the benefit of his disciples;
therefore, it is known that this is indeed a commentary on Dharmottara’s treatise.
It is not that Dharmottara himself composed it, though the title of the treatise contains the name "Dharmottara."
Perhaps this is not the case;
the title in the middle of the treatise lacks the character "wu" (無).
All catalogs state that it is the *Dharmatrāta-abhidharma*.
Some say that it is a separate translation of Dharmatrāta’s *Abhidharma*.
Later, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* was composed by Dharmatrāta.
Comparing these with the two preceding treatises:

The textual meaning is somewhat extensive. *Abhidharmāmṛtarasa-śāstra* (Treatise on the Flavor of the Ambrosia of Abhidharma), two fascicles; alternatively titled *Āmṛtarasa-abhidharma*; composed by the Venerable Ghoṣa; translated during the Cao Wei period by a Tripiṭaka Master whose name is lost. *Anu-lakṣaṇa-śāstra* (Treatise on Following Characteristics), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Guṇabhadra-anulakṣaṇa-śāstra*; composed by Dharma Master Guṇamati; translated by the Chen dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha; alternatively in two fascicles. The above three single-text treatises comprise fourteen fascicles in two volumes.
*The Treatise Compiled by the Venerable Vasumitra Bodhisattva*, ten fascicles (or fourteen or twelve fascicles), composed by the Venerable Vasumitra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabhūti of Kapiśī during the Fu Qin dynasty and others.
*The Single-Volume Treatise on the Two Dharmas*, two fascicles (sometimes without the word "treatise," sometimes called a "sūtra," or in three or one fascicle).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

Second Translation. [Of these two translations, one is missing. Regarding this *Tridharmaka-śāstra*, there is both an original text and a translated version. The original consists of three chapters and nine *tattvārthas* (true degrees), and the commentary also comprises nine sections. Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu wrote a preface stating that the original treatise was composed by the Venerable Śrīlāta, while the commentary was compiled by the Mahāyāna layman Saṃghasena of India. A later record states that it was compiled by the Mahāyāna bhikṣu Śramaṇa Saṃgha. These two accounts differ slightly, and it remains unclear which is correct.

*Abhidharmāvatāra-śāstra*, two fascicles; composed by the Arhat Saṃghabhadra; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Single volume. Upper [section] of the Three Treatises, fourteen fascicles in two bundles.
*Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, twenty fascicles, composed by Harivarman;
totaling one hundred and two chapters, or alternatively twenty-four fascicles;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
*The Standalone Treatise on the Establishment of the World Abhidharma* (Lishi Apitan Lun), ten fascicles (sometimes without the character "lun"),
one volume, or fifteen fascicles;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen Dynasty.
The Standalone *Vimuttimagga* (Treatise on the Path to Liberation), twelve fascicles or thirteen fascicles,
one volume;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghavarman of Funan during the Liang Dynasty.
The *Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*, twenty-two fascicles (or twenty or thirty fascicles),
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśa together with Dharmagupta during the Yao Qin dynasty.
The *Pañcavastuvibhāṣāśāstra*, two fascicles— also known as the *Abhidharmapañcavastuśāstra*— composed by the Venerable Dharmatrāta.
The Single-Volume Diagram of the Translation of Scriptures Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang,
Volumes 1–24 of the Two Treatises.
It is an error to record the *Abhidharma-pañcavastuka-śāstra* separately within the *Dazhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalogue).

The fourteen-fascicle *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* also states: "The *Vibhāṣā-abhidharma-śāstra*, composed by Ārahan Saptadhāpani; translated by the Kasmirian Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabhūti during the Fu Qin dynasty. The standalone *Sammitīya-nikāya-śāstra* consists of three fascicles (though some versions omit the word "nikāya" or list it as four fascicles); its translator is lost. "Sammitīya" means "Right Measure," and this is a treatise from within the Sammitīya school. It is now appended to the Qin records. These two standalone treatises comprise seventeen fascicles in two volumes.

*Fenbie Gongde Lun* (Treatise on the Analysis of Merit), four fascicles; alternatively titled *Fenbie Gongde Jing* (Sutra on the Analysis of Merit), three or five fascicles. Translator lost. Included in the Later Han catalog. Single work. The above treatise explains the meaning of the *Ekottarika Āgama*. It begins with the "Preface Chapter" and proceeds until halfway through the "Disciples Chapter," where it stops at the section concerning the Bhikṣu Rājakumāra. The *Fashang Lu* states that it was translated by Zhu Fahu; however, this is not the case. Within this text, the citations from the sutra and the explanations of its phrases are identical to the extant *Ekottarika Āgama*. It appears that both were translated by the same person. Yet, other catalogs all state that the source is lost. For now, we shall rely on this record. The *Sengyou Lu* claims that Kāśyapa and Ānanda compiled it; this too is incorrect. Since the first fascicle of the treatise cites the teachings of the foreign master Sarvāstivādin, we know it was not compiled by those two venerable ones.

*Catuḥsatya-śāstra*, four fascicles; composed by Vasubandhu; translated by the Chen Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha. *Svayambhū-bodhisattva-pūrva-yoga-śāstra*, two fascicles; translator lost; now appended to the Qin Records. *Aṣṭadaśa-sāstra*, one fascicle; newly identified as a work of lost translation; appended to the Three Qin Records. The above eighteen treatises constitute the first translation.
According to various records, it is unanimously stated that this was translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha during the Liang dynasty.

Now, upon careful examination, since the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha had already translated eighteen treatises, it would not have been appropriate for him to translate the *Samayabhedoparacanacakra* again.
The beginning of this treatise in eighteen sections cites the "Chapter on Differentiation" from the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
Following the chapter, it next states, "Compiled by Master Kumārajīva," and only thereafter does the actual treatise begin.
If this were translated by Kumārajīva,
it would be inconsistent for him to cite the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchāsūtra*— which did not yet exist during the Qin period— and place it at the beginning.
Alternatively, it may be appropriate to compile the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*—based on its text in the *Bie lu* (Separate Record)—as a work of lost translation.
There is no doubt that it was cited as evidence during the Qin period.
If it were a re-translation by Paramārtha, [it would have been recorded accordingly].
