In the commentary on the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the presence of the characters "Qin" (秦) and "words" (言) is inconsistent;
yet, upon examining its literary style and structure, it appears for the most part to have been translated during the Qin period by Kumārajīva.
It is likely that various catalogs omitted these details, leading to this doubt.
The commentaries on the eighteen schools of the *Satyasiddhi* are the *Śāstravibhāga-viniścaya*.
Although this principle exists, I did not dare to point it out [previously].
Later, upon receiving various reports and requests for an authentic record, [I have provided this].

*Samayabhedoparacanacakra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Formation of Doctrinal Divisions), one fascicle; also titled *Samayabhedavyūha-śāstra*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen Dynasty. First translation. *Bhinnasamaya-siddhānta-śāstra* (Treatise on the Tenets of Different Schools), one fascicle. Composed by the Bodhisattva Vasumitra. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Recorded in the *Fanying tu* (Diagram of Translated Scriptures). Third translation. The three treatises above are the same original text translated differently. The six treatises listed above comprise thirteen fascicles and are contained in a single volume.

2. Records of the Biographies of Sages and Worthies, including both translations and original texts. Within the Records of the Biographies of Sages and Worthies, Part Three: one hundred and twelve works in five hundred and ninety-five fascicles, comprising sixty-four bundles. Regarding these "Records": [text continues]
Compiled by the noble disciples after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
although these are not the orthodox scriptures of the Tripiṭaka,
they nonetheless assist in propagating the profound transformation.
Within this, there are five general categories:
first, praising the virtues of the Buddha;
second, elucidating the true principle of the Dharma.
Third, describing the monastic conduct;
fourth, refuting heterodoxy and protecting the Dharma;
fifth, the differing tenets of external schools.
Those that praise the Buddha’s virtues include the *Buddhacarita* (The Acts of the Buddha), the *Śākyamuni-vamśa* (Genealogy of Śākyamuni), and others.
Those that clarify the principles of the Dharma include the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* (Sutra on the Stages of the Bodhisattva Path) and the *Āgama-vibhaṅga* (Distinguishing the Agamas).
The "Biographies" (*Shu seng xing zhuan*) recounts the lives of such figures as Nāgārjuna, Aśvaghoṣa, Faxian, and Xuanzang.
The "Treatises for Defeating the Heterodox and Protecting the Dharma" (*Cui xie hu fa zhe*) includes works such as the *Bian zheng lun*, the *Hong ming ji*, and the *Po xie bian huo lun*.
Regarding the various heterodox systems of external schools, there are two primary categories: the Samkhya and the Vaiśeṣika; no classification of their types exceeds these five.
The arguments presented within these five apply to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
Furthermore, within this context, two additional examples may be distinguished.
The translators of the Sanskrit original are placed first;
those who propagated it in this land follow after.
May the East and West not be confused, so that readers may have their doubts dispelled.

*Collection of Translations from Sanskrit Texts*, sixty-eight works in one hundred and seventy-three fascicles, arranged in fourteen bundles. *The Sūtra on the Life of the Buddha* (Buddhacarita-kāvya), five fascicles. Composed by the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa; also known as the *Sūtra on the Original Deeds of the Buddha*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty. *Sole Translation of the Sūtra on the Original Deeds of the Buddha*, seven fascicles. Also titled the *Biography of the Praise for the Original Deeds of the Buddha*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Śīlabhadra of Liangzhou during the Song dynasty. The above sole translation is recorded in the Great Zhou Catalogue (*Dazhou lu*) and is included among the Mahāyāna re-translated scriptures.
It is an error to claim that this is a different translation of the same text as the sixty-fascicle *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*.
The aforementioned two collections, totaling twelve fascicles, share the same case.
The *Saṃyukta-śataka-vastu-sūtra* consists of ten fascicles.
One fascicle;
translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty,
as recorded in the Neidian lu (Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures).

The *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) was compiled as a separate work and included in the twenty-fascicle *Chuyao jing* (Sūtra of Outstanding Manifestations), or alternatively titled the *Chuyao lun* (Treatise on Outstanding Manifestations), in either nineteen or twenty fascicles;
it was translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Fu Qin period.
The *Xianyu jing* (Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish) exists as a single work in thirteen fascicles, or fifteen, sixteen, or seventeen fascicles.
The *Fanying tu* (Diagram of Translated Scriptures) in its single-volume edition was translated by the monk Huijue and others from Liangzhou during the Northern Wei dynasty at Gaochang Commandery.

I have carefully examined the preface to the *Xianyu jing* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish) by the Liang dynasty monk Sengyou, which states: "The eight monks from Hexi, including Huijue, traveled abroad to seek the Way. Upon reaching the Great Monastery of Khotan, they encountered a quinquennial assembly. The eight men listened separately and each recorded what they heard. Returning to Gaochang, they compiled their notes into a single work; this is precisely the aforementioned *Xianyu jing*. Since the various catalogs of former generations all included it in the Canon (*Jingzang*), one might wonder: as these works were compiled from what was collectively heard rather than being the original recitations of Ānanda, how do they differ from other compilations? Therefore, it seems inappropriate to include them in the 'Correct Canon' (*Zhengjing*). Consequently, I have now moved them to be appended to the 'Collected Biographies and Records' (*Jizhuan lu*). The same applies to the two scriptures, the *Chuyao jing* (Udānavarga) and the *Baiyuan jing* (Avadānaśataka), which are also separate compilations and not original recitations; these too are appended here."

The first two collections comprise thirty-three fascicles in four cases; the first three cases each contain eight fascicles, and the fourth case contains nine fascicles. *Daodi jing* (One fascicle)—sometimes titled *Dazhuxingdao dijing*. This is an excerpt from the *Xiuxing jing*; there is no abbreviated foreign version.

Translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. Included in the *Shiyi*. Second Translation. Regarding the above scripture: it is a partial alternative translation of the later *Xiuxing daodi jing*. According to the preface by Dharma Master Dao’an, the śramaṇa Saṃgharakṣa compiled the essentials of this scripture into one work consisting of twenty-seven chapters. An Shigao selected seven of the chapters compiled by Saṃgharakṣa and translated them into Chinese. Since both the chapter titles and their number correspond exactly, we know this is the scripture produced by An Shigao. These seven chapters total eighteen sheets; the fact that various catalogs state they consist of two fascicles is an error.

*Xiūxíng dàozhì jīng* (Sūtra on the Stages of Practice), six fascicles—or simply called *Xiūxíng jīng* (Sūtra on Practice)—or seven fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty; third translation; one of the three translations is missing. The two aforementioned sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

Seven hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Śramaṇa Saṃgharakṣa of the Western Regions compiled this work; "Saṃgharakṣa" is the local dialectal term for what is called *Saṃgharakṣita* in the Sanskrit of India.
It is unreasonable for the old catalog to include these among the scriptures;
they are no different from the compilers of the later *Saṃgharakṣita-saṃyukta-āgama*.
How can one be recorded as a "True Scripture" while the other is compiled within a collection?
Since the precedents are thus, these are appended here.

The *Saṃgharakṣa-saṃgīta-sūtra* in three fascicles (or five fascicles) was compiled by Saṃgharakṣa and translated during the Fu Qin period. The aforementioned three collections, totaling ten fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

*The Sūtra of One Hundred Parables* (Bai yu jing), four fascicles, composed by Saṃghasena; alternatively, five fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Qi dynasty of the Xiao family. Single-text edition. *The Sūtra of the Original Karmic Conditions of the Bodhisattva* (Pusa benyuan jing), three fascicles; alternatively, four fascicles or two fascicles. Composed by Saṃghasena. Translated by the lay devotee (upāsaka) Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty. Single-text edition. *The Essential Collection of Various Sūtras on the Gate of Practicing the Bodhisattva Path in Mahāyāna* (Dacheng xiuxing pusa xingmen zhu jing yaoji), three fascicles. Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan of Zhixiang Temple during the Great Tang. Newly included in the catalog. The above three collections comprise ten fascicles and are contained in the same volume.

*Fufa zang yinyuan zhuan* (The Tradition of the Causes and Conditions of the Dharma-treasury Transmission), six fascicles—sometimes without the characters "yinyuan" (causes and conditions)—or four fascicles or two fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kiṅkiaya of the Western Regions together with Tanyao during the Northern Wei dynasty. Third translation; two other translations are missing. *Sanzan sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seated Meditation), three fascicles—also titled *Pusa chanfa jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Methods of Meditation) or simply *Chan jing* (Meditation Sūtra)—or two fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. First translation; two other translations are missing. Furthermore, among various catalogs, there is also the *Aluanye xichan fa jing* (Sūtra on the Methods of Practicing Meditation in an Āraṇya), two fascicles.
It is said that this is a different translation of the same original text as the *Zuochan sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seated Meditation).
It is also stated that it was produced by Dharma Master Kumārajīva; upon examining the phrasing from beginning to end, they are entirely identical.
They are merely divided into two separate works due to their distinct titles.
As this is not a separate translation and cannot be circulated alongside the others, the *Buddhavaidūrya-sūtra* (one fascicle), also known as the *Buddhavaidyarāja-sūtra*,
translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Dharmakṣema and Zhi Yue during the Wu dynasty,
has been included here as a supplementary addition.
*The Single-Volume Miscellaneous Difficult Sūtra*, one fascicle;
translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu period and included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection).
*The Single-Volume Sūtra on the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa and Mahākāśyapa’s Journey to the Buddha*, one fascicle; also known as the *Sūtra on Kāśyapa’s Journey to the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa*.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan from the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin Dynasty;
a single-fascicle work on the Bodhisattva’s Method for Rebuking Lust for Physical Form,
also known as the Sūtra translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.

The first translation consists of two versions; one lacks four chapters. *Xuefa jing* (Sutra on Learning the Dharma), one fascicle—sometimes without the word "jing" (sutra)—translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song dynasty;
a standalone text. *Furu niepan miju jin’gang lishi ailian jing* (Sutra on the Buddha’s Entry into Nirvana and the Lamentation of the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada), one fascicle.

*The Single-Volume Sūtra on the Verses of Kātyāyana’s Teaching on the Exhaustion of Phenomena*, translator lost; now appended to the Qin Catalogue. Sengyou’s Catalogue states that Master Dao’an’s list of lost translations now appends this to the Western Qin Catalogue. *The Single-Volume Sūtra on the Buddha’s Treatment of the Body*, also known as the *Sūtra on the Treatment of the Body*. Or it is called the *Sūtra on the Treatment of the Body*.
Sengyou’s Catalog states that Master Dao’an lost the record of its translator;
it is now appended to the Western Jin catalog as a single-text work.
One fascicle of the *Fuzhi yijing* (Sūtra on the Intent of Governing) was included among the "Supplements" (*Shiyi*). Some say it is the *Fozhi yijing*.
Sengyou’s Catalogue states that it is a translation by Master Dao’an whose original translator was lost;
it is now appended to the Western Jin catalogue and included among the "Supplements" in the section on single-text works, Volume 11 of the first collection, totaling eighteen fascicles in one volume.

*Za bao zang jing* (Sutra of the Storehouse of Miscellaneous Jewels), eight fascicles (alternatively said to be twelve fascicles); translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kiṅkara of the Western Regions together with Tanyao during the Northern Wei dynasty. *Dan ben na xian biqiu jing* (The Single-Volume Sutra of the Bhikṣu Nāgasena), two fascicles (alternatively titled simply *Na xian jing* or three fascicles); translator lost, included in the catalog of the Eastern Jin dynasty. The first version consists of two translations, one of which is missing; the upper two collections comprise ten fascicles in the same volume.

*The Essential Methods for the Five-Gate Dhyāna Sūtra*, one fascicle, compiled by the Great Dhyāna Master Buddhamitra; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Jibin during the Song dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). Second translation. *Dharmatrāta’s Dhyāna Sūtra*, two fascicles, also titled *Dhyāna Sūtra on the Practice of the Meditation on Impurity*; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin dynasty. Single volume. [Note: Both Dharmatrāta and Buddhasena were originally from Jibin. They composed these works.
The master Buddhabhadra was a master of dhyāna in that country;
when Zhiyan traveled to the Western Regions,
he also [studied] the dhyāna he had previously learned there.
The fourteen sūtras following "From Sitting Meditation and Samādhi" were included within the middle volume of the *Zhou lu* (Record of Zhou) among the canonical scriptures;
however, as they are not the word of the Buddha, they have now been moved here.

Although the *Zabaozang jing* (Sutra of the Storehouse of Miscellaneous Jewels) collects the Buddha’s words, it also incorporates various other incidental narratives and is not entirely the word of the Buddha;
therefore, it is included among the compiled works.
The *Chanfa yaojie* (Essential Explanation of Dhyāna Methods), in two fascicles, is also known as the *Chanyao jing* (Sutra of Essential Dhyāna).

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty; the first of two translations, one of which is missing. *Canyao heyu jing* (Sūtra on the Essentials of Dhyāna and the Censure of Desire), one fascicle—this is the "Chapter on the Censure of Desire" from the *Canyao jing*.
Translator lost during the Later Han;
included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement) as a single-text edition. *Neishen guan zhangju jing* (Sūtra on the Verses for Contemplating the Internal Body), one fascicle.
One fascicle of the *Dānabhadra-dharmadarśana-sūtra*, translated during the Later Han dynasty and included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) as a standalone text.
One fascicle of the *Sīyuí yàolüè fǎ* (Essential Methods for Contemplation), translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin; alternatively titled the *Jīng* (Sūtra) version,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin, appended as a supplementary collection.
Supplementary entry included in the second translation;
one of the two translations is missing: *The Scripture on the Twelve Wanderings*, one fascicle.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Kālodaka from the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin Dynasty;
supplemented and included as the second translation.
Two translations [of this work] are missing. The *Jiuzapiyujing* (Old Miscellaneous Parable Sūtra) in two fascicles is also called the *Zapiyujijing* (Miscellaneous Parable Collection Sūtra).
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Kang Senghui of Wuchang and India;
collected as a supplementary volume and included here as a single work:
*The Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables* (Yi Ben Za Pi Yu Jing), one fascicle.
Translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Loujiachen of the Later Han Dynasty;
included as a supplementary collection in the single-volume edition, Volume 13 of the Ten Collections, bound together in one fascicle.

*Zapiyujing* (Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables), two fascicles; also titled *Pusa duren jing* (Sutra of the Bodhisattva Saving Humans). Translator lost; included in the Later Han catalogue as a single-fascicle supplement. *Zapiyujing* (Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables), one fascicle, compiled by the Bhikṣu Daolüe. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin; included as a supplement. *Ashewang piyujing* (Sutra of Parables of King Aśoka), one fascicle. Translator lost; now appended to the Eastern Jin catalogue as a single-fascicle supplement. *Ashewang jing* (Sutra of King Aśoka), ten fascicles (sometimes with the character "Da" [Great] added). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of Funan during the Liang dynasty; included as a second translation. The four collections above comprise fourteen fascicles in a single volume.

The *Aśokarājāvadāna* in seven fascicles, also known as the *Mahā-aśokarāja-sūtra*, or in five fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Faqin of Parthia during the Western Jin dynasty. First translation. The two aforementioned translations are different versions of the same text.
More than one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it was only when King Aśoka appeared in the world that this biography first came into existence.

It is an error for the *Da Zhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalog) to include it among the Mahāyāna sūtras; furthermore, the claim in the *Changfang lu* (Changfang Catalog) and others that Saṃghavarman produced a five-fascicle version of the *Aśokarāja-avadāna* is also an error. Since the preceding scripture is itself the biography, it is inappropriate to record it twice.

*The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of King Aśoka’s Son, Haimavata* (one fascicle), also titled *The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Prince Dharmapāla and Haimavata*. Translated during the Qin dynasty by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmanandi of the Former Qin. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). Second translation. [Three translations; two are missing. *A Concise Explanation of the Four Āgamas*, in two fascicles. Compiled by the Arhat Vasubhadra. Translated by the Kuchean Śramaṇa Kumārabuddhi and others of the Former Qin. Included in the *Shiyi*. The three collections of single-fascicle texts above, totaling ten fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

The *Dharmapada-sūtra*, two fascicles; also called the *Dharmapada-saṃgraha*, compiled by the Venerable Dharmatrāta. Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Veṅkaṭananda and others during the Wu dynasty. First translation. One of the two translations is missing. The first volume of the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
As the World-Honored One taught various doctrines for the sake of sentient beings while staying in various villages and towns,
as recorded in the *Dharmapada*, the Venerable Dharmatrāta— translated here as Fajiu— expounded upon these various teachings after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Since it establishes the Chapter on Impermanence for the meaning of impermanence,
and so forth, up to establishing the Chapter on Brahmins for the meaning of the Brahmin,
one knows that this sutra was composed by Dharmatrāta.
The *Zhōu rù zàng lù* (Record of Works Included in the Canon during the Zhou Dynasty) lists this work among the Mahāyāna sūtras and within the collected transmissions;

it is a grave error to record it twice in both places. The *Fǎjù pìyù jīng* (Sūtra of Dharma-Pada Parables), four fascicles—also known as the *Fǎjù běnmò jīng* (Sūtra of the Origins and Endings of Dharma-Pada)—alternatively exists in five or six fascicles. Translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Fālì together with Fǎjù. This is the second translation. One of the two translations is missing. The following [entry] clarifies the similarities and differences between this and the aforementioned *Fǎjù jīng*.
The preceding sutra compiled only the verses and did not include the prose;
this subsequent sutra, however, explains the origins of those verses,
stating that the World-Honored One spoke them only because of certain causes and conditions.
Compared to the preceding verses, this [section] is abbreviated and incomplete.
Furthermore, there are mutual additions and omissions between the preceding and following verses.
It is an error for the *Zhou lu* (Catalogue of the Zhou Dynasty) to include this among the Mahāyāna sūtras.
*The Kāśyapa Saṃnipāta Sūtra*, one fascicle;
translated by An Shigao, the Tripiṭaka Master from Parthia during the Later Han dynasty;
included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection).
The first translation consists of three translations; two are missing. *A Compilation of the Three Piṭakas and the Miscellaneous Piṭaka* (Sanzang ji zanzang zhuan), one fascicle;
translator lost.

Now appended to the Eastern Jin Records as a single-fascicle *Shiyi* (Supplement) and included in the *Sanhui jing* (Sutra of the Three Wisdoms), one fascicle. Sengyou’s Records state that Master Dao’an classified it as a distinct scripture from the Liang region; it is now appended to the Liang Records.

The *Apidan Wufaxing jing* (Sūtra on the Fivefold Practice of Abhidharma), one fascicle— also known as the *Apidan Kuhui jing* (Sūtra on the Suffering and Wisdom of Abhidharma), though some versions omit the character "xing" (practice)—
was translated during the Later Han dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia. It is included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement) section of the standalone editions.

The *Shiyi bianru danben ahankoujie shier yinyuan jing* (Supplementary Compilation of the Single-Volume Oral Explanation of the Āgama on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination), one fascicle— also simply titled the *Ahankoujie jing* (Oral Explanation of the Āgama) or the *Duan shier yinyuan jing* (Sutra on Severing the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination)—
was translated during the Later Han dynasty by the Anxi upāsaka An Xuan, together with Yan Fotiao.
*The Sutra on the Path of the Small Vehicle*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhi Yao of the Western Regions during the Later Han dynasty; included in the *Supplemental Collection*.

*The Sutra on the Vows of Mañjuśrī*, one fascicle, alternatively titled with the character "Verses" (*gāthā*) added, translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin dynasty.

*The Names of Six Bodhisattvas*, one fascicle: included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) as a single work. The *Fang Zhonglu* (Record of Works Included in the Canon) states that it is also titled *The Names of Bodhisattvas* and should be recited and maintained.
Translated during the Later Han dynasty, translator lost; included in the *Shiyi* as a single work. *One Hundred and Fifty Verses in Praise of the Buddha*, one fascicle.
Composed by the Venerable Mātṛceṭa;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang and newly included in the canon.
A Single-Volume Praise in Verse to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one fascicle.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhihui of Foshouji during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang; recorded in the *Dazhou lu*.

The *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) is compiled as a single volume, comprising twelve fascicles in sixteen scrolls within the same case. The *Wuming Luocha Ji* (Collection of the Rakshasa Ignorance),
also known as the *Wuming Luocha Jing* (Sutra of the Rakshasa Ignorance), consists of one scroll— or alternatively two scrolls— and is likewise included in the *Shiyi*.
The standalone text *Biography of Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa*, translated during the Qin dynasty but now lost, is appended here as one fascicle.
*The Biography of Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty, appended to the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) as a separate volume.
*The Biography of Bodhisattva Āryadeva*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty, appended to the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) as a separate volume.

*The Biography of Dharma Master Vasubandhu*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty, appended to the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) as a separate volume. This [master] is called Tianqin (Vasubandhu).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen Dynasty; supplemented and included in the second translation.
One fascicle of the *Verses on the Essential Dharma Taught by the Bodhisattva Nāgadeva to King Śāntaka*, missing from one of the two translations.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kapiśā during the Song Dynasty;
recorded as the first translation in the Old Tang Catalogue: *One Scroll of Essential Verses for Exhorting Kings*.
Compiled by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman;
added as a supplement to the collection.
The Second Translation: *The Verses of Advice to the King by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna*, one fascicle;
translated during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing, newly included in the canon.

Third Translation: The above three collections are of the same original text but differ in their translations. The verses of the first two texts were previously combined into a single fascicle within the *Sūtra-piṭaka*;

they are now divided into two scrolls. *The Scripture on Piṇḍola-Bharadvāja Preaching the Dharma for King Udayana*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty. This is a standalone text; there is also another version titled *The Scripture on Piṇḍola Preaching the Dharma for a King*, one fascicle.
The preface is identical to this [previous entry].
Therefore, it is not listed twice. *The Method for Inviting Piṇḍola* (one fascicle), or with the word "sūtra" added;
translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Huìjiǎn. Second translation. One of the two translations is missing. *A Brief Analysis of Karmic Retribution* (one fascicle).
Compiled by the Bodhisattva Mahāvīra, with additional passages collected;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of India during the Song Dynasty;
appended as a supplement.
*The Scripture on the Transformations of the Future Spoken by the Bhikṣu Dānabhadra*, one fascicle.
This scripture was lost among the translations in Sengyou’s catalogue and is now appended to the Song dynasty catalogue.
Supplemental Compilation:
A Single-Volume Edition of the *Record of the Dharma Abiding as Taught by the Great Arhat Nandimitra*,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang.

The *Sāṃkhyakārikā* (Seventy Verses on the Sāṃkhya), in three fascicles—also known as the *Sāṃkhya-śāstra*—or in two fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen dynasty. From the *Chūn-nei-dian-lu*. Single Text. Original. Number 70. Also: *Sāṃkhya-śāstra*. Or: two fascicles.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen dynasty.
This standalone work is the first treatise on the right [side], composed by the non-Buddhist seer Kapila.
It elucidates the twenty-five principles (*tattva*).

This refers to what is called the *Kapila-śāstra* within the *Sāṃkhya-sūtra*. Regarding the two catalogs of the Inner Scriptures by Chángfǎng, it is an error that both the two-volume *Saptati-kārikā* translated by Paramārtha and the three-volume *Sāṃkhya-śāstra* are listed as existing.

*The Treatise on the Ten Categories of the Victorious School*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. [From] the *Catalogue of Translated Scriptures*, single-text edition. Commentary: This treatise was composed by the victor Śubhagupta (Huiyue). It elucidates the ten categories (*padārtha*) originally established by the owl-ṛṣi Kaṇāda. Although there were originally only six categories, Śubhagupta added four more to complete the ten. Because it is a comprehensive treatise covering both the fundamental and derivative aspects, it is titled *The Treatise on the Ten Categories of the Victorious School*.

The middle section states: "The Vaiśeṣika treatise is this one; its categories are superior to those of the other two treatises. These are not the Buddha-dharma, but are the tenets of various non-Buddhist schools (tīrthikas), and these two are the most prominent among them. I have explained them only so that those who are extensively learned may thoroughly understand the doctrines of heterodox paths."
The first fifteen sets comprise seventeen fascicles in one volume.
This collection of works composed in this land consists of forty-four works totaling four hundred twenty-two fascicles in fifty sets.

The *Mahābuddhanāmasūtra* in sixteen (or fourteen) fascicles was specially ordered by imperial decree on the twenty-third day of the tenth month of the fifteenth year of the Zhenyuan era to be included in the canon; it comprises two sets. The *Śākyaputravaṃśa* in ten fascicles also exists in a five-fascicle version, which differs from this one in its degree of detail.

*Śākyavaṃśasamāsavaṃśa* (A Brief Genealogy of the Śākya Clan), one fascicle, excerpted from the *Fanglu* (Record of the Abbot’s Quarters) by the Śramaṇa Shi Sengyou of Jianchu Monastery during the Xiao Qi dynasty;
newly compiled and included in the canon. (Some versions lack the character "lue" [brief].)
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery during the Great Tang Dynasty: *Shijia fangzhi* (Topography of Śākyamuni), two fascicles;

compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery during the Great Tang Dynasty: *Chu neidian lu xin bian ru zang* (Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures Newly Compiled for Inclusion in the Canon), upper three collections, thirteen fascicles in two volumes.
The Upper Volume contains seven [sections] and the Lower Volume contains six.

*Jīnglǜ yìxiàng* (Diverse Phenomena of Sūtras and Vinaya), fifty fascicles; five volumes. Compiled by the śramaṇa Bǎochàng and others by imperial decree in the fifteenth year of the Tiānjiān era of the Liáng dynasty. Recorded in the Chángfáng Catalogue. Newly compiled and included in the Canon: *Duōluóní pǐnjí* (Collection of Dhāraṇīs), ten fascicles; one volume. The author is unknown.

The aforementioned collection of one dhāraṇī is currently appended to the Liang-lu; however, its inclusion in the Dazhou-lu as a Mahāyāna single-text translation, with the further claim that the translator is lost, is incorrect.
Upon examining its text, it is evident that this is a local compilation rather than a separate translation from an Indian manuscript.
The reasons for this knowledge are that the *Saptabuddha-mantra-sūtra* and the *Dhāraṇī-pātra-sūtra*, among others, were all translated during the Jin dynasty;
furthermore, the *Hugu-zhongtong-dharani-jing* was translated by Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei.
Furthermore, the *Dhāraṇīpātra-sūtra* and the *Duḥkha-parama-vijaya-dīpa-rāja-sūtra* are two versions of the same original text.
Since such sūtras have all been collected and incorporated [into the canon], they are not transmitted as Indic originals.
This must have been compiled within this region;
it is unknown who the specific author was. Therefore, I have recorded it here:

*The Essential Compendium of Various Sutras*, twenty fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Śīlamegha of Ximing Monastery during the Great Tang Dynasty. Newly included in the Canon, Volume I: the first collection consists of twenty fascicles, divided into three bundles; the upper and lower bundles each contain seven fascicles, and the middle bundle contains six fascicles.

*Chusanzangjiji* (Collection for the Propagation and Preservation of the Tripiṭaka), fifteen fascicles; compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Sengyou of Jianchu Monastery during the Liang dynasty; recorded in the Chángfáng catalog; newly compiled and included in the *Zongjing mulu*. *Xiubinruzang zhongjing mulu* (Newly Compiled Catalog of Scriptures Included in the Canon), seven fascicles; compiled by the Śramaṇas Fa-jing and others by imperial decree in the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty; recorded in the Chángfáng catalog; newly compiled and included in the canon. The aforementioned two collections comprise twenty-two fascicles in two volumes: the upper volume contains ten fascicles, and the lower volume contains twelve.

The *Kaihuang Sanbao Lu* (Record of the Three Jewels of the Kaihuang Era), fifteen fascicles; the internal title reads *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Record of the Three Jewels Through Successive Dynasties). Compiled by Fei Changfang of Chengdu, a scholar-translator during the seventh year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. The *Neidian Lu Xinbian Ruzang Zhongjing Mulü* (Newly Compiled Catalogue of the Inner Canon for Inclusion in the Tripitaka), five fascicles; compiled during the second year of the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty.

An imperial edict was issued for the śramaṇas and scholars who were translating the scriptures to compile the *Neidian lu* (Record of Inner Scriptures) and newly include it in the Canon; this consists of the first two collections in twenty fascicles, arranged in two bundles.
The *Dadai neidian lu* (Record of Inner Scriptures of the Great Tang) in ten fascicles constitutes one bundle.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery in the Great Tang: *A New Compilation of the Catalogue of Scriptures Translated within and without the Palace for Inclusion in the Canon*, one fascicle;
compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhisheng of Chongfu Monastery in the Western Capital of the Great Tang:
*A New Compilation of the Illustrated Record of the Translation of Scriptures, Ancient and Modern, for Inclusion in the Canon*, four fascicles.
A New Compilation for Inclusion in the Canon:
A Continuation of the *Record of the Translation of Scriptures Past and Present*, in One Scroll, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Jingmai of the Great Tang;
and compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhisheng of Xichongfu Monastery of the Great Tang.

The Newly Compiled Catalogue of the Great Collection of Scriptures Authorized for Inclusion in the Canon, in fifteen fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Mingquan and others at the Fo-shou-ji Monastery by Imperial Decree during the Dàtáng dynasty;
the Newly Compiled Catalogue of Works Authorized for Inclusion in the Canon, in twenty-one fascicles across two volumes: the first volume in eleven fascicles and the second volume in ten fascicles.
*The Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Kaiyuan Era*, twenty fascicles in two volumes,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhisheng of Xichongfu Monastery in the Great Tang.
The Newly Compiled Supplement to the Kaiyuan Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings, one volume in three fascicles,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuanzhao of Ximing Monastery during the Great Tang, by imperial decree, for inclusion in the catalogue;
and the Newly Determined Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings from the Zhenyuan Era, thirty volumes.
Three fascicles;
compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xìmíng Monastery during the Táng Dynasty by imperial decree, as a new edition included in the canon:
*Yīqièjīng yīnyì* (Phonetics and Meanings of All Scriptures), twenty-five fascicles.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Xuanying, a translator of scriptures during the Great Tang, from the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures):
*Xinyi Dafangguang Fo Huayanjing Yinyi* (Phonetics and Meanings of the Newly Translated Avataṃsaka Sūtra), two fascicles;
compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huiyuan of Jingfasi Temple during the Great Tang.

The Newly Compiled Collection for Inclusion in the Canon, Parts One and Two, twenty-seven fascicles in four volumes: the first volume contains six fascicles; the remaining three volumes each contain seven.

*Record of the Western Regions of the Great Tang* (Dàtáng Xīyùjì), twelve fascicles, compiled by the Tripitaka Master Xuánzàng of the Great Tang; included in the *Neidiǎnlù*. The Newly Compiled Collection for Inclusion in the Canon, Part Three: *A Critical Evaluation of Buddhist and Daoist Doctrines through the Ages* (Gōngjīn Fó Dào Lùnhéng), four fascicles—or two fascicles—compiled by the Śramaṇa Shì Dàoxuān of Xímíng Monastery of the Great Tang; included in the *Neidiǎnlù*. The Newly Compiled Collection for Inclusion in the Canon, Continued Collection: *A Critical Evaluation of Buddhist and Daoist Doctrines through the Ages*, one fascicle, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shì Zhìshèng of Chóngfú Monastery of the Great Tang. The Newly Compiled Collection for Inclusion in the Canon, Parts Four and Five, seventeen fascicles in two volumes: the upper volume contains eight fascicles; the lower volume contains nine.

*Record of the Miraculous Responses of the Triple Gem in the Eastern Lands*, three fascicles; compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery during the Great Tang. From the *Neidian lu*. Newly compiled for inclusion in the Canon. *The Ritual for Śramaṇas Not Bowing to the Laity*, six fascicles; compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Yanzong of Hongfu Monastery during the Great Tang. From the *Neidian lu*. Newly compiled for inclusion in the Canon. The above two collections comprise nine fascicles and are bound together in one volume.

*Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Ci’en Monastery of the Great Tang*, ten fascicles; one bundle. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huili and others of the West Taiyuan Monastery of the Great Tang. Newly included in the canon. *Biographies of Eminent Monks Who Sought the Dharma in the Western Regions of the Great Tang*, two fascicles. Compiled by the Tripitaka Master Yi Jing of the Great Tang. Newly included in the canon. *Record of Faxian’s Travels to India*, one fascicle; also titled *Account of Travels to India*. Recorded by the Śramaṇa Shi Faxian of the Eastern Jin Dynasty concerning his own travels to India. From the Changfang Catalogue. Newly included in the canon. *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, fourteen fascicles; one fascicle is a table of contents. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huijiao of Jiaxiang Monastery in Kuaiji during the Liang Dynasty. From the Changfang Catalogue. The above three collections comprise seventeen fascicles in two bundles: the first bundle contains nine fascicles, and the second bundle contains eight.

*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*, thirty fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery during the Great Tang Dynasty. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Newly compiled for inclusion in the Canon, Upper Collection, thirty fascicles, divided into four bundles: the first and second each contain eight fascicles; the third and fourth each contain seven.

*Biànzhènglùn* (Discourse on Distinguishing the Correct), eight fascicles, one volume, compiled by the monk Fali of Longtian Monastery in the Great Tang; recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Record of Inner Scriptures) and newly included in the canon. *Poxielùn* (Discourse on Destroying Evil), two fascicles or one fascicle.
Compiled by Shi Falin of Longtian Monastery on Mount Zhongnan during the Great Tang Dynasty:
A Newly Compiled Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures for Inclusion in the Canon and Biographies in Three Volumes.
*Zhēnzhèng lùn* (Discourse on Discerning the Correct) in three fascicles,
compiled by Fali; *Xīnbìànhù lùn* (Newly Compiled Discourse on Resolving Doubts through Ten Gates),
in two or three fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Śi Xuānyí of Fóshòujì Monastery during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Fuli of Da Xingshan Monastery during the Great Tang Dynasty, the Newly Compiled *Hongming ji* for Inclusion in the Canon consists of fourteen fascicles.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Sengyou of Jianchu Monastery during the Liang Dynasty, the [original] collection was recorded in the Chángfáng lu; the Newly Compiled version for Inclusion in the Canon consists of twenty-four fascicles in two bundles: the first bundle contains twelve fascicles, and the second bundle contains twelve fascicles.

*Guang hongming ji* (Collection for the Wide Propagation and Clarification of the Teachings), thirty fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery during the Great Tang Dynasty; excerpted from the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures). Newly compiled for inclusion in the Canon, the first collection consists of thirty fascicles, divided into four bundles: the first bundle contains ten fascicles, the second bundle seven, the third bundle seven fascicles, and the fourth bundle six fascicles.

*Ji zhujing lichan yi* (Ritual for Repentance Compiled from Various Sūtras), two fascicles; compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhisheng of Xichongfu Monastery during the Great Tang. Newly included in the Canon. *Dadai nanhai jiguinei fachuan* (Record of the Inner Dharma Sent Back from the Southern Seas of the Great Tang), four fascicles; compiled by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang. Newly included in the Canon. *Biqiuni zhuan* (Biographies of Bhikṣuṇīs), four fascicles; compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Baochang of Zhuangyan Monastery during the Liang dynasty. Newly included in the Canon. *Bieshuozui yaofa* (Essential Rituals for the Confession of Offenses), one fascicle (the character "bie" may be absent); compiled by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang. Newly included in the Canon. *Shouyongsanshui yaofa* (Essential Rituals for the Use of the Three Waters), one fascicle; compiled by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang. Newly included in the Canon. *Humingfangsheng guiyi* (Ritual Procedures for Protecting Life and Releasing Creatures), one fascicle; compiled by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang. The above six collections, totaling thirteen fascicles, are contained in the same volume.
From the *Mahābuddhanāmasūtra* and the *Śākyavaṃśa* down to forty-four works totaling four hundred and twenty-two fascicles,
all were compiled by virtuous scholars of this land.
Nevertheless, it truly serves as a fundamental guide for assisting and glorifying the Great Dharma,
and for maintaining it during these final ages; therefore,
I have compiled this record and prepared it for wide circulation.
In compiling this canon, I have selected and omitted according to my own judgment.
Although various biographies pertain to the Buddhist tradition,
those not by Dharma protectors have not been included herein.
In total, counting the sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras of the Hīnayāna, as well as the collected biographies of worthies and sages currently in circulation,
there are four hundred and fifty-nine works comprising two thousand four hundred and two fascicles.
Two hundred and thirty-four bundles.
*The Biography of the Śramaṇa Falin*, three fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Yancong.
This one work was not included [in the canon] because the old records state that an imperial edict prohibited it and did not permit its circulation.
Now, upon examining this intent in detail,
it appears to pertain to a single occasion;
however, it does not conform to the formal rules of composition.
I hope you will permit its inclusion in the *Zhenyuan Catalogue*.
*The Newly Compiled Catalogue of Śākyamuni’s Teachings during the Zhenyuan Era*, Fascicle 23;
*The Newly Compiled Catalogue of Śākyamuni’s Teachings during the Zhenyuan Era*, Fascicle 24.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xīmíng Monastery in the Western Capital.

Part Two: The Supplementary Record of Translations with No Existing Texts. Section One of the Second Part of the Supplementary Record of Translations with No Existing Texts. Regarding those translations for which no existing text remains:
[The text continues with the list of titles.]
This refers to the textual contents of the Tripiṭaka and the collected works of sages and worthies—
those categories where the titles remain extant but the original texts are missing.
Since the holy teachings first moved eastward, nearly a millennium has passed.
The substance and form have undergone frequent changes, and the bells and tripods have been repeatedly moved.
Furthermore, as Zhou Wuling perished along with his followers of the black robe,
it has caused the lamp of the Dharma to lose its brilliance and the sun of wisdom to withdraw its light.
Essential texts of the Tripiṭaka are frequently scattered or missing;
some were translated recently in the Eastern Capital and had not yet reached the Western Capital,
while others were newly produced in small numbers such that they could not be found despite diligent searching.
How could one have heard of its profound mysteries, having read only the titles in vain?
To have strained my neck in pursuit was already a labor; to now beat my breast in regret is of no avail.
Now, having searched through various catalogs, I have fully recorded what has been lost and omitted.
I hope that many virtuous scholars will join me in investigating and inquiring into this matter.

There are a total of one thousand fifty-five works comprising two thousand thirty fascicles, including those from the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras, as well as the collected writings and commentaries of the sages and worthies, many of which were previously missing.

Mahāyāna sūtras missing: twenty-two works in twenty-five fascicles. Mahāyāna śāstras missing: twenty works in forty-eight fascicles. Hīnayāna sūtras missing: six hundred and five works in eight hundred and fifteen fascicles. Hīnayāna vinayas missing: forty-four works in ninety-two fascicles. Hīnayāna śāstras missing: nine works in sixty-five fascicles. Collected works of sages and worthies missing: forty-seven works in one hundred and eighty-four fascicles. Mahāyāna sūtras missing and Mahāyāna sūtras retranslated and missing: two hundred works in four hundred and eighty-four fascicles. The *Wu pin jing* (Sūtra of Five Chapters) in five fascicles—this is the *Prajñāpāramitā Hṛdaya Sūtra* translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kang Senghui of India;

this is the third translation. The new *Daoxing jing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) in ten fascicles, also known as the *Xiao pin* (Short Chapter), or in seven fascicles; according to the *Yù lù*, it is titled *Gèng chū xiǎo pin* (Another Translation of the Short Chapter).
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty;

this is the fourth translation. According to the catalogs of Changfang and others, it is incorrect to claim that there was another seven-fascicle version of the *Svalpamegha-sūtra* (Small Version Sutra) among the translations of Zhu Fahu.
Since the *New Sūtra on the Practice of the Way* (Xindaoxing jing) translated by Master Hu was not included among the separate records,
there is also a four-fascicle *Sūtra of the Great Wisdom to the Ultimate* (*Dazhidu wuji jing*),
which is likewise said to have been produced by Master Hu.
Since these are identical in meaning to the term *dōgyō* (行道),
they originally should not have been translated separately.
Because both [versions] would be redundant, they have not been retained here.

*Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, four fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jīvaka of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. The three sūtras above are the same text as the fourth assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.

There have been eight translations in total, five of which are extant in the canon while three are missing. According to the catalogs of Changfang and others, there are several instances where the number of scriptures translated by Kumārajīva is recorded incorrectly; specifically, the claim that there was a *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* (the *Fàngguāng bōrě*) in twenty-two fascicles is not correct. Since Master Kumārajīva had already translated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (the *Dàpǐn*), it would be illogical for the *Fàngguāng* to have been produced again; therefore, any such record is an error.

*The Sutra on the Supreme Pure Almsround of the Bodhisattva Śrutarṣi*, in two fascicles; also titled *The Sutra on the Samādhi of Resolving that All Dharmas are Like Illusions*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Yan Fotiao of Linhuai during the Later Han Dynasty. First Translation. The above sutra is the same text as the eighth assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
There have been three translations in total;
two versions are extant in the canon,
while one is missing.

*Renwang Banruo Jing* (Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra), one fascicle, or two fascicles, thirty-one pages; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin—this is the first translation. *Renwang Banruo Jing*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of India during the Liang dynasty. The above constitutes three translations in total.
One copy exists in the Imperial Library; two copies are missing.

*Prajñāpāramitā-naya-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang. Newly included in the catalog. This is the same text as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-mantra-sūtra*.
There are three translations [of this work] in total;
two versions are extant in the canon while one is missing.

The *Dàoxíng jīng* (Treatise on the Way of Practice), in one fascicle, was stated by Master An to be an excerpt from the *Prajñā[pāramitā]* compiled by a person of high learning from the Western Regions, for which Master An composed a preface. Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Zhu Foshuo during the Later Han Dynasty. Although this single scripture is titled *Dàoxíng*, it is [in fact] the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*.
The entire fascicle is very small;
it cannot be considered the same original text as the preceding *Daoxing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā).
For now, let it be recorded separately.

*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-mantra-sūtra*, one fascicle (sometimes without the word *mahā*); translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian. *Mahāprajñā-anuprāpti-citta-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan. Newly compiled and included in the canon. The above ten works, totaling twenty-seven fascicles, following the *Wu-pin-jing* (Wu Division Sūtra), are missing texts from within the Prajñā section.

*Wuliangshou jing* (Sūtra of Immeasurable Life), two fascicles; translated by the Parthian Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. First translation. *Wuliang qingjing pingdengjue jing* (Sūtra of the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment), two fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bo Yan of the Western Regions during the Cao Wei. Fifth translation. [Note: According to the records of Sengchang and others, there was additionally one fascicle of the *Pingdengjue jing* (Sūtra of Equal Enlightenment) among the translations of Bo Yan.
This is precisely what was not redundantly repeated in the preceding sutra.
The two-fascicle *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* (*Wúliàngshòu jīng*) is also titled the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment* (*Wúliàng qīngjìng píngděng jué jīng*),
translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty.

The sixth translation: *The Sūtra of the Tathāgata Amitāyus, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha*, in one fascicle; also known as the *Sūtra on the Joyful Buddha-land* or the *Sūtra on the Land of Ultimate Bliss*.
Translated by the foreign śramaṇa Zhu Fali of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
The seventh translation: *The New Sūtra of Amitāyus*, in two fascicles; also said to have appeared in the second year of the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty;
the eighth translation, the *New Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* in two fascicles;
translated by the śramaṇa Baotán of Liangzhou during the Song Dynasty.
The ninth translation is the *New Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* in two fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Kasmīra during the Song dynasty at Zhenji Temple;
this is recorded as the tenth translation. The above seven sūtras are the same text as the "Assembly on Immeasurable Life" (the fifth assembly) of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*.
This sutra has eleven translations;
four versions are extant in the canon while seven are missing.

*The Scripture on the Chapter on the Training of Bodhisattvas in the Buddha-field of Akṣobhya*, two fascicles. Translated by the Eastern Jin śramaṇa Zhidao Gen. Third translation. This aforementioned scripture is the same text as the sixth assembly, the *Akṣobhyatathāgata-parivarta*.
There are three translations in total;
two are extant and one is missing.

*The Sūtra on the Non-differentiation of the Essential Nature of the Dharma-realm*, two fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. Recorded in the *Fashang lu*. This is the first translation. Note: This single sūtra is identical in its original text to the eighth [sūtra], the *Dharmadhātu-svabhāva-parivarta*.
There are two translations, one of which is extant and the other missing.

*Pumenpin jing* (Sutra on the Universal Gate Chapter), one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. This second translation is the same text as the tenth chapter, the "Assembly of Mañjuśrī’s Universal Gate."
There are three translations in total;
two exist while one is missing.

*The Sutra on Adorning and Purifying the Buddha-field*, two fascicles, also known as the *Sutra on the Pure Land*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Bai Fazang of Henei during the Western Jin dynasty. This second translation is the same text as the fifteenth chapter, the "Mañjuśrī-Prophecy" assembly.
There have been three translations, two of which survive and one of which is missing.

*Bodhisattvapitaka-sūtra*, three fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. This is the first translation. The above sutra is the same text as the seventeenth, the *Pūrṇa-parivarta*.
There are two translations, one extant and one missing.

*Fajing jing* (Sūtra on the Mirror of the Dharma), two fascicles (or one fascicle), translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. This is the second translation; it is recorded among the works translated by Zhi Qian in the catalogues compiled by Sengchang and others.
Furthermore, there is the *Ugra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in two fascicles;
this is none other than the *Dharmadarśana-sūtra*.
It need not be recorded here again to avoid redundancy.

*The Sūtra of the Questions of Ugra* (Yùjiālúyuè wèn púsà jīng), one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Bái Fǎzǔ of Hénèi during the Western Jin dynasty. Fifth translation. *The Sūtra of the Questions of the Householder Ugra* (Yùjiā zhǎngzhě suǒwèn jīng), one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dhammarakṣita of Kapiśa during the Song dynasty. Sixth translation. The above three sūtras are the same text as the nineteenth [assembly], the *Ugraparipṛcchā*.
There have been six translations in total;
three remain extant and three are missing.

*The Sūtra of the Questions of the Girl Prajñā* (1 fascicle). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang. Newly included in the canon. Third translation. This sūtra is identical in text to the thirtieth chapter, "The Assembly of the Girl Prajñā."
There are four translations in total; three are extant and one is missing. *Ajātaśatru-rājña-duhitṛ-āśokadattā-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle.

Translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty]. (First Translation) *Āśokadattā-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin [Dynasty]. (Third Translation) *Āśokadattā-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Song [Dynasty]. (Fourth Translation) The above three sūtras are the same text as the thirty-second assembly, the *Abhayamati-bodhisattva-parivarta*.

There have been five translations in total, two of which are extant and two of which are missing. Furthermore, in the catalogues of Sengyou, Fei Changfang, and others, there is an additional *Aśokadattā-avadāna* (The Story of King Ajātaśatru’s Daughter Aśokadattā) in one fascicle attributed to Dharmarakṣa. However, this is merely a difference in the phonetic transcriptions of the Chu and Jin periods and does not constitute a separate work; "Aśudata" is the Sanskrit term while "Aśokadattā" is its Chinese translation. Thus, the fact that both scriptures are recorded together in these catalogues is an error.

*Yǔhuàn sānmèijīng* (The Scripture on the Illusion-like Samādhi), two fascicles, or one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty—First Translation. *Yǔhuàn sānmèijīng*, two fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty—Third Translation. *Yǔhuàn sānmèijīng*, two fascicles; translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Shilun of Yuezhi during the Former Liang dynasty.
The Postscript to the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi-sūtra*.

Fourth Translation. Newly compiled and included in the canon: *The Holy Sūtra of the Questions of the Devaputra Susthitamati*, four fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty. Sixth Translation. The above four sūtras constitute the same text as the thirty-sixth assembly, the *Susthitamati-devaputra-paripṛcchā*, which exists in seven translations in total; three remain extant while four are missing.

*The Sūtra on the Great Skillful Means Asked by Bodhisattva Prajñottara*, in two fascicles; alternatively, without the title "Bodhisattva," or in one fascicle. Translated by the Śramaṇa Yan Fotiao of Linhuai during the Later Han dynasty. This is the first translation of the *Sūtra on the Great Skillful Means* in two fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. This is the fourth translation. *The Sūtra on the Great Skillful Means Asked by Bodhisattva Prajñottara*, in two fascicles—also known as *The Sūtra of Prajñottara Bodhisattva*, or simply *The Great Skillful Means*, or *The Mahāyāna Upāya*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gaṭa from the Western Regions during the Northern Liang dynasty. This is the fifth translation. The three aforementioned sūtras share the same root text as the thirty-eighth assembly, the *Mahāyāna Upāya-parivarta*.
There are five translations in total;
two remain and three are missing.

*The Sūtra of the Great Vows Asked by Maitreya*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. This is the second translation. The aforementioned sūtra is identical in text to the forty-second assembly, "The Questions of Maitreya."
There have been three translations, two of which survive and one of which is missing.

*The Sūtra on the Pure Conduct of Bodhisattvas*, two fascicles; also called *The Sūtra on the Pure Discipline*. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Kang Senghui of the Wu dynasty. This is the first translation of a separate chapter. This single sūtra is the same text as the forty-seventh assembly, the "Assembly of the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin."
This is the "Ratnaśikhara-parivarta" from the Mahāsannipāta-sūtra;
excluding its original text, there are two translations,
one of which remains extant while the other is missing.

*Śrīmālā-sūtra*, one fascicle; also titled *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahopāya-sūtra*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty. First translation. The above sūtra is the same text as the "Assembly of Lady Śrīmālā," the forty-eighth [chapter].
There are three translations in total;
one is missing.

*Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, three fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śayanāśas during the Northern Zhou dynasty of the Yuwen clan. Regarding the above sutra, although it is called the *Ratnakūṭa*, [it is distinct from the standard version].
Since there is no original text available for collation,
it is unknown with which version this current edition corresponds.
For now, I have recorded it at the end, following the *Wǔliàngshòu jīng* (Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra).
Thirty sections, fifty-four fascicles. This work is missing from the Ratnakūṭa section. *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, twenty-seven fascicles;

translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Later Han—First Translation. *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, thirty fascicles (some editions contain new characters) or twenty-four fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin—Second Translation. The above two sūtras are the same text.
There have been three translations in total;
one version is extant in the canon while two are missing.

*Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Song dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra from India. This is the second translation. The above sutra has four translations in total across its history.

Three versions are extant and one is missing. *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra*, two fascicles (sometimes titled with the character "Da" [Great], or in one fascicle). Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Foshuo during the Later Han dynasty. This is the second translation. *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra*, one fascicle. This is a re-translation of the latter ten chapters. According to the *Yù Lù*, there are versions in one and three fascicles. Translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Loujiachen during the Later Han dynasty. Recorded in the *Jìngtài Lù*. This is the third translation. *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Nianfo Zhang Jing* (Sūtra on the Chapter on Mindfulness of the Buddha in the Pratyutpanna-samādhi), one fascicle. This is a separate translation of the "Practice Chapter" (*Xíng Pǐn*). Translation lost during the Later Han period. This is the fourth translation. *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra*, two fascicles. The Record of Master Ān states: "A further version of the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra* was produced. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Zhú Fáhù. This is the sixth translation. The above four sūtras share the same original text; they comprise seven translations in total, arranged chronologically.
Three versions are extant and four are missing; four are complete texts while three are abridged translations.

*Akṣayamati-bodhisattva-sūtra*, four fascicles. Translated by the Indian śramaṇa Vighnanandin during the Wu dynasty. First translation. *Akṣayamati-bodhisattva-sūtra*, four fascicles. Translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty. Second translation. *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra*, ten fascicles. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of India during the Song dynasty. Fifth translation. The above three sūtras share the same original text and comprise five successive translations.

Two versions are preserved in the Canon; three are missing. Furthermore, according to the catalogues of Daochang and others, there is another *Akṣayamati-sūtra* in four fascicles translated by Dharmarakṣa. However, since Dharmarakṣa had already produced the *Aksayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra*, it is inappropriate for the *Akṣayamati-sūtra* to be issued again. The title of the *Aksayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that in the Jin period it is called *Wujinyi* (Inexhaustible Intention). A footnote in the catalogue notes that it may consist of four fascicles. This is merely a difference between the Sanskrit and Chinese names; in reality, they are one and the same sutra. That two versions are recorded in the catalogues is a grave error.

*The Minor Aśokasūtra*, two fascicles; translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty]. Since this single sūtra is prefixed with the designation "Minor" (xiǎo), it should not be the same text as the aforementioned sūtras.

The *Vaipulya Sovereign Gaganagañja Sūtra* in eight fascicles, also known as the *Gaganagañja-paripṛcchā*, or in five fascicles; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Shengjian during the Qifu Qin dynasty. The above sūtra is an alternative translation of the "Gaganagañja" chapter of the *Mahāsannipāta*.
Even if there were such a text in the Tibetan canon, it would be a separate production titled the *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra*;
it is not a different translation from that translated by Kumārajīva.
Alternatively, this very sūtra may be the translation by Kumārajīva himself.
*The Scripture on the Questions of the Devaputra Non-Saint Firmly Emerged*, five fascicles;

translated during the Northern Zhou Yuwen period by the Tripiṭaka Master Dhyāna-ācārya Jñāyaśas from the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*. From this point in the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* downward, there are thirteen works totaling ninety-seven fascicles. *The Scripture on the Questions of the Devaputra Samādhi-Mind*, five fascicles; currently suspected to be the same text as the *Susthitamati-paripṛcchā-sūtra*. Translated during the Northern Zhou Yuwen period by the Tripiṭaka Dhyāna Master Jñāyaśas. From the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* downward, these constitute thirteen sections comprising ninety-seven fascicles.

*The Scripture on Entering the Inconceivable Wisdom of the Tathāgata*, three fascicles. Missing from the *Mahāsannipāta* section. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Dhyāna Master Jñāyaśas during the Northern Zhou Yuwen period. This is the second translation according to the *Fanying tu*. The above scripture has been translated four times in total.

Three [versions] survive and one is missing. *The Sūtra on the Ten Stages of the Bodhisattva* (1 fascicle), also called *The Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* or simply *The Ten Stages Sūtra*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. First translation: *The Mahāvaipulya Bodhisattva Ten Stages Sūtra* (1 fascicle). Translated by the lay devotee Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin. Second translation: *The Ten Stages Sūtra* (1 fascicle). Translated by the Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin. Third translation. The above three sūtras share the same original text; there have been five translations in total across these periods, of which two survive and three are missing.

*Mahāvaipulya-anutpādānirodha-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the era of the Empress of the Great Tang; newly included in the canon as a single-fascicle work. *Mahāvaipulya-tathāgata-acintya-viṣaya-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the era of the Empress of the Great Tang; included in the canon as a single-fascicle work. *Buddhapiṭaka-mahāvaipulya-sūtra*, one fascicle, also titled *Prajñāpradīpa-paripṛcchā-sūtra*. Translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Daoyan. Regarding the above-mentioned scripture, the catalogue of the Sui dynasty śramaṇa Fajing states:
The "Chapter on the Difficulty of Understanding" from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* has alternative translations.
The old translation is currently missing, while the new translation is found in the sixth fascicle of the old version and the thirteenth fascicle of the new version.

*The Sutra on the Original Acts of the Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; this is also the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, sometimes simply titled the *Sutra on Original Acts*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin dynasty. This is the second translation; together with the original version, there are five translations in total, including the preceding and following ones.
Four copies were originally in the canon. One copy was missing;

since the old version of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* translated by Buddhabhadra did not correspond [to this], this separate edition of the *Karmavibhaṅga* was produced and included in the canon during the Dàzhōu period. I have not yet seen its physical manuscript, though I have described it here. Furthermore, the entry in Chángfáng’s catalog stating that Zhīqiān re-translated the "Pure Conduct Chapter" (*Jìngxíng pǐn*) is an error. The footnote for the *Jìngxíng jīng* states: "Also known as the *Bodhisattva-mūlakarma-sūtra*."

The *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmika-sūtra*, which is the "Ten Stages" chapter. Translated by the lay devotee Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin dynasty. This is the second translation; it includes five translations in total, both preceding and following this version.
Four copies were originally in the canon;

one copy was missing. Furthermore, the catalog of Changfang and others lists another work, the *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmika-sūtra* in one fascicle, claiming it was translated by Buddhabhadra of the Eastern Jin. Upon careful examination, since Buddhabhadra had already translated the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*, it is inconsistent for him to have separately produced this sūtra; thus, Changfang’s catalog is erroneous.

*Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, twelve fascicles; this is the "Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmi*) chapter. Translated by the lay devotee Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin dynasty. This is the third translation; the above includes five translations in total for this chapter and its preceding and following sections.
Four original copies were held in the repository; one was missing.

The *Rāmaka-sūtra* in three fascicles is a small portion of the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Gandavyūha*) chapter. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Anxian of the Western Regions during the Cao Wei dynasty—First Translation. The *Rāmaka-sūtra* in one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty—Fourth Translation. The above includes the present version, totaling five translations across its preceding and succeeding stages.
Three editions exist in the canon while two are missing;
from the *Tathāgataguṇajñānācintyaviṣayāvatāranirdeśa-sūtra* downward, twelve sections comprising seventeen fascicles are missing from within the Avataṃsaka division.

*Fàn bānnièhuán jīng* (Sanskrit Parinirvāṇa Sūtra), two fascicles; the old catalogs state it was formerly called *Hú bān*, now changed to *Fàn*. Alternatively, one fascicle. Translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Zhīlújiāchèn of the Later Han. First translation. *Dà bānnièpán jīng* (Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra), two fascicles. Abridged from the preceding chapters by the foreign Tripiṭaka Master Ān Fǎxián of the Cao Wei, forming three fascicles. First translation. *Dà bānnièhuán jīng* (Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra), two fascicles. Translated by the śramaṇa Zhìmǐng of Yongzhou during the Northern Liáng dynasty at Liangzhou. Sixth translation. *Bānnièhuán jīng* (Parinirvāṇa Sūtra), twenty fascicles. Translated by the lay devotee Zhīqiān of the Wu dynasty. The Preface Chapter and the Lamentation Chapter form two fascicles. Second translation. The above includes both the Mahāparinirvāṇa and the Mahāyāna versions.
Furthermore, there are seven translations of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, including the newly translated *Later Part*. Of these, three versions are extant in the canon while four are missing.

Moreover, the *Catalogue of the Great Zhou* cites the *Record of Zhu Daozu*, stating that in the twelfth year of the Yixi era of the Eastern Jin (416 CE), Buddhabhadra translated one fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* at Daochang Temple—though some say ten fascicles—which constitutes the first ten fascicles of the "Great Version," ending with the *Mahāsāṃghika-paripṛcchā-parivarta*. Upon examining various catalogs and biographies, it appears that the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* translated by Faxian was also translated at Daochang Temple in the thirteenth year of the Yixi era. Since all the scriptures produced by Faxian were translated in collaboration with Guṇabhadra, and since the titles and annotations in various catalogs frequently overlap, it is certain that because the time and place of translation were identical, this was not a second edition. Therefore, I have unified them and shall no longer preserve them as separate works.

The four sections totaling twenty-six fascicles from the *Brahmaparānirvāṇa-sūtra* are missing from the *Nirvāṇa* section. The eight-fascicle *Pu-yao jing* (Lalitavistara) translated during the Shu [kingdom] period has a lost translator;

it appears to have been translated in the Shu territory and was the first translation. It is recorded in the Wei and Wu catalogs as the eight-fascicle, six-fascicle, or four-fascicle *Pu-yao jing*. The third translation was made by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Zhìyán together with Bǎoyún. The two aforementioned scriptures share the same source text as the *Vaipulya-vyūha-sūtra* (Fāngguǎng zhuāngyán jīng); thus, there are four translations in total.
Two extant and two missing.
*Ananta-artha-nirdeśa-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. First translation. The above sutra has two translations, earlier and later.
One version exists and one is missing.
*Fahua sanmei jing* (The Lotus Samādhi Sūtra), six fascicles; one edition includes the character "zheng" (correct/standard).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhīqiānliángjié of the Three Regions during the Wu dynasty.
From the *Chuanjing tu* (Diagram of the Translation of Scriptures), Part One: The first translation is the *Sārvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkāra-sūtra* in six fascicles,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin during the Taishi era.

Regarding the second translation, I have carefully consulted the catalogs of Changfang and others. The *Zhengfahua jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) was translated by Dharmarakṣa in the seventh year of the Dàkāng era; this appears in the catalog of Niè Dàozhēn. It further states that it was also translated in the first year of the Tàiśǐ era. The *Sàyúnfénduólì jīng* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) in six fascicles is recorded in the catalog of Zhú Dàozǔ as being the same single scripture, yet it is listed under different titles. Since the original text remains, the reason for this duplication is not clear; perhaps "Sàyúnfénduólì" is the Sanskrit term while "Zhèngfǎhuā" is the Chinese name, and the cataloguers erred in retaining both.
The *Fāngděng Fǎhuá jīng* (Vaipulya Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) in five fascicles was translated by the Eastern Jin śramaṇa Zhī Dàohèn.
These three translations above share the same base text, and when combined with the *Tiānpǐn* (Augmented Version), there are six translations in total, arranged chronologically.
Three texts are extant and three are missing.

*The Buddha Calls with the Three Vehicles* (Fó yǐ sān chē huàn jīng), one fascicle; translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty]. The above one scripture is an alternative translation from within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This should be the "Chapter on Similes.
The *Old Vimalakīrti Sūtra* in two fascicles,
translated by the śramaṇa Yan Fotiao of Linhuai during the Later Han dynasty.

The first translation is the *Yi Vimalakīrti Sūtra* in three fascicles; Yu states it is distinct from the *Weimojie Jing*, though some versions have the character "si" (思) or consist of two fascicles.
It was translated by the lay practitioner Zhu Shulan of the Western Regions during the Western Jin dynasty.
The third translation is the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-dharmaparyāya Sūtra* in one fascicle, also known as the *Weimojie Jing*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty; this is the fourth translation.

I have carefully examined the *Sengyou lu*, which further records a one-fascicle *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* also said to be translated by Dharmarakṣa. A note below states: "Sengyou’s intention was that the previously produced *Vimalakīrti* was redundant, and thus Dharmarakṣa edited it to remove the missing verses. My current view differs not at all from this, so I have not preserved it separately. Furthermore, the *Zhou lu* contains another two-fascicle *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* also said to have been translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty. Upon checking the *Changfang lu*, this scripture is not found there; the *Zhou lu* is therefore in error.

*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, four fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Gītamitra of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty; the fifth translation. The above four sutras share the same original text and comprise seven translations in total, arranged chronologically.

Three remain and four are missing; as for the five fascicles compiled by the Western Jin śramaṇa Zhimindù from one version by Zhi Qian and two versions by Zhu Fahu, they are not included because they were not separate translations and their original texts are lost.

*Mahāvaipulya-śikhara-rāja-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; this is the second translation. The aforementioned single sūtra has four translations in total, preceding and following this one.

Three translations remain, while one is missing. *Xiánjū jīng* (Sūtra on Dwelling in Seclusion), ten fascicles; translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa—First Translation. *Bēihuā jīng* (Sūtra of the Compassionate Flower), ten fascicles; translated by the Northern Liang Śramaṇa Shi Daogong—Third Translation. These two sūtras share the same original text and comprise four translations in total, consisting of the preceding and following versions.
Two [versions] are extant and two are missing.

*The Sūtra on the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Jibin during the Song dynasty; this is the third translation. The above sūtra has three translations in total, spanning earlier and later periods.
Two [versions] exist and one is missing.

*Mahāyāna-ratnamegha-sūtra*, eight fascicles; translated by the Śramaṇa Subhūti of Funan during the Chen dynasty. This is the second translation. The above sutra has three translations in total, including the preceding ones.
Two [versions] exist and one is missing.

*Samādhi-saṃgīti-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Bai Fazǔ of Hénèi during the Western Jìn dynasty. This is the second translation. The above sutra has three translations in total, spanning earlier and later periods.
Two [versions] exist, one is missing.

*Dhṛtarāṣṭraparipṛcchā-sūtra*, three fascicles; translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty. This is the second translation. The above sutra has three translations in total, spanning earlier and later periods.
Two [versions] are extant and one is missing.
