The *Mañjuśrī-viṣayābharaṇa-sūtra* (also known as the *Xiàn bǎozàng jīng*) is in two fascicles, or alternatively three fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Fǎqīn of Parthia during the Western Jin dynasty. Third translation: the *Mañjuśrī-viṣayābharaṇa-sūtra* in two fascicles, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhī Fǎdù of the Western Jin dynasty. Third translation. The above two sūtras are the same text with four translations in total, arranged chronologically.
Two extant, two missing.

*Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, four fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty; the first translation. Of the above one sūtra, there have been four translations in total, three of which are extant and one missing.

The Mahāvaipulya-nirnimitta-sūtra, five fascicles; also known as the Mahāvaipulya-mahāmegha-sūtra, or simply the Mahāmegha-sūtra, or four fascicles. Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty. This is the second translation; the above sūtra has thus been translated twice, earlier and later.
One version exists while another is missing.

*Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. This is the second translation. The above sutra has three translations in total, spanning earlier and later periods.
Two versions exist and one is missing. *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra*, two fascicles;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Fǎqīn of Parthia during the Western Jin dynasty. Third translation: *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra*, two fascicles, further produced; retranslated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhú Fǎhù of the Western Jin dynasty. Fourth translation: the above was translated by Zhú Fǎhù in the seventh year of Dàkāng.
The *Puchao jing* (Sūtra of Universal Transcendence) was translated again after this;

therefore, its title is marked as "re-translated" (*gengchu*). According to Seng'an's catalog, there is only a re-translation of the *Aśoka-rāja-sūtra*, whereas the *Puchao sanmei* has no such re-translation, as it was previously translated by Zhi Chen. Consequently, it is described as a "re-translation. In Sengyou’s catalog, both versions are recorded.
*Ajātaśatru-sūtra*, two fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; this is the fifth translation. The three sūtras mentioned above share the same original text.
Together with the *Pātra-praveśana-sūtra*, there are six translations in total, three of which survive and three of which are missing.

*The Scripture on the Moon-Lamp Samādhi*, one fascicle; extracted from the seventh fascicle of the *Great Moon-Lamp Scripture*. Translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. First Separate Translation. (Note: This includes both the large version and the preceding and following three translations.)

Two versions are preserved and one is missing. *Xiàngyì jīng* (Sūtra of the Armpit of the Elephant), one fascicle; translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Zhīlújiāchèn of the Later Han. Recorded in the *Fǎshàng lù*. First translation. *Wúsuǒxīwàng jīng* (Sūtra of No Expectation), one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jīduómì of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin. Third translation. The above two sūtras are the same text, with four translations in total across the earlier and later periods.
Two versions exist and two are missing.

*The Sūtra of the Golden Light Crest*, one fascicle; translated during the Former Liang by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Shilun. This is the second translation appended to the record following the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. To the right, this single sūtra is the same text as the *Mahāviśuddhadharmamukha-sūtra* and others.
There were three translations made earlier and later;
two survive and one is missing.

*The Gāthā of Amitābha Buddha*, one fascicle, translator lost, included in the Later Han Record as the first translation. This is the same text as the *Amitābha Gāthā* produced later; of these two successive translations, one survives and one is missing.

*The Sutra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Kasmīra during the Song dynasty. Recorded in the *Baochang lu*. This is the second translation. The above sutra has two translations, earlier and later.

One exists and one is missing. *The Minor Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* (Xiǎo Wúliàngshòu jīng), one fascicle; also known as the *Amitābha Sūtra* or [without the character] "Minor. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. This is the second translation. The above is the same text as the *Amitābha Sūtra*, with three translations in total across earlier and later periods; two exist and one is missing. According to the *Catalogue of the Tripitaka of the Great Zhou*, there was a *Minor Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* whose text was no different from the *Amitābha Sūtra*; therefore, it is considered a missing version.

*Maitreya-buddha-sūtra*, one fascicle; also titled *Maitreya-āgami-janma-sūtra*, seventeen sheets. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. First translation. The above sūtra has two translations, earlier and later.
One exists and one is missing. *Mile danglai xia sheng jing* (The Sutra on Maitreya’s Future Descent), one fascicle;

Sengyou’s Catalog states it was lost among the records of Master Dao’an and is now appended to the Western Jin catalog. First translation. *Mile zuo fo shi shi jing* (The Sutra on the Events of Maitreya Becoming a Buddha), one fascicle; not listed in Sengyou’s Catalog, appearing in Baochang’s Catalog as eight sheets; now appended to the Eastern Jin catalog. Second translation. Translator lost. *Mile xia sheng jing* (The Sutra on Maitreya’s Descent), one fascicle; translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Liang dynasty. Fifth translation. The above three sutras share the same source text and have undergone six translations in total; three exist and three are missing.

*Sarvadharmavīrarāja-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema during the Later Han dynasty; recorded in the *Fashang lu*; this is the first translation. The above sutra has three translations in total, both earlier and later.

Two [versions] survive and one is missing. *Upāyakauśalya-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Kang Senghui of the Wu dynasty. First translation. *Lèyíngluòzhuāngyánfābiàn-jīng* (Sūtra on the Skillful Means of Adornment with Joyful Garlands), one fascicle; also known as the *Dàchéngyíngluòzhuāngyán-jīng* (Mahāyāna Sūtra on Adornment with Garlands) or the *Zhuǎnnǚshēn Púsà* (Bodhisattva Who Transforms the Female Body); translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Fǎhǎi. Fourth translation. The two sūtras above share the same original text and comprise four translations in total, arranged chronologically.

Regarding the two works translated by Dharmarakṣa, the *Shunquan fangbian jing* (Sūtra on Following Expedient Means) in two fascicles and the *Suiquan nü jing* (Sūtra of the Woman Following Expediency) in two fascicles: at the end of the *Shunquan fangbian jing*, it is further stated that it is also called the *Shunquan nü jing*. Since the two meanings of "suiquan" (following expediency) and "shunquan" (conforming to expediency) are similar, and because the *Suiquan nü jing* is recorded separately in Sengyou’s catalogue but is absent from Daoan’s catalogue, we know that it is simply the *Shunquan jing* with a difference in title resulting from the various cataloguers' errors. The *Suiquan nü jing* is now deleted as being indeterminate.

*Śyāma-pūrvayoga-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Śyāma-sūtra*; extracted from the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. This is the second translation. The above includes four translations in total, both preceding and following the original *Ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*.
Three translations survive and one is missing.

*The Sūtra of the Precious Casket of the Wordless* (Wuzi baobie jing), one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas during the Northern Wei dynasty. This is the second translation. The above sūtra has four translations in total, spanning both earlier and later periods.
Three versions survive and one is missing.

*Śrī-vyaya-sūtra* (一卷), one fascicle; Sengyou’s Catalogue states that it was a lost-translation scripture from the record of Master Dao’an. It is now appended to the Western Jin catalogue as the second translation. This single scripture is the same text as the *Candraprabha-kumāra-bodhisattva-sūtra*, among others, and there are four translations in total, arranged chronologically.
Three versions survive and one is missing.

*The Vow Sutra of the Elder’s Son*, one fascicle, translated during the Cao Wei dynasty (translator lost); second translation: *The Bodhisattva Vow Sutra*, one fascicle, translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng. Fifth translation. The above two sutras are the same text, with five translations in total across earlier and later periods.

Three [versions] are extant and two are missing. *Vatsa-sūtra* (also known as *Vatsaputra-sūtra*), one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. Third translation: *Puyang-jing* (or *Ruyang-jing*), one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñātamitra of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. Fourth translation. The above two sūtras share the same original text and comprise four translations in total, arranged chronologically.
Two extant and two missing. *The Scripture on the Adornment of the Woman*, one fascicle;

translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty]; the first translation. *The Scripture on the Woman Heard in the Womb*, one fascicle; recited and brought forth by the Śramaṇa Shi Fahuā of the Xiao Qi [Dynasty]; the fifth translation. The above two scriptures are the same text with five translations in total across three extant and two missing versions.

*The Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*, one fascicle; also titled *The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination Heard at the City*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han. First Translation. *The Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination Missing the City*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Yao of the Western Regions during the Later Han. Second Translation. *The Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination Contemplated Beneath the Peepal Tree*, one fascicle; also titled *The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination Contemplated Beneath the Bodhi Tree*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of Central India during the Western Jin. Fourth Translation. *The Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavṛddhi of India during the Southern Qi. Fifth Translation. The above four sūtras share the same original text and comprise six translations in total, arranged chronologically.

Regarding these four [texts], two are missing. Although the text for the *Wencheng jing* (Sūtra of the City) exists within the Āgama collection, it is identical to the version found under the *Pāṭala* tree; furthermore, the one-fascicle *Shíèr yuánjīng* (Sūtra of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination) is extracted from the forty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*. Therefore, these two sūtras were not transcribed into the canon, as separate versions were sought elsewhere.

*Yiliao benshengsi jing* (Sūtra on the Differentiation of Original Birth and Death), one fascicle. Sengyou’s Catalogue states that it was lost from An’s record and its translation is now appended to the Western Jin catalogue. Of the above, this single sūtra has been translated three times in total.
Two exist, one is missing.

*The Sūtra on the Tathāgata’s Sole Realization of the Samādhi of Self-Vow*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñātāmitra of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty; this is the third translation. The above sūtra has three translations in total, spanning earlier and later periods.
Two [versions] are extant and one is missing.

*Aṣṭamaṅgalika-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Song dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra; the third translation. The above sutra has five translations in total, including those preceding and following it.
Four extant, one missing.

*The Amoghapāśahṛdaya-mantra-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated during the reign of the Great Tang Empress by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India. Included in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. This is the third translation. The above one sūtra has four translations in total, comprising both old and new versions, as well as expanded and abridged recensions.
Three versions are extant and one is missing. *Mahāmāyūrīvidyārājñī-sūtra*, one fascicle.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śrīmitra of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. First translation. *Māyūrī-vidyārājñī-vividha-mantra-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śrīmitra of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. Second translation. *Māyūrī-mantra-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmaruci of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. Third translation. The above three sūtras share the same original text and comprise eight translations in total, including the preceding ones.

Of the five extant and three missing versions, the first six are brief while the latter two are very extensive. As for the *Śrīmitra-vaipulya-saṃyukta-devatā-mantra-sūtra*, which was translated by Śrīmitra, it must be a different recension; since I have not yet seen that scripture, it is difficult to provide a definitive comparison.

*Wuduan di chijing* (Sūtra on Holding Without End), one fascicle; the old catalogues call it *Zongchi*. Translated during the Wei and Wu periods, translator lost. Second translation: *Anan muke jing* (Ānanda-mukha Sūtra), one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Faqin of Parthia during the Western Jin. Third translation: *Wuliang pomoduo luoni jing* (Aparimitāyur-māravidrāvaṇa-dhāraṇī Sūtra), one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Bai Fazhu of Henei during the Western Jin. Fourth translation: [Title lost]. These three sūtras are the same text with eleven translations in total, arranged chronologically.
Eight texts are extant; three are missing.

*Anantapāramitā-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra. This is the second translation. The above sutra has been translated three times in total, both earlier and later.
Two [versions] exist and one is missing. *Dhāraṇī-pada-sūtra*, one fascicle;

the character "chapter" (*zhang*) is missing from the manuscript of Sengyou. Translated during the Eastern Jin dynasty, translator unknown. Third translation. The above sutra is the same text as the *Chiju shenzhou jing* (Sutra of the Divine Incantation of Holding Phrases) and others.
There are four translations in total;
three are extant and one is missing.

*Li-gou-jing-guang-duo-luo-ni-jing* (The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of Undefiled Pure Light), one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog as the first translation. This aforementioned sūtra has two translations in total, one preceding and one following.
One exists and one is missing.

*The Scripture of Avalokiteśvara’s Request*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; the first translation. The above scripture has two translations, earlier and later.
One exists and one is missing. *Neizang jing* (Inner Treasury Sūtra), one fascicle;

alternatively called *Neizang baipin jing* (Inner Treasury Hundred Chapters Sūtra) or *Neizang baibao jing* (Inner Treasury Hundred Jewels Sūtra). Translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. Second translation. The above sūtra has two translations, one preceding and one following.
One version exists while the other is missing.

*The Scripture on the Bathing of the Sangha in the Warm Chamber*, one fascicle; alternatively called the *Warm Chamber Scripture*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. Second Translation. The above scripture has two translations, one preceding and one following.

One version contains [the title] while another omits it; furthermore, one version lacks the character "又" (also). *Śūradatta-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Baiyan of the Western Regions during the Cao Wei dynasty. First translation. *Śūradatta-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle (also known as *Śūradatta-sūtra*). Translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty. Second translation. *Daridraputra-śūradatta-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. Fourth translation. The above three sūtras share the same source and comprise four successive translations.

One [text] is extant; three are missing. The *Dàoshù sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi at the Tree of the Way), two fascicles—An’s catalogue states it was one fascicle—is likely the same as the *Sīhāmèi jīng*. Translator lost; appears in the Zhīmǐndù lù and is now appended to the Eastern Jin catalogue. Second Translation. The above one sūtra is the same original text as the *Sīhāmèi jīng*, with two translations, one extant and one missing. Furthermore, the Chángfáng lù records that Kāṅ Sēnghuì of the Wu period annotated a one-fascicle *Dàoshù jīng*. Since the version annotated by Sēnghuì is the same as that translated by Zhī Qián, this is merely an annotated edition and cannot be counted among the translations.

The Sūtra on the Birthplace of the Bodhisattva, one fascicle; also known as the Questions of the Magadha King. Translated by the Qifu śramaṇa Shi Shengjian. Second Translation. The above sūtra exists in two translations, earlier and later.
One version exists while the other is missing; it was included in the *Da Zhou Lu* (Catalogue of the Great Zhou) but has not been recovered despite recent searches.

*Sì bù kě dé jīng* (The Sūtra on the Four Unobtainables), one fascicle; alternatively, the character "wú" (no) may be absent. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty. This is the first translation. The above sūtra has two translations, one preceding and one following.
One version exists while the other is missing.

*The Scripture on the Maiden Śubhavyūha*, one fascicle; translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Yong. This is the second translation. The above scripture has two translations, one preceding and one following.

*Gāngmíng sānmèijīng* (Sūtra on the Radiance Samādhi), one fascicle. Translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Later Han. Recorded in Sengyou’s Catalogue. First Translation. The above sūtra is the same text as the *Chéngjù guāngmíng dìngyì jīng*; of these two translations, one exists and the other is missing.

*The Sūtra of the Jewel Net*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; this is the second translation. Of the two translations of this single sūtra, one remains while the other is missing.

*The Sutra on the Fifty Matters Concerning the Body of a Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; translated by the lay devotee Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin dynasty. Second translation. The above sutra exists in two translations, earlier and later.
*One exists and one is missing.* *Bodhisattvacaryā-sūtra*, one fascicle.

Translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty]. First translation. *Bodhisattvacaryā-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *The Sūtra on the Practice of the Bodhisattva Gṛhapati Vīryadatta* or *The Sūtra on the Practice of the Gṛhapati*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bai Yan of the Western Regions during the Cao Wei. Second translation. The two sūtras above are the same text, with three translations in total, arranged chronologically.
One version exists and the second is missing.

*Fútián jīng* (Sūtra on the Field of Merit), one fascicle; also known as the *Zhūdé fútián jīng* (Sūtra on the Field of Merit for All Virtuous Ones). Translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju. This is the second translation. The above sūtra has two translations, one preceding and one following.

One version is extant and one is missing. *The Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *The Buddha-Garbha Rectangular Sūtra*. Translated by the Western Jin śramaṇas Dharmasthita and Dharmajvāla. First translation. *The Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Bai Fazang from Henei. Second translation. The above two sūtras are the same text, with three translations in total, arranged chronologically.
One extant, one missing.

*Buddhavacana-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Northern Zhou dynasty of the Yuwen family. Second translation. Regarding the above sūtra, there were two translations, one of which is extant and the other missing.

*The Sūtra of King Suvarṇavarṇa*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmaruci of India during the Northern Wei dynasty. This is the first translation. The above sūtra exists in two translations, earlier and later.
One version exists and one is missing.

*Yǎndàosúyè jīng* (Sutra on the Propagation of the Path for Monastics and Laypeople), one fascicle; one manuscript lacks the character "yè" (karma). Translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty. First translation. The above sutra has two translations, earlier and later.

*The Sutra of the Names of One Hundred Buddhas*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. First translation. Of the above one sutra, there are two translations, one extant and one missing.

*The Sūtra on Praising the Merits of All Buddhas*, three fascicles; also known as *The Collection of Flowers*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. First translation. *The Sūtra of the Names of Present Buddhas*, three fascicles; also known as *The Manifestation of Flowers: The Names of Present Buddhas*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. Second translation. The above two sūtras are the same text with three successive translations: one remains extant while two are missing from the canon. One version within the canon is a translation from the Yuan Wei period that contains the characters "Jin-yu" (words of the Jin); the reason for this is not yet clear.

*Sūtra of the Devaputra Susīma*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty; this is the second translation. The above sūtra exists in two translations, earlier and later.
One version exists while the other is missing.

*The Great Māyā Sūtra*, one fascicle—alternatively without the character "Great" (Dà)—or two fascicles. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhi Yao of the Western Regions during the Later Han Dynasty. First Translation. The above is one sūtra with two translations, earlier and later.
One version exists and one is missing.

*Chuzaihuan jing* (Sutra on the Elimination of Calamities), one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Baiyan of the Western Regions during the Cao Wei dynasty. This is the first translation. Regarding the above sutra, there are two translations, one of which exists and the other of which is missing.

*Paibenzhujing* (The Sutra of the Wise Man), two fascicles; translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Loujiachen of the Later Han—First Translation. *Baijing* (The Sutra of the Wise Man), one fascicle; translated by the Sha-men Shi Shengjian of the Qifu Qin—Third Translation. The above two sutras are the same text, with three translations in chronological order.
One version is extant while two are missing.

The *Guangshiyin Dashizhi Shoujue Jing* (Sūtra on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta) also refers to the "Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin; this is the first translation, titled the *Guanshiyin Shouji Jing* (Sūtra on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara), in one fascicle. Translated by the lay follower Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin; this is the second translation. The above two sūtras are the same text, with three translations in total, arranged chronologically.
One version exists and two are missing.

*Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, four fascicles; alternatively titled with the "New" character added. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty. Second translation. The above one sūtra has two translations, earlier and later.
One exists while the other is absent.

*Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*, two fascicles (or three fascicles), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of Yuezhi during the Later Han; the first translation, *Vaipulya Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, two fascicles, translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of Wu; the second translation, *Shu Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, two fascicles, appearing to have been produced in the Shu region and lost during the Cao Wei; the subsequent translation, *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, two fascicles, lost during the Cao Wei; the fifth translation, *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, two fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bai Yan of the Western Regions during the Cao Wei; the sixth translation, *Yongfu Ding Jing* (Sūtra on the Heroic Subduing Samādhi), two fascicles, which Master Dao’an stated was another version of the *Śūraṅgama*; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin; furthermore, according to the catalogs of Sengyou, Changfang, and others, Dharmarakṣa also produced a *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* in two fascicles.

Now, because the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* and the *Śūraṅgama-vikrāmin-samādhi*—though their Sanskrit and Chinese names differ—are not distinct in content, the postscript to the *Śūraṅgama-vikrāmin-samādhi* states: "The ninth day of the fourth month in the first year of the Yuankang era."
The Bodhisattva Zhìfǎhù (Dunhuáng) held a Hu-language scripture in his hand and recited the Śūraṅgama-samādhi from his mouth;
the upāsaka Niè Chéngyuǎn received it by pen.
By this, one can verify that the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* does not correspond to the *Vīryaparākrama-samādhi*, and the same applies to the two versions of the *Bhadra-kalpika-sūtra*.

The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* has now been discarded and not established [as canonical]. The postscript to the sutra states that "Zhi Fahu" refers to his original family name. *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, two fascicles. Translated by the lay devotee (upāsaka) Zhu Shulan of the Western Jin, from the region of the Western Regions. This was the seventh translation. *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, two fascicles. Translated by the lay devotee Zhi Shilun of the Yuezhi, during the Former Liang. Extracted from the *Postscript to the Śūraṅgama*. This was the eighth translation. [Newly compiled and entered into the canon. The above eight scriptures share the same original text; there are nine translations in total, arranged chronologically.
The ninth is extant;

the preceding eight are all missing. Furthermore, according to the catalogs of Sengyou, Huiyuan, and others, during the reign of Emperor Hui of the Western Jin, the śramaṇa Zhimin-du combined two versions by Zhi and two by Zhu into a single work for circulation. Since these were not translated from original Sanskrit manuscripts, they do not properly count as authentic translations and are therefore not preserved separately.

*The Sutra of the Universal Worthy Contemplation*, one fascicle; also known as *The Sutra of the Contemplation of the Bodhisattva Universal Worthy*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. First translation. *The Sutra of the Contemplation of the Bodhisattva Universal Worthy*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. Second translation. The above two sutras share the same original text and comprise three translations in total, arranged in chronological order.
One version exists and two are missing.

*The Sūtra on the Visualization of the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty. This is the first translation. The above sūtra has two translations, earlier and later.
One version exists while the other is missing.

*The Sutra of the Child Bodhisattva of Inconceivable Light*, one fascicle; also called *The Sutra of the Inconceivable Child* and titled *The Sutra of Inconceivable Light*. The older catalogs simply call it *The Child*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. This is the first translation. The above is one sutra with two translations, former and latter.
One version exists while the other is missing.

*The Scripture on the Ten Stages Severing the Bonds*, in eight fascicles—alternatively titled *The Ten Abodes*—or in four fascicles. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Falan of India during the Later Han Dynasty at Baima Temple. This is the first translation. Thus, this single scripture has two translations, one preceding and one following.

To have one version preserved while another is missing is further evidence that the records of Seng Changfang and others—which state that Zhu Fonian again translated the *Daśabhūmi-pratighāta* in ten fascicles—are in error; this refers precisely to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-sūtra*. Although "bhūmi" (ground) and "vihāra" (abode) are largely synonymous in meaning, there is currently only a single extant edition. We shall now rely on the catalog of Sengyou as the authoritative standard.

The *Bhadra-kalpika-sūtra* in seven fascicles is also titled *Bhadra-kalpa-samādhi* and also titled *Bhadra-kalpa-samāpatti*. The *Yù-lù* (Record of Beneficial Works) states it is the *New Bhadra-kalpika-sūtra*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yaoqin [Dynasty]. Second Translation. The above is a single scripture with two translations, preceding and following.

One version exists while the other is missing; furthermore, in the records of Seng Chang and others, there is additionally a *Bhadra-kalpa-samādhi-sūtra* in seven fascicles among the translations of Dharmarakṣa. Examining this now, it is clear that the cataloguers have erred. "Bhadra" and "Xián" (Worthy) are merely different transliterations of the same Sanskrit term in the Fan (Sanskrit) and Jin (Chinese) languages; thus, the *Xiánjié jīng* (Sūtra of the Worthy Kalpa) begins by stating: "The *Bhadra-kalpa-samādhi-sūtra*; in Jin [Chinese], it is called the *Xiánjié dìngyì* (Sūtra of the Samādhi of the Worthy Kalpa). Within Sengyou’s catalog, only one version exists, yet it was mistakenly divided into two sūtras—an egregious error. Therefore, I have now merged them into one.

*The Scripture on the Names of the Thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa*, one fascicle; translated during the Later Han dynasty, translator lost. Fang [Daozhen] notes that this work contains only the names of the Buddhas and differs from the *Scripture on the Four Truths and the Thousand Buddhas* produced by Dharmarakṣa. The aforementioned list of Buddha names is extracted from the *Bhadrakalpika Sūtra*.

The alternate translations for this missing text are as follows: *Jingdu sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Pure Attainment), one fascicle. Translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan. First translation. *Jingdu sanmei jing*, one fascicle. Translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Baoyun. Second translation. *Jingdu sanmei jing*, one fascicle. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Liu Song dynasty. Third translation. *Jingdu sanmei jing*, one fascicle. Translated by Fanyao, the Director of the Bureau of Monastic Affairs (Zhaoxuantong) under the Northern Wei. Fourth translation. The above four sūtras are different translations of the same original text; however, the *Dazhou ruzang lu* (Catalogue of the Canon Compiled during the Dazhou Period) records that the three-fascicle version of the *Jingdu sanmei jing* is missing. Upon examining its phrasing, it is found to be superficial and shallow, and its doctrinal principles are inconsistent and contradictory. As its content appears to involve human contrivance rather than being a sacred scripture, it has been included in the *Yilu* (Record of Doubtful Texts). One should seek out the authentic sūtra separately.

*Si yi jing* (Sūtra on Contemplating the Mind), one fascicle; also called *Yi jing* (Sūtra on Benefit). Translated by the Śramaṇa Yan Fotiao of Linhuai during the Later Han dynasty. First translation: *Yi yi jing* (Sūtra on Benefiting the Mind), one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kang Daohuo of the Eastern Jin dynasty. Second translation. The above two sūtras are translations of the same original text with different versions; they are both missing from the *Changfang lu* and other catalogs, which all state that they were translated by the monk Sengqunī of the Xiao Qi dynasty. As for the *Yi yi jing* in two fascicles, this is largely an error transmitted by cataloguers.
During the final years of the Southern Qi dynasty, Jiang Mi, a doctoral candidate at the National University, had a daughter who left home to become a nun.
Her name was Sengqie;
with her eyes closed, she could recite twenty-one scriptures from memory.
It consists of thirty-five fascicles in total.
Among them, there are three fascicles of the *Yi-yi jing* (Sūtra on the Meaningful Intent).
Sengchang considered that there must be a cause for such habitual conditioning.
It has been included in the *Zhenglu* (Canon of Authentic Works).
Other catalogs, considering it not to have been translated from an Indic original,
have placed it among the spurious works.
I fear that by retaining this single scripture, we may fall into error.
Its name is sometimes called *Saṃkhyā-nī* and sometimes *Nī-saṃkhyā*;
this is because the character *nī* (尼) is placed either above or below [the other characters].
Yù (Shēngyù) is not recorded in the catalog of Qi;
thus we know that all other catalogs are erroneous. Among the scriptures included in the Zhōu canon, there are two fascicles of the *Yìyì jīng* (Scripture on the Meaning of Benefit).
Examining its textual meaning, it is also a work by a person from Shā; at the beginning of the lower fascicle, there is approximately one page and a half.
The text is identical in every word and phrase to that of the preceding fascicle;
however, regarding the two successive predictions for the Bodhisattva Īśvaraghoṣa,
his names and the names of his lands differ from one another.
None of these types of works are found among the various sūtras.
Therefore, I have compiled this "Chapter on Doubts" and shall further seek out authentic scriptures.

Sengyou’s Catalogue states that Master Dao’an classified the *Bodhisattva-bhūmi Sūtra* (one fascicle) as a lost translation from the Western Jin period; it was formerly included in the Western Jin catalogue. Master Dao’an stated that it originated from the Vaipulya section.

Sengyou’s Catalogue states that Master Dao’an classified the *Bodhisattva-pūrva-caryā Sūtra* (one fascicle) as an ancient scripture of the Han period, which is now appended to the Han catalogue. Sengyou’s Catalogue states that Master Dao’an classified the *Bodhisattva-pūrva-caryā Sūtra* (one fascicle) as a scripture with strange origins from the Guanzhong region, which is now appended to the Qin catalogue.

*Mahāratnakūṭa-vaiśvānara-sūtra*, one fascicle. Sengyou’s catalogue states that this was a "distinct scripture from Guanzhong by Master Dao’an"; it is now appended to the Qin catalogue. *Bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, one fascicle.
Sengyou’s catalogue states that this was a "distinct scripture from Guanzhong by Master Dao’an"; it is now appended to the Qin catalogue. *Bodhisattva-carita-sūtra*, one fascicle.

One fascicle; the old catalogue calls it the *Mañjuśrī-vaipulya-samādhi-sūtra* (or simply *Vaipulya-samādhi-sūtra*). Sengyou’s Record states that it was a distinct scripture from the Liang region according to Master Dao’an;

Sengyou’s Record states that it was a distinct scripture from the Liang region according to Master Dao’an; it is now appended to the Liang records. *Bodhisattva-daśauṇḍa-sūtra*.

*Hu jing* (Hu Sūtra), one fascicle; currently suspected to be the same as the aforementioned *O-hu* (Ugra). These five works, along with the fifty-two scriptures listed under the heading "The Names of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions," constitute the collection.
These were all among the "Newly Collected Translations of Unknown Origin" in Sengyou’s *Lü* (Catalogue) of the Liang dynasty;
they are now appended to the *Lü* of the Song dynasty, following the section on sūtras translated from Indic originals among the various catalogues of scriptures of unknown origin.
Merely the titles remain;
their fundamental texts have long been lost and cannot be consulted.
Thus, it is truly difficult to definitively expound upon the Great and Small Vehicles.
Moreover, even this rough classification involves considerable overlap.
I trust that learned scholars will examine it and correct it.

*Mahāyāna Vinaya*, incomplete original; twenty-two sections in twenty-five fascicles. *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, two fascicles (or three). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kang Mengxiang from the Western Regions during the Later Han dynasty. First translation. Regarding the above, there are two translations: one version exists in the canon, while the other is missing.

*The Sūtra on the Original Action of the Bodhisattva’s Diadem* (Bodhisattvamaulī-karmapatha-sūtra), two fascicles; second translation, translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Zhìyán. *The Sūtra on the Original Action of the Diadem*, two fascicles; also titled *The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Diadem*, translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Dàoyán. The above are three translations, both earlier and later.
One copy exists in the Tripitaka; two copies are missing.
*Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. First translation. (The above comprises three translations in total.)
Two versions survive and one is missing.

*Mañjuśrī-viśuddha-śīla-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the lay devotee Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin dynasty. This is the second translation. The above comprises four translations in total, including the preceding and following ones.

Three versions exist and one is missing. *Bodhisattva-zhai-fa-jing* (one fascicle), sometimes omitting the word "jing"; also titled *Xian-shou-bodhisattva-zhai-fa-jing*, *Zheng-zhai*, or *Chi-zhai*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin—this is the first translation. *Bodhisattva-zheng-zhai-jing* (one fascicle). Translated by the Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin. Third translation. The above is the same text as the *Bodhisattva-shou-zhai-jing*.
There are three translations in total;
one survives and two are missing.

*The Scripture on Mañjuśrī’s Repentance* (one fascicle), also known as *The Scripture on Mañjuśrī’s Confession*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. The above consists of two translations.
One version exists while the other is missing.

*Śāriputra-parivarta-sūtra* (also simply titled *Parivarta-sūtra*), one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. Second translation: *Śāriputra-parivarta-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin. Recorded in the catalog of Fashang. The above comprises three translations in total.
One version exists and two are missing; the third translation is omitted.

*Fǎlǜ sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Dharma-Regulations), one fascicle, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master Ān Shìgāo of the Later Han. According to Fǎshàng’s catalogue, this is the first translation. The above consists of the two preceding and following translations.
*Fó huìguò jīng* (Sūtra on the Buddha’s Repentance), one fascicle;
translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa.

translated by the lay devotee Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin.
*The Method for Repentance of the Bodhisattva Precepts in a Single Volume*, one fascicle; the Fang Catalogue states it is a different version.

Twenty Mahāyāna treatises in forty-eight fascicles, translated during the Wei and Wu periods with the translators lost; these are incomplete works. Among them, the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra-śāstra* in four fascicles was translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati of the Northern Wei;

this is the second translation. Regarding the aforementioned two translations, one exists while the other is missing from the canon. Although it was previously included in the Zhou Tripitaka, I have yet to locate its original text upon searching for it.

*Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Śāstra*, one fascicle; the author is unknown, and it is uncertain whether it is a single or multiple translation. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen dynasty. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra Śāstra*, five fascicles; the author is unknown, and it is uncertain whether it is a single or multiple translation. Newly included in the catalog; the original manuscript has not yet been located. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang. *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra Śāstra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen dynasty. This is the second translation; of the two preceding and subsequent translations, one remains and the other is missing. The above four works are commentaries on sūtras. *Yogācārabhūmi Śāstra*, five fascicles.
Translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Liang Dynasty. This re-edited version is a different translation of the same original text as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
As for its original source, it is currently unknown which of the seventeen stages (*bhūmi*) within that treatise it corresponds to.

*Madhyamaka-śāstra*, one fascicle; the author is unknown, and it is uncertain whether it was translated once or twice. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of India during the Liang dynasty. *Ratnagotravibhāga-śāstra*, four fascicles (or five fascicles); translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of Northern Wei. Regarding the first translation, between these two successive translations, one remains while the other is missing. According to the *Da Zhou Lu Zang Lu*, I have searched for the original manuscript but have not yet obtained it.

*Mahāyāna-pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*, one fascicle. Transmitted from the catalog of the Mahāyāna Monastery of the Chen dynasty; first translation. Composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; translator lost. Newly appended to the Liang catalog. The aforementioned Chen catalog states:
In the fifth month of the fourth year of the Taizhuan era of Emperor Chen, the śramaṇa Huibu arrived from the north.
He produced two translations,
one of which was preserved and the other lost.

*Upāyahṛdaya-śāstra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin dynasty. This is the first translation. Regarding the aforementioned two translations, one remains extant while the other is missing.
*Treatise on the Distinction of the Three Times*, one fascicle;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Liang Dynasty.

*Treatise on Refutation through Counter-Interrogation*, one fascicle. It is now suspected that this is the same as the *Yathābhūta-śāstra* (Treatise on Reality) found in the canon; therefore, its title there is given as the "Chapter on Refutation through Counter-Interrogation" of the *Yathābhūta-śāstra*.
The Single-Volume *Vigrahavyāvartanī*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of India during the Chen Dynasty. One fascicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of India during the Chen Dynasty.
*Ekavyavahārikatrayayānasiddhi-śāstra*, one fascicle;
translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Chen Dynasty.
*Ekavyavahārika-tattvanirdeśa-śāstra*, one fascicle.
A Single-Volume Treatise on Mental Action, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen Dynasty.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen Dynasty.

translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Chen dynasty.
*Pañcavidyā-sthāna-śāstra*, combined into one fascicle: (1) Phonetics; (2) Medical Formulas; (3) Arts and Crafts; (4) Incantations and Techniques; (5) Talismans and Seals.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Ten Stages), ten fascicles, composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; translated during the Northern Zhou Yuwen dynasty by the Indian śramaṇa Ratnabhadra.
A single-text edition.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty;
a single volume. The aforementioned catalog by Changfang states that it was translated by Master Kumārajīva during the Hongshi era.
Upon searching through to the end of the scroll, it resembles the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya*.

In the second volume of the catalog, the *Chen Dynasty Catalogue of the Mahāyāna Temple Collection*, it states: "Also known as the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*. I now suspect this is the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* from within that collection.

*Shi banruo liuzi sanju lun* (Treatise on the Six Characters and Three Phrases of Prajñā), one fascicle; newly included in the canon; single volume; translated and compiled by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of South India during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang. *Jiliang lun* (Treatise on the Compendium of Valid Cognition), four fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yi Jing of the Great Tang; newly included in the canon; single volume. Furthermore, the record of Fashang states that the *She dacheng lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) in twenty fascicles was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha in the second year of the Taicheng era of the Liang dynasty; this must be an error, as it is mostly a transcription mistake for twelve fascicles. Now, according to the Fang catalog, Paramārtha’s translation of the *She lun* dates to the Chen dynasty; since it is absent from the Liang catalog, it is not retained here. In total, the Mahāyāna sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras missing in their original versions are calculated as follows: [list omitted].
A total of four hundred and fifty works in eight hundred and seventy-four fascicles.
*The Newly Compiled Catalogue of Śākyamuni’s Teachings* (Zhenyuan xinding shijiao mulu), Fascicle Twenty-four.
*The Newly Compiled Catalogue of Śākyamuni’s Teachings*, Fascicle Twenty.
Part Six of the Five Separate Records, compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xìmíng Monastery in the Western Capital.

Within the Separate Records, this is Part Two of the Catalogue of Translations for Which the Originals Are Missing: Small Vehicle Sūtras with Missing Originals; Small Vehicle Sūtras with Missing Originals from Repeated Translations; Small Vehicle Sūtras with Missing Originals from Repeated Translations: one hundred and fifteen works in two hundred and sixty-five fascicles. *Madhyama Āgama* (Zhōng Āháng jīng), fifty-nine fascicles. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dánmónántí of the Fúqín [Former Qin] dynasty. First translation. Note: Of the two translations of this single sūtra, one version is preserved in the canon while the other is missing.
The preface to the *Ekottarika-āgama* (Zengyi Ahan Jing) states it consists of fifty fascicles;
some say forty-one fascicles, while others say twenty-four.

Sengyou states it contains thirty-three fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmānanda of India during the Fu Qin dynasty. First translation: the *Kumāra-kāśyapa-sūtra* (Jiumo Jiasheshi Jing), one fascicle, also known as the *Kumāra-kāśyapa-vinaya-praśna-sūtra*. Sengyou’s catalog records this as a work of lost translation.
The *Fajing lu* states that it is extracted from the *Madhyamāgama*.

Volume sixteen contains a separate translation titled *One Scroll of the Sūtra on Kāśyapa the Child Resolving Difficulties*, also known as the *Kāśyapa-tīrthika-sūtra*. Sengyou states that it is extracted from the *Dīrghāgama*.
Translated by the Qifu Qin śramaṇa Śaṅghabhadra.
Fang states that this shares the same original text as the *Kāśyapa-sūtra* translated by Kumārajīva;
however, Kumārajīva’s version lacks the *Kāśyapa* portion. Thus, these two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.
Extracted from the seventh fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
It shares the same original text as the *Paiśunya Sūtra* (Bìsù Jīng).
Both of these originals are missing.

*The Sūtra on the Six Directions of Prostration*, one fascicle; also known as *The Sūtra on Śakrāditya’s Six Directions of Prostration*, or simply *The Sūtra on the Six Directions of Prostration*. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. The above is also included in the *Sūtra of Good Birth* (Susīma-sūtra), the eleventh sūtra of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
There have been three translations, two of which survive and one of which is missing.

*The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Explanation for the Brahmin Āṣāḍha*, one fascicle. This includes the *Madhyama-āgama* (Middle Length Discourses), the *Amagandha-sūtra*, the thirteenth [sūtra] of the *Dīrgha-āgama* (Long Discourses).
There have been three translations, two of which survive and one of which is missing.

*The Sūtra on the Sixty-two Views*, one fascicle; also known as *The Brahmajāla Sūtra on the Sixty-two Views*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. The above is also included within the fourteenth sūtra of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
There have been three translations across different periods; two remain extant while one is missing.

*Luó tán jīng* (Lòu-tán jīng), six fascicles, or five or eight fascicles. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. This is the first translation. *Luó tán jīng*, eight fascicles. Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin. This is the third translation. The above includes the *Jì shì jīng* (Sūtra on the Record of the World) from the fourth division of the *Cháng āhán jīng* (Dīrgha Āgama).
Of the six translations listed above and below, four are extant and two are missing. *The Sūtra on the Practice of the Path of Resolve*, in two fascicles;

the Catalogue of Fang states it was extracted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*, though it may also consist of one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty. *The Great Twelve Gates Sūtra*, in two fascicles (or one); annotated by Master Dao’an. The Catalogue of Fang states it was extracted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty. *The Minor Twelve Gates Sūtra*, in one fascicle. The Catalogue of Fang states it was extracted from the *Āgama*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty.

Commentary by Master Dao’an. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty: *The Sūtra on the Seven Dharmas*, one fascicle. The old catalogues call it either *The Abhidharma Sūtra on the Practice of the Seven Dharmas* or simply *The Sūtra on the Practice of the Seven Dharmas*. Sengfang states it is from the *Dīrgha Āgama*. *The Sūtra on the Increase of the Path*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty. The old catalogues lack the character "Path" (Dao). It is a variant translation of the *Daśottara-sūtra*. Sengfang states it is from the *Dīrgha Āgama*. *The Sūtra on the Decisions on Meaning and Vinaya*, one fascicle; *The Maitreya Sūtra*, one fascicle. Dao’an states these are from the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

"The scriptures whose translators were lost by Master Daoan are appended to the Western Jin catalog under the section of the Kāśyapamātṛ-sūtra; these comprise fourteen works in twenty-eight fascicles, all of which are incomplete versions belonging to the *Dīrgha Āgama*."

*Sūtra on the Four Truths*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kang Mengxiang of the Western Regions during the Later Han dynasty. The above is also included within the *Sūtra on the Analysis of the Noble Truths* in the seventh fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
There are four translations in total;
two are extant and two are missing.
There is also one fascicle titled *The Sūtra on the Demon King Entering Maudgalyāyana’s Belly*, also known as *The Sūtra on the Evil Mara Tempting Maudgalyāyana*.

"Master Dao’an’s ancient catalogue of scriptures is now appended to the Han-lù. This includes, among other texts, the *Jiàngmó jīng* (Sūtra on Subduing Māra), the thirtieth fascicle of the *Zhōng āhán*."
There have been five translations in total;
three remain and two are lost.

*The Rāṣṭrapāla Sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhi Yao of the Western Regions during the Later Han Dynasty. This work combines the *Rāṣṭrapāla Sūtra*, the thirty-first sūtra within the third division of the *Madhyama Āgama*.

There are four translations in total; two are extant and two are missing. *The Scripture on the Venerable Elder Vaikaṭaka’s Sixfold Prostrations*, one fascicle (also titled *The Scripture on Vaikaṭa*).

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gītamitra of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. Second Translation: *The Scripture on the Venerable Elder Vaikaṭaka’s Sixfold Prostrations*, one fascicle. Translated by the lay practitioner Zhu Nanti of India during the Eastern Jin dynasty. The *Yùlù* states: "Master Ān’s lost translations are appended here to the Western Jin catalog. Regarding the single scripture above, it is suspected that it is the same text as the *Ratthapāla Sūtra* found in the thirty-first [fascicle].
*Huanyu jing* (Sūtra on Joyful Delight), one fascicle.

Master Dao’an’s *Jing* (Scripture) on the "Three Matters of Human Folly and Ignorance" in One Scroll, now appended to the Han Records. Master Dao’an stated that it is extracted from the *Madhyama Āgama*.

Now appended to the Han Records: *Fǎpǔyì jīng* (Sūtra on the Universal Meaning of the Dharma), one fascicle; also called *Pǔyì jīng*. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. *The Sūtra on King Bimbisāra’s Questioning of the Buddha Regarding Offerings*, one fascicle; translated by Prince Upaśūna of the kingdom of Ujjayinī during the Northern Wei dynasty. *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *Aṅgulimālaka-sūtra*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. The above includes one additional version, making five translations in total for this scripture from beginning to end.

These are all partial or incomplete versions of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

*Śiṅgālaka-sūtra*, one fascicle; also called *The Sūtra on Prince Śiṅgālaka Clarifying the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions*, also called *Prince Mingxing and the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions*, and also called *The Tiger-Ear Sūtra*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty. Second translation. Of the five translations listed above, four remain and one is missing.

The *Madanī-sūtra* in the Tripiṭaka was translated by An Shigao; there is now a *Śāthokkhāna-sūtra*. Since Madanī and Śāthokkhāna are the same original text, it is inappropriate for both to appear together; yet both versions are currently included, the reason for which remains unclear. Alternatively, this present text may be the *Śāthokkhāna-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa, which has been erroneously cataloged here by the compilers.

*Saṃyukta-piṭaka-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Song dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra from India; the fourth translation. Of the four translations mentioned above, three survive and one is missing.

*Disciple Man’s Exposition of the Sūtra for Jīvaka*, one fascicle; also titled *Disciple Man’s Exposition of Arrogance for Jīvaka*, or *The Disciple’s Playful and Exaggerated Sūtra*. Translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng. Fourth translation. The above is the same text as the *Sūtra on Ānanda Asking about Serving the Buddha* and others.
There are four translations in total; three remain extant and one is missing.

The *Xiǎoběnqǐjīng* (Sūtra of the Minor Account of Past Deeds) in two fascicles—sometimes titled *Xiūxíngběnqǐ* (Account of Past Conduct) or *Sùxíngběnqǐ* (Account of Former Deeds)—was translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhi Yao of the Western Regions during the Later Han dynasty. This is the first translation. The *Tàizǐběnqǐruìyìngjīng* (Sūtra of the Auspicious Responses of the Prince’s Past Deeds) in two fascicles, also known as *Yìngběnqǐ*, was translated by the Tripitaka Master Kang Mengxiang of foreign lands during the Later Han dynasty. The *Guòqùyīnguōjīng* (Sūtra of Past Causes and Effects) in four fascicles was translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin dynasty. This is the fifth translation. Thus, of the six translations listed above, three remain extant and three are missing.

*Fǎhǎizàng jīng* (Sūtra of the Dharma-Ocean Treasury), one fascicle; also known as the *Fǎhǎi jīng*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhú Fálán of India during the Later Han dynasty. This is the first translation. Of the three translations [of this work] recorded before and after, two survive and one is missing.
*The Scripture in Forty-two Sections*, one fascicle.

The *Fang Lu* states that it differs slightly from the version translated by Kāśyapa Mātanga. Translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu Kingdom. First translation. Of the two translations mentioned above, one survives and the other is missing.

The *Nai-nü Qi-yu jing* (Sūtra of the Maiden Qi-yu), one fascicle; also known as the *Nai-nü jing*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. This is the second translation. Of the two translations mentioned above, one remains extant while the other is lost.

*Zuìyèbàiyīng jīng* (Sūtra on the Retribution of Sinful Karma), one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Zhú Tánwúlán of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. This is the second translation. Of the two preceding translations, one remains extant while the other is lost.

*The Scripture on Maudgalyāyana Subduing the Dragon King*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *Without the Character "King"* (i.e., *Subduing the Dragon*), or *The Scripture on Subduing the Dragon King*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. Second translation. Of the two preceding and succeeding translations, one remains extant while the other is lost.

*The Sūtra on the Elder’s Pleasing Voice*, one fascicle; translated by the lay devotee Juqu Jingsheng of the Song dynasty; the second translation. Of the aforementioned two translations, one remains extant while the other is lost.

*Xiūyào jīng* (Sūtra on the Secret Essentials of Dhyāna), four fascicles; alternatively, the title lacks the character "jīng" (sūtra). Translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty]. From the *Śāṭhapañcaka-sūtra* downwards, there are forty-three works in sixty-one fascicles;

these include all re-translated scriptures (excluding the four Āgamas) for which the original texts are missing, as well as single translations of Hīnayāna scriptures for which the original texts are missing—totaling four hundred and eighty-one works in five hundred and fifty-one fascicles.

Among the various catalogs of scriptures of unknown translators,
only the titles remain while the texts themselves have long been lost; thus,
there is nothing available for detailed examination.
It is truly difficult to definitively expound upon the Great and Small Vehicles;
even a rough classification involves much overlap and intermingling.
I trust that learned scholars will examine this in detail and rectify it.

This is the first translation. *Śāriputrābhidharma-bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra*, one fascicle.

Compiled and translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty; this is the second translation. The aforementioned catalogue by Senglang states: "In the sixth year of the Taiyuan era, Tanwushenglan combined the three versions held by Sengchun, Damohu, and Zhu Sengshu into one fascicle. This is recorded in Baochang’s catalogue. Examining various catalogues carefully, we find that Sengchun obtained the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* in the country of Kapiśa and brought it back, where he had Damohu and others translate it. Based on this, it appears that Sengchun and Damohu represent the same original text. As for Zhu Sengshu, his name does not appear in other catalogues; it remains unclear from where the combined version he produced was derived. The above includes the combined version along with the three preceding translations.

One version exists and two are missing. *Bhikṣuṇī-śīla* (The Bhikṣuṇī Precepts), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Bhikṣuṇī-śīla-sūtra*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty. Third translation. [Note: The right-hand entry in Sengfang’s catalogue states that Sengchun obtained the Sanskrit manuscript in the country of Kauśāmbī and that Fonian translated the text; however, the wording was cumbersome, so later Zhu Fatai revised and corrected it. This is recorded in Baochang’s catalogue. Now, I suspect that the translation attributed to Fonian is identical to that of Dharmayaśas. Since both concern the source of the Bhikṣuṇī precepts, why are they preserved separately?
The texts for three translations, both preceding and following this one, are missing. *Mīśāsaka-karman*, one fascicle;

The *Jingqin lu* states:
"Translated by Dharmapriya of Later Qin, in two fascicles: *Shisong lü zashi wen* (Inquiries on Miscellaneous Matters of the Ten-Recitation Vinaya)."
The *Baoshang lu* states that the Kasmirian śramaṇa Dharmayaśas of the Later Qin translated one fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*.
These two accounts are mostly errors regarding the names of the catalogers.
Or perhaps it is the same as the first translator mentioned previously.
Both Sengyou’s *Chu sanzang jiji* and Fei Changfang’s *Lidai sanbao ji* state that this was translated during the Eastern Jin dynasty and not during the Qin period;
thus, these two catalogs should be taken as authoritative.

The *Fanglu* (Record of the Abbot) further states that regarding those who translate the teachings of Dharma, it is extremely important to skillfully distinguish and guard against the mutual entanglement of property belonging to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, as their boundaries are distinct.
There is currently a single fascicle of the *Wubai wenshi jing* (Sūtra on Five Hundred Questions) within the Canon.
There are thirty-three pages which also clarify that the property of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha must not be involved in worldly affairs;
however, the terminology differs,
and the reason for this remains unknown.
The *Yulu* (Supplementary Record) states:
"That which is excerpted from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* concerns matters such as the acceptance of the day for the thirty-nine nights, as clarified in the *Pañcaśata-praśna-sūtra*;
this is consistent with the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*."
However, because the terminology differs,
it has not yet been definitively established;
this shall be further examined by those of broad learning hereafter.

*Detailed and Corrected Exposition of the Dharma for the Ordination of Bhikṣuṇīs*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kasmīra during the Eastern Jin dynasty. *Sole Text: Ritual Text for the Two-Year Training of Bhikṣuṇīs*, one fascicle (sometimes lacking the character "ni" [bhikṣuṇī]). Translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmadhara from the Western Regions together with Fonian during the Fu Qin dynasty. *Sole Text: The Two Hundred and Six Precepts*, three fascicles; *Combined Differences*, two fascicles; the preface includes the characters "Great Bhikṣu. Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan from the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. The above is the combined preface to the precepts, which states:

On the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month in the year of Xinsi, the sixth year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, the bhikṣu Zhu Tanwulan compiled these precepts at the Temple of General-in-Chief Xie; they were recorded on the eighteenth day of the seventh month.

Furthermore, both the *Chángfáng nèidiǎn lù* (Changfang’s Record of Inner Scriptures) and the *Jìngmài jīngtú* (Jingmai’s Diagrams of the Scriptures) state that during the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty,
the śramaṇa Dharmaratna translated the *Īryāpathika-śīla-sūtra* in two fascicles, comprising two hundred and sixty precepts.
Now, examining this statement in detail,
it is certainly not logically tenable.
When the Buddha-dharma first arose, the precepts and regulations were not yet fully established.
From what source did this combination of the precepts arise?
According to my humble judgment,
it was merely that which was compiled by Zhu Tanwulan.
The names and surnames of these two individuals were identical;
the cataloger erroneously transcribed "Tanwu" (曇無) as "Falu" (法蘭),
when it was actually Dharmaratna.

Therefore, in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, it is recorded that among the translations by Dharmarakṣa, only the titles of other sections were indicated, and this name for the precepts did not exist therein;
thus, it has been omitted and not established in this present catalog.
Furthermore, the version by Dharmamitra is a composite work and not a direct translation.
This record should likewise not have been included herein;
however, because these two accounts contain discrepancies,
I have preserved them for the sake of documentation.

The reason for this is unknown. *Abhidharmahṛdaya* (Heart of Abhidharma), sixteen fascicles or thirteen fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kapiśī during the Fu Qin dynasty—first translation. *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* (Heart of Combined Abhidharma), thirteen fascicles; translated by the Śramaṇa Faxian together with Xuangao during the Eastern Jin dynasty—first translation. *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, thirteen fascicles (the root being ten fascicles, continued to form thirteen or fourteen); translated by the foreign Śramaṇas Iyevala and others during the Song dynasty—third translation. Later, Guṇavarman continued the translation until its completion, resulting in thirteen fascicles.

The *Tang neidian lu* (Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures of the Tang) and the *Fanying tu* (Diagram of Translated Scriptures) agree with this.
Now, as for the case of Guṇabhadra, he merely continued what was previously incomplete rather than translating it anew;
thus, leaving the earlier and later versions existing separately is logically improper.
Now these have been combined into a single volume.
Regarding the fourth translation currently in circulation,
the *Chángfáng lù* states:

During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, the Indian śramaṇa Saṃghavarman arrived at Jianye from India in the tenth year of the Yuanjia era. He was profoundly learned in the Vinaya-piṭaka and the *Samyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*. At Daochang Monastery, Huiguan—having previously seen that although the Tripiṭaka masters and others had translated [the text], Saṃghavarman possessed a marvelous understanding of the *Samyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya* and could recite it with complete fluency—[requested him to produce a new translation].
Before he had even finished copying it,
he requested that it be translated again.
Baoyun conveyed this message.
Observing my own manuscript notes, they were all identical upon completion; thus, it is known that the version containing [the sections on] view, conduct, and practice is a later edition.
Of the four translations made earlier and later, one remains extant while three are lost.

Buddhabhadra appeared even later than him.
Pairing [these texts] as having the same source may be inappropriate; therefore,

This refers to works excerpted from within a large collection and circulated separately,
such as the second assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. Indeed,
the Dharma gates are so vast that it is rare for anyone to fathom their limits.
The scriptures are so vast and manifold that their limits are inexhaustible; therefore,
there have been those who, according to what is appropriate for conversion and guidance,
applied them in accordance with the conditions of sentient beings, drawing upon them briefly as needed from within these great collections.
Those who merely search for it do not know its origin;
those who merely study it will not complete its meaning.
Now, I have gathered many strands and unified them, bringing them back to this present treatise.
I have nevertheless revised and pruned the old records, adjusting for additions and omissions,
and have fully recorded the titles to provide a detailed account of discrepancies;
this is intended so that future students may examine the branches and know the source.
Fearing that this may not yet be exhaustive, I hope for future scholars [to supplement it].

Furthermore, it is not definitively known from which sūtras or vinayas these were extracted.

Moreover, the *Renshou Zhongjing Lu* (Catalogue of All Scriptures of the Renshou Era) of the Sui dynasty lists a total of two hundred and thirteen works in two hundred and twenty-seven fascicles under the category of "Separate Extracts of Mahāyāna Scriptures," yet it likewise fails to specify their sources.
Now, upon examining the catalogs of various dynasties, most have already recorded [these works].
It is unreasonable to claim that those catalogs treat such texts as the *Daśakuśalakarmapathasūtra* and the *Gadhinbhikṣusūtra* as separate excerpts (*biéshēngchāo*).

all derive from the *Zapiyu jing* (Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables).
According to the *Catalogue of All Scriptures* (Zhongjing lu) from the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty, there were thirty-nine scriptures [included therein].
Now, regarding the one-fascicle *Māyī jīng* (Scripture on the Meaning of Abuse), various catalogues of successive dynasties state that it was translated by An Shigao.
Since it has now been included within this collection of the Tripitaka, it is omitted here.
As for the *Ṣaṭpuruṣasūtra* (The Sutra of the Six Men), which explains the intent behind the insults, it has already been compiled in the previous volume; therefore, it is excluded from this one.
The *Dedao ticheng jing* (Sutra on the Ladder and Staircase to the Way) also states that it originated from the *Zapiyu jing* (Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables).
For now, as it is not found in the *Daban* (Mahāsaṃnipāta), it has been compiled and included in the canon.

Furthermore, the aforementioned six sutras—the *Wuju jing* (Sutra on Fearlessness), the *Bieyu duyu jing* (Sutra on the Parable of the Turtle and the Parable of Poison), the *Huizi jing* (Sutra on Instructing Sons), the *Mayu jing* (Sutra on the Parable of the Horse), and the *Shouda jing* (Sutra on Shou-da)—all originate from within the *Chusheng jing* (Sutra on the Arising of Life).
The former claim that these were extracted from the *Saṃyukta-avadāna* is an error;
they have now been compiled into that [separate] record, and this [present collection] has also excluded them.

As for the *Kāśyapa-reproaches-Ānanda-dual-crossing-arhat-parable-sūtra*, it is merely an alternative title for the *Kāśyapa-interrogates-Ānanda-sūtra* and should not be listed twice; excluding these ten sūtras, there are twenty-nine others as previously enumerated.
Since it is stated that these were extracted from the *Saṃyukta-avadāna*,
it is unknown from which specific source they originated;
furthermore, upon examining both extant versions of the two-fascicle *Avadāna*, neither contains such sūtras.
Regarding the eighty fascicles that ought to have been produced:
it may be that the *Sūtra of Three Hundred and Fifty Miscellaneous Parables* translated by Master Hu was among them;
this sūtra is recorded within the catalog of missing texts (*quēběn lù*).
