Section Four: The Record for Deleting Redundancies, consisting of one hundred and forty-seven works in four hundred and eight fascicles. Regarding the "Record for Deleting Redundancies": it refers to those [works] which...
That is to say, there are instances where the same original text appears under different names,
or where what was extensive has been abbreviated to such a degree that it becomes redundant;
all such cases shall now be deleted.
However, because the years have long passed, errors have been transmitted together with the authentic praise;
thus, from the fullness of these volumes, much labor has been expended.
Now, I shall carefully collate the differences and similarities to clearly distinguish between what is correct and what is erroneous.
The complete catalog of items is worthy of examination. Newly recovered separate *Bie sheng jing* (Sūtras on Separate Arisings):

sixty-seven works in one hundred and eighty-five fascicles. The *Xukongzang suowen jing* (Sūtra of the Questions of Ākāśagarbha) in eight fascicles; also called the *Fangdeng zhuzhuxukongzang jing* (Vaipulya Sūtra of the Lord Ākāśagarbha), or simply the *Xukongzang jing* (Ākāśagarbha Sūtra), or in five fascicles. The above one sūtra is a separate excerpt from the "Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva Chapter" of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, circulated independently.
The *Dazhou lu* states that it was translated by the śramaṇa Śrīghana during the Qifu Qin dynasty; this is an error.
That translation by Śrīghana lacks the original manuscript.
*The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja Asking about the Amount of Merit Obtained from Upholding this Sūtra*, one fascicle.
The above sūtra is also an excerpted text separately transcribed from within the *Gaganagañja-parivarta* of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*.
It is an error that all catalogs state this was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
[The *Ekottarikāgama-sūtra on the Dānapāramitā practiced by King Sarvada*, one fascicle. The above is one sūtra.
This is from the "Perfection of Giving" (*Dānapāramitā*) section of the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya-sūtra*.
All catalogs state that it was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty, but this is an error.
*The Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha-sūkṣma-guhya-nidhi Sūtra*, two fascicles.

This aforementioned sūtra is an excerpt from the "Tathāgatagarbha-samudgama-parivarta" (Chapter on the Arising of the Nature of the Tathāgata) of the old *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, circulated separately. Its first chapter has been supplemented with the *Śraddhā-pratītyasamutpāda-vidhi* (Sequence of Faith), and the initial *nidāna* (circumstantial origin) of the first assembly has been taken and placed at the beginning.
The statement in the *Chángfángděng lù* (Records of Sengchang and Others) that this was translated anonymously during the Western Jin dynasty is erroneous.

One fascicle of the *Suīyuàn wǎngshēng jīng* (Sūtra on Rebirth According to One’s Vows), also titled the *Guǎngjìng suīyuàn wǎngshēng shífēn jìngtǔ jīng* (Sūtra of the Ten Pure Lands of Rebirth According to Vows through Consecration), is also known as the *Pǔguǎng púsà jīng* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Pǔguǎng). The above constitutes one sūtra.
This is the first of ten volumes of the *Mahābhiṣeka-sūtra*, the "Universal Extensiveness Chapter" (*Puguang-pin*).
Some editions of the sūtra place it as the twelfth;
the catalogs of Changfang and others all state this.
Translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty;
some claim it was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin, but both assertions are erroneous.

*The Scripture of Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabhā*, one fascicle, also titled *The Scripture on Attaining Deliverance from Birth and Death through the Empowerment that Eradicates Transgressions and Sins*. This is the first scripture.
This is the twelfth fascicle of the *Mahābhiṣeka-sūtra*.
There are some manuscript versions of this sūtra that place it in the tenth [fascicle];
the catalogs of Changfang and others all state as much.
The attribution to the Song dynasty monk Huìjiǎn of Lùnyè Monastery is erroneous.

Regarding the two scriptures—the seventy-eight fascicles of the second assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, which the common people of the time titled the *New Translation of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Dàpǐn Fàngguāng), and the eighteen fascicles of the fourth assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, which the common people of the time titled the *New Translation of the Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* (Dàoxíng Xiǎopǐn)—both of these are as follows:
At that time, it was commonly rumored among the people that this was a translation by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing;
they altered the title and transcribed it for circulation.
I searched through Master Jing’s catalogue of scriptures and found that this sutra had never been translated;
furthermore, upon examining its text, I discovered it was no different from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
Fearing that others might not know the full details, I have recorded this here.

The *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra of the Sovereign King of Gods*, eight fascicles, also known as the *New Translation of the Prajñāpāramitā of the Sovereign King of Gods*. This aforementioned sūtra is the sixth assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*;
it is a different translation from the same original text as the old *Prajñāpāramitā of the Sovereign King of Gods*.

The *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra* in two fascicles, also known as the *New Translation of the Mañjuśrī-prajñā*, is one of the aforementioned scriptures; it is precisely the "Mañjuśrī-parivarta," the seventh assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
This is a different translation from the same source text as the *Old Version of the Prajñāpāramitā*.

*The Sūtra on the Essential Principles of Prajñāpāramitā*, one fascicle. The above-mentioned sūtra is precisely the "Section on the Essential Principles of Prajñā" from the tenth assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
The *Miji Jingang Lishi Jing* (Sūtra on the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada) in two fascicles.
Regarding this single sūtra, the *Neidian Lu* (Catalogue of Inner Scriptures) states that the translator is unknown; however, this is incorrect.
Upon examining its original source, it is found to have been extracted from the *Wu Miji Lishi Jing* (Sūtra on the Five Vajrapāṇis).

From the fifth line of the fourth sheet at the beginning of the fourth fascicle, following the five-character verse, through to the end of the fifth fascicle, the wording is identical [to the *Ekottarika-āgama*].
One fascicle of the *Ekottarika-āgama*. The above is one scripture.
From the Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Twenty-one, three sūtras are extracted.
The first clarifies the four merits of Brahmā;
the second clarifies the four kinds of nutriment.
The following clarifies the four translations.
The *Chángfáng lù* (Record of Dharmafang) states that it was translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Dharmaghoṣa; this is an error.
*Xíngqī xíng xiànbào jīng* (Sūtra on the Seven Practices and Manifest Retribution), one fascicle, one sheet. The above sūtra is extracted from the thirty-fourth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
*The Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*, one fascicle, three pages.
The above sūtra is excerpted from the forty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
It was included in the Zhou catalog within the Mahāyāna Piṭaka.

The claim that the *Yun yu baituo shu xia sili shier yinyuan* (Cloud and under the Pippala Tree Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination) is a different translation of the same original text is erroneous.
The *Jiexiangying fa jing* (Sūtra on Dharmas Corresponding to the Precepts), one fascicle—this aforementioned sūtra is extracted from the thirtieth fascicle of the *Za ahan jing* (Saṃyukta Āgama).
The *Chángfáng lù* states:
"The attribution to the Eastern Jin-period Central Asian śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan is erroneous.
*Bǐqiū wèn fó duō yōubōsè mìngzhōng jīng*, one fascicle. The above scripture is also found in the thirtieth fascicle of the *Zá āhán jīng*.
The *Chángfáng lù* states that the claim this was translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Dharmakṣema is erroneous.
One fascicle of the *Dú fù zhǎngzhě jīng* (Sūtra of the Solitary Rich Man): the above sūtra is extracted from the forty-sixth fascicle of the *Zá āhán jīng*.
The *Chángfáng lù* states that the attribution to the Later Han Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao is erroneous.
There is one fascicle titled *Yǒu zhòngshēng sānshì zuò è jīng*. The above scripture is found in the eighth fascicle of the *Chūyào jīng*.
The *Chángfáng lù* states that the attribution to the Western Jin śramaṇa Dharmagupta is erroneous.
*Chūjiā gōngdé jīng*, one fascicle. The above scripture is the first chapter, "On the Merit of Leaving Home," from the *Xiányú jīng*.
The *Chángfáng lù* states that the attribution to the Wu-period upāsaka Zhi Qian is erroneous.
The one-fascicle *Fó wèi niánshào póluómén shuō zhīshàn jīng* (Sūtra on Knowing Goodness Spoken by the Buddha for a Young Brahmin) is extracted from the fourth fascicle of the *Zá āhán jīng*.

The *Chángfáng lù* states that the claim it was translated by the Later Han Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao is erroneous; the *Mūlapariyāya-sutta* (Root-ripening Sūtra) in one fascicle, spoken by the Buddha for the householder Nakula, is found in the fifth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

The *Chángfáng lù* states that the claim it was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han is erroneous. This *Sūtra on Detachment from Desire Spoken for the Sinner Suśīma* in one fascicle is extracted from the fourteenth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

The *Chángfáng lù* states that the attribution of these to the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty is erroneous. *The Sūtra on King Aśoka Giving Half an Āmalaka Fruit*, one fascicle: found in the twenty-fifth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. *The Sūtra on the Fulfillment of Dhyāna Contemplation*, one fascicle: found in the twenty-ninth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. According to the *Chángfáng lù*, both of these translations are erroneous. The five sūtras listed above were included among the missing texts within the *Zhōu lù*.
I have now examined and found their originals;
they both originate from within the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
Since they are merely derivative extracts, I have excluded them and not included them [in this collection].
*The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Makara Fish*, one fascicle;
from the ninth fascicle. *The Sūtra on the Venerable Udāyin Leading Various People to Pay Homage to the Buddha and the Saṃgha*, one fascicle;
from the eleventh fascicle. *The Sūtra on Returning to One’s Native Land and [Meeting] the Father King*, one fascicle.
One fascicle of the *Jātaka of Prince Jālinīprabha*, appearing at the end of the seventeenth fascicle and the beginning of the eighteenth;
one fascicle of the *Sūtra on Giving Things Rightly or Wrongly*, appearing in the nineteenth fascicle;
and one fascicle of the *Sūtra of Instruction to Rāhula*, appearing in the twenty-fourth fascicle.
The *Sūtra on the Wheel of Birth and Death in the Five Destinies*, one fascicle, is extracted from the twenty-fifth fascicle.
The *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Bhikṣu Svāgata*, one fascicle, is extracted from the thirty-fourth fascicle.
The *Sūtra on the Seven Meritorious Deeds with and without Objects*, one fascicle, is extracted from the forty-second fascicle.
The forty-sixth fascicle, "The Causes and Conditions of the Makara Fish," and the nine sutras following it are all extracted from the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*.
The two-fascicle *Sūtra on the Elder Agnidatta Receiving Retribution* is extracted from the second and third fascicles.
The one-fascicle *Sūtra on the Venerable Subhūti and His Pleasant Voice* is [extracted from the same].
From the fourth fascicle: *The Sūtra on the Five Kinds of Water Strainers*, one fascicle.
From the fifth fascicle: *The Sūtra on the Original Causes of Lady Śrīmālā*, one fascicle.
From the seventh fascicle: *The Sūtra on King Prabhāsa’s Faith in the Buddha*, one fascicle.
The *Sūtra on the Retribution for Slaying the Śākyas* in two fascicles, extracted from the eighth fascicle;
the *Sūtra on the Great Mistress Bhikṣuṇī Entering Nirvāṇa* in one fascicle, extracted from the eighth and ninth fascicles;

the *Sūtra on the Buddha Preaching to Nanda Concerning Leaving Home and Entering the Womb* in two fascicles, included in the fourteenth assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa*; and the *Sūtra on Honoring the Dharma and Sacrificing the Body* in one fascicle, extracted from the eleventh and twelfth fascicles.
From the fourteenth fascicle: *The Scripture on Two Boys with False Views Attaining the Fruit* (1 scroll);
*The Scripture on Pure Dignified Conduct* (1 scroll), also known as *The Scripture on Cleansing Dignified Conduct*.

The *Sūtra on the Retribution Received by Mahāmaudgalyāyana*, one fascicle, appears in the sixteenth fascicle. The *Sūtra on the Manifestation of Great Auspicious Omens at Birth*, one fascicle, appears in the eighteenth fascicle. The *Sūtra on the Conversion of Kātyāyana*, one fascicle, appears in the twentieth fascicle. The *Sūtra on the Karmic Causes and Conditions of the Nāga King Elāpattra*, one fascicle, appears in the twentieth fascicle. Regarding the similarities and differences between this *Sūtra of the Nāga King Elāpattra* and the *Sūtra on the Conversion of Kātyāyana*, they are clearly identical.
However, the initial text of the former sūtra exceeds [the latter] by four sheets;
from the section on the causal origin (nidāna) onwards, they are identical with no difference.
Why then was it needlessly duplicated in the *Zhongchao* (Comprehensive Extracts), dividing them into two separate sūtras?
The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Lady Anle, one fascicle;
from the twenty-first volume. The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Saṃpāka, three fascicles;
from the twenty-second, twenty-third, and twenty-fourth volumes. The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Prabhāsa, one fascicle.
The *Sūtra on Subduing Non-Buddhists and Manifesting Great Supernatural Powers*, one fascicle, translated during the twenty-fifth year [of the reign];
the *Sūtra on the Skillful Means of Mahābhaiṣajya*, two fascicles, translated during the twenty-sixth year;
and the *Sūtra on the Buddha Descending from Heaven to Jambudvīpa*, one fascicle, translated during the twenty-seventh and twenty-eighth years.
The *Sūtra on the Ordination of Prāpti Gautamī*, one fascicle, is extracted from the twenty-ninth volume;
the *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Hārītī*, one fascicle, is extracted from the thirtieth volume;
and the *Sūtra on the Nun Dharmadinnā Attaining the Fruits while Remaining a Laywoman*, one fascicle, is extracted from the thirty-first volume.
The *Sūtra on the Arrogance of the Brahmin Jyotipāla*, one fascicle, extracted from the thirty-second fascicle;
the *Sūtra on the Disciple Serving His Teacher*, one fascicle, at the end of the thirty-fourth fascicle and beginning of the thirty-fifth fascicle;
and the *Sūtra on the Seven Kinds of Non-retrogression*, one fascicle, extracted from the thirty-fifth fascicle.
The *Buddha’s Discourse on Heedlessness Spoken for the Elder*, one fascicle, extracted from the thirty-fifth fascicle.
The *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Earthquakes*, one fascicle, extracted from the thirty-sixth fascicle.
The *Sūtra on the Four Seals of Black and White Dharmas*, one fascicle, extracted from the thirty-sixth fascicle.
From the thirty-seventh fascicle: *The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Impending Entry into Nirvāṇa and His Deliverance of Subhadra*, two fascicles;
from the middle of the thirty-seventh fascicle: *The Sūtra on the Two Ministers’ Report to the King Regarding the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa*, one fascicle;
from the thirty-eighth fascicle: *The Sūtra on the Eight Great Kings Dividing the Relics*, one fascicle.
At the beginning of the thirty-ninth fascicle, the textual content of these two preceding sūtras is intermingled;

the *Mahāmātya-rāja-avavāda-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Great Minister’s Exhortation to the King) has been displaced from its later position to the earlier one, resulting in an excess of more than two pages of text.
The *Sūtra on the Division of the Relics* is three or more pages longer than the preceding sūtra,
yet there are no differences in their textual excerpts;
since both sūtras are verbose and inappropriate, they have been omitted.
The thirty-three sūtras following the "Fire" section of the *Gṛhapati* [chapter] all originate from the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*.

Furthermore, there is one fascicle titled "The Circumstances of Anāthapiṇḍada Requesting the Painting of a Monastery," which originates from the seventeenth chapter of the *Kṣudraka-vastu* and the fifth fascicle of the *Vinaya-gāthā*.
From the *Mahā-maṅgala-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Causes and Conditions of the Makara Fish) down to the forty-second scripture, comprising forty-nine fascicles,
these are all the *nidānas* (causal origins) from within the Vinaya of the Sarvāstivāda school.
They were excerpted and circulated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yi Jing.
Since these have already been categorized separately, they are all deleted.
Among them, the *Sūtra on the Lawfulness and Illegality of Bestowing Objects* and the *Sūtra on the Disciple’s Service to the Teacher*,
although slightly expanded or abridged compared to the extensive versions, do not differ from their originals.
Why should these be separately compiled into distinct fascicles?
All such variant translations have been deleted.

A new examination has identified twenty works with different titles but identical texts, totaling fifty-two fascicles: The *Bodhisattvaviṣayāvaivartikadharmamukha-sūtra* (菩薩境界奮迅法門經), ten fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei dynasty. Recorded in the *Baochang lu*. The above-mentioned scripture is an alternative title for the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-putra-sūtra*.
The *Zhou lu* records it separately;
furthermore, the claim that it is a missing text is an error.

The *New Version of the Daoxing jing* in ten fascicles (or seven fascicles), translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. [Recorded by] Cifang and others. Regarding the above scripture, I have examined various editions in the Tripitaka collections.
That which is identical in every word and phrase to the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra in Twenty-five Thousand Lines* (the *Xiǎopǐn*) is an error in the original text.
At the time when Master Dharmarakṣa translated the new *Daoxing jīng*,
the original manuscript was not available.
I have heard that there is a *Hùběn* (Original Protector) in the Eastern Capital;
though I have sought it out, I have not yet obtained a translation of it.
The *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, eight fascicles. The above is one scripture.
It is recorded in both the *Táng nèidiǎn lù* and the *Dàzhōu lù*.
Upon examining its text now, it is precisely the sixth fascicle of the *Hebù dàjí jīng*.
The first two scrolls are titled "Chapter on the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Directions."
This is precisely the *Prajñāpāramitā-naya-sūtra* (or *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, Chapter on the Fifty Evaluations).
The final six fascicles are the *Akṣayamati-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.
It is unknown for what reason this *Prajñāpāramitā-naya-sūtra* was compiled into the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*.
As for those works that exist as separate sections due to their distinct differences,
since they have already been recorded here,
I have now deleted them.
The *Anavatapta-nāgarāja-sūtra* in two fascicles. This single sūtra is identical in both text and wording to the *Hongdao guangxian sanmei jing*;
it differs only in its title.
Now, one copy is preserved.

*He Dao Shenzu Jing* (Sutra on the Divine Footsteps that Accord with the Way), three fascicles. The above sutra is the same title as the *Dao Shenzu Wujing Bianhua Jing* (Sutra on the Infinite Transformations of the Divine Footsteps of the Way), though the texts differ.
*Aiqi Jing* (Sutra of Lamentation), three fascicles, or alternatively two fascicles, in six chapters. The above is one sutra.
This shares the same name as the *Vaipulya-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, though the wording differs.
Since the first chapter of that *Vaipulya-nirvāṇa* is titled "Lamentation" (*Aiqi*),
this title was adopted from that chapter's name to serve as the title for the present scripture.
Compared to the Vaipulya Nirvāṇa [sūtras], this lacks three chapters at the end and is thus incomplete.
*Bao tian hui yin san mei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Wisdom Seal of the Precious Field), one fascicle. The above is one sūtra.
The text of the *Huiyin sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom) is identical in title, though differing in length and detail.
The *Chángfáng lù* states that the *Huiyin sanmei jing* is also titled the *Bǎotián huiyin sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom of the Precious Field).
Both versions of the *Zhou ruzang lu* (Catalogue of Works Entered into the Canon during the Zhou Dynasty) record these two texts;
however, it is a grave error to treat them as one single work.
*Lüzijing* (The Scripture of Mṛgāraputra), one fascicle. The above is this one scripture.
The title is identical but the texts differ;
according to their textual meaning, it should be categorized under the *Mātṛ* (Mother) lineage.
The *Chángfáng lù* (Record of Changfang) calls it the *Mṛgaputra Sūtra*.
It is an error to claim that this was translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty.
One fascicle of the *Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
The above-mentioned sūtra shares the same name as the *Amitābha Sūtra*, yet their texts differ.
Its school is that of the *Shorter Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Qi dynasty;
at that time, the original manuscript was unavailable.
One fascicle of the *Garbha-tantra Sūtra*. The above is one sūtra.
The *Sūtra on the Woman Wugouxian* has the same title but different text.
The *Sūtra on Hearing the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination in the City*, one fascicle—
this aforementioned sūtra has the same title but different text as the *Sūtra on Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination under the Pei-tuo Tree*.
There are variant editions of this *Śrāvastī-sūtra*, but I have not yet been able to find them.
One fascicle (or two fascicles) of the *Mahānāma-anāpāna-sūtra*; the *Neidian lu* states it is in two fascicles while the *Changfang lu* states it is in one fascicle. The above is one sūtra.
The *Yǔ Dà'ānbān Shǒuyì Jīng* (Sūtra on the Great Ānāpāna and Guarding the Mind) is identical in its wording and phrases to [the other], differing only in length;
it is a grave error that two versions of this work were preserved among the various catalogs.
*Shēnrì Jīng*, one fascicle. The above is one sūtra.
This is the same title as the *Candraprabha-kumāra-sūtra* found within the Mahāyāna Piṭaka, though the texts differ;
the father's name is Śreṇika and the son's title is Candraprabha.
Based on these differences, the titles of the scriptures are established separately.
The *Chángfáng lù* states that the claim that the *Shēnrì jīng* was translated by the Wu-period upāsaka Zhi Qián is erroneous.
One fascicle of the *Lúnzhuǎn wǔdào zuífú bàoyìng jīng*: the aforementioned scripture and the *Zuífú bàoyìng jīng* are identical in their titles and wording, differing only in their length.
*The Sūtra of Cāṇḍava*, one fascicle.
This sūtra is identical in title and wording to the *Sūtra of King Cāṇḍava*, differing only in its length;
it was included in the Tripitaka during the Zhou dynasty and is cataloged among the single-fascicle works.
The *Cāṇḍālayavanarājāsūtra* is already included among the retranslations.
To have it recorded in both places is a grave error.

The *Zhenwei shashamen jing* (Sūtra on Authentic and Spurious Śramaṇas), one fascicle, listed in Sengchang’s catalogue; also known as the *Mahābhikṣu sūtra* or the *Kāśyapa-śīla-sūtra*. This concludes the aforementioned scripture.
This is an alternative title for the *Kāśyapa-śīla-sūtra*, with the wording being identical throughout.
Some claim it was translated by the Śramaṇa Huìjiǎn of Lùnyè Monastery during the Song dynasty, but this is an error.
*The Sūtra on Turning the Wheel of Dharma*, one fascicle. Regarding the above sūtra, its original text cannot be found;
it is an error that all the scriptural collections have substituted it with the *Treatise on Turning the Wheel of Dharma*.
A verified original copy was recently obtained at the Eastern Capital and recorded here as being included in the canon.

*The Scripture on Piṇḍola Preaching the Dharma for the King*, one fascicle. The above scripture and *The Scripture on Piṇḍola Preaching the Dharma for King Udāyana* are identical in their wording and names; they differ only in their length.
*Āraṇyaka-cīnadharmaparyāya-sūtra*, two fascicles. The above-mentioned sūtra shares the same name but differs in its text from the *Zuòchán sānmèijīng*.
*Xiányào jīng*, five fascicles. The above-mentioned sūtra.
It is stated that this was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of the Song dynasty,
and that it is a different translation from the same original source as the *Biyao fa* (Secret Essential Dharma) translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
Now, upon examining the preceding and following contexts, it is extremely erroneous and not the original scripture.
The first fascicle is actually the *Secret Essential Method for Treating the Illnesses of Meditation*;
furthermore, it does not reach its conclusion, but stops halfway through.
The portion from the second fascicle onwards is the *Dhyānaguhya-uttama-dharma* translated by Kumārajīva;
it begins from the middle of the first fascicle and extends through the end of the third fascicle, yet the text is not yet complete.
The missing ten or more folios are all comprised within four fascicles;
together with the preceding ones, they form five.
As for the portion translated by Dharmamitra, its original manuscript was missing at that time.

Newly excavated scriptures from the *Chóngshànglù*: eight works in thirty fascicles; the *Bodhisattvabhūmiviniścayasamgrahaṇī* (Pusa dizhī jīng) in ten fascicles—or eight fascicles—also titled the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* and alternatively the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*. The above constitutes one scripture.
It is also titled the *Bodhisattvabhūmiviniścayasamgrahaṇī*.
In this present catalog, it is classified under the Vinaya section to preserve its status as a sūtra,
while its classification as a śāstra is excluded.
The statement in the middle [of the text] that the *Bodhisattvabhūmiviniścaya-sūtra* is missing is an error.
Furthermore, within the Zhou catalog, this single sūtra has multiple titles that differ and contradict one another in their sequence.
In total, there are six instances where the upper [text] has been erroneously transposed:
one instance in the Mahāyāna Sūtras, two instances in the Mahāyāna Vinaya, one instance in the Mahāyāna Śāstras, and two instances in the *Qiuben lu* (Record of Missing Texts).
The number of these [texts] is not limited to one, as they appear repeatedly in other sūtras;
fearing that this would clutter the pages and ink, I have described them briefly here.

The *Anīkadevī-sūtra* (一卷), the *Prathamārthadharmavijaya-sūtra* (一卷), and the *Maitreyabodhisattvapṛcchāpūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra* (一卷)—these three sūtras were erroneously recorded in both sections of the *Dazhou Zhongjing Mulü* (Catalogue of the Canon of the Great Zhou) as single translations and as retranslations.
Now, excluding the single-text version from among the retranslations,
there is one scripture— the *Bodhicittotpāda-sūtra* in two fascicles, also titled the *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra*.
It is an error for it to be recorded in both the Mahāyāna Sūtras and the Mahāyāna Śāstras sections of the Zhou Catalogue of the Tripitaka.
Now, regarding those composed by Bodhisattvas, their titles have been removed and they are preserved in the catalogs of treatises (*śāstra*).

The *Jianwang jing* (Sūtra on Admonishing the King) in one fascicle—also known as the *Daxiao Jianwang jing* (Greater and Lesser Sūtras on Admonishing the King)—is recorded in both catalogs as being included in the Zhou-period canon; however, this is an error, as the text is missing.
The *Dharmapada-sūtra* in two fascicles, also titled the *Dharmapada-saṃgraha*:
the aforementioned scripture is erroneously listed in both sections—the Mahāyāna translations and the collected transmissions—of the Zhou-period canon catalog.
Upon examining the texts, they are identical and cannot be divided into two; although one version was previously translated twice, it is now missing.
This current scripture has been excluded from the collection.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* in twelve fascicles: this is the first treatise.

The *Catalogue of All Scriptures* from the second year of the Kaihuang and Renshou eras of the Sui dynasty, as well as the *Great Zhou Catalogue* of the Tang dynasty’s Buddhist Canon and others, all preserve two versions [of this text],
stating that they share the same original source as the fifteen-fascicle *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, differing only in their translations.
It is an error to claim that both were translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty.
Now, having examined the wording from beginning to end, they are entirely identical;
although the number of fascicles differs, they cannot be divided into two separate works.

Only fifteen fascicles remain; those consisting of twelve [fascicles] have been removed. Newly identified works to be incorporated into the Great Canon: fifty-two works in one hundred forty-one fascicles.

The fifth [section], comprising four hundred and sixty-nine works in one thousand four hundred and fourteen fascicles, is the Supplementary Record of Omissions and Recoveries. This record consists of those [works] that were omitted and subsequently recovered.
This refers to those works that were omitted from previous catalogs or not yet included in new translations;
all such items are now meticulously detailed and fully recorded herein.
It is my hope that the Wheel of Dharma shall remain untainted and the Sun of Wisdom ever increase in brilliance.
May it forever illuminate the dark paths and perpetually moisten those who are parched.

The above concludes the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-ūṣmagata-sūtra*,
part two. A total of one hundred and sixty-four works, comprising two hundred and five fascicles,
are all formerly translated sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras.
The *Da Zhou Guanglu* (Extensive Record of the Great Zhou) contains its title,
yet it is not included among those texts entered into the canon.
It remains uncertain whether this work was recorded in the *Queben lu* (Record of Missing Texts).
There were certain works recorded in the Zhou catalog that were omitted from other catalogs;
these have now all been collected to supplement the omissions and included in the Tripitaka catalog.

To the right of the Avataṃsaka-sūtra are two hundred and twenty-one works.
These comprise seven hundred and forty-one fascicles in total;
all were newly translated after the *Dazhou kanding zhongjing mulu* and the *Kaiyuan shijiao lu*,
which is why they were not included in the earlier catalogs.
These have now all been supplemented and incorporated into the *Zhenyuan xinding shijiao mulu* (Newly Compiled Catalogue of Śākyamuni’s Teachings from the Zhenyuan Era).
Regarding the Vinaya and Abhidharma treatises of the Hīnayāna, there have been no new translations since the *Kaiyuan lu* (Catalogue of the Kaiyuan Era).

*The Biography of Faxian*, compiled by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, in one fascicle, also known as the *Record of Travels to India*;
and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan), compiled by the Śramaṇa Faxian of the Eastern Jin, in fourteen fascicles, of which one fascicle is a catalog.
*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Xu gaoseng zhuan), thirty fascicles, compiled by the Liang dynasty śramaṇa Shi Huijiao;

The *Separate Biography of Shi Falin* in three fascicles, compiled by Shi Falin of Longtian Monastery during the Great Tang;
included in the catalog of the New Compilation of the Zhenyuan Era.

*Collection for Propagating and Clarifying* (Hongming ji), fourteen fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Fuli of the Great Tang;
*Extended Collection for Propagating and Clarifying* (Guang hongming ji), thirty fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Sengyou of the Liang dynasty.
*The Great Tang Monk Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan’s Compilation: The Great Tang Record of the Inner Dharma Sent from the Southern Seas*, four fascicles;

one fascicle of *The Ritual for Protecting Life and Releasing Creatures*, compiled by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang.
The above follows after the *Mahābuddhanāmasūtra* (The Scripture of the Great Names of Buddhas), compiled by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang.
In total, there are seventy-six sections comprising four hundred and fifteen fascicles;
these are all biographies, collections, and records compiled within this land.
However, because the divine power assisted in the propagation and glorification of the Great Dharma, this work was used to supplement previous omissions.
By imperial decree, it was compiled and included in the *Zhenyuan shijiao mulu* (Zhenyuan Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings).
*Zhenyuan xinding shijiao mulu*, Volume 27.
The Newly Compiled Catalogue of Śākyamuni’s Teachings from the Zhenyuan Era, Volume Twenty-Eight,
Supplement Nine,
compiled by the śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xīmíng Monastery in the Western Capital.
6. Doubtful or Repeatedly Detailed Records from the Supplementary Catalogue (Lüelù zhōng yíhuò zài xiánglù). Section Six: Fourteen Works in Nineteen Volumes Recorded as Doubtful.
Since the Brahma scriptures were first propagated in the East nearly seven hundred years ago,
the teachings have undergone periods of flourishing and decline, and their transmission has shifted across time;
the number of translated fascicles now approaches ten thousand.
Since the collection of volumes is so extensive, it is difficult to examine them all thoroughly.
Those who compiled the definitive catalog recorded works as soon as they heard of them, yet they did not carefully investigate their fundamental tenets; thus, some principles may be subject to doubt.
Now, fearing that the genuine and the spurious may be intermingled and right and wrong may overlap,
I have compiled this separate record to show to future generations.
It is my hope that men of profound insight and high standing will further examine and finalize it.

The *Vīra-samādhi Sūtra* in two fascicles; the *Sūtra on the Determination of Sin and Merit* in one fascicle; the *Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Samantagocara-viṣaya-ṛddhi* in one fascicle—I have personally examined its original manuscript, and it is entirely not the word of the Buddha; and the *Sūtra on Protecting Life and Delivering People from the Calamities of Disease*, which is similar in style and phrasing to the *Sūtra on Saving from Illness*.
It is difficult to determine which of these is authentic and which is spurious; the *Zuimiàoshèngdìng jīng* (One Scroll) has a textual style similar to the *Zuimiào chūjiào jīng*.

The *Guānshìyīn sānmèi jīng* (One Scroll), the *Qīngjìng fǎxíng jīng* (One Scroll), and the *Jìshuō kǒnglǎo yánhuí shì wǔbǎi fànzhì jīng*—also known as the *Wǔbǎi póluómén wèn yǒuwú jīng*—state that they were produced from the five teachings. These eight works, totaling nine scrolls, follow below the *Xiàopílúosānmèi jīng*.
In ancient catalogs, these were all classified as spurious and false;
however, they were subsequently included among the authentic scriptures during the Great Revision (Dazhou).
Upon examining them, one finds that their doctrinal principles are frequently inconsistent with the established traditions.
The discussion of the meaning of the syllogism (*pramāṇa*) somewhat involves ordinary worldly sentiments;
for now, it is appended to the section on "Doubts" (*yīkē*), though it is difficult to reconcile with the orthodox record.
Some say that by disparaging the sacred teachings (*āgama*), the fault finds its proper locus.
The Buddha has given this sincere word: "This is not a matter for censure or difficulty.
As the Sūtra says:
"If one gives rise to doubt regarding what I have taught, one should not even accept it; how much less so in cases such as these?"
According to this principle, one must distinguish between what is correct and what is false;

furthermore, we await the collective examination of the worthy ones regarding the authenticity [of these texts]. Among the eight scriptures mentioned above, there are those that were previously classified as spurious in the *Jiulü* (Old Catalogue), yet even within this current list of spurious works, they have been preserved without being expunged. There are several other titles from the *Jiùwèijīngdùlù* (Catalogue of Formerly Spurious Scriptures) that were established as authentic, but as their original texts have not yet been seen, they are not discussed here.

The *Fashè jīng* (Dharma Society Sūtra) in two fascicles; its internal title reads: *Yèbào lúnzhuǎn chángzhài yǐndào dìyù císhàn zhuāngyán fashè jīng* (Sūtra on the Dharma Society Adorned with Charity, Leading the Way through Hell by Repaying Debts through the Cycle of Karmic Retribution). Regarding this one sūtra, the *Dàzhōu lù* states it was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhú Fáhù of the Western Jin dynasty.
I have carefully consulted the records of Sengchangfang and others.
Among the translations by Dharmarakṣa, there is one fascicle of the *Dharmasūtra* (Fashijing).
A footnote states:
The commentary regards this as doubtful.
This is likely the *Fashu jing* (Scripture on the Dharma Society) from among the many spurious records of old.
Furthermore, the title at the beginning of the preceding scripture states:
The Tripitaka Master Huanglu translated this Hu-language scripture;
however, upon examining the meaning and style of this text, it appears to involve human sentiments,
and its titles and annotations are inconsistent, making it difficult to establish a standard for verification.
Furthermore, I shall include this in the *Biān yì lù* (Record of Doubtful Matters) to await further detailed investigation.

Regarding the *Jìng dù sān mèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Pure Deliverance) in three fascicles: among the works compiled and excerpted by Xiào Zīliáng, there is a *Jìng dù sān mèi jīng* in three fascicles.
I suspect this scripture is the *Yiyi jing* (Sūtra on Beneficial Intent) in two fascicles, which was recited by the monk Fa-ni; among his recitations, there is a *Yiyi jing* in two fascicles.
I suspect this scripture is one of these two aforementioned works in five fascicles, which were included in the canon according to the *Dazhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalog).
Upon examining the phrasing and considering human circumstances, this matter must be scrutinized further;
for now, it shall be included in the *Pseudo-Scriptures* (*Wailu*).

One fascicle of the *Ullambana Sūtra*, recited by the nun Sengfa, contains a title that raises doubt as to whether this scripture is authentic. Thus, one scripture is recorded in both the *Changfang Neidian Lu* and the *Er Lu* as having been presented by Mudaoxian in the fifteenth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty.
Since the detailed reasons for this have already been shown to lack a foundation,
it is difficult to determine whether it is authentic or spurious;
for now, it shall be appended to the records of doubtful texts.
*Jingtu ulamben jing* (The Sutra of the Ullambana for the Pure Land), one fascicle; five sheets. Regarding this sutra, it is not recorded in either the new or old catalogs;
nevertheless, it has been circulated among the common people and is being treated as an authentic scripture.
A close examination of the wording also reveals elements of human sentiment;
the matter must be scrutinized with care.
For now, I have appended this to the Record of Doubts.
*The Scripture on the Three Kitchens*, one fascicle. The above scripture is not recorded in either the new or old catalogs;
nevertheless, upon examining its literary principles, it also involves human ingenuity.
Following it in practice has yielded numerous verified results.
Furthermore, these must be examined in detail and provisionally appended to the Record of Doubtful Works.

**Section Seven: Records of Forged and Deceptive Works that Confuse the Authentic within the Separate Record.** The seventh section of the Separate Record, "Records of Forged and Deceptive Works that Confuse the Authentic," comprises three hundred and ninety-three works totaling one thousand four hundred and ninety-one fascicles of spurious scriptures.
Those who create false views thereby disorder the true scriptures.
Since the Great Master withdrew his form from view two thousand years ago,
demonic teachings have vied with one another to arise while the True Dharma has declined.
There have been those among the stubborn and ignorant whose evil views delude their minds,
who falsely fabricate various sutras to deceive the common people and whose heterodox words throw the correct teaching into disorder.
How lamentable this is!
Now I fear that the genuine and the spurious will be intermingled and right and wrong will be treated indiscriminately—
like the precious jade of Mount Kun ming flowing together with common tiles and stones.
Jambūnada gold may be valued equally with lead and iron;
now, by distinguishing the specific characteristics of each, the genuine and the counterfeit can be separated.
Thus, may the Jing and Wei rivers flow apart so that no future harm is incurred.
*Yàoxíng shěshēn jīng* (Sūtra on the Essential Practice of Relinquishing the Body), one fascicle, slightly over three pages;
it contains a "Vow for Relinquishing the Body" at the end, totaling five pages. Regarding this sūtra, it is unknown who composed it, as heterodox factions were prevalent [at the time].
The beginning of the scripture also states, "Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang.
However, upon examining the translations produced by the Master, this scripture is not among them;
the nature of its spuriousness and errors is clearly evident.
Furthermore, I shall describe four matters to enlighten the ignorant mind.
First, a spurious scripture begins by stating:
"The Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha."
The name "Gṛdhrakūṭa" (Vulture Peak) appears in ancient translations of the sūtras;
Master Xuanzang translated it all as "Jiufeng" (Vulture Mountain).
The current rendering as "Lingjiu" (Numinous Vulture) is clearly a corruption.
Furthermore, at the beginning of this spurious scripture, it says:
"Beside the Śītavana charnel ground on Vulture Peak.
According to various biographical records, that Vulture Peak Mountain is located fourteen or fifteen *li* to the northeast of the inner palace city within the kingdom of Magadha.
How could there be a place for abandoning corpses within the capital city?
Since this is not the case, two falsehoods are manifest.
Furthermore, it says in one of the false sutras:
Regarding the Buddha’s statement that he first vowed to sacrifice his body during the time of the past Dīpaṃkara Buddha:
Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata was the teacher who bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon Śākyamuni Buddha at the completion of the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
How could one who has received the prediction that they shall attain Buddhahood die and cast off their body?
This contradicts both fact and principle; thus, three kinds of falsehood are manifest.
Furthermore, within one of these spurious sutras it says:
If there is someone who kills sentient beings throughout the entire Sahā world,
commits the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes, slanders the Vaipulya sutras,
and steals the property of the permanent or the currently present Sangha;
Such sins as these would collectively lead to rebirth in hell;
yet if one can cast off the body, these sins will surely be extinguished.

Those who slander the sutras or commit the heinous crimes (ānantarya) deserve to fall into the Avīci Hell, but by casting off their bodies at death, they may be purified and thus avoid heavy retribution. This is no different from the false calculations of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who claim that bathing in the Ganges River eliminates the stains of sin and that by risking one's life to float upon it, one is born in heaven to receive blessings. How does this notion of purifying sin through death differ from such deluded views? Foolish people commit evil and then use this [method] to eliminate their transgressions.
The wise should reflect upon this so as not to be deceived;
otherwise, one will sink forever into the evil realms with no prospect of liberation.
Since the facts contradict the principles and the four types of falsehoods are manifest, the errors are so numerous that they cannot be recorded in full.

*Yogadharma-ādarśa-sūtra*, two fascicles (or one fascicle); it also includes a spurious preface. This single sūtra is the *Saddharmavipralopa-saṃdeha-vinodana-sūtra* from the old spurious catalogs, with two additional chapters appended to the original text to form a single work.
The initial statement says:
"The Buddha, on the verge of parinirvāṇa, preached the Dharma for Ānanda in the Chapter on the Abiding and Ceasing of the Dharma.
This chapter is derived from the *Buddha-āyuṣ-pramāṇa-nirdeśa-sūtra* (佛臨涅槃記法住經) translated by Master Xuanzang.
The order has been revised, expanded, and reduced, and placed at the beginning.
Next is the "Chapter on the Contemplative Practice Praising the Dharmakāya" of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva;
last is the "Chapter on the Questions of Constantly Bestowing Bodhisattva."
This chapter is identical to the old translation;
however, its textual sequence lacks coherence.
In the first year of the Jinglong era (707 CE), the Sanjie monk Shili forged a preface, falsely claiming therein:
The Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci and the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnākarasiṃha and others translated [this work] together at Chongfu Monastery.
Śīlī stated that there was a Sanskrit manuscript, which Bodhiruci had never seen or heard of.
The old edition was included among the spurious works; I have recompiled it as the *Wangjuan yilu* (Record of Doubts to be Dispelled).
As for the "spurious" version, it is even more spurious, containing numerous errors and corruptions that can be seen at a glance without the need for extensive explanation.

The compiler says: I once personally questioned the Tripiṭaka Master Liu Zhi about this matter, and he said, "I originally had no Sanskrit manuscripts with me, nor did I ever translate this sūtra. His disciple Prajñāgupta was of clear intelligence and great learning, and he fully understood the circumstances. Fearing that because the ages have been so distant, errors might corrupt the true teaching, I have clarified these points here as a warning for future generations. As for the monk Śīla, because he engaged in petty quarrels during his youth, the Imperial Person personally took concern over him and ordered him to return to lay life; was this not because Heaven did not grant him protection and thus brought this punishment upon him?

*The Scripture on Maitreya’s Descent to Birth, Sent by Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta to Exhort and Transform Sentient Beings to Abandon Evil and Practice Goodness for Longevity and Joy*, one fascicle; also simply titled *The Scripture on Longevity and Joy*, ten sheets. *The Scripture on the Bodhisattva Guangmin Asking the Tathāgata about the Appropriate Time for His Appearance in the World and the Universal Proclamation*, one fascicle; eight sheets. *The Scripture on Maitreya Attaining Buddhahood in the Tuṣita Heaven*, one fascicle. *The Scripture on the Vajra Secret Essentials Discussed in the Chapter of the Bodhisattva Xiànshù Questioning the Buddha*, one fascicle; also named *The Scripture on the Origins of the Ten Thousand-Luminosity King*, or alternatively *The Treatise Without Argument*, which also explains Maitreya’s descent to birth; fourteen sheets. The above four scriptures are all forged by heterodox followers.
Among these, it is stated that Maitreya Tathāgata is about to descend to be born, and so forth.

According to the authentic scriptures, after the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni, when fifty-seven koṭis and six hundred thousand years have passed in the human realm and the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa has increased to eighty thousand years, Maitreya Tathāgata will then appear in the world. How could Maitreya descend to be born while the human lifespan is less than a hundred years?
Using such demonic delusions to seduce the ignorant and foolish,
those of shallow understanding mostly accept them with faith;
because of this, they fall into ruin.
This may truly be called lamentable.
Therefore, I have clarified this matter specifically, hoping for your detailed examination.

After the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Ānanda preached the *Lifó chízá jīng* (Sūtra on Paying Homage to the Buddha and Observing the Fasting Precepts) in one fascicle for the fourfold assembly.
Also titled *The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Ascent to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven Spoken by Maitreya Maṇi Buddha on the Awakening of Buddha-nature*, one fascicle;
the colophon of this sūtra reads: *The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Human Existence for Awakening Buddha-nature*, nine sheets;
and *The Sūtra on the Rituals for Observing the Fast*, one fascicle.
*The Sūtra on the Upāsaka Precepts for Pure Conduct*, one fascicle;
alternatively titled *The Sūtra on the Upāsaka Precepts for Pure Conduct, Chapter Thirteen on Spiritual Resonance*; [this work] replaces the *Sūtra of the Bequeathed Teaching* with six fascicles.
*The Sūtra on the Great Flood Disaster of the Jiashen Year*, one fascicle.
Two sheets on the difference between the water-related events of the Jiashen year and the prophecy concerning the alms bowl of that Buddha;
one scroll and two sheets of the *Zixing jing* (Sutra on Self-Reflection);
one scroll of the *Fumuenzhong jing* (Sutra on the Profound Kindness of Parents).
The scripture cites Ding Lan, Dong An, Guo Ju, and others; thus we know that people have produced [the following works]:

*The Secret Essential Treasury of the Tathāgata’s True Teaching*, one fascicle (ten sheets); *The Vinaya Pitaka*, one fascicle (eight sheets); *The Scripture on the Canopy*, one fascicle (the internal title reads: *The Buddha’s Discourse on the Profound and Sublime Meaning of the Dharma: A Treatise Explaining the Profound Meaning of the Path of Birth and Death*); *The Scripture of the Eight Yangs of Heaven and Earth*, one fascicle (seven sheets; at the end of the scroll it is titled: *The Scripture of the Divine Incantation of the Eight Yangs*).
This differs entirely in meaning and principle from the "Eight Yang Divine Incantations" found in the orthodox scriptures.

This work expounds upon the methods for divining the auspiciousness of yin and yang and for averting calamities and eliminating misfortunes. *The Sutra of the Eight Sheets on the Jealous New Wife*, also known as the *Sutra of the Envious Wife*. The aforementioned sutra was composed by a person of recent times; its author's name has been forgotten.
Because his wife was prone to jealousy, he forged this sutra to deceive her;
within it, he states that those who harbor jealousy receive extremely heavy retribution.
*Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, two fascicles; it is also simply called the *Aṅguli-sūtra*.
It shares the same title as the *Zhenjing* (True Scripture).
Among the works compiled by Xiao Ziliang, there are two fascicles of the *Aṅgulimāla-sūtra*.

It is suspected that these may be the same as the *Chonglou jiejing* (One-fascicle Sūtra on the Multi-storied Tower Precepts), the *Qingjing jushi zi duren jing* (One-fascicle Sūtra on the Pure Layman’s Son Saving People), the *Madengqijing* (One-fascicle Mātaṅga Sūtra), and the *Piyujing* (One-fascicle Sūtra of Parables) translated by Huijian of the Song dynasty, among which there is also a one-fascicle *Piyujing*.
Time has no fundamental basis;
it is identical to its name.
Thus, truth and falsehood become confused with one another.

Therefore, both versions are preserved: *The Sūtra of Maudgalyāyana’s Questions*, one fascicle; its name is identical to that of the authentic sūtra, yet its language and meaning differ entirely. *The Sūtra on the Extinction of Minor Dharmas*, one fascicle; its text and meaning differ entirely from the *Sūtra on the Extinction of Dharmas* within the authentic canon. *The Sūtra of the Ringing Bell*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra on the Method of Upholding the Precepts*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of the Golden Turtle’s Decisive Mouth*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of the Hells*, one fascicle. There is also a *Sūtra of the Hells*, one fascicle, whose translator during the Han dynasty is lost.

It is suspected that these are the same work. *The Sūtra of King Utpalaka* (1 fascicle); *The Treatise on Ānanda’s Request for Merit and Retribution* (1 fascicle); *The Treatise on Ānanda’s Questions Concerning the Vinaya* (1 fascicle)—this may be the same as the *Treatise on Ānanda’s Questions Concerning the Precepts*; *The Treatise on the Adjudication of the Two Divisions of the Vinaya* (1 fascicle)—this may be the same as the *Treatise on the Adjudication of the Vinaya*; *The Treatise on the Śramaṇa* (1 fascicle)—this may be the same as the *Treatise on the Śrāmaṇera* found in the *Catalogue of Inner Scriptures*; *The Treatise on the Solitary Begging of Pratyekabuddhas* (1 fascicle); *The Treatise on Questions Concerning the Vinaya* (1 fascicle); *The Account of the Hells* (1 fascicle). From the *Aṅgulimāla Sūtra* downwards, there are nineteen works totaling twenty fascicles.
Furthermore, their doctrines are contradictory and their falsehoods are manifest;
yet, as commentators cite them together, they remain unaware of their deceptions.
Therefore, I have compiled this record to transmit it to future worthies.
If you would happen to realize that these are not the truth, I hope we may together reform this corruption.
Furthermore, the number of such spurious scriptures is truly vast.
I shall wait further to seek out and continue compiling examples of this kind.

The old catalog states that there were thirty-nine works following the *Buddhanāma-sūtra*; now, excluding the *Buddhanāma-sūtra* itself, which has been included in the canon, there should be thirty-eight remaining. Currently, one work is missing, leaving only thirty-seven; the details remain unclear.
From the *Yaoxing sheshen jing* (Sūtra on the Essential Practice of Relinquishing the Body) down to thirty-seven works in forty-one fascicles:

According to my careful examination of various catalogs, these have already been translated twice.
Fearing that this might lead to the false appropriation of a genuine title,
I have preserved its entry.
Furthermore, there is one fascicle of the *Dharmaparyāya-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

These are merely alternative titles for works already recorded; it is an error to include them again here, as they were already listed among the spurious records of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions.

*Zhàomíng Púsà Fāngbiàn Bìyù Zhìbìng Jīng* (One Scroll) *Zhàomíng Púsà Jīng* (One Scroll) *Jiā Tóu tuó Zì Shǒuluó Bìqū Jiàn Yuèguāng Tóngzǐ Jīng* (One Scroll) *Ānán Xiànbiàn Jīng* (One Scroll) *Bōrě Xuánjì Jīng* (One Scroll) *Youshēn Xuánjì Jīng* (One Scroll) *Xuánjì Jīng* (Two Scrolls)

The *Zhou lu* (Catalogue of the Zhou Dynasty) states that there is one fascicle [of this work], while the *Daqijing* (Great Sūtra) consists of four fascicles. The *Zhou lu* also notes that it is alternatively titled the *Mile xiasheng jie dashan qijing* (Sūtra on Maitreya’s Descent and the Great Good Karmic Bonds), or that it consists of three fascicles. There is also a *Faputixin jing* (Sūtra on Arousing the Bodhicitta) in one fascicle; the two-fascicle version currently extant is likely this very sūtra, though while the title is the same, the number of fascicles differs slightly. There is also a *Pusa qiuyan jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Seeking the Five Eyes) in one fascicle, translated by Nie Daozhen; although this sūtra exists, its name is recorded here again as a spurious work that has usurped the title of a genuine text, which is why both the authentic and the counterfeit versions are found together. There is a *Baninihuan hou zhubiqiu jing* (Sūtra on the Bhikṣus After the Parinirvāṇa) in one fascicle; according to Sengyou’s catalogue, this is simply a different name for the *Xiaobaninihuan jing* (Shorter Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa).

There is also a *Xiaobaninihuan jing* in one fascicle, alternatively titled the *Dafamiejin jing* (Sūtra on the Great Extinction of the Dharma). According to the records of An Shigao’s translations, there is already a *Xiaobaninihuan jing*; since the titles are identical and no original manuscript can be verified, its authenticity remains uncertain.

Furthermore, both catalogs record the following: *The Scripture on the Five Turbidities of the Evil World*, one fascicle; *The Great Scripture on the Five Turbidities* (this is likely the same as the aforementioned work); *The Scripture on the Miraculous Transformation of Heaven and Earth*, one fascicle; *The Flower Adornment Scripture on the Ten Evils*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on the Contemplation of the World*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on the Tower of Carbon*, one fascicle; *The Minor Scripture on the Tower of Carbon*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on Mount Sumeru and the Four Continents*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on the King’s Transformation of the Inner and Outer*, one fascicle (also titled *The Scripture on Laozi Transforming the Barbarians*; the bibliographic records state it was composed by Wang Fu, the Libationer during the Jin dynasty; there is also a *Scripture on the Demon’s Transformation of Bhikṣus*, one fascicle). Within Zhi Qian’s catalog, there is a scripture titled *The Scripture on the Good Faith*, two fascicles; within Kumārajīva’s catalog, there is the *Good Faith Mahā-Śrī*. Fearing that these may be forgeries that have stolen the names of authentic works, I have preserved both titles here for reference. *The Scripture on the Divine Incantations of Good Faith*, two fascicles. Within Kumārajīva’s catalog, there is the *Good Faith Mahā-Śrī*.
The *Dhāraṇī Sūtra* in two fascicles: its title is confused with others, and its authenticity remains undetermined;

both versions are preserved. The *Sūtra of the Five Turbidities* in one fascicle. Furthermore, there is the *Minor Sūtra of the Five Turbidities*, which should be this same text. The *Sūtra on Merit and Demerit Spoken within the Huaxian Sūtra* in one fascicle; it is also simply called the *Huaxian Sūtra*. The *Sūtra of the Five Dragon Kings’ Repentance* in one fascicle; also titled the *Sūtra of the Five Dragon Kings’ Repentance for Protecting the Dharma*. The *Sūtra of the Gate of Samādhi for the Complete Precepts through the Repentance of Emptiness and Wisdom* in one fascicle. The *Sūtra of the Most Sublime and Victorious Samādhi* in one fascicle. The *Sūtra of the Indian Śramaṇa* in one fascicle. The *Sūtra on Saving and Protecting Life and Delivering One from the Suffering and Calamity of Illness* in one fascicle; it is also simply called the *Sūtra on Saving and Protecting Life*, or the *Sūtra on Protecting Life and Vitality*. To the right, there is yet another version of this sūtra.
The title reads: *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-dhāraṇī Sūtra*. It initially states that it was translated by the Brahmin Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.

With the addition of one dhāraṇī verse, the remainder of the text is largely identical [to the previous version]. The compiler notes: "Regarding the title of this sūtra, it is unclear whether it is from Paramārtha’s work. If it were a re-translation by Paramārtha, the scriptural language would have matched the old version exactly; however, while the dhāraṇī here differs, the rest is the same. As this cannot resolve people's doubts and there is no basis for investigation, it is impossible to compile it recklessly. Therefore, I have recorded it here according to the original source."

*Mahānārāyaṇa Sūtra*, one fascicle; *Hui-ming Zheng-xing Jing* (Sūtra on Wisdom and Right Practice), one fascicle; *Tian-huang Fan-mo Jing* (Sūtra on the Brahma King Vaśavartin), one fascicle; *An-mu Jing* (Sūtra on Entombing), one fascicle; *An-zhong Jing* (Sūtra on Entombing Mounds), one fascicle; *An-zhai Jing* (Sūtra on Entombing Dwellings), one fascicle. [Note: The *An-zhai Shen-zhou Jing* (Sūtra of the Divine Incantation for Entombing Dwellings) in the *Zheng-lu* (Correct Catalogue) differs from this. *Tian-gong Jing* (Sūtra of the Heavenly Lord), one fascicle; *Du-sheng-si-hai Shen-chuan Jing* (Sūtra of the Divine Ship Crossing the Sea of Birth and Death), one fascicle; *Jiu-yi Sha-mi Jing* (Sūtra of the Śrāmaṇera Saving the Ants), one fascicle. Since I have not yet seen [the latter], I preserve this as well. *Bei-fang Li-fo Zhou Jing* (Sūtra of the Northern Region’s Incantation for Bowing to the Buddha), one fascicle;

*Jing-fu Jing* (Sūtra on Reverencing Merit), one fascicle—its full title is *Ru-lai Zai Jin-guan Zhu-lei Qing-jing Zhuang-yuan Jing-fu Jing* (The Tathāgata in the Golden Coffin Entrusts the Pure and Adorned Sūtra on Reverencing Merit); *A-lo-huo Tiao Guo-wang Jing* (Sūtra of King Arahacchada), one fascicle; *Wu-bai Fan-zhi Jing* (Sūtra of the Five Hundred Brahmacārins), one fascicle.

*Yimǐ yìyǒu yìwú jīng* (Sūtra on Being Both Existence and Non-existence), one fascicle; *Xiūxíng fāngbiàn jīng* (Sūtra on the Expedient Means of Practice), one fascicle; *Jìnglìng jīng* (Sūtra on Commandments), one fascicle; *Dùshì bùsǐ jīng* (Sūtra on Transcending the World and Immortality), one fascicle; *Zhāifǎ qīngjìng jīng* (Sūtra on the Purity of the Fasting Rite), one fascicle; *Wúwéifǎdào jīng* (Sūtra on the Path of Unconditioned Dharmas), one fascicle; *Zhòumèi jīng* (Sūtra on Incantations and Sorcery), one fascicle;

and *Zhèngzhāi jīng* (Sūtra on the Correct Fast), one fascicle—translated by An Shigao. The *Zhǔfǎhù lù* (Catalogue of Dharmarakṣa) also includes the *Zhèngzhāi jīng*; fearing that this might cause confusion and usurp the true titles, [I have omitted it here].
Each preserves its title: *The Śītavana Sūtra* (one fascicle) and *The Sūtra for Summoning Souls* (one fascicle), also called *The Sūtra for Summoning Souls*.
The *Zhou Lu* states: *The Sūtra for Summoning Souls*, one fascicle. The *Fajing Lu* states: [the same].
Upon consulting ancient records, it appears there should have been a separate system for the *dharmasabha* (Dharma society).
However, as this scripture has not yet been seen, let us for now set that aside and clarify what follows. Regarding this single-fascicle *Dharmasabha Sūtra*, three versions have been encountered.
Although the settings described are the same, the wording is different.

Examining their textual meanings, they are all human compositions: one version consists of three sheets titled *The Scripture on the Retribution of Merit and Demerit at the Dharma Society*, another consists of two sheets, and another consists of one sheet. The rest are similar.

*The Sūtra of the Prince’s Praise*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Dharmagupta Seeing the Transformations of Hell*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the People’s Petitions*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of King Yama and Mount Tai in the East*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Seven Jewels*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Treatise on Characters*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra for Saving and Protecting Sentient Beings from Malignant Diseases* (also known as the *Sūtra for Saving from Illness*), one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Parable of the Five Fruits*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Orphan Boy and Orphan Girl*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the King Delivering His Subjects and Commoners through Receiving the Five Precepts and Right Faith to Eliminate Evil*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Samādhi of the Law of the Bequeathed Teachings*, two fascicles. According to the catalogs of the Changfang era and others, as well as the catalog of lost translations, all these sūtras are recorded therein.
Since there is no original text and it is difficult to determine its definitive reality, I shall for now preserve their titles.
The compiler states: "Although I have not seen the complete version of this sutra, most of the passages cited from it appear to be human fabrications."

*The Sūtra of Two Hundred and Fifty Precepts*, one fascicle. The *Fajing lu* states that various catalogs all claim there are six or seven different versions, distinct from those previously issued; therefore, it is included here among the works of uncertain authenticity. To the right, this is verified by the *Liang sengyao lu*, the *Sui fei changfang lu*, and the *Tang daoxuan lu*.
It further states that it was produced during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty by the śramaṇa Shi Fadu;
however, it does not mention a translator, and the meaning of the term "produced" (chu) remains unclear.
Its intent is as follows:
As for what constitutes a spurious compilation,
it is difficult to definitively determine because its original source is missing; furthermore,
the *Yifajinglu* (Catalogue of the Sūtras on Dharma-robes) records it among the spurious catalogues.
*Yī wēiyí* (Diverse Postures), one fascicle. *Fǎjīng lù* states:

Composed by Fǎdù, a disciple of Dharmayaśas, during the Yuánjiā era of the Song dynasty. *Wǔfánfū lùn* (Treatise on the Five Ordinary Beings), one fascicle. The above constitutes eighty-six works in one hundred and forty-one fascicles from the section following the *Ānàhán jīng*.
In the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, the *Catalogue of All Scriptures* (*Zhongjing lu*),
compiled by the śramaṇa Fajing and others, states in its section on "Spurious and Doubtful Scriptures" that these works all have titles that deviate from the truth.
Some begin with golden words but do not elaborate on their prophetic verses;
some first discuss worldly arts and later record Dharma terminology;
some cite the auspiciousness and misfortune of yin and yang.
Some clarify the fortunes and calamities of gods and ghosts; all such works as these are evidently false and deceptive. Now, they ought to be kept secret in order to remedy the world's afflictions.

However, regarding the *Fajing lu* (Dharmaguptaka Catalogue), which classified works such as the *Suiyuan wangsheng jing*, *Leshi jing*, *Fantian shen ce jing*, *Renwang jing*, *Baorulai sanmei jing*, *Zhancha jing*, *Fan jing*, *Wuku zhangju jing*, *Anzhai shenzhou jing*, and the *Yijiao lun* among the "doubtful and spurious" (*yiwei*), this is not correct. The three sutras beginning with the *Suiyuan wangsheng jing* appear in the *Daguanding jing*; the seven sutras beginning with the *Renwang jing* all have authentic sources for their translation. To include them among the doubtful and spurious is improper. They should now be included in the "Authentic Record" (*zhenglu*), and thus they are not recorded here [in the current list].

*Vajragarbha-sūtra*, thirty fascicles; the Zhou catalog states it may consist of thirty-one fascicles. *Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha to Subhūti*, two fascicles; also known as the *Subhūti-sūtra*. *Sūtra on Attaining the Way through Prajñā*, one fascicle; the Fa-jing catalog states: [text continues].
Regarding the *Prajñāprāpti-sūtra*:

it may be that the *Prajñāprāpti-sūtra* is precisely what is recited by the *bhikṣuṇīs* of the Saṃgha-fa-ni school. Among the works translated by Zhu Tanwulan, there are titles for the following sūtras: the *Sūtra on the Creation of Heaven and Earth* (one fascicle), the *Sūtra on the Thorny Garden* (one fascicle), and the *Sūtra on Fragility* (one fascicle). These names appear therein.
Since the original text has not yet been seen, it is difficult to provide a definitive commentary;

for now, both versions are preserved. *The Sūtra on the Fallen Upāsaka*, one fascicle, translated by Zhi Yao of the Later Han dynasty: the title exists, but the original text is certainly non-existent.

Furthermore, there are separately preserved: *The Sutra of the Silver-Hoofed, Golden-Horned Calf*, one fascicle; *The Sutra on Filial Piety and Transformation, the Destruction of Evil Karma, and the Practice of Cultivation*, also known as *The Sutra of the Stepmother*, one fascicle; *The Sutra on the Practice of the Vinaya*, also known as *The Vinaya Practice* (or containing the word "Sutra"), one fascicle; and *The Treatise on the Great Emptiness Prajñā*, one fascicle. The above eleven works, totaling forty-one fascicles, follow the *Vajragarbha Sutra*.

In the second year of the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty, an imperial edict requested that the Venerable of Xingshan Monastery, along with the śramaṇas translating the scriptures and the scholars, jointly compile a catalog of the various scriptures.

Regarding those spurious and doubtful scriptures included within the internal catalog, it is stated: "Within this catalog of spurious works, there is further the *Sūtra on the One Hundred and Forty-eight Vows of Mahāprabhāsa Bodhisattva*. In the record of Sengyou, it is annotated as a 'extracted scripture' (*chao jing*); it now appears separately in this supplementary catalog. It has been removed from the catalog of spurious works."

*The Scripture on the Descent of the Buddhas as Great Dharma Kings*, sixty fascicles; Vinaya Master Xuán states: "I personally saw this text at Féndū. *The Scripture of the Extensive [Teaching] on the Extinction of Sin and the Attainment of Buddhahood*, three fascicles; also called *The Scripture of the Great Penetrating Extensive Repentance for Purifying Sin and Adorning the Attainment of Buddhahood*, or simply *The Great Penetrating Extensive Scripture*. *The Dharmapada*, two fascicles. *The Scripture on Resolving Doubts Regarding Sin and Merit*, one fascicle. *The Scripture on the Five Pungent Herbs*, one fascicle. The *Zōu Lù* (Catalogue of the Zhou Dynasty) states: *The Mahāyāna Prajñā Scripture on the Five Pungent Herbs*, one fascicle; also called *The Scripture of the Initial Teaching*. One source calls it *The Most Sublime Scripture of the Initial Teaching*.

The *Sūtra on the Most Sublime and Victorious Samādhi*, the *Sūtra on the Retribution of Sin* in one fascicle, and the *Sūtra on the Offering of the Sun Disk* in one fascicle, as well as the *Sūtra of Milk Light* in one fascicle—these texts differ entirely from the authentic sūtras.
*The Scripture on the Retribution of Merit for the Offense of Consuming Milk*: one fascicle; *The Jewel Seal Scripture*: one fascicle; *The Ultimate Great Compassion Scripture*:

one fascicle, or three fascicles, or also said to be eight fascicles; *The Treatise on the Pratyekabuddhas*: one fascicle; *The Treatise on the Determination of the Vinaya*: one fascicle; *The Treatise of Upāli*:
one fascicle, or as it is also called, *The Universal Decision Scripture of Upāli*: one fascicle.

and the *Kāśyapa-paripṛcchā-śāstra*; or the *Kāśyapa-paripṛcchā-vinaya-śāstra*,
the *Mahā-īryāpatha-paripṛcchā-śāstra*, the *Ratnamālā-śāstra*, the *Śrāmaṇera-śāstra*, and so forth.

Some say there is one fascicle of the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-śāstra*. The above twenty-two works totaling eighty-seven fascicles, from the *Mahādharmanṛpa-sūtra* onwards, were compiled by the śramaṇa Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery in the capital during the first year of the Linde era of the Great Tang.
Regarding the apocryphal scriptures among the catalogs of the Inner Canon,
Xuán said:
"Various apocryphal sūtras and śāstras are frequently found within the human scriptural treasuries."

The original catalog contains many entries that remain to be examined and recorded. The compiler states: "Within the Inner Canon (Āgama), there is also one fascicle of the *Suvarṇakāya-parinirvāṇa-śāsana-sūtra* (*Jīn guān zhūlèi jīng*), which is the same as the *Jìngfú* mentioned in the *Fǎjīng lù*; therefore, it is not recorded here again. In the first year of the Tiān-cè Wànsuì era of the Great Táng Empress [Wǔ Zetian], by imperial decree, the śramaṇa Míngquán and others of the Fóshòujì Monastery in the Eastern Capital were charged with editing and determining the catalog of spurious scriptures among the various sūtras.
The *Zhou lu* states:
"Traditionally handed down since antiquity, all have claimed it to be spurious and erroneous.
Upon examining its phrasing, one finds it prolix and disordered; its principles and meanings are superficial and frivolous."
Although they steal the name of being spoken by the Buddha, they ultimately expose the nature of human contrivance.
That the masses of sentient beings fall into delusion is entirely due to this. Therefore, I have compiled and listed them in detail as above. The compiler says:

These eighty scriptures were never included in the spurious catalogs of antiquity; it was only the *Zhou lu* (Catalogue of the Zhou Dynasty) that uniquely compiled them. Although it is said that they have been transmitted from ancient times, all agree they are spurious and erroneous, yet it does not specify from which catalog they were drawn. For now, I have itemized them according to the *Zhou lu* as shown above.
*Fófǎ yǒu liù yì dìyī yīngzhī jīng*, one fascicle; [the character "jīng" (sūtra) is absent in the record of Sengyou].
*Liùtōng wú'ài liùgēn jìngyè yìmén jīng*, one fascicle; [the character "jīng" (sūtra) is absent in the record of Sengyou]. The catalog of Fang lists these two works.
In the *Fanglü* (Record of the Scriptural Repositories), there are the two sections and two fascicles mentioned above;
the *Liang Sengyou Lu* states that they were falsely fabricated by the monk Shi Fayuan during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty.
However, since titles and fascicle numbers have already been established, these works will cause confusion and doubt among future generations.

Therefore, it is clearly noted in the *Lù Chángfáng* (Record of Chángfáng): "The world generally includes this among the list, yet treats it as a doubtful scripture; thus, I have recorded it again so that later worthies may recognize its source and fortunately examine it together with diligence.

*Fó suǒ zhì míngshù jīng* (Scripture on the Enumeration of Names Established by the Buddha), five fascicles. This one work in five fascicles is recorded in the *Liáng Sēngyòu Lù* (Lìang Dynasty Record of Sēngyòu).
Compiled during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty by the bhikṣu Shi Wangzong,
this work extracts and gathers from various sūtras, resembling a "Forest of Numbers" (Śālistamba). However,
fearing that it might confuse the names and realities [of the teachings], it is titled as being "Established by the Buddha."

Therefore, it is noted in the *Chángfáng Lù* (Fǎcháng’s Record): "The title of this scripture was included at the head of the catalog; since it is not an authentic scripture, it has been a source of doubt in the world.

*Jièguǒ Zhuāngyán Jīng* (Sūtra on the Adornment of the Fruits of Precepts), one fascicle—some versions omit the word "sūtra"—consists of eight chapters in verse. This one work, one fascicle, is recorded in the *Sòng Fánjīng Xuéshì Fèi Chángfáng Lù* (Record of Fǎcháng, Scholar for Translating Scriptures of the Sui Dynasty).

Regarding the *Xiao* (Pipa Scripture), compiled by the Court Attendant Geng Xie in the fifth year of the Yongming era of the Liang dynasty during the reign of Emperor Wu: it was recorded that he extracted the essential meanings from the scriptures to compose this work. As it was not a forgery but rather a distinct compilation, there was concern that it might be confused with the sacred canons. Consequently, it was included among the apocrypha in the Sui Renshou Catalogue and the Great Zhou Catalogue; we shall likewise include it here in the section on apocryphal works.

all of which were excerpted by Prince Wenxuan of Jingling during the Qi dynasty.
Generally, those characters inscribed above the titles were all copied by Wénxuān.

He copied fifty-nine fascicles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; fifty-nine fascicles of the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*; twenty-six fascicles of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*; and ten fascicles of the *Bodhisattva-niyata-caryā-sūtra*, also known as the *Śuddha-caryā-upāsaka-sūtra*.
The *Fajing lu* states:

In the seventh year of the Yongming era, at the request of King Wenxuan,
